en: Whether she be bewildered by the intoxication of passion, or perhaps stupefied by wine;
Whether she has herself committed an offense or has been led astray by another,
she shall be purified by her menstrual period, even if she has become fallen from dharma.
A woman is purified by her menses, just as a river is purified by its current;
having reached her fertile period, she becomes pure through union with a man.
Likewise: "Women are an incomparable purifier; they are never defiled. Month after month, the menstrual flow of women carries away their misdeeds."
The purification of earthenware is by fire; that of wooden objects, however, is by planing;
that of bell-metal is by ashes; and for women, it is traditionally held to be by their menses.
Fire is never satiated with wood, nor the great ocean with rivers; Death is never satiated with all living beings, nor a beautiful-eyed woman with men.
Vasiṣṭha says: A woman is purified by her menstrual flow; a river is purified by its current;
bell-metal is purified by ash; and that which is made of clay is purified by firing again.
Śaṅkha and Likhita state:
"Indeed, for women there is no vow, no ritual with mantras, and no [independent] duty. Prajāpati says:

The traditional teaching (*smṛtivāda*) states that those who have been taken by the hand (*pāṇigṛhītāḥ*) are not defiled when approached by others if they are seeking offspring; for Vaivasvata says that they are purified by their menstrual flow (*ārtava*). Hārīta says that engaging in sexual intercourse out of desire is an improper act (*akārya*).
[848] Because of that conduct and because of the resulting birth from oneself, there is fault (*doṣa*).
Gautama:
"The teachers say that the Cāndrāyaṇa penance is the means of purification for these [women], or else the Prājāpatya. Hārīta: [same].

One should avoid a woman who causes miscarriage, one who has sexual relations with a teacher, a disciple, or a son, one who is addicted to the vice of drinking, and one who causes the depletion of wealth and grain. Some say that a woman who commits adultery is purified by her menses; others say she is not defiled if she does not share the enjoyment of the act with others. Vasiṣṭha says: "Soma gave them purity, and Gandharva taught them speech."
"And Agni [granted] the state of being edible by all; therefore, women are equal to gold coins. Others say:
"Because they share the same vow and the same nature as spilled semen, and because they are afflicted by the organs of others, they become corrupters of the family."
Yama says: "If a woman is indeed one who acts according to her own will, her abandonment is ordained;
however, one should not perform the shaving of her head, nor the mutilation of her limbs."

Vivasvat declared the abandonment of a wife who acts according to her own will and is unfaithful; however, four types of women must be rejected: she who goes to a pupil, she who goes to a teacher, she who kills her husband, and especially she who approaches a man of lower caste.
Śātātapa says:
"In a village, however, where there has been contact during a journey, in quarrels and the like,
or even in the defilement of a village, no fault attaches to the one who touched."
"In a village," such as on a royal highway and the like; "during divine processions, weddings, sacrifices, and when [rites] have commenced";
and "in all festivals"—contact with those who are untouchable does not cause impurity.
Bṛhaspati also says:
"At a sacred ford, at a wedding, on a journey, in battle, during a national upheaval,
and when a city or village is burning, contact with those who should not be touched does not cause impurity."

Some maintain that these three statements refer to cases where there is no awareness that "I have been touched by this person. Others hold that they refer to cases involving contact with what is left-over (ucchiṣṭa) or impure (aśuci).
Viṣṇu said: thus ends the exception regarding impurity;
now bathing is described.

In that regard is the praise of bathing. Viṣṇu says: "One who has bathed becomes qualified for rites pertaining to the gods and the ancestors, as well as for the recitation of purifiers (*pavitra*) and for giving gifts as enjoined by the rules."
Misfortune, ill-fortune, bad dreams, and evil thoughts—all these perish for one consecrated with even a mere drop [of water]; such is the firm conviction.
Indeed, one who bathes daily does not behold the suffering of the torments of Yama;
even those men who are doers of evil are purified by daily bathing.
Bathing at every dawn, during the twilight, or when the sun has risen,
is equal to the Prājāpatya penance and destroys even the most grievous sins.
The body is utterly impure and endowed with nine openings;
it flows [with secretions] day and night. Morning bathing is its purification.
In one who is fast asleep, the sense-faculties become moist and leak away;
the limbs, both high and low, sink into a state of uniformity.
A man who has risen from bed, covered with saliva and sweat, should not perform any rite whatsoever, such as recitation or fire-offerings, without having first bathed.
Therefore, they praise bathing as auspicious, bringing both visible and invisible benefits;
one whose soul is purified by morning bathing is worthy of all [rites], such as the recitation of prayers (*japa*).
Satyavrata said: Through bathing properly, a person attains strength, beauty, fame, righteousness, knowledge, longevity, happiness, fortitude, health, and nourishment.

The *Yogayājñavalkya* states: By performing the ritual bath (*snāna*), one is liberated from the sin of approaching those who should not be approached, from the sins of accepting improper gifts, and from sins committed in secret.
If one is unable to perform the acts of *juhoti* and *yajati*,
the wise person should purify himself through bathing, meditation, recitation, and giving.
Whatever bath one performs with a purified inner self,
by that very act one obtains the entire fruit of ritual sacrifices and ceremonial rites.
This bath generates clarity of mind, increases physical beauty and good fortune,
destroys grief and evil dreams, and likewise bestows liberation as well as knowledge.
All rites prescribed for human beings in the Śrutis and Smṛtis have bathing as their foundation;
therefore, one should practice bathing, which increases prosperity, nourishment, and health.
For one devoted to the ritual bath, ten qualities are to be accomplished: beauty, splendor, strength, purity,
longevity, health, and freedom from greed.
It destroys bad dreams, and it is austerity and wisdom.
Thus ends the praise of bathing.
Now, the classifications of bathing.
Regarding this, Dakṣa says:
Bathing is said to be of three kinds: daily (nitya), occasional (naimittika), and optional (kāmya). Among these, that which is the daily bathing is further divided into three types.
The removal of impurities by the side [of the body] and in the water is prescribed along with mantras;
that is the twilight bath (saṃdhyā-snāna) performed with both [methods], and these are proclaimed as the locations for bathing.

The cleansing of the body with clay and cow dung is "the removal of impurity. "On the side" means on the bank. "Twilight bathing" refers to ritual sprinkling (mārjana). That should be performed "with both," namely with water and [clay] on land.
Śaṅkha says:
"Bathing is said to be of two kinds, distinguished as secondary (gauṇa) and primary (mukhya).
Of these two, the Vāruṇa (bath by water) is the primary; that, moreover, is of six types."

The daily bath, the occasional bath, the bath for the fulfillment of desires, the bath as an auxiliary to ritual acts, the bath for removing impurities, and the sixth, the ritual bath— thus the bath is proclaimed to be sixfold.
He himself states their characteristics in sequence:
"A man who has not bathed is unfit for recitation, fire-offerings, and other such rites;
therefore, the morning bath is proclaimed as the obligatory daily bath."
Having touched a Caṇḍāla, a corpse, pus, or the like, as well as a woman in her menses, one must bathe;
when one who is already fit for bathing bathes, that is indeed an occasional (naimittika) bath.
O knower of the gods, that which is enjoined by the ritual rules, such as the bathing with flowers and so forth,
and that bathing which one performs as an auxiliary to a rite— that is proclaimed as *kriyāṅga* (ritual bathing).
The bath called "removal of impurities" is preceded by anointing with oil;
its purpose is indeed the removal of impurities, and not otherwise.
In lakes, natural reservoirs, sacred fords, and rivers, the ritual bath (kriyā-snāna) is prescribed; in that context, "ritual" refers to the specific action performed therein.
In that context, "action" (kriyā) refers specifically to bathing; it is "prescribed" (matā), meaning it is enjoined.

Among those, the optional (kāmya) rite should be performed exactly as directed by the injunctions, as well as the obligatory (nitya) and occasional (naimittika) rites, which are limbs of the ritual action and serve to remove impurities.
In the absence of a sacred bathing place (tīrtha), however, one should perform the rite with warm water or water drawn from elsewhere;
likewise for one who has bathed, [one may use] water heated by fire or even water from another source.
The purification of the body should be understood as such, yet it does not constitute the fruit of bathing;
the limbs are cleansed by water, but one obtains the fruit from bathing at a sacred ford (tīrtha).
Since bathing is indeed the primary rite in lakes, natural ponds, sacred fords,
and rivers, it is traditionally taught that the fruit of merit arises from bathing.
Gobhila says: That which is to be performed constantly is the *nitya* [obligatory rite]; that which is beneficial for the fulfillment of a specific desire is the *kāmya* [optional rite];
and that which arises from a particular occasion is traditionally known as the *naimittika* [occasional rite].
By this, the obligatory nature (*nityatva*) of the midday bath is also stated, because that too must be performed regularly. And so says Vaiyāghrapāda:
"One should always be a morning bather; one should always be a bather at the twilight [sacrifices]."
Regarding those who are unable to perform the aforementioned ablutions, Yoga-Yājñavalkya states other forms of bathing as well:
"Due to the incapacity of the body, or in consideration of time, strength, and so forth,
some wise teachers maintain that there are seven types of bathing, beginning with the *mantra-snāna* (mantra-bath)."
The seven baths, in their proper order, are: that with mantras, that on the ground, that pertaining to fire, that pertaining to wind, that celestial, that pertaining to water, and that mental.
He himself states their characteristics:
"The ritual touching of earth with the mantras beginning with *āpo hi ṣṭhā* is the earthly [bath];
bathing with ashes is the fiery; and the dust raised by cows is recorded as the windy."
That bathing which is performed with rain falling from the clouds is called divine;
immersion in water is Vāruṇa, and the contemplation of Viṣṇu is Mānasa.
The bath prescribed according to the instructions, whether performed through the sequence of mantra-bathing,
due to time constraints, place, or lack of capability, is traditionally held to yield an equal result in every case.
Some wise men maintain that mental bathing is the most excellent,
since it was recited by Vyāsa in the praise of the sacred ford of the Self (ātmatīrtha).
Likewise:
"May the waters be auspicious for us," "From the post," "O Waters, you are most beneficent," and "The Expiation of Sin"—
the ritual bath with mantras is declared to be performed with these four Vedic verses.
When impurity has arisen, one should perform a bath in this manner;
likewise, one should perform the ritual sprinkling with the previously mentioned mantras, otherwise it would be ineffective.
Gautama said: "The divine, the aerial, the fiery, the brahmic, the Sarasvata, and likewise the mental— thus the secondary bath (gauṇasnāna) should be known to be sixfold."
Parāśara also says:
"There are five meritorious baths which those who know them have proclaimed;
I shall explain them correctly, as they truly are, in their proper sequence."
The first is that of Agni, the second is that of Varuṇa, and the third is indeed that of Brahmā;
the fourth is that of Vāyu, and the fifth is called the divine (divya).
The fire-related bath is performed with ashes; the water-related bath by immersion; the brahmic bath with the mantra "āpo hi ṣṭhā"; and the wind-related bath consists of the dust raised by cows.
Whether at the proper time or otherwise, when the sun is free from clouds,
the bliss experienced upon seeing it is called divine.
Chāgaleya says:

Bathing with ashes is said to be Āgneya (related to Agni); bathing with water is Vāruṇa; that performed with the hymn "āpo hi ṣṭhā" is Brāhma; and bathing with the dust raised by cows is remembered as Vāyavya.
Bathing with water from the sun's heat and rain is here called the divine bath;
having bathed with these according to the mantras, one obtains the fruit of sacred pilgrimage sites.
In this regard, a specific detail is shown in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*:
"The smearing of the body with sacred ash from the feet to the head," says Bṛhaspati.
The dust of the cows is said to be *vāyavya* (belonging to the wind) when the Lord of Rays (the Sun) is setting.
*Sārasvata* means that which has been attained by the Sarasvatī of the learned; Vyāsa [describes] its true nature as follows:
One who knows the ritual should personally perform the ceremonial bath with due decorum for a twice-born person who has approached him, as well as for a disciple or a son.
O sinless one, may your bath be performed with jars made of gold, filled with the waters of the Ganges by a knower of mantras, accompanied by auspicious rites and declarations of merit.
Having spoken thus, one should proclaim other sacred fords (tīrthas) located at the site of the Jāhnavī;
finally, one should say: "May you have the merit of bathing in all sacred fords."
Thus, by the words of these great-souled best of Brahmins, one becomes well-bathed in all sacred fords and purified; it cannot be otherwise.
"To one who has approached" means to one who is seated nearby; "Dākṣāyaṇa" refers to gold. Jābāla says:
For those engaged in ritual acts, however, bathing may be performed without the head if they are unable to bathe fully.
They know that wiping the body with a moist cloth is also a form of purification for the person.
This is the Kāpila bath.
Regarding it, Bṛhaspati said:
"The cleansing of the body with a wet cloth is remembered as the Kāpila bath."

In the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa: "Bathing is said to be of three kinds: daily (nitya), occasional (naimittika), and optional (kāmya). Libation (tarpaṇa), however, is proclaimed as being an ancillary part (aṅga) of that."
In certain specific circumstances, Āpastamba states an exception to the rule regarding libations:
"Upon touching an untouchable, upon vomiting, upon the shedding of tears, upon shaving, and upon sexual intercourse."
The occasional bath (naimittika-snāna) should be performed, excluding those rites dedicated to the gods and the ancestors.
Regarding this, Viṣṇu states a specific rule:
"One who is entitled to a bath on account of a particular occasion, having already performed an immersion,
should thereafter sip water (ācamana) with self-restraint and then perform the bath according to the prescribed rite."
"Having performed the immersion," the word "silently" is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence].
Likewise, Yogayājñavalkya states:
"A man who is impure should immerse himself only silently."
Having sipped water and become purified, he should thereafter perform his bath according to the prescribed rules.
Vṛddhavasiṣṭha says:
Upon contact with a Caṇḍāla or similar outcaste, one should perform the Vāruṇa bath;
the other four [types of baths] are indeed prescribed according to the circumstances.
"The others" refers to the *brāhma* and other types of baths.
Gārgya also states a specific rule for the daily (*nitya*) bath within the *vāruṇa* bath:
"One should perform the occasional (*naimittika*) bath with cold water, and likewise the optional (*kāmya*) bath."
One should always perform [the rites] either according to one's whim or as one pleases.
"Spontaneous" (*yādṛcchika*) refers to the removal of impurity; for it has been stated by that very same author: "They say that spontaneous bathing is the washing away of impurity."
Regarding the bath for one who is ill, Parāśara says:
"When the occasion for a bath due to illness has arisen, ten times over, those who are not ill shall bathe and touch him; then that sick person becomes pure."
If a woman becomes menstruating when an occasional bath is required,
she should perform the bath using water filtered through another vessel and then observe her vow.
She should somehow have her limbs, including the major and minor parts, sprinkled with water;
she should not wring out her garment, nor should she put on another cloth.
Uśanas: When a woman is overcome by fever and simultaneously overwhelmed by her menses, how may she attain purification? By what ritual act may she become pure?
When the fourth day arrives, another woman should touch her;
having plunged into the water with her clothes on and bathed, she should touch her again after each bath.
She should sip water ten or twelve times again and again;
at the end, she should discard her garments, and thereby she shall become pure.
Then, having given a gift with devotion, she becomes purified by a *puṇyāha* ceremony.
Chāgaleya states the specific rule regarding death occurring during childbirth or within the period of ritual impurity:
"When a woman who has recently given birth dies, how do the performers of sacrifice proceed?
Taking water in a jar, as well as the five products of the cow (pañcagavya)..."
One should consecrate the waters with meritorious mantras; from that, one obtains purity through speech.
Having bathed [the image] with those very waters, one should then perform the ritual bath according to the prescribed rule.
Having bathed the deceased woman who has reached her menses with the five products of the cow,
and having covered her with another cloth, one should cremate her according to the prescribed ritual.
Thus end the varieties of bathing.
Now, the prohibitions for one who performs the bath.
Regarding this, Vyāsa says:
One should not perform a ritual bath at night, nor especially a gift;
however, one may perform occasional (naimittika) baths and gifts even during the nights.
This refers to the intention regarding the "great night" (mahāniśā),
as Manu says:
"One should not perform a bath after eating, nor when ill, nor at the great night."
Nor should one constantly wear clothes together with them, nor [bathe] in an unknown body of water.
Jābāli says:
One should never bathe for another's sake, nor after eating, nor at midnight;
nor should one ever put on a single garment while it is still wet.
Mārkaṇḍeya describes the characteristics of the "great night" (mahāniśā):
"The great night consists of two ghaṭikās during the middle watch of the night;
at that time one should perform occasional rites (naimittika), but not even the slightest optional rite (kāmya)."
"Kāmya" here refers to that for which no specific time has been prescribed. It consists of two *ghaṭikās*: the last part of the second watch and the first part of the third.
Devala states that the period of the two middle watches alone is known as "mahāniśā":
"Mahāniśā should be understood as the two middle watches."
One should not perform a bath in it, except for rites performed for specific desires or occasional observances.
That which is performed for a specific desire is *kāmya*, as prescribed for that particular occasion—for example:
"Then, at every watch of the night, one should bathe with cold water from jars," and so forth. Paiṭhīnasi also says:
For water is always unfit for drinking during the two middle watches of the night;
likewise, one should not perform bathing or the ritual of sipping water (ācamana).
Viśvāmitra says:
The "great night" (mahāniśā) should be understood as the two middle watches of the night;
one should not perform an optional bath or even the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) during that time.
In the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata* as well:
"Water is indeed always unfit for drinking during the two middle watches of the night;
one should not perform bathing there, nor the ritual sipping (*ācamana*) for the sake of specific desires."
However, regarding specific circumstances, even the counter-exception (pratiprasava) for sipping water (ācamana) is mentioned in that very same [text]:
"If a Brahmin performs the sipping of water after urinating or defecating during the dead of night, he must perform an expiation;
he deserves half of a Prājāpatya penance."

"Uccāraḥ" means the voiding of excrement. Since bathing is prohibited specifically during the "great night" (mahāniśā), it is understood that [voiding] at other times during the night is not forbidden. For this very reason, Parāśara says:
The "great night" (mahāniśā) should be understood as the two middle watches;
during the evening or the final watch, one should perform the daytime bath.
"Pradoṣa" refers to the first watch of the night. This should be understood as applicable when bathing during the day is impossible.
As he himself has said:
"Bathing during the day, purified by the rays of the sun, is praised."
Bathing at night is not recommended, except when there is an eclipse of the moon by Rāhu.
Vyāsa says:
Bathing at night is forbidden, except when there is an eclipse of the moon (the appearance of Rāhu);
likewise, one should never bathe in small or public waters without the head.
"Rāhudarśana" means an eclipse; it is mentioned here for the purpose of indicating other occasions such as the transit of the sun (saṃkrānti) and so forth.
For this very reason, Devala says:
"At the sight of Rāhu, at the transit [of the sun], at a wedding, at times of calamity, and at times of prosperity..."
One should perform bathing, giving gifts, and other such rites at night during optional vows.
‘*Atyayaḥ*’ means death; ‘*vṛddhiḥ*’ means birth. Yogayājñavalkya also says:
“During eclipses, weddings, the sun’s passage into a new sign (*saṅkrānti*), journeys, calamities, and childbirths...”
Bathing on special occasions (naimittika) should be known as that which is permitted even at night.
‘Ārti’ means death.
Parāśara also says:
“At the birth of a son, at a sacrifice, and likewise at the transit of the sun...”
Bathing at night is recommended upon the sighting of Rāhu, but not otherwise.
"In the sacrifice," namely at the *avabhṛtha* bath. As for the prohibition of bathing in a river at night stated by Vyāsa:
"A man should avoid bathing in a river by all means once the sun has set."
One who knows the Dharma, having bathed in a river, should not praise another river.
One should not bathe after having hidden oneself, nor at a sacred ford (tīrtha) within the midst of water;
one should not urinate in a wooden trough for water, nor should one cross a river while intending to bathe.
Thus, this refers to the case of touching that which is normally untouchable.
As the elder Śātātapa said:
"If one should touch [an untouchable] at night after the sun has set, having first touched [something else]..."
O Blessed One, by what means would purity be attained? Tell me that with certainty.
If water has been drawn while the sun has not yet set, purification is achieved by using that water in its entirety; however, one must avoid touching a corpse.
Parāśara:
When the sun has set, how is purification prescribed for one who touches a Caṇḍāla, an outcast, a woman, or a woman who has recently given birth?
Having bathed and touched Jātavedas, gold, Soma, and likewise Arka,
one becomes pure with the consent of Brāhmaṇas.
For one who has sipped water or followed after another, bathing at night is not prescribed;
however, bathing or the sipping of water (ācamana) is declared to be performed with water fetched during the day.
Yama says: A Brahmin who has been touched at night by a woman in her courses or by an outcaste should bathe in the presence of the sacred fire using water fetched during the day.
Even water collected during the day, having mixed it with gold,
one should bathe near a fire when the time for the night bath has arrived.
But when water brought during the day is not available, Marīci states this specific rule:
"If the water brought during the day is not present in the house,
one should kindle a fire and then bathe in a river or a lotus pond."
Regarding this, Kātyāyana states a specific rule:
"Pracetās and Varuṇa [reside] in the waters; one should not draw water at night except for the purpose of a dwelling. Standing on the bank, one should perform the ritual bath."

The meaning is that one should not draw water at night except by means of the mantra indicated by the opening words "dhāmno dhāmnaḥ. And with the water thus drawn, one standing on the bank of a river or similar body of water should bathe. The Yajurvedic mantra beginning with "māpo mauṣadhīr hiṃsīr dhāmno dhāmno rājan" is to be used. Paiṭhīnasi states a specific rule regarding the drawing of water:
"If there should be no water in the house, how can purification take place?"
One should take [the fire] into the vicinity of the fire with the mantra "dhāmno dhāmnaḥ."
"In the vicinity of fire" means holding a blazing fire over the water;
and thus says Hārīta:
"Holding the fire above [the water] with the mantra 'dhāmno dhāmnaḥ,' one should take [the water]."
However, on occasions such as the sighting of Rāhu (an eclipse), bathing even at night in a river or similar body of water is recommended.
As Vyāsa says:
"He who bathes in the Jāhnavī during a lunar or solar eclipse..."
Having bathed in all the sacred fords, why does he wander the earth?
In the Devīpurāṇa:
"The Godāvarī is exceedingly meritorious when the moon is joined by Rāhu,
and when the sun is eclipsed by the moon— that form of darkness, O high-minded one."
In the Saura Purāṇa: "Upon touching a corpse in the house of the moon (during the lunar eclipse), and during the transits of the sun,
one may bathe at night in rivers and other bodies of water."
Devala says:
Just as bathing and giving gifts are prescribed during the daytime on the occasion of a solar eclipse,
so too are bathing and giving gifts ordained at night for a lunar eclipse.

The meaning is that where the eclipsed moon sets after sunrise, the bathing and other rites for the occasion of seeing Rāhu must be performed *before* sunrise, and not afterwards. Vṛddha-Vasiṣṭha states: "In the case of an eclipse of Rāhu, there is impurity (sūtaka) for all castes."
One should perform a bath with one's clothes on and avoid food from those who are in a state of ritual impurity due to birth or death.
"Sūtākānna" refers to food from the impurity of Rāhu.
Gautama states: "One should never bathe naked at night."
Baudhāyana says: one should bathe naked, but one should not bathe at night.
Āpastamba says: [the same].
One should avoid immersing the head in water after sunset; bathing [with the head] is not permitted. This prohibition against immersing the head applies specifically to stagnant water.
Thus, it is stated in the Nandipurāṇa:
"Having entered the water, a twice-born man should bathe while submerged in a river's current."
"One should perform the bath visibly in the waters of tanks and the like. Thus [says] Manu:
"One should not perform the bath naked. Thus [he says].
Uśanas:
One should not bathe naked. Hārīta: [The same].
One should not drink water while naked. Śaṅkha and Likhita state:

One should bathe without being submerged and without being naked; one should not urinate in water, nor should one perform rubbing [of the body]; one should not strike the water with a foot or with a hand, because water is indeed all the deities; one should not step into it in vain when it is not being praised, and having sprinkled it, one should avoid impure water; one should not bathe in scant water, one should not plunge into the ocean, one should not speak of a river as a river in rivers, nor of mountains as mountains on mountains.
The *Yogayājñavalkya* states:
A wise man should not strike water with his foot, his hand, a staff, or a cloth; nor should he speak of it, nor should he disturb it.
One should not cause pain to anyone through action, mind, or speech;
one should not perform the ritual ablution, but should instead perform other duties.
Devala says: One should not speak of a river while among rivers, nor of a mountain while among mountains;
likewise, while staying at sacred fords (tīrthas) or shrines, one should not praise anything else.

Standing at one river, one should not speak of another river; standing among other mountains, one should not speak of another mountain, nor praise it. Likewise, the meaning is that while standing at other sacred fords (*tīrtha*), shrines (*āyatana*), or fields of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*), one should not praise another ford or field. Hārīta says:
"One should not bathe at a crossroads or at the gate of a city."
Furthermore, Hārīta states:
"One should not offer the first portion of either the bath-water or the cosmetic paste to anyone other than the gods, one's teacher, or Brāhmaṇas.
Viṣṇu says, with reference to the rule that "one should perform the bath": [the same applies].
One who is suffering from indigestion, one who is ill, one who is naked, nor [should one bathe] at night—except during an eclipse of Rāhu—nor during the two twilights.
Jābāli says: One should never neglect the daily bath, nor that which is performed for specific desires, nor that which is occasional.
It should be performed on the tenth day and subsequent days, and never at random.
"Spontaneous" (*yādṛcchika*) refers to that performed for the purpose of removing impurity.
Āpastamba also says:
"But that bath which is performed by the twice-born for the sake of enjoyment is spontaneous."
That [practice] is prohibited on the tenth day and other such occasions, but not the obligatory (nitya) or occasional (naimittika) rites.
Hārīta says:
He who uses oil on the tenth, the fifth, the full moon day, the thirteenth, the eleventh, or the third [lunar days]— [is guilty of a sin].
His growth will have transcended [the world], and there shall be no decline in his power or lifespan.
Baudhāyana also says:
"On the Nandās, the Riktās, the Pūrṇās, and the Jayās;
on the twelfth and the seventh lunar days; and during the Vyatīpāta and Vaidhṛti yogas."
Furthermore, during the sun's transit into a new zodiac sign, one should not perform an oil massage or a bath.

The *nandās* are the first, sixth, and eleventh lunar days (*tithis*). The *riktās* are the fourth, ninth, and fourteenth. The *pūrṇās* are the fifth, tenth, and fifteenth. The *jayās* are the third, eighth, and thirteenth. Thus, it is stated that one should not perform an oil-bath (*abhyaṅga-snāna*) on any lunar day other than the second.
A prohibition regarding the days of the week (*vāra*) has also been shown by Parāśara:
[bathing on Sunday, Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, and Saturday results respectively in] distress, beauty, short life, wealth, poverty, as well as [the others].
Through anointing [with these oils] on the days of the Sun and other planets, there shall be health and the fulfillment of all desires.
On this point, Pracetas says:
"Mustard oil, scented oil, oil perfumed with flowers, and likewise any other oil mixed with substances, never becomes defiled."
Yama also says:
"There is no fault in using ghee, mustard oil, or any oil perfumed with flowers for bathing and anointing, provided they have been cooked; this applies constantly."
In the *Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa*:
"O King, on the seventh lunar day of both fortnights, at night and during the two twilights,
one who desires learning, sons, or a wife should avoid bathing with sesame seeds."
One should always perform the meritorious bath with sesame seeds, and with *āmalaka* fruits for the sake of prosperity,
except on the seventh and ninth lunar days, the new moon, and during the sun's transit (*saṃkramaṇa*).
In the Vāyu Purāṇa: On the ninth day, on the new moon, on the seventh day, at the sun's transit (saṃkrānti), on Sundays,
and during lunar and solar eclipses, one should avoid bathing with *āmalaka* fruits.
Vyāsa states:
"On the tenth, the third, and likewise on the thirteenth lunar day,
the Vāruṇa bath (the ritual bath in water) should not be performed by Kṣatriyas and the other castes."
Jābāli also says:
"On the thirteenth, the third, and especially on the tenth lunar day,
those born of the Śūdra, Vaiśya, and Kṣatriya castes should by no means perform an ablution."
Regarding this, Garga states an exception:
"At the birth of a son, at a solar transit (saṃkrānti), at a śrāddha, on one's birthday,
and when a daily bath is to be performed, no fault regarding the lunar day (tithi) exists."
Also in the Gāruḍa Purāṇa:
"When the daily bath is to be performed, no defect regarding the lunar day (tithi) exists."
In the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa:
"One should not bathe once the festival has ended, after having concluded the auspicious rites,
having seen off friends and kinsmen, and having worshipped one's chosen deities."
An exception to this rule is also stated in that same source:
"Bathing with oil and mantras is desired on auspicious occasions, during rites for prosperity, and at festivals and seasonal celebrations; it is especially recommended before midday."
Thus end the prohibitions regarding the performer of the bath.
Now, the waters to be accepted and those to be avoided for the purpose of bathing. Regarding this, Manu says:
One should always perform one's bath in rivers, in natural pools dug by the gods, in tanks, in lakes, and also in pits and springs.

A *nadī* is a flowing river with water that cannot be exhausted. This is because bathing is prohibited in small streams whose waters may dry up in the summer. That which is remembered as "dug by the gods" (*devakhāta*) is a natural pool. An artificial reservoir with a dimension of more than two thousand *hasta*s is a *taḍāga*. A body of water larger than a thousand *hasta*s but smaller than a *taḍāga* is a *saras*. The nature of a *gartta* (pit) has been described by Kātyāyana: "Those [water bodies] whose course does not extend for eight thousand *dhanus* [are *garttas*]."
Those hollows are not designated by the word "river"; they are proclaimed to be such.

A reservoir of water situated on a plot of land measuring eight thousand *dhanus* in extent, beyond which there is no further movement or flow, is designated by the term "pool" (*garta*) and not by the term "river. A "springs" (*prasravaṇa*) is a waterfall; the meaning is a flowing stream of water trickling down from a mountain or similar source. Yājñavalkya states:
"One should bathe in rivers, in natural excavations made by deities, in lakes, and in springs."
A "pool" (*hrada*) is a portion of a river with a steady current and exceedingly deep water. It refers to one who is skillful; and knowledge resides in that which is unartificial water.
In the Viṣṇupurāṇa: "One should bathe for the sake of daily rites in rivers, streams, and tanks, in lakes dug by the gods, and in natural hollows and springs."

The "rivers" are those such as the Hiraṇyabāhu and others. Mārkaṇḍeya states that the merit of waters increases progressively: water situated on the ground is more meritorious than that which has been drawn up, and water from a spring is more meritorious than that.
The merit from that [gift] is even more essential than merit; therefore, it is said that nothing should be withheld.
The water of a sacred ford is more meritorious than that, but the water of the Gaṅgā is the most meritorious of all.
"A *tīrtha* is frequented by the virtuous; for that which is occupied by the Arhats is indeed declared to be a *tīrtha*, according to the traditional teaching (*smaraṇa*)."
Viṣṇu also says:

"Water on the ground is more meritorious than water drawn up; therefore, one should not take [water] from a river; even more so, that which is accepted by the virtuous; and above all, that which comes from the Gaṅgā.
Vivasvat also says:
On one side are all the sacred fords, and on the other is the Ganges alone— that river which,
having fallen from the head [of Brahmā] in the world of Brahmā, reached the surface of the earth.
Marīci also said:
Whether situated on the ground or drawn up, whether cold or even warm,
the water of the Gaṅgā quickly purifies sin committed until the end of one's life.
In the Padma Purāṇa: "Water that has been drawn up is indeed auspicious only so long as it is not stale;
however, the water of the Bhāgīrathī never becomes stale."
In the Āditya Purāṇa:
"Even water that has been kept for a long time, or even that which has been touched by a Śūdra,
always purifies one through bathing, giving, and other rites in the Jāhnavī."
For this very reason, Yogayājñavalkya states that one should not bathe with water drawn from [the Ganges] that has been touched by Śūdras and others:
"A man who performs his bath with water drawn [from a source] defiled by contact with the impure shall never become pure."
Likewise:
"Rivers that do not flow to the ocean yield their fruit after three nights;
those flowing to the ocean, however, after a fortnight; and the Lord of Rivers (the ocean) after a month."

"Yielding the fruit of three nights" means that they bestow the fruit of the vow of fasting for three nights; the same applies to [fasting for] a fortnight and a month. As stated in the *Vārāha Purāṇa*:
"The water of the Sarasvatī [is equal to fasting] for three days, but that of the Yamunā for five days."
The water of the Gaṅgā purifies immediately, while that of the Narmadā does so merely by being seen.
The water of rivers that flow into the ocean, as well as that of other rivers, is purifying for bathing and giving gifts; it is recorded in tradition as being equal to the Prājāpatya penance.
Furthermore, whatever large bodies of water there may be that do not flow into the ocean and which cannot be dried up even in the summer season— one should perform one's ablutions in them.
One should never bathe in those small streams that dry up in summer when scorched by the rays of the sun, even if water is occasionally seen in them.
A traditional saying: One should not perform a ritual bath in those rivers on earth that dry up during the summer, nor even in the rainy season when only a cloud is visible.
Kātyāyana states that even for rivers that are otherwise praiseworthy, there is a period of impurity due to dust (rajo-doṣa) during which bathing and other rites are improper:
"When the month of Śrāvaṇa has arrived, all rivers are in their menstrual flow;
one should not bathe in them, with the exception of the Jāhnavī."
"In the month of Śrāvaṇa" is intended as an indication of the rainy season;
for this very reason, Mārkaṇḍeya says:
"During these two months, all rivers here become menstruating."
Therefore, bathing with fresh rainwater during the monsoon season is not recommended.

The rainy season (*varṣākāla*) lasts for two months starting from the *saṃkrānti* of Cancer (*karkaṭa*). This is because of the traditional teaching of Jyotiḥparāśara: "The rains [occur] during Cancer and Leo. The mention of bathing (*snāna*) is intended to indicate libations (*tarpaṇa*) and other such acts as well. As Kātyāyana says:
"Between the months of Nabhas and Nabhasya, all rivers are in their menstrual flow (*rajasvalā*)."
A person should not perform any acts such as bathing and the like in those [rivers].
The meaning is that she remains menstruating for two months beginning from Karkaṭaka.
[871] And likewise during an eclipse of the moon or sun, as well as on the day of the solar transit (saṃkrānti) and so forth;
as he himself has said:
During the rainy season, great rivers are constantly in their menstrual flow;
one should not bathe in them, with the exception of the Ganges.
Regarding the Ganges, however, he himself states that the impurity of menses lasts for exactly three days:
"When the month of Śrāvaṇa has begun, the Gaṅgā is menstruating for three days;
when the fourth day arrives, the daughter of Jahnu becomes pure."
This too refers specifically to the solar measurement; otherwise, it would contradict [the following]:
"In the first [month of] Karkaṭaka, the Goddess Gaṅgā is menstruating for three days; all rivers flow with blood, as does the Karatoyā."

Thus, there would be a contradiction with the statement of Yogayājñavalkya, because in the solar measurement of time, the conventional usage of the months beginning with Śrāvaṇa is observed solely on account of the *saṃkrānti* (the sun’s passage into a zodiacal sign). "Karatoyā" is a specific river. Likewise: "When Cancer begins, the Gomatī is defiled by impurity for three days."
The Candrabhāgā, the Sindhu, the Śarayū, and likewise the Narmadā.
Regarding all rivers other than those already mentioned, he [Yājñavalkya] himself states the specific rule when the two-month period of menstrual impurity (*rajas*) occurs:
"During the two months beginning with Śrāvaṇa, all rivers are in their menstrual flow;
one should not bathe in them, except for those that flow into the ocean."

‘Yavyāḥ’ refers to *māṣa* beans, according to the *Śatapatha-śruti*: "That which is one is the year. Regarding rivers flowing to the ocean, it is stated in the *Bhagavatī-purāṇa* that their menstrual flow (*rajoyoga*) lasts for six nights:
"All rivers are in their menstrual period for two months, beginning with Karkaṭa;
however, for those flowing to the ocean, the menstrual flow is held to last for six nights."
[872] It is stated in the *Vāmana Purāṇa* that even among those rivers flowing to the ocean, there are some in which there is no dust whatsoever:
"The river Sarasvatī is meritorious, as is the river Vaitaraṇī;
likewise the Āpagā, the Narmadā, the Gaṅgā, and the river Mandākinī."
The Madhusravā, the Aṃśumatī, the Kauśikī, and likewise the Yamunā;
the highly meritorious Dṛṣadvatī and the river Hairaṇvatī.
Except for the Sarasvatī,
the waters of all rivers flowing during the rainy season are proclaimed to be meritorious during that very time;
in these [rivers], there is never any state of being "menstruating" (impure).
Kātyāyana also says:
"The Gaṅgā, daughter of Tapaṇa, the Sarasvatī born from the Plakṣa tree,
and those others known as rivers, are not overcome by passion."
"The Sarasvatī at Kurukṣetra is the one that originates from the Plakṣa tree.
Thus, he (the same author) states an exception in certain cases regarding the defect of menstrual impurity:
"At the Upākarma and the Utsarga ceremonies, as well as during the morning bath," [there is no impurity].
And during an eclipse of the moon or sun, the defect of menstrual impurity does not exist.
Gārgya says: Twice-born men should avoid bathing in a river where the water flows backward, where there is a washerman’s bathing place,
or within ten cubits of its upper bank.
"In *pratyāvarta* means 'endowed with whirlpools. Baudhāyana also says:
'Likewise, bathing in a river that has whirlpool waters should be avoided by the twice-born.'"
In that [river], one should avoid the washerman's bathing place by a distance of ten cubits.
Bathing at the washerman’s bathing place, eating in a courtesan’s house,
and sleeping toward the northwest will take away one’s fortune even from Indra.
When the [waters] have ceased, they shall not perform [the work]; in that case, the builder of the bridge shall not be entitled to a share.
Regarding this, Jamadagni states, following the phrase "in flowing rivers":
"A Brahmin should never perform his bath in rivers that are obstructed by another, because [otherwise] he would obtain the fruit belonging to the builder of the dam."
Śaṅkha says: One should not bathe in water that is insufficient, nor should one plunge into the ocean;
this is intended with reference to the availability of abundant water.
As Chāgaleya said:
"When a river is nearby, one should not perform one's bath elsewhere;
nor should one bathe in water that has been drawn up, nor ever in very little water."
The definition of "very little water" is stated in the *Skanda Purāṇa*:
"Water that reaches only to the navel is declared to be 'very little';
one should perform bathing there, but never when it is only knee-deep."
Yogayājñavalkya states:
"When abundant and very pleasant water is available,
a twice-born man should not bathe in a small amount of water, nor should he abandon a river to bathe in an artificial pool."
In the Nāradīya Purāṇa:
"While a river is available, one should not bathe in other waters;
one should not bathe in a small amount of water when abundant water is present."
Marīci states that one may bathe even in ponds and the like when a river is not nearby:
"In the absence of rivers, one may at any time bathe in tanks, lakes,
large reservoirs, or even in wells."
In the Viṣṇupurāṇa:
"A twice-born man should perform his bath in wells where the water flows upward;
otherwise, he should bathe with water drawn out, unless there is a specific preference for another method."
Mārkaṇḍeya also says:
"One should perform the bathing of the ancient kings, the great-souled sages, and the deities in wells and ponds."
By the phrase "of the great-souled ones," it is implied that one should not bathe in wells or reservoirs belonging to outcasts and the like. For this very reason, Vṛddha-Manu says:
[One should not accept gifts] from wealth acquired by unjust means, from an outcast, or from a usurer.

"One should not bathe in public wells; having bathed there, one should perform a *kṛcchra* penance. This same principle is to be understood regarding [water] that has not been consecrated for use. As Vyāsa says:
One should not sit down where permission has not been granted, nor likewise where the ground has not been consecrated.
"Unprepared" means not having established [the ritual site]. "Not relinquished" means not abandoned for the sake of all purposes; that is to say, belonging to another.
For this very reason, Jābāli says:
"One should never bathe in water belonging to another."
Manu also says:
"One should never bathe at water-reservoirs belonging to others; for by bathing there, one becomes tainted by a portion of the evil deeds of the person who constructed the reservoir. [875]
Furthermore, as for that which was stated by Vyāsa:
"One should perform a bath in another's water without having extracted five lumps [of earth]," and that which was stated by Yājñavalkya;
Having removed five lumps [of earth], one should not bathe in the waters of others.
And as Śaṅkha and Likhita state:

"One who is bound by lifelong vows (naiṣṭhika) should satisfy the ancestors. In reservoirs, wells, ponds, and drinking-water sources, having removed seven, five, or three lumps, one should satisfy the gods and ancestors."
Thus it is said; and as for that which was stated by Paiṭhīnasi:
"One should avoid bridges and wells made by others. One who shares in the merit of a bridge should bathe there after having lifted out three lumps [of earth].
This refers to a situation where rivers and other such sources are unavailable.
And so Manu says:
"In the absence of water from divine sources, from lakes, or likewise from rivers,
one should perform the ritual bath in another person's water after having drawn out four handfuls."
Baudhāyana also says:
"Therefore, one should avoid bridges and wells made by others;
or, in times of distress, one may take water after removing three lumps [of earth], but never as a regular practice."
From five lumps of clay that have been set aside, and likewise from three jars taken from a well; as Śaunaka also says:
"If one should ever drink from a large pond, a well, or a lake..."
Having extracted lumps of clay, one should throw either ten or five of them [into the water].
Yogayājñavalkya also says:
"If one should ever bathe at water-reservoirs belonging to others,
one should first extract seven lumps of earth from there and then perform the bath."
Viṣṇu also states:
"One should not bathe in the water-reservoirs of others; however, one may perform a bath there by removing five lumps [of earth], except in times of distress.
Here, the application depends on one's capacity. Thus, it is implied that the liability for that fault applies only in cases where one bathes in another's reservoir without removing [the earth].
Regarding this, Śaunaka says:
"But he who bathes in another person's reservoir of water without having first drawn [some out],"
"Such bathing becomes fruitless, and the performer is smeared with sin.

Here, "fruitless" (vṛthā) means "inefficacious. The underlying sense is that when water has been set aside for all purposes, there is no fault in failing to remove it, as it does not belong to another. Śaṅkha likewise states that bathing in hot water is likewise fruitless.

The purification of the body by means of water heated by fire or even by the water of another person should be understood as mere physical cleansing; however, it does not constitute the fruit of ritual bathing.

Yogayājñavalkya also says: "Bathing in hot water for no purpose, Vedic recitation that is not according to the Vedas, giving gifts to one who is not learned in the Vedas, and eating in the absence of witnesses— all these are in vain."
As for that which was stated by Yama:
"Water is always pure, and fire is its purifier;
therefore, at all times, warm water is remembered as purifying."
Thus it is said; and also in the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*:
"Water is pure by its very nature, how much more so when heated by fire? Therefore, the virtuous praise bathing with warm water."
Thus, that refers to the subject of bathing for the sick;
and likewise Yama says:
"Purified by the rays of the sun, and purified again by fire..."
"It is traditionally taught that boiled water is recommended for the bathing of one who is ill.
When, however, a river or similar body of water is not available, then even for one who is not ill, bathing with warm water is not prohibited; thus he [the same author] says:
"The daily obligatory bath, the occasional bath, the bath as part of a ritual act, and the bath for removing dirt..."
"But in the absence of a sacred bathing place (tīrtha), it should be performed with hot water or rainwater.
As for that which was stated by Vṛddha-Manu: "At death, at birth, at the sun's passage into a new sign (saṃkrānti), at a śrāddha, and likewise on one's birthday..."
Furthermore, upon touching that which is untouchable, one should not bathe with hot water.
On a solar transit, on a Sunday, on the seventh lunar day, or upon seeing a king,
one who desires health, sons, friends, or wealth should not bathe with warm water.
He who bathes with warm water on the full moon day or likewise on the new moon day incurs here the sin committed by killing a cow; of this there is no doubt.

Thus, even when death and other such occasions have been mentioned by him, although there may be an absence of a sacred bathing place (*tīrtha*), one should not bathe with hot water; rather, it is stated that one should bathe with water brought from elsewhere. There is therefore no contradiction. Regarding the specific rule for bathing with hot water, Vyāsa says:
"Hot water, collected in abundance along with mantras, should be poured into cold water."
Knowledge is praised even in the home; otherwise, it would be fruitless.
The "materials" (saṃbhārāḥ) are clay and so forth.
For this very reason, Vivasvat says, in the context of the midday bath:
"The ritual rinsing (upasparśana) is said to be conjoined with the materials for the mantra."
"In bathing and immersion, splashing [the water] is forbidden by rule.
Thus are the waters to be accepted or avoided for the purpose of bathing.
Now, the requisites for bathing:
Regarding this, Dakṣa says:
"In the fourth part [of the day], one should likewise fetch earth for the purpose of bathing,
as well as sesame, flowers, kuśa grass, and so forth, or perform the bath in artificial water."
In this context, it should be understood that the fourth part is divided into eight portions. The *Yogayājñavalkya* states:
"Clay, sesame seeds, cow dung, *darbha* grass, and fragrant flowers..."
At the time of bathing, however, being restrained and pure for the sake of the bath,
one should go to the water's edge and, according to the prescribed rule, place them separately on the ground in the proper sequence.
Śaunaka said:
On the bank of a river, in a pure place, one should fetch earth and *kuśa* grass;
being self-restrained, having taken earth, *dūrvā*, *apāmārga*, and cow dung.
One should set aside a small portion of the clay from one part, and then gradually [from the others].
Jābāli says: Then, for the sake of bodily purification, one should fetch pure clay— free from foul odor and not saline— from a clean place, having made it very fine.
One should collect fresh, pure cow dung from cows that have not eaten impure food, are free from disease, and are without physical defects.
From a region devoid of cremation grounds and the like,
one should fetch fresh, creeping *dūrvā* grass and likewise *apāmārga* for the purpose of purification.
For the purpose of employing all ritual actions, one should bring either kuśa or kāśa grass,
as well as barley and sesame seeds for the sake of the libation (tarpaṇa).
For the purpose of performing the rite of worshipping the deities,
one whose self is purified should take fresh, auspicious flowers as well as a pair of washed garments.
Likewise, one should procure a sturdy vessel made of udumbara wood for the purpose of sprinkling,
and a rosary made of rudrākṣa beads or similar materials for the purpose of recitation;
having thus gathered the necessary materials, one should commence the rite of bathing.
Regarding this, Śātātapa says:
"Seven kinds of earth should not be taken: that from an anthill, from a molehill, from what remains after cleansing, from water, and from the roots of a tree or a path."
In a clean place, free from gravel, stones, and the like, one should collect earth;
it is traditionally held to be of three kinds: red, pale-yellow, and white.
A wise man should not take clay or water at night, nor should he take cow dung at night,
nor should he take cow urine at dusk.

One who rubs himself with sesame, bathes with sesame, remains constantly pure, offers water with sesame, and is an offerer, an eater, and a giver of sesame— such a person, possessing these six qualities of sesame, does not perish.
Marīci says: Earth,
darbha grass, sesame seeds, flowers, dūrvā grass, apāmārga, cow dung,
sesame, āmalaka, and garments— these are for the vessel used for sprinkling.
Having gone to a secluded place with water and washed his hands on the bank,
he should arrange the ritual materials there, each in its proper place and separately.
Aṅgiras: Any bath taken without *darbha* grass, any gift given without water,
and any recitation performed without counting— all that becomes fruitless.
Vyāsa says:
Having taken earth produced on the banks of the Gaṅgā with supreme devotion,
he who anoints his limbs thereby shall possess great merit.
Vasiṣṭha says: Having taken earth, durvā grass, and fresh cow dung while purified,
and having set them down and likewise performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), one should then perform the bath.
Thus end the requisites for bathing.
Now follows the morning bath;
regarding this, Dakṣa says:
The duty for the first part of the day is now prescribed for him:
when the time of dawn has arrived, he should perform purification according to the rules;
thereafter, he should perform his bath preceded by the cleansing of the teeth.
Śaunaka said:
Having performed the morning sipping of water (ācamana) with faith according to the rules,
and having then cleansed his teeth, he should perform the morning bath.
Gautama:
Having properly performed the rules for purification and rinsed his mouth after cleansing his teeth,
he should perform his bath according to the prescribed ritual at dawn.
Jātūkarṇya says:
The morning bath should be performed every single day by all social classes;
however, the twice-born should perform it with mantras, while Śūdras should do so devoid of mantras.
Satyavrata says:
Morning bathing is a means of purification for all four castes;
it should be performed by the twice-born with mantras enjoined by the Vedas.
Baudhāyana says: Immersion in water as a bath is prescribed for all social classes;
however, for the twice-born, sprinkling with water accompanied by mantras is specifically distinguished.
In the Mahābhārata:
"O descendant of Kuru, bathing with mantras is prescribed for the Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas; however, for Śūdras and women, it is indeed to be done silently."
In the *Kūrmapurāṇa*:
"One desiring purity must always bathe before the daily rites of prosperity (*abhyudaya*).
This is declared to be the common duty for the four social orders (*cāturvarṇya*)."
Women and Śūdras should perform the immersion [in water] without the recitation of mantras.
Gobhila says: One should perform the bath every day at dawn before the sun has risen;
likewise, one should satisfy the ancestors with mantras that do not contain masculine gender endings.
Viṣṇu:
[882] One who bathes at dawn should bathe after observing the eastern quarter seized by the rays of the sun.
As for that which is stated in the Caturviṃśatimata:

The statement that "the bath [should be performed] at every dawn, during the twilight (saṃdhyā), and even when the sun has risen" is not in contradiction with the aforementioned texts, because "when the sun has risen" is explained as "facing the rising. Otherwise, there would be a contradiction with such passages as, "The morning twilight [is to be observed] while the stars are still visible," since one becomes entitled to the twilight rites and so forth only after having bathed, according to statements such as, "One who has bathed is qualified [for the rites]. Nor is it correct to argue that the twilight rite itself should be postponed on the strength of this very text; for it is said:
"One should perform the twilight worship during the twilight, neither when the sun has set nor when it has risen."
Thus, because of the traditional injunction regarding the prohibition stated by Yogayājñavalkya, Yājñavalkya says:
"The two twilights must be bathed in by Brāhmaṇas residing in the household;
however, by an ascetic, one must bathe during all three twilights."

"At both twilights" refers to those known as morning and midday. "By those residing in a house" means by householders. "The ascetic" refers to the *yati*, such as Viśvāmitra. Bathing at morning and midday is for the forest-dweller and the householder.
For ascetics, bathing three times a day is prescribed;
however, for the student (brahmacārin), it is ordained that he bathe only once.
Dakṣa says:
Bathing in the morning and at midday is prescribed for forest-dwellers and householders;
for ascetics, bathing three times a day is ordained, while for students it is once a day.
Kātyāyana says: Just as during the day, so too should one always bathe untiringly in the morning;
having cleansed one's teeth in a river or similar body of water, or at home, this [cleansing] is done without mantras.
The phrase "as if without mantras" does not intend a total prohibition of mantras; rather, it is for the purpose of prohibiting a multiplicity of mantras.
As Jaimini said:
"For even in the home of the twice-born, bathing with mantras is prescribed."
"Even if they possess the capability, they should never effect the omission of the prescribed rule.
Thus Vivasvān stated the fault in the total prohibition of the mantra:
"He who should commence the bath without even knowing the Smārta injunction..."
"He goes to a terrible hell"—such is the established doctrine of Dharma.
Vyāsa also says: "They declare that bathing purified by mantras is the bathing that yields fruit;
it is not in vain like water for those ignorant of mantras, being equal to [water for] aquatic creatures."
"Of the *yādas*," meaning aquatic creatures.
In the *Yogayājñavalkya* it is also said:
"The ritual for them, beginning with the formal salutation (*upasthāna*), which has been proclaimed as being accompanied by mantras."
The exponents of Brahman say that the bath concludes with the offering of the oblation.
From conception until the cremation ground, according to the revelation of the Vedas,
no rite whatsoever for the twice-born is performed without a mantra.
But he who performs an action prescribed by rule according to an improper method obtains no fruit at all; for that [action] of his results only in suffering.
Fish, turtles, and frogs remain submerged in the water day and night;
yet even though they dwell there, they never deserve the fruit of bathing.
Whatever action is performed by men, conjoined with faith and according to the prescribed rule,
and with a pure and clean disposition, that conduces to infinity.
Whatever is performed devoid of prescribed rules, corrupted by intention, and done without faith—
that is seized by the Asuras from that deluded person of unrefined soul.
"Bathing with mantras is prescribed for the Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas;
however, for a Śūdra, it is traditionally held that bathing should be performed silently, accompanied only by a salutation.
Therefore, because there is the possibility of omitting rites such as the fire-oblation (*homa*), one should perform the morning bath briefly and without mantras.
As Śāṭyāyani said:

"If one should fear that the performance of the oblation and other rites might be obstructed due to the brevity of time, then one should perform them in brief; however, in every case, they must be performed without mantras."
Kātyāyana also says:
"Because the time for the fire-oblation is short and the ritual of bathing is extensive, the morning bath should be performed concisely; the omission of the oblation is censured."
Yogayājñavalkya states the method for the abbreviated bath:
"If one is unable to perform that supreme procedure for bathing which has been described in detail, then this [abbreviated] procedure is prescribed."
Bathing within the water, as well as sprinkling, sipping,
the consecration of the water, and the visualization of the sacred site (tīrtha).
By reciting the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn three times daily,
this is designated by the great-souled ones as the performance of the ritual bath;
or one may, according to one's desire, employ other mantras dedicated to Varuṇa.
The bath is performed on the twenty-fourth day;
one should perform the bath with those [prescribed] years, or with Vāruṇa mantras together with earth,
or else with the Vyāhṛtis, or even with the verse "yat kiṃ cedam."
Or, as it is said, "like from Drupada," one should offer libations to the gods and humans;
and this libation is an integral part of the bath,
for libation is proclaimed to be its subsidiary element.

Thus, according to the recollection in the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*. Baudhāyana states: "The ascetic practice consists of immersing oneself in water; having satiated the deities, one performs the libation to the ancestors by pouring out water along the edge of the bank with the mantra, 'Carrying strength' (*ūrjaṃ vahantīḥ*). Furthermore, they cite this as well:
While the flowing streams have not ceased, the three twice-born castes,
having risen in the morning, should perform the libations for the gods, the sages, and the ancestors.
In the twenty-four [verses]: Immediately after bathing, one should offer libations to the ancestral deities (*pitṛdevatā*).
And this libation (*tarpaṇa*) must be performed while standing in the water. As Vyāghra says:
Standing in water reaching up to his navel, with his mind directed upwards and reflecting, he says:
"May my ancestors come; may they accept these handfuls of water."
"A wise man standing in water, facing south, should offer three handfuls of water each to the ancestors residing in the sky, making them progressively higher.

Thus, having drawn up [the water] to the height of a span (*prādeśa*), three handfuls should be offered with intent for the father; then, having drawn it up to the height of a cubit (*hasta*), for the grandfather; and then, having drawn it up to the height of a cow's horn (*gośṛṅga*), for the great-grandfather—in this sequence, they become successively higher.
Thus it is said in the *Garuḍa Purāṇa*:
"Having lifted up water to the measure of a span (*prādeśa*), then to the measure of a cubit (*hasta*),
and then to the measure of a cow's horn (*gośṛṅga*), one should offer the water to the ancestors and others."
Having lifted [the water] to the height of a span, one should satisfy the gods and humans.
In the *Brahmavaivarta*: "Standing in water reaching up to the navel, one should perform the libation that is a limb of the ritual bath;
one should offer libations to the gods, the sages, the hosts of ancestors, and one's own forefathers."
One who has bathed with water drawn from its source should not perform the libation for the ancestors (tarpaṇa) as part of the bath at another time;
however, a wise man should never omit the libation that is an integral part of the ritual bath.

Therefore, even at midday, the *tarpaṇa* that is an ancillary part of the bath must be performed while still standing in the water. One should not raise the objection, "How can there be a *pitṛ-tarpaṇa* in the morning, given the Vedic injunction, 'The afternoon belongs to the ancestors' (*aparāhṇaḥ pitṝṇām*)? For if that were the case, then according to the injunction, "The forenoon indeed belongs to the gods" (*pūrvāhṇo vai devānām*), there would be no *deva-tarpaṇa* during a midday bath. Nor should it be said, "Let it not be so," for it is stated:
"And in all baths whatsoever, one should perform the *tarpaṇa* of the ancestors and deities;
one should especially perform that with great effort in the case of both optional and obligatory rites."

Thus, according to the Smṛti of Vyāsa. Therefore, it should be understood that the two [conflicting] Śruti texts refer to matters other than the libation (tarpaṇa). Furthermore, Vasiṣṭha has shown that there is even a fault in failing to perform it: "He who, out of a state of atheism, does not offer libations to the ancestors after bathing..."
"His ancestors, seeking water, drink the discharge from his body. Here, "discharge from the body" (*dehaniḥsrāva*) refers to bodily impurity.
— Kaśyapa.
Having bathed, the wise man, being pure, should satisfy the gods, the sages, human beings, and the hosts of ancestors, for they have him as their support.
Regarding the fruit obtained when this is performed, Dakṣa says:
"The Brahmin who, having risen in the morning, always becomes one who bathes in the morning,
destroys the sin committed in seven lifetimes within three years."
Śaunaka also says:
"The Brahmin who, having risen in the morning, always performs his morning ablutions,
being liberated from all sins, attains the supreme Brahman."
Thus concludes the morning bath.
Now follows the midday bath. Regarding this, Yogayājñavalkya says:
Having heard those words of Yājñavalkya at that time,
the sages of purified souls asked about the determination regarding ritual bathing.
O sinless one, you previously mentioned the bath performed with mantras dedicated to the water-deities;
O Lord, explain that specifically, as well as the ritual procedure for the bath.
Yājñavalkya, of immeasurable luster, with a joyful heart, replied to them:
"Listen, for I shall describe the ritual bath that destroys all sins."
Having gathered earth and other materials and gone to a pure body of water,
the twice-born man should perform his bath every day in the morning and at midday.
Sumantu says: Then, at the time of midday, one should again perform the ritual bath;
thereafter, one should perform the worship of the Sun, as well as the recitation of mantras (japa), fire offerings (homa), and so forth.
Vasiṣṭha and Hārīta also state:
"With the sacred grass (pavitra) in hand, one-pointed in mind, not looking toward the sides,
and free from disease, one should perform the bath especially before midday."
"Free from disease" (*aruk*) means being devoid of illness; thus, it is implied that one who is sick should not bathe. And it has been said by Vyāsa:
"One should perform the midday bath when the food is well-digested and one is free from disease."
One who has eaten should not adorn themselves; one who is ill should not bathe in unknown waters; and one who is distressed should not do so either.
Śaṅkha says:
"The morning bath is intended for the sake of purification in a concise form; however, that which is performed according to the rules with mantras at midday should be elaborate."

Pāraskara: Having taken earth, cow-dung, kuśa grass, sesame seeds, and flowers, and having gone to the edge of water, one should place them in a clean spot, wash one's hands, feet, and sacred thread, tie the topknot, and perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana). [In] the Skanda Purāṇa:
One should wash the sacrificial thread (yajñasūtra) slowly with earth and water.
Bhṛgu says: "Since the sacrificial thread remains upon the body purified by mantras..."
Therefore, the wise person who desires his own welfare should rescue them.
That [impurity] residing within the body must be washed away; it should never be removed [by external means].
Vyāsa says:
Having recollected the syllable *oṃ* and the *gāyatrī*, one should then bind the topknot (*śikhā*).
With the sacrificial grass in hand, having sipped water for ritual purification, he should touch his navel and shoulders.

Baudhāyana: Then, having washed his hands and taken hold of his water-pot and a lump of earth, he should go to a sacred bathing place (tīrtha) and wash his feet three times; then he should wash himself three times. Now, some say that one must not enter a cremation ground, water, a temple, a cow-pen, or a place where Brāhmaṇas are, without first washing one's feet. Yājñavalkya on Yoga says:
Having divided that clay and the cow dung into three parts, the wise man should perform the washing of the lower, upper, and middle limbs with them respectively.
One should perform the washing with separate portions so as not to mix the earth;
having washed the feet with water and earth and performed the ritual sipping (ācamana), one indeed becomes pure.
In this regard, one should wash the area above the navel with the right hand and the area below it with the left hand;
a knower of the Dharma should not employ the right hand for purification below the navel,
nor likewise should he cleanse the area above the navel with the left hand.
Thus, according to the Smṛti of Bhṛgu; and in the Nandipurāṇa:
"In former times, a twice-born man desiring long life should apply clay as an ointment to his head."
One who desires prosperity should first perform the cleansing of the feet with earth.
Regarding the purification of impurities, Vyāsa also states:
"The feet should be washed with six [handfuls of] clay, the shanks and the navel region with four, and the hips with three;
the head should be cleansed with a single handful of clay, after which one should perform the wiping."
Vasiṣṭha also says: "The head should be washed with one application of clay; likewise, the area above the navel with two;
the area below it should be treated with three; and the feet likewise with six."
Having washed the entire body, one should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) twice according to the prescribed rule.
Pāraskara:
"The head should be washed with one application of clay, and likewise the area above the navel with two;
the anus should be cleansed with four applications of clay, and likewise with six."
Then, having washed the waist, the bladder, the thighs, the shanks, and the feet with three [handfuls of water],
and likewise having washed both hands, one should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) twice with a concentrated mind.
In this matter, the specific arrangement follows one's own particular Śākhā.
However, the measurement of the clay and other materials is shown in the Kūrma Purāṇa:
"And the clay is prescribed as being the size of a fresh Āmalaka fruit."
The quantity of cow dung, however, is that by which one should smear the limbs.
And this purification from impurity should be performed on the bank [of a river].
Thus it is said in the Nṛsiṃha Purāṇa:
"Having sprinkled a clean place, one should set down kusha grass, clay, and sesame seeds."
Then, one should externally cleanse one's own body with earth and water.
Yama says: Having then performed the bath for removing impurities, sipped water (ācamana), and become pure while facing east,
one should perform three breath-control exercises (prāṇāyāma) and then meditate upon the Sun.
"Having sipped water," the word "twice" is understood as the remainder [of the instruction]. And this sipping of water (ācamana) should be performed by placing one foot inside the water;
as it is stated in the *Caturviṃśatimata*:
"One who has sipped water on dry land is pure within the water, but one who is in the water is pure on dry land."
"Having placed both feet [in water] and having sipped water (ācānta), one indeed attains purity.
Thus, after cleansing the bathing cloth on the bank, this sipping of water (ācamana) should be performed; having diligently rubbed one's own body with earth and water on the outside.
Having thoroughly cleansed his bathing cloth, the wise man should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana).

Thus, according to the *Marīci-smṛti*, there is no fault in performing the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*) even while standing with the knees raised, on a riverbank that is otherwise unsuitable for sitting and so forth; for Jātūkarṇya says:
"One who stands in the water with the knees raised and performs the sipping of water is not defiled."
Vyāsa says:
Having become pure in a clean place at the water's edge, being composed, one should regularly restrain the vital breaths three times; thereafter, one should commence the bath.

"Having become pure" means having performed the purification of impurities. Because of the inclusion of the word "daily," the purification of impurities and breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) are mandatory even during bathing and other such acts.
Saṃvarta describes the nature of breath control:
"The seven *vyāhṛtis* joined with the *praṇava* [should be recited] daily."
A twice-born person should recite [the Gāyatrī] three times mentally together with the Gāyatrī-śiras while restraining his breath;
this is prescribed as prāṇāyāma.

In this context, first is the filling of the breath through the nose; then, the stabilization of the filled breath; then, the recitation of the mantra three times; and then, the performance of inhalation (*pūraka*), retention (*kumbhaka*), and exhalation (*recaka*) according to the sequence of exhalation. Thus it was said by Vasiṣṭha:
"The inhalation drawn in through the nose, when meditated upon, is called *pūraka*;
*kumbhaka* is the motionless breath; and that which is being emptied is *recaka*."
Furthermore, meditation on specific deities in specific locations during the practices of *pūraka* (inhalation) and so forth was taught by that very same [author]:
"One should meditate, by means of *pūraka*, upon the Great-Souled One, who is dark like the petal of a blue lotus, established in the center of the navel, and possessing four arms."
[892] By means of *kumbhaka*, one should meditate upon the lotus-seated Brahmā, the Lord of Creatures (*prajāpati*), in the region of the heart— he who has limbs as fair as blood and four faces.
"During the *recaka* [exhalation], one should meditate upon Maheśvara, the Lord, situated on the forehead—
resembling pure crystal, stainless, and the destroyer of sins. Thus it is stated in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*.

Then, having recollected the specific place, time, and constituent parts [of the ritual], one should make the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*): "I shall perform the midday bath for the sake of exhausting the accumulated sins. Thereafter, having made a prayer to the water with the verse, "For King Varuṇa has made wide space" (*uruṃ hi rājā varuṇaś cakāra*), and having turned the water clockwise with the verse, "Those hundred [fetters] of yours, O Varuṇa" (*ye te śataṃ varuṇa*), one should take water in the hollowed palms with the mantra, "May they be friendly" (*sumitriyā naḥ*), and with the mantra, "May they be unfriendly" (*durmitriyā naḥ*), one should cast it toward the north, dedicating it to desire, anger, and the like.
Regarding this, the Yogin says:
"Having worshipped the water with the three verses beginning 'For wide' (*uruṃ hi...*), [one should turn] clockwise."
One should stir that water with the three-verse hymn beginning with "ye te śatam."
Recalling the deity, one should raise the joined palms while reciting "sumitriyā naḥ";
then, meditating upon the enemy, one should sprinkle water while reciting "durmitriyāṇaḥ."

In this regard, having divided the clay into two portions and then further dividing [one portion] into three, one should perform the aforementioned cleansing bath (*malasnāna*) with the first portion; then, one should consecrate the remaining portion for the purpose of the clay bath (*mṛttikāsnāna*) with the mantra beginning "aśvakrānte.
And so it is stated in the *Matsyapurāṇa*:
"One should likewise perform the bath with clay, having consecrated it according to the prescribed rule."
"O Earth, trodden by horses, trodden by chariots, trodden by Viṣṇu!"
Immediately after that:
"O Earth, you were lifted up by the boar Kṛṣṇa with his hundred arms;
you were bestowed by Brahmā and consecrated by Kaśyapa."
O Earth, destroy all that evil which has been committed by me;
O Earth, grant me nourishment, for everything is established in you.
By the sin destroyed by you, may I live for a hundred autumns.
Having extracted the earth with this mantra spoken in the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*, and having shown it to the Sun with this verse, "Homage to Mitra and Varuṇa," [he recites]:
"Climbing upon my limbs, release me from all evil;
O Earth, I take you with my offspring and my wealth."
Having smeared the limbs of the body, beginning with the head, with this mantra spoken by Kaśyapa, one should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) twice.
This is stated in the Śiva Purāṇa:
"Recalling the mantra 'aśvakrāntā' and consecrating the clay with that mantra..."
One who is well-composed should extract [the tooth] with the mantra: "Thou art extracted."
Having shown [the sun] with the verse "namo mitrasya" and [the verse] "bhānave," and having touched his limbs with the verse "āruhya," he should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) twice.
Jamadagni said:
One should slowly bring pure earth with the mantra "aśvakrānte";
one should show it to the sun with hands joined in reverence while reciting "namo mitrasya."
Having recited "gandhadvārām," one should smear one's own limbs [with sandalwood paste]. Regarding the mantra for smearing the limbs, the Yogin says:
one should obtain clay for the limbs with the three verses beginning with "idaṃ viṣṇuḥ."
Likewise:
[894] One should gradually wash the limbs with water after water,
from the head down to the navel and all parts, while recollecting the healthy Viṣṇu.
The waist, bladder, thighs, shanks, and feet [are each formed] by three [channels] each.
In the same manner, having sipped water with both hands and paid homage to the water,
one should then bow with palms joined in reverence while reciting the mantra "yat kiṃ cedam."
Jamadagni says: "To Varuṇa with the golden horn"—with this he approaches the waters;
