"May those who are friendly [to us]"—having touched the water with this, he should cast outside those who are unfriendly.
Having stirred the water three times with his hand while reciting "Whatever of the waters is cruel," Baudhāyana says: "Then he approaches the water."
I take refuge in Varuṇa, whose horns are of gold; grant me a sacred ford (tīrtha) when I entreat you.
Whatever I have released toward the unrighteous, whatever acceptance of gifts from the wicked, and whatever evil deed I have committed with my mind, speech, or action—[may it be cleansed].

"May Indra, Varuṇa, Bṛhaspati, and Savitṛ purify us. Then, with his joined palms, he scoops up water, saying, "May the waters and plants be auspicious friends. He sprinkles that water toward the direction in which he has an enemy, saying, "May they be ill-disposed toward him who hates us and whom we hate. Then, having touched water, he turns the water three times clockwise, saying, "Whatever in the waters is cruel, whatever is impure, and whatever is unpeaceful—let that depart.
(From the Matsya Purāṇa.)
One should perform the ritual bath with waters that are either drawn out or not drawn out;
a bathing place (tīrtha) should be prepared, measuring two cubits square on all sides.
But with darbha grass in hand, having sipped water according to the rule, being self-controlled and pure,
the wise knower of mantras should prepare the sacred site (tīrtha) with the root mantra.
"Oṃ namo nārāyaṇāya" is declared to be the root mantra.
[The site] should be four-cornered and square on all sides, measuring four cubits.
Having prepared [the vessel], the wise one should invoke Gaṅgā with these mantras:
"You are born from the foot of Viṣṇu; you belong to Viṣṇu; Viṣṇu is your deity."
"Save us from that sin which begins at birth and ends with death;
Vāyu declared that there are thirty-three million holy fords (tīrthas) and a further ten million."
In heaven, on earth, and in the intermediate space, O Goddess Jāhnavī, these are your names: among the gods you are indeed called Nandinī, and among the Devas, Nalinī.
Dakṣā, Pṛthvī, Vihagā, Viśvakāyā, Śivāmṛtā, Vidyādharī, Suprasannā, and likewise Lokapramāthinī.
Kṣemā, Jāhnavī, Śāntā, and Śāntipradāyinī—
these meritorious names one should recite at the time of bathing;
thereupon, Gaṅgā, who flows through the three paths, becomes present there.
Likewise, there is also the statement of the Gaṅgā: "Nandinī, Nalinī, Sītā, Mālatī, and Mahāyaṇā— the Gaṅgā,
who flows through the three paths, originated from the water-offering at Viṣṇu’s feet."
Bhāgīrathī, Bhogavatī, Jāhnavī, and Tridaśeśvarī.
Wherever one who is intent on bathing remembers these twelve names in any body of water, there I shall always be present for him.
Vasiṣṭha: Having thus performed the purification with the mantras beginning with "aśvakrāntā," [he recites]:
"Right here, O Goddesses, is the nectar in the rivers Pārā and Avyarā."
With the two verses beginning "ye te śatam," the wise man should invoke the sacred bathing places (tīrthas).
Vyāsa: May Kurukṣetra, Gayā, the Gaṅgā, Prabhāsa, and the Puṣkara lakes—
all these sacred fords— be present for me at the time of my bath.
"All of this should be performed in artificial waters alone;
one should mentally recall the Gaṅgā and other sacred fords within artificial waters and the like," according to the traditional teaching of the *Yogayājñavalkya*.
In whatever place there is a sacred ford or a most meritorious river, one should bathe while meditating upon it with the mind; otherwise, bathing elsewhere involves distracted thought.

Thus, because Bhṛgu has prescribed meditation on that very *tīrtha* in the case of natural (non-artificial) ones, and because of the prohibition against recollecting another *tīrtha* while at one—expressed as "one should not speak of a river while at a river"—one should bathe after having invoked the *tīrthas* according to the procedure stated in one's own scripture. Yogayājñavalkya says:
"Purified and facing east, one should enter that water with the mantra 'ud uttamam'."
With the three verses beginning "yena devāḥ pavitreṇa," he should perform the touching.
Afterwards, even though he is already pure, he should sip water with the Mahāvyāhṛtis;
facing the sun, he should immerse himself while reciting the three verses beginning with "āpo asmān."
Jamadagni:
Facing the sun, one should immerse oneself in the waters with the three verses beginning with "āpo asmān.
(From the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa.)
Having recited "āpo asmān" and standing facing the sun,
and having muttered "idaṃ viṣṇuḥ," he immerses himself against the current.
Āpastamba: "One should approach the water slowly, without striking it; facing the sun, one should touch the water. This is the rule for touching water in all cases.
And the requirement of facing the sun applies specifically to stationary water.
And so it is stated in the Narasiṃha Purāṇa:
"A twice-born man should bathe in flowing rivers standing against the current;
in waters such as ponds and the like, he should perform his bath facing the sun."
In the Vāmana Purāṇa:
"One should immerse oneself facing the current where the waters indeed flow;
and in still waters, one should always face the sun."
Yogayājñavalkya says:
Then, having rubbed his limbs, immersed himself, and emerged again,
he should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) and smear himself with cow dung while reciting the Mānastokīya hymn.
Regarding this, Jamadagni states the mantra for sipping water: "At midday, one who sips water [should do so] with the mantra 'May the waters purify me' (Apaḥ punantu);
and at evening and morning, [with the mantra] 'Agni and I, and Sūrya and I'" (Agniś ca me ca sāyaṃ ca prātaḥ sūryaś ca me).
And this sipping of water (ācamana) must be performed after reaching the bank;
regarding that, Baudhāyana says:
"One should purify oneself with darbha grass, using auspicious, flawless, and sanctifying mantras."
With the three verses beginning "āpohiṣṭhā," [he offers] this oblation of water.

With the two verses beginning "O divine waters," with the three-verse hymn beginning "The divine waters," with the verse beginning "As from a pillar," and with the verse "May the goddesses [waters] grant us bliss," [he offers] the essence of the waters.

With a concentrated mind, he should slowly purify himself with the verses beginning "The divine waters, the purifying ones" (*āpo devīḥ pāvamānyaḥ*), the first three verses of the *pāvamānī* hymns, and the nine verses beginning with "Citpati may me... (*citpatir mā*).

And likewise, one should recite the *pāvamānī* verses beginning with "hiraṇyavarṇāḥ," as well as others such as the *taratsamandī*, the *śuddhavatī*, and other purificatory hymns (*pavitra*), according to one's ability.
A Brahmin, standing in the midst of water with a pure disposition, should recite hymns from the Vāruṇī hymnal according to his ability and meditate upon Hari.
With the syllable *oṃ*, the *vyāhṛtis*, and the *gāyatrī*,
one who is composed should perform the sprinkling (*abhiṣeka*) at the beginning and at the end in due order;
likewise, the purification (*mārjana*) is prescribed for one standing in the midst of the waters.

Viṣṇu: Having removed impurities with earth and water, and having immersed himself in the waters and performed the ritual sipping (*upaspṛśya*), he should consecrate the bathing place (*tīrtha*) with the three verses beginning with *āpo hi ṣṭhā*, the four beginning with *hiraṇyavarṇāḥ*, and the verse *idam āpaḥ pravahata*. Then, submerged in the waters, he should mutter the *aghamarṣaṇa* mantra three times; or else the verse *tad viṣṇoḥ paramaṃ padam*, or the *drupadā* verse, or the *sāvitrī*, or the section beginning with *yuñjate manaḥ*, or the *Puruṣasūkta*. Paiṭhīnasi: [same as above].

Having bathed with the hymn beginning "hiraṇyavarṇāḥ" and having performed purification, one should perform three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas) in the midst of the waters. Jamadagni says: One should recite this Aghamarṣaṇa hymn, "ṛtaṃ ca," three times within the waters.
Just as the avabhṛtha bath concludes the Aśvamedha sacrifice, so does the Aghamarṣaṇa rite conclude the ritual bath.
In the continuation of the rule "within the water," Vasiṣṭha says:
"One should perform breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*), the *gāyatrī*, or the *aghamarṣaṇa*;
then, having been agitated by those [faults] as previously described, one should submerge three times like a staff."
The meaning is: by means of the aforementioned forms of the wind’s inhalation, retention, and exhalation.
Baudhāyana states: "Having performed the ritual purification (*mārjana*), having gone into the water, and having performed three breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) with the *aghamaṛṣaṇa* hymn."
The *Yogayājñavalkya* states: "One should recite the *Aghamarṣaṇa* mantra three times while submerged in water;
or one should practice the *Drupadā* verse three times; or the three verses beginning with 'āpo hi ṣṭhā'."
Having repeated three times the verse beginning with "haṃsaḥ śuciṣat," he should then recite it;
furthermore, he should recollect other hymns as prescribed in the Smṛtis.
One should then recite the Gāyatrī mantra three times together with the Vyahṛtis and the Praṇava;
or one may repeat the Praṇava, or meditate upon the imperishable Viṣṇu.
For the waters are the abode of Viṣṇu, and he is called the lord of the waters;
these [waters] are indeed his offspring, therefore one should meditate upon him within the waters.
From Nara, indeed, the waters were produced; therefore they are remembered as "Nārāḥ.
Since those waters are his place of rest (ayana), he is therefore remembered as Nārāyaṇa.
For he is indeed the enjoyer of vows, of the Vedas, of self-restraint, and of discipline;
the enjoyer of sacrifices and austerities, as well as the very meditation of those who meditate.
One should constantly meditate upon Nārāyaṇa during rites such as ritual bathing;
by doing so in all acts of expiation, a person is released from evil deeds.
Whatever part of the ritual action performed during sacrifices may fall away due to negligence, that becomes complete through the mere remembrance of Viṣṇu; such is the Vedic revelation.
One should immerse oneself in the waters again and again with the mantra "tad viṣṇoḥ," for this Gāyatrī belongs to Viṣṇu and is indeed for the purpose of recollecting Viṣṇu.
Bṛhaspati says: That mantra which is [found] in the Vājasaneyaka Veda, beginning with "drupadād iva," if one recites it three times while submerged in water, one is liberated from all sins.
Viśvāmitra said:
That goddess named Drupadā is established in the Yajurveda;
by reciting her three times while submerged in water, one is released from the sin of killing a Brahmin.
Vyāsa also says: "The Gāyatrī named Drupadā, which belongs to the Brāhmaṇa Vājasaneyaka,
removes even the sin of killing a Brāhmaṇa if it is recited once while submerged in water."
Regarding Drupadā, the Kūrma Purāṇa states:
"Having taken water in the hand, having recited [the mantra], and having performed the sprinkling (mārjana),
one who places that water upon the head is liberated from all sins."
Bhṛgu said: Having taken water in his hand, he should recite the Drupadā verse three times.
Having placed that water upon his head, he is liberated from all sins. Vyāsa says:
Likewise, being self-restrained, one should repeat the Sāvitrī mantra three times while submerged in water.
One is liberated from all sins, provided one is not a slayer of a Brahmin.
Hārīta also says:
"The Gāyatrī named Jumbaka, found in the Vājasaneyaka Veda,
removes even the sin of killing a Brahmin when recited once while submerged in water."

The mantra is: *jumbakāya svāhā*. Sumantu also says: "Having approached one's mother, sister, maternal aunt, daughter-in-law, female friend, or having committed any other forbidden sexual act, one becomes purified from that by reciting the *aghamarṣaṇa* hymn three times while submerged in water."

Hārīta also says: "By reciting three times while submerged in water this *ṛc*—*āpaḥ naḥ śam̐sād duriṣṭaṃ yajñasya viśvatomukhāḥ / svāhākṛtāḥ śam̐tamā no bhavantu asmin hi loke uttarasmiṃś ca devāḥ*—one is liberated from all evil. By reciting three times while submerged in water this *ṛc*—*haṃsaḥ śuciṣad vasur antarikṣasad dhotā vediṣad atithir duroṇasat / nṛṣad varasad ṛtasad vyomasad abjā gojā ṛtajā adrijā ṛtam bṛhat*—one is liberated from all evil. Gautama also says:

Alternatively, by reciting the Gāyatrī three times while submerged in water—first foot by foot, then half-verse by half-verse, and finally the whole verse in its entirety—one is liberated from all sin. Dakṣa says:
"The purification [of the breath] should be performed within the water, followed by breath control (prāṇāyāma) wherever one may be."
Subsequently, attendance and recitation are said to consist of the recitation of the Sāvitrī.

The *Śāṭyāyanagṛhya*: "Wearing his garment, he should bathe day after day; having bathed, he should put on another garment after stepping out of the water. Even here, the *tarpaṇa* (libation) that is an ancillary part of the bath must be performed while in the midst of the water. However, in case of incapacity, an abbreviated bath should be performed according to the method previously described. [904]
Vasiṣṭha says:
Whatever twice-born man bathes in water anywhere according to this rule, he obtains the fruit of a sacred ford; at actual fords, the fruit is twofold.
Whatever sin he commits through the actions of mind, speech, and body—
all that goes to destruction like an unbaked clay vessel in water.
Śaṅkha says: "One who has bathed according to this rule obtains meritorious fruit. Thus concludes the midday bath.
Now, regarding the ritual bath (*kriyāsnāna*):
on this matter, Śaṅkha says:
"I shall explain the ritual bath exactly as it is, according to the prescribed rule."
At the outset, purification must be performed according to the rules with earth and water.
Having emerged from being submerged in the water and having sipped water according to the rule, one should perform the invocation of the sacred ford (tīrtha); I shall explain that hereafter.
I take refuge in the divine Varuṇa, the powerful lord of the waters;
grant me the sacred ford I have requested, so that no further sins may arise.
I shall invoke the sacred ford that destroys all sins;
by my grace, let it assume its presence within these waters of mine.
I take refuge in all the Rudras, the givers of boons;
I, seated within the waters, take refuge in all those who dwell within the waters, standing here bowed in devotion.
I take refuge in the divine Agni, the consumer of oblations and the destroyer of sin;
likewise, I seek refuge in the waters, which are meritorious and purifying.
Rudra, Agni, the serpent, Varuṇa, and the waters themselves.
"May they quickly pacify my evil and always purify me.
Having spoken thus, one should then perform the sweeping with *kuśa* grass.
One should perform the rite duly and in proper sequence with the three verses beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā," and likewise with the four verses beginning with "hiraṇyavarṇāḥ" by the seer.
Likewise, one should recite the mantra "śanno devī," as well as "śanna āpaḥ," and "idam āpaḥ pravahata."
Having thus performed the sweeping,
one who is self-restrained should always recollect the *chandas*, the seer, and the deity of the *aghamaṣaṇa* hymn.
The meter of this [hymn] is Anuṣṭubh, its seer is Aghamarṣaṇa,
and it is proclaimed that the deity of this destroyer of sins is Bhāvavṛtta.
Then, while immersing oneself in the water, one should recite the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn three times;
for it is like the Aśvamedha, the king of sacrifices, which destroys all sins.
Likewise, one should recite the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn, which removes all sins;
then, one should apply water to the head while reciting the Vyāhṛtis.

Having bathed according to this procedure, one should change one's bathing garments at a place unfit for purification; then, having changed one's clothes, one should perform the ritual sipping of water (upaspṛśet) on the bank of the sacred ford.
Thus concludes the ritual bath.
Now follows the procedure for one who has emerged from the water.
Regarding this, Baudhāyana says:

Having wrung out his upper garment and put on unwashed clothes that have been washed and aired, having sipped water and sitting upon *darbha* grass while holding *darbha* blades, he should face the east and repeat the *Sāvitrī* one thousand times.
"Washed and aired" means dried immediately after washing.
On this point, Vyāsa says:
"Before the crushing [of the body], a handful of water should be offered on the ground, intended for one who has died without having received the sacraments (*asaṃskṛta*).
Thus it is said in the *Padmapurāṇa*:
"Wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvīta*), with *kuśa* grass in hand, together with sesame seeds..."
One should offer handfuls of water on dry land for those who have died in the unconditioned realm (asaṃskṛta).
Looking toward the southern direction with effort, one should recite this mantra:
"May this water mixed with sesame seeds, which is offered, become inexhaustible for those born of my lineage who have died without the proper rites and have fallen into an evil state."
Vyāsa also says:
"One should cast those who died before receiving the sacraments into a single pit. Those living beings in my family who were not cremated by fire, and those who were not burned at all—"
May they be satisfied by what is given upon the ground; being satisfied, may they go to the supreme goal.
Furthermore, this handful of water must be poured onto dry land while one is still standing in the water; for Sumantu states the fault in doing otherwise:
"If one who is on dry land, yet wearing clothes wet with water, should offer a handful of water, the deceased will drink it by diverting the flow of the water dripping from his garments."
‘Apavārya’ means having cast the water-offering (jalāñjali).
Furthermore, one should remain on the bank for some time for the purpose of draining the water from one’s clothes.
Regarding this, Bharadvāja says:
Since those who belong to the class of slaves, once dead, require water for their clothing,
one should let the water fall upon the ground after it has remained there for some time.
Then one should wring out the bathing garment. Pulastya says:
"Having thus performed the libation (tarpaṇa) and having emerged from the body of water..."
The wise man should wring out his bathing cloth right there on the bank.
The reason why one should wring out [the garment] right there on the bank is stated in the *Vāyupurāṇa*:
"The *Śruti* declares that the water wrung from the garment is the portion for those who partake of the leavings (*ucchiṣṭabhāgin*) at the *śrāddha*; therefore, one should wring it out on dry land."
The prohibition against wringing out [the garment] while in the midst of water is stated in the Nāradīya Purāṇa:
"If any Brāhmaṇa, weak in knowledge, wrings out his garment while in the midst of water, that bath of his becomes fruitless."
Because of the statement, "having performed the libation," one should not wring out the garment beforehand.
Thus says Yogayājñavalkya:
"As long as one has not offered libations to the gods, the sages, and the ancestors..."
One should not wring out the garment so that the one who has bathed does not [become wet] again in the water.
One should not wring out the garment with which one has bathed;
however, he who wrings out the bathing garment before the libation [of water] [incurs a fault].
His ancestors depart hopeless along with the gods and the sages;
so says Parāśara:
"The ancestors depart hopeless when the wringing out of the garment is performed."
Therefore, one should not wring out one's garment without having performed the libation to the ancestors.
In the context of the deities and the ancestors, Śātātapa states:
"They return disappointed when the wringing out of the garment is performed;
therefore, one should not wring out the garment without having performed the libation to the ancestors."
Śaṅkha:
"Indeed, one should not wring out the bathing cloth until water has been offered [to the ancestors]. Viṣṇu: [Silent].
Without having performed the libations for the gods and ancestors, one should not wring out the bathing cloth.
Regarding the manner of wringing out the garment, Sumantu says:
"Standing facing south, with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītī)..."
Wrapping it in a counter-clockwise direction, he should wring out the bathing cloth.
Regarding this, Kārṣṇājini states the mantra:
"Those born in our family who have died childless or as agnates—
may they accept this water from the wringing out of the garment offered by me."
He [the author] himself states that after wringing out the garment, the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) must be performed:
"Then, having wrung out the bathing garment, one should perform the ritual sipping of water again.
And this ritual sipping of water must be performed while standing on dry ground.
As Hārīta says:
"If that lowest of men, while on dry land, sips water while his garment is still wet from water,
his ancestors drink the dripping moisture of that garment as something impure."
Therefore, one who knows the rule, having placed one foot within the water and likewise one on the ground while performing the ritual sipping (ācamana), becomes purified; it is not otherwise.
Paiṭhīnasi also says:

"One who sips water while inside [the house] becomes pure inside; one who sips water while outside becomes pure outside. Therefore, having performed one sip inside and one outside, one should sip water for the feet; thus one becomes pure in all circumstances.
This is stated in the Matsya Purāṇa.
Having bathed in this manner, and thereafter having sipped water according to the rule,
one should rise and put on two clean, white garments.
The remainder [of the instruction] is that one should sip water twice; thus says Vyāghra: "Then, having taken two clean garments, one should touch [them] twice."
Vasiṣṭha also says:
Having sat down in a clean place facing either east or north, one should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) twice.
Between the donning of the garment and the sipping of water, the cleansing of the shins and other lower limbs must be performed.
And so Jābāla and Parāśara state:
"Having bathed and put on another garment, the two shanks should be cleansed with earth and water;
for they have been rendered impure by the water used for bathing the loincloth."
In this context, because the reason is stated as "having become impure," the mention of the shanks (*jaṅghā*) is intended to indicate any part of the body that has become impure.
For this very reason, the *Yogayājñavalkya* states:
"Having bathed in this manner and having put on two clean, unwashed garments..."
Having washed the thighs with earth and water, one should then wash the hands.
Furthermore, one should not discharge feces or urine while wearing clothes wet from bathing.
Thus it is said in the *Liṅgapurāṇa*:
"If, after having bathed, one discharges feces or urine while still wearing wet clothes..."
Having performed three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas), one becomes pure again through bathing.
In the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*:
After bathing, one should not wipe the limbs with clothes or hands,
nor should one shake the hair, nor should one shake the garment.
Regarding this, Vyāsa states the reason:
"There are thirty million and another ten million body hairs;
as many sacred bathing places (tīrthas) flow [through them], therefore one should not wipe [the body]."
Gobhila also says:
"The gods drink from the head; the ancestors drink from the mouth;
all the Gandharvas [drink] from the middle; and all living beings [drink] from below."
Therefore, one should not wipe away water from the body with the hand after bathing or lying down.
In the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*:
"Having bathed, one should not wipe the limbs with the bathing cloth nor with the hand.
Because of the specific mention of the "bathing cloth" (*snānaśāṭī*), some maintain that wiping with another garment is permitted.
Manu: "When bathing the head with oil, one should not touch any other part of the body at all. Laghu-Hārīta: [same as above].
If any twice-born man, having performed his ablutions, takes a flower [for himself], the deities do not accept it; he shall become like wood in ashes.

Viṣṇu: Having bathed, one should not shake one's head; one should not pour water from the limbs; one should not touch oil; and one should not wear a garment previously worn that has not been washed. One should not engage in conversation with Mlecchas, Antyajas, or outcasts. Vyāsa:
One should not apply ointments without having bathed, nor should one wring out one's garment;
rather, after bathing, a person should wear clothes while they are still damp.
Hārīta says:
Having bathed, one should not wipe the limbs, nor shake the head, nor shake the garment, nor exchange the upper garment. Vyāsa and Vasiṣṭha say:
A wise man should never wear his upper garment below, nor his lower garment above; he should never go about without wearing an undergarment.

After sipping water (ācamana), one should apply a tilaka made from clay from a sacred ford (tīrtha) and other substances, and perform the recitation (japa) of the Gāyatrī and other mantras according to one's capacity.
Thus it is said in the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa:
"Having put on a pair of clean white garments, being composed in mind..."
Having thoroughly cleansed the thighs and the shanks, as well as the hands, he should likewise wash them.
Having sipped water twice and sitting upon kusha grass, one should perform the recitation of the Sāvitrī; being self-restrained, one should also recite other meritorious hymns and mantras.
Thus concludes the ritual for emerging from the water. Next are the garments to be worn. Regarding this, Bhṛgu says:
The garment of a Brāhmaṇa is white; that of a king (Kṣatriya) is red and brilliant;
that of a Vaiśya is yellow; and for a Śūdra, blue is prescribed as being like soiled [garments].
‘Ulbaṇa’ means intensely red, and that is indeed a mineral-dyed [color].

For Uśanas has recorded a prohibition against wearing anything dyed with *kaṣāya* for rites dedicated to the gods or ancestors, stating: “One should not perform rites for the gods or ancestors while having a turban wrapped around one’s head, or while wearing garments dyed with dark *kaṣāya*.
It is the established rule that what is unwashed (*ahata*) and dyed with minerals is pure.
And because of his recollection of that [past] favor;
with this very intention, Gautama also said:
"One should not wear clothing that is dyed, ostentatious, or worn by another."
The characteristic of being unblemished has been explained in the section on clothing.
Regarding this, Devala states a specific rule:
"A wise man should perform his religious rites with a garment washed by himself;
never, however, with one washed by a washerman, nor ever with an unwashed one."
"Unbeaten" means unwashed; for the word "unbeaten" is used even in that sense, as stated by Satyatapas:
"The cloth released from the loom is called *hṛta* by the Self-existent One."
That is recommended for auspicious occasions, but only for that specific time, not at all times.
‘Māṅgalikya’ refers to marriage and similar auspicious rites.
In the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa:
“O Lord of Men, the garment used on the wedding bed should indeed be different.”
For one thing indeed is the conduct on the streets of the gods, another is that in worship;
yet another is that in worldly affairs, and quite different is that in the vision of the Lord.
Baudhāyana says:
An upper garment must be worn during these five activities:
the private recitation of the Veda, the ritual dismissal of the sacred fires, the giving of gifts, as well as after eating and when sipping water for purification.
"Utsarga" refers to the voiding of urine and so forth; "bhuktam" refers to eating. From the *Yogayājñavalkya*:
"Bathing, giving gifts, recitation, fire-offerings, Vedic study, and libations to the ancestors..."
A twice-born man should not perform the rites of honoring those who eat at a śrāddha while wearing only a single garment.
In the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa: "One should not engage in acts of giving, recitation, or burnt offerings, nor in ancestral rites, study,
or the ritual of reciting for Brahmins while wearing only a single garment."
"Dvijavācanaka" refers to the recitation for the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāhavācana*).
As stated in the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*:
"The fire-oblation, the worship of the gods, and likewise the recitation by the twice-born."
A twice-born man should not perform the rite of sipping water (ācamana) nor recite prayers (japa) while wearing only a single garment.
Gobhila says:

A man wearing only a single garment should not eat, nor should he perform the worship of the deities, nor should he honor the twice-born; indeed, a person in such a state should not perform any other [religious act].
He [the same author] states the definition of one who wears a single garment:
"One whose cloth is slipped from the left shoulder and worn around the waist—one should know him as a 'single-garmented' person; he is to be avoided at rites for the gods and the ancestors."

He is so described because his garment, which was draped over his left shoulder, has slipped down and is now held at the region of his waist. This should be understood to apply equally to one who is deprived of a second garment. Regarding this, the *Viṣṇupurāṇa* states the definition of a "naked" person: "One who is naked should not even contemplate Vedic or Smārta ritual acts."
Jātūkarṇya said:
During the private recitation of the Veda, in the muttering of prayers, as well as in giving gifts, performing fire-oblations, and worship—
likewise in rites for the gods and the ancestors— one should not bind up one's side of the waist.
If the sash is tied outside the lower garment, it is indeed demonic.
Regarding the wearing of the lower garment here, Pāraskara has shown the mantra:
"I shall put on [this garment] which bestows glory; for long life, may I reach old age; may I live a hundred autumns full of vigor; may I clothe myself in the nourishment of wealth.
The same applies to the upper garment as well.
"May Heaven and Earth grant me glory; may Indra and Bṛhaspati grant me glory; may Bhaga grant me glory; may glory come to me.

These two mantras are to be recited when putting on a new garment, because it has been stated by that same authority: "The mantra is used for a garment, an umbrella, and sandals, provided they are new."

Regarding this, Bhṛgu states what is to be avoided: "A wise man should avoid clothing that is red, excessively bright, or blue; he should also shun that which is less than ten days old, stained with dirt, or contemptible."
Jātūkarṇya says:
They know that according to dharma, an upper garment that is dyed, black, dirty, infested with hair, or has frayed edges is contemptible.
And this prohibition against wearing soiled garments applies when one has the means;
as Gautama says: "When wealth is available, one should not wear worn-out or dirty clothes."
Regarding this, Yogayājñavalkya states the secondary rule:
"In the absence of a washed cloth, one may use a garment of hemp, linen, or wool, or a *kutapa* blanket or a *yogapaṭṭa* band, by means of which one indeed becomes 'doubly clad' (*dvivāsas*)."
The word "should take" is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence]. A *kutapa* is a woolen blanket made from the hair of mountain goats.
Viśvāmitra also says:
"Two sacred threads (*yajñopavīta*) should be worn during rites prescribed by the Śruti and those prescribed by the Smṛti."
And in the absence of clothing, that third upper garment is prescribed.
Jātūkarṇya states the definition of the upper garment (*uttarīya*):
"In the absence of a cloth for an upper garment, one should make that upper garment circular by means of threads alone, measuring one, two, three, or four finger-breadths.
Thus ends the section on garments to be worn around the waist and those not so worn.
Now, the libation (tarpaṇa). Regarding its time and place, Śātātapa says:
"Thereafter, the twice-born Snātaka should perform the libation every day."
Yājñavalkya also says:
"Having bathed, one should likewise satisfy and worship the gods and the ancestors. Vyāsa [says]:
Sages of celebrated vows declare that libation (tarpaṇa) is of two kinds:
one should perform the first while standing in water, and the other while standing on land.
Viṣṇu states the distinction between these two:

"One who has bathed but whose clothes are still wet should perform the libations to the gods and ancestors while remaining in the water; and having stepped out onto the bank of the sacred site, one should do so wearing changed garments.
Hārīta also says:
One wearing wet clothes should perform libations, sipping of water, and recitation in the water;
one wearing dry clothes should perform libations, sipping of water, and recitation on land.

The remainder [of the sentence] is "standing in water. He states the fault incurred by transgressing the aforementioned rule: "Written down by one who is dry inside the water and likewise by one whose garment is wet even on the outside."
Bathing, giving, recitation, fire-offerings, and the libation to the ancestors become fruitless [if performed without this]. This is the Brāhma bath. Therefore Hārīta says:
"The Brāhma bath, as well as giving, and the libations to the deities and ancestors [are perfected by it]."
But one who performs [the rite] in the midst of water while wearing dry clothes incurs a great fault.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
A wise man, standing on dry land, should not perform the libation (tarpaṇa) while wearing wet clothes;
nor should he do so while standing in water reaching up to his knees, unless his bathing garment has slipped off.
Marīci: One should perform the libation (tarpaṇa) while standing in the water as an integral part of the bath;
however, for that which is other than the integral part of the bath, one should perform it at midday while on dry land.
After describing the procedure for recitation following the midday bath, Satyavrata states:
"Having performed the libations to the gods, sages, and ancestors according to this rule,
one should perform that which is prescribed by one's own Vedic school as a separate rite, indeed as a constituent part of the bath."
Vasiṣṭha also says:
One should mutter the mantras and Yajus formulas declared in the Ṛgveda, Sāmaveda, and Atharvaveda;
having thus performed the muttering, one should then perform the libations for the gods, sages, and ancestors.
As for that which was stated by Yogayājñavalkya:
"With one-pointed mind, on the bank [of a river], with palms joined, one should slowly recite the beginning of the Veda,
or likewise the Brahmavidyā, for the sake of accomplishing the Brahmayajña."
Or, having recited the Praṇava according to one's capacity, one should then perform the libation (tarpaṇa).

Thus, the immediate succession to the *brahmayajña* has been stated; that refers to the performance of the *brahmayajña* immediately after the morning oblation (*prātarāhuti*), since it is prescribed there as well. And so says Bṛhaspati: "It should be performed either before the libation (*tarpaṇa*), or after the morning oblation, or at the conclusion of the *vaiśvadeva* sacrifice; but not at any other time except on specific occasions."
Viṣṇu states that when one performs libations while standing on dry land, one should not pour the water of the libation into the midst of the water:
"If a man, standing on dry land, offers water into the water, that water does not reach the ancestors; it is useless for them."
Gobhila, speaking of the libation on dry land (*sthalatarpaṇa*),
says: "Neither in water nor in vessels, neither when angry nor with only one hand—
water that is not offered upon the ground does not reach [the ancestors]."
Therefore, the intention is that one standing on dry land should offer [the water] directly upon the ground. Śaṅkha also says: "One should never pour water into water for the sake of the ancestors."
"Having emerged [from the water], one should perform the libation of water (udakatarpaṇa) in a clean place.
Regarding this, Hārīta states a specific rule:
"Having put on a clean garment, [one should sit] upon a wide expanse of sacrificial grass (barhis) on dry land."
One who knows the ritual rules should perform the libation, but never into an ordinary vessel.
Or, having taken water from the vessel, one should pour it into another auspicious vessel,
or into a pit filled with water, but not onto dry ground devoid of grass.
And regarding this, the Grandfather (Brahmā) has stated: "The vessel for the libation to the ancestors should be made of gold, silver, copper, or bell-metal;
however, one should avoid a vessel made of clay."
The specific manner of spreading the sacrificial grass has been shown by Yogayājñavalkya:
"Having invoked [the deities] as before with the mantras, and having spread auspicious *kuśa* grass,
one should properly seat the gods upon those blades whose tips point eastward, and the ancestors upon those whose tips point southward."
The word "should satisfy" (*tarpayet*) is to be understood as the ellipsis.

Furthermore, regarding a place where [offering] is prohibited—such as by the rule "one should not satisfy the ancestors on a site built of bricks"—or which is impure, Viṣṇu states that one should offer [the water] in water:
"But where the place is impure, one should [offer] the deities and ancestors in water."
One should satisfy [the ancestors] at will with water, for everything is established in water.
However, when one performs the libation (tarpaṇa) while standing in the midst of water, one must not pour the libation water onto dry land. As it is stated in the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*:
"One standing in water should never perform the libation for the ancestors or the gods on dry land;
but one standing on land may do so even while in water, provided the land is impure."
Kārṣṇājini, however, states that the water-offering for those who died without the funeral rites (*asaṃskṛtapramīta*) must always be cast upon dry land:
"One should offer the water-offering to the deities and the ancestors in the water;
but for those who died without the funeral rites, one should again offer the water on land."
[919] Thus concludes the determination of the time and place for the libation (*tarpaṇa*). Now, the means for performing the libation.
Regarding this, Laugākṣi says:
"The libation for the ancestors should be performed with a sword or a pearl in hand;
never with a mere clean vessel, nor one joined with jewels or gold."
‘Khaḍga’ refers to the bone of a rhinoceros. ‘Śuddhena’ means by itself alone. From the *Yogayājñavalkya*: Gold worn on the ring finger and silver on the forefinger.
A man who holds a sword with his little finger shall thereby become purified.
Kātyāyana also says:
Having made the hand non-empty with gold, silver, kuśa grass,
gems, swords, and sesame seeds, one who is purified should perform the libation.
Śaṅkha also says:
"Without silver and gold, without copper and sesame seeds,
and without *darbha* grass and mantras, [the rite] for the ancestors is not accomplished."
Water with sesame seeds offered to the ancestors from a vessel made of gold, silver, or lotus, or from one of udumbara wood, becomes inexhaustible for them.
Whatever is given with snow, or with milk, or even with honey—
that water mixed with sesame seeds for the ancestors likewise attains imperishability.
'Hima' refers to camphor or sandalwood;
'marīci' refers to a ray of light.
[920] One may go mentally toward silver, but when it comes to gold, it must pass through the hand.
And in sesame seeds it takes a moment, but in copper it takes two muhūrtas.
That which is offered on Darbha grass during the seventh Muhūrta with the accompaniment of mantras becomes inexhaustible;
for wherever a person may be, whatever belongs to them shall attend upon them right there.
These statements do not have the purpose of enjoining a collection of gold and other items;
as he himself said:
"One should perform the rite with the hand joined by even one of these."
A wise person should perform the libation with either two, or three, or even all [of the verses].
Yājñavalkya also says:
"If even sesame seeds are unavailable, [one should sprinkle water] containing gold and silver;
in their absence, however, one should sprinkle with *darbha* grass or again with the mantra."
By this, the necessity of the mantra is established. For this very reason, Jābāli says:
"One should employ gold, silver, and *darbha* grass according to what is available."
The wise should never perform the libation rite (tarpaṇa) without a mantra.
Marīci said:
Just as a son finds his mother who has been lost among many cows,
so indeed that which was given by Manu to whomsoever remains established with him.
Yogayājñavalkya says:
One should offer libations in successive order with the names, the lineage, and the utterance of "svadhā";
water should be given with mantras, which increases the satisfaction of the ancestors.
Gautama said:
But even when kuśa grass is not available, one should perform the libation (tarpaṇa) by using kāśa or even dūrvā grass; one must never remain empty-handed.
Regarding this, Prajāpati states the specific rule:
"Whatever rites for the ancestors there may be, such as the libations (tarpaṇa) and others,
they should especially be performed with double-folded darbhā grass together with pavitra blades."
Bhṛgu says:
One should satisfy the gods with [blades of grass] pointing eastward, but the humans with those pointing northward;
having doubled those very same [blades], one should, being self-restrained, satisfy the ancestors.
The phrase "those very same" indicates that even those [materials] employed for the libation to the deities possess suitability for the libation to the ancestors.
Thus it is stated in the Gṛhyapariśiṣṭa:
"Darbha grass, the black antelope skin, the mantras, the Brāhmaṇas, the sacrificial oblation, and the fires."
These, being of undiminished potency, may be employed again and again.
Chāgaleya said:
Holding a small vessel in his hand, as well as a sword made of gold,
silver, or even copper, he should thereby satisfy the ancestors.

Śaṅkha says: One should offer water using a vessel made of gold, silver, udumbara wood, or even a sword-vessel; or one may use a *śaṅku* (a small rod), touching it at the *pitṛ-tīrtha* (the part of the hand sacred to the ancestors).
"Audumbara" means made of copper. "With a *śaṅku*" means with a small stick fashioned from gold or other materials.
Viṣṇu:
"One should perform the libation (tarpaṇa) for the gods with water mixed with barley, and for the ancestors with water mixed with sesame seeds"— this is the remainder of the statement.
In the Kūrma Purāṇa: "One should satisfy the gods and the Brahman-sages with water and unbroken grains (akṣata);
out of devotion to the ancestors, one should satisfy them with black sesame seeds according to the procedure prescribed in one's own Sūtra."
In the *Matsyapurāṇa*:
"One should satisfy the gods with barley, and humans such as Sanaka and others;
one should especially satisfy the ancestors, such as the Agniṣvātta-gaṇas, with black sesame seeds."
And [he should offer it] for himself and for all his ancestors, together with his friends and kinsmen.
Vṛddha-Manu says: Just as a righteous king proceeds accompanied by thousands of warriors,
so does water mixed with sesame seeds reach the deceased.

As for that which is stated in the Rāmāyaṇa: "O Trijaṭā, all of that [merit] belongs to you— washing the feet without anointing with oil, the libation (tarpaṇa) without sesame seeds, and whatever śrāddha is performed without a sacrificial fee."

Thus, even when sesame seeds are obtained, that statement intends [the performance of] libations deficient in them; otherwise, there would be a contradiction with such statements as "if even sesame seeds are not obtained. Gobhila says: "One should satisfy the gods with white [sesame seeds], and humans with variegated sesame seeds."
A twice-born man, however, should always satisfy the ancestors with black [sesame seeds] while performing the libation.
Regarding the specific rules for taking sesame seeds, Marīci says:
"One should give with an open hand and must not display a formal gesture (mudrā) there;
the sesame seeds are to be taken with the left hand, while the right hand remains open."

The *mudrā* is the joining of the tips of the forefinger and the thumb. This refers to the intention of offering libations with water that has not been drawn out [from the vessel]. And as it is said in the *Yogayājñavalkya*:
"If one pours out water that has been drawn out, one should mix sesame seeds into the water."
Otherwise, however, the wise should take up the sesame seeds with the left hand.
"Otherwise"— that is, when the water libation has not been performed—
Śālaṅkāyana states a specific rule for one who is standing in water:
"Having filled his arm with sesame seeds, one standing in water should offer libations to the ancestors."
One who desires the satisfaction of the ancestors should not perform [the rite] while standing on dry land.
And thus it was said by Gobhila:
"He who offers libations to the ancestors after placing sesame seeds upon his hair..."
By that blood and by that impurity, the ancestors were gratified.

Thus, it should be understood that this refers to the context of libations performed on dry land (*sthalatarpaṇa*). However, when one who is standing on dry land performs the libation with water that has not been drawn up, then the libation should be performed by placing sesame seeds upon a hairless part of the left hand or upon a cloth.
Regarding this, Kārṣṇājini says:
"Having placed the sesame seeds upon the hair [of the arm], one should offer libations to the ancestors and the deities."
Having placed them on the ground, whether in water or even upon a cloth.
Regarding the libation with sesame seeds (*tilatarpaṇa*), Marīci states an exception in certain cases:
"On the seventh lunar day, on a Sunday, at home, and likewise on one's birthday,
one who desires servants, sons, and a wife should not perform the libation with sesame seeds."
O King, on both fortnights, during the seventh lunar day and at the junctions of night and day,
one who desires knowledge, sons, or a wife should avoid eating sesame seeds on these five occasions.
On the seventh lunar day, one should not consume neem, apply sesame oil as an unguent, use sesame seeds for libations or collyrium, nor eat from a copper vessel.
In the Kālikā Purāṇa: "Water used for the libation of sesame seeds on the thirteenth day of the sun or Venus, on the seventh day, or at the junctions of night and day, is declared to be blood."
Kauṇḍilya states that there is a prohibition against the libation with sesame seeds for a specific category of qualified persons:
"One whose father is living should not perform the Darśa-śrāddha, the Gayā-śrāddha, the śrāddha of the dark fortnight, nor the libation with sesame seeds."
Thus end the means for the libation (tarpaṇa). Now, regarding the number of añjali-offerings,
Vyāsa says on this matter:
The gods deserve one handful each; Sanaka and the others, two each;
the ancestors, three each; but women, only one handful each.
Satyatapas said:
One should cause the deities, ancestors, humans, and others— who are enjoined by the rules of one's own Vedic branch—
to pronounce their satisfaction with a single handful [of water] each, using the nominative case ending.
In the Viṣṇu Purāṇa:
"One should offer water three times for the gratification of the gods;
likewise for the sages according to the rule, or even once for Prajāpati."
O Lord of the Earth, one should drink water three times for the purpose of pleasing the ancestors.
‘Apavarjayet’ means one should give. In the Kūrma Purāṇa:
“For all the deities, however, one handful (añjali) each is prescribed.”
For sages there should be only one [guardian], for humans likewise two;
for the ancestors there are three times three, but for women there is indeed only one each.
In the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa:
"The wise man, satisfying the gods, should offer two handfuls;
for the sages and humans, he should cause [the offering] to be given only once."
One should offer [the water] three times each for the paternal ancestors, but only once for women;
twice each for the maternal grandfathers, and likewise once for maternal uncles,
as well as once for the guru, the preceptor, fathers-in-law, friends, and kinsmen.
Baudhāyana says: Three handfuls of water should be offered for those others who have been consecrated on earth;
for those who died unconsecrated, one [handful] alone should be cast into the pit.

In this regard, the specific arrangement should be understood according to one's own Vedic school (*śākhā*). However, for those belonging to schools where [the names] are not recited, there is an option (*vikalpa*).
Thus ends the enumeration of the *añjali* offerings. Now follows the sequence of the group of those to be gratified (*tarpaṇīya*).
In this regard, Chāgaleya says:
"Thereafter, one should constantly gratify the gods and the hosts of gods, as well as the sages and the hosts of sages, and the ancestors and the hosts of ancestors."
Śātātapa says: [One should offer] to the gods, the sages, and the ancestors in due order.
Vasiṣṭha also [says the same].

The wise man should, in due order, satisfy the gods, the sages, and human beings; the host of living beings, both moving and stationary; the Vasus, the Rudras, and likewise the Ādityas; then the hosts of ancestors, as well as his own deceased kin.
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*:
"First, being well-composed, one should gratify the gods, beginning with Brahmā;
thereafter, the wise man should fully satisfy the sages, headed by Marīci."
Immediately thereafter, he [created] the Vasus, Rudras, and Ādityas in due order,
as well as the Yakṣas, Paśus, Suparṇas, and the fourfold host of beings.
He likewise [taught] the teachers, the others, and even the divisions of time;
and immediately thereafter, the humans headed by Sanaka.
Then he should offer to Kavyavāla, Nala, and the other groups of ancestors (pitṛgaṇas);
thereafter, he should give to his own paternal ancestors, followed by his maternal ancestors;
then to his maternal grandfathers, and after that, to his paternal uncles.
Then [he should offer] to his wives, his sons, his father’s sister,
his mother’s sister, his maternal aunt, his daughter, his own sister, as well as to his teacher and the officiating priest.
Disciples, kinsmen, friends, and relatives—
these must be gratified in the proper manner and in their respective order.
Then, one should offer a handful [of water] intended for both those who are known and those who are unknown;
thereafter, a separate handful should be offered for those who have died without having received the funeral rites.
Whoever performs the libation for the gods and others in this sequence, by that act they shall be satisfied with nectar; of this there is no doubt.
In the Skanda Purāṇa: [927] First, one should satisfy the six Vināyakas, beginning with Moda and Pramoda;
thereafter, O high-minded one, the gods beginning with Brahmā are to be offered libations.
And thereafter, being purified, one should perform the satiation of Sanaka and the others.
Then, one should perform the satiation for the ancestors, beginning with the Agniṣvāttas and others in their proper order,
and thereafter offer it to Yama Dharmarāja.
Then [he offers] for the fathers, then for the mothers, then for the maternal grandfather,
then for the wives, fathers-in-law, kinsmen, and the relatives of one's sons.
In the Nāradīya Purāṇa:
"O King, the gods beginning with Agni should first be gratified;
thereafter, the sages of celebrated vows beginning with Śatarcins."
Then, endowed with faith, one should satisfy all the Kāṇḍarṣis;
and one should likewise satisfy the human ancestors (manuṣya-pitṛs) in the same order as before.
Satyavrata said:
First, one's own ancestors should be gratified with libations, and afterwards one should gratify others;
one should offer [water] to the paternal ancestors every day, and likewise to the maternal ancestors.
Then [he offered] for his maternal grandfathers, and for his paternal uncle's son.
After the libation to the ancestors and others, Yājñavalkya states:
"Thereafter, one should perform the libation for friends, relatives, and kinsmen."
Yama says: Having first performed the water-rites for the sapindas and kinsmen,
one should then offer handfuls of water to the groups of friends and relatives.

Having performed the water-libation (*udakatarpaṇa*) for as many ancestors on the paternal side as one can name up to the seventh generation, one should perform it for the gurus. Having performed it for the gurus, one should perform it for those on the maternal side. Having performed it for those on the maternal side, one should perform it for their relatives and kinsmen. Having performed it for them, one should perform it for friends.
This is the sequence of the group to be offered libations.
Now, the rules regarding the hand-purification (*hastatīrtha*), the sacred thread (*upavīta*), the knees, and the directions:
In this regard, Yama says:
Having joined the two hands together, one should fill them with a handful of water;
having drawn up water to the height of a cow's horn, one should pour it into the midst of the water.
As for that which was stated by Vyāghra:
"He who offers water with both hands goes to the Kālasūtra hell, headlong, as a fool."
This refers to the subject of *śrāddha* and similar rites.
And so says Kārṣṇājini:
"At a *śrāddha* and at the time of a wedding, [the gift] is given with one hand."
"But the libation (tarpaṇa) shall not be performed in this manner; such is the ancient rule. For this very reason, it is stated in the *Bhaviṣyat-purāṇa*:
"Then, having respectfully joined the palms with both hands..."
One should satisfy the gods, the sages, human beings, and the ancestors.
In the *Matsyapurāṇa*:
"Having filled both hands with water to form an *añjali*,
one who is pure should perform the libation (*tarpaṇa*) for the gods and the ancestors."
Regarding this, Yogayājñavalkya states the specific detail:
"Then, facing the Aparājita direction (the northeast), with both hands having the thumbs enclosed,
or indeed with the left hand supporting [the right]."
"One should pour water"—this is the ellipsis. In the *Vāyupurāṇa*:
"Then, with both hands, one should satisfy the ancestors and the gods."
Or again, with the right hand itself joined by the left hand as an assistant.
Vasiṣṭha states: "One may perform the libation for the gods and ancestors with one hand, or with both hands beginning with the left. This is also stated in the Kūrma Purāṇa.
With his left hand grasped by the right,
the wise man should gratify the divine seers with handfuls of water, and the ancestors with libations of water.
There is an option between grasping [the hand] with the right hand or with both hands joined in añjali.
In the Viṣṇupurāṇa: "Wearing clean garments and having bathed, one should perform the libation for the gods, sages, and ancestors."
For one should perform [the rite] with great concentration at the very same bathing place (tīrtha) as theirs.

"For them"—that is, for the gods and the others; and thus it is stated that the satiation (tarpaṇa) of the gods should be performed with the *devatīrtha*, that of the sages (*ṛṣis*) with the *prajāpatitīrtha*, and that of the ancestors (*pitṛs*) with the *pitṛtīrtha*.
As stated in the *Narasiṃhapurāṇa*:
"One should always perform the satiation of the gods with the *devatīrtha*."
[930] Of all men, beginning with Sanaka, and even of the sages (ṛṣis) in every respect.
Being pure and endowed with faith, one should sprinkle water using the *prājāpatya* [tīrtha];
the wise should perform the libation for the ancestors using the *pitṛtīrtha*. A man who performs the libation otherwise becomes joined with sin.
In the Agni Purāṇa:
"The propitiation of the gods is prescribed to be performed with the Daiva-tīrtha;
one should propitiate the sons of Brahmā with the Prājāpatya-tīrtha."
For the libation to the ancestors should likewise be performed with the part of the hand sacred to them.
Viṣṇu states: "At the very outset, one should perform the libation for the gods with the divine *tīrtha*, and for the ancestors with the ancestral *tīrtha*.
The definition of a *tīrtha* has been stated by Yogayājñavalkya.
Five sacred fords reside in the right hand of a Brahmin:
the Brāhma, the Daiva, the Pitrya, the Prājāpatya, and the Saumika.
The Brāhma [tīrtha] is at the base of the thumb, the Daiva at the tips of the fingers;
the Prājāpatya is at the roots [of the fingers], and the Saumya is established in the middle.
The region between the thumb and the forefinger is proclaimed as the ancestral (pitrya) path;
knowing this, the twice-born are indeed not deluded in any ritual actions.
But by Hārīta:

The *āgneya* [tīrtha] is said to be in the middle. The line to the north of the thumb is the *brāhma* tīrtha; behind the little finger is the *prājāpatya*; the tips of the fingers are the *daiva*; between the thumb and the forefinger is the *pitrya*; and the middle is the *āgneya*. One should sip water with the *brāhma* tīrtha after sneezing, spitting, yawning, eating, licking, voiding urine or excrement, dropping a tooth, speaking with a Śūdra who has been left over from a meal, when desiring to approach a deity, or when about to study. One should perform the sowing of seeds, oblations, and libations with the *prājāpatya* tīrtha; cleansing, worship, the offering of bali, and eating with the *daiva*; rites for the ancestors with the *pitrya*; and receiving gifts with the *āgneya*.
In the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa: "A wise man should perform the rite of offering rice-balls (piṇḍa) and water for the Nāndīmukhas by means of the Prājāpatya tīrtha, and whatever [is offered] to Prajāpati."
Jamadagni says:
Wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (yajñopavītī), one should offer handfuls of water to the gods;
but wearing it around the neck (nivītī), one should perform the libation for humans with due care.
Wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (prācīnāvīta), he should offer water to the ancestors.

Bharadvāja states the definition of the sacrificial thread (*yajñopavīta*) and other such characteristics: "Raising the right arm and placing [the thread] over the left shoulder is called the *yajñopavīta*; it is prescribed for rites dedicated to the gods."
When the sacred thread (brahmasūtra) is positioned over the left shoulder and under the right arm, it is known as the *nivīta* position; this is prescribed for human rites.
When the left arm is raised and rests upon the right shoulder, they call this the *prācīnāvīta* mode; it is used specifically for rites pertaining to the ancestors.
Satyavrata says:
Having performed the upavīta, one should then become nivītī for the gods;
one should then satisfy humans with devotion, as well as the sons of Brahmā and the ṛṣis.
Then, having bent the left knee to the ground, he should perform the rite with the sacred thread over the right shoulder;

holding *darbha* grass in his hand, he should then satisfy the deceased ancestors according to the rule by name and lineage, beginning with the paternal ancestors and then the maternal grandfathers as well.
Pulastya said:
Having placed his right knee on the ground and using *kuśa* grass with its tips pointing eastward,
the twice-born man should daily gratify the gods with a mind purified by faith.
Having touched his left knee with double-folded kuśa grass,
he should devoutly satisfy the ancestors with his mind fixed upon them, while meditating on them.
Gobhila says:
While gratifying the deity, the wise man should place his right knee upon the ground;
likewise, the discerning man should place his left knee when [gratifying] the ancestors.
While performing the libation for humans, one should not let anything fall upon the knees.
Sumantu said:
Having placed the right knee down on the ground, one should perform the libation for the gods;
likewise, having placed the left knee down, one should perform the libation for the ancestors.
In the *Brahmavaivarta*: "Facing the eastern direction, upon *kuśa* grass with its tips pointing east,
the knower of dharma, being self-restrained, should offer water libations (*apohiṣṭhā*) intended for the gods."
Facing the northern direction and upon sacrificial grass with its tips pointing north,
he should constantly offer handfuls of water for the satisfaction of human beings.
Facing the south and standing upon kuśa grass with its tips pointing toward the south,
one should, with a joyful mind, offer water to the ancestors for their satisfaction.
Viśvāmitra says:
Then, with both hands, facing a direction that is not defeated [by obstacles],
one should take up water and properly satisfy the sages and the gods.
Then, looking toward the southeastern or the southern direction,
a man should offer three handfuls of water each, dedicated to his ancestors.
In the *Nandipurāṇa*:
"The libation for the thirty gods should be performed facing the eastern direction;
then, one should offer libations to the sons of Brahmā facing the northeast or the north."
In the southern direction, however, the libation to the ancestors (pitṛtarpaṇa) should be performed.

Thus [end] the rules regarding the hand-tīrtha, the sacred thread, the knees, and the directions. Now follows the description of the individual deities and others to be propitiated with libations (tarpaṇa). In the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa:
First, wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (upavītī), one should satisfy the gods and the Vināyakas:
Moda, Pramoda, Sumukha, Durmukha,
Avighna, and Vighnakartṛ— these are the six Vināyakas.
The *Yogayājñavalkya* states:
One should first satiate Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Prajāpati;
then the gods, the meters, the Vedas, and the sages whose wealth is austerity.
The Ācāryas and the Gandharvas, as well as the Ācāryāṇīs;
likewise, for a year including its fractions, the divine Apsarases.
Likewise, [he saw] the gods, the followers of the gods, the nāgas, the oceans, and even the mountains;
as well as the rivers, humans, yakṣas, and indeed rākṣasas.
And the Piśācas, the Suparṇas, the Bhūtas, as well as the animals,
the trees, the medicinal herbs, and the fourfold collection of living beings.
[934] Śaunaka also said:

Agni, Viṣṇu, Prajāpati, Brahmā, the Vedas, the Ṛṣis, all the meters, the syllable Oṃ, the Vaṣaṭ-call, the Vyāhṛtis, the Sāvitrī, the sacrifice, Heaven and Earth, the intermediate space, days and nights, numbers, the Siddhas, the oceans, the rivers, the mountains, fields, herbs, trees, Gandharvas, Apsarases, Nāgas, birds, cows, the Sādhyas, Brahmins, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, spirits—and likewise others; the Ṛṣis: the Śatarcins, Mādhyamas, Gṛtsamada, Viśvāmitra, Vāmadeva, Atri, Bharadvāja, Vasiṣṭha, the Pragāthas, the Pāvamānyas, the Kṣudrasūktas, and the Mahāsūktas; [and] wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītī): Sumantu, Jaimini, Vaiśampāyana, Paila, the Sūtras, the Bhāṣyas, the Mahābhārata...

"May the teachers of dharma of the Mahābhārata—Bāhavi, Gārgya, Gautama, Śākalya, Vābhravya, Māṇḍavya, Māṇḍūkeya; Gārgī Vācaknavī, Vaḍavā, Prāvītheyī, Sulabhā, Maitreyī; Kahola Kauṣītaki, Mahākauṣītaki, Yogya, Mahāyogya, Suyajña Sāṅkhyāyana, Aitareya, Mahaitareya, Bāṣkala, Gārya, Sujāta, Bakrāma, Audavāhi, Mahaudavāhi, Saujāmi, Śaunaka, Āśvalāyana, and whatever other teachers there may be—all of them be satisfied. [This is repeated] for each individual. Thus says Paiṭhinasi.
Then Gautama, Bharadvāja, and likewise Viśvāmitra;
Jamadagni, Vasiṣṭha, Kaśyapa, and likewise Atri.
Svārociṣa, Uttama, Tāmasa, Raivata,
the highly resplendent Cākṣuṣa, and likewise Vaivasvata are to be gratified.

Thus, wearing the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), facing east, with his right knee bent, upon *kuśa* grass blades pointing eastward, he should satisfy the gods and the seers (*ṛṣis*) with water mixed with white sesame seeds or barley, using the "divine" (*devatīrtha*) part of the hand and *kuśa* blades pointing eastward. Then, wearing the thread around the neck (*nivīta*), facing north or toward the northeast, upon *kuśa* grass blades pointing northward, he should satisfy Sanaka and the others, as well as Marīci and the others, with water mixed with variegated sesame seeds or barley, using the middle of the *kuśa* blades and the "Prajāpati-tīrtha" part of the hand.
Regarding this, Saṃvarta says:
Then, having arranged the sacrificial thread around the neck (nivīta) and facing north,
one should separately satisfy the human beings using the prājāpatya tīrtha.
Having thus gratified the gods and the sages with devotion, he should then,
wearing the sacred thread around his neck (nivītī), gratify human beings, the sons of Brahmā, and the ṛṣis.
Sanaka, Sananda, and the third, Sanātana; Kapila, Āsuri, Voḍhu, and likewise Pañcaśikha—
these seven sons of Brahmā are celebrated as human beings.
Marīci, Atri, Aṅgiras, Pulastya,
Pulaha, Kratu, Pracetas, Vasiṣṭha, Bhṛgu, and Nārada—
one should satisfy these divine brahmin-sages with water and unbroken grains (akṣata).

Then, wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*), facing south, with his left knee bent and resting upon *kuśa* grass whose tips point toward the south, he should begin the libation for the ancestors (*pitṛtarpaṇa*) with water mixed with *kuśa* and sesame seeds, using the *pitṛ-tīrtha* (the part of the hand between the thumb and forefinger) and double-folded *kuśa* blades.
Thus says Yogayājñavalkya:
"Having invoked [the ancestors] with mantras as before, and having spread out auspicious *kuśa* grass..."
Then, having touched his left knee with both hands, he faces the south.
Likewise, one should satisfy all the hosts of ancestors with mantras containing their respective marks;
wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītī), one should pour out water mixed with sesame seeds.
Likewise: Kavyavāhana, Nala, Soma, Yama, Aryaman,
as well as the Agniṣvātta Pitṛs, the Somapas, and the Barhiṣad Pitṛs.
If one whose father is still living should [perform this], he should likewise offer these divine ancestors,
or he should cause the offerings to be given to those to whom his own father would give them.

A twice-born man whose father has died should offer salutations accompanied by the *svadhā* exclamation to these [ancestors] and those who will be mentioned hereafter— the Vasus, the Rudras, and the Ādityas.
These are the fathers of all, and upon them depend human beings;
and the teacher [honors] his own fathers, beginning with the paternal ancestors by name.

If one whose father is living should perform the libation (*tarpaṇa*), then after the libations to the gods, sages, and humans, he should complete the rite by offering libations to the eight divine ancestors beginning with Kavyavāla. Or else, he may perform the libation for those same [ancestors] for whom his father would offer it. However, one whose father is deceased should offer libations to these aforementioned ones—Kavyavāla and the rest—as well as to the Vasus, Rudras, Ādityas, and his own father and grandfather. Regarding the libation to the ancestors, Paiṭhīnasi states:

"Then, having placed the sacred thread over the right shoulder and standing facing the direction of the ancestors (the south), one should satisfy the divine and non-divine ancestors with the *pitṛ-tīrtha* [of the hand].
Here, "divine" refers to the Vasus and others; "non-divine" refers to one's own father and other ancestors.
And those divine ones were revealed by him:
Dhruva, Adhvara, Soma, Āpa, Anala, Nala, Pratyūṣa,
and Prabhāsa— these are proclaimed as the eight Vasus.
Ajaikapād, Ahirbudhnya, Virūpākṣa, and Raivata;
Hara, Bahurūpa, and Tryambaka, the lord of the gods.
Sāvitra, Jayanta, Pinākin, and Aparājita—
these are declared to be the eleven Rudras, the most excellent of the gods.
Indra, Dhātṛ, Bhaga, Pūṣan, Mitra, Varuṇa,
Aryaman, Atri, Vivasvat, Tvaṣṭṛ, Savitṛ, and Viṣṇu.
"These twelve Ādityas are indeed considered the foremost among the gods;
they are the divine ancestors (Pitṛs) who must be worshipped by all with great effort. Thus says Jaimini.
Having gratified the divine ancestors, one should then gratify one's own ancestors. Jābāli says:
Then, standing facing south and meditating upon one’s own ancestors and the others...
Then he should satisfy his mother and the others, as well as the groups of his maternal grandfathers.
He should gratify his teachers, paternal uncles, kinsmen, and others;
as well as friends, relations, other patrons, disciples, and officiating priests.
Thus concludes the individual identification of the deities to be propitiated. Now follows the procedure for the libation (*tarpaṇa*).
Yogayājñavalkya says:
With the left hand held in support, one should sprinkle water with the right hand,
saying "May [they] be satisfied," using the name preceded by the syllable Om.

Since the activity of the one to be gratified is perceived in the expression "tṛpyatām" (let [he/they] be gratified), it is appropriate that the nominative case alone be used for the expressed agent (*abhihite kartari*). Thus, he has demonstrated the following usage: having pronounced the name ending in the nominative case, such as *praṇava*, etc., one should say "tṛpyatām" at its end.
However, Jānūkarṇya has also demonstrated the usage with the *parasmaipada* (active voice):
"tṛpyatu" or likewise "tṛpyatām."
One who knows the ritual procedure should pour water for the gods and all others without exception.
"Of the gods and others" means of the celestial sages (*devarṣi*), humans, and ancestors (*pitṛ*).
Kātyāyana, however, has stated that the verbal form ending in the word *uttamapuruṣa* (the first person) should be employed.
Then one should satisfy the gods with water and the ancestors with water mixed with sesame seeds.
Uttering "Om" at the beginning and saying "I satiate" at the end of each name.
In the Kūrma Purāṇa:
"Then he should satiate the gods, the ancestors, and the hosts of sages,
having first uttered the syllable Om, and at the end [of each name] saying, 'I satiate you, Oṃ namaḥ.'"

Regarding the phrase "I satiate" (*tarpayāmi*), since that which is to be satiated is connected as the object of the action, one should pronounce the name of the deity—beginning with *oṃ*—in the accusative case, and then utter "I satiate, obeisance" (*tarpayāmi namaḥ*) at the end. Thus, it is stated that the formula should be performed either in the singular, such as: *oṃ brahmā tṛpyatām*, *oṃ brahmā tṛpyatu*, or *oṃ brahmāṇaṃ tarpayāmi namaḥ*; or in the plural, such as: *oṃ vedās tṛpyantām*, *oṃ vedās tṛpyantu*, or *oṃ vedāṃs tarpayāmi namaḥ*. In this matter, the application is determined according to one's own Vedic school (*śākhā*).

In this regard, Kaśyapa states a specific rule for the satiation of the Vasus and others: "One should always satisfy the Vasus, Rudras, and Ādityas with water, accompanied by salutations and their names preceded by the syllable Om."
Having gratified King Yama, one should proclaim a salutation.

In this regard, the author of the *Smṛticandrikā* and others have shown the formula as: *oṃ dhruvāya namaḥ*. Others, however, for the sake of completing the sentence, state the formula as: *oṃ dhruvaṃ tarpayāmi namaḥ*. Therefore, one’s own traditional practice (*svācāra*) should be followed. But in the libation to Yama, because the scriptural injunction [939] prescribes the recitation of the name ending in the dative case and followed by *namaḥ*, only formulas such as *oṃ yamāya namaḥ* and so forth are to be employed. Thus says Chāgaleya: "Reciting 'to Yama, to Dharmarāja'..."

"By satisfying Yama with water, one does not see hell at all. Regarding this, some say: "Oṃ, obeisance to Yama; I satisfy Yama. However, by Ṛṣyaśṛṅga, even the use of a word ending in the middle person (the second person) was demonstrated in the libation to the ancestors (*pitṛtarpaṇa*).
One should offer salutations with joined palms to the ancestors and others while reciting the mantras according to the rule, saying "Be satisfied" three times; and likewise to the maternal ancestors.

The meaning is that one should offer three handfuls of water for each individual person, as indicated by the phrase "let the mantras be recited" (*mantrān udīratām*) and so forth, which will be mentioned later, and by the word "thrice" (*triḥ*).
And thus says Paiṭhīnasi:
"For each individual person, there should be the utterance of their name and lineage."
One should cast three handfuls of sesame-water upwards, again and again, with increasing intensity.

From the father’s *añjali*s [of water], the grandfather’s *añjali*s should be offered with the words "ucair ucaiḥ" while raising the hands slightly higher; from those as well, the great-grandfather’s *añjali*s—thus it is explained in the section on bathing. Yājñavalkya says:
"One should pour water according to the rule through the *pitṛtīrtha* on the right side."
One should take [the water] with the right hand alone, near the *pitṛtīrtha*.
Water should be offered to those of the same caste and even to those of different castes; one should satisfy them in due order with their lineage names, personal names, and the utterance of "svadhā."
Baudhāyana also states a distinction regarding the inclusion of the name and so forth:
"It is prescribed that the name of a Brāhmaṇa should end in *śarman*, that of a Kṣatriya in *varman*,
that of a Vaiśya in *gupta*, and that of one born as a Śūdra in *dāsa*."
For all four castes, the ancestors belong to the father’s *gotra*;
for unmarried daughters, the *gotra* remains that of the father, while for those who have been married, it becomes the *gotra* of the husband.
In this context, the recitation of the relationship must also be performed,
because of the traditional teaching of Bhṛgu: "One should recite the names of the lineage, the relationship, and the father during the ancestral rites."
In this context, the plural number is used for the gurus to express reverence in accordance with established custom, while the singular number is used for the younger relatives and the wives.

The formula should be employed as follows: "Oṃ, I satiate my ancestors of such-and-such lineage, named so-and-so, with *svadhā* and obeisance (*namaḥ*). Or alternatively, the formula should be performed as: "Oṃ, may our ancestors of such-and-such lineage, named so-and-so, be satiated with *svadhā*. In the case of younger relatives (or friends), however, the formula is: "I satiate my friend of such-and-such lineage, named so-and-so, with *svadhā* and obeisance. Or alternatively, the formula is: "Oṃ, may our friend of such-and-such lineage, named so-and-so, be satiated with *svadhā*. Regarding this, Paiṭhīnasi says:

Having sprinkled himself with purificatory waters and sipped water, he should pour out water for the Vasus, for Brahmā, and for Vaiśravaṇa. Then, with the three mantras beginning with "udīratām," he should pour out three handfuls of water while pronouncing the names of his paternal lineage, as well as those of the teacher, the mother, the maternal grandfather, and the maternal uncles.
As Yogayājñavalkya says:
"Water should be offered with mantras that increase the satisfaction of the ancestors."
And those mantras were shown by him himself: "May the Aṅgirases rise up," "May they come," and also "Strength," "To the ancestors," and the three-verse hymn beginning with "The winds are sweet.
Meditating upon the ancestors, he should indeed pour [the water] while reciting these mantras in sequence;
then, with palms joined and body bowed, he should say three times, "Be satisfied."

The meaning of this is as follows: At the conclusion of the mantra *udīratām*, one should offer the first handful of sesame seeds (*tilāñjali*) while reciting the formula: "O our fathers of such-and-such lineage (*gotra*), named such-and-such Śarman, may you be satisfied; *svadhā*! Then, at the conclusion of the mantra *aṅgirasena*, one should offer the second handful, uttering the same formula. Then, with the mantra *āyantu naḥ*, one should offer the third in the same manner. In this way, one should offer three handfuls to the father. Then, at the conclusion of the mantra *ūrjaṃ vahantīḥ*, one should offer the first handful to the grandfather, reciting: "Oṃ, O our grandfathers of such-and-such lineage, named such-and-such Śarman, may you be satisfied; *svadhā*! The second is offered in the same manner with the formula *pitṛbhyaḥ svadhā*. The third is offered in the same manner with the formula *ye ceha pitaraḥ*. In this way, one should offer three handfuls to the grandfather. Then, at the conclusion of the mantra *madhuvātā*, one should offer the first handful to the great-grandfather, reciting: "Oṃ, O our great-grandfathers of such-and-such lineage, named such-and-such Śarman, may you be satisfied; *svadhā*! The second is offered in the same manner with the mantra *madhunaktam*. The third is offered in the same manner with the mantra *madhumān naḥ*. In this way, one should offer three handfuls to the great-grandfather. At this point, one should first perform the libation (*tarpaṇa*) for the mother and others, and then for the maternal grandfather and others.
First, the father and others are to be satiated, and then the mother and others as well;
thereafter, the maternal grandfather and the maternal grandmother, and after that, the rest.
Thus, according to the Smṛti of Vyāsa:

"Oṃ, O our mothers, belonging to such-and-such gotra and named such-and-such, be satisfied; svadhā!"—thus to the mother. "O our paternal grandmothers, belonging to such-and-such gotra and named such-and-such, be satisfied; svadhā!"—thus to the paternal grandmother. "O our paternal great-grandmothers, belonging to such-and-such gotra and named such-and-such, be satisfied; svadhā!"—thus to the paternal great-grandmother. In this manner, one should offer a single añjali to each of the mothers and others, using their names alone accompanied by the utterance of *svadhā*.
And likewise, immediately after the injunction regarding the mantras for the father, maternal grandfather, and others, Yājñavalkya says:
"The mother, the mother’s sister, the maternal aunt, the father’s sister, the daughter,
the sister, the pupil, the officiating priest, the kinsmen, and the relatives—
these should be gratified in their proper order with the utterance of 'svadhā' using their names. Thus it is said.

Immediately thereafter, at the end of the mantra "namo vaḥ," one should offer three handfuls of water to the maternal grandfathers (*mātāmaha*) as follows: first, "Oṃ, may our maternal grandfathers of such-and-such lineage, named so-and-so Śarman, be satisfied; *svadhā*! In the same manner, one should offer the second and third handfuls. Thus, one should offer three handfuls for each of the maternal grandfathers. In exactly the same way, one should offer three handfuls each for the great-grandmother's father (*pramātāmaha*) and the great-great-grandmother's father (*vṛddhapramātāmaha*). As for the mantra, "namo vaḥ" alone is repeated again and again. And thus says Yogayājñavalkya:
"Having recited 'namo vaḥ,' one should likewise [offer] to the maternal grandfathers."
One who relies upon the supreme dharma should satisfy them for the sake of compassion.

Then, having uttered the ritual formula (prayoga) for the mother, one offering of water with joined palms (añjali) should be given for each of the maternal grandmothers and others.
