After that, having performed the libations for the wives, the satiation (tarpaṇa) of the paternal uncles and others should be performed following the satiation of the maternal grandmothers.
This is stated in the Garuḍa Purāṇa:
"Then [the libation] for the maternal grandmothers, and immediately after for one's own wives."
And then the libation for paternal uncles, and also for their wives.
One should always [offer] to the father’s sister and her husband, as well as to the maternal uncle;
then to the maternal aunt, the mother’s sister, and her husband.
One should perform the libation for one's father-in-law and also for one's mothers-in-law;
thereafter, one should perform it for one's teachers and for the wives of one's teachers as well.
[He should visit] the kinsmen, the wives of brothers, as well as the son and the daughter-in-law;
likewise the daughter, her husband, the sister, and her husband.
Having satisfied his sister's son, his grandson, his daughter's son, his sacrificial patron, his officiating priest, his pupil, and his friend, as well as their wives in the same manner;
He should also give to others to whom he wishes to give;
having established himself in the supreme dharma, he should offer a single handful of water to each of all his maternal grandmothers and the rest, especially at a sacred bathing place (tīrtha).
In the Vārāha Purāṇa, Dvaipāyana declared: "One who is intent on that, remembering it with the mind, should offer water separately for the deceased; one should also offer water for oneself."
Regarding this, Kātyāyana speaks of the final añjali:

"I satisfy those belonging to my father’s lineage, those belonging to my mother’s lineage, and whoever else deserves water from me"—with these words, one should offer the final handful of sesame seeds.
This is also stated in the Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa.
Wherever they may reside, for those whose selves are afflicted by hunger and thirst,
may this water with sesame seeds offered to them be inexhaustible.
For those in my family whose funeral offerings have been interrupted, and who are bereft of sons and wives—
may this water mixed with sesame seeds, now offered, be for them inexhaustible.
"May that which is given to those who have died in the maternal lineage, and likewise in the paternal lineage, be indeed inexhaustible for them; let this water with sesame seeds be so.
Having uttered this, one should then offer a handful of water into the water. Thus it is said.

One should also offer another handful of water called *kāmodaka*; this is stated in the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*: "O King, having performed the libations for the gods and others, one who desires to benefit all beings should also murmur this mantra and offer water according to one's own wish."
The gods, asuras, yakṣas, gandharvas, uragas, and rākṣasas;
the piśācas, guhyakas, siddhas, kūṣmāṇḍas, trees, and birds.
May all creatures— those that dwell in water, those that live on land, and those that depend on the air—
quickly attain complete satisfaction through this water given by me.
To those who have gone to all the hells and to the various torments,
this water is offered by me solely for their refreshment.
"May those who have no kin, or those who were kin in another birth, and whoever desires [offerings] from us—may they all attain complete satisfaction. Thus it is said.
However, one who is unable to perform the rite in detail should perform the libation (tarpaṇa) in brief according to the method prescribed in the *Matsyapurāṇa*.
Gods, yakṣas, as well as nāgas, gandharvas, apsarases, and asuras;
serpents, cruel beings, suparṇas, trees, jṛmbhakas, and birds.
Those beings who have the wind as their support, those who have water as their support, likewise those who move through space,
those who are without support, and those who are devoted to the Dharma.
Having thus performed the *upavīta* rite and given [the offerings], one should then become *nivītī*.
Sanaka, Sananda, and the third, Sanātana;
May Kapila, Āsuri, Voḍhu, and Pañcaśikha—
may they all attain complete satisfaction through the water offered by me.
I satisfy with unbroken grains and water Marīci, Atri, Aṅgiras, Pulastya,
Pulaha, Kratu, Prācetasa, Vasiṣṭha, Bhṛgu, and Nārada,
as well as all the divine and brahminical ṛṣis.
Then, having placed the sacred thread over the right shoulder and bending the left knee to the ground,
[he should address] the Agniṣvātta, Saumya, Haviṣmat, and Uṣmapa [ancestors].

I satisfy with devotion the Vikālins, the Barhiṣads, and others who move at will, using water mixed with sandalwood and sesame seeds. Then, with darbha grass in hand, one should satisfy the deceased (pretas) according to the prescribed rite.
In the Viṣṇupurāṇa, the extremely concise libation (saṃkṣepatarpaṇa) is described: "Saying,
'May the world, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, be satisfied,' one should offer three handfuls of water while performing the concise libation."

At this juncture, the wringing out of the bathing garment should be performed. Thus says Vasiṣṭha: "Having thus completed the libation to the ancestors on the bank of the reservoir, one should wring out the bathing garment while standing on dry land, facing south."
Therefore, at the midday bath, having performed the *tarpaṇa* as a limb of the bath while standing in the water, one should emerge, wring out the garment, and perform the *ācamana*.
However, the wringing out of the garment should be done after the *tarpaṇa* on dry land.
This has been stated in the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*:
Then, having bathed according to the prescribed rule and having offered libations to the ancestors and the gods,
he should emerge from the body of water and, with a concentrated mind, perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) twice.
The bathing cloth should not be wrung out until after the libations on dry land have been performed;
having performed the libations even on dry land, one may then wring out the cloth.
Thereafter, having touched water twice, one should present the *arghya* offering to Sūrya;
then one should perform the worship of the deities—this is the midday ritual procedure.

Yogayājñavalkya states: Some maintain that the squeezing out of the water from the bathing garment should be done first, prior to the libations for the gods and ancestors; therefore, one should not squeeze it until after those [offerings].
Like the preparation of food, he should wring out that garment with his left hand. Having wrung it out, having sipped water, being restrained and pure,
he should perform the worship of the gods, beginning with Brahmā, free from envy.
Regarding this, Bṛhaspati states the specific rule:
"Having washed his feet and hands, he himself should perform the sipping of water (ācamana) twice.
[946] Śaṅkha declares the fruit for one who acts in this manner:
Having bathed and performed the libation for the ancestors with water mixed with sesame seeds,
one attains the world of the ancestors and likewise gratifies them.
Manu, Śātātapa, and Yogayājñavalkya state:
"Whatever fruit a supreme twice-born man obtains by performing the water-libation for the ancestors after bathing,
by that alone he attains the entire fruit of the performance of the ancestral sacrifice (pitṛyajña)."
In this regard, Yama says in the verses of the ancestors:
"May there be someone born in our lineage who would offer us handfuls of water,
especially in rivers that abound with cool waters."
In this regard, Viṣṇu says:
"May that being be born in our lineage who shall offer us handfuls of water,
especially in rivers abounding in cool waters."
The fault incurred by failing to perform the libation (*tarpaṇa*) is stated in the *Brahmavaivarta*:
"He who does not offer libations to the deities, the sages, and the ancestors,
becomes a debtor to the gods and others and goes down to hell."
Hārīta says: One should not step across a flowing river in vain; for thus said the Grandfather (Brahmā):
"Both the gods and the ancestors look toward the river."
But when they receive nothing, they depart as they came, filled with despair.
Parāśara and Śātātapa state:
"The deities and the highly fortunate ancestors follow a Brāhmaṇa who comes to bathe, having become like the wind and seeking water."
When the water was not granted, they departed in despair after having uttered a curse.
Kātyāyana also says: Just as one afflicted by the summer heat might desire shade,
one thirsty for water, or one hungry for food;
The fool [sees] the mother as the progenitor and the progenitor as the mother;
the woman [sees] the man as the male, and the man [sees] the woman as the female.
Likewise, all beings, both stationary and moving,
desiring prosperity, seek water from the Brahmin.
Therefore, a Brahmin must always perform his duties; by failing to do so, he becomes joined with great sin, for by performing them, he indeed sustains this entire universe.
In the Kūrma Purāṇa it is said:
"The twice-born who thus gratifies all beings every day shall go to the supreme abode, a form of radiant energy, free from all affliction."
Thus concludes the procedure for the libation (*tarpaṇa*). Now, regarding the libation to Yama and Bhīṣma, it is stated therein in the *Skanda Purāṇa*:
When the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight coincides with a Tuesday,
one should bathe in auspicious water and offer libations while reciting the names of Yama.
Regarding this, Vṛddha-Manu says:
"Having reached any river whatsoever on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight—
especially the Yamunā— a Brāhmaṇa with his senses restrained [should perform the rite]."
To Yama, the King of Dharma, to Death, to the Ender,
to Vaivasvata, to Time, and to the Destroyer of all beings.
Salutations indeed to Audumbara, Dadhna, Nīla, Parameṣṭhin,
Vṛkodara, Citra, and Citragupta.
Having thus gratified the god Yama with these name-mantras, beginning with *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending with *namaḥ*, one is liberated from all sins.
In this case, the formula is: *oṃ yamāya namaḥ*.
Regarding this, Vṛddhamanu states the specific rule:
"Having prepared three handfuls of water mixed with sesame seeds for each [deity]."
Whatever evil has been committed throughout one's entire life perishes at that very moment.

In the Padma Purāṇa: Because Yama is his father, the wise man should satisfy him with sesame seeds while facing south using the *apasavya* method; because he is also a deity, he should satisfy him using the *daivatīrtha* (the part of the hand sacred to the gods).
Vyāsa says: On the thirteenth or fourteenth day of the dark fortnight,
[one should offer] to Yama, Dharmarāja, Mṛtyu, and Antaka.
To Vaivasvata Kāla, and to the destroyer of all beings.
With these seven names, which are mantras of salutation, one should offer seven handfuls of water; thus one is liberated from all sins. Yama says:
Having offered seven handfuls of water on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight...
By dedicating it to Dharmarāja, one is liberated from all sins.
At the time when the sun has not yet risen, on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Māgha,
one who bathes and offers libations to Yama is liberated from all sins.
Indeed, by bathing in any river whatsoever on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight and offering libations to Dharmarāja, one is liberated from all sins.
Manu states the fruit for one who acts in this way:
"Whatever sin has been committed in this life and whatever has been committed in other lives,
one dispels that by offering libations on the fourteenth day of the month of Aṅgāraka."
Likewise, they record the libation for Bhīṣma in the Mahābhārata on the eighth day of the bright fortnight of Māgha:
"Whoever offers water to Bhīṣma on the eighth day of the bright fortnight of Māgha,
his sin committed throughout the year perishes at that very moment."
In this regard, the mantra is as follows: "To Bhīṣma, who belongs to the Vaiyāghrapada gotra, the Sāṅkṛtya pravara, and is the son of Gaṅgā, I shall offer water with sesame seeds."
"I give this water for the sake of the protection of Bhīṣma, who is without a son.
Thus is the libation for Yama-Bhīṣma.
Next is the libation as taught by Baudhāyana.

Purified by the five *brahmayajñas*, he satisfies the deities in the waters with water itself, in ascending order: "I satisfy Agni, Prajāpati, Soma, Rudra, Aditi, Bṛhaspati, and the Sarpas—these deities of the eastern gate, together with the constellations, the planets, the days and nights, and the muhūrtas. "I satisfy the Vasus; I satisfy the Pitṛs, Aryaman, Bhaga, Savitṛ, Tvaṣṭṛ, Vāyu, Indra, and Agni—these deities of the southern gate, together with the constellations, the planets, the days and nights, and the muhūrtas. "I satisfy Mitra, Indra, the Mahāpitṛs, the Āpas, the Viśvedevas, Brahmā, and Viṣṇu—these deities of the western gate, together with the constellations, the planets, the days and nights, and the muhūrtas. "I satisfy the Ādityas; I satisfy the Vasus; I satisfy Varuṇa; I satisfy Prajāpati; I satisfy Parameṣṭhin; I satisfy Caturmukha; I satisfy Hiraṇyagarbha; I satisfy the male attendants of Brahmā; I satisfy the female attendants of Brahmā. "Oṃ bhūḥ, I satisfy Puruṣa; Oṃ bhuvaḥ, I satisfy Puruṣa; Oṃ svaḥ, I satisfy Puruṣa; Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ, I satisfy Puruṣa. Oṃ bhūḥ, I satisfy; Oṃ bhuvaḥ, I satisfy; Oṃ svaḥ, I satisfy; Oṃ mahaḥ, I satisfy; Oṃ janaḥ, I satisfy; Oṃ tapaḥ, I satisfy; Oṃ satyam, I satisfy. Oṃ, I satisfy the god Bhava; Oṃ, I satisfy the god Śarva; Oṃ, I satisfy the god Īśāna; Oṃ, I satisfy the god Paśupati; Oṃ, I satisfy the god Rudra; Oṃ, I satisfy the god Ugra; Oṃ, I satisfy the god Bhīma; Oṃ, I satisfy the god Mahān. Oṃ, I satisfy the wife of the god Bhava; Oṃ, I satisfy the wife of the god Īśāna; Oṃ, I satisfy the wife of the god Paśupati; Oṃ, I satisfy the wife of the god Rudra; Oṃ, I satisfy the wife of the god Ugra; Oṃ, I satisfy the wife of the god Bhīma; Oṃ, I satisfy the wife of the god Mahān. Oṃ, I satisfy the son of the god Bhava; Oṃ, I satisfy the son of the god Śarva; Oṃ, I satisfy the son of the god Īśāna; Oṃ, I satisfy the son of the god Paśupati; Oṃ, I satisfy the son of the god Rudra; Oṃ, I satisfy the son of the god Ugra; Oṃ, I satisfy the son of the god Bhīma; Oṃ, I satisfy the son of the god Mahān. Oṃ, I satisfy the Rudras; Oṃ, I satisfy the male attendants of the Rudras; Oṃ, I satisfy the female attendants of the Rudras. "Oṃ, I satisfy Vināyaka; Oṃ, I satisfy Vīra; Oṃ, I satisfy Śūla; Oṃ, I satisfy Ugra; Oṃ, I satisfy Varada; Oṃ, I satisfy Hastimukha; Oṃ, I satisfy Ekadaṃṣṭra; Oṃ, I satisfy Lambodara; Oṃ, I satisfy the male attendants of Vighna; Oṃ, I satisfy the female attendants of Vighna. "Oṃ, I satisfy Sanatkumāra; Oṃ, I satisfy Skanda; Oṃ, I satisfy Indra; Oṃ, I satisfy Ṣaṣṭhī; Oṃ, I satisfy Ṣaṇmukha; Oṃ, I satisfy Viśākha; Oṃ, I satisfy Subrahmaṇya; Oṃ, I satisfy Mahāsena; Oṃ, I satisfy the male attendants of Skanda; Oṃ, I satisfy the female attendants of Skanda. "Oṃ, I satisfy Nārāyaṇa; Oṃ, I satisfy Mādhava; Oṃ, I satisfy Govinda; Oṃ, I satisfy Viṣṇu; Oṃ, I satisfy Madhusūdana; Oṃ, I satisfy Trivikrama; Oṃ, I satisfy Vāmana; Oṃ, I satisfy Śrīdhara; Oṃ, I satisfy Hṛṣīkeśa; Oṃ, I satisfy Padmanābha; Oṃ, I satisfy Dāmodara; Oṃ, I satisfy the goddess Śrī; Oṃ, I satisfy Sarasvatī; Oṃ, I satisfy Puṣṭi; Oṃ, I satisfy Garuḍa; Oṃ, I satisfy the male attendants of Viṣṇu; Oṃ, I satisfy the female attendants of Viṣṇu. "Oṃ, I satisfy Yama; Oṃ, I satisfy Yamarāja; Oṃ, I satisfy Dharmarāja; Oṃ, I satisfy Kāla; Oṃ, I satisfy Nīla; Oṃ, I satisfy Mṛtyu; Oṃ, I satisfy Citragupta; Oṃ, I satisfy Vaivasvata; Oṃ, I satisfy the male attendants of Vaivasvata; Oṃ, I satisfy the female attendants of Vaivasvata. "Oṃ, I satisfy Bhūmideva; Oṃ, I satisfy Kāśyapa; Oṃ, I satisfy Vidyā; Oṃ, I satisfy Dhanvantari; Oṃ, I satisfy the male attendants of Dhanvantari; Oṃ, I satisfy the female attendants of Dhanvantari."
Then [he is] wearing the sacred thread around his neck.

Oṃ, I satisfy the Ṛṣis. Oṃ, I satisfy the Mahārṣis. Oṃ, I satisfy the Paramarṣis. [952] Oṃ, I satisfy the Brahmarṣis. Oṃ, I satisfy the Devarṣis. Oṃ, I satisfy the Rājarṣis. Oṃ, I satisfy the Śrutarṣis. Oṃ, I satisfy the Taparṣis. Oṃ, I satisfy the Satyarṣis. Oṃ, I satisfy the Saptarṣis. Oṃ, I satisfy the Kāṇḍarṣis. Oṃ, I satisfy the Ṛṣikās. Oṃ, I satisfy the wives of the Ṛṣis. Oṃ, I satisfy the sons. Oṃ, I satisfy Kāṇḍa Baudhāyana. Oṃ, I satisfy Āpastamba, the author of the Sūtras. Oṃ, I satisfy Satyāṣāḍha. Oṃ, I satisfy Hiraṇyakeśin. Oṃ, I satisfy Dhyāna. Oṃ, I satisfy the Praṇava. Oṃ, I satisfy the Vyāhṛtis. Oṃ, I satisfy Sāvitrī. Oṃ, I satisfy Gāyatrī. Oṃ, I satisfy the Vedic meters (Chandas). Oṃ, I satisfy the Ṛgveda. Oṃ, I satisfy the Yajurveda. Oṃ, I satisfy the Sāmaveda. Oṃ, I satisfy the Atharvaveda. Oṃ, I satisfy the Atharvāṅgirasa. Oṃ, I satisfy the Itihāsas and Purāṇas. Oṃ, I satisfy all those born of the Vedas. Oṃ, I satisfy all beings. 32.
Then, on the south side, wearing the sacrificial cord over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītī).

I satiate the fathers with *svadhā* and obeisance; I satiate the grandfathers with *svadhā* and obeisance; I satiate the great-grandfathers with *svadhā* and obeisance. I satiate the mothers with *svadhā* and obeisance; I satiate the grandmothers with *svadhā* and obeisance; I satiate the great-grandmothers with *svadhā* and obeisance. I satiate the maternal grandfathers with *svadhā* and obeisance; I satiate the maternal grandfathers' fathers with *svadhā* and obeisance; I satiate the maternal grandfathers' great-grandfathers with *svadhā* and obeisance. I satiate the maternal grandmothers with *svadhā* and obeisance; I satiate the maternal grandfathers' mothers with *svadhā* and obeisance; I satiate the maternal grandfathers' great-grandmothers with *svadhā* and obeisance. I satiate the teachers with *svadhā* and obeisance; I satiate the teachers' wives with *svadhā* and obeisance. I satiate the gurus with *svadhā* and obeisance; I satiate the gurus' wives with *svadhā* and obeisance. I satiate the friends with *svadhā* and obeisance; I satiate the friends' wives with *svadhā* and obeisance. I satiate the kinsmen with *svadhā* and obeisance; I satiate the kinsmen's wives with *svadhā* and obeisance. I satiate the ministers with *svadhā* and obeisance; I satiate the ministers' wives with *svadhā* and obeisance. I satiate all with *svadhā* and obeisance; I satiate all their wives with *svadhā* and obeisance. Having thus crossed over, he sprinkles water, saying: "Carrying strength, carrying immortality, clarified butter, milk, sweet drink, and flowing nectar—you are *svadhā*; satiate my fathers; be satisfied, be satisfied. One should not perform rites for the gods or rites for the ancestors while wearing wet clothes or a single garment; so say some.
Thus ends the libation as taught by Baudhāyana. Now follows the libation as taught by Śaṅkha:
Having bathed and performed his silent prayers (japa), with his hands between his knees and facing north, he should satisfy the gods with water using the divine *tīrtha*.
Now follows the procedure for the libation (tarpaṇa).

"I satisfy the Blessed One; I satisfy the remainder"—these two phrases, "I satisfy" (*tarpayāmi*), are written at the beginning and the end, not in the middle, because they would otherwise be redundant; this is how it should be understood. The seven netherworlds (*pātāla*) are: Kālāgnirudra, Śvetavarāha, Ajita, Rukmabhauma, Śailabhauma, Nīlabhauma, Raktabhauma, Pītabhauma, Śvetabhauma, and Kṛṣṇabhauma. The seven continents (*dvīpa*) are: Jambūdvīpa, Śākadvīpa, Kuśadvīpa, Krauñcadvīpa, Śālmalidvīpa, Gomeda, Puṣkaradvīpa, and Plakṣadvīpa. The world-protectors (*lokapāla*) who endure for a *kalpa* are: the mountain named Lokāloka, Sudhāman, Śaṅkhapada, Ketumān, and Hiraṇyaroman. The seven oceans are: Lavaṇa, Kṣīroda, Dadhyoda, Ghṛtodaka, Surodaka, Ikṣurasodaka, and Svādūdaka. There is also the group of four seas (*sāgara*). The great mountains are: Śṛṅgavān, Śveta, Nīla, Meru, Mālyavān, Gandhamādana, Niṣadha, Hemakūṭa, and Himavat. The seven principal mountain ranges (*kulaparvata*) are: Mahendra, Malaya, Sahya, Śuktimān, Ṛkṣavān, Vindhya, and Pāriyātra. And all the mountains headed by Kailāsa and Maināka; the lakes headed by Bindusaras; the Gaṅgā with its seven streams flowing through the three worlds; the Śatadrū; and the seven Sarasvatīs. The Yamunā; the first Puṣkara, the second Puṣkara, and the third Puṣkara; Prayāga, Naimiṣa, Hayaśīrṣa, and all holy bathing places (*tīrtha*), all springs, and all rivers; the lake, the sacred ford, the lordly trees headed by the Aśvattha, the medicinal herbs headed by barley; the mountain named Mānasottara; and the world-protectors: Indra, Śacī, the thunderbolt (*vajra*), Airāvata, Mātali, and the Gandharvas headed by Citrasena; the Apsarases: the Apsarases named Pramudā, Pṛṣṭā, Āyu, Stāvā, Bhekurī, and Ūrjā; Agni, Sānta, Svāhā, Sānta, Agnīdhra, Yama, Dharma, Priya, Satya, Tapa, Sānta, the sacrificial fee (*yajñadakṣiṇā*), Initiation (*dīkṣā*), Celibacy (*brahmacarya*), Resolve (*vyavasāya*), Dharmarāja, Daṇḍapiṅgala, and his weapon, the noose; Heaven, Death, Citragupta, the servants of Yama, Śyāma and Śabala, Virūpākṣa, Nirṛti, and those preeminent in Dharma. The Daityas, Dānavas, Vidyādharas, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, Piśācas, Diseases, Fever, the Lord of Diseases, Health, Varuṇa, Gaurī, the Nāgas, Vāsuki, Ananta, the Serpents, the lordly trees, the Winds, and all the vital breaths—Prāṇa, Apāna, Samāna, Udāna, and Vyāna—the sense organs, the objects of the senses, and the individual soul (*jīva*). Soma, the constellations, the current constellation, the Pitṛs: the Abhāsvaras, Barhiṣads, Agniṣvāttas, Kravyādas, Upahūtas, Ājyapas, Sukālins; Mahādeva, Pārvatī, Senānī, Skanda, Viśākha, the Skanda-grahas, the child-seizers (*bālahā*), the mother-seizers (*mātṛgraha*), the attendants of Skanda, the female attendants of Skanda, the Bhūtas, the Earth-Rudras, the Intermediate-Rudras, the Heavenly-Rudras, the Assembled-Rudras, the Mothers, the Yogīśvarīs, the wives of the gods, the mothers of the gods, the Gaṇas, and the lords of wealth. Vināyaka, Mitra, Saṃmita, Sānta, Śāla, Saṅkaṭa, Kūṣmāṇḍa, Rājaputra, Dharma, Artha, Kāma, Gati, Prīti, Nidrā, Kṣudh, Aditi, Āyati, Niyati, Kīrti, Prajñā, Vṛtti, Medhā, Ākṛti, Ruci, Śraddhā, Vāṇī, Sarasvatī, Ṛkṣa, the daughters of Dakṣa, Progeny, Prajāpati, Sanaka, Sanātana, Sanatkumāra, Kratu, the Pitṛs, the Brahmarṣis, Devarṣis, Rājarṣis, and the Ṛṣikas; the wives of the Ṛṣis and the sons of the Ṛṣis; Gāyatrī, Uṣṇih, Anuṣṭubh, Paṅkti, Jagatī, and all the meters; Garuḍa, Aruṇa, Havya, Jāta, Surabhi, the midday, the Cow, Uccaiḥśravas, Dhanvantari, the world-serpents, the directional serpents, the family serpents, Viśvakarman, Vaiśravaṇa, Ṛddhi, Nala, Kubera, Revanta, Śaṅkha and Padma, Bahuputra, his wife, and their progeny; Kaśyapa, his wife, and their progeny; Dhanada, his wife, and their progeny; Prajāpati, his wife, and their progeny; Candra, his wife, and their progeny; Ariṣṭanemi, his wife, and their progeny; Kṛśānu, his wife, and their progeny; weapons, treatises, and missiles. The Ṛgveda, Yajurveda, Sāmaveda, Atharvaveda, the Itihāsas, the Purāṇa, the Dhanurveda, Gāndharvaveda, Āyurveda, Phalaveda, Jyotiṣa, Śikṣā, Kalpa, Vyākaraṇa, Nirukta, Chandas, the Dharmaśāstras, the Mahābhārata, Manu, Viṣṇu, Yama, Aṅgiras, Vasiṣṭha, Nārada, Dakṣa, Saṃvarta, Śātātapa, Parāśara, Āśvalāyana, Auśanasa, Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana, Kātyāyana, Bṛhaspati, Gautama, Śaṅkha, Likhita, Hārīta, Atri, Yājñavalkya; and then the Blessed Dharma, Uttānapāda, Yajña, Nārāyaṇa, the Nāsatyas, Varuṇa and Aryaman, the Year, Mitra, Indra and Agni, Marīci and Kaśyapa, Dhruva, Agastya, Dhātṛ, Mārtaṇḍa, Rāma, Vālmīki, the Kalpa, the Mahākalpa, the current Manvantara, the powerful Indra, Svāyaṃbhuva, Svāroci
Oṃ! One light, two lights, three lights, four lights; the one Śakra.

Dviśakra, Triśakra, Īdṛśa, Anyādṛśa, Śānta, Prīta, Prītasadṛśa, Mita, Saṃmita, Asita, Ṛtajit, Satyajit, Suṣeṇa, Senajit, Atimitra, Amitra, Puruṣamitra, Ṛta, Satya, Dhartā, Vidhartā, Varuṇa, Ghṛta, Vidhāraya, Īdṛkṣa, Etādṛkṣa, Asita, Sita, Prītina, Prītisadṛkṣa, Sakṣarasama, Atidhartā, Ugra, Dhuni, Bhīma, Abhiyukta, Ṛkṣapāda, Saham, Dyuti, Vasu, Anādhṛṣya, Vāsa, Kāmajaya, Vijaya, Jaya—these are the forty-nine Maruts. Bhuvana, Bhāvana, Ajanya, Sudhājana, Kratu, Vasu, Mūrdhā, Vāja, Vyasruva, Prasrava, Āpyāyana, and Ṛkṣāmat—these are the twelve Bhṛgus. Manu, Mantṛ, Prāṇa, Apāna, Citi, Naya, Rūpa, Haṃsa, Nara, Nārāyaṇa, Vibhu, and Prabhu—these are the twelve Sādhyas. Savitṛ, Dhātṛ, Mitra, Aryaman, Pūṣan, Aṃśu, Tvaṣṭṛ, Vivasvat, Indra, Viṣṇu, Varuṇa, and Bhaga—these are the twelve Ādityas. Aṅgāraka, Sūrya, Nirṛti, Sakha, Ajaikapād, Ahirbudhnya, Dhūmaketu, Baha, Mṛtyu, Kapālin, and Hara—these are the eleven Rudras. Ātmā, Apa, Sama, Ṛkṣa, Vṛma, Prāṇa, Haviṣmant, Gariṣṭha, Ṛta, and Satya—these are the twelve Aṅgirases. Kratu, Dakṣa, Vasu, Satya, Kāma, Dhuri, Kāla, Rācana, Purūravas, and Ārdravasa—these are the ten Viśvedevas. Dhara, Dhruva, Soma, Āpa, Anala, Anila, Pratyūṣa, and Prabhāsa—these are the eight Vasus. Nāsatya and Dasra are the two Aśvins. I satisfy these nine groups of gods along with their followers, the Self-born (Svayaṃbhū), Sāvitrī, all the gods, the goddess Satī, Lakṣmī, Carī (?), Aniruddha, Pradyumna, Saṅkarṣaṇa, Vāsudeva, the Bhūrloka, Bhuvarloka, Svarloka, Maharloka, Janaloka, Tapoloka, Satyaloka, the Cosmic Egg (Brahmāṇḍa), Earth, Water, Fire, Wind, Ether, Mind, Intellect, the Seat (Āsana), the Unmanifest (Avyakta), and the Puruṣa. Thus the word "I satisfy" (tarpayāmi) is employed at the end. One should offer handfuls of water and flowers with devotion while reciting the Puruṣasūkta, which exceeds the Ṛgveda verses. Then, having placed the sacred thread over the right shoulder (apasavya), facing south, with the knee resting on the ground, one should offer water to the ancestors according to one's faith and according to the light available, using the ancestral (pitrya) part of the hand.
Thus ends the libation (tarpaṇa) as declared by Śaṅkha.
Now, the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) is described.

Since all rites must be preceded by ācamana, and because it is mandatory for those engaged in a rite to perform it even when occasions such as sneezing arise, there is a need for those performing a śrāddha to know the rules for ācamana. Regarding this, Mārkaṇḍeya states that all rites are preceded by ācamana:
Having sipped water properly, one who is pure should diligently perform the rites for the deities, the seers, and the ancestors.
The fault incurred by performing a ritual action without having sipped water (ācamana) is stated in the *Brahma Purāṇa*:
"If an atheist performs a ritual out of delusion without having sipped water, all his actions indeed become futile; of this there is no doubt."
Regarding the occasions for sipping water (ācamana), Manu says:
"Having voided urine or feces, one who has touched the bodily apertures should sip water;
likewise when about to study the Veda, and always when eating food."

Because the root *kṛ* has multiple meanings, "having done" (*kṛtvā*) is understood here as "having discharged. Having discharged urine and feces, and having washed the anus and genitals, one should touch the "apertures"—the sense organs—after having sipped water according to the prescribed rule. The phrase "about to study the Veda" implies that one should not utter the syllables of the Veda without having sipped water after performing other worldly activities. "Eating food" means about to consume food.
[This is taught by] Manu, Aṅgiras, and Bṛhaspati:
"After sleeping, sneezing, eating, spitting, and speaking untruths..."
Having drunk water, and also when about to recite sacred texts, one should sip water for purification, even if one is already pure.

"Having slept," having lain down; "having sneezed," having made a sneeze; "having eaten," having taken food; "having spat," having discharged phlegm from the mouth; "untruth," falsehood; "having drunk water," having swallowed water—the term *prayataḥ* (pure/ready) is connected only with the word *adhyeṣyamāṇaḥ* (about to study). The meaning is that even one who is already pure, when about to study, should perform *ācamana* (ritual sipping of water), for *ācamana* is an ancillary part of the injunction for study. —Viṣṇu.

Having sneezed, slept, eaten, or desired to eat or study; having drunk, bathed, spat, or changed one's clothes; having stepped onto a road, or after voiding urine or feces; having touched the bone of a five-toed animal or its fat; and upon conversing with a *caṇḍāla* or a *mleccha*, one should sip water for purification (*ācamana*). Śaṅkha says: "Having voided urine or feces, or likewise when desiring to eat, one should bathe."
Having eaten, having sneezed, likewise after sleeping, drinking water, bathing,
walking upon a carriage road, and changing one's clothes, one should sip water for purification.

Āpastamba: Having voided urine or feces, or having washed away the remnants of urine, feces, or food, as well as the smears of semen, and having washed his feet and sipped water (ācamana), he becomes pure. Following the rule for sipping water, Devala says:
When there is the discharge of feces, urine, or excrement, or during eating and exhaustion from travel, this kind of purification is prescribed; however, other forms also exist to some extent.
I shall now describe the specific rules of purification regarding eating and shaving; for the general procedure of sipping water (ācamana) has already been indicated as applicable everywhere.
Having touched a person who has food remnants on them, or likewise such food,
one becomes pure by washing both hands and feet and performing the ritual sipping of water (ācamana).
Likewise:
Water that, when used for purification, reaches the ground and perishes there,
or water that has washed something smeared with impurity— one who touches it becomes pure by sipping water (ācamana).

Regarding the sipping of water (ācamana) which is about to be described, Hārīta states: "Having walked upon a road, or being about to sleep, or having voided urine or excrement, or having eaten"— "about to sleep" meaning intending to sleep.
Bṛhaspati states: "Upon the emission of downward wind (flatus), upon shouting, upon the arising of anger,
upon touching a cat or a mouse, upon laughing, and upon speaking untruths..."
On these occasions, one should perform the ritual sipping of water while performing an action for the sake of dharma.
"Upasparśana" means sipping water (ācamana). In the Kūrma Purāṇa:
"Upon conversing with a Caṇḍāla or a Mleccha, or upon speaking with a woman or a Śūdra while they are left-over from their meal..."
Having touched a person who is impure from food remnants, or likewise food of that same nature, one should sip water;
and likewise when tears are shed, or in the case of blood.
Upon touching fire, or cows, or indeed an impure person;
or upon touching women, or oneself, or having adjusted the waist-knot (nīvī); |||

By the word *nīvī*, the lower garment (*adhovāsa*) is indicated here due to its association; for the knotting of the lower garment is indeed the *nīvī*. Āpastamba states: "Upon dreaming, sneezing, blowing one's nose, touching blood, hair, fire, cows, a Brāhmaṇa, or a woman; upon walking on a high road, touching something impure, or touching an unclean person—one should touch water, or put on the *nīvī* (the lower garment), or touch wet cow-dung, herbs, or the earth."
‘Kṣavathuḥ’ means sneezing. ‘Siṅghāṇikā’ is nasal mucus. ‘Aśru’ is tears. The word ‘ārdram’ (moist) is connected with all [the items] beginning with feces. ‘Śakṛt’ means cow dung. Baudhāyana says:
“Having loosened the waist-knot and put on [another garment], one should sip water; or one should touch moist grass, the ground, or cow dung.”

Or he may touch [his ear]. However, touching moist grass and the like should be understood as applicable only when rinsing with water (ācamana) is somehow impossible; otherwise, it would result in an improper option between unequal injunctions. This being the case, when rinsing with water is possible, touching the right ear is not an alternative. As it is stated in the *Yama Purāṇa*:
Upon seeing a Caṇḍāla or others during the recitation of mantras or the fire sacrifice, the best of the twice-born should sip water;
likewise, upon seeing a dog or similar animals, he should touch his right ear.
While performing rituals such as *japa* and *homa*, or upon seeing a Caṇḍāla or a dog, one should perform *ācamana* (ritual sipping of water) or touch the right ear. Furthermore, Vasiṣṭha states:
"Upon sneezing, spitting, sleeping, putting on a garment, or shedding tears..."
Or, among these five, one may touch the tongue, the ear, or the right shoulder.
Thus, as Parāśara has stated with its explanatory supplement:
"Upon sneezing, spitting, when something is stuck to the teeth, likewise upon speaking untruth,
or conversing with those who have fallen from their status, one should touch the right ear."
Manu declared that the sacred fords beginning with Prabhāsa, as well as the rivers beginning with the Gaṅgā,
reside within the right ear of a Brāhmaṇa.
Āditya, Varuṇa, Soma, Vahni, and likewise Vāyu—
these deities always abide in the right ear of the Brahmin.
Thus, this should be understood to apply when even the touching of moist grass and the like—which is prescribed for those unable to perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana)—is impossible.
As it is stated in the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa:
"In the event of sneezing and so forth, one should properly sip water or touch moist grass and the like."
Or one may perform the touching of the right ear.
"For this [is to be done] according to one's means; if the former is not obtained, then the latter.
When the former is available, the attainment of the latter is not desired.
Thus Baudhāyana says that when a cause for impurity has arisen, one should immediately strive for purification as far as possible.
"One should not remain impure even for a moment regarding the domain of the *śakti*.
Āpastamba also says:

"Raising his empty hands toward water, he should touch water; regarding the domain of the *śakti*, he should not remain impure even for a moment. Nor [should he remain impure] while naked, nor is there a requirement for purification for one who is already in the water; rather, having emerged, he should sip water (*ācamet*)."

"Empty-handed" (*riktapāṇiḥ*) means with hands devoid of a water-vessel. "Having exerted oneself for water" (*payase udyamya*) means having made an effort for the sake of water. However, one who is standing in water should, even when the occasion for *ācamana* has arrived, step out of the water before performing the *ācamana*. He states the reason for this: "For one remaining in water" (*apsu sataḥ*), that is, for one staying in water while performing *ācamana*, "the first purification" (*prathamanaṃ*)—namely, purification through exertion (*prayatatā*)—does not exist. Hārīta says, following the word "water": "One should not cross over [a body of water] without having touched [it]."
Yama says: Having emerged from the water and sipped water for purification, one should touch water again after descending [into it].
In this way, one becomes endowed with excellence, and Varuṇa is indeed honored.
Having first sipped water, one should enter the water; thereafter, even after emerging from the water, one should again sip water.
Dakṣa:
Immediately after bathing, the ritual sipping of water (upasparśana) is prescribed. Prajāpati: [Agrees].

At the commencement of a distinguished ritual act, even though one is already purified, one should sip water (*ācāmet*); this is the understood remainder [of the injunction]. Thus it is stated in the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*.

Having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) properly, one should perform the rites such as the worship of the gods, as well as the salutation of the guru; likewise, one should perform the act of eating.

Regarding the section on the water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*), Vasiṣṭha states: "Having performed the necessary duties, one who is most skilled in purification should sip water (*ācāmet*). "Necessary duties" refers to the obligatory rites (*nitya-karmāṇi*).
Hārīta: One desiring to approach the deity should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana).
[From] the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa.
In all cases of doubt, as well as when loosening the topknot,
one should always perform the ritual sipping of water (upaspṛśet) without the sacred thread (yajñopavīta).
Śātātapa says:
One should always rinse the mouth after chewing food, except when chewing betel;
likewise after touching the lips when they are hairy, and after changing one's garment.
Āpastamba states:
"One should touch the lips as far as their dark edges.
The phrase "as far as their dark edges" means starting from the roots of the teeth up to the dark line situated near the beard.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
If one who holds an object in his hand is touched by something defiled by leavings, he should set the object down,
perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), sprinkle the object with water, and then take it up again.

By the word *ucchiṣṭa* (remnant) here, a person who is characterized by impurity requiring sipping of water (*ācamana*) is denoted; or else, it refers here merely to a substance remaining after eating that is fit for consumption. And so Vasiṣṭha says:
"If, while moving among things fit for consumption, one should touch what is *ucchiṣṭa*..."
Having cast that object upon the ground and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), one should proceed once more.
‘Pracaran’ means while serving [food]; ‘among the foods to be consumed’ (abhyavahāryeṣu) refers to food and drink, with the understood sense being “when they have been taken in hand.
Bṛhaspati also says:
“While serving food and drink, if one should touch that which is leavings (ucchiṣṭa),” [one must rinse].
Having placed that object on the ground and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), one should proceed once again.
In the Kūrma Purāṇa: "If a twice-born man, having taken up an object made of metal, should become impure by leaving food remnants on himself,
he should set that object down on the ground, perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), and then proceed with his duties once more."

Baudhāyana says: If one becomes impure while holding a metallic object, he should discard it, sip water, and, before taking it up again, sprinkle it with water. If he becomes impure while holding something other than that [metallic object], he should discard it, sip water, and, before taking it up again, sprinkle it with water. If he becomes impure while holding water, he should discard it, sip water, and, before taking it up again, sprinkle it with water.
"Discarding" means setting it down; "something other than that" refers to food (abhyavahārya) other than that metallic object, meaning while that [food] is still held in his hand.
As for that which was stated by Manu:
"If one who has something in his hand is somehow touched by leavings,
he shall attain purity after sipping water (ācamana) without first setting down that object."

Thus, regarding this matter, Medhātithi has stated the settled rule: "A more valuable object is set aside; another [object] is not set aside, yet one sips water. The author of the *Smṛticandrikā* states: "There is no setting aside of non-edible things such as clothing and the like, because the rule for setting aside applies to other [edible] things. Alternatively, there is no setting aside of objects that are not designated by mantras; there is setting aside of edible and metallic objects, while there is an option regarding clothing and other items distinct from those.
This is stated in the *Kūrmapurāṇa*: "If, having taken up an object without a mantra, one should happen to be accompanied by leavings..."
Without setting that object down, one who has sipped water (ācānta) shall attain purity;
however, there may be an option regarding clothes and such, for the same rule applies when they are touched by those [impure things].
The phrase "tatspṛṣṭau" means "when touched by the remnants"; the meaning is that it should be placed or not placed. Regarding placement, Baudhāyana says:
"This very same [procedure] is reversed; there is an option regarding the wooden vessel (vānaspatya) when it is without a mantra."

But how can rinsing (*ācamana*) be possible when the substance is held in the hand? It is said: for the rule there is that "having washed the hands up to the wrist. What is intended there is merely the contact of the substance with the body, not its being specifically held in the hand. Thus, even when impure, if substances are placed on the shoulder or elsewhere, one who has touched what is leavings (*ucchiṣṭa*) remains indeed impure; likewise, purification occurs for one who has rinsed. Therefore, having taken that substance from the hand to another place—such as the forearm or the armpit—one should rinse. This is the intention: just as it is indeed impure due to connection with human impurity, so too it is pure upon the purification of that [person]. But when one places that substance on the ground and rinses, how is the purity of the substance [attained]? By being grasped by a person who is careful, or by sprinkling (*abhyukṣaṇa*) and other methods prescribed in another *Smṛti*, such as "having rinsed, one should sprinkle the substance. And thus, in this established arrangement:
In the forthcoming statements of Gautama and others, let the word division (*cheda*) be made as desired, either as "anidhāya" (without setting down) or as "nidhāya" (having set down). Gautama says:
"One who has something in hand and is impure from eating should set it down and then sip water."
Śaṅkha and Likhita state:
One who has food in hand and becomes impure by being left-over (ucchiṣṭa) should set it down, sip water for purification, and then sprinkle the object with water.
Regarding the taking of cooked food while performing urination, the verse of Āpastamba should be consulted.
Having placed that object on the ground and performed purification according to the rule,
one becomes pure after sipping water when cooked food has been brought onto one's lap.
This applies to cases of incapacity:
when one has voided urine or feces while carrying goods in hand on a path in the forest, in a waterless place, at night, or where it is infested with thieves and tigers, one does not become pure.
One should first perform purification; then one should wash the feet. Having sipped water and sprinkled oneself, that which has been taken [into the hand] attains purity.
[966] Thus, because of the traditional teaching (smaraṇa) of Bṛhaspati.
Mārkaṇḍeya, however, states that even purification must be performed without setting anything down:
"He who voids urine or excrement while holding cooked food..."
Without even setting that object down, having placed it upon his limb and made it his support.
Having performed purification according to rule and sipped water according to the prescribed method,
one should sprinkle the food with water, lift it up, and show it to the sun; or,
having set aside just the first portion from it, the remainder shall attain purity.
Thus end the occasions for sipping water. Now follow the occasions for sipping water twice.
Regarding this, Yājñavalkya says:
Having bathed, drunk, sneezed, slept, eaten, walked upon a road,
or changed one's garment, one who has already sipped water (ācamana) should sip water again.
Paiṭhīnasi:

Having eaten, having sneezed, having slept, having changed one's garment, and upon the onset of coughing, spitting, or labored breathing, as well as when passing through a road, a crossroads, or a cremation ground—one who has already sipped water (ācamana) shall sip water again.
Manu, Aṅgiras, and Bṛhaspati [state this].
Having slept, having sneezed, having eaten, having spat, having spoken untruths, and having drunk water—
even if one is already pure— one should sip water (ācamana) when about to study.
Gautama, following the rule "one should sip water," states:
"after sleeping, after eating, and after sneezing. Regarding the rules for eating, Hārīta says:

One should meditate on the unmanifest Puruṣa after having stepped upon urine, feces, or a road, and likewise after visiting a cremation ground; having sipped water once, one should sip water again. Thus says Paiṭhīnasi.

Having stepped onto a public road and voided urine or excrement, or having touched the bone or oily residue of a five-toed animal, one who has already sipped water (ācamana) must sip water again; the same applies after conversing with a Caṇḍāla or a Mleccha.
Śaṅkha and Likhita state:
at the times of bathing and eating, one who has already sipped water must sip water again.
Āpastamba:
"One who is about to eat, being pure, should sip water twice, wipe the mouth twice, and touch [the lips] once. Vyāsa: [The same].
Having washed his hands and feet, one who is about to eat should sip water twice. (From the *Kūrmapurāṇa*):
"Having washed his hands and feet, one who is about to eat should sip water twice."
Seated in a clean place, and having eaten, one should sip water twice.

Vasiṣṭha: Having eaten, slept, sneezed, or drunk, one who has performed the sipping of water (ācamana) should sip again; likewise after putting on a garment, touching the lips, or touching the corners of the mouth. [As stated] in the Kūrma Purāṇa.
Having touched the lips when they are hairless, or having put on a garment,
or after discharging semen, urine, or feces, or upon speaking what is untruthful.
Having spat, at the commencement of Vedic study, or likewise upon the onset of desire or breathlessness,
the best of the twice-born, having approached a crossroads or a cremation ground, [should perform purification].
Likewise, at both twilights, even though one has already sipped water, one should sip water again.
Śaṅkha and Likhita state:
"One should sip water again after voiding urine or excrement, spitting, and so forth, as well as when uttering words that are unclean or impure.
Baudhāyana states:
In eating, in offering oblations, in giving gifts, in receiving offerings,
and at the time of consuming sacrificial food, it is not prescribed that one should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) twice.
Vyāsa says: At the time of giving, at the time of eating, during both twilights,
and during the recitation of mantras, fire-offerings, worship, and so forth— one who has not sipped water (ācamana) should sip water again.
Thus end the occasions for the twice sipping of water (ācamana). Now follow the sippings of water for the śrāddha rite.
Regarding this, the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa states:
One who is about to begin a *śrāddha* ceremony should wash his feet and hands as well,
and facing north, he should perform the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*) twice with thoroughly purified water.
Then, in the purified mandala, the twice-born, having washed their feet and standing to the north of the mandala, should indeed perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) twice.
Then, having sipped water once more according to the rule, the performer of the śrāddha,
with darbha grass in hand, should seat the Brahmins upon darbha grass.
Satyavrata said:
When the Brahmins have washed their feet and sipped water twice, the performer himself,
having likewise washed his feet, should then perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana).
In the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa:
[969] Having sipped water and sipped again, and having performed the washing of the feet of the twice-born,
one should wash one's own feet with care and then sip water once more.
Jātūkarṇya says:
Having honored the Viśvedevas and the ancestors with perfumes, garlands, and other offerings,
and having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), one should, with a well-composed mind, perform the offering into the fire (agnaukaraṇa).
Jamadagni says:
Then, having first offered water and subsequently the perfumes and other articles in their proper order,
one should perform the ceremonial sipping of water (ācamana) after causing [the recipient] to recite the words signifying the completion of the worship.
In the Viṣṇupurāṇa: Having worshipped the ancestors with perfumes and other offerings, and having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) in front of the foremost of the twice-born,
one should place vessels made of gold, silver, and so forth.
In the Brahmapurāṇa, however, the sipping of water (ācamana) is prescribed immediately after the offering of the respectful oblation (arghya):
"Having offered water, milk, curd, ghee, sesame seeds, rice grains, mustard seeds, tips of kuśa grass, and flowers, one should then sip water oneself."
In the Āditya Purāṇa: "The wise man should then scatter food on the ground, saying, 'Those who were consumed by fire...';
having himself performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), he should give water to the Brahmins one by one."

Viṣṇu: Having sprinkled water with sesame seeds near the leavings, having scattered food for those who died before receiving sacraments, and having touched water, one should ask whether they are satisfied. Saṃvarta: [The same].
Standing facing the south, he should scatter food upon the ground;
then, having washed his hands and sipped water (ācamana), he should recite the Madhumatī verses.
In the Āditya Purāṇa: "Having performed the offering of the rice-balls (piṇḍa) for the ancestors in their proper order,
as well as for the maternal grandfathers, one should then perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana)."
Kātyāyana says: Having offered the rice-balls while restrained, having sipped water (ācamya),
and having circumambulated from left to right, one should pay homage six times and worship with a single-minded focus.
Viśvāmitra says:
Having placed the rice-balls and honored them with perfumes, garlands, and other offerings, one should then touch water and, free from envy, sprinkle that place.
In the Agni Purāṇa: Having honored the rice-balls (piṇḍas) with perfumes, garlands, and other offerings, and having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) while self-restrained,
one should then offer water along with flowers and unbroken grains (akṣata) into the hands of the twice-born.
Bṛhaspati says: Having completed [the rites] for the Brahmins and having followed them to the boundary,
he should wash his feet and hands and perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) twice.
Pārāśara says: Having completed the śrāddha according to the rules and having dismissed the brahmins as well,
one should perform the twice-daily sipping of water (dvir-ācamana) and then carry out the daily rites such as the Vaiśvadeva offering.
The compiler has stated these seven acts of sipping water (ācamana) in brief:
first, at the end of the washing of the Brahmins' feet, during the worship, when the scattering of grain (vikira) has been performed,
after having offered the rice-balls (piṇḍas), after having worshipped, and likewise after having dismissed the Brahmins.
The performer of the śrāddha should sip water (ācamana) at these seven places:
he should sip twice at the beginning and the end, but only once at each of the remaining ones.
Gobhila says:
"At the beginning and at the conclusion, a double sipping of water (ācamana) is prescribed;
elsewhere, in rites for the ancestors (pitṛkārya), a single sipping is traditionally taught."
Regarding this, some have said:
"At the commencement and conclusion of the śrāddha, at the end of the foot-washing and the worship,
during the scattering of food (vikira), and at the offering of the rice-balls (piṇḍa), double sipping of water (ācamana) is prescribed."

Likewise: "At the beginning, at the end, during worship, when washing the feet of the Brahmins, when scattering grains, and when offering the rice-balls (piṇḍas)— in these six instances, sipping water (ācamana) is prescribed."

And thus it is said. Furthermore, according to that view, rinsing of the mouth (*ācamana*) does not take place immediately after the offering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa-nirvāpa*) and before the turning toward the north; rather, the rinsing is performed only after completing the entire ritual procedure for the offering of the rice-balls, up to the point of giving the fragrant substances (*gandha*) and so forth.
These are the rules regarding the rinsing of the mouth during the *śrāddha*.
Now follows the exception to the rule on rinsing.
In this regard, Yājñavalkya says:
"Droplets from the mouth are pure, as are drops from the act of sipping water;
likewise, the beard and hair within the mouth are pure, and one becomes pure after spitting out what is stuck between the teeth."

"Born from the mouth" (*mukhajāḥ*) means those that have issued from the mouth; "droplets" (*vipruṣaḥ*) are drops of phlegm; they are "pure" (*medhyāḥ*), meaning they do not cause one to become *ucchiṣṭa* (leftover/defiled). From the injunction for sipping water (*ācamana*) after spitting or speaking untruths, it is understood that one who has not sipped water is impure. Since droplets also emerge from the mouth, they are indeed like spittle; therefore, this statement is made as an exception (*apavāda*) to the requirement of sipping water that would otherwise apply here. Likewise, water drops falling from the hand below through the gaps between the fingers while one is sipping water are also pure. "Beard" (*śmaśru*) refers to the hair of the face; even when it enters the mouth—that is, has gone inside the mouth—it is pure. Even food and such stuck to the teeth, one remains pure even without sipping water. However, upon contact with droplets, one must certainly perform the sipping of water (*ācamana*) because of the contact with an impurity.
And likewise Āpastamba says:
"When drops are perceived falling from his mouth, sipping (ācamana) is prescribed for those [drops]; as for those [drops] that fall upon the ground, one should not sip for them—so says one [teacher].
The word "perceived" (upalabhyante) means "touched."
Gautama says: "Drops [of saliva] do not make one impure by leavings, provided they do not fall upon the body. Vasiṣṭha also says the same.
Droplets that do not touch the body do not make one impure by being remnants;
so too Manu says:
"Droplets from the mouth do not make one impure, nor those which do not reach the body."
Nor [should one eat] what has gone onto the beard, nor what is stuck between the teeth.
"Between the teeth" means in the space between the teeth. "Situated" means adhering [to them].
It has been stated that drops from rinsing the mouth are pure; regarding this, Manu states a specific rule:
"The drops that touch the feet of one who is causing others to rinse their mouths..."
Those [waters] on the ground should be known as equal; one should not remain unpurified because of them.
Here, the connection is with the words "the feet" in the phrase "making others sip water."

If one who gives water for rinsing the mouth (ācamana) has his feet touched by drops of water fallen from the hand of the person performing the rinsing, he does not thereby become impure. For those drops are equal to those found on the earth; just as certain quantities of water remaining on unpolluted ground are pure, so too these drops falling from a hand that has been used for rinsing are pure—this is the meaning. Since it is here stated that the purity belongs specifically to the person who caused the rinsing, it is understood that for the one performing the rinsing and for others standing nearby, impurity (aprāyatya) indeed occurs upon contact with the rinsing drops. Baudhāyana also says:
Drops that touch the feet of one who is giving water for sipping to others do not cause a state of impurity; they are equal to those on the ground.
Vasiṣṭha also says: "Even for one who is causing others to sip water, those drops that have fallen upon his feet do not cause him to become impure; they are considered equal to the ground."
In this context, the mention of "feet" is intended to indicate other parts of the body as well;
and thus Yama says:
"The drops that fall from the body of men while they are sipping water [for purification]..."
"There is no fault of impurity from food remnants here; they are considered equal to the ground.
And these [drops] are pure only when they have risen by striking the ground, not when they have been touched while still in mid-air.
As Paiṭhīnasi says:

Drops that have fallen to the ground, when touched, are pure; droplets [on the body] are clean. One should sip water (ācamana) when the hair of the body is wet. There is no state of being "unclean" (ucchiṣṭa) due to whiskers that have entered the mouth.
Devala also says:
"Impurity is not prescribed on account of whiskers that have entered the mouth."
Regarding this, Āpastamba states a specific rule:
"One does not become impure by having food remnants on the beard, provided they remain inside the mouth and do not touch the hand."

The mention of "taking by the hand" (*hastagrahaṇa*) is intended as an illustration for other parts as well, since the rule for sipping water (*ācamana*) is prescribed even upon touching the impurity of another limb, such as the face. Furthermore, that which was stated previously—that there is impurity merely by the discarding of what is stuck to the teeth—should be understood as referring to cases where the substance has fallen off of its own accord; for the Smṛti of Baudhāyana states: "When those [particles] have fallen away, one need not sip water; one becomes pure by their being spat out. "Spitting out" (*saṃśrāvaṇa*) means ejecting from the mouth.
Manu, however, states that for that which has fallen off on its own, purity is attained simply by swallowing it.
While remaining pure, he should swallow those [impurities] as they fall from his state;
"swallowing" means causing them to enter within. And there is an option between swallowing and discarding.
Gautama also says:

"One should know that when [food] has fallen [from the teeth], it is like the *āśrāva*; while swallowing it, one remains pure. Here, "*āśrāva*" means water for rinsing the mouth; the meaning is that just as that [water], even if it falls, does not become impure, so it is with this. By the word "even" (*eva*) in "while swallowing it," it is indicated that during the act of chewing, one must certainly perform the ritual sipping (*ācamana*) as prescribed by Viṣṇu: "One should always sip water while chewing. However, if something stuck to the teeth is forcibly dislodged, one must sip water, according to the traditional teaching of Devala: "During a meal, after removing what is stuck between the teeth, one should perform the ritual sipping."
Food and the like that do not pass beyond the teeth do not make one impure with remnants, just as the teeth themselves do not.
Regarding this, Baudhāyana says:
"Moreover, they also cite [the following verse]:"
That which adheres to the teeth like the teeth themselves, as well as that which may be inside the mouth,
remains pure even after sipping water (ācamana), provided one swallows it.
Vasiṣṭha:
[975] There is no defilement from what has gone onto the beard.
That which adheres to the teeth is like the teeth themselves; and also that which may be inside the mouth.
If there be a remnant after one has sipped water, he becomes pure by simply swallowing it.
Hārīta says:
Regarding food particles stuck between the teeth, as well as whatever may remain inside the mouth after sipping water (ācamana), one becomes pure by simply swallowing that residue.

Paiṭhīnasi states: "Regarding food stuck between the teeth, as with the teeth themselves, one is purified simply by swallowing it while it remains inside the mouth. The rule "as with the teeth" regarding what is stuck between the teeth is to be understood to apply when no flavor is perceived.
Regarding this, Śaṅkha says:
"In the case of food particles stuck to the teeth, they are treated like the teeth themselves, except for the contact with the tongue.
The meaning of the phrase "except" and so forth is that even if no taste is perceived, impurity arises when there is contact with the tongue.
Manu says:
Regarding food particles stuck between the teeth, one remains pure provided they do not come into contact with the tongue, just as with the teeth themselves.
Some, however, say that one is not impure even when there is contact with the tongue, as long as emission does not occur;
and thus Gautama says:
"Regarding what is stuck between the teeth, it is like [what is on] the teeth, except for contact with the tongue, until emission," so some [hold].
The phrase "like a tooth [is what is stuck] to a tooth" intends to refer to a coating that cannot be removed.
And so Devala says:
"One should consider a coating stuck to the teeth as being like the tooth itself, provided it is not removable."
One should not exert much effort again toward its extraction from that place.
[976] There would be extreme impurity if a wound were inflicted by piercing with a blade of grass.
Śātātapa says:
A twice-born man does not become impure by remnants when there is fruit or root stuck to the teeth, nor with edible food, oil, or clarified butter, nor with betel leaf, nor with a stalk of sugarcane.
In this context, "oiliness" refers to the oiliness of food that remains stuck to the hands and so forth, even after one has performed the ritual rinsing (ācamana).
As stated in the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*:
"In the case of betel, fruit, and what remains of food mixed with oiliness..."
If something adheres to the teeth, a person does not become impure by the mere contact of it.
With bark, leaves, roots, and flowers, as well as with items made of grass and wood,
or with fragrant substances, a twice-born man shall not become impure by eating the remnants.
Regarding the phrase "at the contact of what is stuck to the teeth," the remainder [of the sentence] is "by means of the tongue. Parāśara says:
"In the case of betel, sugarcane, fruit, and likewise after applying oil or ointments while eating..."
Manu has declared that in the case of the honey-mixture (madhuparka) and the Soma sacrifice, there is no such thing as "leftover" (ucchiṣṭa).
Regarding Atri and Aṅgiras:

"In the case of the honey-mixture (madhuparka), in the Soma sacrifice, in water, and in the offerings to the vital breaths (prāṇāhutis), a Brahmin shall not be considered impure from remnants; such is the word of Atri."

Because of the proximity of the *prāṇāhuti* offerings in the passage beginning with "In the waters... (*apsu*) and "Thou art the covering of immortality" (*amṛtāpidhānam asi*), the meaning is that when drinking water is to be performed, even one who has already eaten is not considered "leftover" (*ucchiṣṭa*) with respect to the recitation of the mantra.
Vasiṣṭha states: "In the *prāṇāhuti* offerings, in the *soma* sacrifice, and likewise in the *madhuparka* [offering]..."
In all offerings made from the mouth, a twice-born man does not become impure by remnants.
"In mouth-offerings" refers to food remaining after being bitten.
This is an exception to the rule regarding sipping water (ācamana). Now follows the prohibition regarding sipping water.
Regarding this, Hārīta states:

"One should not sip water while wearing the sacred thread (*upavīta*) in the wrong manner, nor with the topknot untied, nor standing, nor laughing, nor talking, nor looking about; nor with water that has not been inspected, nor with hot water, nor turbid water, nor frothy water, nor water containing bubbles.
The term "standing" means with eyes directed upward; "looking about" refers to looking toward the directions—this is the implied meaning—or else looking at one's own reflection in that very water.
Regarding the injunction "one should sip water" (ācāmet), Śaṅkha and Likhita state:
"Not standing, not bowing, not with the fingers [extended], not making a sound with the mouth, not with unwashed feet, not without the sacred thread, and not with the topknot untied.
Baudhāyana says:

One should not perform the ritual sipping (upaspṛśet) with water that is [carried] by the fingers, nor with water containing bubbles, nor with foam, nor with alkaline water, nor with hot water, nor with turbid water; nor should one do so while laughing, nor while looking around, nor while stooping, nor while bowing down, nor with the topknot untied, nor with the hair disheveled, nor without the waistband fastened, nor with the knees outside [the knees of the garment].
"Prahva" means one whose body is bent low.
Likewise:
One should not sip water that is the residue of washing the feet; if one should sip it, one must first sprinkle it upon the ground and then sip.
Āpastamba says: "One should not sip water from raindrops, nor from water in a fissure in the earth, nor from heated water without a specific reason."
‘Crack’ (*pradara*) refers to a portion of ground that is somewhat split and sunken. ‘Without cause’ (*akāraṇāt*) means without a reason such as illness.
Likewise, one should not perform useless acts with the remainder of another's water, nor should one sip water (*ācāmet*) using water stirred by the hand or water drawn up by only one hand.
This follows from the recurring injunction "one should sip water," according to Gautama.
Nor with water offered by a Śūdra, or that which is impure, or poured from a single hand. Vasiṣṭha says: One should not perform ācamana while walking, standing, lying down, or while prostrate.
Āpastamba:
One should not sip water while standing or while bent over. Pracetas: [The same].
One should not sip water while wearing an inner garment, nor without a lower garment, nor shedding tears, nor with uneven feet.
Gautama says: one should not drink from joined palms, nor while standing, nor should one sip water that has not been drawn up.

The meaning is that one should not drink from the mouth like an animal. Regarding the rule "one should sip water" (ācāmet), Vasiṣṭha states: "Not with waters corrupted by color or taste, nor those that have come from impure sources."
Hārīta:
One should avoid water that is discolored, foul-smelling, and frothy. Śaṅkha: [Also says: [One should avoid water that is discolored, foul-smelling, and frothy.]
A twice-born man who is without his sacred thread, or whose hair-tuft is untied,
or whose feet are unwashed— even if he has sipped water for purification— remains impure.
One who touches [the water] with the knees outside [the knees], or with water held in only one hand,
or while standing with shoes on, shall not attain purity at all.
Devala states, following the injunction "one should sip water" (ācāmet):
"Neither while walking, nor while lying down, nor while stumbling, nor while touching others;
nor while laughing, nor while talking, nor even while looking at oneself."
Without touching his hair, his waist-knot, his lower body, or even the ground;
if he should touch these, he must wash his hand again.
"Skhalan" means moving.
Likewise:
"One should not perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) while wearing sandals, or while standing in water, nor with hair loosened,
nor wearing a turban, nor having the head wrapped in a cloth."
One who has a covering even over the region of the beard is "uṣṇīṣī" (one with a turban/head-covering),
according to Vyāsa: "Having covered the head or the neck, or even having one's lower garment or topknot hanging loose..."
Without having washed one's feet, even if one has sipped water for purification, one remains impure.
If a Brāhmaṇa sips water from the tips of his fingernails, that is equal to the drinking of liquor; thus spoke the Seer.
Viṣṇu says: One should not [recite] while walking, nor while lying down, nor while standing, nor while bowing;
nor while touching anything, nor while laughing, nor while talking, nor upon seeing a dog or a Cāṇḍāla.
‘Standing’ means having risen; ‘not touching anything else,’ is the ellipsis. Gobhila says: “And having made one part of the inner garment serve as the upper garment.”

The word "should sip water" (ācāmet) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence. "Inner garment" (antarīya) refers to the lower garment; this rule concerns that portion of the lower garment for which the status of an upper garment (uttarīya) was not previously assigned with a mantra at the time of the first wearing. For in the absence of a second garment, the status of an upper garment is conferred upon the upper half of the very garment used for wrapping. This is because Pāraskara’s Smṛti, immediately following the injunction for taking up the upper garment with a mantra—stating, "If there is but one garment, he covers it with its upper fold"—mentions this practice. Thus says Saṃvarta.
A twice-born man of the highest rank is never purified by water given by a Śūdra, by one who is impure, or by one using only a single hand; nor is he purified while wearing sandals.
Marīci says: One should not [recite] outside the sacred enclosure (jānu), nor in haste, nor while seated on a seat, nor while standing up;
nor while wearing sandals, nor without concentration, but rather pure and with a disciplined mind.
Having eaten and remaining seated, one should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), but never at any other time.
Bhṛgu says:
If one has sipped water while without the sacred thread, or likewise without a washed garment,
or having released the topknot, the entire rite must be performed again.
One who wears a turban, one who sits in the full lotus posture, one who has his feet raised, one traveling in a vehicle,
or one standing on tiptoe in an improper place, does not attain purity by performing the ritual sipping of water (ācamana).
"Baddhaparyaṅka" means one whose lap is covered with a cloth or similar material.
Gobhila states the definition of "prauḍhapāda":
"Either with the feet placed upon a seat, or likewise upon the knees or the shanks."
And he who has placed his foot upon a support is called one with a "stretched foot."
The posture in which the two knees are covered by a cloth shaped like a yogic band is called *avasaktikā*. "Prapada" refers to the tip of the foot. In the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*:
"Whether covering his head or his chest, even when walking on a street or in a marketplace..."
If one has not performed the purification of the feet, one remains impure even if one has sipped water.
‘Āpaṇaḥ’ means a place of buying and selling. ‘Kauśikaḥ’:
some Brāhmaṇa who is impure in his hands, should touch [the water].
All of that becomes impure for him, as does his ritual sipping of water (ācamana).
Viṣṇu says: Standing in water above the knees, one does not attain purity by merely sipping water;
even if one sips it a hundred times while standing below that level, one is not purified.
Since the sipping of water (ācamana) is prohibited when one is below the knees, it is understood that sipping is not forbidden even when standing in water reaching only to the knees.
Thus Jātūkarṇya says:
"Standing in knee-deep water, or on dry land facing east, but not sitting."
Pure in every respect and having sipped water for ritual purification, he stands simultaneously between the two of them.
"Of the two" means "of water and land.
For this very reason, Hārīta says:
"Whether situated in water, or on land, or standing equidistant from both."
One who stands in water is authorized for water-related tasks, and one who stands on dry land for land-based activities;
however, one who stands in both places is authorized for the duties of both.

If one sips water while standing in water, then one is authorized for rites performed in water; but when standing on land, then for rites performed on land; furthermore, if one stands in both places, then one is authorized for the performance of rites belonging to both. [982] Dakṣa also says: "When a Brahmin has bathed, he should sip water while placing his feet in the water and on the land."
When that [mind] is purified in both respects, it will then become capable of performing its function.
Yama says: "That twice-born man who sips water while it is touched by the nails of his hands clearly drinks liquor;
such is the word of Yama."
If a Brāhmaṇa drinks water held up by his left hand,
Svāyambhuva Manu declared that it is equal to the drinking of liquor.
A specific detail regarding this is shown in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*:
"One should not drink water by lifting it with the left hand using the mouth.
The word "mouth" (*vaktra*) implies that it must be a clean mouth.
Śāṭyāyani says:
Having taken water from a gourd, a copper vessel, or a water-pot, and sipping it himself, one does not thereby become impure.
Chāgaleya says:
One should perform the sipping of water (ācamana) with one's own hand using a vessel made of horn, gourd, wood, copper, or leather; furthermore, one should avoid affectionate conversation.
Water that has been in a vessel of horn, as well as water that has been in a copper vessel,
or even in one of gold or silver, can never be purified.
Thus ends the prohibition against sipping water. Now, regarding the waters for sipping:
Regarding this, Manu says:
"Desiring purity, one should always sip water that is not warm, free from froth, and pure according to dharma, while seated and facing either the east or the north."
By the phrase "not hot," the heat produced by contact with fire is prohibited;
one should sip water that is not from fire, not hot, free of froth, not touched by the hand of a Śūdra alone, and not alkaline.
Thus, from the recollection of Viṣṇu: "With those that are not defiled," meaning free from defects such as contact with impure substances;
this follows Yājñavalkya’s statement in the context of "one should sip water":
"But with waters that are in their natural state, devoid of foam and bubbles."
"With those abiding in their natural state" means with water whose odor, color, and taste are unaltered.
Śaṅkha says:
"But with water drawn up that is deficient in foam and bubbles."
And one should not touch [the water] with it unless it has been heated by fire and is free from salt.
The inclusion of the term "drawn up" (uddhṛta) is intended to exclude the water contained within a reservoir from being taken by the mouth. Gautama says:
"One should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) with water that has been drawn up."
In the context of the injunction "one should sip water," Śaṅkha and Likhita state:

[One should sip] waters that have been drawn up, strained, inspected, non-saline, not heated over fire, and free from foam and bubbles. Regarding these terms: "strained" means filtered through a cloth; "not heated over fire" means not warmed by fire.

Āpastamba says: "One becomes pure by sipping water from water that has reached the ground, or from water that one who is already pure causes him to sip. It has been stated that one should not sip water from the water in a crevice; regarding that specific case, Vasiṣṭha says:"
"By those [streams] from a fissure which satisfy a cow— [one] should sip water (ācāmet) is the ellipsis.
Paiṭhīnasi states this while continuing the word "one should sip water" (ācāmet).
"With water that is not boiled, without foam, and without bubbles.
"Not boiled" means uncooked; this refers to cases where one is not ill. For this very reason, Yama says:

Purification by means of water that has not been looked at during the night has been declared for the wise; likewise, for those who are ill, purification is by water, and for those who drink hot [liquids], it is by hot water.
"Of those who drink warm [water]" refers to those who are ill, and not merely to those who are unwell; this is the meaning.
Furthermore, when water with the aforementioned characteristics cannot be found there, Devala is consulted regarding what should be done:
"In whatever regions there are gods, and in whatever regions there are twice-born [brahmins]..."
In whatever regions there is water, and whatever soil exists in those very places;
In whatever places there is a particular purity and whatever kind of righteous conduct exists, one should not despise those things; for in that very place, dharma is of such a nature.
Regarding this water, Yama says that one should not sip water for purification as long as one has not touched it with the left hand:
"A wise man should not touch [the water] until he has touched it with his left hand;
for in the left hand dwell the twelve Ādityas and Varuṇa, the lord of the waters."
Thus are the waters for sipping.
Now, the measure of the water for sipping.

Regarding this, Manu says: "A Brahmin is purified by water that reaches the heart; a Kṣatriya, by water reaching the throat; a Vaiśya, by water that has been tasted; and a Śūdra, by water merely touched at the extremity."

"Reaching the heart" (*hṛdgāḥ*) means they arrive at or reach the heart; "is purified" (*pūyate*) means he attains purity. "With those reaching the throat" (*kaṇṭhagābhiḥ*) means with those that touch only the throat; "a lord of the earth" (*bhūmipaḥ*) refers to a Kṣatriya. "With those tasted" (*prāśitābhiḥ*) means with those that have entered the interior of the mouth but have not reached the throat; [this refers to] a Vaiśya. The suffix *-tasi* here has the sense of the third case (*tṛtīyārthe*). Furthermore, the word *anta* signifies proximity. That [proximity] requires another related term. Consequently, a Śūdra is purified by water touched by a spot adjacent to the spot where the sipping of water is prescribed for a Vaiśya. And the place of the Vaiśya is the tongue; the place adjacent to it is the teeth themselves. Although, in this case, contact with the tongue is unavoidable because of the fluidity of the water placed on the teeth, nevertheless, this [statement] is intended to indicate a slight reduction from the previously mentioned quantity.
Śaṅkha and Likhita state:

A Brāhmaṇa is pure with water that reaches the heart; a Kṣatriya with water reaching the throat; a Vaiśya with water reaching the palate; a woman and a Śūdra with water that merely touches the lips. Vasiṣṭha says:

A Brāhmaṇa becomes pure by water that reaches the heart—provided it is free of bubbles and foam; a Kṣatriya by water reaching the throat; a Vaiśya by water merely sipped; and a woman or a Śūdra by water merely touched. Śaṅkha says: "A Brāhmaṇa is purified by water reaching the heart, while a king (Kṣatriya) is purified by water reaching the throat."
A Vaiśya [is purified] by [water] reaching the palate, and a Śūdra by [water] merely touching the extremities of the lips.
Devala says:
When the water has been drunk and has reached the heart, the Brāhmaṇa is pure;
the Kṣatriya is pure when it reaches the throat; the Vaiśya, when it reaches the mouth; and the Śūdra is pure by mere contact.
Paiṭhīnasi says:

A Brāhmaṇa [should sip] water that reaches the heart; a Rājanya, water reaching the throat; a Vaiśya, water that has reached the mouth; a woman and a Śūdra, water that has merely touched [the lips]. Baudhāyana says:
Moreover, they cite this example:

"A Brahmin becomes pure by water that has reached the heart; a Kṣatriya, by water reaching the throat; a Vaiśya, by water that has been sipped; and a woman or a Śūdra, by contact with the water at the extremity."
Yājñavalkya and Viṣṇu state:
"The twice-born classes are purified by [water] reaching the heart, the throat, and the palate, respectively;
a woman and a Śūdra are purified when it has touched them once at the end [of the mouth]."
Hārīta says:

A Brahmin becomes pure by [drinking] water that has reached the heart; a Kṣatriya, by water reaching the throat; a Vaiśya, by water that has been swallowed; and women and Śūdras become pure even by the mere touch [of the water].
Śālaṅkāyana says: When the water has reached the heart, a Brāhmaṇa attains purity;
a Kṣatriya [attains it] when it reaches the throat; a Vaiśya when it reaches the navel; and a Śūdra or a woman when it reaches the very end [of the mouth].
