When the occasion for a śrāddha has arrived, one should certainly not give way to anger;
nor should one remain in the presence of the ancestors while leaning on something or with a perspiring body.
And one should not ward off hawks, crows, or other such birds from this place;
for it is stated in the Veda that the ancestors arrive there in those very forms.

One should not "give way to anger," meaning one should not produce it. "Sumut" means one who dwells with joy; the sense is that even when there is a cause for shedding tears and so forth, one should remain joyful. "Leaning against" (*āśritaḥ*) means having a portion of the body placed against a wall, pillar, or similar object. The prohibition against warding off hawks, crows, and other such birds pertains to *tīrtha* (sacred) *śrāddha* rites. Otherwise, there would be a contradiction with scriptural statements such as, "Carnivorous birds must not look upon the *śrāddha*. Furthermore, it will be stated in the section on *tīrtha-śrāddha* that one should not perform the warding off of crows and the like at a sacred site (*tīrtha*). — Viṣṇu.

One should not place food upon a seat, nor touch it with the foot, nor spit upon it. The mention of a "seat" (āsana) is intended to indicate any supporting surface; therefore, the meaning is that one should not set down the vessel of food upon such a support.
— Yama.
The Yātudhānas plunder whatever is sacrificed, offered, given, eaten, muttered in prayer, performed as austerity, or studied by a twice-born man whose purity has fallen away.
Likewise, that which is given in anger and that which is eaten in haste—
both of these the Yātudhānas, along with the Rākṣasas, plunder away.
Having invoked the ancestors, one should not become subject to negligence;
therefore, having restrained both speech and anger, one should perform the śrāddha.
One should not harbor anger toward anyone for any reason whatsoever;
for when served by one who is free from anger, the ancestral spirits (pitṛs) are truly gratified at a śrāddha rite.
Baudhāyana says: Lack of faith is the supreme evil; for evil is said to be ignorance. One who is ignorant shall have his dharma lost; one whose dharma is lost is declared to be the lowest.
By faith the intellect is purified; by faith the mind is purified.
By faith Brahman is attained; faith is the liberator from sin.
Therefore, the deities do not consume the oblation of one who lacks faith.
Kātyāyana says:
Endowed with faith, one should perform the śrāddha even with vegetables alone; so says Manu.
Whatever one gives according to the rules, correctly, and endowed with faith,
that becomes infinite and inexhaustible for the ancestors in the hereafter.
Āpastamba:
"Being self-restrained, with a serene mind and contented, one should feed the Brāhmaṇas.
These are the rules for the one who feeds.
Now follows the determination regarding the offering and presentation of perfumes and other items.

In this regard, there is this doubt: should perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, and garments be given to the *brāhmaṇas*, or to the ancestors (*pitṛs*)? On this matter, the author of the *Mahārṇavaprakāśa* maintains that they should be given to the *brāhmaṇas*, based on the perception of the meaning of the scriptural injunctions and the application of logical reasoning. Regarding the scriptural injunction, Marīci states:
"Having made the perfumes the property of the Brāhmaṇa.

Here, because the suffix *sāti* is heard, it is observed that there is an injunction for the meaning that the perfumes and so forth must be made to have the Brāhmaṇa as their owner. For, according to the rule "in the sense of being dependent on that," the suffix *sāti* is taught as denoting a substance whose owner is that [person]. And this state of having the Brāhmaṇa as the owner is only possible when they are given to those very persons, and not otherwise.
This is the statement from the *Brahmapurāṇa*.
Having said, "This is your incense," one should then burn it before them. Thus it is said.

In this context, because the word *tat* (that) is a pronoun (*sarvanāman*), it refers to what has been previously mentioned; thus, those who were denoted by the word *vaḥ* (you) in the phrase "O you [ancestors]," they alone are denoted by the word *tat* in the phrase "before them. Now, if the ancestors (*pitaraḥ*) are intended [by *tat*], then because they are formless (*amūrta*), their status as qualifiers of the object "before" (*agra-pada-artha*) is not tenable. Therefore, since the word *tat* denotes embodied Brahmins, and the referent of the word *vaḥ*—which is pointed to by *tat*—is likewise of the nature of Brahmins, the offering of incense (*dhūpa*) to the Brahmins is established. This is also an illustration for other articles of worship, such as perfumes (*gandha*) and so forth. As for the observations regarding other purposes found in the Purāṇas: [they are not relevant here].
In that regard, the Mahābhārata says:
Having spoken thus to the wise Vāsudeva, to his aged maternal uncle, and likewise to Rāma and the others, the King of Dharma...
Then, for the sake of all [the ancestors], he performed the ancestral rites according to the rules;
he gave jewels, garments, villages, horses, and even chariots.
And likewise, he gave women, ornaments, horses, cows, and desirable excellent wives to the foremost of the twice-born by the hundreds of thousands.
Giving instructions again and again, that best of kings bestowed [gifts] upon the Brahmins,
as well as upon Droṇa, Sātyaki, Bhīma, Somadatta, and Bāhlika.
And [he addressed] King Duryodhana and his sons individually,
as well as all his friends, headed by Jayadratha.
That best of kings gave [the wealth] to the Brahmins, repeatedly instructing them.
Likewise, the one of great splendor performed the funeral rites for his father, as well as for his grandfather and great-grandfather, and for Gāndhāra himself.
In the *Rāmāyaṇa*, following Daśaratha’s departure to the other world:
"When ten days had passed, having performed his purification according to the rules,
he performed the twelfth and indeed the thirteenth *śrāddha* ceremonies."
Then, in honor of his father, he gave wealth to the Brahmins,
as well as precious gems, cattle, horses, and vehicles.
"Bharata" is the understood subject.
And in the Viṣṇupurāṇa, there is the father’s speech:
"Jewels, garments, great vehicles, all objects of enjoyment, and wealth."
When there is wealth, whoever shall give it to the Brahmins on our behalf.
In the Vārāha Purāṇa:
Having seated [the recipient] upon a bright seat, one should provide an umbrella there;
and for the sake of protection, one should cause that cloth to be given to a Brāhmaṇa.
"Then [he gave] all the garments and ornaments to the Brahmin," and so forth.

In all these cases, because of the hearing of the words "to the Brāhmaṇas" (*brāhmaṇebhyaḥ*), it is understood that the gifts are to be given to them alone. This statement occurs after the injunction for turning the two *arghya* vessels face-down in the works of Kātyāyana and Āśvalāyana: "At this time, there is the offering of perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, and garments. Here, although the desired sequence is not obtained through the order of the text (*pāṭhakrama*) alone, the prescription of the sequence by means of the scriptural statement "at this one time" leads to this understanding. For if these two sages had suspected that the gift of umbrellas, sandals, water-pots, and so forth—performed for the sake of securing the welfare of the ancestors—is generally performed at the time of giving the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) because it is enjoined by a general injunction to give and because it has the Brāhmaṇas as its recipients; and if they thought that the gift of perfumes and so forth is likewise similar in being enjoined by an injunction to give and having the Brāhmaṇas as its recipients, and thus might bypass the order of the text to perform the gift of perfumes and so forth at the time of the sacrificial fee—that must not happen. For this reason, the sequence is explicitly stated by the word. Therefore, the intention is understood that for those two [rites], the gift of perfumes and so forth has the Brāhmaṇas as its recipients alone. Otherwise, the phrase "at this time" would be meaningless. Moreover, there is also a logical argument (*nyāya*) here. If the gift of perfumes and so forth were intended for the ancestors, then since they lack a physical body and the like, they cannot be recipients; thus, they could not function as the recipient (*saṃpradāna*). Consequently, in the expression "he gives perfumes and so forth" (*gandhādīn dadāti*), even though the literal sense is possible, it would result in the fault of the word *dadāti* indicating only a part of its own meaning (since the ancestors are not the actual recipients). Furthermore, if the perfumes and so forth were offered to the ancestors and not to the twice-born, then the perfumes and so forth would incur the status of "divine property" (*devadravya*). For a substance is called "divine property" only when it is abandoned with the thought "this is not mine," dedicated to a deity by name in the dative case; it is not, however, that which is abandoned merely for the sake of an image, or where the notion of ownership belongs to a deity such as Viṣṇu. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that what is abandoned for the sake of an incorporeal deity would not be divine property. Even if a deity possesses the cognition that the substance abandoned is for its own sake, nevertheless, in accordance with the fact that they are understood to be conscious beings from the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), it is established that deities and ancestors also possess the cognition of ownership, just like Hari, Hara, and Hiraṇyagarbha.
And it has been stated by Āpastamba: "The ancestors also possess the status of deities; in that regard, the ancestors are the deities, while the Brāhmaṇas serve the purpose of the Āhavanīya fire."

Therefore, fragrances and other offerings dedicated to the ancestors (*pitṛs*) become the property of the gods (*devadravya*); however, that which is dedicated to the Viśvedevas is clearly the property of the gods. Thus, a twice-born man who, having formed the notion of ownership over it, makes use of that substance, becomes a great sinner through the theft of the most excellent divine property and would be liable to punishment according to the rules for grave offenses (*mahāsāhasa*). In this context, the property of the gods is considered the highest form of wealth.
Regarding the definition of its theft, Nārada says:
"Gold, gems, silk, women, draft animals, elephants, and horses..."
And it should be known that the most excellent wealth belongs to the gods, the brahmins, and the king.
The wise declare that theft consists of the removal [of property] from those who are asleep, intoxicated, or heedless, after having washed it away by various means.
Manu and Yama, however, have declared the sin of theft:
"He who, out of greed, misappropriates the property of a deity or the property of a Brāhmaṇa—
that evil-souled man lives in the next world on the leavings of vultures."
Hell overtakes that man of evil deeds who steals the property of the gods, as well as one who seizes the property of a Brahmin.
And it is stated in the section on punishments:
"The same threefold punishment which has been declared by the wise for acts of violence (sāhasa) applies also to theft (steya), according to the sequence of the three types of objects."
In this case of the highest violence (uttamasāhasa), the punishment is declared to be the execution of the men involved, or their banishment from the city, or likewise the amputation of their limbs.
Bṛhaspati said: For women, draft animals, gold, and gems, as well as the property of gods or Brahmins,
and for the finest silk garments— these being superior goods— the fine shall be equal to their value.
"Or rather, kings should determine it as double in relation to the person," so it is said.

Therefore, since it is enjoined only that the sacrificer must honor the Brahmins with perfumes and other offerings already set aside for the ancestors, once this has been done, the Brahmins—having accepted [the invitation] and agreed to the occasion—would have to accept the sacrificial substances being offered as the locus for their disposal. Having accepted them, they would incur some degree of sin until the completion of the ritual procedure; then, having taken the perfumes, flowers, and garments, they would have to depart only after discarding them at the sacrificer’s own home upon the conclusion of the rite. This, however, is not approved by the learned (śiṣṭa). Therefore, the perfumes and other items should be given directly to the Brahmins.
To this it is replied:

*Śrāddha* is defined as an action that brings about satisfaction and pleasure for the ancestors (*pitṛs*). Since satisfaction and pleasure are directly perceived to be produced by the food, ornaments, and other items being given, it is understood that generally whatever is prescribed as the object to be given in a *śrāddha* is to be given to the ancestors. This applies to fragrances and so forth as well; therefore, these must be given with the ancestors in view. Furthermore, that the ancestors experience satisfaction and pleasure through the ancestral rite (*paitra-karman*) is understood from the indicative power of the mantras:
"The ancestors have eaten; the ancestors have rejoiced; the ancestors have been satisfied."

"O Fathers, be purified! Thus [it is said]. And the explanation of this is in the *Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa*: "Having brought water, he pours it out with the words, 'The Fathers have eaten. Verily, he bestows food upon them. With the words, 'The Fathers have rejoiced,' he indeed causes them to rejoice. With the words, 'The Fathers have been satisfied,' he indeed satisfies them. With the words, 'O Fathers, be purified,' he purifies all of them in due order; thus he gladdens them. So it is.

"O Fathers, rejoice here; come to your respective portions. "The Fathers have rejoiced; they have partaken of their respective portions. The explanation of these two [mantras] is found in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa.

There he mutters: "O ancestors, rejoice here; come to your respective portions. By this he means, "Eat according to your respective portions. Then he mutters over the remnants: "The ancestors have rejoiced; they have come to their respective portions. By this he means, "They have eaten according to their respective portions. As for the suffix *-ti* (in *mādayadhvam*), it is explained in this view as intending the existence of the fruit of ownership—characterized by the right to enjoy what has not been forbidden—which arises when fragrances and other items are relinquished to the ancestors. Furthermore, because the Brāhmaṇas who serve as the substratum are regarded as non-different from the ancestors due to the descent of the ancestors into them, or because one relies on the presence of the ancestors, the formula proceeds as if addressed to the ancestors themselves, such as "O ancestors, this is your *arghya*; O ancestors, this is your *piṇḍa*," supported by the use of the word *ca* and the mention of "their front" (*tadagra*). Moreover, in the ritual offerings to the *piṇḍas*, in the verse "This is your garment, O ancestors," the giving of clothing is seen to be directed explicitly to the ancestors themselves by the use of the word *vaḥ*. And in the Purāṇas and other texts, it is heard that the offering of fragrances and other items is made directly to the ancestors themselves.
And so it is stated in the Vārāha Purāṇa: "Fragrances, flowers, garments, incense, lamps, and unbroken grains (akṣata) are recommended for rites for the ancestors, as are sweet food, water, and ice."
"O Vasundharā, he who, endowed with faith, offers these to the ancestors—
he alone is virtuous and does what is pleasing to me."

Those statements from the *Mahābhārata* and other texts which were previously shown as indicators that the giving of perfumes and so forth has Brahmins as its recipients do not actually concern that subject, because they lack any mention of "perfumes" (*gandha*) and the like; thus, they were cited merely under the mistaken impression that they were "observations of another matter. We do not, however, deny that the gifts of jewel-villages and the like taught therein have Brahmins as their recipients. As for the statement of Kātyāyana and Āśvalāyana, "at this time," it is intended to establish a restriction of time by precluding the practice of giving cows and other items at indefinite times. For even those items such as cows, which are recited in this specific sequence, are seen being given without fixed rule—either before the meal or after it. Furthermore, the word "gives" (*dadāti*), even while functioning here as a metonym (*upalakṣaṇa*) for a single part (the cow) just as it does for food and other things, is not contradictory. Indeed, in this very section, it is frequently seen to function precisely as a metonym for a single part. And so it is stated in the *Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa*: [1038]... [text continues].

Now, when one gives to the ancestors month after month in this very manner, he gives at that time when [the moon] is neither seen before nor seen behind. This King Soma is the food of the gods, which is the moon; it wanes during the night. When it has waned, he gives; in this way, he creates concord among them. For if he were to give while it has not waned, he would indeed create discord between the gods and the ancestors. Therefore, he gives only when it is neither seen before nor seen behind. He gives in the afternoon; for the forenoon belongs to the gods, midday to humans, and the afternoon to the ancestors. Therefore, he gives in the afternoon. Regarding the offering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*), he offers there in the same way, saying, "O so-and-so, this is for you," specifically for the sacrificer’s father. Some say here, "And those who follow you," but one should not speak thus. For they are already included with him, and she (the wife) is included with them. Therefore, one should simply say, "O so-and-so, this is for you" for the sacrificer’s father; "O so-and-so, this is for you" for the grandfather; and "O so-and-so, this is for you" for the great-grandfather.

Furthermore, if the offense of stealing the property of the gods (*devasvāpahāradoṣa*) were to apply when the twice-born accept perfumes, flowers, and so forth offered with the ancestors and others as the intended recipients, then that offense would be unavoidable for the twice-born invited to the *vaiśvadeva* rite. For in the formula for the offering of perfumes and other items prescribed in the *Brahma-purāṇa*, the Viśvedevas are seen to be the direct intended recipients:
"This water for the feet and this *arghya*—flowers, incense, and ointment—and this light of the lamp, are offered to the Viśvedevas."

Now, it might be argued as follows: Since this sentence, which teaches the offering of perfumes and other items intended for the Viśvedevas, cannot teach the understanding of the offering of perfumes and so forth to Brāhmaṇas as the recipients found in another sentence (the Brahmapurāṇa), this offering to the Viśvedevas is indeed something distinct. Therefore, having given perfumes, flowers, and the like to the Viśvedevas during the Vaiśvadeva rite, these should be given separately to the Brāhmaṇas. And the learned (*śiṣṭas*) act in exactly this way. For this very reason, in this passage from the Brahmapurāṇa, clothing—which is determined to be the exclusive property of the Brāhmaṇas—is not included among the offerings. But how is it that a general understanding derived from another sentence with a clear meaning is not sublated by a specific statement from the Brahmapurāṇa with a specialized sense? To this it may be replied: A general rule (*sāmānya-śāstra*), whose meaning is initially ambiguous, is sublated by a specific rule (*viśeṣa-śāstra*)—even if that specific rule has a fixed single purpose—once its meaning is established through the logic of examining the sequence of words within the sentence. Furthermore, it is observed that a specific rule is intended solely for its particular case. For example, consider the passage: "Prajāpati led a horse to Varuṇa; he was afflicted by his own deity; he was torn asunder. He saw this oblation to Varuṇa on four potsherds; he offered it, and thus he was released from Varuṇa’s noose. Verily, Varuṇa seizes him who accepts a horse. As many horses as one might accept, so many four-potsherd oblations to Varuṇa should one offer. Here, the understanding that the sacrifice is to be performed by the giver—arising from the examination of the sequence of words—is not sublated by the Maitrāyaṇīya passage, "This horse is accepted," which prescribes a sacrifice performed by the receiver. Rather, the sacrifice is prescribed for the receiver as well. As the author of the Vārttika stated: "If there were another clear sentence regarding the receiver, then the sacrifice would belong to him too; however, that does not prevent the sacrifice from being for the giver. In the present case, however, there is this distinction: that the gift has Brāhmaṇas as its recipients... [text ends]... Numerous and very clear statements establishing this point are found. In that regard, because the two scriptural injunctions regarding the *pratigraheṣṭi* (the sacrifice for receiving gifts) concern two distinct entities—the giver and the receiver—who exist in a state of mutual exclusion, there is no relationship of sublation (*bādhyabādhakabhāva*) between them. In the present case, however, one statement is a general rule (*vyāpaka*) encompassing both the *daiva* (divine) and *pitrya* (ancestral) categories, while the other concerns the specific category of the *vaiśvadevika*. Therefore, since the general rule is set aside by the specific, there is no separate offering of perfumes and other items in the *vaiśvadevika* rite. Furthermore, when perfumes and other items are given to the *viśvedevas*, they are certainly not discarded elsewhere without first performing the worship of the Brahmins. Thus, how could these items, being accepted by the Brahmins, not incur the fault of stealing the property of the gods? As for the claim that "the learned act in this very manner," that is merely a matter of indifference, as it is nowhere actually observed. Therefore, it is logical that one should offer the perfumes and other items directly to the Brahmins, specifically intending them for the ancestors. Moreover, just as when food is offered with the ancestors and others in mind, the Brahmins incur no fault of stealing the property of the gods even while consuming it, so too there is no such fault in the use of perfumes and other items. Now, if it be argued: "Since Kātyāyana’s rule states, 'One invited by one who is blameless shall not depart,' and since non-departure has the purpose of eating and thus extends until that point, no sin arises from performing what is prescribed by the text"—just as in the following example: [The text continues: "Just as when one eats food offered with the ancestors in mind, the Brahmins do not incur the fault of stealing the property of the gods, so too there is no such fault in the use of perfumes and other items. If it is further argued that because Kātyāyana’s injunction "one invited by one who is blameless shall not depart" prescribes non-departure, and since that non-departure culminates in the purpose of eating, no sin arises from performing what is enjoined by the text—just as... [the argument concludes].
A twice-born man who takes grass, wood, fruit, or flowers, or indeed light,
for the sake of cows or Brahmins, is not tainted by sin.

Thus, regarding theft as specifically prescribed by Yama: in that case, would the fault of stealing the property of a deity not follow from eating at a censurable *śrāddha*? If you say, "It certainly does," we reply: no. That [fault] is based on eating what is censurable, not on the theft of the deity's property; for that fault exists even when one eats what is censurable in a manner other than a *śrāddha* meal, provided it is devoid of consuming the deity's property. Furthermore, no other fault is recorded in the tradition for eating at a censurable *śrāddha*. Now, where an object is used while forming the notion that it belongs to a deity, there the fault is caused by theft. But where food used as a means for a *śrāddha* is consumed without forming the notion that it is one's own, that fault does not arise. Nor is there a rule that whatever is used must be used with the notion that it is one's own; for Caitra, while bathing in the Gaṅgā, does not necessarily perceive her as belonging to himself. It is replied: If that were so, then even one who uses well-known property belonging to a deity without forming the notion that it is his own, but rather with the notion that it is the deity’s property, would not be a sinner. Moreover, just as in the case of food, since it is possible to use perfumes and other items even without the cognition of ownership, there would be no connection to sin [in such cases].

[Objection: "Granted that this may be so in the case of odors and the like; but how can there be the possibility of utility for a garment to be enjoyed over a long period of time without the notion of ownership (*svīyatva-buddhi*)?
[Reply: Not so. For even in the case of things to be enjoyed over a long period, such as the flow of the Ganges, we do not observe the notion of ownership.
[Objection: If it is accepted that one enjoys a garment even without the notion of ownership, then when someone else were to seize it, one would not say, 'This garment is mine, not yours.'"

Not so; for just as a king has a claim of ownership over the horses of a horse-herdsman who is imprisoned in a dungeon, and that claim is established by his designation [of them as his own], so too is such a designation possible in this case.
[Objection: In that case, there would be no disposal of the garment at will, just as there is none with respect to the horses and so forth.

[Reply: Not so. Since the invisible fault (adṛṣṭadoṣa) is not perceived because it is a subtle object of inference, and since there is an absence of visible fault (dṛṣṭadoṣa), and because the gift is offered in its essential form, and because there is the delusion of ownership due to the fact that it is connected with one's own action and no other owner is perceived, such [disposal] is indeed possible.

Now, even in the case of eating food at a *śrāddha* ceremony, there is indeed a fault caused by consuming the property of the gods; for this very reason, the learned (*śiṣṭas*) express censure regarding the eating of food at a *śrāddha*. However, this does not entail for the eater the necessity of being excluded from social intercourse (*avyavahāryatva*), punishment, or the performance of major penances (*mahāprāyaścitta*). This is because, according to the statement regarding "not departing," the injunction to eat implies a lightness of sin. Furthermore, even when a prohibition remains in force, the gravity of the sin is determined by certain specific factors despite the act of transgression being the same. For example, in the case of killing a Brahmin committed publicly, the gravity of the sin is established by the teaching that it must be expiated by a twelve-year vow; whereas in that same act committed in secret, the lightness of the sin is established by the demonstration that it can be removed merely by the recitation of the *aghamarṣaṇa* hymns and other such prayers. And in the present case as well, there is an instruction for penance, and it is a light one.
As Śātātapa says:
"A twice-born man who has partaken of a śrāddha meal should drink water ten times while reciting the Gāyatrī;
thereafter he should perform the twilight devotions (saṃdhyā), as well as mutter prayers and offer oblations."
In that case, even when utilizing perfumes and so forth, there is no room for the aforementioned faults.
Thus concludes the determination regarding the recipient of the gift of perfumes and other items. Now, concerning the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
[1042] Regarding that, first, the etymological derivation of the word *dakṣiṇā* is found in the *Śatapatha-Brāhmaṇa*:

"This very sacrifice, when it was slain, did not give a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). The gods invigorated (*adakṣayan*) it by means of sacrificial fees; because they invigorated it by means of sacrificial fees, therefore they are called *dakṣiṇā*. Whatever part of this slain sacrifice was failing, that they now invigorate for it by means of sacrificial fees; thus the sacrifice becomes successful. Therefore, one gives a sacrificial fee."

The act of striking (*hanana*) in a sacrifice—consisting of forms such as threshing and grinding performed with the mortar and pestle, the lower and upper millstones, and so forth—is set forth in the *Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa* itself in the preceding continuous passage. A sacrifice (*yajña*) is the relinquishment of a substance for the sake of a deity; since it possesses this defining characteristic, the *śrāddha* is also a sacrifice. Therefore, because it brings about the success of the sacrifice, the giving of a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is absolutely necessary even in the *śrāddha*. Regarding the necessity of the sacrificial fee, there is another scriptural statement (*śruti*) in the *Śatapatha* itself: "The oblation (*havis*) should not be without a sacrificial fee. Furthermore, in the *Caturviṃśatimata*, the necessity of giving the sacrificial fee is stated specifically with reference to the *śrāddha* itself.
The twilight devotions are in vain if devoid of darbha grass; a gift is in vain without water;
recitation is in vain if not counted; and a śrāddha ceremony is in vain if it lacks a sacrificial fee.
The author of the *Smṛti*, Āśvalāyana, also said: "A *śrāddha* performed by one who is not learned in the Vedas is as good as dead; a sacrifice without a sacrificial fee is dead.
Therefore, [one should give] at least a *paṇa*, a *kākiṇī*, or even a fruit or a flower."
One should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) in the sacrifice; by that, it becomes fruitful.

"A paṇa or a kākiṇī" is the secondary rule (anukalpa). The primary rule (mukhyakalpa), however, should be consulted in the section on materials in the Smṛtis and Purāṇas, beginning with "cows, land, gold, new garments, and beds. The arrangement regarding the deities is found in the Nāgarakhaṇḍa.
Gold belongs to the deities, and likewise silver to the ancestors. Vṛddha-Manu says:
"A wise man should indeed give gold as the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) in the Vaiśvadeva rite."
In the rite for the ancestors (pitrya), however, silver, land, cows, and so forth should be given with devotion.
Pāraskara says:
"Gold is [given] to the Viśvedevas, silver to the ancestors; other than these, there are cows, black antelope skins, and so forth."
"As much as one may be able.

Here, the intended meaning is simply that the gold being given to the Viśvedevas is superior in quality to the silver being given [to them]. It does not mean, however, that silver should not be given to the Viśvedevas nor that gold should not be given to the ancestors (*pitṛs*), for there are injunctions for the giving of gold to the ancestors in such passages as "cows, land, gold, clothes," and so forth. For this very reason, the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa* states only that the giving of silver related to the ancestors is of superior quality.
"The gift of silver is said to lead to infinite, inexhaustible heaven;
by this gift, virtuous sons indeed deliver their ancestors. Thus it is said.

As for what was stated regarding "as much as one is able," that is intended to express that the determination of the number and quantity of divine materials—such as cattle, land, gold, and so forth, which are of various kinds—is limited solely by one's capacity. "Capacity" (*śakti*) refers to the existence of sufficient wealth beyond what is required for the completion of those necessary worldly and Vedic rites, as well as those optional rites one desires to perform, which might otherwise fail due to the non-availability of likely future resources; "incapacity" (*aśakti*), conversely, is the absence of such wealth. Furthermore, Pāraskara permits inequality in the distribution of sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*).

When Brahmins are seated in a single row for a śrāddha meal, the food—both that which is chewed and that which is swallowed—should be given equally; however, the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) may be according to their respective merit.

The meaning is: either according to the relative excellence of the qualities of the recipient, or according to the desire to give arising from the respect shown to the ancestors as conceived through the relative excellence of the relationship and its correlates.
Bṛhaspati also says:
"One should, however, give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to all of them in accordance with their respective worth."
Just as there is satisfaction for those who have eaten when given cows, land, gold, and clothing,
so too must one act, especially by a person who is capable.
He who gives all of this according to the worthiness of the recipient brahmins,
as well as the giving of sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to others according to his capacity, brings about the perfection of the śrāddha.
Śātātapa states the time for the giving of the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā):
"Having fed the Brāhmaṇas, one should give a sacrificial fee according to one's ability;
for the sake of accomplishing one's intended purpose, one should cause them to pronounce auspicious wishes."

In this context, because the general rule for giving—that "it should be given to those who are pure"—is the subject at hand and is applicable here, it is understood that one should give specifically to those who have sipped water (ācānta) and who are the eaters at the *śrāddha*.
Thus Devala says:
"Then one should present the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the twice-born who have sipped water."

By this, it is stated merely that [the rite] occurs after the sipping of water (*ācamana*), and not that it occurs immediately thereafter without any interval. For, after the sipping of water, various ritual items such as the recitation of auspiciousness (*svastivācana*) are mentioned, since the injunction for the giving of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is observed in the *Smṛtis*, *Purāṇas*, and other texts.
Thus, it is said in the *Saura Purāṇa*:
"Having washed his hands, he should indeed perform the recitation of auspiciousness."
"One should give a sacrificial fee according to one's ability and utter the word *svadhā*. Thus it is said. Also in the *Matsyapurāṇa*:
"One should perform the pouring of the *svadhā* and likewise the water for imperishability (*akṣayyodaka*)."
"One should give [the gift] with sesame seeds, mentioning the name and lineage, and according to one's ability, a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).

Thus it is said. Furthermore, in the *Nāgarakhaṇḍa*, after describing the ritual items beginning with the offering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) and ending with the recitation of the *svadhā* formula, the giving of the sacrificial fee is stated:
"Having turned the vessel of water-offering (*arghyapātra*) face upwards, one should give the sacrificial fee. Thus it is said.

Furthermore, it is understood that this sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) should first be given to the twice-born of the Vaiśvadeva rite, and immediately thereafter to the twice-born of the ancestral rite; for in the Śrāddha ceremony, it is ordained that all ritual elements—excluding the formal dismissal (*visarjana*)—must begin with the deities.
And so says Manu:
"One should endeavor to have the rite begin and end with the deities; it should not begin and end with the ancestors."

The term *daivādi* refers to that [rite] in which the items belonging to the deities (*daiva*) and so forth—which precede the dismissal (*visarjana*)—are preceded by those belonging to Viśvedevas (*vaiśvadevika*). Likewise, *vānta* refers to that in which the item belonging to the deities is at the end. The meaning is that having performed all the items beginning with those for Viśvedevas, the dismissal for the Viśvedevas must be performed at the conclusion.
Mārkaṇḍeya also says:
"In a Śrāddha, one should diligently perform everything preceded by the rites for the deities."
Thus, Vṛddha-Manu states an exception to the rule that the precedence of the deities (*daivapūrvakatva*) is understood for the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) through general statements:
"One should give the sacrificial fee first to the Brahmins of the ancestors (*pitṛ*), and thereafter to the two [Brahmins] of the deities.

Having given it first to the Brahmins of the ancestors, one should give it immediately after that to the two Brahmins of the Vaiśvadeva rite. And because they are the recipients (*saṃpradāna*), the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) in the word *dvayoḥ* should be explained as having the sense of the dative.
Jamadagni states the procedure for the giving of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*):
"In all rites, [the ritual action] is performed with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*apasavya*), except for the giving of the sacrificial fee.
By this, it is stated that for the fee, the thread is over the left shoulder (*savya*).
The *apasavya* position was also stated by that very same [author]:

"In that regard, the Lord Matsya said to Manu: 'Savya' means clockwise (pradakṣiṇa), as does the *yajñopavīta*; 'apasavya' means counter-clockwise (apradakṣiṇa), as does the *prācīnāvīta*. Therefore, there is an option (*vikalpa*) between *savya* and *apasavya*. Alternatively, when the Brāhmaṇas are the recipients (*saṃpradāna*) in the giving of gifts, then it is *savya*; when the gift is made with reference to the ancestors (*pitṛ*), then it is *apasavya*—such is the settled rule (*vyavasthā*). And both these positions will be explained."
Then Jamadagni says: "One should give [the gift] with sesame seeds, mentioning the name and lineage, and a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) according to one's ability."

In this regard, regarding the view that the giving of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is directed toward the ancestors (*pitṛs*): having placed the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*apasavya*), one should take in one's hand silver or other materials together with *kuśa* grass, sesame seeds, and water. Having recited the mantra for the object to be given and the mantra for the sacrificial fee, one should announce the names, lineages (*gotra*), and relationships of the ancestors using words in the dative case. Then, saying, "May this such-and-such object, as an imperishable form of sacrificial fee, become *svadhā*; obeisance (*namaḥ*)," one should offer it into the hand of the Brahmin representing each respective ancestor by means of the *pitṛ-tīrtha*. Then, having placed the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*savya*), one should take in one's hand gold or other materials together with barley, *kuśa* grass, flowers, and water. Having recited the two mantras and announced the name of the Viśvedevas in the dative case, one should say, "May this such-and-such [object], as an imperishable form of sacrificial fee, become *svāhā*; obeisance," and offer it into the hand of the Brahmin representing them by means of the *deva-tīrtha*. Regarding the view that the giving of the sacrificial fee is directed toward the Brahmins: having placed the sacred thread over the right shoulder, one should take in one's hand silver or other materials together with sesame seeds, *kuśa* grass, flowers, unbroken rice (*akṣata*), and water. Having recited the mantra for the object to be given and the mantra for the sacrificial fee, one should announce the name and lineage of the ancestors using words in the dative case. Then, saying, "May this such-and-such object, as an imperishable form of sacrificial fee, become *svadhā*; obeisance," one should offer it into the hand of the Brahmin representing each respective ancestor by means of the *pitṛ-tīrtha*. Then, having placed the sacred thread over the left shoulder, one should take in one's hand gold or other materials together with barley, *kuśa* grass, flowers, and water. Saying, "May this such-and-such [object], as an imperishable form of sacrificial fee, become *svāhā*; obeisance," one should offer it into the hand of the Brahmin representing them by means of the *deva-tīrtha*. Regarding the view that the giving of the sacrificial fee is directed toward the Brahmins [alone]: having placed the sacred thread over the left shoulder, one should take in one's hand silver or other materials together with sesame seeds, flowers, unbroken rice, *kuśa* grass, and water. Having recited the mantra for the object to be given and the mantra for the sacrificial fee, one should announce the name and lineage of the [recipient] Brahmin using words in the dative case, and one's own [name and lineage] using words in the nominative case. Then, saying, "For the sake of the stability (*pratiṣṭhā*) of [myself], named So-and-so Śarman, I bestow upon you this such-and-such sacrificial fee; obeisance," one should offer it into the hand of the Brahmin representing the ancestors by means of the *deva-tīrtha*, and likewise give gold and other materials to the twice-born representing the Viśvedevas.

Thus concludes the determination of the necessity for defining the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), the distinction between the primary and secondary ritual procedures (*mukhyakalpa* and *anukalpa*), the disparity in its quantity, and the sequence of its timing.
Now follows the determination regarding the recipient of the sacrificial fee.

In this regard, some maintain that the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) should be given to the ancestors (*pitṛs*). For they say: because Jamadagni prescribed in the context of giving the sacrificial fee the connection with sesame seeds (*tila*), the wearing of the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*apasavya*), and the mention of the ancestors by name and lineage; and because the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*, after enumerating the materials for the sacrificial fee, states that "everything should be given to the ancestors," thereby establishing a connection with the ancestors—it is understood that the sacrificial fee should be given intended for the ancestors.

On this point, the author of the *Smṛticandrikā* has stated both the objection and its resolution. First, the objection: if the relinquishment of property (*dravyatyāga*) is made with reference to the ancestors (*pitṛ*) and others, and not with reference to the twice-born (*dvija*), how then can the Brāhmaṇas possess ownership over the gift-material (*dakṣiṇā-dravya*)? The resolution, however, is as follows: Just as in the giving of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā-dāna*) at the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), it is said that "the rice (*odana*) is for the sake of the Brāhmaṇas," and when the rice is offered by the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) acquire ownership over that rice solely by virtue of being performers of the ritual (*karmakaratva*), even though there is no formal relinquishment of the rice specifically for their sake; so too here, upon the offering of gold, silver, and so forth, the Brāhmaṇas acquire ownership therein solely by virtue of being performers of the ritual. Or again, just as in the case of consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) and the like, when one relinquishes garments, ornaments, and so forth with reference to the deity during the consecration, the preceptor (*ācārya*) takes all the implements at the conclusion of the consecration; by virtue of being supported by the scriptural statement that he is the performer of the ritual, ownership belongs to the preceptor—so too here.
Having fed the Brahmins, one should give them a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) according to one's ability.

On the grounds that the Brāhmaṇas acquire ownership even when a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is relinquished for the sake of another, because they act as officiants (*karmakara*) supported by this very statement, this opinion appears to be untenable. For if the twice-born are indeed the recipients (*saṃpradāna*), then since the giving of the fee is an ancillary part of the ancestral rite (*pitryakarman*), it is inherently related to the ancestors; thus, its connection with sesame seeds and the *apasavya* (leftward) arrangement is perfectly logical. Furthermore, in the scriptural injunction "with sesame seeds, [pronouncing] name and lineage," the intention to refer to the name and lineage associated with the Brāhmaṇas is also possible. Moreover, this is recorded in the rules regarding the procedure for giving.

"Having pronounced the name and lineage of the recipient and of oneself, they bestow the gift; however, in the case of giving a daughter in marriage, three males [are mentioned]. Even here, regarding the statement "it should be given to the ancestors," it can be understood through figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) that it means "it should be given to the Brahmins who represent the ancestors. Therefore, for the reasons stated previously, it is not possible to conclude with certainty that the ancestors are the intended recipients (*uddeśyatva*).

As for what was said—that ownership of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* rice belongs to the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) solely by virtue of their performing the ritual work even before it is given—that is not so; for this rice is indeed given.
Therefore Āpastamba says:
"He gives them the *anvāhārya* [fee], saying, 'O Brahmins, this is the rice.'"

For this very reason, the statement "it has been accepted" applies to the Brahmins. However, when an object has been relinquished for the sake of a deity, even though the officiating priest (ācārya) takes it as his established fee, his ownership is not contradictory because there is a scriptural declaration that he "should take it. But in the present case, no such declaration exists. Furthermore, it is established that the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is the non-excessive remuneration for those performing the sacrificial acts. Therefore, for the sake of the consistency of the term *dakṣiṇā* and for the sake of maintaining the well-known worldly conception of ownership, it is understood that it is logical that the sacrificial fee should be given to the Brahmins alone.
And there are statements on this point:
"Then one should bestow the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) upon the twice-born who have sipped water.
Likewise:

"One should give the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) first to the Brahmins of the ancestors, and then to the two [Brahmins] of the other [lineage]. Although the giving of the *dakṣiṇā* has the Brahmins as its recipients, this statement is made because the status of being an ancillary part of the ancestral rite (*pitryakarman*) does not cease; thus, it follows that one must indeed perform it with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*apasavya*). As it is said: "All rites are to be performed *apasavya*, with the exception of the giving of the *dakṣiṇā*."

Lest the exclusive application of the *savya* (left-hand) method be undermined by the exception regarding the *apasavya* (right-hand), the rule for the *apasavya* is stated once again in that very same context. Therefore, because it is both prescribed and prohibited, there is an option (*vikalpa*). Furthermore, this serves as a meaningful purpose for the injunction of the *apasavya* method. By the passage beginning with "to the twice-born who have sipped water," it is stated that a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) should be given to those who eat at the *śrāddha*.
Bṛhaspati, however, says that the fee should be given even to others—namely, to those who eat the remainder of the food prepared for the *śrāddha*, and to others who arrive at that time:
"Relatives, kinsmen, guests, and likewise other guests."
One should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to all of them in accordance with their respective merit.

"Kinsmen" (*jñātayaḥ*) are those related through the father; "relatives" (*bāndhavāḥ*) are those related through the mother. This is the determination regarding the recipient of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
This concludes the description of the sacrificial fee.
Now follows the determination of the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice.

In this regard, the times for cooking are matters of doubt. First, there is a doubt concerning the alternative: is the single act of cooking for the *vaiśvadeva* and other rites the same as that for the *śrāddha*, or are they distinct? In this matter, the cooking for the *nitya-śrāddha* included within the five great sacrifices (*pañcamahāyajña*) and the *vaiśvadeva* and so forth is indeed one and the same. For the daily cooking performed every day serves the purpose of all rites, as it is not completed until all the duties have been accomplished. However, in the case of specific periods of impurity (*āśauca*), since the *vaiśvadeva* and other rites do not take place before the eleventh day, there is no possibility of doubting the identity of the cooking during the *navāha-śrāddhas* (the nine-day funeral rites) performed at that time. But regarding the *śrāddha* on the eleventh day, the *vaiśvadeva* must be performed with a separate act of cooking.
"However, in the case of *ekoddiṣṭa* rites, one should discard the remainder to the Brahmins.

Since Devala thus prescribes that in the *ekoddiṣṭas* known as *navaśrāddha*, all remnants of food must be given to the Brahmins, and since this will also be stated regarding *pretaśrāddhas*, there is no doubt concerning the cooking intended for the *amāvāsyā-śrāddha*. As for the annual (*sāṃvatsarika*) and other such rites, which are modifications (*vikṛti*) of the *amāvāsyā-śrāddha*, their determination follows precisely from the determination of the archetype (*prakṛti*). Therefore, how could there be any doubt regarding the cooking for the *amāvāsyā-śrāddha*, given the absence of conflicting opinions?

Now, what is the root of this conflict? It is the two opposite determinations—correct and incorrect—arising from a reason and a fallacious reason respectively, which depend upon different disputants. For instance, there arises an incorrect determination produced by a fallacious reason: "The daily *śrāddha* is performed with the same cooked food intended for the *vaiśvadeva* sacrifice; therefore, another [separate] rite must also be performed. Conversely, there is a correct determination: "Since there is no application of one purpose elsewhere without a specific cause, the *darśa-śrāddha* cannot be performed with the food intended for the *vaiśvadeva*. This is the root of doubt. Alternatively, for one who does not perceive a distinguishing feature, doubt arises from seeing both possibilities. Indeed, it is observed that even among many rituals, there is a rule that some are accomplished by a single cooking while others require multiple.

In this regard, the teacher Karka first established his own doctrine that the *śrāddha* should be performed with the very same food intended for the *vaiśvadeva* offering; he then presented the opposing doctrine—that it should be performed with a separate cooking—as a prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*). For instance: it is not possible for food already used for one purpose to be fit for use in another rite without a scriptural injunction. This is known from the injunction regarding the offering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*), which states: "Having asked permission regarding the remaining food, one should place the rice-balls near the leavings. Furthermore, if food already used elsewhere were inherently fit for use in another rite, then the food served to the Brahmins would by its very nature be fit for the act of offering rice-balls, and the request for permission would be redundant.

Furthermore, if the *śrāddha* were to be performed from the same food intended for the *vaiśvadeva*, then it would contradict the scriptural injunction: "Then one should perform the *gṛhabali* (household offering). For here, the *gṛhabali* is prescribed as occurring after the *śrāddha*; and that *gṛhabali* is a constituent part of the rite known as *vaiśvadeva*. Therefore, this very *vaiśvadeva* is what is being stated as occurring after the *śrāddha*. Since the *śrāddha* would have to precede this [if they shared the same food], that is not tenable; for the *vaiśvadeva*, which is accomplished by means of a cooking (*pāka*) prepared for its own sake, must come first, while the *śrāddha*, which subsists on what has been prepared for another, must come later. Nor should it be argued that one might cook solely for the purpose of the *śrāddha*, perform the *śrāddha*, and then perform the *vaiśvadeva* with that same cooking—thus making both rites share a single cooking (*ekapākatva*). For if there is a single cooking, since the *vaiśvadeva* is capable of accomplishing all rites that require food and subsists on the food prepared for its own sake, it does not necessitate a separate commencement of action; thus, the cooking for the *śrāddha* must indeed be distinct from the cooking for the *vaiśvadeva*. Having thus presented the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), he stated his own established conclusion (*siddhānta*): because the cooking intended for the *vaiśvadeva* is already available as it is required for all rites, or because of a specific scriptural statement regarding separate cooking, the *śrāddha* should also be performed using the very same food intended for the *vaiśvadeva*. For this very reason, by the injunction beginning with "But having completed the *pitṛyajña*," the performance of the five great sacrifices (*pañcamahāyajña*)—characterized by the *pitṛyajña* and including the ancestral water-libation (*tarpaṇa*), the *vaiśvadeva*, and the fire-oblation (*homa*)—is taught as occurring prior to the *śrāddha*. Then follows the *śrāddha*. This sequence is logical if the *śrāddha* subsists on the food intended for the *vaiśvadeva*; otherwise, since the *śrāddha* would be accomplished by a cooking independent of the other, it might even be performed before the *vaiśvadeva*. Nor should it be argued that this sequence applies to the *śrāddha* together with the *piṇḍapitṛyajña* alone, and not with the five great sacrifices such as the ancestral libations; for the *piṇḍapitṛyajña* is not denoted by the term "pitṛyajña" alone.

As for the injunction that one should perform the *gṛhabali* (household offering) after that—that is, after the *śrāddha*—it does not refer to the *bali* belonging to the five great sacrifices (*pañcayajña*), which consists of the *vaiśvadeva* offering; rather, it refers to another entirely, namely the worship of the deities of the site (*vāstudevatā*).

Furthermore, as for the formula of permission used during the offering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*), like the question regarding satisfaction, it is intended for the purpose of sanctifying the food in an invisible manner (*adṛṣṭa*), and not for the purpose of removing the defect of being subsequently employed in another ritual action.

This doctrine of the teacher Karka, together with its prima facie arguments and their refutations, is untenable. For that request for permission is not for the sake of offering the *piṇḍas*, but rather for the sake of [allowing] disposal according to one's desire. It is for this very reason that the granting of permission is in the form "let it be eaten along with those you wish," and not "let it be used for the sake of the *piṇḍas*. Furthermore, if this were the case, then whenever the offering of *piṇḍas* were to be performed prior to the feeding of the Brahmins, there would follow both the request for permission at the commencement of the Brahmin-feeding by asking "the remaining food? and the granting of permission in the form "let it be used for the feeding of the Brahmins."

As for what was stated—that since it is to be accomplished by cooking performed by oneself, one must first offer the domestic *bali*—that too is untenable as a prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), because for the Naiyāyika, the sequence [of actions] may occur otherwise due to the power of the verbal injunction. Furthermore, as for the claim that "all things already exist," that also is not correct; for it is determined that the daily cooking is solely for the purpose of the rites performed every day, and not for the sake of the *śrāddha* on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*) and so forth. And as for the statement beginning with "having completed the sacrifice to the ancestors" (*pitṛyajñaṃ tu nirvartya*), which asserts that the five great sacrifices (*pañcamahāyajña*), such as the water-libation (*udakatarpaṇa*) for the ancestors, should be performed prior to the *śrāddha*.

That is not so, because here the term *pitṛyajña* denotes the *piṇḍapitṛyajña*. For even the word *pitṛyajña* alone is seen to refer to the *piṇḍapitṛyajña* in passages from the *Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa*, such as: "Then he performed this with the *pitṛyajña*" and so forth. As for the statement, "But having completed the *pitṛyajña* called *tarpaṇa*," that too is not contradictory, as it merely restates the *piṇḍapitṛyajña* itself by the name *tarpaṇa* because it is a means of satisfaction (*tṛpti*).

Therefore, the established conclusion that the *amāvāsya* and other *śrāddhas* should be performed with the very same food cooked for the sake of the *vaiśvadeva* sacrifice is untenable. Consequently, this is stated: the cooking intended for the *amāvāsya* and other *śrāddhas* must indeed be distinct from that intended for the *vaiśvadeva*. For, once an oblation has been set aside for one [deity], it is certainly not offered to another. As for what was said by the teacher Karka—that there is no mention of separate cooking—that is incorrect; for Laugākṣi says:
"One should prepare the cooking for the sake of the ancestors and likewise for the sake of the *vaiśvadeva*."
The Vaiśvadeva rite is not for the sake of the ancestors, nor is the Darśa rite for the sake of the Vaiśvadevas.

In this context, although in the first half [of the verse] it might appear that one should prepare a single cooking for both purposes—thinking "one should prepare [the food] for both"—nevertheless, by the second half, a distinction between the two types of cooking is made clear: "The *vaiśvadeva* is not for the sake of the ancestors. Food cooked for the sake of the *vaiśvadeva* and for the sake of the daily fire-oblation (*nityahoma*) is called *vaiśvadeva*; that is not for the sake of the ancestors, nor is it for the sake of the *darśa-śrāddha*. This is because it is determined that the sacrifices performed daily—which are designated as sacrifices to the gods, ancestors, spirits, and humans—are accomplished by means of a single cooking; therefore, it is not for the sake of the *darśa-śrāddha*. Food cooked for the sake of the *darśa-śrāddha* is called *dārśa*; that is not for the sake of the *vaiśvadeva*. By the word "darśa" here, all *śrāddhas* ending with the *ekoddiṣṭa*—whether obligatory (*nitya*), occasional (*naimittika*), or optional (*kāmya*)—are indicated by way of secondary implication (*lakṣaṇā*), because they possess the same procedural requirements (*itikartavyatā*) as the *darśa-śrāddha*. By the word "vaiśvadeva," the sacrifice to beings (*bhūtayajña*), the sacrifice to ancestors (*pitṛyajña*), and the sacrifice to humans (*manuṣyayajña*) are also implied. But how can there be a suspicion that something intended for one purpose could serve another? For one does not accept the application of what has already been assigned to one thing to another purpose without a reason, even through secondary indication based on the underlying substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna-lakṣaṇā*).

True. It is not that the possibility of one thing serving another purpose when it already exists for a different purpose has been suspected or refuted here; rather, the suspicion regarding the *tantratā* (simultaneous performance) of the offering (*nirvāpa*) and the cooking (*pāka*) has been set aside. Furthermore, there is the possibility of *prasaṅga* (incidental application) where something existing for one purpose may also apply elsewhere. In that regard, *prasaṅga* and the suspicion [of it] arise because, when actions occurring at proximate times can be accomplished by a single cooking, there is an economy in the employment of the means of accomplishment. Here, as for what was stated by a portion of Laugākṣi’s statement—that "the Vaiśvadeva [rite] is not for the Darśa"—this is to be understood as applying only when the Vaiśvadeva is performed either before or during the Śrāddha, and not at a time subsequent to it.
For Paiṭhīnasi says:
"He who performs the Vaiśvadeva rite by taking food from the portion set aside for the ancestors—that śrāddha becomes asuric; it does not reach the ancestors."

But is it not the case that the word "having extracted" (*uddhṛtya*) is redundant? For it is impossible to perform an oblation (*homa*) without having first cut off a portion (*avadāya*). And cutting off a portion is simply the extraction of a part from the whole.

Not so. For here, by the term *pitṛpāka* (the cooking for the ancestors), the state of the cooking in which it has the ancestors as its designated deity (*saṃkalpita-pitṛ-daivatyatva*) is denoted. And the extraction (*uddharaṇa*) of a portion from that state is precisely the removal of that very state; it is not merely a division, nor is it that state itself. Furthermore, such removal is only possible once the connection with the previous deity has been severed. Therefore, this "extracts" (*uddharati*) signifies a removal from the ancestors as deities; it is not performed without having first established [the new recipient]. And this [removal] is possible either before or during the *śrāddha*, by setting aside a specific intention (*saṃkalpa*) of the form: "I shall perform this cooking, which has the ancestors as its deity, at the time of the offering (*nirvāpa*). It cannot, however, be done at a later time. For it is impossible to sever [the portion] from that which has already been relinquished in favor of the ancestors, since its status as having them as its deity is already accomplished. Indeed, what is already accomplished cannot be made unaccomplished.

[Objection: Surely we do not say that what is already accomplished is made unaccomplished; rather, it is said that it is destroyed. [Reply: Not so, because a cause of destruction is impossible. [Objection: If you say that the extraction performed with reference to another deity is the cause of destruction, [Reply: No, because there is no evidence that it destroys the connection with the previous deity when its purpose is merely to establish a connection with a subsequent deity. [Objection: Since the subsequent connection cannot be established without the destruction of the previous connection, its status as a destroyer of the former is inferred. [Reply: No, because the two connections are not mutually exclusive in a single substrate. [Objection: If you say that the cutting away (*āccheda*) taught by the scriptural injunction is the destroyer, [Reply: ... (text continues)

Not so. For being "dedicated to that deity" (tad-daivatyatva) consists precisely in the state of being relinquished with reference to that deity. And that state, having come into existence only after the completion of the act of relinquishment, has already perished. Therefore, what is there to be destroyed by the act of confiscation, and what is the meaning of the doctrine of "removal" (uddhṛtyavāda)? [Objection: But in this way, even for an object relinquished with reference to a deity presiding over an image or the like, the connection with the deity would have perished immediately after the relinquishment; consequently, since the substance would have been lost, there would be no fault of theft regarding the deity in the case of its seizure.

Not so. For, in the first place, regarding that substance which has been relinquished for the sake of being enjoyed as an image and so forth, its status as dedicated to that deity persists as long as the enjoyment lasts, because that status has enjoyment as its fruit; for if it were destroyed, it would be difficult to maintain the occurrence of the occasional (*naimittika*) state once the occasioning cause (*nimitta*) has ceased.

As for that substance whose enjoyment has been completed, let there be a prohibition against taking it—treating the deity’s ownership as a secondary characteristic (*upalakṣaṇa*)—just like a *nirmālya* (an offering already used). Therefore, since the connection of the cooked food with the ancestors (*pitṛ-sambandha*) has perished after the *śrāddha*, what is there to be destroyed by a confiscation? In reality, however, there is no connection with the ancestors at all in the remnants of the *śrāddha*; what, then, could be destroyed? For in the case of remnants of what has been consumed, that [connection] exists merely as a secondary characteristic; and in such a state, it does not deserve to be revoked. Now, why is it not explained as "having set aside from the remnants of the ancestral cooking, one should divide [the portions]"? That has already been largely answered by the point regarding the futility of such a removal. Therefore, the meaning of the statement is this: if one performs the *vaiśvadeva* rite after having set aside [food] from the cooking intended for the ancestors—whether the ancestral rite has not yet begun or is still incomplete—that *śrāddha* becomes *āsura* (demonic). And this is logical. Even common people consider any act improper if something prepared for a specific purpose is given to another without first being offered to that intended recipient—even if it is a worldly matter. How much more so when something is prepared for the ancestors or the deities, yet given to another beforehand! But when it is given to that intended recipient and then given to another, no one considers it defiled or improper. Furthermore, it has been stated that even the food intended for the *śrāddha* may be employed in the *vaiśvadeva* rite after the time of the *śrāddha*.
And so says Paiṭhīnasi:
"Having performed the Śrāddha according to the rules, one should then perform the Vaiśvadeva and other rites; thereafter, one should give alms and likewise offer betel-nut and other such items."

Here, by the word *tataḥ* (from that) in the first [verse], the meaning of the preceding verse is stated as a reason. By the second [word], it is stated: "from the food remaining after the *śrāddha*. Thus, the meaning is this: since the *śrāddha* would become *āsura* if the *vaiśvadeva* were performed with food extracted from the *pitṛ-pāka* (the cooking for the ancestors) prior to the *śrāddha*, therefore, having completed the *śrāddha*, one should take a portion from that food remaining after the *śrāddha* and perform the *vaiśvadeva* and other rites. Nor should it be argued here that the food is unfit to be referred to by the pronoun *tat* because it was not previously mentioned; for in the preceding verse, "having extracted [food] from the *pitṛ-pāka*," the food is introduced. That which is proximate is what is referred to by a pronoun. Nor is there a rule that proximity exists only through explicit mention; rather, it is accepted that proximity consists in being present in the mind (*buddhi-saṃnidhi*).

Here, by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), all daily rites (*naityaka-karma*) accomplished through food are included. Consequently, the obligatory *śrāddha* (*nitya-śrāddha*) must also be performed using the remnants of the cooking employed for the *darśa-śrāddha*. Thus, if one performs the *vaiśvadeva* at the conclusion of the dismissal of the Brahmins, it is done with that very same cooking intended for the *śrāddha*. However, if one performs the *vaiśvadeva* at any of the times prior to the dismissal of the Brahmins—in the manner to be described later—then it is to be performed with a separate cooking. Regarding this, the author of the *Smṛticandrikā* states:

Having cited the statement of Laugākṣi beginning with “one should offer cooked food for the sake of the ancestors” and ending with “this is not the Vaiśvadeva portion of the Darśa,” and having explained that food set aside for the purpose of the Darśa-śrāddha does not become available for the Vaiśvadeva even after the śrāddha has been performed, he further stated that this refers specifically to the case of a Darśa-śrāddha performed by one who maintains the sacred fires (*sāgnika*). He provided the following reasoning: since the Vaiśvadeva is prescribed for one who maintains the fires *prior* to the Darśa-śrāddha, it is impossible to perform the Vaiśvadeva at the end of the śrāddha using the remnants of the śrāddha. However, this very reasoning establishes a meaning that is precisely the opposite of what he intended to convey. Since there is no possibility of performing the Vaiśvadeva at a later time (after the śrāddha), there can be no point in prohibiting it; therefore, this prohibition must apply only to the earlier time, and thus it would concern both those with and without the sacred fires (*sāgnika* and *anagnika*). If it is argued that, despite the impossibility of the prohibition due to the lack of such a contingency, it may be a mere restatement (*anuvāda*) of an obligatory rule, then two faults would follow: first, the fault of being a redundant restatement (*anuvādatva*), and second, the fault of purposelessness (*ānarthakya*). Furthermore, there would be an inconsistency: if this applies exclusively to those with the sacred fires, it would have to refer to both the Vaiśvadeva performed before the śrāddha and the one performed after. In that case, the injunction would be a prohibition regarding the former, while it would be a redundant restatement of a prohibition regarding the latter. Therefore, because the Vaiśvadeva prescribed for times prior to the dismissal of the Brahmins is prohibited from sharing the same cooking vessel (*pākaikyaniṣedha*) as the śrāddha, let the statement of Laugākṣi apply to both those with and without the sacred fires. As for the one who thinks... [text ends].
Having performed the śrāddha according to the rules, one should then perform the vaiśvadeva and other rites.

By such statements as these, one should be informed as follows: the injunctions prescribing the performance of the *vaiśvadeva* and other rites with the remnants of the *śrāddha* apply to *śrāddhas* such as the annual (*pratisāṃvatsarika*) ones, which are modifications (*vikṛti*) of the *darśa-śrāddha*; however, the rule "not the *dārṣa-vaiśvadevika*" applies specifically to the *darśa-śrāddha* itself. All these general rules are taught in reference to the *darśa-śrāddha* alone; there is no *anārabhyavāda* (independent injunction) here whatsoever. Even if such an independent injunction were to exist, nevertheless, by the maxim "or [it belongs] to the archetype (*prakṛti*) because of being stated twice,"—just as in the case of the rule "his *juhū* ladle is made of *parṇa* wood"—there is a fixed rule that it must belong to the archetype, and thus its application is restricted to the *darśa-śrāddha* alone. If it is argued that an independent injunction (*anārabhyavāda*) finds its place in a modification (*vikṛti*) when the archetype is already occupied by contradictory duties taught in reference to it (*ārabhyādhīta*), that is not so; for the contradiction with what is taught in reference to the archetype has already been resolved by the aforementioned determination of the scope (*viṣaya-vyavasthā*). Therefore, it must be stated here whether this injunction pertains to the *darśa-śrāddha* or not.
Regarding the division of cooked food prior to the offering of the *piṇḍas*, another Smṛti states:

"That which is cooked for the sick, for those who have renounced the world, and for children, one should not perform the *vaiśvadeva* rite; nor should one perform it for that which is cooked for the purpose of a *śrāddha*."

Likewise: The food prepared for a *śrāddha* should not be given to one who maintains the domestic fire, to a child, to a deity, to an ascetic (*yati*), or to a student (*brahmacārin*), as long as the rice balls (*piṇḍas*) have not been offered.
Pracetas has also said:
"Having performed the *bali* offering from the domestic cooking and having completed the sacrifice to the ancestors (*pitṛyajña*),
one should first offer that food which has been set aside for them."

The term *gṛhya* refers to that which pertains to domestic rites (*gṛhyakarma*). Here, the *bali* offering is the *vaiśvadeva*. Having "completed" (*nirvartya*)—that is, finished—the *pitṛyajñiya*, which is the *piṇḍapitṛyajña* together with its ancillaries (*sāṅga*), "then" (*tataḥ*), immediately thereafter, one should "announce"—that is, offer—that food which has been set aside for the purpose of the *śrāddha* "to them," meaning to those intended as the recipients of the *śrāddha*, "first" (*agre*), i.e., previously. By implication, one should give it to others at a later time.
This is the determination regarding the *vaiśvadeva* cooking.
Now follows the determination regarding the time for the *vaiśvadeva*.

In this regard, first, there arises the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) concerning the doubt as to whether or not one who maintains no sacred fires (*anagnika*) should perform the *vaiśvadeva* offering prior to the *śrāddha*. According to the injunction for the *vaiśvadeva* itself—namely, "one should perform the *vaiśvadeva* oblation"—it follows that the *vaiśvadeva* performed by one who maintains no fires must be performed at some time; thus, its performance at the time preceding the *śrāddha* is already established as an optional possibility. As for the prohibition of that prior timing found in the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*: "If the daily oblation is performed at the beginning of the *śrāddha*, the gods do not accept the *havya* and likewise the ancestors do not accept the *kavya*."
And as for the prohibition made by Gautama:
"He who performs the Vaiśvadeva rite without first performing the ancestral Śrāddha—that Śrāddha becomes as if unperformed; it does not reach the ancestors."

It should be understood that the performance of the Vaiśvadeva rite must occur at the time preceding the Śrāddha cooking itself, and not when performed with a separate cooking. For this very reason, Vasiṣṭha states that once the Vaiśvadeva has been performed, the remainder of the food is unfit for the Śrāddha:
"One who maintains no sacred fire (anagnika) should perform the Śrāddha even without having performed the Vaiśvadeva;
however, if the oblation is offered in the common (laukika) fire, the remainder does not reach the ancestors."
And regarding this very point, the statement of Paiṭhīnasi has been shown: "Having set aside [a portion] from the food cooked for the śrāddha," and so forth.

This [text] does not prohibit the performance of the Vaiśvadeva after having set aside a portion from the food cooked for the śrāddha at a time subsequent to the śrāddha. Even in the view of one who considers that the verb *uddharati* in the phrase "having set aside from the śrāddha-cooking" denotes merely a separation, there would arise a contradiction with the requirement to perform the remnants of the śrāddha as established by such statements as "having completed the śrāddha according to rule. Therefore, for one without a sacred fire (*anagnika*), the Vaiśvadeva-homa before the śrāddha using a different cooking is not prohibited by anyone; thus, it must be performed by him as well.

It is said: since it is prescribed that the Vaiśvadeva rite is to be performed with the remnants of the *śrāddha* food at the time following the *śrāddha*, its performance is prohibited using a portion extracted from the *śrāddha* cooking itself; therefore, those [texts] are explained as referring to times other than that. Likewise, because the Vaiśvadeva is entirely forbidden at a time prior to the *śrāddha*, they must also be explained as referring to times other than that. Thus, for one who maintains no sacred fire (*anagnika*), the Vaiśvadeva may be performed even with the *śrāddha* cooking at the time after the *śrāddha*. However, during the course of the *śrāddha* itself, it is never to be done with the *śrāddha* cooking, but only with a separate cooking. But prior to the *śrāddha*, it is not to be performed at all.

[Objection: Surely, there would result a threefold restriction regarding all prohibitions against performing the *vaiśvadeva* offering as part of a single cooking (*ekapāka*). For instance: (1) the agent in general—which is implied by the verbal root and denoted by the suffix, or denoted by the suffix and delimited by number—would be restricted from its two-fold scope (both those with and without a sacred fire) to the specific case of only one who lacks a sacred fire; for the *vaiśvadeva* performed by one with a sacred fire is necessarily prior in time and thus cannot occur at the intermediate time [of the *śrāddha*]. This is the restriction of the agent. (2) The restriction of the action: the generic action of *vaiśvadeva*, which is understood from the word *vaiśvadeva* alone and pervades many individual instances of *vaiśvadeva* occurring at both prior and intermediate times, would be restricted to a single instance of *vaiśvadeva* occurring simultaneously with the *śrāddha*. Precisely for this reason, there is a restriction of time. Thus, a threefold restriction results. Furthermore, if this were the case, the requirement that the *vaiśvadeva* performed by one with a sacred fire be accomplished through the same cooking as the *śrāddha* would not be negated. And if the prohibition of priority applied only to one without a sacred fire, there would be a restriction of the agent. [Response: To this it is replied: First, this must be considered. Is this prohibition—"the *vaiśvadeva* oblation is not to be performed before the *śrāddha*"—to be explained as applying to both those with and without a sacred fire, by being construed as a single syntactic unit with another sentence such as "it is not to be performed apart from the *śrāddha* cooking," in order to maintain the connection between the agent in general (understood from the verbal root) and the action in general? Or is it to be taken as applying only to one without a sacred fire, as a prohibition of the *vaiśvadeva* in its mere essential form, in accordance with the literal sense of the text? Regarding this:
Because of independence, because of the abandonment of what is heard [in the text], because of the transition to another thing to be enjoined,
and because of the consequence of meaninglessness, this [statement] does not form a single syntactical unit with anything else.
Nor is its connection with that which possesses fire perceived as having occurred previously,
because it is sublated by the instruction regarding the prior time.
In this case, the fault of mutual dependence (anyonyāśraya) would clearly follow regarding the positive concomitance (anvaya);
for positive concomitance exists when there is a single unified statement, and that [unified statement] occurs only when the positive concomitance has already been established.
Nor can a connection [of the words] be established by recalling their syntactic unity with the thing to be proven,
by one who recognizes the multitude of faults already set forth.
Nor is it held that the authority of a ritual manual (*kalpa*) is supported by the sublation of perception;
