for the ritual manual, through its commonality of authorship, sublates the scriptural prohibition.

A statement whose purpose is established even by the prohibition of the nature of the *vaiśvadeva* does not require syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) with another statement; nor does the other statement require it. If there were such syntactic unity, the prohibitive injunction would lose its status as having the expressed prohibition of the nature of the *vaiśvadeva* as its purport, and instead would have to be assumed to have the purport of prohibiting the performance of the *śrāddha* cooking. This being the case, even the charge of pointlessness (*ānarthakya*) does not apply, because the purpose is fulfilled by those very [texts] that prohibit the performance of the *śrāddha* from a single cooking. This is the meaning of the first verse. The second and subsequent verses, however, have their meanings clearly evident. Therefore, this prohibition—that the *vaiśvadeva* is not to be performed before the *śrāddha*—refers exclusively to one who maintains no sacred fires (*anagnika*). The prohibitions regarding the performance of the *śrāddha* cooking, on the other hand, refer to both those who maintain the fires (*sāgnika*) and those who do not. Among these, since for the fireless person (*anagnika*) the *vaiśvadeva* is prohibited at all times prior to the *śrāddha*, the texts take him as the agent performing the *vaiśvadeva* during the intermediate period. For the one who maintains the fires (*sāgnika*), however, he is the agent during the earlier period. Consequently, the previously mentioned defects of over-narrowing (*saṅkoca*) do not apply. However, a restriction of those [prohibitions] away from the earlier time of the fireless person is indeed logical based on the explicit scriptural statement; therefore, the fireless person must never perform the *vaiśvadeva* prior to the *śrāddha*. Furthermore, the rule prescribing the intermediate and later periods also concerns exclusively the fireless person, since for him the *vaiśvadeva* has been precluded from the earlier period. Nor should it be said that the prohibition is useless because it resides within a Smṛti text; for if, in this way, even the claim of a general connection with the agent fails to achieve syntactic unity with another statement, how much less will it achieve a connection with a specific particular such as the fireless person?
Regarding the necessity of performing the Vaiśvadeva rite during the course of a Śrāddha, the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa states:
"One should offer the Vaiśvadeva oblations into the fire prior to the feeding of the Brāhmaṇas;
it is traditionally taught that one should perform the Bhūtayajña and other rites after having completed the Śrāddha."

By the statement, “prior to the feeding of the Brāhmaṇas,” it is indicated that one should offer the Vaiśvadeva oblations immediately after the *agnaukaraṇa*. By the statement, “having performed the Śrāddha, the *bhūtayajña* and so forth are prescribed,” it is shown that the *bhūtayajña* alone is to be performed at the conclusion of the Śrāddha; thus, since its purpose has been fulfilled, the offering of the *bali* should be made immediately after the Vaiśvadeva oblations—so says the author of the *Smṛticandrikā*.
This is one time for the Vaiśvadeva rite for those without a sacred fire (*anagnika*); a second time is also mentioned in the *Bhaviṣyatpurāṇa*:
“Having gratified the ancestors according to the rule, one should offer the *bali* according to the injunction.”
Then one should perform the Vaiśvadeva rite, followed by the recitation by the Brāhmaṇas.
The word *bali* is also explained in that very same place:

"O Hero, know that whatever a wise man should cast upon the ground with a mantra for those who have been consumed by fire— that is always to be understood as the *bali* offering in the rite of *śrāddha*."

By this, it is stated that one should perform the *vaiśvadeva* rite after offering the *bali* known as the *vikira* and prior to the recitation of the *svasti-vācana*. This constitutes the second time for its performance. A third time is also mentioned in the *Smṛtis*, *Purāṇas*, and other sources. Regarding this, Manu says:
"The remnants of the meal should remain until the Brahmins have been dismissed;
thereafter, one should perform the domestic *bali*—thus is the law established."
The commentary on this, composed by Medhātithi, is stated as follows.

While the twice-born are eating, the food that remains stuck to the vessels used for eating or has fallen upon the ground must not be wiped away from that spot until the Brāhmaṇas have departed. Then, once the Śrāddha rite is completed, one should immediately perform the Vaiśvadeva oblation and the daily duties such as feeding guests; this is because the word *bali* is intended to be illustrative. Others, however, say that the term *bali* is more commonly known to refer specifically to the *bhūtayajña* (sacrifice to beings), and therefore the performance of the fire-oblation (*agnau homa*) prior to the Śrāddha is not contradictory. One should not argue: "How can another ritual act be performed in the midst of a rite dedicated to the ancestors (*pitrya*) when it has already begun? For just as there is no contradiction in performing the morning and evening fire-oblations (*homakaraṇa*) before the Śrāddha when the Brāhmaṇas have been invited on the previous day—even though the Śrāddha itself has not yet been performed—likewise, there is no contradiction in performing the Vaiśvadeva oblation belonging to the *aupasadika* period in the interim. Therefore, when the *bhūtayajña* is postponed, by the principle of postponing what follows the first (*tadādyutkarṣanyāya*), the items subsequent to the *bhūtayajña* are postponed, but those preceding it, such as the Vaiśvadeva, are not. To this it is replied: If the Vaiśvadeva oblation were performed before the Śrāddha, then the Śrāddha would come first and the *baliharaṇa* (the offering of the *bali*) afterwards; in that case, the *devayajña* and *bhūtayajña* would become separated. Consequently, the established sequence consisting of immediate succession between the two—as taught in such injunctions as "one should perform the Vaiśvadeva and likewise the daily *bali"—would be subverted. Indeed, the principle of postponing up to the end (*tadantotkarṣa*) is also resorted to precisely to avoid subverting a fixed sequence. Therefore, in order not to subvert that [sequence], the postponement up to the end should be adopted in some cases. Nor does this result in a contradiction with the rule regarding the postponement starting from the first (*tadādyutkarṣa*). For that rule is mandatory only where the postponement of the first item would subvert its own sequence and time. And even when the Śrāddha has been performed, the performance of the Vaiśvadeva does not subvert the sequence and time pertaining to the latter. Therefore, the performance of all the Great Sacrifices (*mahāyajña*) occurs after the Śrāddha. [On MDh 3.255]
Here ends the commentary composed by Medhātithi.
This same point is stated in the *Matsyapurāṇa*:
"The remnants of the meal should remain until the Brahmins have been dismissed."
"Then one should perform the Vaiśvadeva rite once the ancestral rites (pitṛkarman) have been concluded. Thus it is said in the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa:
"O mighty-armed one, having performed the Śrāddha and having dismissed the Brāhmaṇas..."
Then, O lord of men, he should perform the Vaiśvadeva and other rites. As stated in another Smṛti:
"When a man desires to give a Śrāddha to the ancestors..."
Then, once the śrāddha rite has been completed, one should perform the vaiśvadeva offering.
Paiṭhīnasi says:
"Having performed the Śrāddha according to the rules, one should then perform the Vaiśvadeva and other rites; thereafter, one should give alms and likewise offer betel nuts and so forth."
Upon the completion of the *śrāddha*, Mārkaṇḍeya says:
"Then one should perform the daily rites and likewise feed the guests;
thereafter, the man should eat that food together with his servants and others."

The *nityakriyā* consists of the *vaiśvadeva-homa*, the offering of oblations (*bali-haraṇa*), the daily ancestral rite (*nitya-śrāddha*), and so forth. Thus, for one who performs the *vaiśvadeva* and other rites without a sacred fire (*anagni-kartṛka*), there are three times: one immediately after the *agnaukaraṇa*; another after the scattering of rice (*vikira*); and a third after the dismissal of the Brahmins. This concludes the determination of the times for the *vaiśvadeva* performed by those without a sacred fire.
Now follows the determination of the *vaiśvadeva* performed by those with a sacred fire (*sāgni-kartṛka*).

Its performance occurs neither in the middle of the *śrāddha* nor at its conclusion, but rather while the *śrāddha* has not yet been performed; for the *piṇḍapitṛyajña* is prescribed before the *śrāddha*, and the *vaiśvadeva* is even prior to that.
Thus says Devala: "But when the *vaiśvadeva* has not been performed, the *sthālīpāka* offerings are prescribed."
But apart from the piṇḍayajña, it is prescribed for the afternoon.

In this context, the rites accomplished by means of the *sthālīpāka* (pot-cooking) are designated by the term *sthālīpāka*. These, being distinct from the *piṇḍapitṛyajña*, are performed even when the *vaiśvadeva* has not yet been performed. However, the *piṇḍapitṛyajña* is performed later in the afternoon, after the *vaiśvadeva* has been completed.
Furthermore, Manu has stated that the *pitṛyajña* precedes the *śrāddha*:
"A Brahmin who maintains the sacred fires, having performed the *pitṛyajña* on the new moon day..."
"One should perform the *piṇḍānvāhāryaka* Śrāddha every month.
Regarding this very point, Laugākṣi states clearly:
"Having performed the rites at the end of the fortnight and the *vaiśvadeva* sacrifice, one who maintains the sacred fires [should perform the Śrāddha]."

"Then the wise man should perform the piṇḍayajña, and after that, the anvāhāryaka. Here, "the rite at the end of the fortnight" refers to the *agnyanvādhāna*; "anvāhārya" refers to the *darśaśrāddha*.

Now, since the Vaiśvadeva is prescribed precisely between the Pakṣādi-sthālīpāka and the Piṇḍapitṛyajña, its performance by one who maintains the sacred fires (*sāgnika*) is already understood; why, then, is the term *sāgnika* explicitly mentioned? It is for the purpose of excluding the *aupāsana* fire from the performer of the Piṇḍapitṛyajña who is without sacred fires (*niragni*). Therefore, like others who are without sacred fires, even such a person must perform the Vaiśvadeva at the times previously stated in the section [of the text]. Gobhila also states in this sūtra—“either before the ancestral rite (*pitrya*) or after the words of benediction (*svastyayana-vākya*)”—that the Vaiśvadeva occurs at the very beginning of every kind of Śrāddha. Even in the Śruti, the Vaiśvadeva is heard of as occurring first for one who maintains the sacred fires: “They should not eat what has not been offered, nor should they give what has not been offered. However, in a specific type of Śrāddha, even for one who maintains the sacred fires, the Vaiśvadeva occurs only afterwards.
And so it is stated in the *Pariśiṣṭa*:
"When the *pārvaṇa* śrāddha or likewise the *ekoddiṣṭa* has arrived, the Vaiśvadeva rite should take place first; on the eleventh day, however, it should be performed afterwards."

In this context, the mention of the *pārvaṇa* [śrāddha] is intended as an illustration for those rites dedicated to multiple deities. Consequently, the determination is that for one who maintains the sacred fires (*sāgnika*), the *vaiśvadeva* offering must be performed prior to all *śrāddhas* except for the eleventh-day rite (*ekādaśāhika*); however, in the case of the eleventh-day rite alone, it is performed afterwards.
Thus said Śālaṅkāyana:
"One who maintains the sacred fires should perform the *vaiśvadeva* indeed before the *śrāddha*."
"Excepting the rites of the eleventh day, for it is prescribed there at the end.
Thus concludes the determination of the time for the Vaiśvadeva performed by one who maintains the sacred fires (*sāgnika*).
Now follows the determination of the time for the *bhūtayajña* and other offerings.

On this point, the teacher Karka maintains that at the very time of the *vaiśvadeva* offering, immediately following it, is the *bali* known as the *bhūtayajña*. As for the *bali* to the household deities (*gṛhabali*) which Manu mentions at the end of the *śrāddha*—saying "one should perform the *bali* thereafter"—that is directed toward the deities of the site (*vāstudevatā*) and is not the one called *bhūtayajña*. For this very reason, Pāraskara, after describing the dismissal of the Brahmins, says:
"Having dismissed them, one should worship the household deities with the offering of the *bali*.
Śaṅkha-dhara also [states the same].

Whenever the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice is performed, at that very same time the Bhūtayajña must follow immediately thereafter. One must never allow an interruption between the Vaiśvadeva and the Bhūtayajña by performing other rites in the interval, because of the injunction regarding non-interruption. For it is said: "The Devayajña is prescribed first, and the Bhūtayajña follows after that."
Likewise: "One should offer the *bhūtabali* from the remnants of the food offered to the gods."

Furthermore, as for the statement regarding the *bhūtayajña* occurring after the *vaiśvadeva* has already been performed, its purpose is to indicate that even when the *bhūtayajña* has been performed immediately following the *vaiśvadeva*, one must perform that specific portion again as an integral part (*aṅga*) of the *śrāddha*. Likewise, as for the statement regarding the *gṛhabali* at the conclusion of the *śrāddha* after the *vaiśvadeva* has been performed, that too is intended for the sake of performing that specific portion again as an integral part of the *śrāddha*, even though the *gṛhabali* was already performed at the time of the *vaiśvadeva*. This [interpretation] is untenable. It contradicts the fact that the *bhūtayajña* and other such rites are parts of the *śrāddha* which serves the human purpose (*puruṣārtha*). If you argue that there is no contradiction because a single rite can serve both purposes according to the principle of "separateness of connection" (*saṃyogapṛthaktva*), we say no; for since no direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) or other evidence establishing the *śrāddha* as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) is observed, the principle of "separateness of connection" is not established here. If it is argued that this is simply a different ritual (*karmāntara*) whose status as a part of the *śrāddha* is established by the context (*prakaraṇa*), that too is not correct. This is because the *bhūtayajña* is recognized as being the very same rite serving the human purpose, just like the *vaiśvadeva*. Otherwise, in the rule "one should then perform the *vaiśvadeva*," there would follow the absurdity of prescribing a different *vaiśvadeva* as a part of the *śrāddha*. Nor is this logical, as it involves unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*). For in the case of merely prescribing the sequence, there is the merit of simplicity (*lāghava*) and the support of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*). Therefore, based on the explicit statement, even an interruption [of the sequence] may occasionally be accepted. And the statement has been shown by the author of the *Smṛticandrikā*: [The text continues with the cited verse.]

"One should offer the Vaiśvadeva oblations into the fire prior to the feeding of the Brāhmaṇas; however, it is traditionally taught that the Bhūtayajña and other rites are to be performed after having completed the Śrāddha. [1067] Nor should it be thought that because only the oblation (*āhuti*) is mentioned here, the *baliharaṇa* (food offering) which is an ancillary part of the Vaiśvadeva must not be performed afterwards. This is because the latter half of the verse prescribes the Bhūtayajña and the others specifically for the time immediately following the Śrāddha. For this very reason...
"One should perform the Vaiśvadeva and the daily bali offering.
Thus, within the very section on Śrāddha, the *Matsya Purāṇa* has stated the immediate succession of these two.
This concludes the determination of the time for the sacrifice to beings (*bhūtayajña*) and the others.
Now follows the determination of the times for the daily *śrāddha*.

Although the daily *śrāddha* has already been determined within the section on the sacrifice to beings (*bhūtayajña*) and others, it is introduced again here in order to state certain specific details.
Regarding this, Mārkaṇḍeya says:
Then he should perform his daily rites and likewise feed the guests;
thereafter, the man should eat that food together with his servants and others.

"Thereby"—that is, by means of that food remaining from the *śrāddha*—"the daily rite" (*nityakriyā*) which is accomplished through food; therefore, the daily *śrāddha* (*nityaśrāddha*) should also be performed with that very same [food]. Alternatively, the daily *śrāddha* should be performed with a separate cooking (*pāka*). This is because, since it consists of a *śrāddha*, there is the possibility of employing a separate cooking for that which constitutes the *śrāddha* rite.

For this very reason, with reference to the daily *śrāddha*, it is stated in the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*: "The daily [rite] is [performed] with a separate cooking. The meaning of this is: the daily *śrāddha* should be performed with a cooking separate from the cooking used for the *śrāddhas* of the new moon day (*darśa*) and so forth.

Others, however, say "no" to this; the meaning is that they believe the obligatory *śrāddha* (nitya-śrāddha) should also be performed with the remnants of the cooked food from the *śrāddha* of the new moon (*darśa*) and other such occasions. And this [obligatory rite] is not mandatory when another *śrāddha* has already been performed. As it is said in that very same place: "Some men desire the obligatory rite for the ancestors."
Nor for the ancestors; likewise, one should perform the remaining rites as previously described.

The "daily rite for the ancestors" (*pitṛṇāṃ nityakriyā*) refers to the daily *śrāddha* (*nityaśrāddha*). Regarding this alternative form of the daily *śrāddha*, the following rule applies: in the case of *śrāddhas* performed on common occasions such as the new moon (*amāvāsyā*), as well as in *nāndīmukha* and *tīrtha-śrāddhas*, the daily *śrāddha* need not be performed separately because it is accomplished by way of incidental connection (*prasaṅga-siddhatayā*), since the deities of the daily *śrāddha* are already intended to be worshipped there. However, in the case of annual *ekoddiṣṭa* rites and the like, the daily *śrāddha* must certainly be performed, because there is no fixed rule that all the deities of the daily *śrāddha* are to be sacrificed to in those specific rites. As for the "remainder," such as the *vaiśvadeva* offering and so forth, one should "perform it as before"; the meaning is that one should perform it according to the established rule.
Thus it is said in the *Camatkārakhaṇḍa*:
"One should not perform the daily *śrāddha* where it is accomplished incidentally;
when another *śrāddha* has been performed elsewhere, one should not omit that [daily one] because of its obligatory nature."
Thus concludes the determination of the times for the daily *śrāddha*.
Now, regarding the prayers (*japya*):
therein, Bhṛgu states the prayers to be recited by the Brāhmaṇas who partake in the *śrāddha*.

When addressed, one should mutter the *dogdhṛ* mantra while seated; for those carrying a quiver, however, they should do so standing. Having eaten at a *śrāddha*, one does not incur fault if one recites the *Vāmadevya* hymn.

"Having been invited" means after having accepted the invitation; "the milch-cow" (*dogdhrīm*) refers to the fixed *yajus*-formulas beginning with "May the Brahmin be born endowed with Vedic luster" (*ā brahman brahmaṇo brahmavarcasī jāyatām*) and ending with "May our acquisition and security be provided for" (*yogakṣemo naḥ kalpatām*), which are indicated by such phrases as "the milch-cow. "Seated" means seated upon a seat of *darbha* grass prepared at the site of the *śrāddha*. Regarding "those bearing quivers": he should mutter these five mantras containing the word "quiver-bearer" (*niṣaṅgin*): the first is "Homage to him who runs with his full equipment, to the lords of beings"; the second is "Homage to the deceiver, to the one who deceives all around, to the lords of the sinews"; the third is "Homage to the bold and to the one who touches [all]"; the fourth is "Those who frequent the sacred bathing-places (*tīrthas*)"; and the fifth is "He with arrows in hand, he with quivers. Then he should mutter the *vāmadevya*, the triplet beginning with "With what [help], O Citra, will you come to us? (*kayā naś citra ābhuvat*). "Having eaten" means having consumed the food of the performed *śrāddha*; he should mutter this after the dismissal of the guests. The *vāmadevya* is a specific *sāman*, the triplet beginning with "With what [help], O Citra, will you come to us? (*kayā naś citra ābhuvat*).
Gobhila says:
One who has been invited should mutter the *doha* verses; one who is appointed [to the task] should mutter the *ṛṣabha* verses;
and having likewise muttered the *aniṣaṅga* verses right there, the best of the twice-born should eat.
Having eaten and sipped water, one should, with a concentrated mind, recite the *padastobhas* there,
and in the middle of that, the *gosūkta*, the *aśvasūkta*, and the *manīṣā*.
Having gone and sat down in a clean place, he should then recite the Vāmadevya hymn;
thus covered by the Sāman chants, the best of the twice-born may eat.
He is not defiled by the great faults associated with eating at a *śrāddha* feast;
for one who eats otherwise at offerings to the gods (*havya*) or the ancestors (*kavya*), being ignorant of the mantras,
causes himself and the giver of the food to fall into a demonic state.
Thus end the prayers to be recited by the Brahmins who partake of the *śrāddha*. Now follow the prayers to be recited by the patron (*yajamāna*).
Regarding this, Manu says:
At a rite for the ancestors, one should indeed cause [the guests] to hear the private recitation of the Veda, as well as the treatises on Dharma,
narratives, histories, Purāṇas, and the supplementary texts (khilas).

‘Svādhyāya’ refers to the Veda. ‘Dharmaśāstras’ are the treatises composed by Manu and others. ‘Ākhyānas’ include the Sauparṇa, Maitrāvaruṇa, Pāriplava, and so forth, which are recited in the Ṛgveda; there are also other ancient stories related to the ancestors, such as the narrative of the Seven Hunters (Saptavyādha) and others. ‘Itihāsas’ are the Mahābhārata and similar works. ‘Purāṇas’ are the scriptures characterized by the five topics beginning with creation (sarga). As it is said: “Creation, secondary creation, genealogy, the periods of the Manus (manvantaras), and the history of the dynasties (vaṃśānucarita). [1070]
And the *vaṃśānucarita*—thus the Purāṇa has five characteristics.

The term ‘*khilāni*’ refers to the *strīsūkta*, *mahānāmnikā*, and so forth. One should cause the Brāhmaṇas who are eating to hear these [texts], as found in the *Pādma*, *Mātsya*, and *Prabhāsakhaṇḍa* sections.
During the ancestral rite (paitrya), one should cause [the ancestors] to hear the recitation of sacred texts (svādhyāya), the Purāṇas, and the Khilas,
as well as various hymns of praise dedicated to Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Arka, and Rudra.
Regarding this, Śaṅkha and Likhita state a specific rule:
"With the *pavitra* in hand, seated upon *darbha* grass, one should mutter the verse, 'The winds are sweet' (*madhuvātā*).

“With the *pavitra* in hand” means with *darbha* grass in the hand. “Seated upon *darbha*” means sitting on top of *darbha* grass. One should mutter the three verses beginning with *madhuvātā ṛtāyate*. And this is intended as an illustration for all prescribed mutterings (*japa*). For it is stated in the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*: “With *kuśa* grass in hand, seated on *kuśa*, wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*upavītī*), one should then mutter the Vedic purifiers (*pavitra*), the *purāṇas*, and the *khilas*.”

In this context, the recitation of "madhuvātā" and so forth must be performed by one wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītī). However, that which is performed by the sacrificer in front of the Brāhmaṇas while they are eating must be done with the sacred thread over the left shoulder (yajñopavītī), as will be stated later.
Furthermore, Yama has stated that the recitation is to be performed at the beginning:
"One should properly cause [them] to hear the Vedic study and the Dharmaśāstras repeatedly."
One should recite various historical narratives in their presence;
being joyful oneself, one should gladden the Brahmins and feed them food slowly.
"In front of them" means before them.
Pracetās states that even one standing in front must act while facing [them]:
"While the Brahmins are eating, [one should recite] the characteristics of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma [Vedas]. [1071]
One should recite the mantra while facing [the deity], especially when it concerns the ancestors.

The phrase "characterized by the *Ṛg*, *Yajus*, and *Sāman*" has "that which is to be recited (*japyam*)" as its ellipsis. Among these, the *Ṛk* is that wherein the arrangement of quarters (*pāda*) is determined by the sense; the name *Sāman* applies to chants; and for the remainder, the word *Yajus* is used. "Pertaining to the ancestors" (*pitrya*) means having the ancestors as its deity. Regarding the *Nigama*:

while they are eating, one should recite purificatory mantras (*pavitramantra*), the *Ṛg*, *Yajus*, and *Sāman* verses, the *Itihāsas* and *Purāṇas*, the *Rakṣoghna* and *Pāvamānī* hymns, the verse beginning with "udīratām," those beginning with "avaram," those beginning with "adhvan," those beginning with "avatī," and mantras consisting of twelve or eight syllables and so forth.

The fifteen verses beginning with *rakṣoghnīḥ* and *kṛṇuṣva pājaḥ prasitiṃ na pṛthvīm*; the twenty-five verses beginning with *rakṣohaṇaṃ vājinam ājiṣṭham*; the twenty-five verses beginning with *indrāsomā tapataṃ rakṣa ujjalam*; the nine *pāvamānī* verses beginning with *agne haṃsi ny atriṇam*; the sixteen verses beginning with *punantu mā pitaraḥ*; the section beginning with *taratsamandī*; the thirty verses beginning with *pavasva viśvacarṣaṇe*; the thirty-two verses beginning with *tvaṃ sāmā*; the fourteen verses beginning with *udīratām avaraḥ*; the *madhumatī* verses beginning with *madhuvātā ṛtāyate*; those of similar form beginning with *tad vā narāsanayedam*; and the eleven verses beginning with *pinuṃ nu stoṣam*—these constitute the *annavatyaḥ*.
Baudhāyana says: One should cause the *madhūrcas* and the *pavitrāṇi* to be heard, and one should recite them softly.
The term *madhūrcas* refers to verses containing the word "honey" (*madhu*). The term *pavitrāṇi* refers to hymns such as the *Puruṣasūkta*.
Hārīta says:

Whatever one considers pure, one should recite the sixteen *pāvamānī* verses beginning with "May the fathers purify me," specifically reciting the first three. Whatever else one considers to have the characteristic of purification (*pāvana*), that too one should recite. These are the sixteen *pāvamānī* verses beginning with "May the fathers purify me. Among these, one should especially recite the first three mantras. Pracetās says:
The Yajus formulas, the Rudras, the verses that destroy demons,
the Pāvamānī hymns, the Purāṇas, and indeed the Dharmaśāstras.
The word "rudrān" means that one should recite the mantras that reveal Rudra, such as the Śatarudriya; this is the ellipsis [to be supplied].
In the context of the recurring term "japed" (one should recite), Śaṅkha and Likhita state:
"Having caused the Pavitra, the Dharmaśāstra, the Apratiratha, and the Gāyatrī to be heard in the middle."
The author of the Bhāṣya says that the *sāman* is the "Apratiratha. Others say it consists of the twelve verses beginning with "āśuḥ śiśānaḥ.
[Then] Viṣṇu [says]: "Then, while the Brahmins are eating, one should recite the hymns 'ye me prakāmāḥ', 'ahorātraiḥ', and 'yad vaḥ kravyāt', as well as the Itihāsas, Purāṇas, and Dharmaśāstras."
The explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) for this is stated in the *Āditya Purāṇa*:
"In the world of the ancestors, most wonderful rivers of nectar flow;
[this is so] when the *Itihāsas* and *Purāṇas* are recited during the ancestral rites."
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"Whatever [is ordained] for me by days and nights at my pleasure, and likewise whatever is for you, O flesh-eater;
as well as the *Itihāsas*, the *Purāṇas*, and the treatises on Dharma."
One should cause the twice-born who are eating to hear the supreme mantra of the seven flames (the Gāyatrī).
In the Saura Purāṇa: "Then one should cause the Brāhmaṇas to hear the Dharmaśāstras, the Purāṇas, as well as the Atharvaśiras, and the Aindra and Pauruṣa Sūktas."
In the Pādma, Mātsya, and Prabhāsa-khaṇḍas,
one should recite the Indreśa, Soma, and Sūkta hymns, as well as the Pāvamānī verses, according to one's ability.

The three hymns beginning with *surūpakṛtnu mūtayaḥ*, each consisting of ten verses, and the three hymns beginning with *indramid ghāthinaḥ*—these are dedicated to Indra (*aindrāṇi*). The eleven-verse hymn beginning with *imā rudrāya tavase kapardine*; the nine-verse hymn beginning with *kadrudrāya pracetase*; the fifteen-verse hymn beginning with *ā te pitar marutāṃ sumnam etu*; and the four-verse hymn beginning with *imā rudrāya sthiradhanvane giraḥ*—such are the hymns dedicated to Īśāna (*aiśānāni*). The four hymns beginning with *svādiṣṭhayā* are dedicated to Soma (*saumyāni*). [This is stated] in the *Bhaviṣyottara* and *Bhaviṣyat Purāṇas*.
While the twice-born are eating, one should recite the Śuddhavatī, Kūṣmāṇḍa, Pāvamānī, and Taratsamandī verses,
as well as the hymns that destroy demons, the Pitṛ-sūktas,
and other auspicious mantras.
Yājñavalkya:
Having recited the purificatory mantras until satiety, as well as the previously mentioned prayers, [one should proceed].

The "prior recitation" (*pūrvajapa*) consists of the *Gāyatrī* verse with the *Vyāhṛtis*, and so forth, as previously stated. For example, for the followers of the *Bahvṛca* school, it includes the nine-verse hymn beginning with "I praise Agni" (*agnim īḷe*), and "O Vāyu, come hither, O beautiful one" (*vāyav āyāhi darśata*). It also includes the twelve-verse hymn beginning with "May the Aśvins come, do not harm us" (*aśvinā yantv aririṣaḥ*), and "The singers sing thee, the Gāyatrī-singers" (*gāyanti tvā gāyatriṇaḥ*). Furthermore, there are eight verses beginning with "All have magnified Indra" (*indram viśvā avīvṛdhan*), and the fifty-two-verse hymn beginning with "Of this lovely, grey-haired Hotṛ" (*asya vāmasya palitasya hotuḥ*). There is also the section from the *Āraṇyaka* beginning with "O Maghavan, know, know the path" (*vidā maghavan vidā gātum*). However, for the followers of the *Sāṅkhyāyana* school, there is the nine-verse hymn beginning with "Nine indeed are the gods who increased hunger" (*navā u devāḥ kṣudham id vṛdhann aduḥ*). Finally, there are the eleven hymns beginning with "I praise Agni, the domestic priest" (*agnim īḷe purohitam*).
Now follow the recitations for those who study the Yajurveda.

Regarding this, Hārīta states: "O Pitṛs, here" is a Yajus; "Homage to you, O Pitṛs" is a Yajus ending with *smā*; "The winds are honey for the one who follows the Ṛta"—these three verses; and the section beginning with "May the Pitṛs purify me. Also, "O Soma, you are wise"—this is the Saṃhitā pertaining to the Pitṛs. By reciting these, one gratifies the Pitṛs, and for him, there is an inexhaustible [reward] for the Pitṛs.

"May we be the most excellent among them"—this is the end [of the formula]. Because it occurs in the context of the *yajus* formulas, the recitation of this by those who are eating before [the others] brings satisfaction to the ancestors (*pitṛs*). Furthermore, the food of these [ancestors] becomes inexhaustible.
Baudhāyana says: "And the *Sāman* chants that destroy demons, and the *yajus* formulas containing the word *svadhā*."

"Rakṣoghnāni" refers to those [mantras] possessing the characteristics for slaying demons (*rakṣas*), known by the name *devavrata*. "Staumbhikāni" refers to the *sāmans*. Alternatively, the *sāman* with the *prastāva* "dvā utviśyati śvitā," the *ūha* "vāho," and the *nidhana* "iḍā" is the demon-slaying (*rakṣoghnā*) *sāman*. With "sanād agne," the *prastāva* is "āhovohāsanād agnā iha mṛṇasi yātudhānān," and "viśvapāyā" is the *nidhana*. "Svadhāvanti" means those joined with the word *svadhā*, such as the *yajus* formulas beginning with "svadhāvibhyaḥ svadhā namaḥ.
[These are found] in the *Mātsya*, *Pādma*, and *Prabhāsa-khaṇḍas*.
Likewise, the Śāntikādhyāya and the Madhubrāhmaṇa,
as well as the Maṇḍalabrāhmaṇa and whatever else brings joy;
One should recite all of that— both for the Brahmins and for oneself—
the study of the Mahābhārata and its poetry, which is most dear to the ancestors.

The chapter on pacification (*śāntikādhyāya*) begins with "May the wind blow auspiciously for us" (*śanno vātaḥ pavatām*). The Madhu-brāhmaṇa begins with "This earth... (*iyaṃ pṛthivī...*). The Maṇḍala-brāhmaṇa begins with "That orb which shines... (*yad etan maṇḍalaṃ tapati...*). Likewise, whatever brings pleasure to the Brahmins while they are eating, as well as to himself—such as historical narratives (*itihāsākhyāna*) and the like, or the sounds of the lute (*vīṇā*) and flute (*veṇu*)—he should cause that also to be performed, just like the Vedic recitation (*vedajapa*), with a mind purified by faith.
And so it is said in the *Brahma-purāṇa*:
"Or he should present the sound of the lute and the flute to the Brahmins."
There are also other purifying recitations [to be performed] according to traditional practice. For example:

For the Taittirīyas: the sacrificial formulas (*yajūṃṣi*) beginning with *divo vā viṣṇava uta vā pṛthivyāḥ* and ending with *viṣṇave*; those beginning with *agna udadhiyāta iṣur yuvānām* and ending with *vanyapañcamaḥ*; the section (*anuvāka*) beginning with *rakṣohaṇo vo balagahano vaiṣṇavān khanāmi*; the section beginning with *somāya pitṛmate puroḍāśaṃ ṣaṭkapālaṃ nirvapet*; the section beginning with *uśantas tvā havāmahe uśantaḥ samidhīmahi*; the section beginning with *asau vā ādityo ’smin loke āsīt*; the section beginning with *dhruvāsi dharuṇāstṛtā*; the section beginning with *indro vṛtraṃ hatvā*; the two sections beginning with *vaiśvadevena vā prajāpatiḥ prajā asṛjata tā varuṇapraghāsair varuṇapāśād amuṃ cātayat*; the three sections beginning with *ayaṃ vā vayaḥ pavate*; the section beginning with *acāṃ prācī mahatī dig ucyate*; the five sections beginning with *amṛtopastaraṇam asi*; the three sections beginning with *brahmamerumām* (the *trisuparṇa* and others); the section beginning with *aṇor aṇīyān mahato mahīyān*; the four sections beginning with *medhāma indro dadātu medhā devī sarasvatī*; the section beginning with *na kaṃcana vasatau pratyācakṣīta* and ending with *ya evaṃ vedopaniṣat*.

For the Vājasaneyins, however, one should recite the Gāyatrī mantra together with the Praṇava and the Vyāhṛtis either three times or once; then the five verses beginning with *kṛṇuṣva pājaḥ* which destroy the Rākṣasas; the six sections beginning with *agnaye kavyavāhanāya svāhā*; the seventeen verses beginning with *surāvantam*; the nine ancestral mantras (*pitryamantra*) beginning with *ādyājānu*; the Puruṣasūkta consisting of sixteen verses beginning with *sahasraśīrṣā*; the seventeen verses beginning with *āśuḥ śiśānaḥ*; the six verses beginning with *apatirathaṃ yaj jāyata*; the Piṇḍapitṛyajña-Brāhmaṇa beginning with *śivamaṅkalpaṃ prajāpatiṃ vai bhūtāni*; the Pitṛyajña-Brāhmaṇa beginning with *mahāhaviṣā*; and [the section] beginning with *pañcaiva mahāyajñāḥ*.
The *Brahmayajñabrāhmaṇa* begins with "Where indeed of Indra... and so forth; the *Surāhomabrāhmaṇa* begins with "To the gods, to the Surās... and so forth.
For the Maitrāyaṇīyas, however, there are five sections (*anuvākas*) beginning with "For food thee," "For prosperity thee," "Ye are Vāyus," and "O God Savitṛ, you...

For the Kaṭhas, however, there is the section beginning with "To Soma accompanied by the Pitṛs, the ghee for the Pitṛs seated on the sacrificial grass (*barhiṣad*)," followed by the sections beginning with "We invoke you, who desire us... and the section beginning with "The Pitṛyajña is not before the [offering]... and so forth.
Now follow the recitations for the Chāndogas. Regarding this, Gobhila says:

"While they are eating, one should recite the Sāvitrī preceded by the Vyāhṛtis, as well as the Gāyatra [Sāman] upon it, the Pitryā Saṃhitā, and the Mādhuchandasa; thus one is magnified in the heavenly world, and this [merit] of his becomes inexhaustible."

"Let them eat" (*aśnantu*) refers to while they are eating. "Sāvitrī" is that which has Savitṛ as its deity, and that is indeed the *gāyatrī*. Regarding the *vyāhṛtis*, one should recite the other five, excluding the pair "mahaḥ" and "janaḥ. These are to be preceded by *prāṇāyāma* (breath control). According to the *Varatantu-smṛti*: "Having performed the five ending with *satya* preceded by *prāṇāyāma*, one should recite the *gāyatrī* together with the *praṇava* and the *vyāhṛtis*. The meaning is: having performed the five ending with *satya*—namely, *oṃ bhūḥ*, *oṃ bhuvaḥ*, *oṃ svaḥ*, *oṃ tapaḥ*, *oṃ satyam*—one should chant the *gāyatrī* preceded by the *praṇava* and the *vyāhṛtis* (*bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ*). And upon that *gāyatrī*, one should sing the *gāyatra-sāman*: "tat savitur vareṇyam" is the *prastāva*; "ā" is the *nidhana*. Alternatively, there are two verses beginning with "yad vā ja vi śya tiḥ" and "sanād agne akṣan na gām adantaḥ," and "abhivr̥taḥ pṛṣṭhaḥ arkaṃ samudraḥ kanikranti"—this is the *saṃhitā* for the ancestors (*pitryā*). The *sāman* for Mādhucchandasa is "tvām id āhyo naraḥ. Its *prastāva* is "tvām id āho ihīyonarā e"; the *nidhana* is "rasā gāḥ hā inu iḍā idaṃ hy anvojaseti," and the first and last [parts]. The *prastāva* of the first is "idam aihiyān na ojā asā"; the *nidhana* is "vāsā. The *prastāva* of the second is "ojasā"; the *nidhana* is "ghr̥taś cyutāḥ," and also "surūpakr̥tnum. The *prastāva* is "surūpakr̥tnum ūtaye sudughr̥svāmā"; the *nidhana* is "jyotīḥ pavasva soma madhumāṃśatāveti. The *prastāva* is "hā haiḍahāi ihāpavasva somamadhumārutāvā"; the *nidhana* is "drāyānāḥ."
In the Matsya, Padma, and Prabhāsa-khaṇḍas,
as well as in the Bṛhat and Rathantara [sections], likewise in the Jyeṣṭhasāman and Saraurava.

The word "should recite" (*japet*) is to be understood as the remainder of the sentence. The *Bṛhat* is the Sāman known by that name. Its *prastāva* is: *tvām iddhi havāmahāe*. Its *nidhana* is: *hassurathantaram*. The *prastāva* is: *abhitvā śūranonumo vo*. The *nidhana* is: *apsu*. The *Jyeṣṭhasāmans* are the three [Sāmans] sung upon this *ṛc*: *mūrdhānaṃ divaḥ*. Among them, the *prastāva* of the first is: *ājyadohaṃ mūrddhanaṇ dāi*. The *nidhana* is: *ājyadoham*. The *prastāva* of the second is: *tvidohaṃ mūrddhānam*. The *nidhana* is: *vyohaṃ mūrddhāi*. The *prastāva* of the third is: *vyohaṃ mūrddhādāi*. The *nidhana* is: *ṛtam*. The *prastāva* of the Sāman called *Raurava* is: *punānaḥ somādhārāyā*. The *nidhana* is: *ṇyayā ūho vā*.
Pracetas [taught] the Puruṣa-vratas, the Jyeṣṭha-sāmans, and various other [hymns].

The "Puruṣa-vratas" are the five Sāmans sung in the Puruṣasūkta. Among them, the Prastāva of the first is: *sahasraśīrṣā puruṣaḥ*; the Nidhana is *iṭ iḍā*. The Prastāva of the second is: *tripād ūrdhva udait puruṣaḥ*; the Nidhana is *ū*. The Prastāva of the third is: *puruṣa evedaṃ sarvam*; the Nidhana is *iṭ*. The Prastāva of the fourth is: *etāvān asya mahimā*; the Nidhana is *iṭ iḍā*. The Prastāva of the fifth is: *tato virāḍ ajāyata*; the Nidhana is *īṭ*. [Thus it is stated] in the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa.
One should cause the Sāman hymns of Āditya-Brahman, as well as those of Viṣṇu and Rudra,
to be heard at the Śrāddha, and likewise many others in abundance.

The *Ādityasāmans* are twenty-one Sāmans known as the *Ādityavrata*. "Brahma jajñānaṃ prathamaṃ purastāt" is the *Prastāva*; "Iḍā" is the *Nidhana*. The Sāmans of Viṣṇu and Rudra have been shown specifically for the Chāndogas in the *Puṣyagrantha*. "Idaṃ viṣṇuḥ," "prakṣasya vṛṣṇaḥ," "prakāvyam," and "uśale ca bruvāṇaḥ"—this is the Vārāha; and another is the *Puruṣavrata*. This is the Saṃhitā named Vaiṣṇavī; by employing this, one pleases Viṣṇu. "Āvorājā," "tad vo vargaḥ," the *Ājyadohas*, and the *Devavratas*—this is the Saṃhitā named Raudrī; by employing this, one pleases Rudra. Other Sāmans should also be sung according to established practice (*sāmācāra*). For example, those of the Śārdūla-branch: "Sa pūrvo mahānām" has the *Madhuśrut* as its *Nidhana*; the *Prastāva* is "sa pūrvomihānām," and the *Nidhana* is "madhuśrutāḥ. "Purām bhindur yuvā kaviḥ" is the Māruta; the *Prastāva* is "purām bhindur yuvā kaviḥ," and the *Nidhana* is "puruṣṭutāḥ. "Ho iḍā upaprakṣe madhumatī kṣiyantaḥ" is the Vācasāman; the *Prastāva* is "oṃ vā upaprakṣe madhumatī kṣiyantaḥ oṃ vā," and the *Nidhana* is "ūpā. These seven sections beginning with "tāi ho vāca" belong to the Kauthuma branch. Or, the fifteen Sāmans beginning with "yad vā uviśyatir" constitute the chapter "asau vā ādityo deve madhye" for the Rāṇāyanīya branch. The Mahānāmnī Sāman: the *Prastāva* is "e vidā maghavan vidā," and the *Nidhana* is "evā hi devāḥ."
Now follow the recitations for those who know the Atharvaveda:

the Apratiratha hymn beginning with "The vehicle of Indra"; the three Prāṇa-hymns beginning with "Obeisance to Prāṇa"; the Puruṣa-hymn beginning with "Thousand-armed is the Puruṣa"; the Kāla-hymn beginning with "May Time, the horse with seven reins, carry [us]"; and the Upaniṣad concerning the inner self (*adhyātma*), namely the *Prāṇāgnihotra-mahopaniṣad*. In the event that the performance of all these aforementioned types of recitation is impossible, an alternative method is stated in the *Matsyapurāṇa*:

In the absence of all these vidyās, one should begin the recitation of the Gāyatrī. Furthermore, there are other mantras to be recited mentioned in the Purāṇas. Among them is the Saptārci-mantra, found in the Viṣṇudharmottara, Bhaviṣyatpurāṇa, Brahmavaivarta, Brahmapurāṇa, Vāyupurāṇa, Prabhāsakhaṇḍa, and Bhaviṣyottara.
It is said: "It destroys sin, it is purifying, and it is equal to the Aśvamedha sacrifice."
Therefore, I shall declare the mantra, which is nectar created by Brahmā.
Salutations to the deities, to the ancestors, and to the great yogis; salutations to Svadhā and Svāhā, always, salutations again and again.
One should always recite this three times at the beginning and the end of a Śrāddha ceremony;
for when honored and worshipped by the twice-born, it yields the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice.
The ancestors attain satisfaction and the Rākṣasas flee;
moreover, this mantra delivers the ancestors throughout the three worlds.
One who desires sovereignty should always recite this mantra without weariness during a *śrāddha* ceremony, while being attended by disciplined exponents of the Veda.
This increases vigor, all success, heroism, fortune, and longevity;
by means of this recitation and observance, the ancestors are gratified.
Thus ends the mantra of Saptārcis. Now follows the Viṣṇuhṛdaya mantra, according to the Gāruḍa Purāṇa.
Whoever, being self-restrained, recites the Viṣṇuhṛdaya mantra during śrāddha ceremonies,
by him the ancestors are gratified as if with milk and ghee.
May that Viṣṇu be gracious to me, who is offered oblations with four, four, two, and five, and again with two.
I bow to that Acyuta, by whose remembrance and by whose name being uttered, whatever is deficient in asceticism, sacrifice, ritual acts, and so forth, immediately attains completeness.
One who is faithful, self-controlled, and pure, reciting the Viṣṇuhṛdaya mantra at the beginning, middle, and end [of the rite], attains the world of Viṣṇu.
Whatever action may be deficient or excessive, let it all become exactly as prescribed; thus one shall deliver the ancestors.

*Oṃ śrāvaya* consists of four syllables; *astu śrauṣaṭ*, four; *yaj*, two; *ye yajāmahe*, six; and *vauṣaṭ*, two. He who is offered with these is the Sacrificial Person (*yajñapuruṣa*), Viṣṇu; the meaning is: "May he be gracious to me. Accordingly, a statement to this effect is also seen in the *Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa*.

This is the unexhausted power of the sacrifice: "Śrāvaya," "Astu Śrauṣaṭ," "Yaja," and "Yajāmahe Vauṣaṭ. There are seventeen syllables in these *vyāhṛtis*: "Oṃ Śrāvaya" has four syllables; "Astu Śrauṣaṭ" has four syllables; "Yaja" has two syllables; "Ye Yajāmahe" has five syllables; and the *vaṣaṭ*-call has two syllables. This is Prajāpati, the seventeenth, established both with respect to the deities and with respect to the self. He who knows this becomes firmly established through offspring and cattle in this world, and through immortality in that world. Thus ends the Viṣṇuhṛdaya mantra.
Now begins the hymn to Saptārchi,
found in the Prabhāsakhaṇḍa, the Brahmāṇḍapurāṇa, and the Viṣṇudharmottara:
"I shall proclaim the auspicious hymn to Saptārchi, which bestows all desires."
I always pay homage to those ancestors of radiant splendor, both formless and embodied, who are meditative and possess the eye of yoga.
I bow to those bestowers of desires, the progenitors of Indra and the other gods, as well as of Dakṣa, Marīci, the seven ṛṣis, and the ancestors.
I bow to all those ancestors who are the progenitors of Manu and the others, as well as of the sun and the moon, and who dwell within the waters and the oceans.
With palms joined in reverence, I always pay homage to the constellations and the planets, as well as to the winds, the fires, and the ancestors, and to heaven and earth.
I pay homage to those grandfathers, the progenitors of the divine sages, who are honored by all the worlds and who are the protectors of all beings.
With palms joined in reverence, I always bow down to Prajāpati, to the cows, to Agni, to Soma, to Yama, and to the Lords of Yoga.
Homage to the seven groups of ancestors in the seven worlds;
having paid homage to the Self-Existent Brahmā, the eye of the world.
This is that which has been spoken of as the seven-rayed one, worshipped by the hosts of Brahman-sages;
for it is supremely pure, glorious, and the destroyer of Rākṣasas.
A man who is engaged in this rite obtains three boons;
the ancestors on earth bestow food, long life, and sons.
One who, endowed with supreme devotion, full of faith, and having conquered the senses,
recites the seven-flamed [mantra] daily with a concentrated mind,
shall become the sole sovereign over the earth with its seven continents and oceans.
Thus ends the hymn to Saptārcis. Now follows the praise of the Pitṛs from the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa.
And Brahmā, having heard the desire of that Brahmin Ruci, said:
"You shall become a Prajāpati; progeny must be created by you."
O Brahmin, having created those beings and likewise having brought forth the ritual acts,
you shall attain perfection once you have fulfilled your duties both performed and yet to be performed.
Therefore, act according to what has been said by your ancestors: take a wife;
and while reflecting upon this desire, perform that worship of the ancestors.
And thus satisfied, the ancestors will grant you your desire;
when they are content, what would the grandfathers not give—wives and sons?
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having heard these words of the seer Brahmā, whose birth is unmanifest,
he performed the libations for the ancestors on a secluded sandbank of the river.
Then, becoming single-minded and self-restrained, with his neck bowed low in devotion, the brahmin, being honored, praised the ancestors with these hymns.
Ruci said:
"With devotion I pay homage to the ancestors and those who are their presiding deities,
who are indeed gratified even by the gods at the śrāddha rites with offerings preceded by the svadhā-call."
I pay homage to the ancestors in heaven who are gratified by the great seers with devotion through mental śrāddhas, performed by those desiring both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
I pay homage to those heavenly ancestors whom the perfected ones (siddhas) gratify at the ancestral rites (śrāddha) with divine intentions and unsurpassed offerings.
With devotion I pay homage to the ancestors who are worshipped in heaven by the Guhyakas, who,
desiring identification with them, seek ultimate and auspicious prosperity.
I pay homage to the ancestors who are always honored by mortals on earth,
and who, through the ancestral rites (śrāddha) performed with faith, bestow the attainment of desired worlds.
I pay homage to the ancestors who are always honored on earth by the wise;
they grant the status of Prajāpati and bestow the attainment of one's desired objects.

I pay homage with devotion to the ancestors who are always worshipped on earth by the fortunate ones— those of restrained diet whose sins have been destroyed by austerity— through the performance of śrāddha rites.
I pay homage to the ancestors who are constantly gratified by the Brahmins through their meditative absorptions, as they remain perpetually self-restrained and devoted to lifelong celibacy.
I pay homage to those ancestors whom the kings satisfy at the śrāddha ceremony with all kinds of funeral offerings according to the rules— those who bestow the fruits of both worlds.
I pay homage to the ancestors who are always worshipped on earth by the Vaiśyas,
who are constantly devoted to their own duties, with flowers, incense, food, and water.
I pay homage to the ancestors who, even when propitiated with devotion by Śūdras during the śrāddha rite, satisfy the entire world; they are renowned by the name Sukālins.
I pay homage to those ancestors who, in the netherworld (pātāla), are always gratified by the great asuras with offerings of nectar at the śrāddha rites, having forever abandoned deceit and pride.
I pay homage to the ancestors who are honored with ancestral offerings (śrāddha) in the subterranean realm (rasātala) by the Nagas,
who desire all various enjoyments and objects of their longing.
I pay homage to the ancestors who are always gratified by the serpents at the śrāddha ceremony,
right there with various mantras accompanied by an abundance of enjoyments.
I pay homage to the ancestors who dwell visibly in the worlds of the gods, upon the earth,
and likewise in the intermediate space, being worthy of worship by the gods and others.
May they accept what has been offered by me.
I pay homage to the ancestors who have become subtle atoms and dwell formless within celestial chariots,
whom they worship with minds free from impurity.
The lords of yogis [practice] for the sake of liberation from the afflictions.
I pay homage to the ancestors who dwell in heaven in embodied form, who partake of the *svadhā* offering when there is an intent for desired fruits,
and who are capable of bestowing all things wished for.
Those who grant liberation regarding things that have not been intentionally aimed at.
May all the ancestors who are here be satisfied—
those who grant the desires of those who wish for them, [bestowing] the state of a god, the state of Indra, or even a status superior to that.
Take the sons of Vasu, Kṣyāma, and Abalā to their homes.
May those ancestors who always dwell in the rays of the sun, in the lunar orb, and in the white celestial palaces, be satisfied in this [offering] with food and water.
May those who possess satisfaction through fragrance and other such things proceed.
Those who find satisfaction in the oblation poured into the fire,
those who eat while residing within the bodies of Brahmins,
and those who attain joy through the offering of funeral cakes— [to them I bow].
May those ancestors be satisfied in this rite with food and water.
By the gods with their desired rhinoceros meat,
by the great and excellent sages with black, divine, and charming sesame seeds, and with kāla vegetables.
Being fully gratified, may they find joy herein.
May there be the presence here of all those poetic works which are most desired by you, and which are highly honored by the immortals—
of those [works], let there be the presence through this flower-offering.
In the perfumes, waters, and foods brought by me.
Those who receive worship day by day, those on earth who are to be honored at the end of a month during the Aṣṭakā rites,
and those who are to be honored at the end of a year on festive occasions— [all these are satisfied].
May my ancestors attain satisfaction today through you.
Those who shine like the moon among the white water-lilies are worthy of worship among the twice-born;
those with the hue of the rising sun are so among the kṣatriyas; and likewise, those with the luster of gold are so among the vaiśyas.
And those who resemble indigo are of the śūdra class.
May they all, together with me, attain satisfaction in this world through my offering of flowers, incense, perfumes, food, water, and so forth,
as well as by means of the fire-oblation (agnihoma).
I am forever bowed down before those ancestors.

Those who, even when they were formerly gods, eat the sacrificial offerings for the ancestors brought by the virtuous for the sake of satisfaction— those progenitors of the earth who become satisfied; [1087] those who, even when they were formerly gods, eat the sacrificial offerings for the ancestors brought by the virtuous for the sake of satisfaction— those progenitors of the earth who become satisfied.
May they be satisfied with this; I bow down to them.
Expelling the Rākṣasas, Bhūtas, and fierce Asuras, and thereby removing all that is inauspicious for living beings,
they are the primordial ones of the gods and are worthy of worship by the immortals.
May they be satisfied here; I bow down to them.
May the Agniṣvātta Pitṛs, the Barhiṣad Pitṛs, the Ājyapa Pitṛs, and likewise the Somapa Pitṛs, attain satisfaction in this Śrāddha, having been gratified by me.
May the Agniṣvātta classes of ancestors protect my eastern direction;
likewise, may those ancestors who dwell on the sacrificial grass (Barhiṣad) guard the southern quarter.
Likewise, the drinkers of clarified butter [protect] the western direction, and the drinkers of Soma the northern;
likewise from Rakshasas, Bhūtas, Piśācas, and from the evil of the Asuras.
May Yama, the sovereign lord of them all, grant me protection. Viśva, Viśvabhuj, Ārādhya, Dhanya, Dharma, Sanātana, Bhūtida, Bhūtidā, and Bhūta— these are the nine hosts of the Pitṛs.
Kalyāṇa, Kalpaka, Kartṛ, Kalpa, Kalpatarāśraya,
and Kalpatāhetu— these six are remembered as the classes of the sinless (anagha).
Vara, Vareṇya, Varada, Tuṣṭida,
Puṣṭida, Viśvadhātṛ, and Dātṛ— these seven are likewise the Gaṇas.
Mahān, Mahātman, Matimān, and Mahābala—
these five hosts of the ancestors likewise destroy all sins.
One is said to bestow happiness, another wealth, another the Dharma, and another prosperity;
thus is this fourfold group of ancestors described.
The thirty-one classes of ancestors, by whom the entire world is pervaded—
may they be satisfied here by me, may they prosper, and may they always bestow what is beneficial.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
As he was thus offering praise, a mass of radiant energy with upward-flaming crests suddenly appeared, pervading the entire sky.
Seeing that immense radiance standing there, having completely enveloped the world,
Ruci knelt upon the ground and sang this hymn of praise:
Ruci said: I always bow down to those ancestors of immeasurable splendor, both those who possess form and those who are formless, who are ever meditative and endowed with divine vision.
I bow to Dakṣa and Marīci, the progenitors of Indra and the others, as well as to the Seven Sages and other such bestowers of desires.
I bow down to all those progenitors of Manu and the others, as well as those of the sun and the moon, and to the ancestors who dwell within the oceans.
With palms joined in reverence, I pay homage to the constellations and the planets, as well as to wind, fire, and space, and likewise to heaven and earth.
With palms joined in reverence, I pay homage to those who are the progenitors of the divine seers, who are worshipped by all the gods, and who are the constant bestowers of fearlessness.
To Prajāpati, to Kaśyapa, to Soma, and to Varuṇa,
as well as to the Lords of Yoga, I offer salutation with palms joined in reverence.
Homage to the seven assemblies, as well as to those in the seven worlds;
I pay homage to the Self-Existent One, to Brahmā, who possesses the eye of yoga.
Since those hosts of ancestors are indeed the supports [of all beings] and possess forms of yoga,
I therefore pay homage to Soma, the father of the worlds.
Likewise, I pay homage to those other ancestors who have the form of fire,
since this entire universe consists entirely of Agni and Soma.
But those who are composed of splendor, whose forms are Soma, Sūrya, and Agni,
who are indeed the very nature of the world and likewise the very nature of Brahman—
To all those yogis, my ancestors, with a restrained mind, I offer salutation after salutation; salutations to you! May the consumers of the *svadhā* offering be pleased with me.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
O best of sages, having been thus praised by him,
those Pitṛs then emerged from that splendor, illuminating the ten directions.
Then he saw them standing before him, adorned with the perfumes, garlands, and ointments that he had offered.
Having prostrated again with devotion and once more with palms joined in reverence, he spoke with distinct respect: "Homage to you! Homage to you!"
Then the gratified ancestors said to that best of sages,
"Choose a boon," and he, with his neck bowed, spoke to them.
Ruci said: "Now that the office of creator has been assigned to me by Brahmā,
I desire a wife who is blessed, divine, and capable of bearing offspring."
The Pitṛs said:
"This very day, your wife shall become Manoramā;
and by her, a son shall be born who will be a beautiful and excellent sage."
The wise lord of the Manvantara, distinguished by your very name,
shall attain renown throughout the three worlds as Rucya, the son of Ruci.
That great-souled one shall also have many sons,
who will be possessed of great strength and great heroism, and will be protectors of the earth.
And you, having become Prajāpati, have created the fourfold progeny;
now that your office has been fulfilled, O knower of dharma, you shall thereafter attain perfection.
For whoever shall satisfy us with devotion by means of this hymn, O Ruci,
we, being pleased, shall grant him enjoyments and supreme knowledge.
Those who desire physical health, sovereignty, sons, grandsons,
and the like, should constantly and diligently praise [the deity] with this hymn of praise.
And he who, standing before the foremost of the twice-born while they are eating at a śrāddha feast, shall recite with devotion this hymn that brings us pleasure;
When our presence is established through the joy of hearing this hymn of praise,
that śrāddha ceremony of ours will undoubtedly become inexhaustible.
Even if a Śrāddha is performed by one who is not learned in the Vedas, or if it should be defiled,
or if it is performed with wealth acquired through unjust means, or otherwise improperly.
Even if offerings are presented by those unworthy of receiving the śrāddha,
or if they are offered at an improper time, in an improper place, or even if the rite is devoid of its prescribed rules;
Even if a śrāddha is performed by faithless men relying on hypocrisy,
it still serves for our satisfaction through its mere recitation.
Wherever this hymn, which brings us happiness, is recited at a śrāddha ceremony,
our satisfaction there lasts for twelve years.
This hymn, when heard, bestows satisfaction for twelve years during the winter season,
and for twice that number of years during the cool season.
In the spring, sixteen [verses] are for satisfaction in the śrāddha rite;
and in the summer, these same sixteen are recited as the cause of satisfaction.
Even when a śrāddha has been performed incompletely, if it is purified by this hymn,
O Ruci, our satisfaction becomes inexhaustible during the rainy season.
Even that which was recited in the autumn, when offered at the time of a śrāddha ceremony,
provides us with satisfaction lasting for fifteen years through these men.
In whichever house this remains written at all times,
we shall be present there whenever a *śrāddha* has been performed.
Therefore, O highly fortunate one, this should be recited by you before the Brahmins while they are eating at the śrāddha ceremony; it is the cause of our great delight.
Now, there are also other passages to be recited from the Bhaviṣyottara, Vārāha, and Viṣṇu Purāṇas:
"The wise man should cause the Brāhmaṇas to hear these verses from the Purāṇas."
May my father, grandfather, and likewise my great-grandfather,
abiding today within the bodies of the Brahmins, attain satisfaction.
May my father, grandfather, and likewise my great-grandfather,
their forms nourished by the fire-oblation, attain satisfaction.
May my father, grandfather, and likewise my great-grandfather,
attain satisfaction through this rice-ball (piṇḍa) offered by me upon the earth.
May my father, grandfather, and likewise my great-grandfather attain satisfaction through this which has been uttered by me with devotion.
May my maternal grandfather, his father,
and even his father be forever satisfied by my libations to the twice-born, by my burnt offerings, and by the offering of funeral cakes.
May his maternal grandfather attain satisfaction,
as well as his father and his other paternal ancestors;
and may the Viśvedevas reach the highest state.
May the Yātudhānas meet their destruction and find no satisfaction.
Lord Hari, the Master of Sacrifice, the imperishable Self who partakes of all sacrificial offerings and ancestral oblations, is the Sovereign here;
by His presence, let [all obstacles] depart immediately.
All the Rākṣasas without exception and all the Asuras.
In this regard, the learned also recite the verses praising Gayā as spoken in the Brahmavaivarta and Vārāha Purāṇas:
"What is given at Gayā, on Dharmapṛṣṭha, at the lake of Brahmā,
and likewise at the Banyan Tree of Gayāśīrṣa, becomes inexhaustible for the ancestors."
At Gayā, Janārdana himself exists in the form of the ancestors;
by beholding that lotus-eyed one, one is liberated from the three debts.
One should offer a funeral ball (piṇḍa) at Gayāśiras, even if it is only the size of a śamī leaf;
thus one shall uplift seven lineages and a hundred and one members of the family.
Those established on the [lower] stages go to heaven, and those dwelling in heaven are destined for liberation.
Among the realms of heaven, the netherworld, and the mortal world, there is no sacred site equal to Gayā.
By offering a funeral cake at Gayāśiras, the ancestors attain the state of gods.
In the Kālikā Purāṇa:
One should recite the original Purāṇas,
as well as the treatises on one's own dharma approved by the ancestors.
And for the satisfaction of the Brahmins, [he told] the story and indeed the history of Viriñci and the others.
In the *Kūrmapurāṇa*:
"One should indeed cause them to hear the *svādhyāya*, the treatises on Dharma (*dharmaśāstra*),
the *Itihāsas* and *Purāṇas*, and the auspicious ritual manuals for *śrāddha*."
In the Nāradīya Purāṇa:
"One should cause the twice-born who are eating to hear the narratives of the ancestors and the verses sung by the ancestors for the sake of inexhaustible satisfaction at the śrāddha rites."

It has been stated that one should cause the ancestral narratives (*pitṛ-khyāna*) to be heard; among these, the narrative of the Seven Hunters (*saptavyādha-khyāna*) is to be found in the section on the praise of *śrāddha*. The narrative of Purūravas (*paurūravasa-khyāna*) is to be sought in the section on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*). The narrative of Acchoda (*acchoda-khyāna*) is to be understood as having been set forth in the section on the *aṣṭakā* rites. Other ancestral narratives, such as those mentioned in the *Brahma-purāṇa* and the narrative of Marīci mentioned in the *Mārkaṇḍeya-purāṇa*, have not been written here for fear of excessive prolixity; they should be sought out and recited from their respective *purāṇas*. However, one who is unable to read the entire narrative of the Seven Hunters should recite these two verses from the *Matsya-purāṇa* and *Padma-purāṇa*, which serve as a summary thereof.
The seven hunters were deer in the Daśārṇa forest;
on Mount Kālañjara they were cakravāka birds; and on the island of the lake Mānasa they were swans.
They too were born in Kurukṣetra as Brahmins who had mastered the Vedas;
they set out upon a long journey, and you have come to them for refuge.
The verses concerning the ancestors (*pitṛgāthā*), however, are presented here having been collected from various *Smṛtis* and *Purāṇas*.
Among them, in the *Yama-smṛti*:
"Those who know the past recite the verses sung by the ancestors."
May there be born in our lineage one who would offer [this] to us on the thirteenth day.
One should offer milk-rice mixed with honey during the shadow of an elephant falling toward the east,
and during the Maghā constellation in the rainy season, using a goat made entirely of gold.
Viṣṇu said:
Now, there are two verses sung by the ancestors:
"O best of kings, might someone be born in our lineage..."
During the rainy season, on the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight, being composed in mind.

He who performs a śrāddha with honey-abundant milk-rice (pāyasa) throughout the entire month of Kārttika, or even during the time when the shadow of an elephant falls eastward, [attains the highest merit].
Paiṭhīnasi says: "With a goat made of all metals, during the rainy season and under the Maghā asterism,
a son or even a grandson should offer [the Śrāddha] on the thirteenth lunar day."
Bṛhaspati said:
[1095] Ancestors, fearing a fall into hell, long for sons, thinking:
"Whoever shall go to Gayā, he will deliver us."
He will perform the rite of releasing a bull, as well as sacrifices and works of public utility;
he will establish a household, offer ancestral oblations, or give gifts daily.
Yājñavalkya says: May that being be born in our family who shall offer us a handful of water,
especially in rivers abounding in cool water.
"Will there not be born in our family some supreme among men who,
with a concentrated mind, would perform a śrāddha at the Gayāśīrṣa banyan tree?"
In the *Yama*, *Yājñavalkya*, *Viṣṇudharmottara*, *Brahmavaivarta*, *Bhaviṣyottara*, and *Kūrma Purāṇas*: "One should desire many sons, for even if only one among them goes to Gayā,
or performs the Aśvamedha sacrifice, or releases a dark-colored bull."
From the *Matsyapurāṇa* and the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"Henceforth, O tiger among kings, I shall proclaim those verses which were celebrated by the ancestors, desiring [to dwell] in their own city."
Perhaps there may be someone in our own family who would constantly perform the ancestral rite (śrāddha),
even if only with water, roots, fruits, flowers, sesame seeds, or water again.
Perhaps there may be someone in our own family who would offer us a handful of water at rivers that abound with water, especially those that are cool.
Perhaps there may be someone in our own family who, being composed in mind, would offer us a handful of water mixed with gold, combined with sesame seeds and honey.
Perhaps there might be someone in our own family who would offer us milk-rice mixed with honey and clarified butter on the thirteenth lunar day during the rainy season under the Maghā asterism.
Perhaps there might be someone in our own family who would diligently perform a *śrāddha* offering even once with rhinoceros meat, or else with black potherbs.
Black pot-herbs, great pot-herbs, honey, and the food of sages,
as well as rhinoceroses devoid of horns— we shall subsist upon these until the sun’s end.
At Gayā, during an eclipse of Rāhu, one should feed a yogin with the meat of a rhinoceros; indeed, by doing so for us while we are in the shadow of an elephant,
our satisfaction shall endure until the end of the aeon.
The donor shall become a master who acts according to his will in all worlds for the duration of the period until the dissolution of all beings; there is no need for deliberation on this matter.
Since we shall always attain infinite satisfaction with even one of these five, how much more so with their complete abundance?
Perhaps there might be one in our own family who would release a bull,
or who would give a cow while she is in labor to an eminent Brahmin.
"Perhaps there might be some most excellent man in our own family who would bestow upon us a house equipped with all necessary furnishings."
O best of men, it may be that someone from our own family gives a black antelope skin, complete with its horns and hooves, according to the prescribed rite.
"Could there perhaps be some most excellent man in our own family who would give a horse of every color, especially one that is white and blue?"
Perhaps there may be someone in our own family who, endowed with faith,
would perform the gift of gold, the gift of cows, and even the gift of the earth.
"Could there perhaps be some most excellent man in our family who is a builder of wells, groves, ponds, and large reservoirs?"
Perhaps there may be someone in our family who, with his whole being, would go for refuge to Hari, Viṣṇu, the Lord of Gods, the slayer of Madhu.
In the Vāyu Purāṇa and the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa,
those conversant with antiquity recite these verses sung by the ancestors;
I shall now proclaim them correctly, so listen attentively.
May he be born in our lineage who would give us milk-rice mixed with honey and ghee on the thirteenth lunar day, under the shadow of an elephant,
with a goat made of all metals, during the rainy season and under the Maghā asterism.
One should desire many sons, so that even if only one among them goes to Gayā,
or marries a wife who is a Gaurī, or sets free a dark-colored bull.
In the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa,
the ancestors spoke this ancient verse, O beloved:
"If a son is unable to go to Gayā by any means whatsoever..."
Then one should go with effort to the supreme sacred ford of Goṣpada.
With bulbs, roots, fruits, or even oil-cakes and iṅguda seeds, [one should pray]:
"May there be born in our family one who will offer a śrāddha here."
In the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa:
"O Lord of the Earth, the verses of the ancestors (pitṛgāthāḥ) are always sung here by those who discourse on Brahman— those which were formerly sung by the ancestors in secret."
When shall there be born in our lineage a preeminent son,
who on this earth shall offer funeral cakes with the remnants of food consumed by yogins?
Or at Gayā, one should offer a funeral cake (piṇḍa) consisting of rhinoceros meat as a great oblation,
or black potherbs with sesame and other grains, or kṛsara, for the sake of complete satisfaction.
The meat of the rhinoceros, offered to the Viśvedevas and Soma, is the supreme oblation;
we hope that those rhinoceroses, excluding their horns, shall remain until the end of the sun.
Likewise, on the thirteenth day of the rainy season and under the Maghā asterism,
one should offer milk-rice mixed with honey and clarified butter according to the prescribed rite during the sun's southern course.
In the Mahākālakhaṇḍa and the Varāhapurāṇa,
there are likewise verses sung by the ancestors; hear them, O best of beings,
and having heard them, you should remain steadfast in soul.
Blessed indeed would be the man born in our family who,
free from stinginess regarding his wealth, shall offer us funeral cakes with devotion.
When you have the means, you will give to the brahmins, on our behalf, wealth such as jewels, garments, the Mahāyāna, and all manner of enjoyments.
Or, at this time, a man whose wealth is limited to that alone, with a mind bowed in devotion, shall feed the foremost of Brahmins according to his ability with food.
If one is incapable of giving food, one shall give grain or vegetables according to one's ability to the foremost of the twice-born, or even a very small sacrificial fee.
Even there, O twice-born one, one who is possessed of incapacity will bow down and give to some eminent brahmin the sesame seeds situated at the very tips of his fingertips.
If, bowing with devotion, he shall offer us a handful of water mixed with seven or eight sesame seeds;
Having obtained it from anywhere at all, or even a cow's daily ration from cows,
one who is endowed with devotion will give it to us to please us in its absence.
In the absence of all else, having gone to the forest and displaying roots and tubers,
he shall recite this aloud to the world-protectors, beginning with the Sun.

I have no wealth, no riches, nor anything else suitable for offerings to the ancestors; bowing to my own forefathers, may they be satisfied by this devotion of mine. May those two [parents] likewise be gratified.
His two arms were fashioned as the path for the wind.
Having prepared barley, milk-rice, śyāmāka grain, or nivāra rice, as well as groats mixed with honey and sesame seeds, he will offer them as funeral cakes (piṇḍas).
By that offering of funeral cakes, our residence shall be in the triple heaven;
and whoever here, with a concentrated mind, should perform a libation for us even with seven or eight sesame seeds, he too shall lead us to supreme satisfaction.
In the Kūrma Purāṇa: "The ancestors sing songs and the wise are satisfied;
one should desire many sons who are virtuous and endowed with good qualities."
If even one among those who have gathered together should go to Gayā,
or having reached Gayā, should perform a śrāddha even incidentally;
We have been delivered by him; he goes to the supreme goal, especially on Mount Varāha and at Gayā.
Especially in Vārāṇasī, where Lord Hara himself resides. In the Nandipurāṇa:
"Hear now their settled opinion regarding the ancestors."
This secret was proclaimed by those sages of purified souls.
Those who offer vegetables, roots, or even fruits for the sake of a *śrāddha*,
having sprinkled them with water from a sacred bathing place;
They [attain] the fruit of sons among those who have sons—sons of excellent character.
Neither the performer of sacrifices nor the knower of all the Vedas, nor one who has gone to Gayā, is dear to the ancestors;
that son alone is beloved and esteemed by the ancestors.
Whoever should offer water with devotion even just once.
Enough indeed with gifts, Vedic study, ascetic penances, and other such restraints;
there is one supreme, most holy ford.
Having attained that which removes evil and casts out all defects.
A self-controlled man should also offer water mixed with sesame seeds here to the ancestors;
by him, a Śrāddha has been performed for a thousand years.
The ancestors declare this to be a secret.
Thus end the recitations.
Now, the case endings:
one should correctly set forth the names together with the lineage and the relationship.

Because of this statement, the utterance of the word that serves as the cause for the realization of the lineage (*gotra*) must be performed; and since that cannot be done without case-endings (*vibhakti*), Nārāyaṇa says that when a particular case-ending is applicable, a restriction is made by the scripture regarding that specific case-ending, such that "in the *śrāddha*, one should give with those very specific case-endings. For it is said: "That which is given to the ancestors and deities joined with case-endings becomes inexhaustible when offered; otherwise, it is fruitless."

"Pitṛdaivatam" means substance intended for the ancestors and for the deities, conjoined with case-endings (*vibhaktibhiḥ*). It is connected with case-endings—such as the dative and others—as prescribed by the authors of the *Dharmaśāstras* on *vyāsādi*. This is intended to express the relationship of the substance being offered indirectly through the connection of the case-ending with the word denoting the deity who is the object of the dedication. It does not, however, mean a direct connection of the case-ending with the word denoting the substance itself, because the injunctions to be shown later establish a rule regarding the dative and other case-endings for the word denoting the deity who is the object of the dedication. In the view that [the term] functions as an adverbial modifier (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*), nothing is untenable. Therefore, the meaning is: "Substances such as perfumes and the like are to be given, having dedicated them to the gods and the ancestors by means of words ending in the dative and other case-endings. "Viparītam" (contrary) means lacking the prescribed case-endings. "Anarthakam" (meaningless) means fruitless.
Also in the *Nāgarakhaṇḍa*:
"If a śrāddha is performed in a manner contrary to the rules, being devoid of the proper divisions, one should know that it is as if unperformed; it does not reach the ancestors."
Therefore, with every effort, a wise Brāhmaṇa should always perform the Śrāddha rite with the three divisions as they have been described.

‘From the opposite,’ that is, from error. ‘By those as stated,’ meaning by those prescribed according to the scriptures. ‘By three’ is a Vedic usage regarding the case endings (*vibhakti*). Therefore, the *śrāddha* should always be performed with these three case endings. This should not be understood to mean that the *śrāddha* is connected only to these three case endings, because four case endings will be mentioned later. How then is it that the four [case endings] are not connected solely to the *śrāddha*? Because in the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite, due to the absence of the invocation (*āvāhana*), the second case ending does not appear in the mantra. If one asks what those case endings are, it is stated in that very same place: “The first, the fourth, and the sixth should be used for the accomplishment of the *śrāddha*. By the word ‘and’ (*ca*) in the phrase ‘the first and...’, its specific form, the vocative (*saṃbuddhi*), is included. By the subsequent ‘and’ (*ca*), the second case is included. Thus, one should accomplish the *śrāddha* by employing the first, the vocative, the second, the fourth, and the sixth case endings as appropriate.
Vyāsa states the application of the aforementioned case endings:
"The dative case is prescribed for the seat and for the formal resolve (saṃkalpa);
the nominative is declared for the libation (tarpaṇa), while others have said it is the vocative."

The phrase "and always on the fourth [day] on the seat" (*caturthī cāsane nityam*) is intended to indicate that this is observed frequently, but not to mean that it is mandatory, since its non-mandatory nature will be demonstrated later. Alternatively, the word "always" (*nityam*) is connected with what follows, because the intention regarding food (*anna-saṃkalpa*) is not fixed. "Libation" (*tarpaṇa*) refers to the offering of water intended for the ancestors and others. In that regard, one should perform the ritual either using the nominative case: "May our ancestors of such-and-such lineage be satisfied" (*amukagotrā asmatpitaraḥ tṛpyantu*), or using the vocative: "O our ancestors of such-and-such lineage, may you be satisfied" (*amukagotrā asmatpitaraḥ tṛpyadhvam*).
