The statement beginning with "the vocative" (*saṃbuddhim*) constitutes a separate sentence. "Others" means in other instances, such as the offering of the *arghya* water; those learned in the scriptures say that the vocative case should be employed there.
Dharma said:
Regarding the questions at the inexhaustible seat, the sixth and fourth [fingers] are considered appropriate for the seat.
Likewise, there is the water for the guest-offering (arghya), the water for washing the feet (avanejana), the rice-ball (piṇḍa), and the water for the subsequent washing (pratyavanejana).
Having fully understood these, one who is proficient in all the scriptures should act accordingly.

"Request" (*pṛcchā*) refers to the formal inquiry for permission regarding the purpose of the Brahmins at the commencement of a *śrāddha* rite; "imperishable" (*akṣayya*) refers to the offering of water for the sake of imperishability. Bhṛgu states:
"The sixth case ending is indeed used in the request and the seating, as well as in the offering of the imperishable water."
The accusative case should be used in the invocation; this is the settled conclusion of the scriptures.

In the offering of water for honor (arghya), the water for washing the feet (āvanējana), the funeral cake (piṇḍa), and likewise in the subsequent washing of the feet (pratyāvanējana), one should employ the nominative case;
in all other instances, the genitive case is prescribed.
One who desires to follow the ritual procedure for the fourth [day] should offer perfume, garlands, incense, lamps, and food together with a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) without distinction—
that is to say, without differentiation or inequality.

Pracetās says: One should offer these [libations] counter-clockwise, one by one, according to the order of the ancestors; having addressed them by their lineage and name, one should say, "This is your *arghya*."

Among these—the father, grandfather, and great-grandfather—one should address each one individually according to the paternal line by their *gotra* and name, using honorific terms such as "father" (*pitṛ*) and so forth to indicate the relationship, and announce: "This is your *arghya*.
In the *Brahmapurāṇa*, it is stated that one should offer this water for the feet (*pādya*) and the *arghya* using the dative case ending.

In this context as well, the meaning is that one should first recite the words for the name, lineage, father, and so forth, ending in the vocative case (saṃbuddhi), and then apply the word *vaḥ*—just like the pronoun *yuṣmad*—in the dative case. As stated in the *Nāgarakhaṇḍa*:
"Thereafter, water with sesame seeds should be offered using the dative case."
Having taken up the purifiers, one should proclaim "Svadhā."
The author of the *Saṃgraha* also states the sixth case in the context of inexhaustible offerings (*akṣayyadāna*):
"The sixth case is prescribed for the two [terms] *akṣayya* and *āsana*; the second case is remembered for the invitation;
the fourth case should be used for the gift of food; and the remaining cases are remembered as the vocative (*saṃbuddhi*)."
In the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa as well: "The dative case (caturthī) is prescribed for all ritual acts; the locative case (ṣaṣṭhī vibhaktiḥ) is remembered for the libation (tarpaṇa);
and the genitive case (ṣaṣṭhī vibhaktiḥ) is used according to rule for the rite for the ancestors (pitṛkārya) when it concerns that which is inexhaustible."
In this matter of ritual option, the determination is according to one's own specific Vedic school (*śākhā*).
However, regarding the invocation (*āvāhana*), the *Nāgarakhaṇḍa* states that there is a rule for the use of the accusative case and a prohibition against other case endings:
"The invocation must be performed using the accusative case ending."
All those who do not come have been summoned individually.
Otherwise, one should never invoke the ancestors using the case endings;
for even if they are hungry, those illustrious ones will not arrive.

The word *atha* means "immediately after the offering of seats. Following this, one should perform the invocation (*āvāhana*) of the ancestors with the words, "May the ancestors come; O ancestors, come! This is stated as a prohibition against other [forms], since there is the possibility of using other case-endings (*vibhakti*). However, others have stated the application of the case-endings simply by observing the use of words accompanied by such endings. Regarding that, the procedure for the recitation has been stated in the *Bahvṛca-Pariśiṣṭa* according to the prescribed sequence: "One should correctly state the lineage (*gotra*), the relationship, and the names. In all cases, the lineage name ends in a vowel during the rite of the inexhaustible offering (*akṣayya-karman*)."
One should perform the satiation of the lineage in this manner; thus the donor does not become deluded.

‘Gotram’ refers to the word *gotra*; ‘ending in a vowel’ (*svarāntam*) means ending in an *ac* vowel. This applies everywhere, with the exception of its own specific exceptions; furthermore, the word *gotra* itself ends in an *ac* vowel. Since the sense of the locative case is impossible here, the locative will be excluded by its very unsuitability for usage. Alternatively, regarding the phrase “ending in a vowel,” according to the maxim that when any quality of ending in a vowel is applicable, the first [vowel] should be restricted, the letter *a*—being the first mentioned in the traditional list of phonemes (*dharmasamāmnāya*)—is understood to be the final constituent. Thus, it is understood that the word *gotra* should be pronounced as ending in the letter *a*. Alternatively, “ending in a vowel” (*svarāntam*) refers to that which ends in an acute accent (*udātta*). Among the vowels, which are forms of the properties of phonemes, the acute accent is designated by the unqualified term ‘vowel’ (*svara*) because it is the first and the most prominent; this is because it alone can be identified [by that term]. Consequently, it is only a phoneme characterized by the acute accent that constitutes the end, not any other phoneme. Therefore, in this context, the word *gotra* possesses the status of ending in a vowel only when it occurs in the vocative case (*saṃbuddhi*). Here, words such as *pitṛ* (father) in the masculine singular are intended as illustrations, since they serve as the primary examples, whereas words such as *mātṛ* (mother) and *mātāmaha* (maternal grandfather) appear in the feminine plural. Thus, the formula used here is: *amukagotra pitaramukaśarman etat te ’rghyam* (“O father of such-and-such lineage, such-and-such name, here is your *arghya*”). The same applies to the paternal grandfather and others. For the *akṣayya* offering, the formula is: *amukagotrasya pitur amukaśarmaṇo ’kṣayyam astu* (“May there be inexhaustibility for the father of such-and-such lineage, such-and-such name”). The same applies to the paternal grandfather and others. For the libation (*tarpaṇa*), the formula is: *amukagotraḥ pitā amukaśarmā tṛpyatu* (“May the father of such-and-such lineage, such-and-such name, be satisfied”). The same applies to the paternal grandfather and others. In the same way, one should infer the formulas for the offering of seats and so forth. However, the detailed application of these formulas for each case-ending and each specific object will be shown in the section explaining the afternoon rites.
Bṛhatpracetā also says:
"In all cases, the *gotra* ending with a vowel is used for the rite of offering inexhaustible merit (*akṣayya-karman*);
however, for the libation (*tarpaṇa*), the *gotra* alone is prescribed; by doing so, the performer does not err."
In all cases, the father is declared to be the "father" (pitṛ) in the rite of libation;
however, at the time of offering the inexhaustible water (akṣayya) for the father, what is given becomes inexhaustible for the ancestors.
In the *Nāgarakhaṇḍa*, however, its application is stated to be preceded by the use of words such as "father" (*pitṛ*) ending in case-terminations:
"In all cases, 'O Father' (*pitaḥ*) is prescribed in the rite of libation (*tarpaṇa*);
but at the time of the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*), it is 'to the paternal ancestors' (*pitryam*); and when offering the inexhaustible water (*akṣayyodaka*), it is 'to the father' (*pitur*)."
In all cases, the *gotra* name ends in a vowel; in the rite of libation (*tarpaṇa*), it is [in the dative] "to the *gotra*";
in the giving of grain, however, it is "to Śarman"; and in the rite for the inexhaustible [offering], it is "of Śarman."

"At the time of forming the intention" means at the time of renouncing food. "In the giving of grain" means in the giving of food. Even though it is feminine, the application [of the forms] is found right there by observing the use of words ending in case-terminations. For *mātṛ*, *mātre*, and likewise *mātaḥ*; for *āsana*, *kalpana*, and *akṣaya*;
for *gotra*, *gotrām*, and *gotrāyāḥ*—these are the nominative and subsequent case-endings.
One should likewise pronounce [the name] for the goddess as "Devī," for the divine lady as "Devī," and similarly for the mother.
Gobhila also says:
"One should employ the *gotra* in the case of the seat, and the *gotra* also in the cases of the *arghya* offering and the rice-ball (*piṇḍa*)."
At the time of the inexhaustible [offering], one should perform the renunciation for the lineage (gotrā);
likewise, one should perform the invocation for the lineage when it is in the feminine gender—of this there is no doubt.

Other such statements regarding case endings, such as "One should first offer food even to those facing east with the words 'Obeisance to all the gods' (namo viśvebhyo devebhyaḥ)," will be demonstrated in that very context due to their inclusion in the ritual application. Thus ends the section on case endings.
Now follows the determination regarding the *prācīnāvīta* and *yajñopavīta* modes of wearing the sacred thread.

In this regard, by way of that general principle, there are indeed four kinds of ritual action (*karma*) here: some are *pitrya* (pertaining to the ancestors) because they relate exclusively to the ancestors, such as the offering of the *svadhā*; some are *daiva* (pertaining to the gods) because they relate exclusively to the gods, such as the recitation, "May the Viśvedevas be pleased"; some are of both natures because they relate to both, such as the cooking and sprinkling enjoined with reference to materials like *śamī* wood; and some are purely worldly (*laukika*) because they lack connection to either gods or ancestors, such as inquiries after one's welfare (*svāgata*). Regarding these, Manu states that what pertains to the ancestors and what is of both natures must be performed with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*). [Note: The commentary portion regarding the relationship between primary and subsidiary elements has been integrated into the translation for clarity.]
Wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder, with the offering properly made counter-clockwise, unwearied,
and holding *darbha* grass in his hand, he should perform the ancestral rite according to the rules until the conclusion.

"By one wearing the *prācīnāvīta* [garment]" means with the sacred thread (*brahmasūtra*) placed over the right shoulder and under the left arm. "Until the end" means until its completion. Regarding the phrase "with *darbha* grass in hand," this is intended to exclude the practice from being used in rites for the ancestors (*pitrya*), and not to exclude it from rites for the gods (*daiva*) or humans (*mānuṣa*), because Viṣṇu has taught that it applies to all by stating: "Having sprinkled the place of the *śrāddha*, one should perform everything with *darbha* grass in hand. Here, because of the mention of "for the ancestors," the rule of wearing the *prācīnāvīta* is prescribed for whatever action is related to the ancestors. Therefore, whatever is connected solely to the ancestors, as well as that which is common to both gods and ancestors, should be performed with the *prācīnāvīta*. Even in the case of what is common to both, the ancestral rule is more appropriate than the divine rule; for when there is a conflict between the primary and secondary rules of the principal and subordinate elements, the rule of the principal is stronger. Furthermore, regarding the view that the *agnaukaraṇa* (offering into the fire) consists of both the divine and ancestral aspects, the statement of an option between the *yajñopavīta* and the *prācīnāvīta* belongs only to the opinion of a particular authority and is thus not contradictory. Consequently, even in the case of what is common, the *prācīnāvīta* alone should be used; however, in rites for the gods, the *yajñopavīta* alone should be used. For this very reason, Āśvalāyana says:

The most excellent Śrāddha for the gods should be performed with the sacred thread over the left shoulder (savya), while that for the ancestors (pitṛs) should be performed with it over the right shoulder (apasavya), according to the instruction of the Vedas.

The *śrāddha* for the gods—which is a constituent part of the *pitr-śrāddha*, the *vaiśvadeva*, and other varieties of *śrāddha* shown in the section on the classification of *śrāddhas*—must be performed with the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*yajñopavītin*), moving clockwise (*prādakṣiṇyena*). Here, the word *śrāddha* serves as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for all rites dedicated to the deities, such as the *homa* and others. And the *śrāddha* for the ancestors must be performed with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītin*), moving counter-clockwise (*apasavyam*), and not clockwise. Here, the word *śrāddha* serves as an indicator for all rites dedicated to the ancestors. The phrase "on account of the evidence of the Śruti" means that this is seen in the supplementary portion of the injunction regarding the sacred thread: "The *prācīnāvīta* is for the ancestors; the *upavīta* is for the gods."
Also in the *Prabhāsakhaṇḍa*:
"One who understands [the rules] should perform rites for the gods with the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*yajñopavītin*),
and likewise all rites for the ancestors with it over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītin*)."
In the *Nāgarakhaṇḍa*, however, an exception to the *prācīnāvīta* [wearing of the sacred thread] is shown in certain cases:
"Thus all rites pertaining to the gods should be performed with the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*savyapūrvikā*),
and those pertaining to the ancestors (*paitṛkya*) with it over the right shoulder (*apasavyena*), with the single exception of the *svastivācana*."

Regarding the *svastivācana* (the recitation for well-being) directed toward the paternal Brahmins, there is the injunction for the *svastivācana*; however, those acts connected solely with the Brahmins—such as rising to greet them, welcoming them, and inquiring after their welfare—which are worldly (*laukika*) because they constitute honors due to distinguished persons and are not integral parts (*anaṅga*) of the *śrāddha*, in these cases one should follow the rule that the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) is worn in the ordinary manner, as established by general rules such as "one who constantly offers water" and "one who constantly wears the sacrificial thread. Thus concludes the general determination regarding the *prācīnāvīta* (wearing the thread over the right shoulder). Now follows the specific determination regarding the *prācīnāvīta* and other modes of wearing the thread.

In this regard, although it might be possible to argue that acts such as purchasing—which serve as the means for accomplishing the rice and other materials related to the ancestors—are denoted by the word *pitrya* (pertaining to the ancestors) in Manu’s verse because they are somehow connected to the ancestors, nevertheless, what is intended here by the *taddhita* suffix and the direct statement (*śruti*) is specifically that which is *enjoined* (*vihita*) as being related to the ancestors, and not merely anything related to the ancestors. Thus, when there is a requirement for delimitation to avoid over-extension (*prasaṅga*), it is logical to adopt the proximate, internal meaning of the word presented by its own linguistic context. Furthermore, purchasing and the like are not themselves enjoined; rather, their performance is undertaken only as a matter of course (*arthāt*) because they serve to accomplish the enjoined rice and other materials. Therefore, these acts do not possess the property of requiring the *prācīnāvīta* (wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder). Alternatively, if in the aforementioned verse of Manu—"It should be done with the *prācīnāvīta*"—the word "enjoined" (*vidhi*) is construed with the term *pitryam*, then the resulting injunction would be: "That *pitrya* rite which is *enjoined* (*vihita*) and accompanied by the injunction (*vidhiyukta*) must be performed with the *prācīnāvīta*. In this way, since the purpose of the injunction is fulfilled, the *prācīnāvīta* does not apply to unenjoined acts such as purchasing. Consequently, for acts occurring within the ritual procedure—such as buying, farming, receiving gifts, and so forth—which are unenjoined, there is no rule regarding proximity to the primary act; they may be performed at any time. For the same reason—that they are unenjoined—the *prācīnāvīta* does not apply to acts such as threshing, winnowing, husking, grinding, and binding.

[Objection: But surely, just as in the *sthālīpāka* performed on the occasion of the new moon and other festivals, threshing and other such rites are obtained by extension (*atideśa*) in the *śrāddha* rites; why then is there no injunction for them? [Reply: It is said in response: For threshing is prescribed for grain that has already been set aside (*nirupta*). And here, there is no setting aside of grain in its raw state. If it is argued that this too should occur by extension, we say: No.

"One who maintains the sacred fires should perform the offering for the ancestors, or else with handfuls of parched barley flour (*saktu*). [Thus, the ritual form is established without requiring the specific preparatory acts of grain.]
Saying, "I offer to the ancestors," he should place [the offering] to the south of everything.

Since the word *pāka* (cooking) is mentioned in this statement from the *Padmapurāṇa*, it is understood that the act of *nirvāpa* (offering) applies specifically to the substance in the state of rice, which is proximate to the means of cooking. Therefore, the *nirvāpa* pertaining to the state of grain—which would otherwise apply by extension—is set aside. Consequently, in the case of threshing and other such rites, although the *nirvāpa* might generally apply by extension, it is restricted to being performed only with the sacred fires (*sāgnika*), because of the specific injunction "the fire is in front" (*prācīnam agnim*).

In that case, let it be that the *prācīnāvīta* (wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder) applies to the subsidiary element consisting of the purification of clothes, which is enjoined as something to be done and is common to both rites for the gods and the ancestors.

Not so. In the case of a rule (*vidhi*) concerning a pure substance, it is only the *time* for the mental application (*bhāvanā*) of washing clothes—which is already established by the requirements of the situation—that is enjoined, not the essential nature of that mental application itself; therefore, the rule regarding wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvīta*) does not apply here. Furthermore, even in the case of cleaning objects such as damaged vessels, there is no rule enjoining a mental application of purification toward the substances themselves. Likewise, one who fails to perform purification out of a desire to discard an impure substance when other easily available, pure substances exist, would incur sin. Moreover, because this specific purification is not part of the primary context (*aprākaraṇika*), the *prācīnāvīta* does not apply. As for the purification of vessels used for drinking and eating, which is mentioned in the section on the preparation of materials for sweeping and cleansing—such as "having performed the purification of the vessels"—since it is not understood to have the sacrificer as its fixed agent, the connection with the *prācīnāvīta* is not mandatory there. Even the mental application of smearing the ground at a *śrāddha* is merely restated as something already obtained by implication from the injunction to designate a place for the *śrāddha* characterized by purity; it is not being enjoined anew. For this very reason, learned people perform *śrāddhas* in places that have been made level and smeared by anyone at all, and cleaned by someone such as a son, a pupil, or a wife, regardless of whether they are personally involved. Thus, there is no fixed rule.

[Objection: Let it be then that the *prācīnāvīta* [wearing mode] applies to the meal on the preceding day—which is enjoined by the statement "having eaten once without meat"—as a constituent part (*aṅga*) of the invitation (*nimantraṇā*).

[Reply: Not so. For there is no injunction for eating here; rather, since eating is already established through natural inclination (*rāga*), the rule regarding its being meatless and so forth is what is enjoined.

[Objection: In that case, since the rule is enjoined as a constituent of the ancestral rite (*pitrya*), the *prācīnāvīta* must indeed be performed when the eating qualified by that rule is carried out.

That is not so. For substances, actions, qualities, and the like, "restriction" (*niyama*)—which is synonymous with the "pervasion of the entire performance" (*kṛtsnaprayogavyāpti*)—consists in the attainment of that part which has not yet been attained. Moreover, this does not entail an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) within a single performance. Otherwise, there would be no infinite regress even regarding the sixfold excellence (*ṣāḍguṇya*) of a single performance. Therefore, since even in the case of an injunction of restriction (*vidhi-niyama*), there is an absence of anything further to be performed beyond the essential nature of the restriction itself, the wearing of the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvīta*) is not obtained by its force.

But if that were the case, since it would be possible for a single agent—or even multiple agents—to wear [the sacred thread] in every manner, it would follow that the injunction has as its sole purpose something to be performed (*anuṣṭheya*). Furthermore, since there would be no performance distinct from the nature of the restriction already established prior to the restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*), the injunction would result in being entirely meaningless. Therefore, you too must admit that when, in each performance, there is the possibility of adopting materials and so forth that constitute the "alternative" (*pakṣa*), the "restriction" (*niyama*) consists in the attainment [of one specific alternative] by subverting that absence of attainment; and that restriction, being a property of the subject to be restricted, is something distinct [from the mere absence] and must indeed be performed in each performance. Consequently, through its application, the wearing of the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvīta*) is attained.

Ah! Even though there is no duty to be performed other than the very nature of that which is to be restrained (*niyamyasvarūpa*), the injunction has the purpose of excluding substances that would otherwise give rise to optionality. Furthermore, in the case of such exclusion, there is nothing at all to be performed, because performance consists essentially in activity (*pravṛtti*). Therefore, the wearing of the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvīta*) is not prompted by that [exclusion].

Not so. Even in the case of cessation (*nivṛtti*), there exists something to be performed (*anuṣṭheya*) in the form of the persistence of the impelling effort (*vidhāyaka-prayatna*), because even there one has been set in motion by an injunction alone; for even a prohibition cannot be established without an injunction. Now, if you think that the purposefulness of an injunction lies merely in its enjoining the performance of that very form [of cessation] by way of excluding what was not previously obtained in certain applications, then—since the performance of that very form is itself enjoined—the application of the *prācīnāvīta* [wearing of the sacred thread over the right shoulder] follows all the more clearly in that case.

Now it is said: since there is no distinction as to which applications involve the removal of non-attainment and for which the attainment is effected by an injunction, and furthermore, because there is no certainty regarding the performance of the *prācīnāvīta* [wearing of the sacred thread over the right shoulder] due to this lack of differentiation, one might think that the *prācīnāvīta* must be performed in all cases to avoid the risk of unintended defects (*vaiguṇya*). Nor should it be argued: "Why not simply do the opposite out of fear of performing an act not enjoined? For there is scope for such a position based on the principle that "it is better to omit what is enjoined than to adopt what is not enjoined," and that adopting the latter does not incur any excess fault. Therefore, when performing the restriction of abstaining from meat and so forth—which is enjoined as dependent upon eating—one must perform the *prācīnāvīta*.

To this it is replied: Since the nature of eating is established by natural inclination (*rāga*), the restrictive rule (*niyama*) concerning it—such as the requirement of being meatless—is for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*), because it serves the purpose of the invitation to a *śrāddha* and is thus for the sake of ritual action (*karmārtha*). And that which is for the sake of ritual action is stronger than that which is for the sake of the person. Therefore, by subverting the wearing of the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvīta*) which is prompted by the injunction of the restrictive rule for the sake of ritual action, one must perform the wearing of the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*yajñopavīta*) prompted by the nature of eating for the sake of the person. Furthermore, eating is the substrate (*dharmin*), while the rule dependent upon it is the property (*dharma*). Between a property and its substrate, the substrate is stronger; therefore, in this case, the wearing of the sacred thread prompted by eating must be adopted. Moreover, according to the statement of Āpastamba, "One should eat wearing the sacred thread and with an upper garment," the wearing of the sacred thread dependent on eating is primary as a matter for the person, whereas the restriction of being meatless is not. Thus, the wearing of the sacred thread is more powerful. Consequently, when there is a conflict between the two, the wearing of the sacred thread prompted by eating for the sake of the person prevails. This is the conclusion. Furthermore, the wearing of the sacred thread is prescribed for all ritual acts, whereas the restriction of being meatless applies only to the specific occasion of the *śrāddha*. Therefore, the former is more powerful. For these reasons, the wearing of the sacred thread prompted by eating for the sake of the person is indeed to be adopted here. This is the final position. Thus ends the discussion. Now begins the consideration of the following: "The sacred thread should be worn over the left shoulder at the time of the *tarpaṇa*. Regarding this, the doubt arises as to whether the wearing of the sacred thread over the left shoulder is prompted by the *tarpaṇa* itself, or whether it is prompted by the nature of the act of sipping water (*ācamana*). To resolve this, the following is stated: "The wearing of the sacred thread over the left shoulder is prompted by the *tarpaṇa*. Why? Because it is prescribed specifically for that occasion. Just as the *prācīnāvīta* is prescribed for the *śrāddha*, so too is the *yajñopavīta* over the left shoulder prescribed for the *tarpaṇa*. Therefore, it is concluded that the wearing of the sacred thread over the left shoulder is prompted by the *tarpaṇa*. However, others hold that it is prompted by the nature of the *ācamana*. They argue: "The wearing of the sacred thread over the left shoulder is prompted by the *ācamana*. Why? Because it is prescribed for all ritual acts. Since it is prescribed for all ritual acts, it is understood that it is prompted by the nature of the *ācamana*. Therefore, it is concluded that the wearing of the sacred thread over the left shoulder is prompted by the *ācamana*. But this view is incorrect. It is not prompted by the *ācamana*. Why? Because it is prescribed for the *tarpaṇa*. Since it is prescribed for the *tarpaṇa*, it is understood that it is prompted by the *tarpaṇa*. Therefore, it is concluded that the wearing of the sacred thread over the left shoulder is prompted by the *tarpaṇa*. Furthermore, the wearing of the sacred thread over the left shoulder is prescribed for the *tarpaṇa*, whereas the wearing of the sacred thread over the right shoulder is prescribed for the *śrāddha*. Since they are prescribed for different occasions, there is no conflict between them. Therefore, the wearing of the sacred thread over the left shoulder is prompted by the *tarpaṇa*. Since the *prācīnāvīta* (wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder) of one who has been invited is subordinate as a constituent part of the invitation (*nimantraṇāṅga*), it is not primary; and when there is a conflict between the primary and the subordinate, it is logical that the subordinate is set aside by the strength of the primary. Therefore, there is no performance of the *prācīnāvīta* prompted by the rule of abstaining from meat and so forth. Furthermore, regarding the *prācīnāvīta* obtained through its connection with ancestral rites (*pitryatva*), once the invitation has been performed again according to the injunction beginning with "one should invite them, preceded by the *apasavya* [wearing the thread over the left shoulder], starting with the ancestors" from the point of the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) onwards, the previously established *prācīnāvīta* is excluded (*parisaṃkhyāyate*) by the new rule. Here, the sending of sons or disciples for the sake of the invitation is for the purpose of showing respect, and approaching the place of those to be invited is restated for the purpose of avoiding worldly negligence; thus, even for these reasons, the *prācīnāvīta* does not function as the cause [for the entire rite]. Consequently, the recollection, chanting, and breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*) of specific chosen deities—which are practiced by the virtuous as a form of preliminary purification (*puraścaraṇa*) for the sake of purity of speech and body—are not prompted by the *prācīnāvīta* because they are auxiliary parts of the *śrāddha*. The declaration of the *śrāddha* after proclaiming the place and time (*deśakāla-saṃkīrtana*) is to be performed by one wearing the *yajñopavīta* (sacred thread over the left shoulder), since it lacks the exclusion (*parisaṃkhyā*) of being a subordinate part. Likewise, the invitation of the twice-born for the *vaiśvadevika* portion must be done by one wearing the *yajñopavīta*. As he himself says: "Having prostrated with the left [hand], one should invite those intended for the *vaiśvadeva*. By "with the left," he means distinguished by the *yajñopavīta*. One should understand that the connection with the *savya* (left/over-left) and *apasavya* (right/under-right) applies respectively to the two procedures (*itikartavyatā*) of inviting the gods and the ancestors, ending with the rules such as touching the knees, as detailed in the section on invitation. And the observance of rules such as celibacy (*brahmacarya*), because it is prescribed for the sake of the *śrāddha*, must be performed by one wearing the *yajñopavīta*; for although it pertains to the ancestors (*pitrya*), it is mixed with many divine and human duties characterized by the *yajñopavīta*, and thus, by the maxim "of many things, the nature of the majority prevails," it should be done by one possessing the *yajñopavīta*. If it is argued: "In the case of the Brahmins performing the acts—such as reciting hymns, muttering mantras, brushing teeth, cutting nails and beard, applying ointments, accepting what is offered, eating, vomiting, and so forth—the *prācīnāvīta* should apply because these are ancestral acts"—this is not so. It is mostly refuted by the aforementioned reasoning. Since all the injunctions for the *prācīnāvīta*, such as "by the *prācīnāvītī* correctly," are connected solely to the performer of the *śrāddha*, what occasion would there be for it among the Brahmins? Furthermore, acts such as smearing the cooking ground, sprinkling water, bringing the firebrand, scattering sesame and mustard seeds, binding the cloth, removing the refuse, gathering the vessels, washing, placing rice on the fire, cooking, and serving, though pertaining to the ancestors, are performed by the husband and others as well because they are prescribed as common to both the gods and the ancestors; therefore, they cannot be said to be restricted to the duty of the *prācīnāvīta*. Thus, even when performed by the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), these acts must be done with the default duty of the *yajñopavīta*. However, the pouring out of rice and other materials, which is performed by the sacrificer using mantras such as "I pour out for you, acceptable to the fathers" and "I pour out for you, acceptable to the grandfathers," is properly accompanied by the *prācīnāvīta*. In this context, since the cooking for the ancestors and the cooking for the *vaiśvadeva* is one and the same, it is not for the sake of the *vaiśvadeva* alone. Even if there were a separate pouring out, the state of wearing the *yajñopavīta* should not be asserted as being prompted by that [specific act].

But then, how is it that there is a separate statement regarding the performance of the Vaiśvadeva offering, namely: "One should perform the cooking for the sake of the ancestors, and indeed for the sake of the Vaiśvadeva"?

Not so. For the term *vaiśvadeva* refers to the sacrifice to the gods (*devayajña*) included among the five great sacrifices (*pañcamahāyajña*), as it is well known by that name. If one asks how this is so, it is not [uncertain], because it forms a single syntactical unit with the phrase "the *vaiśvadevika* portion of the *darśa* [sacrifice]. Here, indeed, the status of being *vaiśvadevika* for the *darśa* is prohibited; yet this does not apply to the *vaiśvadevika* rite that is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) of the *darśa-śrāddha*, since that too is included within the meaning of the word *darśa*. Furthermore, a prohibition of the *darśa* itself cannot logically apply to something other than the *darśa* itself. However, the bringing of materials for bathing—such as cow’s hair, wool, the clipping of nails, tooth-sticks, oil, and *āmalaka* fruits—must be performed by one wearing the sacrificial cord in its usual position (*yajñopavīta*), because these acts are devoid of the specific division between rites for the gods and those for the ancestors. This absence of division regarding the aforementioned specific rules is understood from the injunction concerning the subsequent item: "one should give with *audumbara* vessels, preceded by the *vaiśvadeva* [rite]," which indicates a distinction between the ritual properties of the gods and the ancestors. Regarding the act of giving, the phrase "preceded by the *vaiśvadeva*" serves as an indicative mark (*liṅga*) for the instruction on the specific ritual properties of the gods and ancestors; thus, the distinction between the sacrificial cord (*yajñopavīta*) and the cord over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvīta*) is also understood. When the performance of the obligatory daily rites (*nityakarman*) and the bath are carried out simultaneously (*tantra*), their two respective ritual properties—the *yajñopavīta* and the *prācīnāvīta*—are in conflict. Since one of the two must necessarily be abandoned, the incidental (*āgantuka*) *prācīnāvīta* should be set aside, and the original (*autsargika*) *yajñopavīta* alone should be adopted.

Now, one might argue that the ritual bath (*karmāṅga-snāna*) is indeed a modification (*vikṛti*) of the obligatory daily bath (*nitya-snāna*), because it adopts the procedural details (*itikartavyatā*) prescribed for the latter. Furthermore, there is the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) which, being established as a general rule (*anārabhyādhīta*) by such statements as "it should be performed while wearing the sacred thread" and "it should be performed over the right shoulder," applies to the obligatory daily bath due to its being the primary model (*prakṛti*). Therefore, the directly enjoined (*aupadeśika*) *prācīnāvīta* (wearing the thread over the left shoulder) will serve as an exception (*bādhaka*) to the *yajñopavīta* obtained through extension (*atideśa*). Nor should it be said that the *prācīnāvīta* is not even directly enjoined, since its prescription could apply to another vessel, setting aside the ritual bath as a constituent part of a rite. This is because it is improper to restrict a direct injunction merely to conform to an extended application. Moreover, there is no rule requiring the simultaneous performance (*tantrānuṣṭhāna*) of the obligatory daily bath and the ritual bath as a constituent part, as their respective properties (*dharma*) differ. Consequently, when the ritual bath is performed separately, what can prevent the *prācīnāvīta* from applying all the more?

It is said in reply: By the statement "the rite for the ancestors (pitrya) [is performed] up to the conclusion," the *prācīnāvīta* mode of wearing the sacred thread is prescribed for the ancestral rite (*pitrya*) in general by means of the invitatory verse (*anuvākyā*). Furthermore, even in the case of funeral rites (*pretakriyā*), it is possible to designate them as "ancestral" (*pitrya*) because the term *pitṛmedha* is employed therein, and because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the word *svadhā* prescribed in the *Vaijavāpa-gaṇa*: "They should offer one handful of water to the deceased, saying, 'Svadhā to such-and-such a person'. Therefore, since bathing is an ancillary part of that [funeral rite], there is a general application of the *prācīnāvīta* mode due to its being an ancestral act; moreover, specific injunctions for the *prācīnāvīta* are indeed observed in that context.
And so Śaṅkha and Likhita state:

"The relatives of the deceased, having descended into the water according to their seniority, shall not rub [themselves] but shall pour out water once, facing the north; the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya do exactly the same, having placed their lower garment and sacrificial thread over the right shoulder (apavīta)."

‘Of the deceased’ (*pretasya*) means of one who has passed away; ‘relatives’ (*bāndhavāḥ*) refers to the *sapiṇḍas*, *samānodakas*, and so forth; ‘according to seniority’ (*yathāvṛddham*) means without transgressing the order of age; ‘having descended into the water’ (*udakam avatīrya*) means having plunged into the water located in a reservoir; they should not rub their limbs with the hand, a cloth, or anything else. Then, having returned to the bank, there they should, with joined palms (*añjali*), ‘once’ (*sakṛt*)—that is, a single time—facing the north-eastern direction (*pradakṣiṇābhimukhāḥ*). The qualification ‘once’ and so forth also applies to the descent into the water. The same applies to Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas. Having descended into the divine water as a Brāhmaṇa does, they should sprinkle water; ‘with the sacred thread over the right shoulder’ (*apasavyam*) means having placed the upper garment (*vāsaḥ*) and the sacrificial thread (*yajñopavītam*)—the latter being the *brahmasūtra*—in such a way that both are positioned over the right shoulder, meaning having arranged them with effort so that they take the form of the *prācīnāvīta*. However, because the Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas are mentioned separately, it is understood that they may face other directions as well. For this very reason, Pracetas says:

The relatives of the deceased, descending into the water in order of seniority, should not rub [themselves] but should sprinkle water at the water's edge with their sacred threads and garments over the right shoulder (aprasavya). Facing south for a Brāhmaṇa, facing north for a Kṣatriya, and facing east for a Vaiśya, they should perform the rite.
It must be stated that the term *apasavya* here is connected specifically with the act of sprinkling, because its connection with bathing is also clearly established.
Thus it is stated by Baudhāyana:

But at a death, having placed the elders in front according to seniority, having made their sacred threads (*yajñopavīta*) inauspicious—that is, having worn them as *prācīnāvīta*—having descended to the very water’s edge, having submerged and emerged three times, and having poured out water for that purpose, they then descend and sip water.
Regarding "inauspicious," it means they are not auspicious; the meaning is that they are worn as *prācīnāvīta*.
Pāraskara also says this with reference to the death of a relative:

Wearing a single garment with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītin), they immerse themselves facing south, holding water with the thumb and ring finger of the left hand while reciting: "May the waters wash away our sin" (*naḥ śośucad agham*).

"Ekavastrāḥ" means those devoid of an upper garment (*uttarīya*); and this [act], together with the rule "having placed the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*apasavya*)," is presented as an option alongside the mention of the upper garment, or is restricted to specific Vedic branches (*śākhā*). Having "removed" (*apanodya*) the particles of water and the *amalaka*-berries, grass, etc., from that place with the ring finger and the next-to-last finger of the left hand, the relatives, facing south, should perform the bath while reciting the mantra: "May the waters burn away our sin" (*āpo naḥ śośucad agham*). Thus, since the rule for the *prācīnāvīta* (the sacred thread over the right shoulder) applies specifically to the bathing for the deceased, one concludes that the exclusion of the *prācīnāvīta* applies to baths performed for the sake of desire, such as the *pārvaṇa-śrāddha* and others.

[Objection: But surely the statement of Manu beginning with "prācīnāvītī" is recited in the section on the *darśa-śrāddha*; therefore, it should not apply elsewhere than to that context. Since the rule for wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvīta*) would thus not apply to the bathing for the deceased (*preta-snāna*), how can there be an exclusion (*parisaṃkhyā*)? Nor should it be argued that because this statement stands as an isolated injunction (*anārabhyavāda*), it applies universally; for there is a fixed rule that isolated injunctions are restricted to their respective specific subjects.

It is said: although the *prācīnāvīta* (wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder) is an integral part of the *darśa-śrāddha*, its application to the bathing that forms part of the funeral rites (*pretakriyā*) occurs by extension (*atideśa*), just as it does for the model sacrifice (*prakṛti*). Therefore, since the *prācīnāvīta* is obtained through extension, its specific prescription for this particular bathing constitutes a restrictive injunction (*parisaṃkhyā*). Alternatively, because of the observation of a Vedic indicative mark (*liṅga*) stating "the *prācīnāvīta* for the ancestors" (*pitṝṇām*), the *prācīnāvīta* is generally applicable to all ancestral rites (*pitrya*) in their general form. Consequently, it is established that in any bathing other than that which is an integral part of the funeral rites—such as the bathing that is an integral part of the *darśa* and other *śrāddhas* directed toward the ancestors—the *prācīnāvīta* is not used; rather, the standard *yajñopavīta* (wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder) must be employed. Furthermore, the ritual rinsing of the mouth (*ācamana*) for the purpose of bathing during an ancestral rite must be performed while wearing the *yajñopavīta*, because in the rule "one should bathe wearing the *yajñopavīta*" (*yajñopavītī snāyāt*), the *yajñopavīta* is prescribed for the bathing along with its entire procedure (*setikartavyatāka*). Moreover, those ritual rinsings of the mouth which are integral parts of the *śrāddha*—performed at the commencement of the *śrāddha*, the washing of the Brahmins' feet, the worship, the scattering of food (*vikiro*), the offering of rice balls (*piṇḍa*), and at the conclusion of the *śrāddha*—must also be performed while equipped with the *yajñopavīta*, due to the same prescription of the *yajñopavīta*.
For this very reason, Gautama says regarding the putting on of the *yajñopavīta*:
"Wearing the *yajñopavīta*, having washed his hands up to the wrists, remaining silent, and touching his heart, he should sip water three or four times" (GDh 1.35).

Here, due to the firmness of the practice of the learned (*śiṣṭa*), the word *yajñopavīta* intends to refer to the *brahmasūtra* endowed with the specific configuration previously explained, and not merely to the *brahmasūtra* in general.
Regarding the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*), Hārīta states a rule for wearing the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) by way of prohibiting its absence:
"One should not [perform it] without the sacred thread, nor with the topknot untied," and so forth.
Śaṅkha also says the same.
"One should not [perform rites] with unwashed feet, nor while lacking the sacrificial cord (*yajñopavīta*).

Now, one might object: these general statements are sublated within their own scope by this specific statement that "the ancestral rite (*pitrya karma*) must be performed with the sacred thread suspended over the left shoulder (*prācīnāvītin*)."

Not so. First of all, the direct hearing of the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) *pitryam* denotes an action prescribed as being related to the ancestors (*pitṛ*). In that regard, some things are "related to the ancestors" (*pitrya*) because they are directly prescribed as such, such as the giving of perfumes and so forth to the Brahmins representing the ancestors; and some are "related to the ancestors" because they are auxiliary parts of the ancestral rite (*pitṛkarman*), such as cooking and sprinkling. In this context, regarding the act of sipping water (*ācamana*), since it is directly related to the ancestors, the status of being an ancestor arises through the consideration of the finality [of the sequence] as understood from the means of knowledge known as *prakaraṇa* (context) and *ārabhya* (commencement). Consequently, the scriptural injunction for wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvīta*) applies to that [act of sipping] only after a delay. However, the scriptural injunctions for wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*yajñopavīta*) apply immediately to the entire act of sipping water, without having to wait for the operation of other intervening means of knowledge. Therefore, even though sipping water is an auxiliary part of the ritual action, the *yajñopavīta*, which is first established, is not set aside by the *prācīnāvīta*, which is established later and finds its scope only in matters other than the sipping of water. Thus, in that case too, the *yajñopavīta* alone must be employed; as for facing south (*dakṣiṇāmukhatva*), that must be done by virtue of a specific scriptural statement. And so says Devala in the section on sipping water:
"First, standing facing the east, one should slowly wash one's feet;
or facing north for rites pertaining to the gods, and facing south for those pertaining to the ancestors.

As for those sips of water (*ācamana*) required during the performance due to causes such as sneezing, there is no requirement for the *prācīnāvīta* (the sacred thread over the right shoulder) precisely because they do not constitute an integral part of the ritual action itself.

But surely, even for those [purificatory acts], there must indeed be a status as auxiliary to the ritual (*karmāṅgatva*), by way of removing impurity—which is a cause of deficiency—and by way of producing purity, which brings about the sixfold excellence (*ṣāḍguṇya*). It was with this very intention that the Teacher [Śabara] stated, when introducing the sipping of water (*ācamana*) for the sake of Smṛti-purification, in order to avoid the contradiction with the time and other factors of the Śruti-ritual: "When one has prepared the Veda [the sacrificial grass] and then, without having prepared the altar (*vedi*), sips water or sneezes, he is said to be 'preparing the altar itself' at that moment."

It is said in reply: By the statement "the rite must be performed by one who is pure," the status of purity as an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the ritual action is understood. And that purity, being accomplished during the performance of the sacrifice through *ācamana* (sipping water), which is prescribed for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*), is connected to the sacrifice as well by way of a single application (*tantra*). Nor should it be argued that the *ācamana*, though intended for the person, may also serve the purpose of the sacrifice—like the use of *khadira* wood [which serves both purposes]—because there is no such "separation of connection" (*saṃyogapṛthaktva*). The statement of the Teacher is intended only to show that the purity produced by *ācamana* does not constitute an interruption; for they themselves have stated that it is the mere fact of purity that does not interrupt.
"For one should indeed perform the *vedi* without sipping water; otherwise it would become defective.
To make that very [act] complete with its qualities, one should not be separated from purity.
Thus [it is said]. Śaṅkha states the fault incurred when the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) is absent during the sipping of water for the sake of purification:
"A twice-born man without his sacred thread, likewise with his topknot untied, or with unwashed feet—even if he has sipped water—shall remain impure. Thus it is said.

Furthermore, regarding those ritual rinsings (*ācamana*) performed here for reasons of impurity that are not due to an emergency (*anāpad*), there is no doubt at all that the *prācīnāvīta* position applies; thus, everything is faultless. Since the cutting and fetching of *darbha* grass are already established by the rules for *darbha* itself, they are merely restated (*anuvāda*) here and are excluded from the formal ritual procedure (*prayoga*); therefore, like agricultural work and similar activities, they possess the default characteristic of the *yajñopavīta*. Moreover, since the *prācīnāvīta* is taught for the fetching of what has been invited to the site of the *śrāddha*, its absence is understood to apply to the fetching of what has not been invited. Furthermore, because the sprinkling and fetching—accompanied by the procedural details (*itikartavyatā*) such as the *varuṇasruti*—are intended for all purposes including the five great sacrifices (*pañcamahāyajña*), they share the same characteristics as other [ritual acts]. By this logic, the *yajñopavīta* must be employed for the materials intended for the *śrāddha*; however, the act of fetching them toward the *śrāddha* site must be performed with the *prācīnāvīta*.
One should slowly bring everything from the right side using the apasavya method.

This is according to the statement in the *Matsya Purāṇa*. Since the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) of the materials pertains to both the gods and the ancestors, it belongs to the ancestral (*pitrya*) category; therefore, its performance is done with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*apasavya*). As for the invitation of the Brahmins, since it is merely a restatement of what is already implied by the purpose of the rite, it must be performed as before, with the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*yajñopavītin*). On the contrary, acts such as rising to greet them, asking if they have arrived well, feeding them, seating them, removing dust from their feet on the path, washing their feet, and the like, as well as the decoration with perfumes and garlands, are worldly in nature and must be performed with the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*savya*). Furthermore, the two subsequent invitations should be understood in the same manner as the first invitation, distinguishing between the positions for the gods and the ancestors using the *savya* and *apasavya* methods, based on the *Āpastamba* injunction: "As the first, so the second and the third. Considering that the drawing of the circles (*maṇḍala*), their worship, the washing of the Brahmins' feet, their honoring, the offering of the *arghya*, and so forth, belong to both the divine and ancestral categories, these should be performed according to the distribution of the duties of the sacred thread as established by the general rules proclaimed by Āśvalāyana. Regarding certain items here, verses from the *Nāgarakhaṇḍa* which prescribe the *savya* and *apasavya* duties will be shown in the practical application. The disposal of the remnants of materials used for the washing and worship of the feet of the gods and ancestors follows the same *savya* and *apasavya* distinction. Even the arrival at the site of the *śrāddha* is naturally governed by this division. Both the recitation of the success of the *śrāddha* (*śrāddhasiddhi-vācana*) and the act itself, being of a dual nature and being prescribed, should be performed by one wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītin*).

An objection is raised: since the rule for the sacrificial thread (*yajñopavīta*) is prescribed in the context of "recitation, benediction, and the proclamation of auspiciousness" (*japāśīḥsvastivācana*), and since this [present rite] has the form of a *ṛṣi*-text, how can there be the "wearing of the thread over the right shoulder" (*prācīnāvīta*)?

Not so. Since this [rite] consists of a request, it shares the nature of a benediction for satisfaction; because it is connected solely to the ritual action as a means to accomplish the essential form of that action, the *prācīnāvīta* (wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder) is prescribed by that [connection]. By this very principle, one should apply the *prācīnāvīta* in the following cases: the worship of ancestors (*paitṛkābhyarcana*), the offering of rice balls (*piṇḍadāna*), the *śrāddha*, the declaration of the fulfillment of the resolve (*saṃkalpasiddhivācana*) regarding the ancestral Brahmins, and the declaration of the absence of defects (*acchidravācana*). The preparation of the *śrāddha* ground—including smearing with cow dung and cow urine, circling with a firebrand (*aulmuka*), scattering *kuśa* grass and sesame seeds, and tying on a cloth—must likewise be performed while wearing the *prācīnāvīta*. The preparation of the seats, the placing of *kuśa* grass beneath the feet of the twice-born guests, the seating of the guests, the scattering of sesame seeds with the mantra "Apatā" (the evil spirits are struck down), the placing of vessels, lamps, and other items, the drawing of a boundary with ashes and other materials to prevent confusion of rows, the washing of the vessels, the giving of water for hand-cleansing, and the pouring of clarified butter (*ājya*) into each vessel—these acts should be performed according to the respective context of the divine or ancestral station by those wearing either the *yajñopavīta* or the *prācīnāvīta*. The seating of the guest, the praises of the earth and other elements, the praise of the deities, and the breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*) should be done using the left hand alone. The announcement of place and time, and the interrogative formula "I shall perform [this] with your permission," should be uttered by one wearing the *prācīnāvīta*.

Pracetas states that even the recitation of specific mantras occurring prior to the utterance [of the main formula] possesses the characteristic of being performed with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (prācīnāvīta):
"Then, having placed the sacred thread over the right shoulder and having recited the Vaiṣṇava mantra..."
"Having recited the Gāyatrī and the Praṇava, one should then commence the Śrāddha. Thus it is said.

The word "then" (*tataḥ*) means immediately after the Brāhmaṇas have been seated and after the *prāṇāyāma* has been performed. The commencement of the *śrāddha* consists in making the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*). The recitation of the *Saptārcis* and other mantras must be done with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvīta*), because the rule "but as for the recitation while they are eating" restricts the application of the exceptions regarding the *prācīnāvīta* specifically to the time of the meal. Furthermore, the tying of the waist-knot (*nīvībandha*) must be performed with the thread over the right shoulder, based on the scriptural statement that "the waist-knot belongs to the ancestors" (*pitṛdevatyā vai nīviḥ*). The rites pertaining to the Viśvedevas—from the offering of the *darbha* seats up to the covering—must be performed with the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*yajñopavītin*).
Regarding the ancestral rite (pitrya), Bṛhaspati says that it begins and ends with the sacred thread worn over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītī).

Having offered straight darbha grass to the gods with the left hand while circumambulating to the right, one should offer double-folded grass to the ancestors with the sacred thread over the right shoulder, following the procedure for the ancestors.

Here, by the terms *savya* and *apasavya*, the *yajñopavīta* and *prācīnāvīta* are intended, and not right-handedness (*pradakṣiṇatva*) and left-handedness (*aprakṣiṇatva*). This is because those two are mentioned separately from *pradakṣiṇa* and *apasavya* by means of distinct words. "Darbhas" refers to a seat of darbha grass; and this occurs on the left side at the end of the giving of coverings, immediately after the completion of the section of ritual items belonging to the *vaiśvadeva*.
By teaching the *prācīnāvīta* at that time, Yājñavalkya indicates the continued application of the *yajñopavīta* for that duration:
"Then, having performed the *apasavya* rite, one proceeds to the left for the ancestors. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.239)
Having offered double-folded kusha grass while reciting the verse "uśantas tvā," [one should offer] to the ancestors.

The word "āvāhayed" (he should invoke) is to be connected with what follows. And this [practice], being worn over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvīta*), continues up until the covering, setting aside the application of the remnants of the *arghya* water. For this very reason, in certain items occurring within the ritual sequence from the seat of *darbha* grass to the covering, the explicit mention of the *prācīnāvīta* is observed. Thus, it is stated in the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*:
"Then, having placed the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*apasavya*) and taking up sesame seeds while self-controlled, he should ask the north-facing Brahmins: 'I shall invoke the ancestors.'"
Regarding the *arghya* vessels, the *Gṛhya-sūtra* composed by Vaijavāpa states:

"One should place the vessels, with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvīta*), not filled [with water], provided with *darbha* grass, and containing sesame seeds, to the west of the fire upon *darbha* grass."

Regarding "of Agni," such as the *Anvāhāryapacana* fire and so forth: therefore, the ritual section pertaining to the ancestors (*pitrya-karmakāṇḍa*), beginning with the offering of the *darbha*-grass seat and ending with the covering, must be performed with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*apasavya*). It should not be argued that the offering of perfume, flowers, incense, lamps, and clothing is intended for the Brahmins alone and not for the ancestors, because that would be a worldly act and thus subject to the rule of wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*yajñopavīta*). This is because it has been stated that the gift is indeed for the ancestors, with the Brahmins serving merely as the locus (*adhiṣṭhāna*) for that offering. As for the *agnaukaraṇa* (offering into the fire), however, those following the school of Kātyāyana must perform it with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītin*) starting from the request for permission (*anujñābhyarthanā*) onwards. Those following the school of Āśvalāyana must perform it with the sacred thread over the right shoulder starting either from the request for permission or from the subsequent items thereafter. Alternatively, all may perform it with the sacred thread over the right shoulder or over the left shoulder (*yajñopavīta*) from the very beginning. All of this will be explained in detail in the section [1122] concerning the determination of the *prācīnāvīta* and other details within the procedure for *agnaukaraṇa*. However, the disposal of the remnants of the oblation (*hutaśeṣa-pratipatti*) must be performed by everyone with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvīta*), since Śaunaka states here that the *apasavya* rule applies universally.
Having offered [the oblation] into the fire, he should immediately pour the remainder into the vessels for the ancestors;
then, having made the announcement, he should perform the serving of food with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (apasavya).

In this manner, such a procedure (anvaya) is to be understood. For Kārṣṇājini says: "The ancestral rite (pitrya-kṛtya) must be performed entirely with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (apasavya), with the exception of the offering of food; the same applies to the rites for maternal grandfathers."

In this context, "giving food" (*annadāna*) is intended to mean serving it; it does not refer to the relinquishment of food with the ancestors as the intended recipients. This is because such an act is directly connected to the ancestors and is primarily denoted by the term *pitrya* (pertaining to the ancestors), and thus falls primarily within the scope of the rule regarding the *prācīnāvīta* (the sacred thread worn over the right shoulder).
The same author states the fault in serving food with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*apasavya*):
"But he who offers food to the Brāhmaṇas with the sacred thread over the right shoulder..."
All those ancestors and all those best of the twice-born eat excrement.

In the *vaiśvadevika* (rite for the Viśvedevas), the acts of touching the vessel, placing the thumb [into the food], bowing, relinquishing [the food], eating, and giving commands should be performed with the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*savya*). In the *pitrya* (rite for the ancestors), these should be performed with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*apasavya*). For the guest, everything must be done while the sacred thread is worn over the left shoulder (*yajñopavītayukta*). The recitation of verses such as "The father, the grandfather," etc., prior to the meal, and the subsequent recitation of the *Gāyatrī*, "Madhuvātā," etc., are performed with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*apasavya*). Although here, by virtue of the general statement of Jamadagni—"Pradakṣiṇa, 'May the waters be auspicious,' and the recitations and blessings"—it is said that one should wear the sacred thread over the left shoulder for all recitations (*japa*), nevertheless, other *smṛtis* state: "Except for the recitation of *sūktas* and *stotras*" and "Except for the recitation made while they are eating. Since these show an exception regarding the wearing of the thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvīti*) specifically for certain types of *japa*, the *āpośāna* rite—which is prescribed for every regular meal—is performed exactly as ordained. Because this [guest] lacks the relationship of being the "father" (which would require *apasavya*), even though the offering is made by the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), it is still a *pitrya* act; therefore, it must be performed with the sacred thread over the left shoulder. While the Brahmins are eating, the recitation of *pitrya* *sūktas*, *stotras*, mantras, *gāthās*, and narratives must be performed with the sacred thread over the left shoulder.
And likewise Marīci says:
"Circumambulation, auspicious water, the recitation of *japa*, the invocation of blessings (*svastivācana*),
and the giving of sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) to Brahmins— these six are declared to be performed with the right side toward the object (*savya*)."

‘Pradakṣiṇa’ refers to the act of circumambulating the Brāhmaṇas who are standing upon the maṇḍala after departing outside following the dismissal (*visarjana*). ‘Śivā āpaḥ’ indicates the rite consisting of water, flowers, and unbroken grains (*akṣata*) performed with mantras such as *saṃcit* and others. ‘Japa’ is the recitation of mantras and so forth for the sake of an unseen spiritual merit (*adṛṣṭa*). ‘Āśīḥ’ (blessing) is intended to mean the prayer for fruits pertaining to the sacrificer, such as “May our donors increase,” and not merely the prayer for the attainment of dharma connected solely to the nature of the ritual itself. ‘Svastivācana’ is the recitation of “May you say ‘Svasti’ (well-being). ‘The giving of sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) to the Brāhmaṇas’ refers here to the specific act where the fee is given to the Brāhmaṇas alone while using the mantra dedicated to the ancestors (*pitṛs*) and others; it does not include that which is offered to the Brāhmaṇas acting as the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) for the ancestors, because of the specific qualification by the word ‘Brāhmaṇa. These six rites are ‘with the sacred thread over the left shoulder’ (*savya*), meaning they possess the characteristic of the *yajñopavīta*.
Jamadagni also says:
"The entire Śrāddha should be performed according to the rules with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (apavīta),
except for the recitation of hymns and praises, the chanting of prayers, and the dismissal of the Brahmins."

The hymns and praises (*sūktastotra*) have been explained. That which is performed with the tip of a *kuśa* blade while reciting the verse "In strength after strength" (*vāje vāje*) is called "dismissal" (*visarjana*); that too, even when related to the ancestors, must be performed with the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*savya*). The mention of "hymns and praises" is intended as an illustration for all that is to be muttered (*japya*) while the Brahmins are eating. Thus says Vṛddha-Śātātapa:
"Having placed the sacred thread over the left shoulder, one should perform whatever muttering is done by those who are eating."

The phrase "of those eating" (*aśnatām*) means the silent recitation (*japa*) performed by the sacrificer while the Brahmins are eating. Because of the inclusion of the term "eating," the *prācīnāvīta* (the sacred thread over the right shoulder) must be worn for any recitation occurring at times other than the time of the Brahmins' meal. The scattering of food (*vikira-dāna*), together with all one's remaining limbs turned toward the east and north, is to be done with the *apasavya* (the thread over the left shoulder). The single offering of water for rinsing the mouth (*gaṇḍūṣa*) intended for the removal of the vessels should be performed by one wearing the *yajñopavīta* (the thread over the left shoulder), because it follows the same rule as the offering of *āpośāna* water. The inquiry "Are you satisfied? (*tṛptāḥ stha*) and the inquiry regarding the disposal of the remaining food should be performed with the *apasavya*, since they are intended to be common to both the rites for the gods and the ancestors. When the twice-born have sipped water, the sprinkling of the *śrāddha* deities with the formula "May it be well-sprinkled" (*suprokṣitam astu*)—though interwoven with a request for blessings—is to be performed by one wearing the *prācīnāvīta*, because it is connected to the same ritual act as the request for the completion of the *śrāddha* procedure. However, the offerings of water, flowers, and unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*) into the hands of the Brahmins—such as the mantra "May the waters be auspicious" (*śivā āpaḥ santu*) and others—which are accompanied by mantras expressing blessings appropriate to the sacrificer, are to be performed by one wearing the *yajñopavīta*, because they are connected to generally auspicious acts and are performed without reference to the ancestors.
And thus, on this point, Śaṅkhaḍhara has cited the Chāgaleya-smṛti:
"With his left hand, holding water, and with *darbha* grass in his hand, one should offer flowers individually, while restraining speech, mind, and body."

Therefore, the teacher Karka says: "After they have sipped water, the ritual for the ancestors (pitrya) follows the one for the gods (daiva), ending with the offering of water, flowers, and unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*); then [the procedure] is performed with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*apasavya*). However, some desire it to be done with the thread over the left shoulder (*savya*). That is not correct, because of the connection with the act of giving. The mode of performance is like that of the Piṇḍapitṛyajña, because of the instruction regarding the state of being a father."

That [position] has been refuted by the continuous presentation of reasoned arguments and scriptural statements, and thus appears as something that should not be accepted. Furthermore, since the *akṣayyodaka* (the water for inexhaustibility) is prescribed for the sake of the gods and for the sake of the ancestors and others, it should be performed with the sacrificial thread over the right shoulder (*yajñopavīta*) for the gods, and with the thread over the left shoulder (*prācīnāvīta*) for those who are not ancestral. Regarding the recitation of benedictions such as "May the ancestors be free from cruelty," "May our lineage increase," and "May our donors prosper," as well as the *japa*, *āśīḥ*, and *svastivācana*, their performance with the sacrificial thread over the right shoulder is established by the previously cited statement of Jamadagni. Moreover, because the *svadhāvācana* (the invocation of *svadhā*) constitutes a rite for the ancestors, it possesses the characteristics of the *prācīnāvīta*; likewise, the pouring out of the remnants of the *arghya* water contained in the vessels, and the turning of the face-down vessel upward, must be performed with the sacrificial thread over the left shoulder (*prācīnāvītin*).
For this very reason, Atri says immediately after the acceptance of the benediction: "Then,
having placed the sacred thread over the right shoulder (apasavya), being composed, he should cast down the darbha-strainers by the side of the pindas and then release the residual drops."

Thus, the giving of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is performed by some for the sake of the Brahmins alone; by others, however, who desire an excellence of merit toward the ancestors, it is performed with the Brahmins merely as the substratum for the ancestors. In that regard, the former should act with the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*yajñopavīta*), while the latter should act with it over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvīta*). For this very reason, Jamadagni has shown two alternatives:
"All ritual action is to be done with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*apasavya*), except for the giving of the sacrificial fee."

Likewise: "Every rite mentioned here is to be performed with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (apasavya), with the single exception of the offering to the south and the dismissal of the Brahmins."

Regarding the recitation for the gratification of the Viśvedevas, the wearing of the *yajñopavīta* has already been mentioned previously. The performance of the washing of the eating vessels at the places designated for the gods and the ancestors must be carried out according to the distinction between the left (*savya*) and the right (*apasavya*). Some perform the *svastivācana* as belonging to the ancestors, while others do so as belonging to the sacrificer; yet both must be performed by one wearing the *yajñopavīta*, because of the rule stating that the *japa*, the benediction (*āśis*), and the *svastivācana* are all to be done thus. Furthermore, it was shown earlier that the dismissal (*visarjana*) in both the rites for the gods and the ancestors must be performed by one wearing the *yajñopavīta*. Śaunaka also says:

Having offered the *svadhā* with the words "May there be *svadhā*," he should dismiss [the ancestors] with "So be it, *svadhā*"; furthermore, the following behind [the Brahmins] must be performed while wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītin*).

In the act of circumambulating a Brāhmaṇa, the duty of wearing the sacrificial thread (*yajñopavīta*) applies. Furthermore, the acceptance of flowers and unbroken rice (*akṣata*) given by a Brāhmaṇa, the utterance of pleasant words such as "Today my birth has become fruitful," the recitation of mantras, massaging, accompanying [the guest] to his place, requesting permission to depart, and following him to the boundary—all these must be performed while wearing the sacrificial thread, because they are worldly acts consisting of the virtuous conduct of a distinguished person being sent off. As for the covering of the leavings (*ucchiṣṭācchādana*), since it is performed solely for the sake of the ritual purpose—just like the daily meal—it is purely worldly and must therefore be accomplished with the sacrificial thread. As for the restriction of time seen here, prescribed by texts such as "That leavings should remain... and so forth, that does not contradict its worldly nature. Regarding the eating of the middle *piṇḍa* performed by the wife: because it is enjoined in connection with the desire for a son, it has the singular character of an optional rite (*kāmya*). Consequently, the offering of the *piṇḍa* to the wife by the sacrificer lacks any connection to the ancestors; thus, it possesses the characteristic of the sacrificial thread (*yajñopavīta*). However, as for the disposal (*pratipatti*) of the *piṇḍas* which is an ancillary part of the offering, enjoined by texts such as "The *piṇḍas*, however, [should be given] to cows, goats, or Brāhmaṇas," this is characterized by the *prācīnāvīta* (wearing the thread over the right shoulder) because it is connected to the ancestral rite (*pitrya*) due to its relation to the ancestors. Even though this disposal is mentioned in connection with a specific desire, it possesses both a permanent (*nitya*) and an optional (*kāmya*) form. Therefore, because of its inherent ancestral character, it is proper to determine that the procedure must indeed be performed with the *prācīnāvīta*; the *prācīnāvīta* does not cease simply because it is performed under an optional motive. Finally, regarding the eating of the remnants of the *śrāddha* performed by one's own kinsmen or by the sacrificer himself: although it assists the *śrāddha* by providing sustenance to all, all learned authorities (*śiṣṭas*) are seen to practice the rule of the sacrificial thread, considering it to be outside the formal ritual procedure (*prayoga*) because it occurs after the performance of the five great sacrifices (*pañcamahāyajña*) which are enjoined for the period following the conclusion of the ceremony. Thus, its possession of that characteristic (the *yajñopavīta*) must be accepted.
Thus ends the specific determination.
Thus ends the determination regarding the *prācīnāvīta* (the sacred thread worn over the right shoulder).

This concludes the section titled "The Section on General Rules" (*paribhāṣāprakaraṇa*) within the *Śrāddhakalpa* of the *Pariśeṣakhaṇḍa* of the *Caturvargacintāmaṇi*, composed by the illustrious Hemādri, the scholar (*paṇḍita*) and chief minister of all affairs to the illustrious Mahādevīya, the illustrious Great King of Kings.
The Tenth Chapter.
[1127] Now begins the eleventh chapter. To Bali, the preeminent among givers in the matter of charity, and to Dvaipāyana in the matter of speech—

He who surpassed all sages in asceticism and was a preceptor in the excellence of wisdom— this very same Hemādri, now remembering the Lord of the Daughter of the Ocean, undertakes to declare the ritual procedure for the *śrāddha* as it has been ordained.

First, he introduces the section on the invitation therein: the ritual procedure (*vidhi*) in which the host of subtle and excellent objects of the sacrifice has been extracted by the light of expanded wisdom,
and whose extensive range of refined applications has been scrutinized by the virtuous.
It shall abide as the locus of intentions becoming thickened with the nectar of bliss.
Now, regarding the invitation (*nimantraṇa*).

Here, indeed, when the performance of a *śrāddha* is about to commence, since the selection of Brahmins suitable for that rite would otherwise follow even without an invitation, the specific rule of invitation is set forth for the purpose of establishing the restriction that the selection of Brahmins must be carried out precisely by means of the formal procedure of invitation.
In this regard, the *Vāyupurāṇa* states:
The twice-born who have bathed after completing all Vedic vows, who purify the rows [of diners],
who are foremost among those who know the commentaries, and who are devoted to grammar;

Those who study the Purāṇas and likewise the Dharmaśāstras; one who has mastered the Tṛṇāciketa fire-ritual, one who maintains the five sacred fires, one who knows the Trisuparṇa hymns, and one who is learned in the six Vedāṅgas.
The son of a Brāhmaṇa gift, a singer of the *Chāndoga* hymns, and a chanter of the *Jyeṣṭhasāman*,
who have performed their vows and taken ritual ablutions at sacred deities and holy fords;
One should indeed invite to the śrāddha those who have performed the ritual ablutions at the principal sacrificial sessions (satras),
those who always observe immediate vows, those who are devoted to their own duties,
and those who are free from anger and intent on peace.
"And those who are always established in the ten virtuous deeds, constantly devoted to their own duties—these one should invite to the *śrāddha* ceremonies. Thus it is said.

"‘All the Vedas’: this refers to a single, complete branch (*śākhā*) consisting of both Mantra and Brāhmaṇa, as well as all the vows associated with it, including those of the *kṛcchra* type and others; or alternatively, ‘all the Vedas’ refers to the three branches known as Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma, along with their related scriptures and vows. In that regard, ‘bathed’ (*snātāḥ*) means those who have reached the further shore, being proficient or established therein. ‘Of rows’ (*paṅktīnām*) refers to the successions of Brahmins seated for the purpose of a meal; ‘seated in the midst’ of these, they become ‘purifiers’ (*pāvanāḥ*), meaning they bring about purity.
