"One should scatter sesame seeds there and tie goats on all sides;
everything defiled by an *āsura* [rite] is purified by sesame seeds and by a goat."

Immediately thereafter, desiring to begin the cooking, one should remove from the cooking area those persons mentioned in the section on those to be excluded: the loathsome, the envious, the intoxicated, the rogue, the Śūdra and his wife, the outcaste, the heretic, the eunuch, the one-eyed, the one with a withered arm, the killer of an embryo, the leper, the one afflicted with skin disease, the woman in her menses, the unchaste woman, those of mixed birth, the hunchback, the dwarf, those with missing, deficient, or redundant limbs, the lame, the dog, the boar, the donkey, the camel, the elephant, the cock, the dog, the mongoose, the cat, the Caṇḍāla, and those wearing indigo-dyed or astringent-stained garments; having driven them far away, one should arrange the cooking vessels and utensils as appropriate. Then, once the ground has been thus prepared and the new vessels have been cleaned, one should proceed to perform the cooking.
And likewise Devala says:
"In that same manner, the donor, having bathed in the morning and being properly restrained,
together with his kinsmen and wearing new garments, should begin the commencement of the food with new vessels."

This is the meaning: having bathed, he himself—provided he has the capacity—should perform the entire commencement and completion of the cooking together with his wife, who has likewise bathed and is wearing white garments that have been washed by a washerman. If he is incapable, having performed the commencement himself, he should have the subsequent supervision (*anvārambha*) carried out by his kinsmen or relatives. Regarding this, there is an alternative reading: *anvārambhaṃ ca bāndhavaiḥ*. There is also another reading: *annārambhavatāṃ vidhiḥ*.
As for the point that the cooking must be performed by the wife’s own hand, there is an indicative mark (*liṅga-darśana*) on this matter in the *Camatkārakhaṇḍa*.
Then,
at the command of Rāma, that virtuous lady born of Janaka herself, endowed with humility, prepared it for his sake.
Also in the *Prabhāsakhaṇḍa*:
"Then Sītā, the daughter of Janaka, quickly cooked these [grains].
And this commencement of cooking must be performed by one possessing the sacred fire, preceded by the pouring of water accompanied by mantras."
And so it is stated in the *Padma-purāṇa* and the *Matsya-purāṇa*:
"One who maintains the sacred fire should offer the *caru* oblation for the ancestors with handfuls of unhusked grain,
saying 'I offer this to the ancestors,' and he should place everything to the south."

Because of the mention of "rice" (*caru*), it is understood that the pouring out (*nirvāpa*) applies only to the boiled rice (*odana*) and not to the soup, vegetables, and so forth. Regarding the phrase "with unequal handfuls," this means with handfuls of uneven number.
On this point, some who maintain that the requirement for "new vessels" applies only to the annual rite (*sāṃvatsarika*) and not elsewhere, cite the following statement:
"The preparation of new vessels and likewise the anointing of the Brahmins..."
"Before the *śrāddha*, there shall be non-giving; thus, for each year, there are three [items].

This is incorrect, because the mention of "each year" (*pratyabda*) is understood as being for the sake of showing great respect, and because it would result in the postponement (*utkarṣa*) of new vessels and other items prescribed in the section on the *darśa-śrāddha*.
This was stated in the *Devalasmṛti* and the *Kūrmapurāṇa* immediately after the consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the ground and the vessels.
Then, one should prepare food that is well-prepared, consisting of various condiments and edibles, and abundant in things to be sucked and drunk, according to one's ability.

The meaning of this is as follows: [a feast] consisting of various preparations—abounding in many kinds of most wonderful garments and the essence of flavors; primarily made of derivatives of rice, barley, and wheat; with small side-dishes fashioned from stalks, buds, fruits, flowers, bulbs, and sprouts that suit one's desire; possessing the essence of the juices of exceedingly delicious *kūrcikā*, syrups, decoctions, and mangoes; featuring exquisite cooked specialties prepared with black sesame, mung beans, rhinoceros meat, goat, sheep, and mungo-bean flour; and enriched with pepper, jaggery, sugar-candy, salt, asafoetida, and camphor.

One should prepare food—distinguished by the varieties of what is to be chewed, eaten, licked, sucked, and drunk—that is processed with saffron, cardamom, incense, and other ingredients, and endowed with fragrance, color, and flavor. This should be prepared according to one's capacity.
Therefore, Gautama says:
"One should enhance the qualities, preparations, and rules regarding food according to one's ability."

The "qualities" (*guṇāḥ*) of foods consist in their possessing correct species, form, taste, smell, and touch. "Refinement" (*saṃskāraḥ*) is the imparting of excellence through substances, actions, and so forth. One should "enhance" (*prakarṣayet*) these two—meaning one should bring them to excellence according to one's capacity—in accordance with one's ability.
Thus says Parāśara:
"On occasions of sacrifices and charitable works, on the anniversary of a death, on festival days, on full-moon and new-moon days, and on the eighth lunar days..."
One should, according to one's ability, provide sweet food to those who possess worthy vessels.
In this regard, it has been stated in the section on the Vaiśvadeva and related rites that one who maintains the sacred fires (sāgnika) must perform a separate cooking for the sake of the Vaiśvadeva.
Once the cooking is completed, the purification of the site for the Śrāddha must be performed. Regarding that, the ground suitable for Śrāddha is described in the Viṣṇudharmottara:
"And in houses where the Śrāddha rite is to be performed, which have been smeared with cow dung..."
In delightful, diverse, charming,
and supreme gardens, as well as in various sandy and level tracts.
In the *Padma Purāṇa*: "A wise person should offer the *śrāddha* at sacred fords, temples, and cow-pens, as well as on islands, in gardens, and in houses, provided they are secluded and well-swept."
Yama said: Having examined an auspicious site that slopes toward the south, is smooth, secluded, and possesses favorable characteristics, one should quickly smear it with cow dung.
In the *Matsya* and *Padma Purāṇas*: "One should begin the *śrāddha* with devotion on ground smeared with cow dung that slopes toward the south, or in a cow-pen, or in the vicinity of water."
Regarding this, Manu says that one should strive even with great effort to ensure the ground slopes toward the south:
"One should smear a clean and secluded place with cow dung and,
with diligent effort, ensure that it slopes toward the south."

‘Pure’ means not defiled by ashes, bones, potsherds, and the like. ‘Secluded’ means spacious and not crowded with many people. ‘Sloping toward the south’ means inclined in the southern direction. One should diligently prepare such a site and smear it with cow dung.
As stated in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*: “A site sloping toward the south, smooth, secluded, and possessing auspicious characteristics.”
One should smear a clean and secluded place with cow dung.
Paiṭhīnasi:
Having smeared a clean place— whether in a cow-pen, a fire-sanctuary, or elsewhere— with cow-dung,
and having presented an offering of flowers;
"An offering of flowers" (*puṣpāṇām upahāraḥ*) means bringing or scattering them; this is to be connected with the subsequent phrase, "he should cause the twice-born to sit.
Viṣṇu says:
"And one should perform the *śrāddha* in an enclosed place; one should not look upon a woman in her menses, nor a dog, nor a village pig."
One should diligently ensure that a village cock sees the *śrāddha* being performed by a goat.

The mention of "one in her menses" (*rajasvalā*) and so forth is intended as an illustration for all those such as the naked person (*nagna*) and others who were specified in the section on those to be excluded. "Goat" (*aja*) means a he-goat. One must act with such diligence that it is ensured the goat, being tied nearby, shall see the *śrāddha* being performed.
[This is stated] in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*.
A menstruating woman, a eunuch, dogs, pigs, and cocks—
care must be taken by the wise man so that these do not see the śrāddha. O Lord of Men, for the sake of its protection, their exclusion must be ensured.
Likewise,
O subduer of enemies, the presentation of a goat's woolen blanket is always recommended at a śrāddha, as is the presence of a kutapa cloth and a black antelope skin.
In the *Brahmāṇḍapurāṇa*:
"Therefore, one should give [the offering] while it is surrounded and scatter sesame seeds over it;
for the protection against Rākṣasas is by means of sesame seeds, and that against dogs is by means of the enclosure."
In the Mahābhārata:
"Dogs and those who defile the row of diners (paṅktidūṣa) should not look [at the food] under any circumstances;
therefore, one should give [the offering] while it is enclosed and scatter sesame seeds around it."
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*: "Formerly, Viṣṇu slew the two Dānavas, Madhu and Kaiṭabha;
then Mahendra slew Vṛtra; thereafter the earth was covered with their fat."
Therefore, that ground is indeed known by people in the world as "artha" (wealth/meaningful).
Consequently, at a *śrāddha* ceremony, it should be smeared with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), likewise purified with firebrands (*ulmuka*),
covered with white clay, and strewn with sesame and mustard seeds.
"With firebrands" means by placing firebrands all around; in that context, the mantra taught for the Piṇḍapitṛyajña, beginning with "ye rūpāṇi," should be employed.
Regarding the Śrāddha performed at a *kola* (an anthill made by boars), the Brahmapurāṇa states:
"Having scratched the earth with its tusks and sprinkled it with water..."
Having smeared it with the arising of dharma and scraped it again with kusha grass,
one should lead her around with a firebrand and sprinkle her repeatedly.

Since Varāha performed such a preparation of the ground while performing the *śrāddha* here, it is understood from this indicative mark (*liṅga*) that others should also act in exactly this manner. Furthermore, although the digging tool is prescribed as a *vajra* (thunderbolt) in the *Pitṛyajña*, which serves as the archetype for the *śrāddha*, the mention of the "tusk" is not intended to be restrictive. "Source of Dharma" (*dharmodbhava*) refers to cow dung. "Having circumambulated" means having enclosed [the area] by moving a firebrand (*ulmuka*) all around in a counter-clockwise direction.
When the domestic rites have been thus completed, Hārīta describes the duties of the household members:
Those who have completed their tasks—along with women, children, and the elderly—should bathe with fragrant substances, be pure, and wear clean garments.
"Bathed with fragrant substances" means bathed with substances such as scented oils and the like. And this [rule] generally pertains to occasions of auspicious celebration (*abhyudayika*).
This must be so;
for it is stated in the Bhaviṣyapurāṇa: "On that day, those performing the śrāddha rite should bathe along with women, children, and the elderly."
And they must remain fixed in that state until the śrāddha ceremony is completed.
Then they say: when one and a half *praharas* have passed, one should cause the invited Brahmins to have their nails and hair trimmed.
As stated in the *Vārāha-purāṇa*:
"When the night has turned into dawn and the sun has risen..."
Having brought a Divākīrti, one should present him to a Brāhmaṇa according to the prescribed rites.
O beautiful one, one who is devoted to his father should likewise perform the trimming of his beard and the clipping of his nails,
and he should provide him with bathing and anointing.
A *divākīrti* is a barber.
In the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa*: "One should give oil, unguents, and a bath only in the forenoon."
One should also have the nails and beard trimmed while on the grounds of a śrāddha feast.

The specific types of vessels for the offering of oil, massage powders, and so forth, are shown in the Devalasmṛti and the Kūrmapurāṇa. Then, at midday, once [the ritual] has concluded, he should approach the twice-born whose hair and nails have been trimmed and provide them with a tooth-stick according to the prescribed rule.
One should offer oil, unguents for rubbing the body, bathing water,
and various kinds of bath-powders using vessels made of udumbara wood, beginning with the offerings to the Viśvedevas.

"Luptaromanakhān" means those whose body hair and nails have been clipped. "Yathāmārgam" means according to the prescribed rule. "Snānam" refers to warm water for the purpose of bathing; "snānīyam" refers to fragrant substances and other materials used as implements for bathing. "Audumbaraiḥ" means made of copper, or else made from sacrificial trees such as the *udumbara*. The offering of oil should be understood to apply to those lunar days on which the use of oil is not prohibited. Regarding the phrase "tato'nivṛtte madhyāhne," one should observe that the vowel *a* is elided (praśleṣa) in the word "anivṛtte" to form "anivṛtte. Otherwise, there would be a lapse in the time for the principal rite (*pradhānakarma*) and a contradiction with the previously mentioned morning time (*pūrvāhṇakāla*).
Therefore, Mārkaṇḍeya says:
"When six muhūrtas of the day have passed, he should then send those twice-born men one by one, through messengers, with water containing *āmalaka* for bathing."

The meaning is that after twelve *ghaṭikās*, one should send attendants to the invited Brahmins with the instruction, "Give this *āmalaka* paste to each of the invited Brahmins for the purpose of bathing. This offering of *āmalaka* paste is to be understood as applying to those lunar days (*tithis*) on which the use of oil is prohibited. The author of the *Smṛticandrikā* maintains that it should be given even on those [prohibited] days, provided they are other than the new moon (*amāvāsyā*). This is because of the prohibition against bathing with *dhātrī* fruit on the new moon: "One should not bathe with *dhātrī* fruits on the new moon," which prohibits bathing with *āmalaka* water on the new moon. However, regarding a lunar day when the use of oil is not prohibited, it has already been shown in the statement of Devala that oil and such should be given for the purpose of bathing.
In the *Kātyāyana-smṛti* and the *Prabhāsakhaṇḍa* as well:
"One should give oil, unguents, a bath, and even a tooth-cleansing stick to those whose hair and nails have been cut on the following day."

The meaning is that one should give oil and other requisites for bathing, as well as wood and other materials for cleaning the teeth, to those who have been invited and whose hair and nails have been trimmed.
As for that which was stated by Pracetas:
"One should indeed give oil, unguents, and the bath during the forenoon itself."
"One should not cause those who have partaken of the *śrāddha* meal to have their nails or hair cut. Thus it is said.

In this context, the prohibition against cutting the nails and so forth for those eating at a *śrāddha* refers specifically to the occasion when the razor-work (shaving) is forbidden on certain lunar days (*tithi*). Alternatively, it may be explained as follows: the performer of the *śrāddha* should provide oil and other necessities to those eating at the *śrāddha*, but he himself should not have his nails and so forth cut. It has been stated that oil, unguents, and the like should be sent to the houses of the Brahmins. However, regarding those who have come from another village and have no home of their own, Yama says that the sacrificer should have them perform the shaving of the beard and the anointing with oil once they have arrived at his own house.
At the time of the *śrāddha*, one should adorn those invited twice-born men with shaving,
head-bathing, incense, oil-anointing, and collyrium.
One should provide them with a seat— a *kutapa* blanket or another pure cloth.

The materials required for the *śrāddha*, such as vessels, seats, perfumes, flowers, incense, and so forth, must be prepared in the forenoon itself. Then, the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), according to his means, should perform the midday ritual bath at a sacred ford (*tīrtha*) and the bath that is an ancillary part of the rite (*karmaṅga*) simultaneously. For it is stated in the *Matsyapurāṇa* regarding the commencement of the rite:
"Purity and purity of intention do not exist without bathing."
Therefore, for the sake of purifying the mind, bathing is prescribed at the outset.
Also in the *Nāgarakhaṇḍa*:
"Whatever substance is given to Brahmins on behalf of the ancestors by mortals who have bathed and are wearing clean garments, that shall become a source of great satisfaction."
"He is the lord of all the gods of the ancestors"—such is this Vedic revelation.
Regarding the *śrāddha* ceremony here, there is a specific rule in the *Bhaviṣyat-purāṇa*:
"The performer should bathe at the sacred site in the morning or at midday;
or, if unable, he should do it once with warm water."
Then, having performed the libations for the gods, sages, and ancestors, and having stepped out of the water, he should put on two new, washed, white garments as before.
And so Vasiṣṭha says:
"During recitation, burnt offerings, and fasting, one should always wear washed garments."
Adorned, pure, silent, and with senses subdued, he should attend at the time of the śrāddha and other rites.
Pracetas said:
"The performer of the śrāddha should wear white garments.

As for the statement by Vyāsa cited in the section on clothing—which records that even cloth dyed with mineral pigments (dhātu-rakta) is considered pure—that refers to occasions other than the śrāddha, or it pertains specifically to Kṣatriyas and others.
Baudhāyana speaks in condemnation of one who wears saffron-dyed robes:

"If one performs recitations, burnt offerings, or accepts gifts while wearing saffron-dyed garments, that does not reach the gods; likewise, the sacrificial oblation among offerings to gods and ancestors does not reach them."
"In rites for the gods and ancestors" (*havyakavyeṣu*) means in those rituals accomplished by them.
Another distinction is found in the *Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa*:
"Restraining his speech, having washed his feet, and clad in torn garments..."
Therefore, with the belt fastened outside and likewise with the hands outside the knees.
Having thus put on the two garments and sipped water twice, and having performed the midday sandhyā-rite, he should fetch water from a sacred bathing place for the sake of his ritual acts.
As stated in the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa:
"After performing the fetching of water, he should afterwards feed the Brahmins."
In this regard, the specific procedure for fetching water and gathering *kuśa* grass is described in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*:
"On the following day, having gone toward the southern direction with a concentrated mind,
one should fetch pure *darbha* grass together with its roots, which has tips pointing southward."
‘Dakṣiṇāgram’ means a body of water flowing toward the south, or one situated on the southern side. Having performed the invitation on the previous day, Hārīta says:
“Then, when the next day has dawned, having gone toward the southern direction, he should fetch southward-pointing *darbha* grasses along with their roots, and waters that have not been appropriated.
‘Aparigṛhītāḥ’ means those previously unappropriated by anyone else.
Then Yama said: "In the ancestral rite of Śrāddha, the Darbha grass should be used with its roots;
by means of the root, one conquers the worlds of the high-souled Śakra."
Here, the detailed characteristics of the *darbha* grass, the characteristics of the water, and the procedure for fetching both have been stated previously.
Regarding the fetching of water for the sake of the *śrāddha*, there is a specific rule in the *Mahābhārata*:
"And when bringing water, the Lord Varuṇa should be praised."

Since no specific form of praise is mentioned here, it is understood that one should offer praise with any mantra dedicated to Varuṇa, such as "imaṃ me varuṇa" (RV 1.24.11) and others. Furthermore, it was already established previously that if it is impossible to fetch water for sprinkling from a sacred bathing place (*tīrtha*), it may be fetched even from a water-jar (*maṇika*).
Regarding the use of water fetched from a *tīrtha* or from a water-jar and the like, Yogayājñavalkya states:
"Having sprinkled the ritual materials with that water and having performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*) again at home..."
Then one should perform certain prescribed ritual actions.
The procedure for the sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) and other ritual requirements will be explained in the section concerning the rites of praising the Earth and so forth.
Therefore, it is stated in the *Viṣṇudharmottara* that one should perform the worship of Nṛvarāha:
"On the day of the Śrāddha, being purified, having bathed, having sipped water, and being well-composed..."
Clad in white garments, he should worship Janārdana in the form of the supreme Boar.
The ellipsis is "one should begin the *śrāddha*. In the *Śivapurāṇa*:
"Having worshipped Śiva with devotion, one should perform the *śrāddha* for the ancestors."
Having performed the śrāddha according to the prescribed rules, one should eat that which was enjoyed by the ancestors.

In this regard, one who maintains the sacred fires (*sāgnika*), intending to perform the *amāvāsyā* Śrāddha, should first perform the Vaiśvadeva and the Piṇḍapitṛyajña in their proper sequence. However, it has been explained previously that one who intends to perform another type of Śrāddha should first perform the Vaiśvadeva, the Bali-offerings, and so forth.
Thus concludes the ritual concerning the cooking and other preliminary duties. Now follow the requirements for the perfection of the Śrāddha.
In that regard, the objectives to be accomplished are as follows:
Manu, Vasiṣṭha, Yama, Hārīta, and Śātātapa [state]:
"The afternoon, sesame seeds, darbha grass, and likewise the preparation of the site."
Creation, refinement, the foremost twice-born, and the perfections in the performance of śrāddha rites.

In this context, *aparāhṇa* (the afternoon), *tila* (sesame seeds), and *darbha* (sacrificial grass) have already been explained previously in their respective sections. "House" (*vāstu*) refers to a dwelling for the purpose of a *śrāddha*; its "preparation" (*saṃpādana*) consists of producing what does not yet exist, acquiring through means such as purchase what already exists but belongs to another, and the consecration of the site by leveling it so that it slopes toward the south, smearing it with cow-dung, sweeping it, and so forth. "Release" (*sṛṣṭi*), "emission" (*utsṛṣṭi*), "sending forth" (*utsarga*), and "renunciation" (*tyāga*) are synonymous; here it means the giving of condiments and other items without stinginess. "Purification" (*mṛṣṭi*) means cleansing or deliciousness. "Foremost" (*agryāḥ*) refers to those distinguished by qualities such as being learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*). These items are the "perfections of the *śrāddha*" (*śrāddhasaṃpadaḥ*), meaning the abundance of materials required for the *śrāddha*. By the use of the word "perfection," it is indicated that all these things must be prepared by one who desires to perform a *śrāddha*.
Having thus described the perfection of the rites for the ancestors (pitrya-karma), they [the sages] likewise stated the perfections of the rites for the gods (daivika-karma):
"Darbha grass, the purifier, the forenoon, and all kinds of sacrificial food (haviṣya),
as well as whatever purifier was mentioned previously— these should be known as the perfections of the oblation (havya)."

Here, by the first term *apavitra* (impure), one means either the mantra, or a cloth for the purpose of straining water and so forth, or *kuśa*-grass strainers (*pavitra*). "Forenoon" (*pūrvāhṇaḥ*) has already been explained. "Purification" (*pavitram*) refers to purifying conduct, such as pure behavior and the like. Furthermore, that which was previously mentioned—beginning with the preparation of the site (*vāstu-saṃpādana*)—is indicated by the word *havya* (sacrificial offering) as referring to divine rites (*daivika-karma*) and the feeding of Brahmins associated therewith. As stated in the *Mahābhārata*:
"The Brahmin is the time for the *śrāddha*, and curd, ghee, and milk are the vessels."
The waning of the moon and the month—then that forest, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
Regarding the phrase "of the śrāddha," one should complete it by adding "these are the perfections.
Parāśara says:
"The time, the recipient, as well as the place, the substance, the performer, and the ancestors."
The wise say that these are the causes for the accomplishment of this action.
Satyavrata says:
The substance, the recipient, the son, and the ritual procedure are the causes for the satisfaction of the ancestors.
Among these, the recipient is the most important; therefore, one should strive for the perfection of the recipient.
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*:
"One should prepare there kuśa grass cut once together with their roots,
barley, sesame seeds, reeds, a bronze vessel, and pure water collected [from a clean source]."
The vessels should be made of leaves, silver, or copper;
there should be sacrificial fuel, honey, flowers, incense, fragrant substances, and the like, as well as a linen thread and a stirring-ladle.

"In that place" means at the site of the *śrāddha*. "Grass-seats" (*vṛśī*) are seats made of *kuśa* grass and other materials suitable for those observing vows. "Bell-metal" (*kāṃsya*) refers to a vessel made of bell-metal for the purpose of the *agnaukaraṇa* offering and so forth. "By pure ones" refers to the carriers; "collected" is an adjective qualifying the water. By this, the prohibition against preparing water that is forbidden is indicated. "Made of leaves, silver, and copper" means fashioned from leaves, silver, and copper. These should be prepared according to one's capacity. "Linen thread" refers to silk thread. A "stirring-spoon" (*mekṣaṇa*) is a ladle made of sacrificial wood. The preparation of the grass-seats and the eating vessels must be done for each individual Brahmin. In the phrase "fragrant substances, etc.," the word "etc. includes unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), lamps, coverings, and so forth.
In the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa: "An ascetic with three staffs, compassion, a silver vessel,
a daughter's son, the Kutapa period of time, a goat, and likewise a black antelope skin."
White, black, and likewise wild—these three kinds of sesame seeds were created by Brahmā himself for the satisfaction of the ancestors; these ten [items] were thus ordained.

In this context, "tridaṇḍī" is an attribute of the ascetic (yati), "rājata" is an attribute of the vessel, and "kutapa" is an attribute of the time. White sesame seeds, black sesame seeds, and wild sesame seeds are three substances corresponding to their qualities; thus, the number ten is achieved. Devala says:
"In the ritual for the Aṣṭakā, purity is both the primary requirement and the means of purification."
For the ancestors desire purity; they are free from longing and have washed away their defilements.
Darbha grass, sesame seeds, the shadow of an elephant, a daughter's son, honey, clarified butter,
a kutapa blanket, and a blue goat— these he declared to be purifiers in rites for the ancestors.

"In the *aṣṭakā-vidhi*" means in the ritual for ancestral offerings (*śrāddha*). Harihara states that the term *aṣṭakā-vidhi* is intended as an indicative mark (*upalakṣaṇa*) for all rites pertaining to the ancestors (*pitryakarman*). "A dark-spotted one" refers to a dark-colored bull. [This is from] Paiṭhīnasi.
"Sesame seeds, the *dauhitraka* grass, and *kutapa* wool are purifiers at a *śrāddha*; truthfulness, freedom from anger, purity, and proper conduct are praised. Thus says Viṣṇu:
"Vessels containing *kutapa* wool, a black antelope skin, sesame seeds, white mustard, and unbroken grains (*akṣata*) are destroyers of demons."
Or he should give [it].
Manu said:
"Three things are purifying at a śrāddha: a daughter's son, a kutapa blanket, and sesame seeds."
And in this matter, they praise three things: purity, freedom from anger, and lack of haste.
In the Padma Purāṇa: "For the ancestors residing in the celestial realm, the southern direction is praised;
likewise are the prācīnāvīta [wearing mode], water, sesame seeds, and the left side of the body."
Placing the *svadhā* offering at the forefront, one always gratifies the ancestors.
Barley, millet, mung beans, sugarcane, white flowers,
and clarified butter are always beloved and highly praised by the ancestors here in this world.
In the *Matsyapurāṇa*: "The sacred thread worn over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvīta*), water, sesame seeds, the left side of the body, barley, wild rice,
mung beans, white flowers, and clarified butter."
These are always dear and praiseworthy for the ancestors here in this world.
In the *Kūrmapurāṇa*: "Dry land, figs, garments, silver, and even a sword,
as well as fruits and sacrificial fuel— these are highly purifying items at a *śrāddha*."

‘Sthalodumbara’ refers to vessels made of *udumbara* wood grown on dry land. These items, which are declared to be pure and dear to the ancestors (*pitṛs*), must be procured prior to the *śrāddha* at the site of the *śrāddha*.
Regarding the procedure for their collection, the *Mātsya* and *Pādma Purāṇas* state:

He should slowly bring from the south, with the sacred thread over the right shoulder, a water-pot, a bronze vessel, a stirring-ladle, sacrificial fuel, *kuśa* grass, sesame seeds, vessels, fine garments, perfumes, incense, and ointments.

"Apasavyena" means with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (prācīnāvīta) or by moving counter-clockwise. Here, the mention of the water-vessel and so forth is intended as an illustration for other items used in the Śrāddha, such as flowers and the like.
Regarding the materials for the Śrāddha, the *Brahmāṇḍa-purāṇa* and *Bhaviṣya-purāṇa* state:
"One should bring [the materials] from the north of the altar and dismiss them to the south."
The "vedī" is the site for the śrāddha. "Visarjana" is the leading [of the offerings] from the śrāddha location to another place.
These are the objectives to be accomplished through the śrāddha.

Now, among those things to be accomplished by the śrāddha, some are described as being accomplished in their essential form (svarūpa), while others are described according to their essential nature, praise, and application (viniyoga).
In that section on the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa: "Brahmins, a woolen blanket, cows, silver, fire, guests,
sesame seeds, darbha grass, and time— these nine are remembered as the 'kutapas'."
But Paiṭhīnasi has stated a specific rule regarding the *kambala* (woolen blanket) and provided an etymological explanation for the word *kutapa*:
"Midday, a sword-shaped vessel, as well as a Nepalese woolen blanket,
silver, darbha grass, sesame seeds, cows, and the daughter's son is remembered as the eighth."
They say that "pāpa" means contemptible; since these eight cause torment for one who possesses such [sin], they are therefore renowned as "kutapas."

The woolen blanket originating from the country of Nepal is called a "Nepāla-kambala. However, Harihara has explained it thus: "A cloth in the shape of a blanket made from the wool of mountain-dwelling goats, well-known in the northern regions. Śātātapa says:
"In the eighth part of the day, the sun becomes dim."
That time is called Kutapa; what is given to the ancestors at that hour becomes inexhaustible.
Paiṭhīnasi says:
"If a Śrotriya is seen from anywhere at the time of the Śrāddha, he indeed purifies the Śrāddha; therefore, he is designated as a Kutapa."
Vṛddha-Śātātapa says:
That which is seen on the forehead of a daughter like the horn of a rhinoceros—
the vessel belonging to that horn is celebrated as the "son of the daughter" (dauhitra).

The ghee that may be produced from the milk of a cow that has drunk the water of a moonless night is declared to be "daughter's son's ghee" (dauhitra-ghṛta), and it is honored in rites for the gods and the ancestors.

The meaning is as follows: on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*), when the moon has waned, whatever cow drinks water, the ghee that is produced from the milk resulting from the transformation of that water is designated by the term "daughter's son" (*dauhitra*). Here, the word "water" (*āpaḥ*) is intended as an illustration for medicinal plants (*oṣadhī*), for on the new moon day, Soma enters both the medicinal plants and the waters, according to the Vedic revelation: "He enters here the waters and the medicinal plants.
Furthermore, the status of being a "daughter's son" is attributed to ghee derived from a specific type of cow even apart from the new moon day, as stated in the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*.
The offspring of a daughter, as well as a rhinoceros and likewise a bowl,
and that which was carried by the Kapila cow— this is proclaimed as "the son of a daughter" (dauhitra).
Uśanas said:
Kuśas are known as darbhas, as well as kutapas and vṛsas;
and those who are the sons of a daughter are proclaimed to be dauhitras.
*Kuśa* refers to *darbha* grass; the items denoted by the word *kutapa* [are as follows]; *vṛṣayāḥ* [refers to those born of a bull]; and these sons of a daughter are *dauhitras*.
Now, Yama says: "One should diligently feed a *dauhitra* at a *śrāddha*, even if he is a child observing vows."
Having offered a seat made of kutapa grass and having scattered sesame seeds over it, one should proceed.

One should feed with special care—that is, with particular reverence—the son of one’s daughter who has been initiated (*upanīta*) and is established in his vows (*vratastha*), even though, due to his childhood, he is not yet a fit receptacle for excellence in knowledge and the like. One should provide him with a *kutapa*, a specific type of woolen blanket as previously described, as his seat. It should not be thought that this seat or the sesame seeds are connected exclusively with the daughter’s son; for, having recited this very verse, in order to dispel such a doubt, it is said: "Three things are pure at a *śrāddha*: the daughter’s son, the *kutapa*, and sesame seeds."
In one of these verses, Manu has stated in general terms that the *kutapa* cloth and other such items are connected with the *śrāddha*. Viṣṇu says:
"One should drive away the *yātudhānas* with sesame seeds or even mustard seeds."
The word "scattered all around" is to be understood as the ellipsis. Yama says:
"Darbha grass protects against the Asuras; sesame seeds protect against the Rākṣasas."
A knower of the Vedas protects food; that which is given by one who restrains himself becomes inexhaustible.
Hārīta says: Sesame seeds protect against the Daityas; Darbha grass protects against the Rākṣasas;
those learned in the Vedas protect the assembly; and the guest protects everything.
In the *Prabhāsakhaṇḍa*: "The gods have declared that *kuśa* grass and black sesame seeds, which originated from the body of Viṣṇu, are for the purpose of protecting the *śrāddha*."
Hārīta says:
That which is given with *darbha* grass, water, and sesame seeds—even if offered silently—attains heaven;
when offered according to the prescribed rule and in the proper sequence, it is ordained to be inexhaustible.
Offered with darbha grass and other materials according to the mantras upon golden vessels and the like,
these offerings reach the ancestors inexhaustibly, becoming nectar through great waves.
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*:
"Rākṣasas seize that which is offered without *darbha* grass, mantras, sesame seeds, gold, silver, or water; therefore, one should not give [an offering] alone."
The meaning is that *rakṣas* demons seize what is given without *darbha* grass and the like, as well as without water.
In the *Vāyupurāṇa*:
"The proximity, the sight, and the gift of a black antelope skin..."
It destroys demons, bestows Vedic splendor, and grants cattle and sons.
However, the essential nature, praise, and application of the remaining items should be understood from their respective contexts.
Thus concludes the essential nature, praise, and application of the items to be prepared for the *śrāddha*.
This concludes the perfections of the *śrāddha*.

Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Duties of the Forenoon," in the *Śrāddhakalpa* of the *Pariśeṣakhaṇḍa* of the *Caturvargacintāmaṇi*, composed by the illustrious Hemādri, the scholar (*paṇḍita*) and chief minister (*sarvakaraṇādhipati*) of the illustrious Mahādevīya, the great king of kings (*mahārājādhirāja*).
[1180] Now begins the thirteenth chapter:
[The Chapter on] the Summit of the Diadems of All Neighboring Kings Without Exception.
With his footstool attended by the sprouts of jewels,
the preceptor Hemādri performs the collection of rites belonging to the afternoon during the Śrāddha ceremony with all its qualities.
Now follows the afternoon ritual.

In that regard, after describing everything from the invitation of the Brahmins up to the declaration of the success of the *śrāddha*, as well as the sending of bathing requisites to the Brahmins here and the resulting performance of the bath because it serves a visible purpose, it is stated in the *Prabhāsakhaṇḍa*:
"Then, at the time of the afternoon, the performer of the *śrāddha*, being composed..."
He himself should invite the Brahmins, or those of the same caste who have bathed together.
‘Samāplutān’ means those who have bathed;
according to the Varāha and Viṣṇu Purāṇas:
“One should honor the twice-born who have come to the house by washing their feet and other such services.”
"One should honor" means one should show respect; by the word "etcetera," it is implied that this includes even the offering of water for sipping (ācamanīya).
Thus, it is stated in both the Devalasmṛti and the Kūrmapurāṇa:
"Then, having risen with palms joined in reverence toward those who have returned from their bath..."
One should offer water for the feet and water for sipping in due order.

Regarding the phrase "to those who have returned from their bath" (*snānān nivṛttebhyaḥ*): this refers to those who have arrived at the sacrificer’s house after the completion of the bath, having been summoned. "Having risen" (*pratyutthāya*) means having joined one's palms in reverence and asked, "Welcome to you. Then, in order to remove the impurity resulting from their walking along the road, he should provide water for washing the feet and for sipping (*ācamana*). The meaning is that after performing the foot-washing, he should give the water for sipping.
Regarding this, Mārkaṇḍeya states that for those who have arrived at the house after being summoned, a greeting should be offered individually to each person.

"Having bathed, he should honor those who have bathed and been invited individually with a welcome. Regarding "with a welcome," this refers to the interrogative phrase, "A welcome to you all. "He should honor" means he should show them respect. "Individually" means one by one Brahmin. Since a question requires an answer, and because it is traditionally remembered that in such matters a response must be properly given, they should each say in reply, "A very warm welcome to us. Śaṅkha and Likhita state that this inquiry of welcome should be performed by one who possesses qualities such as being composed and so forth.
"Being self-restrained in the afternoon, pure, and wearing white garments, standing upon *darbha* grass,
he should say, 'Welcome. Thus,
the two words "self-restrained" (*prayata*) and "pure" (*śuci*) are intended so that he may be endowed with the two kinds of purification, namely external and internal.

In this context, by teaching that the place where those [guests] are situated is the one for whom the greeting is to be performed, Dharma makes it clear that the greeting and other such acts belong to the afternoon ritual.
"But having honored with a welcome those who have arrived in a secluded place strewn with sesame seeds and *barhis* grass in the afternoon... (MDh 3.105).

Having honored with a welcome as prescribed those initiated *vipras* who have arrived at the house of the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) in the afternoon—whether that be the second part of the day divided into two, the third part of the day divided into three, the fourth part of the day divided into five, or the half-yāma following the two and a half yāmas—he should cause them to sit upon seats; this is the connection with what will be stated hereafter.
As it is said in the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa* and the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*:
"Having honored these twice-born ones who have approached his house with a welcome..."
With the sacred grass in hand, he should cause those who have sipped water to sit upon their seats.

Citing the statement of Āpastamba, "At this occasion, there is an invitation on the preceding day," one should perform a second invitation for those Brahmins who were invited on the previous day, just as before.
And when the Brahmins have been summoned at the time of the Śrāddha, one should cause them to be comfortably seated and adorned.

Thus, according to the words of Yama, one should adorn [the guests] with perfumes, garlands, collyrium, and incense. And it is stated in the Devalasmṛti and the Kūrmapurāṇa: "One should adorn all those who are seated with ornaments, such as flower garlands, head-wraps, incense, lamps, and unguents."

The Nigama states: "Having honored [the guests] the next day with a barber, oil massage, dry rubbing, bathing, tooth-cleaning, and so forth; and having honored those who have bathed with water for the feet, water for sipping, excellent seats with *darbha* grass, ointments, incense, and flowers, he asks: 'Shall I invite the ancestors?'"

"Tomorrow" (*śvaḥ*) means on the day following the invitation. The mention of "anointing" (*abhyaṅga*) is intended to include the grooming of the nails and so forth. And that [grooming] is to be performed by "one's own barber" (*svanāpitena*), meaning by the barber provided by the sacrificer after payment of wages and so on. Furthermore, this—from rising to meet [the guests] up until the invitation and the end of the decoration—is purely human (*mānuṣa*) in nature because it consists of hospitality toward men and the like, not ancestral (*pitrya*); therefore, it must be performed according to worldly custom by one who possesses the *yajñopavīta* and other such ritual attributes, and not by one who follows ancestral rites.

Now, as for that which is to be performed— namely, the preparation of the mandala and its worship, the washing of the feet, and so forth, as prescribed in the section on general rules (paribhāṣā) concerning the duties pertaining to the Viśvedevas or the ancestors— regarding that, Baudhāyana first describes the making of the mandala: "On a level, clean spot that has been smeared with cow-dung and is endowed with whiteness,
[one should draw] a square, a triangle, a circle, or a half-moon."
The mandala should be constructed in due order among the Brahmins and the other castes.

"Among the Brāhmaṇas and others" refers to the patrons (*yajamāna*). The meaning of "in due order" (*ānupūrveṇa*) is as follows: when the patron is a Brāhmaṇa, it is square; for a Kṣatriya, triangular; for a Vaiśya, circular; and for a Śūdra, in the shape of a half-moon.
Regarding this, a specific rule concerning the Śūdra is stated in the *Saurapurāṇa*:
"The [maṇḍala] of a Brāhmaṇa is square, that of a Kṣatriya is triangular."
That of a Vaiśya is circular, and for a Śūdra, sprinkling is prescribed.
Regarding this, Śambhu states the specific detail:
"At the door, which has been swept and smeared, one should construct a mandala;
it should slope toward the north in the northern part, and it should slope toward the south in the southern part."

"At the door" (*dvārī*) means in the courtyard area situated facing the house door. Regarding "two mandalas" (*maṇḍale*), because of the dual number, there are two; one is to the north, and the other is to its south. Among these, that which is to the north is "sloping toward the north" (*udakplava*); this means it is inclined downward in the direction of the north. Likewise, the other is "sloping toward the south" (*dakṣiṇāplava*). Therein, first, one should prepare the northern one according to the ritual rules for the Vaiśvadeva, saying: "Oṃ, I prepare the Vaiśvadeva maṇḍala. Immediately after that, one should prepare the southern one according to the ritual rules for the ancestors, saying: "Oṃ, I prepare the Pitrya maṇḍala."
And these [rites] are to be performed with cow urine and cow dung; this has been stated in the *Matsya* and *Padma* Purāṇas:
"Having thus brought all that together, one should scatter it on the ground before the deity, upon a mandala smeared with cow dung and [prepared] with cow urine."

"In this manner"—that is, by the method previously described in the statement, "One should bring everything with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (apasavya) from the south"—having "prepared" all the implements for the *śrāddha* and having "placed" them in the *śrāddha* area, one should draw a mandala with cow dung on the ground in front, which has been purified by smearing with cow dung and the like, located in the courtyard facing the entrance of the house.
Regarding the specific requirement for the cow dung here, Jābāli says:
"Of cows that do not eat impure food, that are not emaciated, and likewise healthy..."
And one should fetch fresh, pure cow dung from animals that are free of physical defects.
Bhṛgu states a prohibition regarding specific types of cow dung:
"One should not fetch the dung of a cow whose body is extremely decayed, nor especially that of one who is barren, nor of one that is afflicted, nor of one that has recently calved."
Regarding the dimensions of the circles, Laugākṣi says:
"The circle for the Vaiśvadeva rite should be made two cubits in measure;
to its south, for the purification of the feet of the ancestors, it should be four cubits."
Vyāghrapāt describes the worship of these two mandalas in sequence with unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), *kuśa* grass, and so forth:
"The two mandalas should be prepared on ground sloping toward the south.
On the northern [mandala], one should arrange *kuśa* grass joined with unbroken rice grains, with their tips pointing eastward."
To the south, the twice-born should place [the vessels] with their tips pointing southward and containing sesame seeds.

The mention of *akṣata* (unbroken rice) and so forth is intended as an illustration for perfumes and flowers, based on the forthcoming statement from the *Matsyapurāṇa*. Here, the northern mandala is understood to belong to the *vaiśvadeva* (deities) by virtue of its being situated toward the north and other such characteristics of the *vaiśvadeva* rite; likewise, the southern [mandala] belongs to the ancestors (*pitṛs*) by virtue of its being situated toward the south and other such characteristics of the ancestral rite. Therefore, facing either east or north, wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*yajñopavītī*), and bending the right knee, one should worship the mandala situated to the north with perfumes, flowers, barley, and straight *kuśa* grass with tips pointing eastward, saying: "Oṃ, I worship the *vaiśvadeva* mandala. In the same manner, facing south, wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*), and bending the left knee, one should worship the mandala situated to the south with perfumes, flowers, sesame seeds, and *kuśa* grass that is doubled over and has tips pointing southward, saying: "Oṃ, I worship the ancestral (*pitrya*) mandala. The procedure from the invitation of the Brahmins up to the end of the worship of the mandalas, including certain specific details, is described in the *Nāgarakhaṇḍa*: [1185] "Having performed the *pādya*, *arghya*, and *ācamana* rites, and having offered perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, food, and betel-leaf, he should worship the two mandalas. He should worship the northern mandala with perfumes, flowers, and unbroken rice (*akṣata*), and the southern mandala with perfumes, flowers, and sesame seeds. Having worshipped the northern mandala with perfumes, flowers, and unbroken rice, he should worship the southern mandala with perfumes, flowers, and sesame seeds. Having worshipped both mandalas, he should invite the Brahmins. Thus it is said. Furthermore, regarding the specific details: "He should place the *akṣata* and so forth upon the mandalas, and likewise the perfumes, flowers, and incense. Having placed the perfumes, flowers, and incense, he should offer the lamp. Having offered the lamp, he should offer the food. Having offered the food, he should offer the betel-leaf. Having offered the betel-leaf, he should perform the *svasti-vācana* (recitation of auspiciousness). Having performed the *svasti-vācana*, he should perform the *puṇyāha-vācana* (declaration of an auspicious day). Thus it is said. And furthermore: "He should worship the northern mandala with perfumes, flowers, and unbroken rice, and the southern mandala with perfumes, flowers, and sesame seeds. Having worshipped the northern mandala, he should worship the southern mandala. Having worshipped both mandalas, he should invite the Brahmins. Thus it is said. And furthermore: "He should worship the northern mandala with perfumes, flowers, and unbroken rice, and the southern mandala with perfumes, flowers, and sesame seeds. Having worshipped the northern mandala, he should worship the southern mandala. Having worshipped both mandalas, he should invite the Brahmins. Thus it is said. Having worshipped the northern mandala, he should worship the southern mandala. Having worshipped both mandalas, he should invite the Brahmins. Thus it is said. Having worshipped the northern mandala, he should worship the southern mandala. Having worshipped both mandalas, he should invite the Brahmins. Thus it is said. Having worshipped the northern mandala, he should worship the southern mandala. Having worshipped both mandalas, he should invite the Brahmins. Thus it is said. Having worshipped the northern mandala, he should worship the southern mandala. Having worshipped both mandalas, he should invite the Brahmins. Thus it is said. Having worshipped the northern mandala, he should worship the southern mandala. Having worshipped both mandalas, he should invite the Brahmins. Thus it is said. And furthermore: "He should worship the northern mandala with perfumes, flowers, and unbroken rice, and the southern mandala with perfumes, flowers, and sesame seeds. Having worshipped the northern mandala, he should worship the southern mandala. Having worshipped both mandalas, he should invite the Brahmins. Thus it is said. And furthermore: "He should worship the northern mandala with perfumes, flowers, and unbroken rice, and the southern mandala with perfumes, flowers, and sesame seeds. Having worshipped the northern mandala, he should worship the southern mandala. Having worshipped both mandalas, he should invite the Brahmins. Thus it is said. And furthermore: "He should worship the northern mandala with perfumes, flowers, and unbroken rice, and the southern mandala with perfumes, flowers, and sesame seeds. Having worshipped the northern mandala, he should worship the southern mandala. Having worshipped both mandalas, he should invite the Brahmins. Thus it is said. And furthermore: "He should worship the northern mandala with perfumes, flowers, and unbroken rice, and the southern mandala with perfumes, flowers, and sesame seeds. Having worshipped the northern mandala, he should worship the southern mandala. Having worshipped both mandalas, he should invite the Brahmins. Thus it is said. And furthermore: "He should worship the northern
Having prostrated and invited those most excellent Brahmins for the sake of the śrāddha,
one should then bring them all at the time of *kutapa* and offer this prayer to them.
May the illustrious Viśvedevas of great power come;
may those who have been appointed to this śrāddha rite remain attentive.
Then, having performed the rite with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (apasavya), he should pray to those ancestors:
"O ancestors born of my mother’s side who were previously invited by me,
please remain attentive toward these ancestral rites."
Having thus worshipped them all and performed a circumambulation,
one should place both knees upon the ground and then offer the *arghya* with this mantra, O King of Kings, using flowers, unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), and sandalwood paste.
O best of the twice-born, please accept this *arghya* offered by me;
for the purpose of washing the feet, perform what is pleasing to me.
Having spoken thus, one should then scatter darbha grass together with grains of rice upon the smeared surface of the earth, and invoke the Viśvedevas.
Then, having moved to the left (apasavya), one should scatter double-folded darbha grass mixed with sesame seeds there, intended for one's own ancestors.
Thus, it is stated in the *Saura Purāṇa* that after the two mandalas have been worshipped in this manner, the washing of the Brahmins' feet should be performed:
"Then one should wash the feet upon the auspicious, worshipped mandala.
This is also stated in the *Matsya Purāṇa* and the *Padma Purāṇa*.
Having honored him with unbroken grains and flowers while wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (apasavya),
he should wash the feet of the Brahmins, bowing down to them again and again.

"With unbroken grains and flowers" refers to the worship of the *deva*-maṇḍala, because it is associated with the *deva*-dharma. And this [phrase] is intended as an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the worship of the *pitṛ*-maṇḍala, beginning with "with sesame seeds and flowers," and so forth. "With the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*apasavya*), he should wash the feet of the Brahmins" refers to the washing of the feet of the Brahmins belonging to the *pitṛ* rite, because it possesses the characteristics of the *pitṛ*-dharma. And that is an elliptical indication of the previously occurring washing of the feet of the Brahmins belonging to the *vaiśvadeva* rite. Therefore, first, the washing of the feet of the Brahmins belonging to the *vaiśvadeva* rite must be performed at the maṇḍala situated to the north.
And likewise in the *Brahmanirukta*:
"One should first cause the water for the feet (*pādya*) and the respectful offering (*arghya*) to be presented to the deities.
Also in the *Vārāhapurāṇa*:
A twice-born man should offer a welcome, as well as water for the hands and feet and a seat of darbha grass;
having first performed the Vaiśvadeva rite and offered libations into the fire, he should proceed.
In the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*:
"One should offer this water for the feet (*pādya*) and the respectful oblation (*arghya*), [addressing the deity] with the name ending in the dative case.
The mantra for washing the feet is found in the *Brahmanirukti*.
"One should cause the water for washing the feet (pādya) to be offered with the mantra 'śaṃ no devī'. Thus it is said.
Also in the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa:
"One should wash the feet of the Brahmins with the verse 'śaṃ no devīḥ'."
He should personally wash his feet with humility.
When one has the capacity, one should do it oneself; but when one lacks the capacity, one may have another person do it.

Herein is the procedure for washing the feet (*pādaprakṣālana*). Wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*yajñopavītin*), bending the right knee, and facing north, one should recite the mantra: *śaṃ no devīr abhiṣṭaye āpo bhavantu pītaye | śaṃyor abhisravantu naḥ*. Then, having applied the formula: *oṃ purūrava ārdravaḥ-saṃjñakā viśvedevā idaṃ vaḥ pādyaṃ svāhā namaḥ*, one should pour water containing fragrance, flowers, unbroken rice (*akṣata*), and *kuśa* grass into the joined palms using the *devatīrtha* (the part of the hand sacred to the gods) at the feet of each individual Brahmin seated on a seat placed within the outer circle, or standing while treading upon the circle according to custom. After pouring this, one should wash their feet with other water. Here, by the word "and" (*ca*), worship and the offering of the guest-water (*arghya*) following the foot-washing are indicated. Therefore, for each [Brahmin], one should worship from the feet to the head in the manner to be described with fragrance, flowers, and unbroken rice, reciting the verse beginning with *sahasraśīrṣā*. Then, having offered the *arghya*—using a vessel of gold or other materials as available, filled with water mixed with fragrant substances such as scent, flowers, unbroken rice, and *kuśa* grass—one should recite the ritual formula as in the case of the foot-washing.

"One should offer water for sipping (ācamanīyaka) in the region to the north of the mandala," according to the traditional teaching of Laugākṣi; therefore, one should offer water for sipping to those seated to the north of the mandala. And the Brahmins should sip water in such a way that the water used for sipping does not come into contact with the water used for washing the feet, because the Nāradīya Purāṇa mentions a fault in their mixing:
"Where the waters for sipping [are mixed] with the waters for washing the feet..."
"The wise gather together; that [gathering] they declare to be demonic.
On this point, Śaṅkha and Likhita say:

"Having offered water for the feet, the guest-offering (arghya), and water for sipping (ācamanīya), and having touched the feet of the Brāhmaṇas, he should cause them to sit down after touching their seats."

"Water for sipping" (*ācamanīyodaka*) is water intended for the purpose of sipping. "Having taken hold" (*upasaṃgṛhya*) means having grasped it with the right hand; "having touched" (*anvālabhya*) means having touched the seat placed at the site of the *śrāddha* with the left hand, one should cause him to sit there. Then, after giving the water for sipping to the Brāhmaṇas of the Vaiśvadeva section, the performer—facing south, wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*), and keeping the left knee bent (*anvācita-savyajānu*)—should begin the offering of the water for the feet (*pādya*) and other honors to the Brāhmaṇas of the ancestral (*pitrya*) section who are seated facing north on seats placed in the southern mandala, starting from the west and ending toward the east, following the order of the ancestors. According to the principle of viewing the distinctions between divine, human, and ancestral deities as mentioned in the section on the deities: a twice-born man should meditate upon and recite the names of all the ancestors in the form of the Pitṛ named Somapa; a Kṣatriya in the form of the Pitṛ named Haviṣmat; a Vaiśya in the form of the Pitṛ named Ājyapa; and a Śūdra in the form of the Pitṛ named Sukālin. Any performer of the *śrāddha*, whether a Brāhmaṇa or another, should likewise meditate upon and recite the names of the father, grandfather, and great-grandfather in their respective forms as Vasu, Rudra, and Āditya; or as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara; or as Pradyumna, Saṃkarṣaṇa, and Vāsudeva; or as the month, the season, and the year. While doing so, he should perform all the ancestral rites, such as the offering of water for the feet, worship, the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*), the *arghya*, and the giving of *darbha* grass and seats. And therein:
According to the statement, "The name and lineage of the ancestors are what convey [the offerings] of the *havya* and *kavya*," one should declare the relationship,
names, and lineages of the ancestors.

According to this statement, one should address each ancestor—father and the others—individually by their lineage (*gotra*), relationship, and name. Having invoked them, and reciting their names beginning with "Ājyapa" and so forth according to the prescribed divisions, using those very names in the vocative case, one should pour a handful (*añjali*) filled with fragrance, flowers, sesame seeds, *kuśa* grass, and water onto the feet of each individual Brāhmaṇa representing the ancestors. After bowing down, one should wash their feet with another portion of water. The formula for the ritual procedure (*prayoga-vākya*) is as follows: Having recited "śanno devīḥ" and so forth, one should say at the station of the father: "Oṃ, [Name] of such-and-such lineage, our father [Name], together with your wife, in the form of Vasu; this is your water for washing the feet (*pādya*), Svadhā! Obeisance! At the station of the grandfather, having recited "śanno devīḥ" and so forth, one should say: "Oṃ, [Name] of such-and-such lineage, our grandfather [Name], together with your wife, in the form of Rudra; this is your water for washing the feet, Svadhā! Obeisance! At the station of the great-grandfather, having recited "śanno devīḥ" and so forth, one should say: "Oṃ, [Name] of such-and-such lineage, our great-grandfather [Name], together with your wife, in the form of Āditya; this is your water for washing the feet, Svadhā! Obeisance!"

Then, in the manner previously described, at the conclusion of the mantra *śaṃ no devīḥ*, one should recite: *oṃ amukagotrā asmanmātāmahāḥ amukaśarmāṇaḥ sapatnīkā vasurūpā idaṃ vaḥ pādyaṃ svadhā namaḥ* for the place of the maternal grandfather (*mātāmaha*). Having uttered the mantra beginning with *śaṃ no devīḥ*, and having spoken *oṃ amukagotrā asmatpramātāmahāḥ* or *mātuḥ pitāmahāḥ*, followed by *amukaśarmaṇaḥ sapatnīkā rudrarūpā idaṃ vaḥ pādyaṃ svadhā namaḥ*, one should do so for the place of the maternal great-grandfather (*pramātāmaha*). Then, in the same way, having recited the mantra beginning with *śaṃ no devīḥ*, and having addressed them as *oṃ amukagotrā asmadvṛddhapramātāmahāḥ* or *mātuḥ prapitāmahāḥ*, followed by *amukaśarmāṇaḥ sapatnīkā ādityarūpā idaṃ vaḥ pādyaṃ svadhā namaḥ*, one should utter this for the place of the maternal great-great-grandfather (*vṛddhapramātāmaha*).

After washing their feet, one should worship each of the Brahmins belonging to the paternal lineage (pitṛvarga) in sequence, from head to foot, with perfumes, flowers, and sesame seeds, using the mantra beginning with "svadhā to the fathers, svadhā to the fathers" according to the method to be described. In the same manner, one should worship those belonging to the maternal lineage (mātāmahavarga) with the mantra beginning with "namo vaḥ pitaraḥ. Immediately thereafter, having offered *arghya*—using a vessel of silver or similar material filled with water mixed with auspicious substances such as perfumes, flowers, sesame, and *kuśa* grass, and reciting the appropriate ritual formula (*prayogavākya*) according to availability—one should give it in the same order as the *pādya*. Then, one should provide water for sipping (*ācamanīya*) to the twice-born who are seated to the north of the Vaiśvadeva circle. They, in turn, should sip the water for sipping and the water used for washing the feet without mixing them together.

Then, following the tradition of the highly skilled and disciplined (śiṣṭa), one should place the remnants of the materials used for the rites beginning with the worship of the mandala and ending with the sipping of water (ācamana) upon each respective mandala. Then, as stated in the forthcoming ritual injunction beginning with "the sacrificer, with darbha grass in hand, having sipped water twice," the sacrificer—without allowing the water from washing the feet of the Brahmins to come into contact [with himself]—should first wash his own feet, sip water twice, and together with the Brahmins, arrive at the site of the śrāddha. Having addressed the Brahmins, saying, "May you say, 'May the success of the śrāddha be accomplished! and being told by them, "May the success of the śrāddha be accomplished!", he should prepare seats for their seating.
And likewise Yama says:
"Then, having said 'Success,' [he should sit] upon the prepared seats"; the connection is with the subsequent [verse] beginning with "Sit down" (*ādhvam*).
Thus ends the section beginning with the invitation of the Brahmins and concluding with the declaration of the successful completion of the śrāddha.
Now follows the preparation of seats for the purpose of seating the Brahmins.
Atri says:
There, seats should be provided, as well as sesame seeds together with *kuśa* grass;
on each individual seat, lamps should be placed using sesame oil.

In that place where the *śrāddha* is performed, seats should be provided; the meaning is that *tila* seeds together with *kuśa* grass should be offered and scattered upon the ground of the *śrāddha*. A single lamp should be placed near each individual seat; thus they are to be given, and the verb "should be given" (*deyāni*) is to be supplied here by modification. Alternatively, the connection is that upon those seats, *tila* seeds together with *kuśa* grass should be offered separately for each. The mention of sesame oil is intended to indicate excellent unguents such as clarified butter (*ghṛta*) and the like, and to exclude unwholesome unguents such as fat (*vasā*). As for the seats, because they are most highly recommended, if available, they should be made of wool known as *kutapa* or in the form of *vṛṣī* mats. Their high recommendation is stated in the section on the perfection of the *śrāddha*; in their absence, [seats] made of excellent white wool or wood such as *śrīṇī* and so forth are used, and in their absence, those made of any wood not prohibited.
Gārgya states a prohibition regarding specific types of seats:
"A wise man should always avoid a seat made of cow dung or clay, one that is broken, one made of acacia wood, one made of palāśa wood, one bound with iron, or one that is red."

"Made of cow-dung" and "made of clay"; "broken" means cracked. This is a prohibition regarding whatever is of a natural (unrefined) substance. "Akṣa" means made of *vibhītaka* wood. "Pālāśa" means made of the *kiṃśuka* tree. "Loha-baddha" means equipped with strips, pins, and so forth, of black iron (*kāla-ayas*). By this, the prohibition of all [other] types of iron is further indicated. The word "loha" (iron/metal) is intended as an indicative term for base metals such as lead and the like. "Ārka" means made of *rūpikā* (copper). The syntactical connection is that one should always avoid these. [This is stated] in the *Kālikā Purāṇa*.

Having smeared the ground with cow-dung for the sake of the ancestors, one should place the twice-born in a pure location prepared for the ancestral rite, upon a layer of *kuśa* grass strewn with sesame seeds, in an unbroken vessel made of materials other than iron.
The wise donor, having first entered himself, should cause the Brahmins—
who have already performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana)— to sit upon the prepared seats in the purified hall.
Regarding the method for arranging the seats for the divine and paternal ancestors, there is a distinction between the *Devalasmṛti* and the *Kūrmapurāṇa*:
"Those Brahmins who have been previously invited here as the Viśvedevas—
these are their seats, facing east and provided with two blades of *darbha* grass."
The seats for the ancestors are arranged facing south,
with single blades of darbha grass pointing toward the south, and are sprinkled with water mixed with sesame seeds.

It should be understood that in the phrase "facing east and joined with those facing south," the word *mukha* (face) is used with reference to the designated front part of the *vṛṣī* seats and so forth, while in the case of woolen blankets (*kambala*) and the like, it refers to the fringe or tip. The term "placed upon two *darbha* blades" (*dvidarbhopahitāni*) means that for each [seat], a pair of *darbha* tips is placed upon it facing eastward. "With a single *darbha* blade having its tip pointing south" (*dakṣiṇāgraikadarbhāṇi*) means that a single *darbha* tip is placed upon each, with its tip pointing toward the south.
Furthermore, in the *Mahābhārata*, concerning the *vṛṣī* seat, it is said to King Nimi, the performer of the *śrāddha*:
"Place this [offering] with its head toward the east, and you likewise face the north.
The word "you" (tvaṃ) implies "in the rite for the gods" (daive).
Likewise, it is stated in the *Dānadharma* section of the *Śrāddhakalpa*.
On the new moon day, the highly wise king, having summoned and honored the brahmins,
himself prepared all the ritual seats provided with sacrificial fees.
Then, blades of darbha grass with their tips pointing south were placed upon the seats,
as well as at the feet of the brahmins who were partaking of the food.

"Having summoned" means having caused them to enter their own home by invitation. "Honored" means those worthy of honor, or those adorned with collyrium, ointments, and so forth. "Dakṣiṇāvṛttikaḥ" refers to those whose heads are turned toward the south; the meaning is that their heads are directed toward the southern direction, though some say their heads are placed on the right side of the body. On the *viṣṭaras*—seats such as those made of *vṛṣī* grass—and for the purpose of placing the feet of the twice-born, *darbha* grass blades are laid down with their tips pointing southward. From this indicative mark (*liṅga*), it is understood that others should also act in this manner. Furthermore, those seats should be arranged in such a secluded manner that there is no mutual physical contact among the Brahmins seated upon them.
For this very reason, Kratu said:
"With darbha grass in hand, having sipped water twice, wearing light garments, and with his senses subdued,
[he should perform the rite] in an enclosed, pure place smeared with cow dung."
On seats made of darbha grass in a secluded place sloping toward the south, he should cause those who have properly sipped water, being restrained and pure, to sit down.

‘Laghuvāsāḥ’ means one whose garment is free from the heaviness caused by dirt and so forth due to having been washed, or one who wears fine clothing. ‘Pariśrite’ means covered on all sides with a cloth or other screening material. ‘Vivikteṣu’ means in places that have sufficient space between them to avoid mutual contact for those seated there. The rest is self-evident. Gārgya states the reason for this:
“In every instance of physical contact, sin arises from being assigned to the same row.”
Therefore, it is appropriate to exercise discrimination regarding those in a row who follow inferior conduct and the like.

For as many times as one of superior conduct may come into contact with a person of inferior conduct seated in the same row, for that many times they incur impurity (*aprāyatyam*). And for those who perform rituals while being impure, there is sin (*pratyavāya*); furthermore, there is a deficiency in the ritual itself (*vaiguṇyam*). Thus, both kinds of evil would arise; therefore, separation must be made. This [separation] occurs when the inferiority of conduct is not yet determined—then it applies to the seats—but once it is determined, it applies to the row itself.
Bṛhaspati states the means for effecting the separation of rows:
Those who sit in a single row without touching one another,
having established a boundary with ashes, for them there shall be no confusion of castes.

In both the Bārhaspatya-smṛti and the Prabhāsakhaṇḍa, two things are taught here as means for breaking the row: not allowing mutual contact and drawing a line of ashes in the intervening space. [As it says:
"Whether by fire, or by ashes, or even by a pillar, or by water..."
Even by shifting through the gates, a breach in the row is proclaimed.
"A thicket" means a shrub; in some readings, it is "by means of a pillar. And "passage" refers to the doorway—these are the two means. "Passage" means the path.
This concludes the preparation of the seat for the purpose of seating the Brāhmaṇas.
Now follows the seating of the Brāhmaṇas.
Regarding this, Manu and Bṛhaspati both say:
"When separate seats have been prepared, each provided with sacrificial grass (barhis)..."
Once those Brahmins have properly sipped water, he should cause them to be seated.

‘Upon those prepared’ means established; ‘provided with *barhis* grass’ means covered with *darbha* grass. ‘Separately’ means for each individual Brahmin in a distinct manner. ‘Having touched water’ means having performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*).
According to the *Vārāha-purāṇa* and the *Viṣṇu-purāṇa*:
“With sacred grass in hand, he should cause those who have sipped water to sit upon their seats.”
Regarding this, Śāṭyāyani states the specific rule:
"With their hands, feet, and faces moistened, having sipped water for purification and being well-composed, the Brahmins should be seated upon those seats in that same order."

"Moist in hands, feet, and mouth" means that they have not yet dried their washing or sipping, and water still clings to them; the sense is that they should be seated without delay as long as moisture does not leave the mouth, hands, and feet. And so Viṣṇu says:
"In the afternoon, he should seat the Brahmins—who have bathed well and performed the ritual sipping (ācamana)—in order according to their relative learning, upon seats covered with *kuśa* grass."

"According to their greater knowledge" (*yathābhūyovidyam*) means in accordance with the abundance of their learning. This is intended as an elliptical expression for the abundance of asceticism and other such qualities, since Sumantu said: "For those who are superior in learning and asceticism, the first seat is prescribed."
For those seated in a single row, the food, including the fragrances and other offerings, should be equal.

"First" means placed in the first position and preeminent in qualities. Other things—such as perfumes, flowers, and so forth—and food for eating should be given "equally," that is, alike to all; it must not be given unequally by way of distinguishing between superior and inferior.
[1195] Yama also states who are worthy of the foremost seat according to their specific stage of life (āśrama): "If a mendicant (yati) likewise does not eat before the patron (yajamāna)..."
The host of Rākṣasas carries away what is undesirable and marvelous for him.
Therefore, a self-restrained ascetic, or a Vedic scholar, or a celibate student, should be fed at the principal seat by those performing a sacrifice; by that, the sacrifice is not rendered deficient.
Sumantu states the fault in transgressing the prescribed order:
"While worthy persons are present, a gift should not go to one who is unworthy;
[the giver] takes upon himself the misdeeds of the row and is deprived of his lifespan."

"Among those who are worthy (*arheṣu*), for one who is unworthy (*anarhāya*), there should not be a superior seat (*varam āsanam*). The meaning is that an unworthy person should not occupy a superior seat. If, however, he should occupy it, then he "incurs" (*harate*) the misdeed of the entire row; he is also deprived of his "life-span" (*āyuṣā*).
Hārīta also says:
"When worthy persons are seated together, if an unworthy person takes the foremost seat..."
He takes on that impurity from the row and is deprived of his life-span.
"While they are present" means while they exist. "Impurity" refers to evil deeds.
Yama is generally a fool, devoid of traditional knowledge and mantras.
He who, out of a sense of superiority, goes to the seat of honor,
being of deluded mind, sees no other danger than the most terrible hell upon the destruction of his body.
He who is neither learned, nor a student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārī*), nor established in a stage of life (*āśrama*), nor purified by mantras,
yet eats the sacrificial oblations while standing at the yoke.
He eats the impurities and defilements of the row.

"Seated at the head" (*dhuristhitaḥ*) means seated on the foremost seat. One should sit on the foremost seat only after being permitted by the patron with the words, "Please be seated here," and not without such permission.
Thus, Paiṭhīnasi states immediately after the description of those who purify the row (*paṅktipāvana*):

Each one of them, when appointed to the row and seated at its head, purifies even a row defiled by thousands [of others]; therefore, one who is not so appointed should not take the seat of honor. If he should do so, he takes upon himself the evil deeds of the row. Even if a row is defiled by thousands of row-defilers, each one among those previously mentioned "purifiers of the row," being appointed by the sacrificer and seated at the head on the foremost seat, purifies—that is, cleanses—it.
Thus say Śaṅkha and Likhita.
One who has not been invited should not go to the seat of honor.

In this regard, the seating of those for the Vaiśvadeva rite must be performed first, while that of those for the Pitṛs is to follow later; for, with the exception of the washing of hands smeared with food remnants and the formal dismissal, all ritual items pertaining to the Śrāddha are preceded by those of the Vaiśvadeva. Regarding this, Kātyāyana says:
"The ancestral rite (śrāddha) is preceded by the rite for the gods; the procedure regarding the ancestors is like that of the Piṇḍapitṛyajña.
The word "should be performed" is to be understood as the ellipsis.
Śaṅkha and Likhita state the reason for this precedence of the rite for the gods:
Those who are appointed before the ancestors and seated first protect the śrāddha for the gods and others, as well as themselves. Hārīta also says:
They say that the divine is immortality, while that pertaining to the ancestors is ordained as death;
therefore, from the divine they proceed, for they abide among the immortals.

The "immortals" (*amṛta*) are the gods; because it is connected with them, the rite is also called "immortal. The ancestors, however, are mortal; because it is connected with them, the rite is also called "mortal. For this reason, the Śrāddha rites should be commenced beginning from the divine portion. Likewise, they should be concluded within the Vaiśvadevika rite among the immortals—this is the meaning. When it is performed in this manner, the inauspicious rite known as "mortal" becomes auspicious itself, being enveloped on both sides by the "immortal" rite which is of an auspicious nature. The fault of reversing the aforementioned sequence of the divine and ancestral rites has been shown in the Manu passage beginning with, "One should endeavor to have that [rite] begin and end with the divine."
Yama also said:
"That ancestral rite (śrāddha) which is first devoid of the deities would become demonic;
therefore, in all śrāddhas, one should avoid placing the ancestral offering first."
One should first perform the rite for the gods and afterwards that for the ancestors according to the rule;
one who performs the ancestral rite first will soon see his lineage perish.

"Āsura" means fit for the enjoyment of Asuras, because the Vaiśvadeva [seats] intended to ward off the Asuras have not yet been established. Therefore, the seating of the Vaiśvadeva [guests] occurs first, followed by that of the Pitrya [guests]. And that must be done in due order, facing east and facing north respectively.
Thus it is stated in the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa:
"One should first seat two Brāhmaṇas facing east as the deities."
One should always seat three Brahmins facing north for the ancestors.
