"Two" is intended as an indicative mark (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the number of Brahmins invited for the sake of the *vaiśvadeva* rite; and "three" is for the number of Brahmins invited for the sake of the *pitrya* rite.
For this very reason, it is stated in both the *Vārāha-purāṇa* and the *Viṣṇu-purāṇa*:
"One should feed the Brahmins facing east, who represent the dual nature of the gods."
And one should also feed those representing the paternal and maternal ancestors, facing the north.

"Those who possess both natures" refers to those connected to the two *vaiśvadeva* offerings for the sake of the two types of *śrāddha*: that for the ancestors (*pitṛ*) and that for the maternal ancestors (*mātāmaha*).
Regarding these two, O King, some say the performance of the *śrāddha* should be separate;
others, the great sages, perform it in one place with a single cooking.
‘Of the two’ refers to the groups of the paternal and maternal ancestors.
In the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa and the Brahma Purāṇa it is said:
“Facing east, one should perform the ritual intentions for the gods; facing north, one should perform them for the ancestors.”
Yājñavalkya: With the sacred grass (pavitra) in his hand, he should seat those who have sipped water on their seats—
two facing east for the rite to the gods (daiva), three facing north for the rite to the ancestors (pitrya), or even one for each.
Viṣṇu also says:
"Two for the gods facing east, three for the ancestors facing north, or one for each of the two groups.
Śaṅkha also says the same.
A wise man should feed two Brahmins facing east for the rite to the gods, and three facing north for the rite to the ancestors, according to the rules; or he may feed one in each case.
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"Two [seats] for the gods facing east, three for the ancestors facing north, or one for each of the two groups;
those intended for the ancestors should be bathed and arranged according to their sequence of learning and qualities."
One should have them sit upon seats strewn with sesame seeds and *darbha* grass. Kātyāyana also says:

"Having seated those who have bathed, are pure, and have sipped water (*ācamana*), facing east for the rite to the gods (*daiva*)—in pairs according to one's ability—and facing north for each individual in the rite to the ancestors (*pitrya*)."
Uśanas says:

"Having trimmed their beards, nails, and body hair, and having seated them on darbha-grass seats in a pure place—the Vaiśvadevika guests facing east and the others facing north—one should seat them according to the specific Veda.
Thus, there is a distinction in seating based on the specific Veda.
According to the Śātātapa-smṛti and the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa:
"In the rite for the gods, one should seat two Atharvan Brahmins facing east;
in the rite for the ancestors, however, three—namely a Bahvṛca, an Adhvaryu, and an Āmagāna—facing north."
Regarding this, Paiṭhīnasi says:
"One should seat the Viśvedevas facing east on seats provided with sacred grass (barhis), and the ancestors to the south-east. Thus it has been stated.

One should seat the *brāhmaṇas* for the *vaiśvadeva* rite, dedicated to the *viśvedevas*, facing the east; and the *brāhmaṇas* for the *pitṛ* rite, dedicated to the ancestors, facing the south-east. Now, with reference to those seated for the *vaiśvadeva* rite, all this—that they are placed in rows in the south-eastern direction (the *āgneyī* quarter) facing north—is "stated," the remainder being understood as "in the *Gṛhyasūtra*."

Hārīta, however, having criticized the position that the ancestral (pitrya) Brahmins should be seated facing north, stated that they should be seated facing east and the Vaiśvadevika Brahmins facing north: "One should feed auspicious Brahmins who have sipped water for rinsing the mouth upon pure Darbha grass with its tips pointing south; [one may feed them] facing east or facing north. According to Maitrāyaṇi, because of the specification toward the east, these [ancestors] are fierce; when facing [the guests], they become harmful. Therefore, one should feed the Brahmins facing east. Here, due to their predominance and the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the Darbha grass with tips pointing south, the Brahmins intended are specifically those for the ancestral rite. However, some believe that one should feed them facing north. Alternatively, this facing north of the ancestral Brahmins should not be performed. The reason for this is the aforementioned specification toward the east and so forth; since these Brahmins were designated and appointed by the prior invitation to eat in the place of the ancestors and others, therefore—
For the ancestors indeed attend upon those twice-born who have been invited.

Because of this statement, the teacher Maitrāyaṇi considers that those [Brāhmaṇas] presided over by cruel-natured ancestors become harmful when they face south while facing the sacrificer who, facing south, performs the ancestral rite (*pitrya-karma*). Therefore, one should feed them only while they face east. However, those for the Viśvedevas should face north; for since they are presided over by the Viśvedevas, the protectors of the *śrāddha*, they become protectors when facing the sacrificer who, performing the rite, faces the southern direction.
Baudhāyana also [says]:

On seats prepared with six types of grass, he should cause two to sit for the rite to the gods (*daiva*), three for the rite to the ancestors (*pitrya*), or one in each case; they should face either eastward or northward.

Thus, regarding the orientation toward specific directions here, there are five positions. Among them: (1) the Vaiśvadeva [deities] face east and the Pitṛs face north; (2) the Vaiśvadevas face north and the Pitṛs face east; (3) both face north; (4) both face east; and (5) the Vaiśvadevas face east and the Pitṛs face the southeast (āgneya). Of these, this very position—where the Vaiśvadevas face east and the Pitṛs face north—is the one adopted by the majority. In this regard, according to the statement of Baudhāyana, "For the gods it is clockwise (pradakṣiṇa), but for the Pitṛs it is counter-clockwise (apradakṣiṇa)," whatever task belongs to the gods must be performed with a clockwise movement. Consequently, the seating of the Vaiśvadeva group should begin from the south and conclude in the north, while that of the Pitṛs should begin from the west and conclude in all directions. As for what was stated by Yama:
"They should sit with their right sides toward [the center] and should not touch one another.

In this context, the analysis of the compound *dakṣiṇasaṃsthāḥ* is: "those whose position (*saṃsthā*) is on the side of the right arm. And this is consistent with a row that begins from the west and ends in the east.
For this very reason, Chāgaleya says:
When one begins in the west and concludes in the east,
this indeed constitutes the southern orientation for the ancestral rite of Śrāddha.
Alternatively, this statement regarding the placement toward the south is made with reference to the seating of those invited for the ancestors (*pitrya*), which is performed facing east.
The method of seating has been stated by Śaṅkha and Likhita:
"Having greeted the Brahmins, he should cause them to sit down while touching their seats."
Regarding the clasping of the hands of the Brahmins and the touching of their seats, Yama states the specific requirement desired and the formula for seating them:
"Touching the seat with his left hand and clasping the Brahmins with his right hand, and having said, 'Be seated' (samādhvam), he should cause them to sit."
He himself stated another sentence for seating with this verse:
"One should say to them, 'Be seated,' even while touching the seat.
This is also stated in the Kūrma Purāṇa.
He should have them sit upon those seats, even while merely touching the seat, having addressed them with the words, "Be seated"; then they should sit down individually.
Vyāsa, however, states another verse:
"One should say 'Be seated' to them while touching the seat;
they should sit upon those seats that have been spread out, but they should not touch one another."
"On the *upastīrṇa* [seats]" means on those where *darbha* grass has been spread either above or nearby.
Regarding the seating, Dharma states the mantra:
"Then, having touched [the seats], one should seat the gods, and then the ancestors."
He should cause them to sit upon their seats with those same *vyāhṛti* formulas.

Regarding this, Aparārka and the author of the Smṛticandrikā have explained that the *vyāhṛtis* are used only when the paternal ancestors (the *paitṛkas*) are seated. Since no specific distinction is made there, it is indicated that the application of the *vyāhṛtis* occurs during the seating of both [groups of ancestors]. As for the term *anvārabhya*, the author of the Smṛticandrikā reads it as *jānvārabhya* and states that the seating of the Brāhmaṇa is preceded by touching his knee. We do not know from where he has brought this reading, as it is not found even in many original manuscripts of the *smṛti*; furthermore, we do not see how learned practitioners (*śiṣṭas*), who without contradiction grasp the right hand of the Brāhmaṇa, have failed to observe this.
Also in the *Bhaviṣyatpurāṇa*: "Having uttered 'Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ,' one should cause them to sit down properly.

Here, the formula for the ritual act of seating with the mantra is as follows: the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) should utter either "Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ, sit down" (*samādhvam*) or "sit here" (*atrāsyatām*). Thereafter, the twice-born (*dvija*s) should also sit down while responding, "Oṃ, we sit well" (*susamāsmaha*). Having thus seated the Brahmins for the sake of the *śrāddha* for the ancestors (*pitṛ*s) and so forth, he should also seat those for the sake of the *śrāddha* for the maternal grandfather (*mātāmaha*).
And likewise, having established the seating of the Brahmins for the sake of the *śrāddha* for the ancestors and others, Yājñavalkya says:
"The same applies to the maternal grandfathers; or else, the ritual procedure (*tantra*) for the Vaiśvadeva [deities] [is common]."

"In this manner," meaning as in the *daiva* and *pitrya* rites for the *pitṛ-śrāddha*, one should seat separate *brāhmaṇas* for the *daiva* and *pitrya* portions intended for the *mātāmaha-śrāddha*. Alternatively, one may seat only those for the *pitrya* portion separately; however, one should designate the same *daiva* deities for both. This is what is meant by the phrase "or a single ritual procedure (*tantra*). Having performed the *vaiśvadevika* rite—that is, the rite dedicated to the Viśvedevas—only once, it should be understood as serving as a subsidiary part (*aṅga*) for both *śrāddhas*. Thus it is stated in the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa* and the *Brahma Purāṇa*: "And likewise for the maternal grandfathers, the *vaiśvadevika* ritual procedure may be common."
Likewise, some other men maintain that those two are distinct from one another.
Sumantu states what must be done by those seated upon their seats:
"All of them, with sacred grass (pavitra) in hand and observing a vow of silence,
should avoid mutual contact with those who have food remnants (ucchiṣṭa)."

The meaning is that all those Brahmins—intended for the gods and intended for the ancestors—with purifiers (pavitra) in their hands and observing a vow of silence, should remain until the conclusion of the meal, avoiding any contact with food-leavings arising from negligence. From the word "and" (ca), it is understood that the performer of the Śrāddha also should remain observing the vow of silence. Regarding the expiation for the breach of silence through negligence, it has been stated in the section on observances (niyamaprakaraṇa). And this [vow of silence] is intended as an illustration for the previously mentioned observances. Yama states an exception to the application of the vow of silence in certain cases:
They should engage in conversations concerning Brahman; this is what the ancestors desire.
It has already been stated that even when the Brāhmaṇas have thus been seated, one should also seat any guest who has arrived in the row of the Śrāddha.
This concludes the seating of the Brāhmaṇas.
Now follows the ritual for the praise of the Earth and other duties.

In that regard, having sat down upon a seat before the Brāhmaṇas who are seated on the ground strewn with *kuśa* grass, wearing the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) and facing east, one should first perform the remembrance of Puṇḍarīkākṣa (Viṣṇu) either to remove impurity caused by negligence that was previously unknown or to achieve a state of superior purity. For the *Kratu* states that the remembrance of Puṇḍarīkākṣa effects purification:
"Whether one is impure or pure, or even if one has reached every possible state of being..."
Whoever remembers the lotus-eyed Lord (Puṇḍarīkākṣa) becomes pure both externally and internally.

Immediately thereafter, a praise of the Earth (pṛthivīstuti) should be performed. Accordingly, in the *Śrāddhakalpa* of the *Mahābhārata*, there is a statement by Atri regarding one who has been invited: "In this rite, the Earth, which bears the dripping of the funeral offerings (*nivāpa*), should be praised."
Vaiṣṇavī, Kāśyapī, and likewise here Kṣayā.

Regarding the *nivāpa*—the offering dedicated to the ancestors (*pitṛ-devatya*)—since the earth is the substratum for that which is to be poured out (*āścyota*), the earth should first be praised. The particle *iti* is used to demonstrate that [the names] such as Vaiṣṇavī function as the instruments (*karaṇa*) in the act of praise. Consequently, for the purpose of manifesting the praise, names such as "Vaiṣṇavyasi" and so forth should be uttered; or else, the root *stu* may signify propitiation (*ārādhana*). In that latter case, the names Vaiṣṇavī and others should be employed preceded by the *praṇava* (Oṃ) and followed by the dative case ending and the word *namaḥ*. For example: Oṃ vaiṣṇavyai namaḥ; Oṃ kāśyapyai namaḥ; Oṃ kṣayāyai namaḥ. The form *kṣayā* is derived from the verbal root *kṣi*, meaning "to dwell" or "to go."
In the Vārāha Purāṇa:
Having bowed one’s head to the earth, the sustainer of the funeral offering,
by the names Vaiṣṇavī, Kāśyapī, and Akṣayā.
The words of the Boar addressed to the Earth are also found in that very same place:
"O Goddess, having bowed my head and arrived at this place of libation,
I shall praise you with devotion while remaining steadfast in this mantra."
You are Medinī, the Mother of the World, Kṣiti, Urvī, Dharā, Mahī, Bhūmi, and the Rock of the Mountains; you are the Firm One—homage, homage to you!
Dharaṇī, Kāśyapī, Kṣauṇī, Rasā, Viśvambharā, and Bhū;
O Mother, you are the foundation of the world and Vasudhā—homage be to you! You are Vaiṣṇavī, the goddess of all beings, and Pṛthivī—homage be to you!

Then, having meditated upon the site of the *śrāddha* as being Gayā itself and upon Gadādhara situated in one part of it, and having performed obeisance to those two, one should proceed with the subsequent rite.
This is stated in the *Brahmāṇḍapurāṇa*:
"Having meditated upon the *śrāddha* ground as Gayā, and having meditated upon the Lord Gadādhara..."
And having paid homage to those two, one should then proceed with the śrāddha ceremony.

In the phrase "to those two" (*tābhyām*), the dative case is used in the sense of the accusative. And the salutation (*namaskāra*) should be performed with mind, speech, and body. Among these, the verbal salutation should be made using their names as follows: *oṃ bhagavatyai gayāyai namaḥ* (Oṃ, obeisance to the Blessed Lady Gayā); *oṃ bhagavate gadādharāya namaḥ* (Oṃ, obeisance to the Blessed Lord Gadādhara).
Regarding that which is to be chanted prior to the commencement of the *śrāddha*, Pracetas says:
"Then, having placed the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*apasavya*), one should chant the Vaiṣṇava mantra."
Having recited either the Gāyatrī or the Praṇava, one should then commence the Śrāddha.
The "Vaiṣṇava mantras" are those beginning with "tad viṣṇoḥ paramaṃ padam" and so forth. In the Brahmapurāṇa:
"Having seated [the guest], the wise one should recite the Gāyatrī with his permission."

Now, having honored space and time—which are subtle divisions of the physical plane and serve as auxiliary factors for the rite—by citing the authority of the conduct of the learned (*śiṣṭācāra*), one should perform an inquiry regarding the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) to be described hereafter, in order to obtain the permission of the Brahmins.
In this regard, the *Brahmapurāṇa* provides an indicative scriptural passage (*liṅgadarśana*) concerning the Śrāddha performed by Varāha:
"Taking up the *kuśa* grasses with their tips pointing eastward, which reside within the pores of his skin..."
He asked in the hearts of the sages, "I shall perform the libation for the ancestors."

"Pointing eastward" (*prāgagrān*) means having their tips directed toward the front, facing the direction that is turned toward oneself. "Situated within the pores of the skin" (*romakūpāntarasthitān*): this is said because the Sacrificial Boar (*yajñavarāha*) has hair made of *barhis* grass. He questioned the sages—who had been meditated upon with the mind—“in the heart,” that is, in the mind itself.
Regarding the fault of not questioning, it is stated in the *Kālikākhaṇḍa*:
“O Pārvatī, that man who should practice [the rite] without questioning the Brahmins...”
The gods, headed by me, do not act in a way that is pleasing to him.
Regarding the proper procedure in the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*:
Having placed both hands evenly between the knees,
he should respectfully inquire after all the best of the twice-born as they are seated.

"Full of courtesy" (*sapraśrayaḥ*), meaning endowed with humility, he should ask. To manifest this humility, he describes the bodily posture: "Both," and so forth. With both knees, the two hands should be "even," meaning situated at the same level and in the same position, placed directly in front [of the body]—the sense being that he has formed the *añjali* (palms joined). Alternatively, "even with the knees" means having the same configuration as the two knees; having placed them between the knees themselves, he should ask. And this posture is possible only for one who is seated. By the statement "full of courtesy, he should ask the Brahmins," it is understood that he must also direct himself toward the Brahmins. Consequently, seated thus facing the Brahmins, he should ask them all; and the option of asking all of them is optional.
For this very reason, Kātyāyana states: "In the case of questions, he asks the head of the row, or all of them."

From the use of the plural form in the word "praśneṣu" (in questions), it is understood that this [procedure] applies to all types of inquiries. One who is seated at the head of the row—that is, at the beginning of the row—is "the head of the row" (*paṅktimūrddhanya*). When a question is directed toward one person, he alone should answer; when a question is directed toward all, they should all answer. Specifically, regarding the ritual duties to be performed by each respective row, only the one who is the head of that particular row should be questioned; or else, all those situated in that particular row should be questioned. In this regard, the formula for the questioner’s inquiry is found in the *Brahmapurāṇa*.
"I shall honor the fathers,
the grandfathers, and all the great-grandfathers, as well as their fathers, in due order with food."

The plural number in "pitṝn" and so forth is for the sake of honor. Likewise, in other instances as well, the plural should be employed according to established custom. The question, together with the response of the best of the twice-born, is found in the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*:
"With a concentrated mind, one should ask the Brahmins: 'I shall perform the Śrāddha.'"
Being told by them, "Do so," he should then offer a seat of darbha grass.

In this context, after performing three breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) preceded by the remembrance of Śrī Viṣṇu, who is the Supreme Brahman and the Person of Sacrifice (*yajñapuruṣa*), one should—wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*) and seated upon *darbha* grass with its tips pointing south according to the previously mentioned posture facing the twice-born ancestors—ask [the questions] using the formula established by the practice of the learned. In all such inquiries and responses here, the applications must be preceded by the syllable *oṃ*.
Thus it is said in the Mahābhārata, in the Śrī Bhagavad Gītā:
"Therefore, having uttered 'Oṃ', the acts of sacrifice, charity, and austerity [are performed]."
They proceed constantly, as prescribed by rule, for those who discourse upon Brahman.

[1208] As for the formulation of the question: having recited the *saṃkalpa* formula—beginning with "Oṃ, here on this earth... and ending with "...desiring to satisfy the ancestors"—as demonstrated in the section on the invitation (*nimantraṇa*), one should declare at the end, "I shall perform [this rite] with your permission. This very question is designated by the author of the *Smṛticandrikā* as the "intermediate *saṃkalpa*. After the question, being authorized by the Brahmins with the words "Do so," one should offer seats of *darbha* grass, preceded by the rites for the Viśvedevas. It is stated in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*, *Brahmavaivarta*, *Brahma-purāṇa*, *Vāyu-purāṇa*, *Prabhāsakhaṇḍa*, and *Bhaviṣyottara* that the *Saptārcis* mantra should be recited three times prior to the offering of the *darbha* seats.
I shall therefore proclaim this mantra, which destroys all evil, which is equal to the Ashvamedha sacrifice, and which is nectar fashioned by Brahma.
Salutation to the deities, to the ancestors, and to the great yogis; salutation to Svadhā and Svāhā, always, salutation, salutation!
"One should always recite this three times at the beginning, middle, and end of the *śrāddha*;
or, being composed in mind, one should recite it during the offering of the funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*).

Furthermore, learned Brahmins (*śrotriya*) recite the first verse of the *Saptārcis-stotra*, as declared in the *Prabhāsakhaṇḍa*, the *Brahmapurāṇa*, and the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*, three times at the beginning, middle, and end of the *śrāddha*.
"I always bow to those ancestors of radiant splendor— both formless and embodied— who are meditative and possess the eye of yoga.
Others, however, also recite another mantra spoken by Vyāsa:
“May that Viṣṇu be gracious to me, who is offered oblations with four, four, two, and five [verses], and again with two.

At this point, the binding of the *nīvī* (the end of the lower garment tucked between the legs) must be performed; for, based on the indicative mark (*liṅga*) found in the *Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa* stating, “The *nīvī* indeed has the ancestors as its deity,” one understands that a rite dedicated to the ancestors must be performed while wearing the *nīvī*.
In the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa: "One should likewise tie the waist-knot and must not look at wicked people;
one should remain thus restricted as the performer until the śrāddha is completed."

Likewise, while explaining the *Kātyāyana-sūtra*—"Having loosened the *nīvī*, he makes the *añjali* with the words 'namo vaḥ'"—which occurs within the section on the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña*, the teacher Karka stated as follows: "Since the loosening of the *nīvī* is prescribed here, it is understood by implication that the binding of the *nīvī* must be performed at the commencement of the rite. In this context, once bound according to the injunction, this *nīvī* remains unloosened during the occasions for the rites pertaining to the *Viśvedevas* and continues until the salutation to the *piṇḍas*. Here, *nīvī* refers to the concealment of the ends of the upper garment, which are provided with sesame seeds and *kuśa* grass, by wrapping them around the outer part of the cloth attached to the left hip. At the binding of the *nīvī*, the devout performers of the *śrāddha* recite the mantra to be shown later during the scattering of sesame seeds, beginning with "I destroy everything that is impure"; immediately thereafter, for the sake of protection, they should first scatter barley grains in the area designated for the *Viśvedevas*.
For it is stated in the *Brahma Purāṇa*, concerning the *śrāddha* performed by Varāha, regarding the protective role of barley for the gods:
"The wielder of the discus and mace (Viṣṇu) performed the protection of the deities with unbroken grains (*akṣata*).
Indeed, barley-grains are medicinal herbs that have arisen from the weapons of all the gods."
For they have been created for the purpose of protection; indeed, they guard all the gods among the devas, dānavas, daityas, yakṣas, and rākṣasas.
Indeed, no one in the world of moving and unmoving beings is able to cause them any injury;
for they were appointed by Viṣṇu in ancient times to serve as the chariots of the gods.

This being the case, even at the place designated for the Vaiśvadeva, it is the sesame seeds (*tila*) alone that must be scattered, and not barley (*yava*), because there is no scriptural injunction for them. Furthermore, as for what Upādhyāya Karka stated—that what is performed with sesame seeds does not become non-divine (*adaiva*)—it should be understood that this is based on a failure to thoroughly examine the Purāṇas. Thus, having scattered barley in the region for the gods, one should scatter sesame seeds and white mustard (*gaurasarṣapa*) all around in the region for the ancestors.
Accordingly, the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa states:
"One should recite mantras that destroy demons and scatter the earth with sesame seeds."
And white mustard seeds should be used for protection, for there is indeed much deception in the *śrāddha* rite.
"Deceit" (*chala*) refers to obstacles created by *yātudhānas* and others. In the *Saura Purāṇa*:
"Then, having seated the Brahmins and having offered them *kuśa*-grass seats..."
Thereafter, one should scatter sesame seeds for the protection of the śrāddha.

The connection is that one should provide a seat of *kuśa* grass and cause [the guest] to sit down. Furthermore, in this context, black sesame seeds (*tila*) are to be taken; likewise, it is stated in the *Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa*:
"The scattering [of the ground] should also be performed with white mustard seeds (*siddhārthaka*) and black sesame seeds."
And one should also diligently seek a vision of the sun, fire, and garments.
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"The scattering of sesame seeds should be performed for the destruction of the Yātudhānas.
Likewise:
"May the Asuras depart by means of two [verses];
one should diligently perform the expulsion of the Yātudhānas with sesame seeds, or else with white mustard seeds."

“Let the Asuras who have the form of Pitṛs depart—those who wander about assuming various forms; let Agni drive away from here those who attack our fortresses and our enemies. “Let the Asuras who dwell among the Pitṛs depart. Let the lower, the higher, and the middle Pitṛs rise up—the gentle ones who have gone to the life-breath, who are free from malice and knowers of Truth; may they protect us, O Pitṛs, in our invocations.
Likewise: “I strike down everything that is impure.”
All the asuras and dānavas have been subdued by me;
those who are rākṣasas and those who are piśācas and guhyakas—
all the yātudhānas have been slain by me.
With this mantra, one whose self is well-restrained should scatter sesame seeds and mustard seeds in all directions;
for in whatever region this mantra is recited, [it becomes protected].
The Rākṣasas indeed avoid that place.
In the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*:
"There, one should scatter white mustard seeds on the ground to ward off demons;
and in all directions, one should scatter sesame seeds with this mantra."
I shall destroy everything that is impure,
and all the asuras, dānavas, rākṣasas, yakṣas, piśācas, and guhyakas shall be slain by me.
"And all the Yātudhānas have been slain by me.
This mantra for the scattering of sesame seeds and *kuśa* grass at the doorway, as stated in the *Skanda Purāṇa*, is observed in the practice of the learned (*śiṣṭa*).
"May the sesame seeds protect against the Asuras; may the *darbha* grass protect against the Rākṣasas."
"A learned Brahmin (śrotriya) should indeed protect the row [of guests], for the guest is the protector of all.
Regarding the scattering of sesame seeds around the site of the *śrāddha* in the directions starting from the east and in the center, the mantras are given in the *Bhaviṣyatpurāṇa*:
"May the Agniṣvātta ancestors protect my eastern direction."
Likewise, may those ancestors who abide in the southern quarter, seated upon the sacrificial grass (barhiṣad), protect us.
Likewise, the drinkers of clarified butter [should be placed] facing west, and the drinkers of Soma facing north;
they should also be placed below, above, in the corners, and in the intermediate corners in every direction.
From Rākṣasas, Bhūtas, and Piśācas, and likewise from the malice of Asuras—
may Yama, the lord over them all, grant me protection everywhere;
and may there be eternal satisfaction for the Vāyus, Bhūtas, and Pitṛs.

Having thus divided these mantras according to their respective characteristics, one should scatter sesame seeds in the eastern and other directions, below, above, in the corners, and everywhere. It is as follows: "May the Agniṣvātta groups of ancestors protect my eastern direction"—thus in the east. Likewise, "May the Barhiṣad ancestors who reside there protect"—thus in the south. "In the same way, may the Ājyapa protect"—thus in the west. "And may the Somapa protect"—thus in the north.
And likewise below, above, in the corners, and in the intermediate corners, everywhere.
Likewise, from the harm of Rākṣasas, Bhūtas, Piśācas, and Asuras;
May Yama, the sovereign over them all, grant me protection;
and may there be eternal satisfaction for the ancestors who have become the wind.
Thus, one should scatter sesame seeds below, above, in the corners, and everywhere.
As stated in the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*:
"For the protection of the ancestral sacrifice (pitṛsatra), [one should scatter them] three times in every direction."
One should scatter sesame seeds while reciting the mantra beginning with "apahatāḥ."
An explanatory statement (arthavāda) regarding this has also been stated in that very same place:
"Whoever performs this worship of the ancestors at the time of the śrāddha, that śrāddha shall become inexhaustible, protected by the ancestors. Thus it is said.
In the *Nigama*, however, a different mantra is prescribed for the scattering of sesame seeds and the like:
"The Asuras and Rakṣasas have been struck down, they who sit upon the altar"; with this, one should scatter thickly sesame seeds and white mustard seeds upon the ground of the *śrāddha*.
"Dense" means thick.

The authors of the *Smṛticandrikā* and others, however, have cited such a Vedic statement (*nigama-vākya*) as: "Having driven them away, one should scatter sesame seeds. Here, they have also presented the mantra indicated by the opening words (*pratīka*): "Driven away are the Asuras, the Rakṣasas, and the Piśācas from the earth;
let them go hence to where their minds have gone" (Manu). There is also another mantra in the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*.
Saying, "May they go away from all sides, leaving the ancestors and the Brahmins," and reciting,
"Those who have gone to the life-breath," he should scatter sesame seeds while keeping his sacred thread over the right shoulder (apasavya).

"May the Paṇis depart, those who are ill-disposed and haters of the gods; may Yama grant him a dwelling clearly distinguished by days, nights, and mornings"—this is one mantra. Another, characterized by the words "asuṃ ya īyuḥ," begins with "udīratām avaraḥ.
It is as follows:

"May the fathers—those below, those above, and those in the middle—be uplifted; may the Soma-loving ancestors who have gone to the life-breath, who are free from malice and knowers of the *ṛta*, protect us in our invocations. After scattering the sesame seeds and other items, one should place the food in a certain vessel to remove any defect caused by the gaze of a cat or similar animal, whether it has occurred through negligence, been observed, or is suspected. Having consecrated water with the *kuśa-śuddhavatī* verses and other mantras as previously described, one should sprinkle the entire cooked food. It is declared that food defiled by the falling of a malignant gaze or other such causes becomes pure through this sprinkling. Thus, having performed the sprinkling of all the cooked food, one should sprinkle all other useful items brought to the site of the *śrāddha*, such as *kuśa* grass, flowers, and so forth.

And likewise, Vasiṣṭha states: "One should sprinkle the cooked food and other items with the *śuddhavatī*, *kuṣmāṇḍī*, and *pāvamānī* verses. The *śuddhavatī* and others have already been explained. It is specified that a Sāman-chanting sacrificer uses the *śuddhavatī* verses, one who studies the Yajurveda uses the *kuṣmāṇḍī* verses, and a Rigvedic priest uses the *pāvamānī* verses. This is merely illustrative; it includes the *taratsamandī* verses mentioned in the section on the purification of cooked food. By the word "and others" (*ādi*), flowers and other items used in the *śrāddha* are also included.
For this very reason, it is stated in both the *Brahmāṇḍa* and *Bhaviṣyat Purāṇas*:
There should be sprinkling with water for flowers and the like, as well as for grasses and sacrificial offerings;
likewise, for materials brought from elsewhere, one should set them down and sprinkle them again.
One should not touch anything that has not been sprinkled with water during rites for the gods or for the ancestors;
the various rules for the *śrāddha* have thus been proclaimed according to their common application.
"Uccāvacāḥ" means of various kinds.
Yājñavalkya, demonstrating the fault incurred by transgressing the aforementioned prohibitions, states the rule for sprinkling:
"One who offers oblations and gives gifts without having sprinkled [the food] and without having touched water [is at fault]."
The portion for Nirṛti should be set aside; therefore, one should perform the sprinkling.
Thus concludes the section on the worship of the Earth and other preliminary rites.
Now, by Hemādri, whose splendor is graced by a multitude of virtues,
this section on the Vaiśvadeva worship is thus expanded.
Now follow the ritual items, beginning with the seat of darbha grass.

And since everything is preceded by the divine (*daiva*), these [rites] must first be performed for the twice-born of the gods, and thereafter for the twice-born of the ancestors (*paitrya*). In this regard, although it is understood through an examination of the logic—consisting of the favoring of proximity to the principal act as permitted by the injunction of performance—that all ritual items (*padārtha*) inherent in the rites for the gods and ancestors should be performed according to the sequence of individual items (*padārthānusamaya*), nevertheless, by virtue of the authority of the statements of Yājñavalkya and others, it has already been stated that from the offering of the *darbha* grass seat up to the covering, these should be performed for both the divine and ancestral rites according to the sequence of sections (*kāṇḍānusamaya*). Among those, one who desires to perform the offering of the *darbha* seat should first prostrate with the knees.
And so says Ṛṣyaśṛṅga:
"One should always cause the right knee to touch the ground when attending upon the gods;
one should then cause the other knee to touch the ground when attending upon the ancestors."
Immediately after prostrating at the knees and before offering a seat, one should pour water into the hand of the twice-born.
Thus says Yājñavalkya:
"Having given water for washing the hands, one should also give *kuśa* grass for the purpose of seats."

Although it may appear at first glance from the wording that one should give water for washing the hands into the Brahmin’s hand and also give *kuśa* grass for the seat (*viṣṭara*) right there, nevertheless, the author of the *Smṛticandrikā* maintains that it should be understood that one gives the *kuśa* grass for the seat after placing them on the seat, because of the specific use of the term "for the sake of the seat" (*viṣṭarārtha*).
For this very reason, it is stated in the *Kāṭhaka*:
"One should offer *darbha* grass on the seat, but never on the hand."
Pracetas has also said:
"One should provide *darbha* grass for the seat, but never upon the hand;
otherwise, there will be eternal resentment among the ancestors, the gods, and human beings."

*Ruṣṭiḥ* means quarrel. Because the sacrificial seats (*tīrthas*) of the gods, ancestors, humans, Prajāpati, and Agni all reside in the hand of the Brāhmaṇa, a quarrel would arise among the gods and others over the *darbha* grass placed in the hand, each claiming, "This is mine! This is mine!
For this very reason, the *Nāgarakhaṇḍa* states that giving a seat of *darbha* grass in the hand is fruitless:
"Water should be poured into the hand, but by no means should *darbha* grass be [placed there]."
If one devoid of wisdom offers a blade of darbha grass as a seat in his hand,
the ancestors do not take their place upon that seat.

As for that which was stated by Pracetas, "They should take those *kuśa* blades," that too should be explained as meaning they should accept them mentally, and not that they should grasp them with their hands; therefore, there is no contradiction. Devasvāmin, however, maintains the following: the prohibition regarding the offering of *darbha* grass into the hand refers to *darbha* used for spreading as a seat (*āsana*). But the rule regarding taking [the *kuśa*] is, upon a consideration of the other statements of Yājñavalkya, restricted to the *kuśa* intended for the *viṣṭara* (seat-mat) and applies specifically to the hand. That is incorrect, because since it is impossible to offer *darbha* grass intended for spreading a seat into the hand of a Brahmin, there is no occasion for such a prohibition.
Regarding this, the specific location for placing the *kuśa*-grass seat upon the *kutupa* and other types of seats to be offered is shown in the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*:
"One should offer a seat upon the seat, either on the left or even on the right.

Here, "left" refers to the area situated on the left side of the Brāhmaṇa who is seated upon his own seat; likewise for "right. In this context, "right" pertains to the *vaiśvadeva* (ancestral) rite, while "left" pertains to the *paitṛka* (paternal) rite.
And so it is stated immediately after that very point:
"In rites for the ancestors, [the seat] is indeed on the left; in rites for the gods, on the right.

Furthermore, this seat for the gods should be offered with *darbha* grass mixed with barley, while for the ancestors it should be with *darbha* grass mixed with sesame seeds. For this very reason, having stated "one should offer *darbha* grass upon the seat," it is said in the *Kāṭhaka*:
"Darbha grass with barley is for the gods, and together with sesame seeds for the ancestors.
Baudhāyana, however, has stated another distinction:
"For the gods it is clockwise, but for the ancestors it is counter-clockwise."
Darbha grass with barley is for the gods; for the ancestors, it is twofold [in length] along with sesame seeds.
The word "together" (sahitāḥ) is to be understood as the ellipsis. In the *Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa*:
"One should place on the seat for the ancestors double-folded blades of darbha grass along with sesame seeds."
"Dviguṇān" means doubled by being broken in the middle;
for this very reason, Śaunaka says:
"Having offered water, one should offer darbha grass, doubled and broken, upon the seat."
By this, the doubling [of the number of items] up to the point of exhaustion has been stated. "Water" refers to that for the purpose of washing the hands.
In the *Brahmapurāṇa*, regarding the procedure for the *śrāddha* performed by Varāha:
"One who knows the Vedic declarations [should offer] *darbha* grasses with their roots and tips joined together, along with sesame seeds."
Having placed them upon that seat, he offered the *āsana* with his left hand.
Regarding the term *aśliṣṭamūlāgrāḥ*: those whose roots and tips are joined together, being doubled over, are "those with unjoined roots and tips.
By stating that for the ancestors they are "doubled" on the left side of the seated Brahmins, Baudhāyana implies by implication that for the gods they are "straight."
Therefore, Bṛhaspati said:

"Having placed the straight darbha grasses with the left hand for the rite to the gods, one should offer them clockwise; for the rite to the ancestors, one should offer double-folded grasses counter-clockwise, following the counter-clockwise procedure."

"Upright" means free from doubling. "With the left" means with the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) resting on the left shoulder; "with the right" means the opposite of that; "like the right" means counter-clockwise.
As stated in the *Nāgarakhaṇḍa*:
"With straight blades of *darbha* grass accompanied by grains of rice and water, [one should offer] toward the southern direction."

One should offer a seat for the gods and for the ancestors in their proper order. With an odd number of *darbha* grasses, doubled in quantity, together with sesame seeds, placed on the left side— in the southern direction, that is, on the right side of the Brāhmaṇa— one should offer the seat for the gods using an even number of *darbha* blades.
Pracetas, however, instructing each Brāhmaṇa regarding the offering of the *darbha* grasses for the Vaiśvadeva seats, states the mantra for their acceptance:
"In the rite for the gods, straight *darbha* blades should be given individually;
they, for their part, should accept those *kuśa* blades with the mantra: 'I am Dharma.'"

With this Yajurvedic mantra, "I am Dharma, established as the king of the people (viś)," the Brāhmaṇas invited to the Vaiśvadeva rite should take up the *kuśa* grass. The meaning of the word "should take" (*gṛhṇīyuḥ*) has already been explained previously. Some, however, mention a variant reading: "Dharmāsi. According to that view, the mantra is as follows: "Thou art Dharma, the virtuous Dharma; for me, maintain the *brahmans*, maintain the *kṣatriyas*, maintain the people (*viś*); by means of that, having sipped water, mayest thou cause [the sacrifice] to overflow. Regarding the rule for the directions when offering seats and other items, Kratu says:
Facing north for the gods and facing south for the ancestors,
one should offer the seat, the water for the hands (arghya), and so forth, keeping the sacred thread over the left shoulder (savya) according to the prescribed rule.

Regarding the offering of seats, the specific case endings have already been shown: the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) and so forth for "imperishable seats" (*akṣayyāsana*), while the dative (*caturthī*) is optional according to rules such as "always [use the dative] for the seat. Furthermore, concerning the genitive, it is stated in the *Nāgarakhaṇḍa*:
"One should cause the seat to be offered to them with the preceding case ending."

In the *iṣṭi-śrāddha*, the offering of seats and other items should be presented using the names of the Viśvedevas as established by the divisions of the *śrāddha* found in scriptural injunctions such as "Kratu and Dakṣa. Thus, the procedure for offering the seat to the Vaiśvadeva deities, as derived from this collection of statements, is stated as follows: Facing north, having bent his right knee, wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*yajñopavītī*), and with his hands between his knees, he should hold the raised right hand of the twice-born guest with his own left hand. Taking two straight blades of *darbha* grass together with water and barley, and having uttered either "This is the seat for the Viśvedevas known as Purūravas and Ārdrava," or "This is the seat for the Viśvedevas known as Purūravas and Ārdrava," he should pour that water into the hand of the twice-born guest. Then, on the southern part of the seat—such as a woolen blanket or the like—he should place those two blades of *darbha* grass using the *devatātīrtha* (the part of the hand sacred to the gods). The Brahmin, for his part, should recite the Yajus mantra: "I am Dharma, the king established in the people" (*dharmo 'smi viśi rājā pratiṣṭhitaḥ*), and say, "May there be a seat for me" (*svāsanam astu*).

And so it is stated in the *Nāgarakhaṇḍa*: "When offering perfumes, garlands, seats, and the like, the best of the twice-born should utter such words as: 'May there be fragrance! May there be a beautiful lamp! and so forth."
Here, immediately after offering the seat, one should pour water into the hand of the twice-born. Thus says the Āśvalāyana Gṛhyasūtra:
"Having offered water, having offered Darbha grass folded double as a seat, [one offers] water again.
This concludes the offering of the Darbha seat.
[1220] Now follows the third invitation;
and thus it is stated in the *Padma* and *Matsya* Purāṇas:
When the seats provided with darbha grass have been prepared according to the rule,
he should invite the Brahmins, having seated them after they have sipped water.

Indeed, it is widely accepted that by the phrase "having seated them on seats," the priority of time is expressed for seating upon seats made of woolen blankets (*kambala*) and so forth, rather than for the offering of a seat of *darbha* grass. Therefore, if the invitation were performed after first offering a *darbha* seat in the interval following the seating upon blankets and such, then this scriptural indication of priority—namely, the word "having seated" (*upaveśya*)—would be contradicted.

Not so; for in such cases as "one should go after having eaten" (*bhuktvā gacchet*), no contradiction is observed even when there is an intervention by another action between the eating and the going, since the grammatical suffix *ktvā* teaches only priority in time (*pūrvakālatā*). Furthermore, the rule governing the suffix *ktvā* refers merely to priority in time, and not specifically to immediate priority. Or, let us grant that it does refer to that [immediate priority]; nevertheless, in this case, because it is supported by other injunctions prescribing intervening actions, one must assume that its intended meaning (*tātparya*) refers to a priority in time that is indeed intervened. Moreover, by virtue of its commonality with the scriptural mention of the seat (*āsana*), this statement can also denote the immediate sequence of sitting upon the *darbha* grass seat. For this very reason, the author of the *Gṛhyasaṃgraha* says immediately after the offering of the *darbha* seat: "Then, having again offered water, he should invite them for the rite to the gods, saying, 'May the moment be made' (*daive kṣaṇaḥ kriyatām*); then the Brahmin should say, 'Om, so be it' (*oṃ tathā*); the performer should say again, 'May you receive it' (*prāpnotu bhavān*); the Brahmin should say again, 'I have received it' (*prāptavān*). Baudhāyana, however, has shown the invitation formula as: "The moment should be made for all the gods" (*viśvebhyo devebhyaḥ kṣaṇaḥ kartavyaḥ*). As for the interpretation given by the author of the *Smṛticandrikā* regarding the statement from the *Brahmapurāṇa*, "Having taken hold of [the hand] without the thumb, one should summon the Viśvedevas"—which explains that once the invitation is performed by taking hold of the Brahmin's hand without the thumb, the summoning of the Viśvedevas must be done immediately thereafter, and thus concludes that in the invitation one must take hold of the twice-born's hand without the thumb—that is incorrect. Here, there is no evidence for supplying the act of invitation (*nimantraṇa*) as the implied object. Furthermore, since the *Brahmapurāṇa* mentions the "taking without the thumb" in the context of the invocation (*āvāhana*), stating "I shall invoke the gods," and since this phrase "without the thumb" does not appear as connected to anything else in a passage devoid of the introduction of other ritual acts, its connection is understood to be with the invocation itself. Therefore, as before, this invitation too must be performed with the hand placed upon the knee of the Brahmin.
Thus ends the third invitation. Now follows the invocation (*āvāhana*).
Regarding that, the questions concerning the procedure for the invocation and the granting of permission are found in the *Kālikā Purāṇa*.
Then, for the sake of protection, one should employ those known as the Viśvedevas there;

the remainder [of the sentence] is "for the protection of this Śrāddha. "One should employ them there" means one should cause them to be present among those Brāhmaṇas by means of invocation (*āvāhana*). "Then" means immediately after the third invitation. Some, however, perform the invocation after placing the *arghya* vessels in front of the Brāhmaṇas.
And so it is stated in the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa and the Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
"Having given *kuśa* grass for the purpose of a seat and having prepared the *arghya* offering according to the rule, one should perform the invocation (*āvāhana*). Thus it is said.
In the *Nāgarakhaṇḍa* as well, after stating "and having prepared [the vessel] with perfumes and flowers," and so forth, the invocation is described.
However, the sequence following the invitation is respected because it is agreed upon by many scriptures.
Chāgaleya says:
"Having offered straight *darbha* grass for the seat and likewise water..."
Being authorized, he should invite the Viśvedevas while keeping them in mind.

In this context, although the phrase "having offered *darbha* grass" (*atra darbhān pradāya*) expresses that the offering of the *darbha* seat occurs prior to the invocation (*āvāhana*), one should understand—as in the previous case—that there is no contradiction with the scriptural injunction regarding priority even if the invitation (*nimantraṇa*) is performed in the interim, in accordance with other Smṛtis. Regarding the term "recollecting" (*anusmaran*), one should reflect upon the previously mentioned origins, majesties, and essential natures of the Viśvedevas. As for the word "permitted" (*anujñāta*), the specific detail that it is by the twice-born associated with the Vaiśvadeva rite is understood from proximity, the state of being the locus of the invocation, and propriety.
And it is stated in the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*:

"The wise man should perform the invocation (*āvāhana*) of the gods with their permission. By the phrase "with their permission" is meant with the permission of the twice-born who serve as the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) for the deities to be invoked. Accordingly, the question addressed by the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) is also implied, since there can be no occasion for permission in the absence of a question. The nature of the question and the permission, however, is shown in the *Brahmapurāṇa*.
"I shall invoke the gods," he says; "Invoke them! they reply. Having taken hold [of the vessel] with the thumb, he should then summon the Viśvedevas.

In the phrase "without the thumb" (*niraṅguṣṭham*), the word "the hand of the twice-born" (*dvijahasta*) is to be understood as the ellipsis. Others, however, mention an alternative reading: *viprāṅguṣṭham*. Furthermore, because of the injunction that "it must be performed according to the right-hand tradition" (*dakṣiṇācāreṇa kartavyam*), it should be understood as "the right thumb. "Having taken" (*gṛhītvā*) means having held [the water] with one's own right hand. When the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) has posed the question to the twice-born who represent the Viśvedevas, "I shall invoke the gods" (*devān āvāhayiṣye*), those brahmins should reply to that sacrificer, "Invoke them" (*āvāhaya*). Therefore, the word "all" (*viśvān*) should be employed before the word "gods" (*devān*) in the interrogative sentence.
For Kātyāyana says:
"Having spread darbha grass upon the seats, he asks, 'Shall I invoke the Viśvedevas? and, being permitted with the words, 'Invoke them,' [he does so]."
The sacrificer asks, having been authorized by the twice-born.

In this *ceṣṭiśrāddha*, for the sake of making meaningful such scriptural injunctions as "Kratu and Dakṣa are to be invoked in the Vaiśvadevika [portion]," the two specific names of the Viśvedevas—beginning with Kratu and Dakṣa—must be employed by the performer of each respective *śrāddha* prior to the word "viśvān devān. Furthermore, that these names are to be used in a *dvandva* compound has been explained in the section on deities (*devatāprakaraṇa*), and that they are to be used in the accusative case has been established in the section on grammatical inflections (*vibhaktiprakaraṇa*). Moreover, that they must end in the plural number is stated in the very same section on deities. Here too, it is understood that they must be placed at the end [of the phrase] in order to maintain grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the plural-ended term "viśvān devān. Consequently, in the *pārvaṇa* and other rites, the interrogative formula is formulated as: "I shall invoke the Viśvedevas known as Purūravas and Ārdrava," and so forth. However, for those who do not know their specific names, only the phrase "I shall invoke the Viśvedevas" (*viśvān devān āvāhayiṣye*) should be employed.
Paiṭhīnasi states the specific prayer for the invocation, the inquiry, and the response when the gods and ancestors are together:

"Having requested permission with the words, 'I shall invoke the gods and the ancestors,' and having said, 'May they be gracious (saumyāḥ),' one requests permission with the words, 'I shall perform the offering in the fire' (*agnau kariṣyāmi*).
Based on this corresponding prayer, "May they be gracious," it is inferred that the reply of the twice-born should likewise be, "May they be gracious."
And so it is stated in the Śaunaka-sūtra:

"Then he should request permission, saying, 'I shall invoke the gods and the ancestors,' and then he should perform the invocation. Having been granted permission with the words, 'May they be gentle,' he should first invoke the gods.
[He should do so] having been permitted by the twice-born—this is the ellipsis."
In the *Pippalāda-sūtra* as well:

"Having requested permission with the words, 'I shall invoke the gods and the ancestors,' one should perform the invocation. When [the officiant] has said, 'May they be auspicious,' one should first invoke the gods.
And Yama states that this question must be made by the sacrificer with barley in his hand.
Then Yavahasta, having informed the gods regarding the invocation,
should perform the invocation with the permission [of the elder], using the verse beginning "viśvedevāsaḥ."

The meaning is that, having addressed the gods, one should respectfully inquire of the twice-born who are officiating at the Vaiśvadeva rite in the manner prescribed. Here, by the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) that "for the gods, there are *darbha* grasses with barley," it should be understood that the hand is joined with *darbha* grass and barley. The purpose of the hand being so equipped is to serve as the instrument for their invocation (*āvāhana*). And this invocation must be performed by moving clockwise (*prādakṣiṇyena*).
For this very reason, it is stated in the *Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa*: "One should invoke the gods with barley; [one should invoke] the ancestors counter-clockwise (*apasavya*) with sesame seeds."

By the instrumental case in the word *yavaiḥ* ("with barley"), the barley's status as the instrument for the invocation (*āvāhana*) is stated; this occurs by way of the scattering (*vikiraṇa*), which is a subsidiary part of the invocation to be described later. By the term *apasavyam*, since the rule of non-pradakṣiṇa (counter-clockwise) is prescribed for the ancestors (*pitṛs*), it is indicated that for the deities (*devās*) one should proceed with *pradakṣiṇa* (clockwise). Although it might appear here that the questioning should be performed while facing eastward—seated opposite the twice-born (*dvija*) of the Vaiśvadeva rite—in order to prevent the destruction [of the rite], to maintain the conduct of the learned (*śiṣṭas*), and to accomplish the task consisting of the supreme address in a straightforward manner, nevertheless, that practice must be set aside due to the force of the injunction to face northward (*udaṅmukha*).
For it is said in the Kūrma Purāṇa:
"Then, with the permission of the Brāhmaṇas, one should invoke the gods facing north, according to the rule, with the Ṛgvedic verse beginning 'viśvedevāsaḥ'."

For here, the connection of facing north is understood to be with the ritual of invocation (āvāhana) along with its constituent parts; therefore, the question must also be made while facing north. And this [question] should be directed either toward one person at the head of the Vaiśvadeva row or toward all those who partake in that row.
Thus concludes the rules for the invocation, the questioning, and the granting of permission. Now follow the ritual items, beginning with the mantras.
In that regard, the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa* states:
"Having offered the sacred threads (*pavitraka*) to them and having obtained their permission,
the wise twice-born man should perform the invocation (*āvāhana*) of the gods with mantras."

"Having given the *pavitrakas*," meaning those placed in the *arghya* vessels, "into the hands of the twice-born"—this is the ellipsis. And this should be understood as being according to the opinion of those for whom the invocation (*āvāhana*) occurs after placing the *arghya* vessels in front of the twice-born. "With the mantra" means with a sacred verse.
In response to the question "With which mantra?", Yājñavalkya says:
"One should invoke, having received permission, with the *ṛc* beginning 'viśve devāsaḥ'."

"Scattering with barley grains" (*yavair anvavakīrya*) refers to the invocation (*āvāhana*), which is the sending forth and bringing of the deity from its own abode to the place of the ritual; this verse is the manifestation of that act. "Scattering with barley grains" means that, having released the thumb of the Brāhmaṇa’s hand, one scatters clockwise on the ground before the twice-born the *kuśa* grass and barley grains held in one's own hand. However, some, reciting the invocation mantra, perform the scattering of barley grains upon the very body of the Brāhmaṇa as part of the mode of worship. And so says Bhartṛyajña:
"O King, with this mantra, 'O Viśvedevas, come hither,' their invocation should be performed using unbroken rice grains (akṣatas), ending at the head.
This means starting from the right foot up to the head; the procedure for that will be explained [later].
Kātyāyana says: "Having invoked with the verse, 'O Viśvedevas, come hither,' having scattered [the offerings], and having murmured, 'O Viśvedevas, hear this'."

"O Viśvedevas, come; hear this invocation; sit down upon this sacrificial grass (*barhis*). Having performed the invitation (*āvāhana*) with this verse, one should thereafter mutter the following *ṛc* with palms joined in reverence: "O Viśvedevas, hear this my invocation—you who are in the intermediate space, you who are in the highest heaven, you whose tongue is Agni, or you who are worthy of sacrifice—sit upon this sacrificial grass and rejoice. In the two Purāṇas, the *Pādma* and the *Mātsya*, the scattering of barley with mantras is prescribed immediately after the muttering of this mantra.
Having invoked [the deity] with these two verses beginning with "viśvedevāsaḥ," one should scatter barley grains [with the mantra]:
"You are barley, the king of grains; you belong to Varuṇa and are mixed with honey.
You are the cleanser of all sins, a purifier praised by the seers."

Here, because of the dual number in the word *ābhyām* ("by these two"), it is understood that a pair of *ṛc*-verses is specified as the means for the invocation (*āvāhana*). Immediately following that is the scattering of barley (*yava-vikiraṇa*). Furthermore, by way of manifesting the barley during that scattering, the mantra beginning with "You are barley" (*yavo 'si*) is also prescribed.
However, according to Yama, clockwise circumambulation (*prādakṣiṇya*) and a different mantra are prescribed for the scattering:
having recited "O Viśvedevas, listen! (*viśvedevāḥ śṛṇuta*), one should then take up the unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*).
One should scatter [the grains] clockwise while reciting the mantra beginning with "oṣadhayaḥ."
In this regard, by way of a representative example, the mantra is shown as follows: "O King, the plants spoke together with Soma the king: 'Whomever a Brāhmaṇa serves, him, O King, you shall protect.
Furthermore, in the *Brahma Purāṇa*, silence and the mantras for the invocation (*āvāhana*) are prescribed:
"Then, remaining silent, one should mutter the mantra: 'O Viśvedevas, come hither!'"
And one should recite the second mantra: "O Viśvedevas, listen!"
One should recite the third mantra, which is ancient and increases merit:
"May the highly fortunate Viśvedevas of great power come;
may those who are appointed to this śrāddha be attentive."

Regarding this, the third mantra mentioned here is to be understood as intended for one who is ignorant of the specific names of the origin of the Viśvedevas. Accordingly, after describing the visualization of the origin of the Viśvedevas or the recitation of their names, it is stated in the *Bhaviṣyatpurāṇa*: "A wise man, not knowing [the names], should recite [the mantra] once at the beginning of all Śrāddhas dedicated to the gods, in the presence of Brahmins."
“May the highly fortunate ones come,” and so forth, as before. “Not knowing” should be explained as not knowing the origin of the Vaiśvadeva offering or their specific names. And thus says Śaṅkha:
“Those twice-born who do not know the name and likewise the origin [of the deities]...”
They would go to this world, having approached the Brāhmaṇas.

"May the highly fortunate ones come," and so forth. By this, it is understood that those who know their origin and their specific names should perform the invocation while recollecting their origin and employing those specific names. Their origin has been shown in the section on deities as being "born from Dharma in Viśvā, the daughter of Dakṣa. And the employment of the names is as follows: having uttered "those known as Purūravas and Ārdrava," one must recite the mantra beginning with "O Viśvedevas, come hither. In the *Mānava-Śrāddhakalpa*, after saying "I shall invoke the Viśvedevas," and being permitted by the Brahmins, [one recites] "O Viśvedevas, increasers of Truth... O Viśvedevas, you who are never-failing... and so on.

One should scatter barley grains. These two mantras are written here: "May the Viśvedevas, who increase the cosmic order (*ṛta*) and hear our invocation according to the seasons, enjoy the oblation; O lords of food, come! and "May the Viśvedevas, who are never-failing, possessed of creative power (*māyā*), and free from malice, enjoy the sacrifice. In this rite for the Viśvedevas (*vaiśvadevika*), although there is only one [deity], the invocation (*āvāhana*) is not repeated for each individual Brāhmaṇa. This is because the presence (*saṃnidhāna*) of the deity is possible through a single invocation even when presiding over multiple Brāhmaṇas. However, after the invocation, since the presence of the deity resides in each individual Brāhmaṇa, the deity also undergoes a conditional differentiation (*aupādhiko bheda*) according to the distinction between the Brāhmaṇas. Therefore, whatever subsidiary act (*saṃnipatyopakāraka*)—such as the spreading of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa-prathana*)—is performed after the invocation for the purpose of propitiating the deity, all of that must be repeated for each Brāhmaṇa. For in the case of a subsidiary act, the accomplishment of the purpose is not achieved in another Brāhmaṇa without such repetition. As for the silent recitation (*japa*) of mantras such as "O Viśvedevas, listen," although it is performed after the invocation, it is a remote auxiliary (*ārādupakāraka*); thus, being performed only once, it is capable of generating the benefit for all, and so it is not repeated.

Thus are the ritual items, beginning with the mantras. This is the invocation. Now follow the seating, the reclining, and the water for the feet, the guest-offering, and the water for sipping, intended for the deities.
In the Mahābhārata: "The wise man, having mentally designated the seat of kusha grass already offered to the summoned Viśvedevas, should bow down and cause them to sit."
Addressing them, "O illustrious ones, please sit upon these seats," he should then have them settle down, saying, "Please sit comfortably."
In this context, "lying down" refers to a momentary, unblinking rest for the sake of repose of one exhausted by traversing a long journey;
the application [of the term] here is as follows.

Wearing the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), facing east, and bending his right knee, he should seat them with the mantra: "Oṃ, O highly fortunate Viśvedevas named Purūravas and Ārdrava, please be seated on this seat," having visualized them as being present due to the invocation previously performed—possessing two arms with hands equipped with arrows and bows, their limbs adorned with beautiful necklaces, armlets, crowns, bracelets, earrings, and other ornaments, wearing costly lower garments, decorated with fragrant flowers from excellent trees, anointed with various perfumes and unguents, and whose pride surpasses that of Kandarpa (the God of Love) while mocking the excellence of refined gold. Then, he should settle them with the mantra: "Oṃ, O Viśvedevas named Purūravas and Ārdrava, rest here in comfort."

[1229] However, some maintain that the application of these two mantras is based on the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the text: "Sit down upon this sacrificial grass (*barhis*); rejoice. But the offerings of water for the feet (*pādya*) and so forth are mentioned after the invocation (*āvāhana*) in the *Śrāddhakalpa* composed by Kauśika and accepted by Śaunaka and the Atharvaṇas. Now, wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*yajñopavītī*), one should consecrate a vessel of water with the *Sāvitrī* and pour it into the hands of the Brahmins, saying: "Water for the feet, water for honor (*arghya*), and water for sipping (*ācamanīya*) for the Viśvedevas. A vessel filled with water is called an "udapātra. The filling with water should be performed with the mantra beginning with "śanno devīḥ. Thus, it is stated in the *Pippalādātharvaṇasūtra*: "Having consecrated a full vessel of water with the *Sāvitrī* using the mantra 'śanno devīḥ,' one should pour it into the hand of the twice-born, saying: 'Water for the feet, water for honor, and water for sipping for the Viśvedevas. The *Sāvitrī* is the verse addressed to the deity Savitṛ, beginning with "tatsaviturvareṇyam. The mantra cited by its opening words, "śanno devīḥ," is written out here: "May the divine waters be auspicious for our aid; may they be for our drinking; may they flow toward us for our well-being and prosperity."
Now follows the detailed description of the *arghya*.

*Arghya* is the offering of excellent substances before those worthy of honor for the purpose of showing respect. Regarding this, the procedure for the *vaiśvadeva-arghya*, distinguished by specific materials, is described in the *Vārāha Purāṇa*:
"Having offered *kuśa* grass for the seat and having filled the *arghya* vessel according to the rule..."
One who knows the ritual procedure should offer the *arghya* to the gods with barley-water.

"Having filled the *arghya*": having collected the materials for the *arghya* in the vessel. Regarding this, Yājñavalkya and others state that the filling of the *arghya* vessel occurs after the invocation (*āvāhana*); however, Vaijavāpa and others state it occurs prior to the invocation. It is also stated previously in the Viṣṇupurāṇa:
"Having given *kuśa* grass for the seat (*viṣṭara*), one should fill the *arghya* according to the rule."
The wise one, having received their permission, should perform the invocation of the deities;
and knowing the ritual procedure, he should offer the *arghya* to the deities with barley and water.
Also in the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa:
"Having offered *kuśa* grass for the purpose of seats and having fully prepared the *arghya* offerings according to the rule,
with purifiers (*pavitra*) in hand, and having given them [the materials] and obtained their permission,"
The wise twice-born man should perform the invocation of the deities with mantras;
thereafter, he should indeed offer the arghya water for the Vaiśvadeva rite using barley and water.

It will be stated here that the purifiers (pavitra) are to be placed upon the arghya vessel. Having given those purifiers into the hands of the brahmins and having obtained their permission for the invocation (āvāhana), one should perform the invocation; this is the meaning.
Thus concludes the procedure for the offering of the arghya, characterized by its specific materials. Now follows the consecration of the vessels and other implements.
In that regard, the purification of the vessel is first stated in the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*:
"One should indeed purify for the sake of the *arghya* offering vessels made of gold, silver, lotus, or gems; or else an auspicious leaf-cup and the like."

"Golden" means made of gold; "silver" means originating from silver. And that [silver] is to be employed only in rites for the ancestors (*pitrya*), because its prohibition is seen in the case of rites for the gods (*daiva*). Thus, concerning silver, the *Matsyapurāṇa* states:
"Since it originated from the eye of Śiva, therefore it is dear to the ancestors."
That which is inauspicious should be avoided with effort in rites dedicated to the gods.

“Born from Śiva’s eye” means originating from the tears of Rudra; for the *Taittirīya* Śruti states: "That tear which was shed became silver and gold. Precisely because it originates from tears, it is inauspicious. For this very reason, Vaijavāpa declares that silver is preeminent only in rites pertaining to the ancestors (*pitrya*): "Silver vessels are recommended for ancestral rites, while golden ones are for those pertaining to the gods (*daivika*)."
Or alternatively, copper vessels may be used for the rite of the arghya offering in the ceremonies for the gods and the ancestors.
Here, in the latter half [of the verse] as well, the word "praśastāni" (praiseworthy) is to be supplied.

‘Ambhoja’ means made of copper, because in the science of alchemy (*rasaśāstra*) it is well known that the word ‘kamala’ denotes copper. ‘Maṇipātrāṇi’ are vessels fashioned from gems such as rubies (*māṇikya*), emeralds (*marakata*), and crystal (*sphaṭika*). ‘Patrapuṭāḥ’ are vessels made from *palāśa* leaves. ‘Yajñiya’ means made from sacrificial wood; the sacrificial trees include the *palāśa*, *aśvattha*, *udumbara*, *vikaṅkata*, *kāśmarya*, *bilva*, *khadira*, *śamī*, and so forth. By the word ‘etcetera’ (*ādi*), other vessels mentioned in the section on vessels are also included. ‘Saṃskaroti’ means he should purify (*saṃskuryāt*). Although this is expressed in the present tense, it is understood as an injunction regarding something not otherwise established, just as in the case of the rule “one offers in the *agnihotra*. ‘For the sake of the *argha*’ means for the purpose of preparing the *arghya*. Here, although the essential form of the *arghya* can indeed be produced even with unpurified vessels, nevertheless, one cannot produce it in its distinguished form using unpurified ones; therefore, purification must be performed for that purpose. And that purification consists of wiping, placing, sprinkling, and inserting a *pavitra* (strainer). Once the vessel has been placed, it should be filled with water and other substances.
Regarding this, Prajāpati said: "A wise man should fill with water for the *arghya* offering a sacrificial vessel made of gold, silver, iron, copper, or likewise of gemstone, or even a wooden cup."

The singular number in the phrase "made of gold" (*sauvarṇam*) and so forth is not intended to be restrictive (*avivakṣita*). This is because we observe in other Smṛti texts cited below that there may be multiple vessels, and that the rule for filling applies to each individual vessel. Furthermore, even when there are multiple vessels, the singular number is used to indicate that the filling must be performed separately for each one. Regarding this filling of the vessels, Yājñavalkya—preceded by the injunction for the procedure of filling accompanied by the duality of two vessels, stating that it should be done after placing two *darbha*-strainers (*darbhapavitra*) within the vessels—says:
[1232] "Then, having scattered barley grains, [one should pour water] into the vessel containing the strainer."
Having poured milk with the verse "śanno devīr" and likewise barley grains with the verse "yavo 'si," he should proceed.

The phrase "having scattered barley" (*yavair anvakīrya*) has already been explained as serving to establish the procedure for the invocation (*āvāhana*). Alternatively, this has been explained by Śambhu as follows: when a vessel containing a *pavitra* grass-ring is to be prepared for the sake of the *arghya* offering to the Viśvedevas, one should pour water into it with the verse "The divine waters for our aid" (*śaṃ no devīr abhiṣṭaye*), and then scatter barley grains with the mantra "Thou art barley" (*yavo 'si*).

On this point, some say: "Since the deities to be honored are one, the *arghya* offerings are also one; therefore, it is logical that there should be only one vessel for that *arghya*. Thus, the locative singular 'in the vessel' (*bhājane*) is appropriate, not the dual of another case-ending. This is incorrect. Even when the deity is one, if there is a plurality of Brahmins who serve as its substrates, then because the deity is superimposed upon each substrate, a distinction arises based on those limiting conditions (*upādhi*); consequently, a distinction of vessels is indeed logical.

But if that were so, then the two vessels for the *arghya* offering would apply only to the case of two Brahmins; however, when there is an increase in the number of Brahmins, an increase in those vessels would also necessarily follow.

This would indeed be the case if it were asserted that the distinction between deities, conditioned by their respective substrates, is itself an independent cause for the distinction between vessels. But that is not what is being said here. Rather, [the deity-distinction] is dependent, acting as a support for the authoritative evidence (*pramāṇa*) that establishes the distinction between vessels qualified by specific numbers, by means of refuting the logic consisting in the identity of the deity which would otherwise result in the identity of the vessel. And that [dependent factor] remains established in a manner that does not contradict what is to be supported [by the evidence]. Therefore, whether there is the position of two Brahmins or even the position of more than that number of twice-born, there is only a duality of vessels because of the dual ending in the phrase "on two vessels provided with *pavitra*-strainers."
And the duality of the vessels is clearly stated in the *Padma* and *Matsya* Purāṇas:
"Having worshipped the Viśvedevas with barley and flowers, beginning with the offering of seats,
one should fill the pair of vessels while placing *darbha* grass purifiers upon them."
One should offer water with the mantra "śaṃ no devī" and likewise barley with the mantra "yavo 'si."

This being the case, even when there is only one Brāhmaṇa, there must indeed be two *arghya* vessels. Nor should it be argued that this is not so because of the absence of the principle of auxiliary support (*anugrāhaka-nyāya*), for a scriptural injunction has no requirement for such auxiliary support. Nor can there be a single vessel based on custom (*ācāra*), since the Smṛti is more authoritative than custom. Furthermore, the statement of Pracetas, "He should pour the *arghya* water for each individual Brāhmaṇa," does not imply that the number of vessels corresponds to the number of Brāhmaṇas; for that text fulfills its purpose merely by enjoining the pouring of *arghya* water for each Brāhmaṇa. As for the reading "he should pour it into the vessel" (*pātre vinikṣipet*), it finds its application in the context of the rite for the gods (*daiva*) involving two Brāhmaṇas, and in the rite for the ancestors (*pitrya*) involving three Brāhmaṇas.

The Mānavas and Maitrāyaṇīyas, however, prescribe even a single vessel. [Pāraskara says: "One should prepare three vessels: two for the Vaiśvadeva and one for each of the other two," or "one for both.

This rule regarding a single vessel is to be explained as applying to the case of a single Brahmin, and also to the case of multiple Brahmins when multiple vessels cannot be obtained. Regarding this, Pāraskara states the mantra for the preparation of the *pavitra* and the placing of the *pavitra* upon the *arghya* vessel.
Having prepared the strainer with the mantra "pavitre sthaḥ" and placed it in the vessel,
he should pour water into it with the mantra "śaṃ no," and then add barley for the rite for the ancestors, or sesame seeds.
The meaning is: "therefore," that is, immediately after the Vaiśvadeva rite, when the ancestral (paitra) rite is about to be performed. Pracetās also says:
"The wise man should prepare the two strainers (*pavitra*) with the mantra *pavitre sthaḥ*."
Having placed those [flowers] in the arghya vessels, one should pour water with the mantra "śaṃ no devī".

The two mantras indicated by the pratīka "pavitre" are established according to different Vedic branches and are shown in their entirety in the section on *darbha* grass. Here, the nominal stem *pavitra* refers to a tuft of *darbha* grass cut according to specific rules; consequently, the dual number applied to it denotes only the duality inherent in those two tufts. Therefore, although the mantra "pavitre sthaḥ," joined with the dual, is primarily applicable to the two *pavitra* tufts used in the *vaiśvadeva* rite—and not to the three used in the *pitrya* rite—it must nevertheless be employed even when making three, because Kātyāyana has prescribed this application there as well: "He cuts two *kuśa* blades that are equal, unscattered, and with tips containing the inner core, using other *kuśa* blades, saying 'pavitre sthaḥ'; or he may use three. This application is also seen in the *Vājasaneyibrāhmaṇa*: "Then he makes the *pavitra*; having said 'pavitre stho vaiṣṇavyau,' then there may also be three. When this mantra is used for three *pavitra* tufts, it should be employed without any modification (*ūha*) of the plural number, because Kātyāyana prohibits the modification of mantras used in the archetype (*prakṛti*), stating that such modification does not apply to archetypal mantras. However, in the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite, since only one *pavitra* is obtained through extension (*atideśa*), this mantra should be used with the singular number modified accordingly. Regarding the plural "in the vessels" (*pātreṣu*), it is not based on a plurality of various types of vessels like gold ones being optionally chosen; rather, these two *pavitra* tufts are to be placed separately in each vessel. Thus it is stated in the *Caturviṃśatimata*.
Having placed two sticks each into the vessels of the gods, one should pour water [into them]. In the *Kūrmapurāṇa*:
