"Having taken two purifiers (pavitra) and having washed this vessel again..."
Having sprinkled water with the mantra "śanno devīḥ," he likewise [sprinkles] barley grains with the mantra "yavo 'si."
When this [grain] has been thrown into the vessel, it is washed and cleansed with water; the mantra for the pouring of water, *śanno devīḥ*, has already been shown previously.

In the *Mānava-Maitrāyaṇīya-Sūtra*, another mantra is also stated: "Pouring out water, [one says] *samaṃ nyāyanti*. [The verse reads: "Flowing together, others come together; the rivers fill themselves equally. The pure waters have surrounded him, the shining one, the protector of the waters (*apām napāt*). Regarding the scattering of barley, which is performed in one manner as a subsidiary part following the invocation, it is said: "*yavo 'si*" (you are barley).

Gobhila states the same thing with a different reading: [1235] "In sacrificial cups made of wood suitable for sacrifice, with strainers placed inside each one, he pours water into each one with the verse *śanno devīḥ*. Into each one he scatters barley with the formula: *yavo 'si somadevatyo gosavo devanirmitaḥ | pratnamadbhiḥ pṛktaḥ svāhayā viśvān devān prīṇāhi naḥ svāhā*. Since the pouring of water and other substances into each individual vessel is already established by the fact that the vessels are distinct, it is understood that this injunction is intended to ensure the repetition of the mantra for every single vessel.
In the *Nāgarakhaṇḍa*, however, a different mantra beginning with "yavo ’si" is shown.

One should pour [water] into the arghya vessel with the mantra "śanno devīḥ. Then, one should scatter unbroken rice grains (*akṣatān*) there with the mantra "yavo ’si, yavayāsmad... (You are barley; keep [evil] away from us).

‘Akṣatān’ means barley grains. ‘Tatra’ refers to the vessel into which the arghya water has been poured. One should pour them in with this mantra: “Thou art barley; drive away our hatred; drive away the enemy. Following the pouring of the barley, the pouring of scents and flowers is prescribed in the *Saura Purāṇa*:
“Having poured water into the vessel along with the pavitra-grass, [reciting] ‘śanno devī’...”
One should likewise cast in barley with the mantra "yavān yavo 'si" and also fragrant flowers.
The application of these two mantras, *gandhadvārām* and *śrīś ca te*, for the offering of perfumes and flowers is shown in the *Caturviṃśatimata*:
"Having placed two purifiers each upon the vessels of the deities, one should pour milk [into them];
[one should offer] water with the mantra *śaṃ no devīḥ* and barley grains with the mantra *yavo ’si*."
With the mantra "Śrīśca te" one offers flowers, and with "Gandhadvārā" one offers sandalwood paste;
thus a person should worship the vessels of the deities with flowers, incense, and other offerings.

Here, by the word "etcetera," the lamp is also included. Immediately after the offering of perfumes and so forth, fanning is mentioned in the *Mānava-Maitrāyaṇīya-Sūtra*: "Having fanned [the fire] with *sumanas* flowers and having scattered barley grains..."

The meaning is as follows: immediately after pouring water, one should cast barley grains there with the mantra beginning "yavo 'si," place *sumanas* flowers with the mantra "śrīś ca te," perform the purification (*utpavana*) as in the case of the *prokṣaṇī* water, and then offer the *arghya* according to the method to be described. Subsequently, these *arghya* vessels are to be consecrated with the *Sāvitrī* mantra, because of the statement in the *Padma* and *Matsya Purāṇas*: "Having consecrated the water-vessel with the *Sāvitrī*.
One should offer water with the mantra "śanno devīḥ" and barley grains with the mantra "yavo 'si."
Having honored them with perfumes and flowers, one should place [the offerings] toward the Vaiśvadeva fire.

"Facing the Vaiśvadeva," that is, in front of the Brāhmaṇas invited for the Vaiśvadeva rite, one "should place," meaning one should set down, the *arghya* vessel. Regarding this placement, Jātūkarṇya says it should be preceded by the question, "May there be the perfection of the *arghya* vessel," followed by the formula, "Svāhā-arghyā. Then, having caused the best of the twice-born to recite the prayer for the perfection of the *arghya* vessel, one should place the *arghya* vessel before them with the words, "Svāhā-arghyā. *Svāhārghyā iti vinyaset* || 1.254 || Then, having caused the best of the twice-born to recite the prayer for the perfection of the *arghya* vessel, one should place the *arghya* vessel before them with the words, "Svāhā-arghyā. (Jātūkarṇya) *tato 'rghyapātrasaṃpattiṃ vācayitvā dvijottamān | tadagre cārghyapātraṃ tu svāhārghyā iti vinyaset ||* Then, having caused the best of the twice-born to recite the prayer for the perfection of the *arghya* vessel, one should place the *arghya* vessel before them with the words, "Svāhā-arghyā. (Jātūkarṇya) *tato 'rghyapātrasaṃpattiṃ vācayitvā dvijottamān | tadagre cārghyapātraṃ tu svāhārghyā iti vinyaset ||* Then, having caused the best of the twice-born to recite the prayer for the perfection of the *arghya* vessel, one should place the *arghya* vessel before them with the words, "Svāhā-arghyā. (Jātūkarṇya) *tato 'rghyapātrasaṃpattiṃ vācayitvā dvijottamān | tadagre cārghyapātraṃ tu svāhārghyā iti vinyaset ||* Then, having caused the best of the twice-born to recite the prayer for the perfection of the *arghya* vessel, one should place the *arghya* vessel before them with the words, "Svāhā-arghyā. (Jātūkarṇya) *tato 'rghyapātrasaṃpattiṃ vācayitvā dvijottamān | tadagre cārghyapātraṃ tu svāhārghyā iti vinyaset ||* Then, having caused the best of the twice-born to recite the prayer for the perfection of the *arghya* vessel, one should place the *arghya* vessel before them with the words, "Svāhā-arghyā. The meaning of this is as follows:

with palms joined in reverence, one should ask the gods and the Brahmins, "May there be the attainment of the vessels for the divine *arghya* offerings. When the Brahmins have replied, "Oṃ, may there be the attainment of the vessels for the divine *arghya* offerings," one should lift up each vessel individually together with the spread *darbha* grass and place them before the Brahmins of the Vaiśvadeva rite using the formula, "Svāhā, [this is] the *arghya*. Immediately thereafter, the pouring of water from those vessels into the hands of the twice-born of the Vaiśvadeva rite must be performed. Regarding that, Pracetas states that it should be accompanied by a mantra.
Having scattered barley with the mantra "yavo 'si," and having worshipped it well with perfumes and flowers,
one should pour the *arghya* water into their hands with the mantra "yā divyā."

Having scattered [the *darbha* grass] and placed it into the *arghya* vessel, the performer of the *śrāddha* should pour the *arghya* water—contained within that purifier (*pavitra*) and well-honored with perfumes, flowers, and so forth—into the hands of the twice-born (brāhmaṇas) while reciting this mantra: “May those divine waters which were produced from the milk, those which are in the intermediate space, and those which are on earth; O golden-colored ones, may those waters worthy of sacrifice be auspicious and favorable to us. In this regard, if there are two brāhmaṇas for the Vaiśvadeva rite and two *arghya* vessels, then according to the principle that "it should be equal," the first *arghya* should be given with the first vessel into the hand of the first brāhmaṇa, and the second *arghya* with the second vessel into the hand of the second. If, however, there are four brāhmaṇas, then having placed the purifier (*pavitra*) from the first *arghya* into the hand of the first twice-born and having poured a small amount of the *arghya* water from there into his hand, one should take that purifier and place it in the hand of the second brāhmaṇa, and pour the remaining water from that vessel into his hand. In this manner, having placed the purifier from the second *arghya* vessel into the hand of the third brāhmaṇa, one should perform the fourth [pouring] with that vessel as before. Thus, when there are eight [brāhmaṇas] for the Vaiśvadeva, the *arghya* water contained in the two vessels should be distributed equally and poured [into their hands]. When, however, there is only one *arghya* vessel and many brāhmaṇas, then the *arghya* water contained in that vessel should be poured separately and in small amounts into the hand of each of them. And for each pouring, the mantra is to be repeated.

On this point, some say: since the manifestation of the substances contained in the arghya vessel has already been accomplished by the single utterance [of the mantra], there is no purpose for manifesting them again; therefore, the mantra should be employed only once.

That is not so; for since a single portion of the substance to be given into the hand of a Brāhmaṇa is consecrated by a single act of reciting the mantra, it is logical that the mantra should be repeated for the sake of consecrating other portions. Furthermore, its repetition occurs for each individual substance if the mantra is intended for the act of pouring (*prakṣepa*). However, if it is a mantra for subsequent consecration (*anumantraṇa*), the application is performed only once; this is to be understood from the principle that will be stated in the section on the *arghya* offering for the ancestors (*pitrya*). Moreover, this mantra is employed for this very purpose in the *Yājñavalkyasmṛti*, the *Saura-purāṇa*, and the *Kūrma-purāṇa*. In the *Mānava-maitrāyaṇīya-sūtra*, however, before the pouring of the *arghya* water, the two *pavitra* strainers situated in the *arghya* vessel are placed into the hand of the Brāhmaṇa, and a different mantra—a sentence containing a vocative—is prescribed for the giving of the *arghya*: "Having placed [the strainers] in his hand who holds the *pavitra* in his hand, and having said, 'O Viśvedevas, this is your *arghya*—[those waters] which are golden-colored, pure, purifying... "Those waters which are golden-colored, pure, and purifying; those which Kaśyapa begot well-born; those which Indra [and] Agni, being of various forms, held as their embryo—may those waters be most auspicious and easily invoked for us. Furthermore, the pouring of the *arghya* into the hand of the twice-born must be performed after honoring the Brāhmaṇa. For this very reason, after describing the worship of the *arghya* vessel with perfumes and flowers, the *Padma-purāṇa* and *Matsya-purāṇa* state: "Having honored him with perfumes and flowers... and so forth.
"Having adorned [the deity] with perfumes and flowers, one should offer the *arghya* with the mantra beginning 'yā divyā'.
Regarding this worship, Gārgya states that it follows immediately after the offering of the *pavitra* placed in the *arghya* vessel, and describes its specific procedure:
"Having placed the *pavitra* in [the deity's] hand and having performed the worship starting from the feet..."
One should pour the *arghya* into their hands with the mantra beginning "yā divyā."

Regarding the statement, "Having placed the *pavitra* in the hand here, one should pour the *arghya* into the hands," since there is a contradiction between the singular and plural numbers found in the opening and the conclusion, and because the opening is not yet subject to contradiction, it is proper to interpret the conclusion in accordance with it; thus, the plural number is not intended to be significant (*avivakṣita*). "From the foot" (*pādataḥ*) means from the feet up to the head. And so says Pracetas:
"The worship of the gods with flowers is performed from the feet up to the head."

As for the tradition of worship (*pūjā-saṃpradāya*), the offering of flowers is performed in this sequence: first on the right foot, then on the left foot, on the right knee, on the left knee, on the right hand, on the left hand, on the right shoulder, on the left shoulder, and finally on the head. Furthermore, the offering of the water of honor (*arghya*) should be performed by uttering the *arghya* formula at the end of the mantra. And because of such statements as "In the rite for the Viśvedevas, Purūravas and Ārdrava are indeed to be proclaimed," one should employ the names beginning with Purūravas joined with either the vocative or the dative case, according to the optional rules stated in the section on case endings.
And regarding the application of the dative case, there is an indicative mark seen in the *Brahma Purāṇa*:
"Having offered the *arghya* with *kuśa* grass, perfumes, barley, and flowers,
saying 'To the Viśvedevas,' the Boar then questioned them."

Regarding the statement, "I shall invoke the ancestors," and the formula, "This is for you: water for the feet and the *arghya* offering," the phrase "this is for you" (*idaṃ vaḥ*) should also be employed.
Furthermore, Gārgya has stated that the word *svāhā* should be used here;
likewise, at the end of the mantra, the address to the ancestors should be "Svadhā."
And one should utter "svāhā" when performing the oblation-rite for the gods.

"At the end of the mantra" means as a constituent part of the sentence being recited at the conclusion of the mantra. Here, the word *homa* (oblation) applies even to the *arghya* offering, because it consists of the nature of relinquishment and casting [into the fire]. As stated in the *Nāgarakhaṇḍa*:
"Having offered sandalwood, perfumes, flowers, and incense in due order..."
With hands holding the purifiers (pavitra), one should, being composed,
offer the arghya water with the mantra "yā divyā," accompanied by the utterance of svāhā.

At the end of the word *svāhā*, the word *namaḥ* should also be employed, according to the Vedic revelation (*śruti*) stating, "Obeisance to the gods" (*namo devānām*). And all this pertaining to the Vaiśvadeva rite should be performed while facing north.
Thus it is said in the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa:
"One should face north for the gods, but face south for the ancestors."
One should offer the seat, the water for honoring (arghya), and all other items exactly according to the prescribed rule.
Thus concludes the detailed exposition on the arghya offering.

Herein is described the ritual application of water for the feet (*pādya*) and other offerings, as established by this textual arrangement and supported by the practice of the learned. Having cleansed vessels made of gold or any other suitable material with ash, earth, and so forth, and having rinsed them with pure, faultless water, the performer—wearing the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), having placed his right knee on the ground, and standing near the twice-born invited for the *vaiśvadeva* rite—should spread upon the sprinkled ground *darbha* grass according to the characteristics mentioned in the section on *darbhas*: with tips pointing eastward and ends either toward the east or toward the north. Upon these, he should place two vessels face down, sprinkle them, and then turn them face up; or he may set them down already face up. Immediately thereafter, in each vessel, he should place two straight blades of *kuśa* grass called *pavitra*, with their tips pointing either east or north. Then, using the *devatīrtha* (the part of the hand sacred to the deities), he should pour pure water while reciting, "May the goddesses... (*śaṃ no devīḥ*). Finally, he should cast *yava* grains into them while reciting the previously mentioned mantra, "Thou art barley" (*yavo ’si*).
"I invoke here Śrī, the goddess who has fragrance as her door, who is invincible, ever-nourishing, bestowing abundance, and the sovereign of all beings. Thus it is said.

Having placed the fragrant substance (*gandha*) with the mantra, "May Śrī and Lakṣmī be your two wives; day and night your two sides; the constellations your form; the Aśvins your open mouth; may you grant us the desired boon, O Unmada, may you intoxicate the whole world," he should place the flowers. Then, having consecrated that vessel with incense and lamps, purified it, and empowered it with the *Sāvitrī* mantra, he should face the Brāhmaṇas with palms joined and say, "May there be the perfection of the vessels. When the Brāhmaṇas have replied, "May there be the perfection of the vessels," he should lift up each vessel individually along with the spread *darbha* grass and the *pavitra* strainers. Having placed them in the area in front of the Vaiśvadeva twice-born with the formula for offering the *arghya*, "Svāhā, the *arghya*s," he should place the pair of *pavitra* strainers from the vessel into the hands of the twice-born, either pointing eastward or northward. Having honored the twice-born in the manner prescribed, he should lift the vessel with both hands (or with the right hand alone), meditate upon the Viśvedevas as before, recite the mantra beginning with "The divine waters... (*yā divyāḥ*), and employ the formula: "O Viśvedevas known as Purūravas and Ārdrava, this is your *pādya*; Svāhā! Namaḥ! He should then pour the water contained in that vessel into the hand of each twice-born person using the vessel tilted toward the *devatīrtha*. In the same way, he should offer the *arghya* using the formula "This is your *arghya*" or "This *arghya* is for you. Likewise, he should give the *ācamanīya* (water for sipping) using the formula "This is your *ācamanīya*."
Thus [are described] the rites of seating, reclining, water for the feet (pādya), the respectful offering (arghya), and water for sipping (ācamanīya).
Now follows the offering of fragrance and the other [substances];
therein first is the procedure.
In the *Kūrmapurāṇa*: "One should offer perfumes, garlands, incense, and so forth, according to one's ability.
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the lamp is also included.
And so it is stated in the Viṣṇupurāṇa:
"Having offered fragrant incense and lamps to them according to the prescribed rule,
one should arrange everything for the ancestors with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (apasavya)."

"To them" means to all the gods (*viśvebhyo devebhyaḥ*). And this offering of fragrance and so forth should be performed after the offering of the *arghya* water. Thus it is stated in the *Vārāha Purāṇa*:
"Having offered the *arghya* to the gods with barley-water according to the rule, the knower of the ritual..."
And having offered fragrant incense and lamps to them according to the prescribed rite.
Also in the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*:
"Then, having offered the *arghya* with barley and water for the Vaiśvadeva rite,
and having properly presented perfume, garlands, incense, and a lamp."
Yājñavalkya, however, has stated that the offering of perfumes and so forth must be preceded by water:
"Having offered water, one should offer perfume, garlands, incense, and a lamp."

In this context, Gautama has stated that all gifts prescribed by injunctions—such as "the giving of alms, and likewise in the case of righteous gifts, one gives preceded by water" (GDh 5.18–19)—must be preceded by water. Therefore, in the instruction for the purpose of establishing that the gift of perfumes and other items about to be performed must be preceded by water, the verb *dadāti* (he gives) should be understood as meaning "merely pouring down. Consequently, even though the word *datvā* ("having given") is used in the sense of mere pouring down, it should be taken as having a transformed meaning when it is applied elliptically (*anuṣajyamāna*) after water has been poured into the hand of the twice-born without a formal gift-formula, and its form has been modified. Furthermore, another usage of *datvā* should be considered. Thus, with reference to the Viśvedevas, the paste of fragrant substances such as sandalwood and saffron intended for anointing should be offered into the hand of the Brāhmaṇa according to the formula that will be shown. Moreover, the offering of perfumes and so forth should be performed in the hand of the twice-born who serves as the locus of the deity, specifically with the deity in mind; it is not a gift to the Brāhmaṇa as a recipient, as has already been explained at length. After the perfumes, water should be given, and then the clarified butter (*ājya*) prepared from jasmine and other flowers should be offered. This is an illustration for the vessels prescribed for use along with the flowers. Then, after giving water again, the offering of incense produced from prescribed substances such as *guggulu* should be performed. "Together with a lamp" means accompanied by the offering of a lamp; this too should be performed preceded by water. Immediately after this, the offering of clothing (*ācchādana*) should be performed. For this very reason, Śaunaka says:
"At this time" refers to the offering of perfumes, garlands, incense, lamps, and clothing.

"At this time" means that, following the sequence immediately after the offering of the *arghya*, the giving of items beginning with perfumes and ending with clothing should be performed. "Clothing" (*ācchādana*) refers to a garment.
This is also stated in the *Saura Purāṇa*:
One should offer perfumes, garlands, incense, and garments according to one’s ability.
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*, however, the giving of ornaments is mentioned after the gift of clothing.
Then, having offered [the gifts] to the Brahmins, the self-restrained donor should next present water for the feet and the respectful offering (*argha*) in due order.
With perfumes, flowers, incense, garments, and ornaments,
one who is faithful and composed should worship the Brahmins according to one's ability.
First, one should honor the Brahmins seated for the Vaiśvadeva rite;
thereafter, one should honor those seated for the ancestral (Pitrya) purpose.
The discrimination between permitted and prohibited perfumes, flowers, and so forth, has already been established in the technical definitions (*paribhāṣā*).
Thus ends the rule for the offering of perfumes and other items.
Now follows the procedure for the offering of perfumes and other items.
In that regard, the *Brahmapurāṇa* states that the perfumes offered should be used for anointing the Brahmins:
"One should give white sandalwood, camphor, and saffron, as well as other auspicious substances, for the purpose of anointing, along with whatever else is dear to the ancestors."
The performer of the śrāddha should apply ointment to the twice-born, or they themselves may do so.
Regarding this, Vyāsa states the specific rule for the mantra:
"With a pavitra in hand, one should worship them with perfumes, [reciting] 'gandhadvārā'."

Having offered scents into the hands of the Brāhmaṇas with the mantra "Gandhadvārā," the performer of the Śrāddha, having removed the *pavitra* grass from his hands, should worship the Brāhmaṇas with those scents; the meaning is that he should smear them on their limbs, such as the forehead, neck, chest, belly, and armpits. This rite of removing the *pavitra* applies only to the performer of the Śrāddha while he is performing the smearing, and not to the twice-born who are smearing their own limbs with the scents held in their hands. For this very reason, Vṛddha-Śātātapa has stated the fault specifically regarding the performer of the Śrāddha when he performs the smearing while still holding the *pavitra* in his hand.
"But he who, holding the *pavitra* in his hand, anoints the twice-born, that *śrāddha* becomes for the *rākṣasas*; the ancestors depart disappointed. Thus [it is said].
"Anointing" (*samālambhana*) means smearing with fragrant substances.

Regarding this, someone says: "In the passage 'having placed the *pavitra* in the hand,' there is a prohibition against wearing a *pavitra* with a knot; however, this does not apply even to one without a knot, because by the statement of Vyāsa, 'with hands possessing *pavitra*s,' various types of *pavitra*s are prescribed, and not a state devoid of *pavitra*s.

This is incorrect, as it arises from mere imagination. Furthermore, what he himself said—that even Brāhmaṇas, while applying ointment to their limbs, might employ a *pavitra* with a knot—should also be disregarded due to its lack of authoritative basis.
Regarding the performer of the *śrāddha* who applies perfumes to the bodies of the Brahmins, another rule is stated in the *Devalasmṛti* and the *Bhaviṣyatpurāṇa*:

"In rites for the gods (*daiva*) and for the ancestors (*pitrya*), one must never remove the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) from the shoulders of the Brahmins, for the sake of accomplishing the worship with perfumes and other offerings."

The meaning is that for the sake of accomplishing the application of perfumes and other unguents, the *anulepaka* (the applicator of ointments) should not remove the sacrificial thread (*yajñopavīta*) of the Brahmins. Śātātapa also says:
"He who, having formed three marks on his hips, smears himself with perfumes..."
In the sacrifice to the ancestors, there may be a deficiency when the ancestors depart disappointed.

The *citram* is the gateway for the entry of Rākṣasas and others who destroy the Śrāddha rite; the *tripuṣkaram* is the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*). Therefore, for the sake of ease in applying ointments, one should not remove the sacred thread from the shoulder and place it at the waist. This is also an indicative mark for the removal of the upper garment (*uttarīya*), for by removing that, one would be dressed in only a single cloth (*ekavastra*). And that is prohibited: "One who wears a garment slipped from the left shoulder should be known as wearing a single cloth; he should be avoided in rites for the gods (*daiva*) and the ancestors (*pitrya*)."
Likewise:
"One should never perform any rite prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti while wearing only a single garment, nor on an island, nor in the intermediate space, nor ever while impure."

Śaṅkha has stated that a fault occurs if the sacrificial thread (*yajñopavīta*) of a Brāhmaṇa who is performing the *śrāddha*, or even of one who is merely applying ointment, is removed by anyone at all:
"If one applies body-ointment having placed the sacrificial thread around the waist,
or if one eats while wearing only a single garment, the ancestors depart disappointed."
In this regard, a circular or crescent-shaped *tilaka* should not be made.
And so says Kratu:
"Having seen a sectarian mark (*puṇḍraka*) on the forehead, and likewise a garland on the shoulder..."
The ancestors depart in despair upon seeing the husband of a Vṛṣalī.

In this case, since the prohibition to be inferred by the force of the scriptural mention of a fault must be formulated without contradicting the established injunction for the vertical *ūrddhvapuṇḍra*, it is logical that it refers specifically to circular and other types of *puṇḍras*. Because the Smṛti texts record a fault in wearing a garland on the shoulder, it is understood that wearing one on the head is permitted. Regarding even the head, Vṛddha-Manu specifies a particular location for the garland being worn: "Having set aside the state of the sacred thread (*upavīta*), one should apply ointments;
when so enjoined, one may wear a garland on the head, with the exception of the topknot (*śikhā*)."
The term *niyuktaḥ* refers to a Brahmin who has been invited to a *śrāddha*.

Viṣṇu, however, states the mantra for the offering of flowers as "puṣpavatīḥ" and "puṣpam. The word "dadyāt" (should give), heard in the preceding sentence, is supplied here by ellipsis (*anuṣajyate*). The mantra is applied by means of its middle portion, "puṣpavatīḥ. That mantra is: "Oṃ, O plants, rejoice in him; you who possess flowers and bear good fruit. This embryo of yours, born in due season, has taken his seat in the ancient dwelling-place."

Vyāsa states the mantra for the offering of incense: "Having said 'dhūpaṃ ca dhūr asi' (and the incense, [saying] 'you are the burden'). The meaning is that one should offer the incense after reciting this *yajus*: "dhūr asi dhūrva dhūrvataṃ dhūrvantaṃ yo ’smān dhūrvati taṃ dhūrvayaṃ dhūrvāma" (You are the burden; crush him who crushes, crush him who is crushing; he who crushes us, crush him; let us crush him). Although this *yajus* is employed for the touching of the yoke-pole of the cart used in the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices—due to its inherent capacity to denote a yoke-pole (*dhūs*)—nevertheless, because it is specifically enjoined by this statement for the offering of incense as well, it must, through some figurative application (*vṛtti*), illuminate the subject at hand, just as in the case of the injunction "he worships the *gārhapatya* fire."
In the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa, however, another mantra is stated:
"This divine incense, the essence of the forest tree, rich in fragrance and most enchanting, fit to be smelled by all the gods—may it be accepted. Thus.
Incense should be offered with the wind from a fan or the like, not with the wind from the hand.
For this very reason, Śātātapa says:
"Those best of the twice-born who inhale incense struck by the wind of the hand..."
That śrāddha becomes in vain; therefore, one should avoid him.
Having thus offered incense, one should offer a lamp ignited with the aforementioned oil, wick, and so forth.
Regarding this, Vyāsa said:
"Having declared, 'This is light,' one should offer the lamp with a concentrated mind."

Immediately after this, having given a garment and a sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), ornaments, an umbrella, a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*), and so forth, should be given according to one's capacity. Regarding the gift of sandals, however, there is only the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) at that time; the actual procurement must be performed only at the time of the Brahmin’s departure. Concerning the gift of a garment, Śātātapa states the mantra and the substitute in its absence:
"One should give a cloth with the mantra 'yuvā suvāsāḥ'; and in its absence, a sacred thread."

"The youth, well-attired and girt about, has come; he becomes even more excellent as he is born. The wise poets, seeking the gods with their minds, raise him up"—with this mantra, one should give a garment;
this is the meaning. Atri, however, mentions another mantra:
"One should devoutly give garments with the mantra: 'You two [give] garments'."

The mantras, however, are: "May you two clothe yourselves in fat garments; between you two are seamless, continuous streams. You have cast down all falsehoods; O Mitra and Varuṇa, you are united with Truth.

And regarding these mantras for the offering of fragrance and so forth, their common applicability to both rites for the gods (*daiva*) and the ancestors (*pitrya*) is stated in the *Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa*:
"One should carefully offer fragrance with this mantra beginning 'gandhadvārām'."
And [he offers] flowers with the verse "puṣpavatī," and incense with the verse "dhūr asi."

"In rites for the gods and the ancestors, one should give a lamp with the mantra 'This is a light' and garments according to one's ability with the mantra 'May you two [accept] the garments. Furthermore,
in this context, after the recitation of the mantra, the formulas for the offering of perfumes and other items should be uttered.
And these are shown in the *Brahma Purāṇa*:
"O Viśvedevas, this water for the feet (*pādya*), the respectful offering (*arghya*), flowers, incense, and ointment, as well as this light of a lamp, is now presented to you."
Likewise:
having said, "This is your fragrance," he should offer a most beautiful scent;
and having said, "This is your flower," he should present the flowers.
Having said, "This is your incense," one should then burn it before them;
having said, "This is your lamp," one should present a beautiful lamp.
"That which is a fine garment not clinging to the body shall be a pair of auspicious cloths;
having said, 'This garment is for you,' one should present either a pair or a triad.
Having said, 'This garland is for you,' one should give a most beautiful garland. Thus it is said.

‘Mālya’ refers to strung flowers. Regarding the acceptance of the perfumes and other items being offered here, Devala has stated that they are to be addressed as ‘Brāhmaṇas’: “This is light; O Light, O Excellent Light! and so forth.
"This is the light," thus should the performer of the śrāddha announce the light.

The meaning is that those Brahmins should also say, "Excellent light" (*sujyotis*). By the word "also" (*ca*), it is indicated that at the time of acceptance, they should say, "One's own seat," "fragrant scent," "fine flowers," "excellent incense," "bright lamp," and "fine covering.
For here, indeed, is the ritual procedure for the offering of scents and the other articles.

The performer, having assumed the *upavīta* position as previously described and being thus endowed with the divine (*daiva*) ritual duty, shall silently pour water into the hand of the first seated Brāhmaṇa of the Vaiśvadeva group. Taking a paste of fragrant sandalwood and other substances in his own hand, he should recite the mantra beginning with *gandhadārāṃ*, declare, "O Viśvedevas known as Purūravas and Ārdrava, this is your fragrance," and offer it into the hand of the Brāhmaṇa into whom water was poured. Having offered it in the same manner to the hands of the second and subsequent Brāhmaṇas in sequence, he should again give water into the hand of the first Brāhmaṇa, take excellent flowers and so forth, recite the previously mentioned verse containing the word "flower" (*puṣpavatī*), declare, "O Viśvedevas known as Purūravas and Ārdrava, this is your flower," and place it in his hand; he should then give it to the second Brāhmaṇa's hand in the same sequence. Likewise, having again given water, he should offer incense produced by the burning of substances such as *guggulu*, reciting the mantra *dhūr asi*, declare, "O Viśvedevas known as Purūravas and Ārdrava, this is your incense," and cause the Brāhmaṇas to smell it by means of a fan or similar device. Similarly, having given water in their hands, he should declare, "This is your light" or "This is the illumination of your lamp," and offer the lamp along with its circle of light. Likewise, having given water, he should recite the mantra beginning with *yuvā suvāsāḥ*, declare, "O Viśvedevas known as Purūravas and Ārdrava, this is your garment," and offer a garment to each one individually. Immediately thereafter, having offered the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), he should offer ornaments such as rings according to his ability, as well as items such as an umbrella. Following that, with palms joined in reverence (*añjali*), the performer should say to the Brāhmaṇas of the Vaiśvadeva group, "May the worship of the Viśvedevas be complete. When they have replied, "May the worship be complete," the performer should say, "May you all say, 'May the fulfillment of the resolve (*saṃkalpa*) be attained'. The Brāhmaṇas should reply, "May the fulfillment of the resolve be attained. This has been authenticated by the author of the *Smṛticandrikā* as being stated by the author of the *Saṃgraha*. Thereafter, being extremely humble, he should recite the verse of prayer found in the *Bhaviṣyatpurāṇa*.
O best of the twice-born, may this śrāddha— though deficient in mantras, deficient in ritual acts, and deficient in materials—
attain completeness through your grace.

"May it reach completion" means "may it be performed according to the rules. Having recited the verse beginning with *yasya smṛtyā* (Śiva Purāṇa 4.38.1), one should recite the verse beginning with *devatābhyaḥ pitṛbhyaś ca* (Viṣṇu Smṛti 68.42) three times. Immediately thereafter, one should perform the sipping of water (*ācamana*) as described in the section on the sipping of water that is an ancillary part of the *śrāddha*.
This concludes the procedure for the offering of scents and other items.
Thus ends the offering of scents and so forth; this is the time for the worship of the *vaiśvadeva* deities.
Since the Goddess of Fortune was adorned by Hemādri with such humility,
this section is therefore called the *Kāṇḍa* on the worship of ancestors and Brahmins.
Now, regarding the offering of the *darbha* seat for the ancestors and so forth:

it has already been stated previously that, in accordance with the injunctions of Yājñavalkya and others, this section of ritual items beginning with the offering of the *darbha* seat and ending with the covering [of the seats] should be commenced only after the completion of the section of Vaiśvadevika items. Furthermore, the *Padma* and *Matsya Purāṇas* state that this must be preceded by obtaining permission from the twice-born (Brahmins) of the Vaiśvadeva rite:
"Having honored them, and being dismissed by those two, one should commence the sacrifice to the ancestors (*pitṛyajña*)."

Having honored the two Brāhmaṇas representing the Viśvedevas with perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, and garments, and having worshipped them, the performer—being "dismissed," that is, permitted by them—should perform the "Pitṛyajña," which consists of the worship of the ancestors through the offering of seats of Darbha grass and other rites. From the mention of this permission here, it follows that a formal inquiry is also implied. Therefore, after the performer has made the request, "By your permission, I shall perform the worship of the ancestors," and the two Brāhmaṇas representing the Viśvedevas have replied, "Do so," he, being thus authorized by them, should begin the worship of the ancestors—the father, grandfather, and so forth—among the Brāhmaṇas representing the Pitṛs.
In that regard, the specific questions to be addressed to the Brahmins representing the ancestors and others are stated in the *Brahma Purāṇa*:
"Having first worshipped the Viśvedevas prior to the invocation and other rites, [one should ask]:
'O Brahmin, I invite you for the Vasus,' and then, 'I invite you for the Rudras.'"
"O Brahmin, I feed you for the sake of the suns," he should say to them.

"First" (*pūrvam*) means initially. Having worshipped the Viśvedevas with the entire sequence of rites beginning from the invocation (*āvāhana*) up to the covering (*ācchādana*), he should inquire of the Brahmins representing the ancestors and others. In that regard, he should ask the Brahmin representing the father: "O Brahmin, shall I feed you for the sake of the Vasus? He should ask the Brahmin representing the grandfather: "Shall I feed you for the sake of the Rudras? And he should ask the Brahmin representing the great-grandfather: "Om, O Brahmin, shall I feed you for the sake of the Ādityas? Having asked thus, he should sequentially inquire of the Brahmins representing the maternal grandfather and others in the same manner. In all cases, the response "Om, let him feed [me]" (*bhojaya*) should be understood as corresponding to each question. Here, because the question concerns the feeding along with its constituent parts (*sāṅga-bhojana*), it is indeed appropriate that this [inquiry] occurs prior to the offering of the *darbha* seats.
In that regard, there is the offering of a seat of *darbha* grass.

Here, the statements concerning the offering of seats for the ancestors (*pitrya*), as declared in the *Smṛtis*, *Purāṇas*, and *Vikalpasūtras*, have already been presented at the very occasion of explaining those seats, because they cannot be separated from the statements regarding the offering of seats for the gods (*daivika*).
Bṛhatpati states the necessity of proclaiming the lineage (*gotra*), relationship (*saṃbandha*), and name (*nāman*):
At the offering of the seat, the arghya water, the funeral cake (piṇḍa), and the ritual washing,
one should recite the relationship, the name, and the lineage as is appropriate.

The mention of "seating" (*āsana*) and so forth is intended as an illustration for the ancestral rites (*pitryakarma*), such as the invocation (*āvāhana*). Words such as "father" (*pitṛ*) and "mother" (*mātṛ*) denote the relationship. "Lineage" (*gotra*) refers to well-known names such as Kāśyapa or Kauṇḍinya. "Name" (*nāma*) refers to conventional designations such as Caitra or Maitra. "As is fitting" (*yathārham*) means according to what is appropriate. Regarding the ancestors and elders, the optional use of either the genitive or dative case with the plural number is established in the section on case endings (*vibhaktiprakaraṇa*). The meditation upon and the recitation of the names of the ancestors in their forms as the Vasus and other deities have been established in the section on deities. By the rule beginning with "he should cause the other knee to touch the ground for the ancestors," the worship is said to be performed while bending the left knee.
Regarding the *prācīnāvīta* (the sacred thread worn over the right shoulder), the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa* states:
"One should arrange everything for the ancestors with the thread over the right shoulder (*apasavya*).
This is also stated in the *Vārāha* and *Viṣṇu Purāṇas*.
"One should arrange everything for the ancestors with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (apasavya),
but facing north for the gods";
by such statements, the practice of facing south is prescribed.
Devala also said:
"The twice-born, as prescribed, should remain self-restrained and face the north;
the patron, however, should worship according to the rules while facing the south."

The ritual procedure (*prayogapaddhati*) is now described: Facing south, wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*), and having placed the left knee upon the ground, one should take three *kuśa* blades with the middle joint bent and doubled, hold the hand of the twice-born (*dvija*) with the left hand, and, after pouring water into his hand, say: "Oṃ, this is the seat for our ancestors, of such-and-such lineage (*gotra*), named so-and-so, together with their wives, who are of the nature of the Vasus. Having spoken thus, one should pour water into the hands of each of the Brahmins seated in the place of the ancestors and, placing those *kuśa* blades on the left side of the seat—such as a woolen blanket—with the *pitṛ-tīrtha*, one should again give water into the hand of the twice-born. In the same manner, substituting "grandfathers" (*pitāmahānām*) for "ancestors" (*pitṝṇām*) and "of the nature of the Rudras" (*rudrarūpāṇām*) for "of the nature of the Vasus," one should offer the seat to the grandfathers using that very same formula. Likewise, in place of the ancestors' names, one should utter the name of each maternal grandfather and so forth in the genitive plural; and in their respective places, one should sequentially apply the individual names of the Vasus and others. Once these three formulas have been completed and the Brahmins have been seated in the places of each maternal grandfather and so forth, one should offer the seat to each with the respective formula. Here, immediately after the throwing of the *kuśa* blades, the Brahmin should respond: "Oṃ, let there be a good seat" (*svāsanam astu*). In this context, the phrase "together with their wives" (*sapatnīkānām*) should be used only if the wife of the father or other ancestor has died, and not otherwise. Regarding the use of the singular instead of the genitive plural, some authorities employ the singular; however, it should be understood that this is determined by local custom (*yathācāra*). Thus it is said.
Thus ends the offering of the ancestral seats.
Now follows the third invitation.

That too is prescribed for the ancestors by the very same words stated in the section on inviting the gods; and that is exactly like the first invitation, as established by the statement of Āpastamba: "As the first, so the second and the third" (ĀpDhS 2.17.15).

"Having touched the right knee, you too are invited here"—from this statement in the *Matsyapurāṇa*, it is understood that [the invitation] is preceded by the touching of the knee. Therefore, while touching the right knee of the Brahmin representing the ancestors, one should invite each of the Brahmins seated in the positions of the father and others, in due order, individually with the previously shown formula: "May a moment be granted for the Śrāddha of our father, of such-and-such gotra and such-and-such name, together with his wife, who is of the nature of Vasu," and so forth.
This is the third invitation.
Now, the invocation (*āvāhana*). Regarding that, the question concerning the procedure for invocation and the granting of permission is stated in the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*:
"Having offered double-folded *darbha* grass and having obtained permission from them..."
A wise person should perform the invocation of the ancestors preceded by the recitation of mantras.

Having given double-folded *darbha* grass for the purpose of a seat (*viṣṭara*) according to the prescribed method, having offered water into the hand of the twice-born, and having performed the third invitation as ordained in another *Smṛti*, and having obtained permission for the invocation of the ancestors whose forms will be described, one should perform the invocation of the Pitṛs—namely the father, grandfather, and so forth—who have departed to the other world, preceded by the mantra to be mentioned hereafter.
As stated in the *Vārāha-purāṇa* and the *Viṣṇu-purāṇa*:
"Then, having obtained permission and having given the *darbha* grass divided in two..."
A wise person should perform the invocation of the ancestors preceded by the recitation of mantras.

The syntactical connection here is as follows: having placed *darbha* grasses there, and immediately thereafter having obtained permission, one should perform the invocation (*āvāhana*). In this context, Gobhila and Kātyāyana—presenting the sequence of ritual items (*padārthānusamaya*) and thereby establishing the ancestral invocation after the invocation for the Viśvedevas—state the nature of the inquiry and the permission:
"Then he asks, 'I shall invoke the ancestors,' and being permitted with the words, 'Invoke them.
The sacrificer asks; he is permitted by the twice-born.
This very point has been clearly stated in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*, preceded by a slight modification of the question and answer:
"Having himself said with a concentrated mind, 'I invoke the ancestors,' he is then addressed by the twice-born, 'Invoke them!'— then, with his mind fixed on that."

In this context, even though the invocation (*āvāhana*) belongs to the future, it is designated by a word ending in a suffix prescribed for the present tense on account of its proximity to the present (*vartamānasāmīpye vartamānavat*). "Himself" (*svayam*) refers to the agent; "with mind fixed on that" (*tanmanāḥ*) means having a one-pointed mind directed toward the rite about to be performed. This [term] is to be understood as being connected with the verb *āvāhayet* (he should invoke), which will be mentioned later.

In the *Brahmapurāṇa*, however, the question regarding the re-invocation (*pratyāvāhana*) is shown to be employed at a slightly different interval of time, following the completion of the worship of the Viśvedevas.
Having offered the guest-water (arghya) with kusha grass, fragrant scents, barley, and flowers,
the Boar then addressed them with the verse beginning "To all the Viśvedevas."
"I shall invoke the ancestors, both those who are divine and those who are human. Being thus addressed by the others, "Invoke them," he, being pure, performed the invocation.

In this context, the sentence ending with "to all the gods" (viśvebhyo devebhyaḥ) is connected to the worship of the Viśvedevas; thereafter, the passage beginning with "them" (tān) is connected to the question and answer regarding the invocation of the ancestors, where "them" means the Brahmins representing the ancestors. "Sūkaraḥ" refers to the Sacrificial Boar (Yajñavarāha).

Formerly, while performing a *śrāddha* at Kokāmukha, he was instructed by the other twice-born (*dvija*) guests who were eating the *śrāddha* food, saying, "Invoke [the ancestors]. Thus permitted, he should perform the invocation of the ancestors. By this indication of the text, it is understood that anyone else performing a *śrāddha* should also perform the invocation of the ancestors after addressing the ancestral Brahmins with the question, "I shall invoke the ancestors, both those who are divine and those who are human," and being permitted by them with the prescribed response. The connection of the words "those who are divine," etc., is as follows: "I shall invoke those ancestors who are divine in the form of the Vasus, Rudras, and Ādityas, and those who are human in the form of the sacrificer’s father and so forth. According to the view of the Purāṇas, it should be understood that the invocation occurs prior to the offering of the *darbha*-seats; for there, having stated the invocation with the words "the pure one should invoke," it subsequently states the offering of the seat with the words "he gave the seat with his left hand. In the *Nigama* as well, it is said that after saying "I shall invoke the ancestors," one should place double-folded *darbha* grass on the seats and others on the feet. In the *Kaṭha-sūtra* also, after seating those worthy of the oblation and saying "I shall invoke the ancestors," the invocation is stated to occur before the offering of the *darbha*-seats, following the seating of the twice-born. Baudhāyana, by saying "I invoke the ancestors" and then "Let a moment be granted to the Viśvedevas," etc., indicates that the invocation takes place prior to the granting of the moment (*kṣaṇa*). Yama, however, has stated that the invocation occurs after the *agnaukaraṇa* (offering into the fire); that will be shown in the context of the *śrāddha* for one who maintains the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*). In the *Vaijavāpa-gṛhya*, it is taught to occur after placing the filled *arghya* vessel; that statement will be shown in this very section. In the *Pādma* and *Mātsya Purāṇas*, however, it is stated to occur after placing the *pavitra* (strainer) from the *arghya* vessel into the hand of the twice-born.
"I shall invoke the ancestors," he said, and they replied, "So be it.
The connection with the subsequent phrase is: "one should invoke them here. And among these alternative views, the arrangement is according to one's own Vedic school (*śākhā*).

Regarding the interrogative formulas shown here, such as "I shall invoke the ancestors (*pitṝn āvāhayiṣye*)," the word *pitṛ* (ancestor) is intended as an elliptical indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for words such as *pitṛ*, *pitāmaha*, and so forth, which denote the relationship with the deceased persons who are the objects of each respective *śrāddha*. This is stated in the *Mānava-Śrāddhakalpa*: "Having said, 'I shall invoke the fathers and grandfathers,' he is authorized by the Brahmins. Furthermore, the employment of the terms *pitṛ* and so forth in this context is also intended as an elliptical indicator for the use of specific names such as Devadatta and others; for it will be shown later in the section on mantras that the *Vaijavāpa-Gṛhya-sūtra* states, "one should invoke [them] by their names. Once the use of the name and the connection to the deity is established, since we observe the constant association (*sāhacarya*) between those two and the connection to the lineage (*gotra*), it is inferred that the proclamation of the lineage, such as Kāśyapa and others, must also be performed.
And so says Ślokagobhila:
"O best of Brahmins, at the invocation, [one should say] 'our fathers, grandfathers, and great-grandfathers of such-and-such gotra, [named] Śarman'. Then it should be so.

When the ritual act consisting of the invocation of the ancestors (*pitr-āvāhana*) is being performed, regarding the employment of the interrogative sentences that constitute its subsidiary parts, the phrase "O [you of] such-and-such *gotra*, our fathers, [named] such-and-such *śarman*," should "become"—that is, it should attain—that state; the meaning is that it should be uttered. All these interrogative sentences of the manner shown above should be uttered preceded by the *praṇava* (the syllable *oṃ*).
Likewise, in the *Maitrāyaṇīya-sūtra*:
"Having uttered the *praṇava*, having addressed the Brahmins with the words 'I shall invoke the ancestors,' one should invoke them, just as in the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña*."
This instruction is for the purpose of attaining qualities such as facing the south.

Furthermore, in the *Brahma Purāṇa*, after establishing the nature of the question and answer, a statement is made by the author while prescribing another directive, stating that the question must be addressed to the ancestral Brahmins: "I shall invoke the ancestors; then he should speak to the remaining Brahmins.
[1257] "I shall invoke the ancestors," he should say to the remaining Brahmins thereafter.
"Having been told by them, 'Invite [the ancestors],' [the sacrificer says], 'May they be attentive.

The meaning is that 'the others,' namely the remaining Brāhmaṇas of the ancestral (pitrya) rite, are those among whom the invitation was made during the Vaiśvadeva rite. Here, after the question and answer regarding the invitation, the sacrificer should say to those Brāhmaṇas, 'May you be attentive. And from this, the response of the twice-born, 'We are attentive,' is understood.

However, in the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*, it is stated that the question should be addressed to the ancestral Brāhmaṇas by the sacrificer wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*) with sesame seeds in his hand."
Then, having placed the sacred thread over the right shoulder and taking sesame seeds while remaining self-controlled,
he should ask the brahmins facing north, "I shall invoke the ancestors."
"Facing north" means facing the direction of the ancestors (*pitrya*).

Here, by the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) stating "for the ancestors, with double-folded sesame seeds," it is understood that one should take sesame seeds together with double-folded *darbha* grass; for the statement from the *Brahmapurāṇa*, "uttering [the names] while holding sesame and *barhis* grass," which pertains to the scattering of sesame as a subsidiary part of the invocation (*āvāhana*), will be shown later. Furthermore, having sesame seeds in hand here is for the purpose of making the sesame seeds an instrument (*sādhana*) for the invocation. Thus it is said in the *Nāgarakhaṇḍa*:
Then, one should invoke the ancestors with sesame seeds while reciting the mantra "uśantas tvā.

By the word "tilaiḥ" (with sesame seeds), ending in the instrumental case, the status of sesame seeds as the instrument for the invocation is established. And this instrumental status is [understood] through the act of scattering them, just as in the case of barley (*yava*).
Pracetas also stated that sesame seeds serve as the instrument and that the movement should not be clockwise.
Having been authorized, one should perform the invocation with sesame seeds, moving in a counter-clockwise direction.

"Counter-clockwise" (*apradakṣiṇa*) is that which is other than clockwise (*pradakṣiṇa*). Clockwise refers to the completion of an action toward a region characterized by the left side of a person facing oneself; for example, starting from the foremost Brahmin in a row of divine guests seated facing east, and ending with the last Brahmin in that row. Counter-clockwise is characterized by the opposite of what has been described; for example, starting from the chief Brahmin in a row of ancestral (*pitrya*) priests seated facing north, and concluding with the final Brahmin seated in that row. Furthermore, this question should be posed while standing.
Likewise, it is stated in the *Vaijavāpa-gṛhya* immediately after placing the vessel filled with *arghya* materials:
"Standing, one should address [the ancestors], saying, 'I shall invoke the ancestors.

Here, "standing" (*tiṣṭhan*) means standing upright. By this, it should be understood that the seeking of permission (*anujñā-grahaṇa*) must also be performed while standing; for, by the phrase "standing, one should address," there is understood a connection between the addressing and its own purpose, which consists in the seeking of permission.
The invitation, the inquiry, and so forth should be performed facing the south. Thus it is stated in the Kūrma Purāṇa:
"Then, having placed the sacred thread over the right shoulder (apasavya), one facing south should perform the invitation for the ancestors."
Whether sitting, standing, or bowing, where no such rule is specified,
that [rite] should be performed while sitting, and not while bowing or standing.

According to this statement from the *Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa*, one should sit down and perform the invocation (*āvāhana*) and subsequent rites after the conclusion of the question and answer. Now, the practical application of the question and answer, as established by this textual context, is described. Wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*), taking sesame seeds equal in measure to a double-folded broken blade of *kuśa* grass in his right hand, facing south, standing upright with palms joined in reverence (*añjali*), he should address the twice-born ancestors and others with the interrogative formula: "I shall invoke the ancestors, both those who are divine and those who are human. Then he should say: "Oṃ, I shall invoke our father, belonging to such-and-such *gotra*, named so-and-so Śarman, together with his wife, in the form of Vasu; Oṃ, I shall invoke our grandfather, belonging to such-and-such *gotra*, named so-and-so Śarman, together with his wife, in the form of Rudra; [Oṃ, I shall invoke our great-grandfather, belonging to such-and-such *gotra*, named so-and-so Śarman, together with his wife, in the form of Āditya]. He may say "I shall invoke," "I invoke," or "I will invoke. The Brahmins should respond with the reply: "Oṃ, invoke! or "Oṃ, do invoke! Then, turning toward the twice-born who represent the maternal grandfather, he says: "I shall invoke the ancestors, both those who are divine and those who are human. Then he should utter the interrogative formula: "Oṃ, I shall invoke our maternal grandfather, belonging to such-and-such *gotra*, named so-and-so Śarman, together with his wife, in the form of Vasu; Oṃ, I shall invoke our maternal great-grandfather (or grandfather on the mother’s side), named so-and-so Śarman, together with his wife, in the form of Rudra; Oṃ, I shall invoke our maternal great-great-grandfather (or great-grandfather on the mother’s side), named so-and-so Śarman, together with his wife, in the form of Āditya. The response of the Brahmin is as before. Immediately thereafter, the sacrificer should again issue the command: "Oṃ, may you all be attentive! and the Brahmins should give the reply: "Oṃ, we are attentive."
Thus end the [sections on] invocation, the inquiry for permission, and the granting of permission. Now follow the ritual items, beginning with the mantras.
Regarding this, Śaṅkha and Likhita state:

Having obtained permission from the Brahmins with the words, "I shall invoke the ancestors," he should cause them to grant permission with the response, "Invoke [them]," by means of the formula, "I shall invoke the ancestors. Then, having caused the Brahmins to grant permission, he should invoke them with this verse: "We place you, who desire [us], within [our hearts].
Thus it is stated in the *Padma* and *Matsya* Purāṇas.
One should invoke the ancestors with the two *ṛg* verses beginning "uśantas tvā āyantu.

The term "ancestors" (*pitṝn*) refers to the father and others, as well as the maternal grandfather and others. These two *ṛg*s, which are situated in the statement of Gobhila, will be shown below. Here, although both *ṛg*s appear to function as mantras for the invocation due to the use of the instrumental case, nevertheless, it should be understood that only the first functions as the instrument [of invocation], while the second is to be known merely as a mantra for subsequent consecration (*anumantraṇa*).
And this has been stated in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*.
Then the wise one should perform the invocation with the verse "uśantas tvā";
having invoked them, and being authorized by them, he should then recite the mantra "āyantu naḥ."

"Then," meaning after the worship of the Vaiśvadeva deities; "authorized by them," meaning authorized by the Brahmins representing the ancestors, he should perform the invocation (*āvāhana*). Having invoked them, he should recite the mantra "āyantu naḥ" (may they come to us); such is the grammatical connection. Here, having invoked the father, grandfather, and great-grandfather, he should recite the mantra "āyantu naḥ" once. The same applies after the invocation of the maternal grandfathers and others.
It is stated in the *Saura Purāṇa* that the invocation must be performed with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*apasavya*):
"Then, having placed the sacred thread over the right shoulder, the twice-born should invoke the ancestors."
"Having invoked [the ancestors] with the verse *uśantas tvā*, and by their permission,
one should recite the verse *āyantu naḥ*.

Here, for the purpose of indicating the locus [of the invocation], the placement of the hand upon the knees of the twice-born and the visualization (*dhyāna*) of the ancestors and others are shown in the *Brahmapurāṇa*.
In the same manner, Varāha, with one hand placed upon his knee, invoked those ancestors preceded by meditation upon them.

Regarding the phrase "with the hand placed upon the knee," the specific detail—that it should be placed with the palm facing upward at the level of each brahmin's knee—must be understood from established custom (*samācāra*). As for the word "with one [hand]," this refers specifically to the right hand; however, because the ritual service for the ancestors (*pitṛs*) is performed in a counter-clockwise direction (*apradakṣiṇa*), one should keep in mind that the left side of the twice-born’s knees is intended.
But if this is so, would it not follow that even the sacrificer’s left hand would become the instrument for the ancestral rites?

True. To dispel this very doubt, Medhātithi—while providing an explanation based on grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) for the verse of Manu stating, "One should pour out water with the hand not turned to the right (*apasavya*), saying 'Be pure'"—described it as: "With the *apasavya* hand, that is, the right hand, one should pour out the water. Furthermore, the mention of "pouring out water" is intended as an illustration for ancestral rites (*pitryakarman*) in general; for Śaunaka, Āśvalāyana, and others, by stating "with the right hand grasped by the left," have demonstrated in various places that the right hand alone is the instrument for performing ancestral rites.
Where an action is prescribed but the specific limb of the agent is not mentioned,
it should be understood that the right hand is the one that brings the ritual acts to completion.
And because this statement from the *Bhaviṣyatpurāṇa* establishes that the right hand alone is the means for accomplishing all ritual actions.

In this context, because the grasping of the knee is observed in the rite for the ancestors (*pitrya*), some believe that it should also be performed in the rite for the gods (*daiva*). That is incorrect; for there is no authoritative basis for applying what is taught in connection with the ancestors to the connection with the gods. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that even the wearing of the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvīta*) and other such acts prescribed in connection with the ancestors would also apply to the connection with the gods. Therefore, it is proper to conclude that the invocation for the gods is to be performed by grasping the hands of the twice-born without the thumb, whereas the invocation for the ancestors must be performed by grasping the knee. Regarding the phrase "preceded by meditation upon them" (*tadanudhyānapūrvakam*): the meaning is that it is preceded by meditation upon those ancestors and others, both in their respective individual human forms and in their forms as the Vasus and other deities.

The *Vaijavāpagrahya* states that the invocation (*āvāhana*) is not to be performed solely preceded by meditation, but may also be performed preceded by the utterance of the names associated with the father and other ancestors:
"With the verse *uśantas tvā*, having invoked the sacrificer’s father, grandfather, and great-grandfather by their names, and having muttered *āyantu naḥ*, he assigns the vessels.

Here, because of the separate mention of "the father," "the grandfather," and so forth, since the invocation must be performed separately for each individual basis (*adhiṣṭhāna*), the mantra used for the performance must also be repeated that many times.
Regarding the invocation (*āvāhana*) in this context, Yama also states that one should recite the lineage names (*gotra*):
"One should, without weariness, first proclaim the father, and likewise the grandfather,
and the great-grandfather of the father, by their names and lineages."

At the conclusion of the mantra "uśantas tvā," one should invoke the ancestors, beginning with the father and including the maternal grandfather, using such formulas as: "Oṃ, O our fathers of such-and-such lineage, named so-and-so, together with your wives, in the form of the Vasus, come here! Immediately following each respective invocation, one should scatter sesame seeds and *kuśa* grass in front of the twice-born who serves as the locus for that ancestor, moving in a counter-clockwise direction (*aprādakṣiṇya*).
This is stated in the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*:
"Having been authorized, one should invoke the ancestors with the verse 'uśantas tvā'."
Having cast the sesame seeds with the sacred thread over the right shoulder, while meditating on the ancestors with a concentrated mind,
he should properly recite the mantra "āyantu naḥ" in its entirety.
"Apasavya" means counter-clockwise; in the phrase "having scattered sesame seeds," it should be understood that one scatters the sesame seeds and *kuśa* grass previously taken up.
And thus, this has been stated together with the mantra in the *Brahmapurāṇa*:
"May those who are in between depart," while uttering [the mantra] over the sesame seeds and *barhis* grass.
The boar, uttering "May they go away from the ancestors and the brahmins," departed.
Those who have departed for that [state] performed protection by means of both the *ṛc* verse and the *apasavya* rite;
having performed the invocation (*āvāhana*), he called out the names and lineages of the ancestors, uttering:
"O ancestors, swift as thought, come hither!"

‘Barhiṣaḥ’ refers to *kuśa* grass. The two mantras beginning with ‘*apeta yantu ye...*’ are well known in the *Kapiñjala-Kaṭha* recension. The two mantras beginning with ‘*apeto yantu asuṃ ya īyuḥ...*’ were shown previously. These two mantras for the invocation, beginning with ‘*etat pitaraḥ...’’, are to be combined with the mantra ‘*uśantas tvā...*’ because the plural form in the upcoming statement of *Pracetas* [1263] intends to include other mantras. This combination is as follows: one mantra is ‘*etat pitaro manojavā āgacchata pitaro javaiḥ ye nikhātā ye paroptā garbhā ye ca pedire*’; the other is characterized by the two words ‘*āgacchata pitaraḥ*’. That is as follows: ‘*sarvāṃs tān agra āvāhayat pitṝn haviṣe attave | āgacchata pitaro manojavasaḥ pitaraḥ śudhaṣvam*’. However, Baudhāyana has shown another mantra for the invocation: ‘*pitṝn āvāhayaty āyāta pitaraḥ saumyā gambhīraiḥ pathibhiḥ pūrvaiḥ | prajām asmabhyaṃ dadato rayiṃ ca dīrghāyuṣṭvaṃ ca śataśāradaṃ ca*’. Those who follow the *Gṛhya-sūtras* of Āśvalāyana and others explain the phrase ‘*kṣiptvāpasavyaṃ ca tilān*’ as meaning that one should scatter sesame seeds non-clockwise (*aprādakṣiṇyena*) upon the limbs of the twice-born. They invoke the ancestors while scattering sesame seeds on the limbs of the twice-born with the mantra ‘*uśantas tvā...*’.
And so it is stated in the *Nāgarakhaṇḍa*:
"Then, with the mantra 'uśantas tvā,' one should invoke the ancestors with sesame seeds;
thereafter, O best of kings, one should recite the mantra 'āyantu naḥ'."

Here, by means of the instrumental case (the third case), it is indicated that the status of being the instrument belongs to both the mantra and the sesame seeds; furthermore, by the use of the word "ca" (and), it is implied that this applies to them as combined together. In the *Mānava-Maitrāyaṇīya-Sūtra*, however, another mantra is also mentioned: "Desiring you, we call upon you; come back to us, O Soma-loving ancestors!"—with these words, one should scatter the sesame seeds. Furthermore: "Come back to us, O Soma-loving ancestors, by deep and ancient paths; having granted us here auspicious wealth, bestow upon us riches consisting of all heroic sons. The author of the *Smṛticandrikā*, however, has presented the mantra "namo vaḥ" (salutations to you)—which is prescribed for worship with flowers—as applicable here; since that lacks a scriptural basis (*nirmūla*), it should be disregarded. Regarding the sequence of parts during the scattering of sesame seeds, it should be understood according to established custom: first on the head, then on the left shoulder, the right shoulder, the left hand, the right hand, the left knee, the right knee, and finally on the right foot.
Kātyāyana says: "Having invoked with the verse *uśantas tvā* and having scattered [sesame seeds], one should mutter *āyantu naḥ*"; the word "having scattered" implies "sesame seeds."
Yājñavalkya says: Having offered double-folded *kuśa* grass and having invoked the ancestors with the verse "uśantas tvā," he should,
being permitted by them, recite thereafter the verse "āyantu naḥ."
"But the purpose served by barley should be performed with sesame seeds.
Having provided double the amount of *kuśa* grass for the sake of a seat, one should scatter sesame seeds;
thus says Pracetas.
Facing the south, one should indeed mutter the *uśantā yantu* mantras.

In this context, by the use of the plural "mantrān," other instrumental mantras (*karaṇamantra*) and consecratory mantras (*anumantraṇamantra*) taught in the *Kalpasūtras*, *Smṛtis*, *Purāṇas*, and *Itihāsas* are also permitted. According to the *Kaṭhasūtra*: "Having said, 'I shall invoke the ancestors,' and having scattered sesame seeds on all sides with the two [verses] beginning 'May the Asuras depart' (*apayantv asurāḥ*), one should invoke them after muttering the two [verses] beginning 'Come here, O ancestors' (*eta pitaraḥ*). The two mantras beginning with "May the Asuras depart" and the two mantras beginning with "Come here, O ancestors" have already been shown previously. The remaining two mantras are now written down: "O ancestors, invoked by the Virāj, come to your portion from the ocean and from the waters; in this sacrifice, may you obtain all desires and enjoy these inexhaustible [offerings]. "I have hidden [the ancestors] behind the mountains and the great earth, and behind the fire in heaven with infinite [spaces]; I have hidden those ancestors who are boundless, behind the seasons, the days and nights together with the twilights, and the half-months."
Viṣṇu says:

"Then, permitted by the Brāhmaṇas, he should invoke the ancestors with the two verses beginning 'May the Asuras depart,' while scattering sesame seeds; having thus performed the dismissal of the Yātudhānas, he should perform the invocation with the verse 'Come, O fathers, all of you; may Agni lead them hither; I have placed a barrier between. [Thus it is stated] in the Viṣṇudharmottara.
"O Agni, bring all those ancestors here with the words 'these, O fathers';
let them come, having thus proclaimed, 'these, O fathers, are yours'."
"O ancestors, this is your portion, the nectar accompanied by *svadhā*, placed in these vessels; may you subsist upon it as long as it lasts. Rejoice in this *svadhā* offered by me," so says Gobhila.

"Desiring you, we set you down; desiring you, we kindle you. Desiring them, bring the desiring ancestors to eat the oblation. "Come here, O Soma-loving ancestors! "Om! May the Soma-loving ancestors, those consumed by fire (*agniṣvātta*), come to us by the paths traveled by the gods, rejoicing with the *svadhā* offering at this sacrifice. May they speak for us; may they protect us. "The *apahatāḥ* [mantra]—thus, having scattered sesame seeds"—this is the mantra "Come here, O ancestors... which is written here: "Come here, O Soma-loving ancestors, by the deep paths traveled by the ancestors; grant us long life and progeny, and attend upon us with abundance. The *apahatāḥ* mantra has been shown previously. And this scattering of sesame seeds is to be performed at the conclusion of the invocation (*āvāhana*).

And likewise, in the *Brahma Purāṇa*, after describing the invocation accompanied by other mantras to be recited, the scattering of sesame seeds within the interior of the house with a mantra is stated immediately thereafter:
"Then, while reciting 'uśantas tvā,' one should invoke the ancestors—
those who are accompanied by Soma, those who sit upon the sacrificial grass (*barhiṣad*), and those who are consumed by fire (*agniṣvātta*)."
May all our ancestors, possessed of nourishment and glory, come to us.
Then, endowed with supreme faith, one should scatter sesame seeds in that house in a counter-clockwise direction while reciting the mantra "āpo hatāḥ."
[1266] In that house where the *śrāddha* is performed; "house" here is an indication for the place of the *śrāddha*. The mantra beginning with "apahatāḥ" has been shown previously.
Now, the manual of procedure (*prayogapaddhati*) is stated.

Immediately after the conclusion of the invitation (*āvāhana*) and the exchange of questions and answers, he should sit down facing south with his left knee bent. Wearing the *prācīnāvīta* (the sacred thread over the right shoulder), he places his own right hand—palm downward and holding the previously taken sesame seeds and *kuśa* grass—upon the left knee of the first Brahmin representing the paternal ancestors. Meditating on his own father in human form, he recites the verse *uśantas tvā*. At the end of that, saying, "Oṃ, fathers of such-and-such gotra, named such-and-such Śarmans, together with your wives, in the form of Vasus, come here," he invokes the father into the first Brahmin who serves as his locus, while pointing at the knee. He then scatters a few sesame seeds and *kuśa* grass on the ground before him in a counter-clockwise direction. In the same manner, he should perform the invocation and scattering for the second and subsequent Brahmins who serve as the loci for those ancestors. Then, placing his hand upon the left knee of the Brahmin representing the first grandfather (*pitāmaha*) as before, he recites *uśantas tvā*. Saying, "Oṃ, grandfathers of such-and-such gotra, named such-and-such Śarmans, together with your wives, in the form of Rudras, come here," he invokes the grandfather into the first Brahmin who serves as his locus, while pointing at the knee. He scatters sesame seeds and *kuśa* grass before him in the same way, and likewise performs the invocation and scattering for the second and subsequent Brahmins who serve as the loci. Next, placing his hand upon the knee of the Brahmin representing the first great-grandfather (*prapitāmaha*) as before, he recites *uśantas tvā*. Saying, "Oṃ, great-grandfathers of such-and-such gotra, named such-and-such Śarmans, together with your wives, in the form of Ādityas, come here," he invokes the great-grandfather into the first Brahmin who serves as his locus, while pointing at the knee. He scatters sesame seeds and *kuśa* grass before him in the same way, and likewise performs the invocation and scattering for the second and subsequent Brahmins who serve as the loci. Having thus invoked the father and the others, he should join his palms in reverence and mutter the mantra *āyantu naḥ* once. Immediately thereafter, at the end of the *uśantas tvā* mantra, he says, "Oṃ, maternal grandfathers of such-and-such gotra, named such-and-such Śarmans, together with your wives, in the form of Vāyu, come here. Having performed the invocation and scattering of sesame seeds for each maternal grandfather into the respective Brahmins who serve as their loci, he repeats the aforementioned mantra and says, "Oṃ, maternal great-grandfathers of such-and-such gotra, or 'our mother's grandfathers,' named such-and-such Śarmans, together with your wives, in the form of Rudras, come here. Having likewise invoked the maternal great-grandfather into their respective loci and scattered the seeds, he repeats the previous mantra and says, "Oṃ, maternal great-great-grandfathers of such-and-such gotra, or 'our mother's great-grandfathers,' named such-and-such Śarmans, together with your wives, in the form of Ādityas, come here. Having likewise invoked the maternal great-great-grandfather into each of their respective loci and scattered the sesame seeds and *kuśa* grass for each, he joins his palms and mutters *āyantu naḥ* and so forth once. One who is capable of incorporating other mantras taught in the *Kalpasūtras*, *Smṛtis*, *Purāṇas*, and *Itihāsas* may, according to his ability, employ such invocation mantras as *somavanto barhiṣadaḥ*, *eta pitaraḥ somyāsaḥ*, *sarvāṃs tān agne*, *āmeyantu*, *antardadhe*, *āyāta pitaraḥ*, *āgacchata pitaraḥ*, and *etad vaḥ pitaraḥ*, as well as the subsequent consecration (*anumantraṇa*) mantras. However, followers of the *Gṛhyasūtras* of Śaunaka and Āśvalāyana, after the invitation and the exchange of questions and answers, should sit near the Brahmins, place the *prācīnāvīta* over their shoulders, and scatter sesame seeds counter-clockwise from head to foot upon the bodies of the twice-born while reciting the verse *uśantas tvā*. Then, having touched the knees of the Brahmins as before, they should perform the invocations into the respective loci using the aforementioned formulas. Joining their palms in reverence before the Brahmins, they should mutter the consecration mantras beginning with *āyantu naḥ* once, according to their ability. Followers of the Kaṭhas, Viṣṇu, and others, however, after the questions and answers, should scatter sesame seeds in the *śrāddha* area while reciting the two verses beginning with *apayantv asurāḥ*. Joining their palms in reverence, they should mutter *etat pitaraḥ*, perform the invocation using the previously mentioned formulas, and then recite the consecration mantras. Finally, all performers of the *śrāddha* should, after the recitation of the consecration mantras, scatter sesame seeds inside the house while reciting the mantra beginning with *apahatā asurā rakṣāṃsi*.
Thus are the ritual items, beginning with the mantras.
This concludes the invocation.
Now follow the rites of seating, reclining, water for the feet, water for the guest-offering, and water for sipping.
Regarding the continuation of the phrase "one should invite" therein, it is stated in the *Pippalātharvaṇasūtra*:
"With the words 'Come, O Fathers,' one should invite the ancestors; with the words 'Seated,' one should cause them to sit."

The syntactical connection is as follows: one should invoke the ancestors with the mantra "Come, O Pitṛs," and cause them to sit down with the mantra beginning "Seated... [The mantra reads: "Come, O Pitṛs, who are worthy of Soma, by the deep paths traveled by the Pitṛs; having partaken [of the offerings], come back again to our house, possessing good offspring and brave sons, while we offer the oblation within. Seated in the lap of the ruddy cows, bestow wealth upon the mortal donor; O Pitṛs, grant that wealth to his sons, and bestow vigor here.
