In the *Śaunaka-sūtra*, however, both the act of seating accompanied by other mantras and the act of reclining accompanied by mantras are prescribed.

With the words "Come hither," he should invoke the ancestors; with the words "Having bent the knees," he should cause them to sit down; with the words "May they lie down," he should cause them to recline.

Here, the two mantras well-known in the *Atharvaveda* and employed with the two phrases "ācyājānu" and "saṃviśantu" are written down: "Having sat down to the south with knees bent, may all these [ancestors] graciously accept this our oblation. O ancestors, do not harm us in any way for whatever offense we, being men, have committed against you. May the ancestors lie down here, making their own place comfortable and extending our lifespan. I am wary of them as they move about; may they live many autumns. Regarding this, Viṣṇu states the following concerning the water for the feet (*pādya*): [1269]

Having offered water for the feet (*pādya*) with fragrant water mixed with *kuśa* grass and sesame seeds while reciting the verses "yās tiṣṭhanti amṛtāvāg" and "yan me mātā," one should likewise present the water of honor (*arghya*).

The meaning of this is as follows: Having placed three-fold pairs of *kuśa*-strainers (*darbhapavitra*) into each of the vessels, such as swords and the like, which have been prepared for as many deities as there are, one should pour water into each with the verse beginning *śaṃ no devīḥ* using the *pitṛtīrtha* (the part of the hand sacred to the ancestors). Then, having cast sesame seeds into each vessel with the mantra: *tilo ’si somadevatyo gosavo devanirmitaḥ | pratnamadbhiḥ pṛktaḥ svadhayā pitṝn lokān prīṇāhi naḥ svadhā namaḥ*, and having cast perfume with the mantra *gandhadvārām*, and having cast flowers with the mantra *śrīś ca te lakṣmīś ca*, one should offer the *pādya* (water for washing the feet) into the hands of the respective Brahmins who serve as the representatives of each ancestor—using the mantras beginning with *yās tiṣṭhanti* and so forth—and likewise offer the *arghya*. In this context, two mantras are prescribed for the *pādya* of each ancestor by means of the two introductory phrases (*pratīka*): *yās tiṣṭhanti* and *amṛtā vāk*. Among the three mantras indicated by the introductory phrase *yan me mātā* and recited in sequence, each one is combined with the two previously mentioned mantras and applied separately to the *pādya* for the ancestors. These mantras are as follows: *yās tiṣṭhanti yā dhāvanti adugdhāḥ pari saṃstuṣīḥ | adbhir viśvasya dhātrībhir antaranyān pitṝn dadhe || amṛtā vāg amṛtā āpo ’gnir vāco ’nṛtaṃ tat trivṛd ekadhāma | tābhir matprattobhiḥ svadhayā madadhvam ihāsmabhyaṃ vasīyostu devāḥ ||* [The second mantra is: *yan me mātā...* [etc., as cited in the source].]
Whatever my mother lusted after, and whatever she practiced in her longing, may my father take that seed; let another man be cast down by these names.
Whatever my grandmother lusted after and whatever she practiced according to her vow—may my grandfather take that seed of mine; let another man cast it down upon this name.
Whatever my great-grandmother lusted after and whatever she practiced in pursuit of [her desire], may my great-grandfather, named Vaṅka, cause another’s seed to fall upon me.

In the *Brahmapurāṇa* as well, after reciting the two mantras beginning with "yās tiṣṭhanti," the specific application (*viniyoga*) of the two mantras beginning with "yan me mātā" is shown for the distribution of the three *arghya* offerings to the father and the others: "The mantra 'yās tiṣṭhanti' refers to those who stand; and 'yan me mātā' indeed belongs to the father.
Likewise, with 'yan me pitāmahī,' he offered the *arghya* to the grandfather."

Saying "To my great-grandfather," Janārdana offered [the oblation] to his great-grandfather from the right side (apasavya), mixed with kusha grass, fragrant scents, sesame seeds, and flowers; he performed the same rite for his maternal grandfathers as well.

The phrase "in the same manner" (*tadvat*) means that just as the water for the feet (*pādya*) and other offerings were given to the father, grandfather, and great-grandfather, so too should the water for the feet and other offerings be given to the maternal grandfather (*mātāmaha*) and the others. By this extension (*atideśa*), since these very same mantras are applied to the water for the feet and other items for the maternal grandfather and the rest, one must perform a modification (*ūha*) of the words "mother" (*mātṛ*) and so forth with the words "maternal grandmother" (*mātāmahī*) and so forth in the three mantras beginning with "yan me mātā," in order to ensure they are contextually appropriate. For example:

*yat me mātāmahī pralulubhe yac cacārānuvrataṃ | tan me reto mātāmaho vṛṅnāmābhir anyo ’vapadyatām ||* (Whatever my maternal grandmother craved and whatever she practiced according to her vows—may my maternal grandfather take that seed; let another fall away by name.)
Whatever my paternal grandmother lusted after, and whatever she practiced without restraint—may Vṛddhapramātāmaha take that seed of mine; let no other man fall upon it.
"Whatever my great paternal grandmother craved and whatever she practiced without devotion—may my great paternal grandfather take that seed of mine; may another [seed] descend through these names.
And in the Viṣṇu statement, by the words "one should likewise offer the arghya," the procedure for the *pādya* (water for the feet) is extended by analogy to the offering of the *arghya*.
For this very reason, in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*, the procedure beginning with the mantra is stated as common to both the *pādya* and *arghya* offerings:
"With kuśa grass and sesame seeds mixed together, along with water and fragrance;
[the two verses] 'Those who stand' and 'The immortal speech'."
"And likewise, one should cause the water for washing the feet (*pādya*) and the respectful offering (*arghya*) to be brought with the mantra 'yan me mātā'.

[1271] Regarding the term *vārā*, it means "with water. In the *Kaṭhasūtra*, however, the water for sipping (*ācamanīya*) is also mentioned after the *arghya*: "With the three mantras beginning with 'yās tiṣṭhanti amṛtā vāk' and 'yan me mātā', one should bring the waters for the foot-washing, the *arghya*, and the sipping."
"Ānayet" means he should cause it to reach the hand of the twice-born.
In the *Śrāddhakalpa* accepted by Śaunaka and the Atharvaṇas, other mantras for the water for the feet (*pādya*) and so forth are also stated:

"He should prepare three vessels of water; having mixed them with perfumes, garlands, and sesame seeds, he should pour them, verse by verse, using the three [verses] beginning with 'udīratām,' into the hands of the Brāhmaṇas which hold the *pavitra* grass, saying: 'This is the water for the feet, the *arghya*, and the water for sipping, for the great-grandfathers, the grandfathers, and the fathers.'"

"Three" refers to the three groups beginning with the father. "Verse by verse" means that, following the order starting from the great-grandfather (*prapitāmaha*), one should pour those waters contained in the water-vessels onto the hands of each Brāhmaṇa respectively, using each single verse beginning with *udīratām*. "In those [vessels] provided with *pavitra*-strainers" means in the vessels containing the water for the feet (*pādya*) and so forth, which are equipped with *pavitra*-strainers whose tips point toward the south. Among these verses, *udīratām* has already been shown; the second and third are now presented: "I have found the Pitṛs who are well-disposed, and I have found the protection and the stride of Viṣṇu. Those who sit upon the sacrificial grass (*barhiṣad*) and partake of the *svadhā*-libation, may they, being most eager to come, come here. "May this homage be today to the Pitṛs—those who were before and those who came after, those who have settled in the earthly realm, or those who are now among the virtuous clans. Regarding the dedication to the deities starting from the great-grandfather down to the father, this applies only to those belonging to that specific *śākhā*, for they perform the entire *śrāddha* in that manner. For others, however, it follows the order of the father and so forth. Thus, in the *Pippalādātharvaṇa-śrāddhakalpa*, after stating that the offering of the water for the feet and so forth is performed with those very same verses in the order of the father and so forth, the ritual attendance (*upasthāna*) is stated with the verses beginning with *ācyā* and *ānvityā*.

Having prepared three water-pots mixed with perfumes, garlands, and sesame seeds, he should pour them out, verse by verse, using the three verses beginning with *udīratām*, into the hands of Brāhmaṇas who hold purifiers (*pavitra*), while pronouncing the names of the father, grandfather, and great-grandfather, bending his knee. The mantra for "bending the knee" has already been shown; the other is written here: *yad vo rudraṃ pitaraḥ somyaṃ ca tena sacadhvaṃ svayaśaso hi bhūtaḥ | tair vāṇaḥ kavayaḥ śṛṇota suvidatrāvidaye hūyamānāḥ ||* "O Fathers, with that which is yours—both the fierce and the Soma-like—be united, for you have become self-glorious. O wise ones, listen to our voices, you who are well-disposed when invoked for the sake of finding."
Now, the ritual application consistent with the conduct of the learned (śiṣṭācāra), as revealed by this continuous discourse, is being set forth.

Facing south, with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*), and having bent the left knee, he should visualize his own father standing before him, who has been summoned and made present through the individual human form and the collective form of the *Vasu* deities. With palms joined in reverence (*prāñjali*), he should recite either one or both of the two mantras—beginning with the *praṇava* (*oṃ*)—alternatively as "sit down" (*āsīnāsaḥ*) or "having bent the knees" (*ācyājānu*). Then, mentally designating the previously prepared seat of darbha grass, he should seat the father at each instance of invocation (*pratyadhiṣṭhāna*) with the formula: "O our fathers of such-and-such lineage (*gotra*), named so-and-so (*amuka-śarman*), together with your wives, in the form of the *Vasus*, please sit here. In the same manner, meditating on the grandfather (*pitāmaha*) in his previously experienced human form and as the deity known as the *Rudras*, and having performed the recitation of the mantras as before, he should designate the previously prepared seat and seat the grandfather at each instance of invocation with: "Oṃ, our grandfathers of such-and-such lineage, named so-and-so, together with your wives, in the form of the *Rudras*, please sit here. Likewise, meditating on the great-grandfather (*prapitāmaha*) in his experienced human form and as the deity known as the *Ādityas*, and having uttered the aforementioned mantras as before, he should designate the seat and seat the great-grandfather at each instance of invocation with: "Oṃ, our great-grandfathers of such-and-such lineage, named so-and-so, together with your wives, in the form of the *Ādityas*, please sit here. Then, the performer, characterized by the aforementioned qualities, meditating on the maternal grandfather (*mātāmaha*) in his human form and as the *Vasu* form, and after the mantra recitation as before, he should designate the seat and seat the maternal grandfather at each instance of invocation with: "Oṃ, our maternal grandfathers of such-and-such lineage, named so-and-so, together with your wives, in the form of the *Vasus*, please sit here. Similarly, meditating on the maternal great-grandfather (*pramātāmaha*) in his own form and as the *Rudra* form, at the end of the mantra he should say: "Oṃ, our maternal great-grandfathers—the grandfathers of our mother—of such-and-such lineage, named so-and-so, together with your wives, in the form of the *Rudras*, please sit here," and seat the maternal great-grandfather at each instance of invocation. In the same way, meditating on the maternal great-great-grandfather (*vṛddhapramātāmaha*) in his human form and as the *Āditya* form, he should state: "Oṃ, our maternal great-great-grandfathers—the great-grandfathers of our mother—of such-and-such lineage, named so-and-so, together with your wives, in the form of the *Ādityas*, please sit here," and seat the maternal great-great-grandfather at each instance of invocation. Then, the performer, endowed with the aforementioned attributes, visualizing his own father standing before him in the two previously mentioned forms, should recite the mantra "May the ancestors sit here" (*saṃviśantv iha pitaraḥ*) and seat the father at each instance of invocation with: "Oṃ, our fathers of such-and-such lineage, named so-and-so, together with your wives, in the form of the *Vasus*, sit here comfortably. In the same way, meditating on the grandfather with the two forms mentioned for seating, he should recite that same mantra "May they sit here" (*saṃviśantv iha*) and seat the grandfather at each instance of invocation with: "Oṃ, our grandfathers of such-and-such lineage, named so-and-so, together with your wives, in the form of the *Rudras*, sit here comfortably. Likewise, meditating on the great-grandfather with his two forms, he should recite "May they sit here" and so forth, and seat the great-grandfather at each instance of invocation with: "Oṃ, our great-grandfathers of such-and-such lineage, named so-and-so, together with your wives, in the form of the *Ādityas*, sit here comfortably. Similarly, meditating on his maternal grandfather with his two forms, he should recite "May the ancestors sit here" (*saṃviśantv iha pitaraḥ*) and seat the maternal grandfather at each instance of invocation with: "Oṃ, our maternal grandfathers of such-and-such lineage, named so-and-so, together with your wives, in the form of the *Vasus*, sit here comfortably. In the same way, meditating on the maternal great-grandfather with his two forms, he should recite "May they sit here" and seat the maternal great-grandfather at each instance of invocation with: "Oṃ, our maternal great-grandfathers—the grandfathers of our mother—of such-and-such lineage, named so-and-so, together with your wives, in the form of the *Rudras*, sit here comfortably. And likewise, meditating on the maternal great-great-grandfather with his two forms, he should recite "May they sit here" and so forth, and seat the maternal great-great-grandfather at each instance of invocation with: "Oṃ, our maternal great-great-grandfathers—the great-grandfathers of our mother—of such-and-such lineage, named so-and-so, together with your wives, in the form of the *Ādityas*, sit here comfortably. Now, remaining endowed with the aforementioned characteristics, on ground that has been well-sprinkled, in vessels made of materials such as rhinoceros horn or silver obtained as available, which are most pure and arranged in a row ending to the right according to the number of ancestors, he should place three-folded *kuśa* blades with their tips pointing south into each vessel. Having poured pure water with the *pitṛtīrtha* (the part of the hand sacred to the ancestors) while reciting "The goddesses... (*śaṃ no devīḥ*), having thrown sesame seeds with the mantra "Thou art sesame" (*tilo 'si*), having placed sandalwood paste with "The door of fragrance" (*gandhadvārām*), and having scattered flowers with "Prosperity and... (*śrīś ca te*), he should then consecrate those vessels with incense and lamps, empower them with the *Sāvitrī*, and taking each vessel in turn, place it before the twice-born (*dvija*) who serves as the locus for the father and others. Having placed the *kuśa* blades from the vessel for the father into the right hand of the first Brahmin representing the father with their tips pointing south, he should take that vessel held in his own hand and recite the three mantras: "Those who stand... (*yās tiṣṭhanti*), "The immortal speech... (*amṛtā vāk*), and "That which my mother... (*yan me mātā*). Then, saying: "Oṃ, our fathers of such-and-such lineage, named so-and-so, together with your wives, in the form of the *Vasus*, this is your water for washing the feet (*pādya*), svadhā, obeisance," he should pour some of the water from the vessel onto the right hand of that Brahmin—which holds the *pavitra* blades—using the *pitṛtīrtha*. Taking the *kuśa* blades from that hand, he should place them in the right hands of the second and subsequent Brahmins who serve as the loci for the other ancestors, repeating the process of pouring water until the end. If there is only one Brahmin, he should pour all the water from the vessel into the hand of that single person. Immediately thereafter, he should place the three *kuśa* blades from the vessel for the grandfather into the right hand of the Brahmin representing the grandfather with their tips pointing south. After reciting the three mantras "Those who stand...", "The immortal speech...", and "That which my grandmother...", he says: "Oṃ, our grandfathers of such-and-such lineage, named so-and-so, together with your wives, in the form of the *Rudras*, this is your water for washing the feet, svadhā, obeisance," and pours the water from that vessel into the hands of the Brahmin representing the grandfather as before. Next, in the same way, after reciting the three mantras "Those who stand...", "The immortal speech...", and "That which my great-grandmother...", he says: "Oṃ, our great-grandfathers of such-and-such
Thus [are described] the rites of seating, reclining, water for the feet (*pādya*), and water for sipping (*ācamanīya*).
Now follows the determination of the *arghya* offering.
Having thus stated the invocation (*āvāhana*), Yājñavalkya declares the procedure for the presentation of the *arghya*.
If the purpose is barley, it should be performed with sesame seeds; one should perform the offering of water for the hands (arghya) and so forth as before.

"Like the previous" means like the *arghya* offerings and so forth belonging to the *vaiśvadeva* rite. By the word "and so forth," the offering of scents, flowers, and other items is included. In this extended application (*atideśa*), one should understand that there is a sublation by stronger injunctions: the sacred thread worn over the left shoulder (*yajñopavīta*) is sublated by the thread worn over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvīta*); facing east is sublated by facing south; circumambulation from left to right (*pradakṣiṇa*) is sublated by circumambulation from right to left (*apradakṣiṇa*); kneeling on the right knee is sublated by placing the left knee on the ground; the two-fold purity of the tuft of hair (*pavitra-śikhā*) is sublated by its three-fold nature; the scattering of barley (*yava*) is sublated by the offering of sesame seeds (*tila*); the *devatīrtha* (the part of the hand between the thumb and forefinger) is sublated by the *pitṛtīrtha* (the base of the little finger); the word *svāhā* is sublated by the utterance *svadhā*; the names such as Purūravas and Ārdrava are sublated by the names of the ancestors; and the wearing of the sacred thread over the right shoulder along with the instruction regarding sesame seeds is taught here in the *Vaijavāpa-gṛhya-sūtra*. Some of these have already been shown previously, while others are presented here together with the instruction for the *prācīnāvīta* and the use of sesame seeds.

Wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītī), he should have the vessels— even those not yet filled— placed behind him upon the darbha grass with their tips pointing forward, along with darbha grass and sesame seeds.
Kātyāyana also states this in the Chāndogya-Pariśiṣṭa.
Then, keeping the right shoulder uncovered, he should pour water into the vessels for the ancestors as before;
thereafter, he should offer sesame seeds with the mantra "Tilo 'si," as well as perfumes and flowers.
"‘As before’ means by means of the verse *śaṃ no devīḥ*. In the *Śaṅkha-Likhita-smṛti* as well:

‘Having placed the garment and the sacrificial thread over the right shoulder (*apasavya*), having scattered sesame seeds, and having poured water into vessels mixed with all kinds of fragrant sesame seeds, [one recites] *śaṃ no devīḥ*.’”

In the *Vārāha* and *Viṣṇu Purāṇas*, it is stated that a twice-born man should offer the *arghya* and other oblations with sesame-water while wearing his sacred thread over the right shoulder (*apasavya*).

One should not think, however, that this instruction for the use of sesame seeds applies even as a conjunction with barley; for this is an instruction for their use in the specific function of barley, since it has been declared that the purpose served by barley is to be fulfilled by sesame seeds.

It is also stated in the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa: "O highly fortunate one, one who is intent on pleasing the ancestors should likewise perform the rite with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (apasavya), using barley for the arghya offering and sesame seeds."

In the Caturviṃśatimata, however, the instruction for the three-pronged [form] is given regarding the ancestral rite (pitrya). This is the specific rule for the vessel of the ancestors: one should scatter sesame seeds with the mantra "tilo 'si.
Furthermore, in the Pārvaṇa rite, there shall be three prongs each in the vessels of the ancestors.
"In an *ekoddiṣṭa* rite, one should offer water after placing a single *śloka* [of rice]. Thus it is said.

As for the instruction regarding facing the south, it will be shown in another context within the words of Dakṣa; likewise, the instruction against circumambulating clockwise is found in the words of Vṛddha-Vasiṣṭha and Pracetas; the instruction regarding the *pitṛ-tīrtha* is in the *Brahma-purāṇa*; and the instruction regarding the names of the ancestors and so forth is to be seen in many statements. Therefore, this extension (*atideśa*) from Yājñavalkya—namely, "as before"—applies specifically to the vessel and the strainer (*pavitra*), the pouring of water with the mantra "aśnan no devīḥ," and the placement [of the water] upon the hands of the twice-born with the mantra "yā divyāḥ.
Thus concludes the rule for the offering of the *arghya*.
Now follows the consecration of the *arghya* vessel.

Regarding this, the procedure for performing the consecration as taught in the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa* has been shown in the section on the *arghya* for the Vaiśvadeva rite. The nature of the consecration and its utility are also explained in that very same place. As for the vessels, they have been described in the section on vessels within the general rules (*paribhāṣā*). Among those vessels, one should accept whichever are available, whether they are made of a single material or of different materials. In this regard, Śaunaka and Āśvalāyana state: "In three types of vessels—those made of metal, stone, or clay—or even in those made of a single material."

"Made of metal" (*taijasam*) means consisting of gold, silver, copper, bronze, and so forth. "Made of stone" (*aśmamayam*) means consisting of rubies, emeralds, crystal, and so forth. "Made of clay" (*mṛnmayam*) is well known as having earth as its material. For the three ancestors beginning with the father, there is one vessel each made of the respective types of materials such as metal; thus, the vessels are fashioned from different kinds of substances, or alternatively, there may be three vessels for all three ancestors made of the same types of substances such as metal. Gobhila also says:
These may be made of gold, silver, udumbara wood, iron, or precious stones, or they may be any other available vessels;
these arghya-vessels should be taken as exactly three in number for the pārvaṇa rite.
And so it is stated in the Mānava-Maitrāyaṇīya-Sūtra:
"One should prepare three bowls of water."

"Udapātrāṇi" refers to vessels for holding water intended as the means for the *arghya* offering; one should "prepare," that is, employ, exactly three of these for a *śrāddha* dedicated to the deities of the father, grandfather, and great-grandfather. The intention here is as follows: although many Brahmins may be invited in place of each individual ancestor, or only one may be invited for all, nevertheless, because the ancestors—the fathers and so forth—who are the intended recipients of the *arghya* offering are three in number, it is appropriate that there be exactly three vessels, rather than their number being determined by the number of Brahmins. Since the procurement of the vessels for the *arghya* is for the purpose of the *arghya*, and since the *arghya* is for the sake of the deity, it is logical that the distinction in the vessels—which are subordinate to it—should follow the distinction in the principal deities, and not the distinction in the Brahmins who serve as the physical substrates (*adhiṣṭhāna*) for those deities.

Because the consecrated base (*adhiṣṭhāna*) is not a determining factor for the *arghya* and other offerings, so too, when there is identity of deity, there is identity of vessel, but not identity of Brahmins. Hariharā holds that even if the sacrificer has two fathers, two grandfathers, or two great-grandfathers, there should nevertheless be exactly three *arghya* vessels because of the scriptural injunction;
this has also been stated by Śaunaka and Āśvalāyana: "In three vessels... and so forth.
Pracetas has also said:

"Having prepared three water-vessels made of clay, udumbara wood, or aśvattha wood—or of other materials—containing sesame seeds, equipped with *pavitra* strainers, and honored with perfumes and garlands.
Śaṅkha also says:
There are exactly three vessels containing water with sesame seeds, kuśa grass, and fragrant scents. Thus it is said.

And three vessels each are prepared for the paternal ancestors and the maternal ancestors. For thus it has been stated by Upādhyāya Karka in his commentary on the words of Kātyāyana: "One should offer to each [ancestor] with one [vessel]; whatever rite pertains to each individual ancestor and so forth must be accomplished with a single vessel. Likewise, because of the extension (*atideśa*) of this rule to the maternal ancestors, three separate vessels must be prepared for the group of maternal ancestors as well. As for the fact that the *Nigama* text will show only a single vessel for the sake of the group beginning with the maternal grandfather, that applies only to those for whom the practice is performed according to their own ancestral tradition, and not for others; for even regarding the group of maternal ancestors, the employment of three vessels is observed through the tradition of the learned (*śiṣṭa*). And having placed those three vessels facing south, wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*), and bending the left knee, one should pour water upon the ground that has been sprinkled, upon the *darbha* grass blades in front [of the vessels] in the order beginning with the paternal ancestors, arranging them face-upward with their rims toward the south. Then, having placed *pavitra* strainers—each consisting of three strands—with their tips pointing south, one should pour water [over them].
Regarding this, Viṣṇu says:
"One should pour water into the cups, which have their darbha-grass blades pointing south and are arranged from right to left, with strainers placed inside them,
reciting 'śaṃ no devīḥ'."

The meaning is that one should pour water into each cup (*camasa*)—which have been placed upon *darbha* grass with the tips pointing south and arranged so that they incline toward the south—and into the *arghya* vessels, over which purifiers (*pavitra*) have been placed, while reciting the mantra "śanno devīḥ. Regarding this, some place the cups face down, sprinkle them, turn them face up, and then pour water into them once the purifiers have been placed within; however, that should be performed by only those who follow such local custom. Furthermore, it has already been shown in the previous presentation of the *Caturviṃśatimata* that the purifiers should be made with three points.
Regarding this, Pracetas states that the pouring of water (anvāsecana) should be performed for each vessel:
"One should pour water into each of the sacrificial wooden cups (camasa) after a strainer (pavitra) has been placed inside.

Since the act of pouring water into each individual vessel is already established by the fact that there are distinct vessels, it is understood that this injunction is intended to ensure the repetition of the mantra for every single vessel.
The scattering of sesame seeds after the pouring of water is stated in the *Kūrmapurāṇa*:

"Having poured water into the vessel with the mantra *śanno devīr*, and likewise having scattered sesame seeds with the mantra *tilo ’si*, one should then offer the *arghya* as before, or again into their hands."

Now Kātyāyana describes the sowing of sesame seeds accompanied by mantras for each vessel: "Into sacrificial wooden cups (*camasa*) with strainers (*pavitra*) placed inside, he pours water into each one with the verse *śaṃ no devīḥ*; into each one he sows sesame seeds with the formula: *tilo 'si somadevatyo gosavo devanirmitaḥ pratnavadbhiḥ prattaḥ svadhayā pitṝn lokān prīṇāhi naḥ svadhā namaḥ*. Here, the sowing of sesame seeds is performed using the *pitṛ-tīrtha* (the part of the hand sacred to the ancestors); and in the *Nāgarakhaṇḍa*, the mantra is shown with the reading *pitṛdeva* in place of *somadevatya*.
In the same manner, one should pour water into the *arghya* vessels for the ancestors with the mantra:

"Thou art sesame (*tila*), whose deity is the ancestors; thou art the *gosava* sacrifice, created by the gods. As an ancient purifier, do thou satisfy these ancestors with the *svadhā* offering in these worlds. Then, with care, one should separately place sesame seeds into those very vessels using the *pitṛ-tīrtha* (the part of the hand sacred to the ancestors).

Regarding the phrase "in the same manner": one should place sesame seeds individually into each vessel, using the mantra "May the goddesses [grant] us... (*śanno devīḥ*) and the supplementary mantra beginning with "Thou art sesame" (*tilo 'si*). Here, it should be understood that the remainder of the mantra, "to us, *svadhā*, obeisance" (*naḥ svadhā namaḥ*), is to be recited immediately after the word "do thou satisfy" (*prīṇāhi*).

Showing the variant reading *pratnavadbhiḥ pṛktaḥ*, Gobhila says: "In sacrificial vessels made of wood, with strainers placed inside each one, he pours water while reciting *śaṃ no devīḥ*. Then he scatters sesame seeds while reciting: *Tilo 'si pitṛdevatyo gosavo devanirmitaḥ pratnavadbhiḥ pṛktaḥ svadhayā pitṝn imān lokān prīṇāhi naḥ svadhā*. (1283)

In the *Āśvalāyanagṛhya*, having poured water into three vessels containing the same substance, or into [a single vessel] covered with *darbha* grass, and having consecrated them with the mantra "śaṃ no devīr abhiṣṭaye," he scatters sesame seeds into them with the formula: "Thou art sesame, whose deity is Soma; born from the cow-sacrifice, fashioned by the gods, mixed with the ancient ones, through the *svadhā* offering, do thou gratify these ancestors and these worlds for us, *svadhā*! [He does this] with his left hand turned away (*prasavya*), between the thumb and forefinger of the other hand, because of the *upavīta* position, or with the right hand while the left is held underneath.

Regarding this, it has already been explained previously that there are three vessels containing the same substance. However, it is written again—specifically "placed upon *darbha* grass"—in order to fulfill the requirement for a substratum (*ādhāra*). Into these vessels, which are joined with *darbha*-strainers (*pavitra*) consisting of triple-strands doubled over, one should silently pour water and perform the consecration (*anumantraṇa*) over them with the mantra beginning "The divine waters for our aid" (*śaṃ no devīr abhiṣṭaye*). Since it is possible to consecrate all the water simultaneously by the principle of the common procedure (*tantranyāya*), even though it is placed in three vessels, the sprinkling of sesame seeds (*tila*) should be performed into each vessel individually with the mantra "Thou art sesame" (*tilo 'si*), and so forth. In this case, the mantra is repeated for each sprinkling; for the mantra used during the performance of an action is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to that very action as it is being done. It is not possible for the three sprinklings of sesame to be performed at one single time. Therefore, because the times differ and the common procedure is impossible, the repetition of the mantra is necessary. As for the consecration (*anumantraṇa*), however, since it is performed once the actions have been completed, it serves the benefit of all without distinction and thus does not require repetition; such is the intention of Hari-hara. He describes the manner of pouring the water, sesame, and other substances with the words "with the left hand" (*prasavyena*), and so on. "With the left" means with the left hand; "of the other" refers to the right hand, which is positioned between the forefinger (*pradeśinī*) and the thumb. This is what is meant: the pitṛ-tīrtha (the part of the hand sacred to the ancestors) of the right hand should be joined to the region of the root of the little finger of the left hand. The reason for this is stated as "because of the state of the *upavīta*. Just as for one performing a rite with the right hand, the status of wearing the *yajñopavīta* (sacred thread) is maintained by its resting on the left shoulder, so too for one performing a rite with the left hand, the status of the *upavīta* is maintained by its resting on the right shoulder. Alternatively, everything including the sprinkling of sesame should be done with the right hand, "held by the left," meaning touched by the tip of the fingers of the left hand.

One should perform the rites in regular succession; it is stated in the *Padma* and *Matsya* Purāṇas that the scattering of perfumes and flowers should be done immediately after the sowing of sesame seeds.
Having first provided seats of darbha grass, one should fill three vessels;
having first placed sacred grass (*pavitra*) within them, one should pour water into them with the mantra "śaṃ no devī."
One should offer sesame seeds with the mantra "tilo 'si," and likewise offer perfumes, flowers, and so forth.
And this vessel for perfumes and flowers is said in the *Brahma Purāṇa* to be for the purpose of worshipping the water contained in the bowls:
"Then, having taken pure water in vessels made from sacrificial wood together with *kuśa* grass, one should pour it out while reciting the mantra *śaṃ no devīḥ*."
And scattering sesame seeds over them while reciting "Thou art sesame" (tilo 'si) in succession,
they should be worshipped according to the scriptures with water for the guest-offering (arghya), flowers, and perfumes.

The word "tataḥ" means after the scattering of sesame seeds following the invocation (*āvāhana*). "Tāḥ" refers to those waters placed in the vessel; "arghyāḥ" refers to the waters which are to be honored with flowers and perfumes. "Śāstravat" means according to the scriptures.

In this regard, Baudhāyana states that there is only one vessel, the mantra for the removal of the vessel, the reversal of the order in the throwing of water and sesame seeds, the mantras for the sprinkling of *svadhā*, the throwing of perfumes, flowers, and unbroken rice grains accompanied by mantras, and the covering with *darbha* grass on top.

To the south of the fire, he should place the vessel for the *svadhā* offering with the mantra: "O ancestors, come from the path of the gods. Having placed sesame seeds with the mantra: "Thou art sesame, whose deity is Soma; thou art produced by the cow-sacrifice and fashioned by the gods. Mixed with *svadhā* by the ancients, satisfy these ancestors and these worlds for us; *svadhā*, obeisance," he then recites: "The winds blow sweetly for the one who follows the cosmic order; the rivers flow with sweetness; may our plants be full of sweetness. Sweet be the night and the dawns; may the earthly realm be full of sweetness. May the sky, our father, be sweet; may the tree of the forest be full of sweetness for us, and may the sun be full of sweetness. May our cows be full of sweetness. Then, with the mantras: "Thou art the splendor of Soma" and "May the divine waters be auspicious for our aid, may they be auspicious for our drinking; may they flow toward us for peace and well-being," he mixes the offering with *svadhā*. Having cast away a small portion with the words: "The head of Namuci is cast out," he honors the ancestors with perfumes, flowers, and unbroken grains, saying: "Obeisance to the fathers, obeisance to the grandfathers, obeisance to the great-grandfathers," and then covers them with *darbha* grass.

The meaning of this is as follows: To the south of the fire—either the *anvāhāryapacana* or the *āvasathya* fire—one should place the *svadhā* vessel, which is a receptacle for holding the *arghya* water, while reciting the mantra beginning with "O ancestors who have come, [come] from the path of the gods. Immediately thereafter, having cast sesame seeds into it with the mantra beginning with "Thou art sesame," one should mix the *svadhā* consisting of honey, ghee, and water by means of the mantras beginning with "Honeyed are the winds. In that context, the addition of honey is performed with the three verses beginning with "Honeyed are the winds" because they manifest honey; the addition of ghee is performed with the mantra "Thou art the splendor of Soma," because ghee is indeed splendor (*tejas*) and these verses manifest splendor; and the addition of water is performed with the verse "The goddesses covered... because it manifests water. Then, one should perform the removal of the refuse with the mantra "The head of Namuci is cast out. Having cast perfume, flowers, and unbroken rice grains individually with each of the three mantras beginning with "Homage to the fathers," one should place three blades of *kuśa* grass upon them.

And those mantras are: "O ancestral fathers, come from the path of the gods, from the milk-ocean, from the river, from heaven; may you obtain all desires at this sacrifice, and may what is inexhaustible be carried forth. 'I take this for you, for the ancestors'. "The winds blow sweetly for the one who follows the cosmic order (*ṛta*); the rivers flow with sweetness; may the plants be sweet for us. Sweet is the night and sweet are the dawns; sweet is the earthly realm. May the sky, our father, be sweet; may the lord of the forest be full of sweetness for us; may the sun be full of sweetness. May the cows be sweet for us. "Thou art the brilliance of Soma; may my brilliance be like thine"—this is the *yajus*. "The head of Namuci is cast out"—this much indeed is the *yajus*.
Hārīta, however, has stated a different mantra for the sprinkling of water and has also prescribed the purification (*utpavana*):
"Having placed [the materials] near the water-vessels, one should sprinkle water with the mantra beginning 'samanyāyanti' and purify the *sumanas* flowers.

This is the meaning: having poured water into the *arghya* vessels with the mantra whose first quarter is 'samanyāyanti', and having placed *sumanas* flowers therein, one should take up a *kuśa* purifier with the thumbs and ring fingers of both hands and perform the purification (*utpavana*) as in the case of the *prokṣaṇī* water.

The mantra cited here as a representative example (*pratīka*) has been shown in the section on the *vaiśvadeva* *arghya*. However, the purification (*utpavana*) should be performed silently (*tūṣṇīm*). Some, however, perform the purification with this *yajus*: "May the divine Savitṛ purify you with a flawless strainer, with the rays of the Vasu Sūrya. In the ritual manual (*nigama*), regarding a six-deity *śrāddha* performed by one who maintains the sacred fires (*sāgnika*), there are four *arghya* vessels. These are placed upon lines drawn facing south, filled with water, and provided with the six substances beginning with a garland (*srak*). Other mantras are also prescribed therein: "Having drawn [lines] on the southern line and prepared four metal cups (*camasa*), having mixed them with a garland, sesame, milk, curd, honey, and ghee, and having filled them with water using the *mahāvyāhṛtis*, the *āpo hi ṣṭhā* verses, and the *śanno devīḥ* verse..."

‘Srak’ means a garland of flowers. ‘Lauha’ refers to those fashioned from metallic substances other than tin, lead, and black iron. Having placed those four [vessels] upon the aforementioned line—wherein it will later be stated that the fourth is for the purpose of the *arghya* offering to the maternal grandfather and others—and having prepared them with the six materials beginning with the garland, one should fill them with water using the *Mahāvyāhṛti* and other mantras. The *Mahāvyāhṛtis* are “bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ. The ‘Āpohiṣṭīya’ is the hymn of nine verses beginning with “āpo hi ṣṭhā mayobhuvaḥ. Others, however, state that the six materials for the *arghya* are water, sesame seeds, *kuśa* grass, flowers, barley, and fragrant scents. Thus it is said in the *Kālikā Purāṇa* regarding the continuation of the rule "one should offer the *arghya*":
[1287] With sesame seeds, perfumes, barley, flowers, water, and *darbha* grass—all consecrated (*mantrita*).

Regarding the term "consecrated," the mantras for the sesame seeds and water are stated right here; for the barley, the mantra "Thou art barley" (*yavo 'si*) was mentioned previously. For the perfume and flowers, however, the two mantras "O Goddess, thou whose door is fragrance" (*gandhadvārām*) and "Prosperity and Fortune are thine" (*śrīś ca te lakṣmīś ca*) were shown in the section on the *pādya* and other offerings. Furthermore, since it was stated in the section on the *pādya* etc. that after filling the vessel one should consecrate it with the *Gāyatrī*, one should understand that the *kuśa* grass and the other items whose sequential mantras will be mentioned below likewise possess mantras.
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*, however, eight substances for the *arghya* offering are mentioned:
"Having said, 'This is your *arghya*,' one should then give them in eight portions:
water, milk, curd, ghee, sesame seeds, rice, and mustard seeds."
Having offered blades of kusha grass and flowers, he himself should then perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana).

The term "eightfold" (aṣṭadhā) means that one should offer water together with eight kinds of substances, beginning with milk, to the ancestors and others with the formula "This is for you, the *arghya*," and then perform the ritual rinsing (*ācamana*).
This concludes the consecration of the vessels and other items.
Now follows the offering of the *arghya*.

There, immediately after placing the *arghya* materials in the vessel, he should ask the Brahmins representing the ancestors with palms joined: "Oṃ, may there be the perfection (*saṃpatti*) of the *arghya* vessels for the ancestors. When they have replied, "Oṃ, may there be the perfection of the *arghya* vessels for the ancestors," he should lift each one of those *arghya* vessels together with the *darbha* grass placed beneath them using both hands, and place them in front of the Brahmins representing the ancestors and others, respectively, with the tips pointing south, while reciting the mantra: "Oṃ, svadhā, the *arghya*!
Regarding this, Jātūkarṇya says:
Then, having had the best of the twice-born recite the formula for the perfection of the arghya vessels,
one should place the arghya vessels before them with the words, "svadhā arghya."

Immediately after that, based on the forthcoming statement from the *Brahma-purāṇa* beginning with "Having poured water and *darbha* grass into the hand," one should first pour water into the hand of the Brāhmaṇa, place the *kuśa* purifier situated in the *arghya* vessel with its tips pointing southward, honor the Brāhmaṇa, and then present the *arghya*.
To this effect, Dakṣa and Gārgya state:
"Having placed a threefold purifier measuring a span in the hand..."
Having performed worship, one should indeed offer the *arghya* facing the direction of the ancestors (the south).

"Trivṛt" means three-pronged. "Pūrvataḥ" means at the beginning. Here, it should be understood from the *Mānava-Maitrāyaṇīya-sūtra*, which will be cited later as an alternative view, that the very same *pavitra* (strainer) that was previously placed in the *arghya* vessel must be given into the hand of the Brāhmaṇa, and no other. This is because, by virtue of being the subject under discussion (*prakṛta*), that [specific strainer] alone remains present in the mind. However, some take another [strainer], arguing that the former has already served its purpose. That is incorrect; for we observe elsewhere the employment of *darbha* grasses even after they have been used for one purpose in another context. Thus, the teacher Karka also raised this objection and established the same conclusion.
It is stated in the *Vārāha Purāṇa* that worship (*arcana*) should be performed with fragrant flowers:
"Having performed worship with fragrant flowers, one should offer water with sesame seeds into the hand.
The method of worship is described in the *Kālikā Purāṇa*.

Having worshipped according to the rules with devotion through the method of emanation (*sṛṣṭinyāya*), the knower of mantras should then offer the *arghya* water using vessels made from the leaves of the *brahmavṛkṣa* tree.

The practice of performing [the worship] from the head downwards is the "method of emanation" (*sṛṣṭinyāya*); alternatively, it may be performed starting from the head, because the *Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa* records the scriptural teaching that creation proceeds from the head, stating, "He is born being born from the head. This is indeed optional;
for this very reason, Gārgya and Ślokagautama state:
"One should properly worship either from the head or from the feet."
As before, one should worship each [deity] individually, one by one, in sequence.

Regarding this, Śaṅkhadhara has explained that one should worship the ancestors from the feet up to the head, but the gods only from the feet upward. The phrase "as before" means that with the mantra beginning "The divine ones," one should worship each ancestor, such as the father, with a single *arghya* offering. However, the author of the *Smṛticandrikā*, considering that one should worship each Brāhmaṇa with a single *arghya*, stated that this rule applies specifically to the case where there are three [Brāhmaṇas] for the paternal side. Pracetās says that the worship performed from the feet should extend up to the head, and that which is performed from the head should extend down to the feet, to be carried out with specific mantras.
For the worship of the gods with flowers, one proceeds from the feet up to the head;
for the ancestral rites (paitṛka), one proceeds from the head down to the feet, saying "Obeisance to you."

Herein, the mantra beginning with "namo vaḥ" according to the Vājasaneyī Śākhā is first written down: "Homage to you, O ancestors, for your sap; homage to you, O ancestors, for your dryness; homage to you, O ancestors, for your life; homage to you, O ancestors, for your *svadhā*; homage to you, O ancestors, for your terrible power; homage to you, O ancestors, for your wrath; homage to you, O ancestors, O ancestors, homage to you; give us houses, O ancestors; we shall give to you what exists, O ancestors. However, those belonging to other branches will be shown in the context of the offering of rice-balls (*piṇḍa*). This very sequence is stated in the *Skanda Purāṇa* regarding worship.

One should worship the ancestors and the twice-born at the beginning with offerings for the head, the shoulders, the hands, the two knees, and the pair of feet, using sesame seeds, perfumes, and flowers.

The meaning of this is as follows: one should perform the worship of the Brahmins representing the ancestors with sesame seeds, scents, and flowers in this sequence: first on the head, then on the left shoulder, the right shoulder, the left hand, the right hand, the left knee, the right knee, the left foot, and the right foot. Here, the procedure (*kriyākrama*) is that, wearing the *prācīnāvīta* (the sacred thread over the right shoulder), with the left knee bent, facing south and meditating upon the ancestors, one should pour the water contained in the *arghya* vessel into the hands of the Brahmins—which hold the *pavitra* grass—using the *pitṛ-tīrtha* (the part of the hand sacred to the ancestors) while reciting the mantra "yā divyā" preceded by the utterance of the names and lineages (*gotra*) of the father and others, saying, "This is your *arghya*. By this, it is shown that although items such as the *prācīnāvīta* and so forth are established by general statements, they are specifically set forth by us who collect even those seen in particular scriptural texts; in this regard, the meditation on the ancestors and the *prācīnāvīta* have been stated by Pracetas: [Text omitted in source] (Note: The specific verses from Pracetas are not provided in the source text, but the commentary indicates they concern these two points.)
"Visualizing the ancestors, he should pour [the water] over the Brāhmaṇas with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (apasavya).
This means that visualizing the ancestors within the bodies of the Brāhmaṇas, he should pour it.
Facing south, the mantra "yā divyā," the substance to be offered, and the locus of the offering are described in the *Nāgarakhaṇḍa*:
"In rites for the ancestors, with face turned toward the south for the satisfaction of the *pitṛs*,
one should cause the offering to be placed in their hands with the mantra 'yā divyā'."

The agent, distinguished by the "southern face"—that is, by a mouth looking toward the southern direction—should "cause the *arghya* to be given," meaning he should offer the water intended for the *arghya*. The nature of the mantra beginning with "yā divyā" will become clear from the statements of Kātyāyana and others. Śaṅkha and Likhita state that the water for the *arghya* should be poured into the hands of the Brāhmaṇas, which are covered with *pavitra* grass:
"One should pour water into the hands of the Brāhmaṇas while they are covered with *pavitra*."

Regarding the placement of the *pavitra* grass: some perform the rite by placing the *pavitra* in the hand of the Brāhmaṇa; others, however, accomplish it by holding the *pavitra* crosswise in front of the *arghya* vessel. As for the rule concerning the *pitṛ-tīrtha*, it will be shown in the citation from the *Brahma-purāṇa* beginning with "Then, with this [water]... and so forth.
The requirement to precede the offering with the utterance of the names of the father and others is stated in the *Sāṅkhyāyana-gṛhya-sūtra*:
"Having scattered sesame seeds over the water-vessels, he assigns them to the Brāhmaṇas, addressing each with 'O [Name], this is for you.'"
"One should pour [the water] into their hands.
Thus, the phrase "this one" (asau) refers to the specific name of the fire for the father and others.
For this very reason, the practice of first uttering the name and the lineage (gotra) is stated in the Padma and Mātsya Purāṇas.
Having thus consecrated the vessels according to what is available, free from envy,
he should place them in the hands of those holding darbha grass, using the formula "yā divyā" along with the names and gotras of the ancestors.

The meaning is that one should offer the *arghya* water into the hand of a Brāhmaṇa joined with *darbha* grass, having pronounced the name and lineage (*gotra*) of the father and the others. Because of the use of the singular "in the hand" (*kare*), the intention is that the offering of the *arghya* should be made into the single right hand of the twice-born.
However, Vaijavāpa has stated that the *arghya* is offered into the hollowed palms (*añjali*):

"He assigns the vessels, saying, 'O Father, this is your *arghya*; O Grandfather, this is your *arghya*; O Great-grandfather, this is your *arghya*,' and he should pour the contents of the vessels into the hollowed palms of the Brāhmaṇas."

"Vessels" (*pātrāṇi*) refers to the materials for the *arghya* offering, such as water and so forth, which are contained within the vessels. Here, by employing the words "father" (*pitṛ*) and so on in the vocative singular, it is indicated that the personal name and the lineage name (*gotra*) should also be used in that same form [ending in the vocative singular]. Thus say Pracetas and Vṛddhavasiṣṭha:
"One should offer these to each one of them, starting with the father, in non-pradakṣiṇa order."
Having addressed him by name and lineage, saying, "This is your arghya water," he should offer it.

"Of these"—that is, of the father, grandfather, and great-grandfather—"in the order of the ancestors," meaning in the sequence beginning with the father, "one by one," having "addressed them by name and lineage," that is, having brought them to mind by the utterance of their names and lineages; by this, it is understood that the vocative case is to be employed. The ellipsis is: "saying 'This is your *arghya*,' he should offer the *arghya* into the hand of the Brahmin who serves as the locus for the father and the others. To ensure the logical connection with the word "to you" (*te*), the use of the singular endings for both the name and the lineage should be observed. It should be understood here that the mention of "name and lineage" is an illustration for the declaration of the relationship.
And so Vyāsa says:
"Proclaiming the lineage, the relationship, and the names of the ancestors,
one should offer the vessel of *arghya* to each individual Brahmin."

Regarding the phrase "but for each single Brahmin," some explain it as follows: even though many Brahmins may have been invited to take the place of a single ancestor such as the father, one should nevertheless honor only one Brahmin among those who serve as the locus for a single deity with the *argha* offering intended for that specific person, and not a second or subsequent Brahmin who serves as a locus for that same deity.

Others, however, say: "The *arghya* water contained in that vessel should be given into the hands of as many Brahmins as have been assembled on account of their connection to a single deity. The phrase 'to each one' (*ekaikasya*) is intended to indicate that the ritual action is to be commenced separately for each Brahmin. And according to this view, the statement 'one should cause the *arghya* to be given into the hands'—which specifies the connection of a single portion of *arghya* water with a single hand—would otherwise be inconsistent. Thus, the giving of the *arghya* would be made to correspond to the individual objects being offered, such as the perfumes and flowers."
The application of formulas ending in *saṃbuddhi* (vocative) for the expression of relationship is stated in the *Mānava-Maitrāyaṇīya-Sūtra*:

"Having placed the purifier (*pavitra*) in the hand of the Brahmin, having pronounced the name and lineage [of the deceased], one says: 'O my father, this is your *arghya*; O my grandfather, O my great-grandfather.

Regarding this, some, considering the right hand alone to be the means for accomplishing all ritual acts, perform the pouring of water from the vessel and the offering of the *arghya* with that very hand. Others, however, lift the vessel with both hands and pour the *arghya* from the vessel using those same two hands.
And so says the Dharma:
"Taking up the vessel with both hands while reciting 'The divine waters,' and having taken hold of the name and lineage, one should offer the *arghya* with the pavitra-grass held in the hand.
[1293] However, in the *Brahmapurāṇa*, a different method for the pouring of the *arghya* is shown.
Then, having taken the cups in sequence with the left hand,
one should [pour] that water with the right hand using the *pitṛ-tīrtha*.
Having placed darbha grass and water in the hands of each of the Brahmins individually,
one should then recite the mantra "yā divyā āpaḥ" while muttering it,
saying: "O [Name], of the [Gotra] lineage, may this water with sesame seeds be for you."

The meaning of the injunction is that, holding a vessel with the left hand and pouring water from it with the right hand, one should pour it into the hand of the Brahmin using the *pitṛ-tīrtha* (the part of the right hand sacred to the ancestors). In this context, instead of the formula "This is your *arghya*," one should recite: "May this water with sesame seeds be for you. It is understood that this mantra generally pertains to *śrāddha* rites performed by those who maintain a sacred fire (*agnimat*), for in the *śrāddha* of one who maintains a fire, the rule for pouring water is observed even without the word "*arghya*.
For this very reason, Baudhāyana [states]:

Now, when he is about to cause [the guests] to receive this water mixed with sesame seeds, some authorities prescribe that he recite "Svadhā, obeisance to so-and-so; svadhā, obeisance to so-and-so" three times for the sesame-water. One should offer food first, then the sesame-water twice, and the third time after they have finished eating. Thus it is said.

"Intending to cause the Brāhmaṇas to accept water" (*apaḥ pratigrāhayiṣyan*) means intending to have them take hold of water; after the names of the father and others, one should utter "Svadhā Namaḥ. Regarding the word "three times" (*triḥ*) and so forth: "some" (*eke*), namely certain authors of Sūtras, prescribe the offering of water with sesame seeds (*tilodaka*) three times in the performance of the Śrāddha. He states the times for this: "twice before the food" (*puro ’nnaṃ dviḥ*); that is, twice prior to the formal renunciation of the food (*annatyāga*). Among those, one is after washing the feet upon the circle of cow-dung (*gomayamaṇḍala*), and the second is prior to the *agnaukaraṇa* (offering into the fire). "And the third when they have eaten" (*bhuktavatsu ca tṛtīyam*): the meaning is that the third, called the "imperishable water" (*akṣayyodaka*), is offered when the twice-born have finished eating and rinsed their mouths. For this very reason, he says elsewhere: "Having given the *svadhā*, saying: 'Svadhā namaḥ to the fathers, svadhā namaḥ to the grandfathers, svadhā namaḥ to the great-grandfathers. *Svadhā* has already been explained. The connection with what follows is: "having placed those [waters] in the hands of the Brāhmaṇas, one should perform the *agnaukaraṇa*."
The *nigama* also says:

"Having taken up an interconnection from them like a portion of the sacrificial cuttings (*avadāna*), he pours water into their hands while pronouncing the name of each, beginning with the fourth [generation], saying 'of so-and-so,' for the purpose of washing the maternal grandfather and the others."

‘From those’ refers to the cups (*camasa*), since it has been stated that the fourth [cup] is for the maternal grandfathers (*mātāmaha*) and so forth. Having poured water from three of the cups and drawn it up with the hand, one should pour it into the hands of the respective Brahmins while pronouncing the name of each ancestor—the father and the others—in the genitive case, such as *amuṣya*. He describes the manner of drawing [the water]: “In an interlaced manner (*vyatiṣaṅgam*), like the portions (*avadāna*). Just as in the *Cāturmāsya* sacrifices, during the great oblation to the ancestors (*paitra mahāhavis*), the portions are taken in an interlaced manner, so it is here as well. For example: having taken [water] from the cups of the father, grandfather, and great-grandfather, one should first pour it into the hand of the Brahmin representing the father. Then, having taken [water] from the cups of the grandfather, great-grandfather, and father, one should pour it into the hand of the twice-born representing the grandfather. And then, having taken [water] from the cups of the great-grandfather, father, and grandfather, one should pour it into the hand of the twice-born representing the great-grandfather. Thus it is said.

The followers of Āśvalāyana, however, perform the *arghya* offering by placing the *arghya* vessel within the space between the thumb and forefinger of the right hand while the left hand holds it, using water poured from another vessel; or they do so with the vessel held by the right hand assisted by the left. This has already been demonstrated in the *Āśvalāyana* injunctions, such as "with the left hand [encircling] between the thumb and [fingers of] the other hand. Furthermore, Āśvalāyana states that there is a different mantra for the offering of the *arghya* than the mantra for consecrating the vessel, and he specifies the application of the mantra "yā divyā" for consecrating the water that has flowed from the hand of the Brāhmaṇa.

Intending to cause [the ancestors] to accept [the offerings] in succession, saying, "Father, this is for you; Grandfather, this is for you," and so on, [he offers] once with the words, "Svadhā! Arghya! When the waters have been offered and consecrated, [he recites]: "The divine waters which were produced upon the earth, those which are in the intermediate space, and those which are terrestrial—those waters, golden-hued and worthy of sacrifice, may they be most comfortable and auspicious for us."

[1295] Regarding this, after the sowing of sesame seeds, one should offer the *arghya* water into each vessel respectively with the mantras: "O Father, this is your *arghya*; O Grandfather, this is your *arghya*; O Great-grandfather, this is your *arghya*," following the sequence beginning with the father. However, the authors of the *Bhāṣya* maintain that these are not the actual formulas for the offering of the *arghya*.

Regarding "those" waters contained in the vessels: intending to cause the Brāhmaṇas to receive them, he should mutter the mantra "svadhā arghyāḥ" once for each. The meaning is that by means of this [mantra] he should cause them to receive [the water]. Because of the expression "once for each," its recitation must be performed exactly three times; however, there is a repetition according to the number of different Brāhmaṇas. When they have been poured out—that is, when they have gone from the hands of the Brāhmaṇas onto the ground—he should consecrate them with the verse beginning "yā divyāḥ. And it has already been stated previously that the consecration is to be performed only once for all of them.

Kātyāyana, however, has read *payasā* (with milk) in place of *pṛthivyām* (on the earth): "He gives to each [guest] with one [substance] into their hands which hold the *pavitra* grasses: 'The celestial waters which have come together with milk, those which are intermediate, and those which are terrestrial; those which are golden-hued and worthy of sacrifice—may those waters be auspicious and easy to invoke for us! [And then: 'O So-and-so, this is your *arghya*.'"

Gobhila, however, has recited this same mantra with the addition of the word *śivā*: "When the *pavitra* blades have been offered, he gives [the water] to each guest one by one with the mantra: 'May those divine waters which have arisen from the milk, those which are atmospheric and those which are terrestrial, those which are golden-hued and worthy of sacrifice—may those auspicious waters be pleasant and easy to invoke for us, O So-and-so! This is your *arghya*.

As for the *arghya* mantras beginning with "those that stand" (*yās tiṣṭhanti*) and so forth, which are mentioned in the *Viṣṇusmṛti*, the *Viṣṇudharmottara*, and the *Brahmapurāṇa*, they have already been shown in the context of the presentation of the *pādya* and other offerings.

In the *Maitrāyaṇīya-sūtra*, one should pour [the water] into the hand of a Brāhmaṇa, designating each [libation] for the father, the grandfather, and the great-grandfather. From the use of the dative case in the designations "to the father," "to the grandfather," and so forth—such as "This *arghya* is for our father, [named] so-and-so, of such-and-such lineage" (*amukagotrāya amukaśarmaṇe asmatpitre ayam arghyaḥ*)—it is understood that these specific formulas for the offering of the *arghya* should be employed.
Hārīta says:

"Having been authorized by the Brāhmaṇas with the words 'Bring the fuel,' and having invoked the fires beginning with Agniṣvātta, one should honor the Brāhmaṇas standing in place of those fires with vessels of water according to the requirement."

In this context, because of the hearing of the permission granted by the Brāhmaṇas with the words “O, fuel-sticks!”, one should understand that there is a request such as, “May I kindle the fire. Having thus obtained permission and having cast wood into the fire for the purpose of kindling, one should then invoke the ancestors with the previously shown mantras beginning with “etad pitaraḥ”. Then, with the water-vessels prepared beforehand, one should worship the Brāhmaṇas representing the Agniṣvātta and other ancestors—the term “ādi” (etc. including the Havirbhuk and so forth—according to their respective order; specifically, those with which the purpose of the Śrāddha is accomplished for each caste, according to the honors prescribed for them. These [ancestors] are those previously shown by the statement of Manu: “The Somapas are the name for the Brāhmaṇas,” and so forth.

Since it is stated that at the very moment of invocation, the ritual visualization (*saṃkalpa*) and worship of the Agniṣvātta and other ancestors is performed by means of the names of the three ancestors—father, grandfather, and great-grandfather—according to their actual status as presiding deities for those whose fathers are deceased; and since it is understood from this very [text] that one whose father is living performs the worship of two [ancestors], Yama says:
"Then, having brought water, he should offer it silently along with the *pavitra* grass."

By the word "silently" (*tuṣṇīm*), one should understand the absence of a mantra; therefore, it should be considered that the *anumantraṇa* mantras such as "that which is divine" (*yā divyā*) and so forth are optional (*vikalpa*) or performative (*karaṇa*) mantras. Alternatively, this absence of a mantra during the offering of the *arghya* water should be understood according to the established rule (*vyavasthā*) that it applies only to those for whom it is practiced through the tradition of the elders, and not to everyone. "Accompanied by the *pavitra*" means provided with all the *arghya* materials, such as the *pavitra* grass and so on. And in this view, different *kuśa* blades should be placed in the hand of the Brāhmaṇa. In the same manner, for the maternal grandfather (*mātāmaha*) and others as well, one should perform the consecration of the *arghya* vessels and the offering of the *arghya* into the Brāhmaṇa’s hand—accompanied by the mention of their respective names, *gotras*, and relationships—in accordance with the sequence of items (*padārthānusamaya*). This is because of the extended application (*atideśa*) recorded in the text, "The same for the maternal grandfathers," and because it should be understood from the previously cited statement of the *Brahmapurāṇa* that the sipping of water (*ācamana*) must be performed immediately after the offering of the *arghya*.
Thus ends the offering of the *arghya*.
Now follows the application of the remnants (*saṃsrava*) and so forth;
regarding this, the *Āśvalāyanagṛhya* states:
"Having poured together the remnants, he who desires a son anoints his face with that water.
The "remnants" (*saṃsravāḥ*) are the portions of water remaining in the *arghya* vessels. Regarding this, there is an indicative mark (*liṅga*) seen in the *Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa*:
"For indeed, the remnant alone remains over."

Some, however, explain that the water for the *arghya* offering which flows out from the gaps between the fingers of the Brahmins' hands is called *saṃsrava*. According to their view, at the very time of giving the *arghya*, the flowing water is collected into the first vessel. "Having poured together" (*samavanīya*) means having gathered them in one place. And so says Kātyāyana: "Having poured the *saṃsravas* together into one [vessel], one who desires a son anoints his face. Since there is an expectation of a relative to the "face," and because the person in close proximity—the officiant—is understood as the relative, it is understood that the sacrificer who desires a son should anoint his own face. "Into one" means into the first vessel for the ancestors.
And so says Vṛddha-Śātātapa:
"Having collected all the remnants (saṃsrava) into the first paternal vessel,
he should then anoint his face if he desires a son."

Having collected all the *saṃsravas* (overflowing drops) into that first vessel among the *arghya* vessels of the ancestors—since the word "all" here refers to the vessels of the ancestors due to their proximity, and not to those standing in the *vaiśvadeva* vessel—one should recite the mantra over the *saṃsravas* and apply collyrium to the eyes.
Śloka-Kātyāyana, however, has stated the mantra for the consecration of the *saṃsravas* and the application of collyrium:
having said, "The *arghya* is for *svadhā*," one should consecrate the *saṃsravas*.
One desiring a son should touch his mouth with the mantra beginning with "ye devāḥ. Here, the mantra cited by its opening words is written out in full:

"Those gods who are fathers and those who are humans, those who are in the womb, O Maruts, and those who have passed away; those who have emerged and those who are buried—may they all rejoice here in this grain."
In the *Brahmapurāṇa*, however, it is stated that a sacrificer desiring a son should look at his own reflection in the residual water (saṃsrava) remaining in those very vessels.
Into those vessels of residual water filled with water, he who desires a son should look at his face; facing eastward, he should recite the mantra:
"May the worlds, the abodes of the ancestors, be purified; you are the abode of the ancestors."
In the *Nāgarakhaṇḍa*, however, the sprinkling of the eyes with the residual water is prescribed for one desiring long life:
"Having placed the *arghya* vessels one by one into the vessel of the ancestors,
he who desires long life should sprinkle that water upon his two eyes."

"In the father’s vessel" means in the *arghya* vessel of the father. By metonymy, "the *arghya* vessels" refers to the remnants of water remaining in those vessels. "Having collected," meaning having poured them together, one should sprinkle them with the eyes. Others, however, say that one should place the remaining *arghya* vessels into the *arghya* vessel of the father, pour water from them while they remain in that state into the hand, and perform the sprinkling of the eyes with that water. According to the practice of the Vājasaneyins, another person performs the consecration of the sacrificer—who is seated facing east—by taking the water of the *saṃsrava* (remnant) collected in the first vessel in his hand and saying: "May these waters, auspicious, most auspicious, peaceful, and most peaceful, grant you healing. Furthermore, these acts such as the application of collyrium to the face must be performed by the sacrificer wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*yajñopavītin*) during rites for specific desires (*kāmya*). This is because the facing east indicates that these are not rites belonging to the ancestors (*apaitṛka*), and because, like the *godohana* vessel, they lack the status of being auxiliary parts of the primary rite due to their being means for attaining a specific fruit. Thus, the application of these specific optional acts such as the cleansing of the face has been stated here. In that regard, if a portion of those items used remains, or if there is an absence of desire for the result, a specific disposal (*pratipatti*) must be performed. That too should be done either at that very moment, or after collecting them until the recitation of the *svadhā* formula; specifically, in the case where the first paternal vessel is turned face down, it is done at that time, but in the case where it is held face up, it is done immediately prior to the recitation of the *svadhā*. For those who adopt the view that the water on the fingers of the hand is called *saṃsrava*, those very waters should be used for the previously mentioned acts such as applying collyrium to the face. However, the disposal to be described later applies only to the *arghya* remnants remaining in the vessels; according to the view of those who turn the vessel face down along with the *saṃsrava*, the purification of both types of *saṃsrava* is to be performed.
In that regard, according to the *Vaijavāpa-gṛhya*, the ritual practice immediately following the offering of the *arghya* water is as follows:
one murmurs over the remnants on the *darbha* grass, "May there be inexhaustibility for the ancestors."

The meaning is that one should pour the water remaining in the vessel used for the *arghya* offering onto the *darbha* grass spread upon the ground. Immediately thereafter, one should place that vessel in some unblemished spot. Accordingly, the Maitrāyaṇīya Sūtra states: "One should pour the remainder onto the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), sprinkle [the vessel], and set it down. "Sprinkling" refers either to sprinkling the vessel or to the location where it is to be set down. "Setting down" (*pratyāsādana*) means placing back in some spot that which was previously brought forward, used, and finished its purpose. Regarding the disposal (*pratipatti*) of those remnants (*saṃsrava*), Atri has stated that it should be performed after collecting them together and before the recitation of the *svadhā* formula.
Then, having placed his upper garment over the right shoulder and being composed,
he should cast the *darbha* purifiers into the vessel for the rice-balls and then release the residual drops.

Furthermore, this containment of the overflow occurs only when the vessel is placed with its opening facing upward, and not otherwise; therefore, it should be understood that by implication, the placement of the vessel with its opening facing upward is what is being prescribed here. However, according to this view, the paternal vessel, having been made the receptacle for the overflow, must be covered by the paternal grandfather’s vessel—whether turned face down or face up.
And so say Yama and Kātyāyana:
"One should place the paternal vessel first, and upon it, the paternal grandfather’s vessel."
Then, having placed [the mantra] upon the great-grandfather, one should not remove it nor cause it to waver.
Atri also says:
"One should cause it to be covered with a third [vessel]; and in the absence of a third, with another."

Having covered the vessel for the father with the vessel for the grandfather, one should cover it with the vessel for the great-grandfather; in the absence of the vessel for the great-grandfather, one should cover it with any other vessel whatsoever, or with the vessel for the great-great-grandfather. However, the absence of the vessel for the great-grandfather is to be understood as applying to a *śrāddha* where the great-grandfather is still living. And this placement of the vessels—since no specific distinction is mentioned—is common to both positions: either placing them face-up (*uttāna*) or turning them face-down (*nyubja*). In that regard, the mantra for turning [the vessels] face-down along with the pouring of the remnants (*saṃsrava*) is stated in the *Kūrmapurāṇa*.
Then, with a concentrated mind, he should collect all the remnants into a vessel;
he should cause the vessel to be placed face down, saying, "Thou art the station of the ancestors."

"In the vessel" means the *arghya* vessel for the father; with the mantra "Thou art the place for the ancestors," one should cause it to be placed "face down," that is, with the opening downward. The placement of the remnants (*saṃsrava*) in the vessel for the father is stated in the *Kātyāyana-sūtra*:
"Having poured the remnants together into the first vessel, [one places it] face down with the words, 'Thou art the place for the ancestors.'"
Regarding the statement "he prepares the vessel":

it is clearly understood that among the *arghya* vessels for the ancestors, the *arghya* vessel for the father comes first. Gobhila, however, prescribes the recitation of this mantra after the act of turning the vessels face down.
Having poured the remnants into the first vessel and turned the vessel face down, one should mutter: "Thou art the place for the ancestors.
The word "should mutter" is to be understood as the remainder of the sentence.
Regarding the specific location for overturning the vessel containing the *saṃsrava* (remnants), it is stated in the *Nāgarakhaṇḍa*:
"Then one should place that vessel face down in a secluded spot.

The word "that" (*tat*) refers to the vessel in which the *saṃsravas* were collected on the side of the ancestors (*pitṛpakṣa*). "Secluded" (*vijane*) means in a place free from the defects caused by the movement of people who bring, remove, or serve the materials for the *śrāddha*.
Pracetas states that it should not be placed just anywhere, but specifically to the north of the row of twice-born men belonging to the Vaiśvadeva rite:
"Having placed [the vessel] in the *pitṛ* vessel, he should then set it down face-down to the north;
having placed it with the words 'Thou art the place for the ancestors,' he should then honor the twice-born."

Having placed the *saṃsrava* (residual water) on the side of the ancestors, one should place that vessel face down (*nyubja*) in front of the Brahmins with the mantra: "Thou art the station for the ancestors. Immediately thereafter, one should honor the partakers of the *śrāddha* with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
This is also stated in the *Padma-purāṇa* and the *Mātsya-purāṇa*:
"Having offered the *arghya* with the verse 'yā divyāḥ,' one should then give the perfumes and other items."
And having given the upper garment and the rest in successive order, one should first offer the residue of the offering water.
Having placed it in the vessel for the ancestors, one should then set it down upside down to the north;
having set it down with the words, "Thou art the seat for the ancestors," one should serve the food.

The meaning of this is as follows: having offered the *arghya* water with the mantra beginning "yā divyā," one should then, first of all, pour the *saṃsravas*—the remnants of water remaining in the vessels for the grandfather and others—into the vessel for the ancestors. Having placed that vessel face-down to the north of the row of twice-born guests who are to eat, using the mantra "pitṛbhyaḥ sthānam asi," one should set it down. After setting it down, one should offer perfumes and so forth—namely, perfume, flowers, incense, and lamps—and having given garments in their proper order, those which are to be given as upper cloths (*uttara-vastra*), and having performed the *agnaukaraṇa* rite, one should serve the food.
Yājñavalkya states that the vessel for the remnants (saṃsrava) should be turned face down on the ground itself, and not upon a stool, a grass mat, a wooden trough, or similar objects:
