"Having offered the arghya water and having placed the remnants of those offerings in the vessel according to the rule, he turns the vessel face down below, saying: 'Thou art the place for the ancestors.'"
*Adha* means on the ground itself;
for this very reason, [it is said] *pracetāḥ*.
However, having collected all the remnants (*saṃsrava*) into the first vessel for the ancestors (*pitṛpātra*),...
Having said, "This is the place for the ancestors," he should place [the vessel] face down upon the ground.
And this [rite] must be performed face-down upon ground covered with *kuśa* grass;
likewise, the traditional teaching (*smṛti*) has been shown here by the teacher Bhāḍala.
"One should place it face down upon *darbha* grass.
Thus [it is said]. We too shall present the statement of Kātyāyana on this point.
Dakṣa describes the sprinkling of the ground where the vessels are to be placed, accompanied by mantras:
With the words, "May the worlds be purified," he should sprinkle [water] on the ground and scatter *kuśa* grass with the formula, "Thou art the place for the ancestors.
The *yajus* consists of this much: "May the worlds, the seats of the ancestors, be purified."

In the *Kātyāyana-vacana* presented by Śaṅkhadhara and Aparārka, however, another mantra is prescribed for the overturning [of the vessel]. Having sprinkled it with water and sesame seeds using the mantra, "May the worlds, the seats of the ancestors, be purified," one should place that vessel face-down with the mantra, "Thou art the seat of the ancestors. Regarding this, Śaṅkhadhara maintains that because the purpose of the action is identical here, this [mantra] is an alternative to the mantra, "Thou art the place for the ancestors."

[1303] However, Pracetas has stated that the mantra "May they be purified" (*śudhyantām*) is to be employed when touching the vessel that is about to be set down; he also prescribed turning the vessel, which contains the *pavitra* grass, face-down and placing *kuśa* grass upon it.

One should touch the vessel for the remnants of the *arghya* water with the mantra "May they be purified" (*śundhantām*), and one who possesses the *pavitra* should turn it face-down with the mantra "Thou art the place for the ancestors" (*pitṛbhyaḥ sthānam asi*).
"Having placed *kuśa* grass upon that [vessel]" means:

having taken those purifiers (*pavitra*) which were removed from the *arghya* vessels and placed in the hands of the Brahmins, one should turn the vessel face down together with them; and this "togetherness" is as follows. In this regard, those who perform the pouring of the *svadhā* offering upon those very purifiers place them with their tips pointing south beside the turned-down vessel. However, for those who perform the pouring of the *svadhā* offering upon *darbha* grass distinct from those [purifiers], they turn the vessel face down upon those very purifiers. Vaijavāpa also [states this].
Having placed *kuśa* grass upon that, one should offer [the oblation] beginning with the gods;
the phrase "one should offer" and so forth is a constituent part of the subsequent sentence.
Kātyāyana said:

"Herein is the offering of perfumes, flowers, incense, and lamps. Regarding the word "herein" (*atra*), it refers to when the vessel has been turned face down. Some, however, explain that "herein" means at this specific occasion there is the offering of perfumes and so forth to the Brahmins. That too is not contradictory, as it is seen to be in agreement with other scriptural statements. Atri, for his part, states that the turning of the vessel face down occurs only after the spot has been honored with perfumes, flowers, and the like; that the covering of the vessel once it is face down is done with the very same mantra used for worship; and that the covering vessel itself must also be worshipped:
"Having worshipped that [spot] with perfumes and so forth, one should cover it with the third [mantra]."
With the words, "Thou art the place for the ancestors," he should worship in a clean and consecrated spot.
In this context, it should be understood that one should cover [the vessels] with a second [lid].
However, in the *Brahmapurāṇa*, the worship of the ancestors with water for the feet (*pādya*) and other offerings is stated to take place once the vessels have been turned face down;
subsequently, while those *arghya* vessels remain covered, one [worships] the ancestors.
One should worship them, beginning with the ancestors, with water for the feet, respectful offerings, flowers, and so forth.

Although it has been stated that "one should worship [the vessels] with covers," nevertheless, the worship must be performed in the supreme vessel (*sarvottara-pātra*) which is without a cover. This is because the word *sāpidhāna* (with a cover) is commonly applied even to that which lacks a cover. Therefore, for the sake of the straightforwardness of the statement "in the *arghya* vessels with covers" regarding these *arghya* vessels, one should not imagine another non-*arghya* vessel to serve as a cover for the *arghya* vessels.

Furthermore, Āpastamba and Yama state that this worshipped vessel, having been turned face-down (*nyubjīkṛtya*), must not be lifted up until the time of the dismissal of the Brahmins and other subsequent rites.
One should not lift up first the vessel from which the *arghya* was offered to the ancestors; they remain seated there, surrounded, until the dismissal of the Brahmins.

"First" means before the dismissal of the Brahmins, or prior to the time of dismissing the Brahmins, or prior to the time of the inquiry regarding their satisfaction. "The vessel turned face-down for the *arghya* of the ancestors" refers to the vessel placed upside down during the *arghya* rite for the ancestors; one must not lift it up. For the ancestors remain there, covered by that vessel. The explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) states that if it were lifted, they would depart like householders whose houses have been destroyed, even though they were previously sheltered. Therefore, one must not lift it before the three aforementioned times, since the mention of the dismissal of the Brahmins is intended to indicate all three points in time.
Also in the Āśvalāyana Gṛhyasūtra:
"One should not remove first the vessel from which the water-offering (arghya) for the ancestors was poured;
the ancestors remain there enclosed," so said Śaunaka.
The fault in such an extraction is also stated in that very same place:
"If a Brāhmaṇa, weak in knowledge, should extract [the portion] for a worthy recipient,
that Śrāddha becomes unfit to be eaten once the assembly of ancestors has departed in anger."
Āpastamba and Yama have also stated the fault:
"If the vessel is lifted up, or if it should be uncovered,
that śrāddha shall become unfit to be eaten by the gods together with the hosts of ancestors."
Uśanas, however, has stated that there is a fault even in lifting [the vessel]:
"When the vessel for the ancestors is turned face up or uncovered,
that food becomes unfit to be eaten, as the hosts of ancestors depart in anger."
"Exposed" means uncovered.
However, Yama and Kātyāyana have stated that there is a fault in touching such a thing:
"That which has been touched, lifted up, moved elsewhere, or likewise uncovered [is considered abandoned]."
Upon seeing the vessel, the ancestors depart quickly and utter curses.

"Spṛṣṭam" means touched by the hand or other limbs; "uddhṛtam" means lifted up; "anyatra nītam" means moved to another place; "udghāṭitam" means having the lid removed; "pātram" refers to the vessel for the *arghya* offering. Having seen these, the ancestors "depart," that is, they abandon the site of the *śrāddha*, and they "curse," meaning they utter words of undesirable results directed at the sacrificer, such as, "May you be childless, short-lived, or poor. In this context, since the capacity to perform actions such as lifting exists only through touching, the mention of the fault regarding mere touching establishes the fault in lifting and so forth as well. Nevertheless, they are mentioned separately to indicate an intensification of the fault. Alternatively, they are mentioned separately so that a fault may apply even when one lifts [the vessel] with a staff or similar object without direct contact.
Thus [ends] the section on the application of the remnants and so forth.
Now follows the manual for the ritual procedure (*prayogapaddhati*).

The performer, endowed with the ancestral rites (*pitr-dharma*) as previously described, having sprinkled the ground, shall place three blades of *darbha* grass with their tips pointing toward the south. Upon these, he shall set down the vessels for the paternal group—three in number—one for each—made of different materials such as metal, stone, or clay; or alternatively, all of one material, such as metal or others as specified in the section on vessels. He may do so either silently or with the mantra beginning "āmāgantu. Whether he maintains the sacred fire (*sāgnika*) or not, he places them near the fire or near the Brahmins respectively, with their tips pointing south and turned face-down. To the west of those, in the same manner, he shall likewise arrange three vessels (or one) for the maternal grandfather’s group (*mātāmaha-varga*), following the sequence of placement, and sprinkle them. Then he should turn them face-up, or set them down face-up from the start. In each of these, he shall place *pavitra* strainers made of three blades of grass doubled over, with their tips pointing south. With the mantra "śanno devīr," or with the *mahāvyāhṛtis* and the *āpohiṣṭhīya* verses, he shall pour water into each vessel using the *pitṛ-tīrtha* (the part of the hand between the thumb and ring finger) of his right hand, while his left hand is joined to the space between the index finger and thumb or merely touched by it. Immediately after, he shall scatter sesame seeds with the mantra beginning "tilosi," and place fragrant paste with the mantra "gandhadvārām" or silently. He shall scatter flowers with the mantra "śrīś ca te" or silently. A performer following Baudhāyana should also add honey and clarified butter with the mantras beginning "madhuvātā. However, the scattering of fragrance, flowers, and unbroken rice (*akṣata*) should be performed with the three mantras beginning "namaḥ pitṛbhyaḥ. One following the *Nigama* tradition should place the aforementioned substances along with milk and curd. One who respects the *Kālikā-purāṇa* and *Brahma-purāṇa* should also add barley, mustard, sesame, rice, and the tips of *kuśa* grass. Thereafter, every performer, having cast away impurities with the mantra "nirastaṃ na mumuceḥ," shall take the *kuśa* strainers from the vessels with both thumbs and ring fingers using the mantra "devo vaḥ savitā" or silently. Having purified them and placed three *kuśa* blades upon them, he shall consecrate them with the *Sāvitrī*. With palms joined, he asks the paternal Brahmins: "Oṃ, may there be success (*saṃpatti*) for the paternal *arghya* vessels? When they reply, "Oṃ, may there be success for the paternal *arghya* vessels," he shall place the *arghya* vessels, together with the spread *darbha* grass and with tips pointing south, before the twice-born, saying "svadhārghyāḥ. Then, having given water into the hand of the first paternal Brahmin and placed the *kuśa* strainer from the first *arghya* vessel with its tip pointing south into his hand, he shall meditate on his father in his true form. Worshipping the Brahmin from head to foot or foot to head with sesame, fragrance, and flowers while reciting "namo vaḥ," he shall lift the *arghya* vessel with both hands, utter the mantra beginning "yā divyā," and offer the *arghya* water from the vessel into the hand already holding the strainer, using the *pitṛ-tīrtha* of his right hand, while pronouncing: "Oṃ, O [Gotra], O [Name] Śarman, our father, accompanied by your wife, in the form of Vasu, this is your *arghya*, svadhā, obeisance! This is your *arghya*, svadhā, obeisance! A performer following the schools of Āśvalāyana or Śaunaka shall lift the *arghya* vessel with the left hand and pour the water from the vessel into the hand using the *pitṛ-tīrtha* of the right hand, tilted downward. One who respects the *Brahma-purāṇa* mentioned below shall, after pronouncing the *gotra* and name in the vocative case, say "this *tilodaka* is for you," and while pouring water with the right hand from the vessel lifted by the left, he shall give the *arghya* through the *pitṛ-tīrtha* of the right hand. Immediately after, taking the *pavitra* from that vessel and placing it in the hand of the second Brahmin (who represents the grandfather), he shall pour some of the *arghya* water from that vessel into that hand as before, leaving behind a small portion known as the *saṃsrava*. One who considers the term *saṃsrava* to refer specifically to what has flowed from the Brahmin's hand need not leave a remainder; rather, he should hold that which flowed from the hand in another vessel for the purpose of the *saṃsrava* rite. Then, having given water into the hand of the first Brahmin representing the grandfather, and placing the *kuśa* strainer from the grandfather’s vessel with its tip pointing south into his hand, he shall meditate on the grandfather in his true form and worship the Brahmin. Lifting the vessel and reciting "yā divyā" etc., he shall address him: "Oṃ, O [Gotra], O [Name] Śarman, our grandfather, accompanied by your wife, in the form of Rudra... and perform everything as before using the grandfather’s *arghya* vessel into the hands of the Brahmins representing him. Similarly, having given water into the hand of the Brahmin representing the great-grandfather, and placing the *pavitra* from the great-grandfather’s vessel with its tip pointing south into his hand, he shall meditate on the great-grandfather in his true form and in the form of Āditya. Reciting up to "yā divyā" and addressing him: "O [Name] Śarman, our great-grandfather, accompanied by your wife, in the form of Āditya," he shall perform everything as before using the great-grandfather’s *arghya* vessel into the hands of the Brahmins representing him. After this, he shall offer *arghya* to the maternal grandfather’s group (*mātāmaha-varga*) in the same manner as the paternal group, preceded by the respective *gotra* and other details. In both groups, one should note that the use of the vocative case is optional with respect to the dative case when pronouncing the *gotra* and other details. One following the *Nigama* school shall take the *arghya* water from the cups (*camasa*) of the paternal, paternal-grandfather, and paternal-great-grandfather, and according to the prescribed procedure, first pour it into the hand of the paternal Brahmin, preceded by the *gotra* etc. in the genitive case. Then, taking from the paternal-grandfather’s, great-grandfather’s, and paternal cups, he shall pour it into the hand of the paternal-grandfather’s Brahmin; and taking from the great-grandfather’s, paternal, and paternal-grandfather’s cups, he shall pour it into the hand of the great-grandfather’s Brahmin, completing the rest as before. Finally, the performer, wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*yajñopavītī*) and facing east, shall collect the remaining water from the paternal *arghya* vessels—or the *arghya* water trickling from the fingers of the paternal Brahmins—into the paternal *arghya* vessel. Having consecrated it with the mantra "arghyaṃ svadhā yāḥ," he shall take the *saṃsrava* water in his right hand and, if desiring sons, anoint his own face with the mantra "ye devāḥ."

Respecting the *Brahmapurāṇa*, one who desires a son, wearing the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) and facing east, should look at the reflection of his own face in the remaining *arghya* water contained in the vessels belonging to the father and others, using the mantra beginning with "May the worlds be purified" (*śundhantāṃ lokāḥ*). However, one who desires long life, while maintaining the ritual requirements such as the sacred thread, should pour the remnants of the father’s *arghya* into the father’s *arghya* vessel, or place the grandfather’s vessel into the father’s vessel and the great-grandfather’s vessel into that; then, having poured water from those very vessels into his own right hand, he should silently apply collyrium to his eyes. Following the custom of the Vājasaneyins, however, someone seated on the row of Brahmins invited for the ancestors (*pitrya*), facing north and wearing the sacred thread, should perform an aspersion upon the sacrificer—who is seated facing east and wearing the sacred thread—using the remnants collected in the first paternal vessel, with the mantra: "The waters are auspicious, most auspicious" (*āpaḥ śivāḥ śivatamāḥ*). Thereafter, wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvīta*) and facing south, one who has no desire [for a son or long life] should pour all the remnants used for the ritual of applying collyrium to the mouth and so forth—either by pouring them out repeatedly or not at all—into the *darbha* grass placed beneath the vessels, using the mantra: "May there be inexhaustibility for the ancestors" (*pitṛbhyo ’kṣayyam astu*). Then, having sprinkled the area defiled by the movement of water to the north of the row of twice-born invited for the Viśvedevas, and having spread *kuśa* grass with the tips pointing south, he should turn the paternal vessel upside down with the mantra: "Thou art the seat of the ancestors" (*pitṛbhyaḥ sthānam asi*) or "Thou art the dwelling of the ancestors" (*pitṛṣadanam asi*), along with the *pavitra* strainers. He should then cover that with the grandfather’s vessel, and that with the great-grandfather’s vessel, placing *kuśa* grass on top. Alternatively, having touched the vessel with the mantra "May the worlds be purified," he may perform everything from turning it upside down to placing the *kuśa* grass. One who maintains the flow of the remnants until the recitation of the *svadhā* should place the vessel face up there and perform the covering and so forth as before. Immediately after, he should worship the ancestors—the deities of the *śrāddha*—with perfumes, flowers, incense, and lamps. One should act in the same manner for the *śrāddha* of the maternal grandfathers and others.
Thus ends the description of the *arghya* offering. Now follows the presentation of the fragrance and other items.
Regarding this, Manu and Bṛhaspati state the following rule:
Having seated those Brahmins on the censured seats,
he should worship them with fragrant perfumes and garlands, beginning with the gods.

The meaning of this is as follows: After they have been seated, one should honor those seated Brahmins with perfumes (*gandha*) and garlands (*mālya*). "Perfumes" refers to saffron, camphor, and the like; "garlands" refers to flower wreaths. The inclusion of the word "fragrant" (*surabhi*) is an adjective qualifying the garlands; therefore, one should not give flowers that lack fragrance. This same qualification is also appropriately applied to the perfumes for the purpose of excluding unpleasant odors. Alternatively, the mention of "fragrant" may be explained as an independent term intended to include incense (*dhūpa*). Regarding the phrase "previously" (*pūrvakam*): having first given to the gods and the Brahmins, one should then give to the ancestors (*pitṛs*). They say that this repetition of the rule regarding precedence for the gods is for the purpose of indicating that once the meal has commenced, there is no such restriction regarding the serving of drinks, side dishes, and so forth. Otherwise, what would be the point of stating it again? "Ablameable" (*ajugupsitān*) means blameless Brahmins. This is a restatement (*anuvāda*), since only such individuals were previously prescribed. Alternatively, even though the suffix indicates a past action (*bhūtapratyaya*), this is actually a prohibition against performing the action denoted by the verbal root. Thus, it means: "one should not feel contempt for or revile those who are seated. He considers it better to abandon the meaning of the suffix than to abandon the meaning of the entire word. For if it were merely a restatement, the entire word would be redundant.
Baudhāyana, however, states that the offering of perfumes and other items follows immediately after the *arghya* water:

"Then, having caused these [Brāhmaṇas] to accept water mixed with sesame seeds, and having adorned them with perfumes and garlands. Here, "then" (*atha*) means immediately after they have been seated; "these" (*etān*) refers to the Brāhmaṇas representing the ancestors; and "water" (*apaḥ*) refers to the water intended for the *arghya* offering.
Śaṅkha and Likhita have also stated that the gift of incense should be made, saying:
"having adorned [the deity] with perfumes, garlands, and incense. This is found in the Nāgarakhaṇḍa.
Then, however, one should procure sandalwood and other such illuminating substances.
"Then" means immediately after the offering of the *arghya*.

In the *Kauśikasūtra*, however, the presentation of both collyrium and the mirror is also mentioned: "The bringing of perfume, garlands, incense, collyrium, the mirror, and the lamp. Since the purpose of bringing these is visible, it should be understood that the duty to provide them must be fulfilled among the Brahmins.
In the *Āśvalāyanagṛhya*, however, the gift of clothing is also mentioned:
"At this time, there is the offering of perfumes, garlands, incense, lamps, and clothing. The word "at this time" (*etasmin*) refers to the period immediately following the offering of the *arghya*.
In the Bodhāyana-sūtra as well:
"Then, having honored these [deities] with garments, perfumes, incense, lamps, and garlands according to what is available, he asks: 'Let [the fire] be taken out'."

‘Yathopapādam’ means according to the excellence of one’s birth, qualities, and caste; ‘pṛcchati’ means that he should ask the seated Brahmins, for the purpose of the *agnaukaraṇa* rite, by making the inquiry: “Let all kinds of food be brought forth. Likewise, regarding the phrase “having offered the *svadhā*, having honored the ancestors with clothing, food, fragrance, flowers, incense, and so forth, and having obtained their permission,” the term ‘*svadhā*’ refers to the water for the *arghya* offering. Although the tradition prescribes the giving of clothing prior to the offering of fragrance and other items, nevertheless, setting aside the order of the text, that [offering of clothing] should be performed immediately after the offering of incense and lamps.
And so it is said in the *Kālikā-purāṇa*:
"Then, having first worshipped the gods and established the presence of the ancestors,
one should worship them with effort according to the rule, using perfumes, garlands, and other offerings."
But at the conclusion of the incense and lamps, one should offer a garment.

"Having imagined their presence" means having imagined the proximity of the ancestors through the rite of invocation (*āvāhana*); or alternatively, having imagined and established the presence of the Brahmins representing the ancestors immediately after the worship of the Viśvedevas, one should worship the ancestors there. "With perfumes and so forth" means with fragrant substances; "with perfumes" refers to sandalwood and the like. One should also worship them with garlands. "One should provide clothing" means one should provide it by joining it with one's sons and others—that is, one should give it for their sake.
This is also stated in the *Padma* and *Matsya* Purāṇas.
Having offered the *arghya* with the verse beginning "That divine," one should then offer the fragrance and other items;
having given the garments and so forth in due order, starting from the beginning, one should offer the remnants of the previous offerings.

Having offered the *arghya* with the mantra "yā divyā," one should offer the "fragrances and so forth"—namely, perfume, flowers, incense, and lamps—as well as the "upper garment"—the cloth which is given—unto the ancestors. Then, having placed the remaining water from the vessel into the ancestral vessel (*pitṛpātra*), one should turn that vessel face down in the northern direction; this is the connection [of the passage]. "In due order" (*anupūrva*) means sequentially: first having offered perfume, then flowers, then incense and lamps, and finally the covering.
According to Vaijavāpa, however, after the gift of the covering garment, the gift of the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) is prescribed:
"Having placed *kuśa* grass upon it, one should first offer perfumes, flowers, incense, and a lamp, as well as cloth and the sacred thread, beginning with the deities."

Having placed *kuśa* grass, fragrance, and flowers upon that vessel turned face-down (*nyubjīkṛta*), one should offer the fragrance and other items into the hands of the Brahmins representing the ancestors (beginning with the father), preceded by those representing the Viśvedevas. By this sequential instruction of the offering of ancestral fragrance and so forth together with the divine (*daiva*) fragrance and so forth, it is understood that the worship (*arcana*) for both the gods and the ancestors must be performed according to the method of "sequential performance of individual items" (*padārthānusamaya*). Therefore, an option between this *padārthānusamaya* and the "sequential performance of sections" (*kāṇḍānusamaya*) mentioned by Yājñavalkya should be recognized. Nor should it be said that this [method] applies only from the offering of fragrance onwards, while prior to that there is only *kāṇḍānusamaya*; for that would result in an inconsistency in the ritual procedure (*prayoga-vairūpya*). Furthermore, Paiṭhīnasi has recorded that the performance prior to the offering of fragrance and so forth—such as requesting permission with the words, "I shall invoke the gods and the ancestors"—is indeed prescribed. Moreover, the immediate succession of the placement of *kuśa* grass upon the face-down vessel to this offering of fragrance and so forth should also be understood as optional, because the aforementioned Matsya Purāṇa passage, cited continuously, makes it clear that it must necessarily be performed even before that. Regarding the phrase "clothing and sacred thread" (*vastrayajñopavītake*): one should give clothing and the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*). Nor does this mean that "in the absence of clothing, the sacred thread [is given]" (*vastrābhāve yajñopavītakaṃ*).

It should be understood that the sacrificial thread (*yajñopavīta*) prescribed by Vṛddha-Śātātapa is merely a substitute for the [actual] garment, because this would contradict the compound word which expresses a conjunction [of items], and because it would result in subverting the instruction for the gift of an independent sacrificial thread demonstrated in the section on the *yajñopavīta*.
Viṣṇu, however, has also mentioned the gift of ornaments:
"Having offered [the deity] unguents, garments, flowers, ornaments, and incense, one should worship the Brahmins according to one's ability."

The meaning is that having presented the ointments and so forth to the Brahmins with the ancestors and others in mind, and having honored and adorned them with those offerings, one should perform what is about to be described.
This concludes the procedure for the offering of perfumes and other items. Now follows the manner of performing the offering of perfumes and other items.

In this regard, the mantras demonstrated for the offering of perfumes (*gandha*) and other items to the *Viśvedevas* should be understood to apply to the offering of perfumes and other items to the ancestors (*pitṛs*) as well. This is because the statement from the *Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa*, beginning with "And this lamp is the light in the rite for the gods and the rite for the ancestors," which establishes their commonality, was presented in the section on the offering of perfumes and other items to the *Viśvedevas*. In exactly the same way, even when the performer of the *śrāddha* performs the anointing of the limbs with perfumes, the act of making them sacred (*pavitrakaratva*) is performed again by the twice-born (*dvijas*); this should be understood here as well, based on the statements presented in that specific context. Likewise, for the sake of accomplishing the worship with perfumes and other items, the rules are to be understood as identical: the non-removal of the upper garment (*uttarīya*) and the sacred thread (*upavīta*) from the shoulder of the Brāhmaṇa by the performer of the *śrāddha* and the Brāhmaṇa himself; the non-making of circular sectarian marks (*puṇḍra*); the wearing of garlands by the Brāhmaṇa only upon the crest-lock (*śikhā*); and the precedence of water in the offering of perfumes and other items. However, the specific distinction is now stated: at the conclusion of reciting the mantra beginning with *gandhadvārām* during the offering of perfumes and so forth, one must utter the names and lineages (*gotra*) of the father, grandfather, and great-grandfather.
And so it is said in the Ādityapurāṇa:
"Therefore, one who knows the Dharma should burn incense for this purpose, dedicating it to the ancestors;
having proclaimed their names, lineages, and so forth, he should offer it to each one individually."

Since by the offering of incense an inexhaustible satisfaction arises for the ancestors (*pitṛs*), for this reason one should burn incense—such as *guggulu* and the like, mixed with clarified butter and honey—as prescribed in the section on incense, before the Brahmins, after first pronouncing the names and lineages (*gotra*) while designating the ancestors; and one should offer it to them, meaning one should present it with the ancestors in mind. Although here the pronouncing of the name, lineage, and so forth is understood specifically in connection with the offering of incense, it should nevertheless be applied to the offering of perfumes (*gandha*) and other items as well.
Therefore, Paiṭhīnasi says:
Having pronounced the names and lineages, one endowed with faith should offer perfumes and other articles to the Brahmins on behalf of the ancestors, beginning with the deities.
By the word "etcetera" (ādi), flowers, incense, and coverings are included. For this very reason, Hārīta says:

"Having taken the scents and having uttered the name of the paternal lineage, and having touched water, one should likewise offer incense, lamps, garlands, and coverings for the other two [ancestors]."

Having poured water into the hand of a Brāhmaṇa for the sake of the ancestors, and having taken fragrant substances such as sandalwood, saffron, camphor, and so forth, he should pronounce the name and lineage of the father in the manner to be described. Having given the fragrance into the very hand of the Brāhmaṇa and sipped water, he should likewise offer flowers, incense, a lamp, and a garment. Regarding "the other two"—that is, the grandfather and great-grandfather—"in the same way" means just as with the father; having given the items from the fragrance down to the garment into the respective hands of those Brāhmaṇas, he should touch water. Having thus performed the offering of the fragrance and the rest, the performer of the Śrāddha, with palms joined in reverence, should mutter this *ṛc*: "The Ādityas, the Rudras, and the Vasus."
And likewise, there is a scriptural indication in the *Brahma Purāṇa*:
"Having worshipped them again with perfumes and other offerings, and having offered incense with devotion,
the Lord recited the *ṛc* verse beginning with 'ādityā rudrā vasavaḥ'."
Having honored those ancestors, beginning with the father, with fragrant flowers and performing the rites up to the offering of garments, Varāha recited this verse:

"May the Ādityas, Rudras, and Vasus, having well-prepared the earth, the ground, and the intermediate space, release the sacrifice; may the gods, being of one accord, raise up the banner of the rite. From this it is understood that even by another person performing a *śrāddha*, this verse should be recited at the conclusion of the offering of perfumes and other items. However, in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*, it is stated that while looking at the twice-born (the Brahmins), one should mutter this very mantra.
Having always reverently honored the Brahmins with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings,
he should then gaze upon the twice-born— who are the Ādityas, Rudras, and Vasus— and recite the mantra.

In this context, although the simultaneity of reciting and looking is understood from the expression "one should recite while looking," nevertheless, the looking at the twice-born must be performed precisely at the conclusion of the utterance of the mantra, because in that case it serves as the *karaṇa-mantra* (instrumental mantra).
And so Viṣṇu says:
"Having honored the Brahmins, one should look [at them] with the mantra: 'The Ādityas, Rudras, and Vasus'."
Here, because of the use of the instrumental case—as in the mantra, "He grasped this rein of Truth"—it is understood that these are *karaṇa-mantras* (instrumental mantras).
However, a different set of mantras is stated in the *Kaṭha-sūtra*:

"With the three verses beginning 'Those who stand uninvoked,' 'Speech,' and 'That which my mother,' he should bring the water for the feet, the guest-offering (*arghya*), and the water for sipping (*ācamanīya*); with these very same [verses], 'The Ādityas, Rudras, and Vasus,' he asks, 'Shall I perform the fire-ritual (*agnau karavāṇi*)? while looking at them."

In this context, since the mantras have already been introduced by the pronoun "by these" (*etābhiḥ*), the phrase "the Ādityas, the Rudras, the Vasus" should be explained as being intended merely to convey the actual form of the words, including the particle *iti*.

In this regard, the procedure for the offering of perfumes (*gandha*) and other items is as follows: The performer, endowed with the ancestral rites (*pitryadharma*) such as wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvīti*) as previously described, takes a paste of fragrant sandalwood and the like from the hand of the first seated Brāhmaṇa representing the ancestors. Reciting the mantra beginning with *gandhadvārām*, he says: "Oṃ, O our fathers of such-and-such lineage (*gotra*), named such-and-such Śarman, together with your wives, in the form of the Vasus—this perfume is for you; *svadhā*! Salutations, salutations! Having said this, he offers it into the water-sprinkled hand of the Brāhmaṇa. When the Brāhmaṇa replies, "It is fragrant," the performer should touch water and proceed in the same manner to offer the perfume to the second and subsequent Brāhmaṇas seated in the place of the ancestors. Then, substituting the word *pitāmaha* (grandfather) for *pitṛ* (ancestor), and *rudra* for *vasu*, he should offer the perfume to the Brāhmaṇas representing the grandfather in those same two places, sequentially substituting *prapitāmaha* for *pitāmaha* and *āditya* for *rudra* for the Brāhmaṇas representing the great-grandfather. He should perform the offering of perfume to the Brāhmaṇas representing the maternal grandfather using the same formula as before, saying: "O our maternal grandfathers of such-and-such lineage, named such-and-such Śarman, together with your wives, in the form of the Vasus. Then, substituting *pramātāmaha* (maternal great-grandfather) or "mother’s grandfather" for *mātāmaha*, and *rudra* for *vasu*, he should offer it to the Brāhmaṇas representing the maternal great-grandfather. Subsequently, substituting *vṛddhapramātāmaha* or "mother’s great-grandfather" for *mātāmaha*, and *āditya* for *rudra*, he should offer the perfume to the Brāhmaṇas representing the maternal great-great-grandfather using the same formula for the maternal grandfather. Thereafter, the performer of the *śrāddha* should, in order, smear those perfumes on the foreheads and other limbs of the Brāhmaṇas, or they may do so themselves. Immediately after, taking auspicious flowers and leaves along with the perfumes, and reciting the verse *puṣpavatīm*, he should substitute the word *puṣpa* (flower) for *gandha* (perfume) and offer flowers and leaves to the hands of the Brāhmaṇas using the same formula as before. In the same way, reciting *dhūr asi*, he should substitute *dhūpa* for *gandha* and offer incense using the previous formula. Likewise, he should offer a lamp by substituting *dhūpa* with one of these phrases: "This is a lamp," "This is your light," or "This is the illumination of a lamp. In this same manner, having uttered the words denoting each specific item to be given, he should present garments, ornaments, and so forth. After that, with palms joined in reverence, the performer should say to the Brāhmaṇas representing the ancestors, "May the worship of the ancestors be complete. When they reply, "May the worship be complete," he should perform the rites from "May the fulfillment of the resolve (*saṃkalpa*) be attained" up to the sipping of water (*ācamana*), just as in the *vaiśvadeva* rite. Following that, he should gaze at the Brāhmaṇas while reciting the mantra beginning with "The Ādityas, the Rudras, the Vasus. Having thus completed the offering of perfumes and other items, he should perform the cleansing of the *śrāddha* site and other duties. As it is stated in the *Kālikā Purāṇa*: [The text continues with the citation from the Kālikā Purāṇa.]
Having thus completed the ritual according to the injunctions of the Brahmins and in accordance with the rules,
he should again purify the ground and perform the rites for the space between the rows.
Then he should provide the vessels, and thereafter, in due order, perform the purification of the hands.

"In this manner," by this method, "by the instruction of the Brāhmaṇas" (meaning with the permission of the Brāhmaṇas), having completed the ritual actions ending with the offering of perfumes and so forth—actions involving materials such as *kuśa* grass and flowers that have fallen into the course of the worship—one should "purify" (meaning make clean) the ground damaged by the footfalls of the worshippers by removing the fallen *kuśa* grass and so forth and wiping it with the hand. Then, one should create a separation between the "rows" (meaning the space sufficient for placing the eating vessels) by means of circles drawn all around with lines of ash and other substances. One should "give the vessels" (meaning place the eating vessels) in the middle of the aforementioned circles. Then, having given water for the Brāhmaṇas to wash their hands, one should perform the washing of the vessels.
The fault in reversing the sequence of establishing the boundary and washing the hands is stated in the *Matsya Purāṇa*:
"If one should perform the purification of the hands without first establishing the boundary, that *śrāddha* becomes *āsura*; it does not reach the ancestors."

Here, by the word *maryādā*, exactly what has been explained as the interval between rows is meant. The mention of "ashes" (*bhasma*) is intended to include the flour of wild rice (*nīvāra*) and so forth.
For this very reason, it is said in the *Brahmapurāṇa*:
"And mandalas should be made with auspicious powders of wild rice."
One should avoid earth that is white, or even well-prepared ashes, as well as earth mixed with stone powder or brought from afar.
By Bhṛgu, however, the specific method for establishing the maṇḍalas according to the division of castes such as the Brāhmaṇa and others, as well as their ritual procedure, was stated:
"Then one should cause the maṇḍala to be made either with ashes or with water;
it should be quadrangular for the foremost of the twice-born (Brāhmaṇa), but triangular for the Kṣatriya."
The Vaiśya’s [purification] is said to be in the form of a circle, while that of the Śūdra is known to be by sprinkling.
"Maṇḍalākṛti" means circular in shape.
However, in the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*, the disposal of the water used for washing the hands and the vessel is stated:
"Having washed the hands, the vessel, and so forth, one who knows the ritual procedure should afterwards [dispose of them] with water."
One should pour the washing water, mixed with darbha grass and sesame seeds, into pure ground.
And it is the traditional practice of the learned that this [water] is poured into the circle for washing the feet.
Thus ends the procedure for the offering of perfumes and other items.
And the section on the worship of the ancestors is completed.
Hemādri, honored by King Mahādeva,
respectfully and skillfully composes this meritorious determination regarding the *agnaukaraṇa* rite.
Now follows the determination regarding the offering into the fire (agnaukaraṇa).

In this regard, a doubt arises as to whether the *agnaukaraṇa-homa* (the oblation into the fire) should be performed by one wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*) or by one wearing it over the left shoulder (*yajñopavītī*). Regarding this, some maintain that it should be performed by the *prācīnāvītī*, on account of the connection with the deities in the form of the ancestors and the employment of the word *svadhā* within the mantras. To explain: from the wording of the mantras shown by Śaṅkha, Likhita, and others—namely, "Svāhā to Agni Kavyavāhana" and "Svāhā to Soma Pitṛmat"—it is understood that the deity is Agni characterized as the "carrier of offerings to the ancestors" (*kavyavāhana*), and Soma characterized as "possessing the ancestors" (*pitṛmat*). In this context, "kavya" refers to the food and other substances offered to the ancestors; since these have no connection with the gods, they must be carried by Agni specifically to the ancestors. Furthermore, this is heard [stated] in the *Pitryeṣṭi* sacrifice.
"He sacrifices to Agni Kavyavāhana; he thus sacrifices to that very fire which belongs to the ancestors.
So says the Śatapatha Śruti: "Havyavāhana indeed belongs to the gods, and Kavyavāhana to the ancestors; therefore one says, 'Recite for Agni Kavyavāhana!'"

Therefore, in this context, the deity is Agni in the form of the ancestors (*pitṛ*). Now, it may be argued that a deity must be defined by the very word by which it is enjoined, and not by another; for if it were defined by another, it would indeed become something else. For this very reason, they maintain that the essential nature of the deities Indra and Mahendra—who are integrated into the ritual act—is indeed distinct. Consequently, how can the deity enjoined by the term *kavyavāhana* be said to be in the form of the ancestors?

Not so. Just as there is no contradiction in designating those who are designated by the terms *pitṛ*, *pitāmaha*, and so forth, by the single term *pitṛ* (father/ancestor), the same will hold true here as well. If it is argued that even in that case there is a contradiction, that is not correct. For if that were so, the application of the ritual properties prescribed for the *pitrya* (ancestral) rite would not be established in a rite dedicated to the *pitāmaha* and other deities. Alternatively, if it is argued that the designation by the word *pitṛ* is not contradictory because their status as ancestors is stated in another scriptural passage (*vākya*), and because they are understood to be the deities (*devatā*) from the injunction "one should give to the *pitṛs*," then—by that same logic—the designation of the fire *Kavyavāhana* by the word *pitṛ* does not lose its validity, since his nature as an ancestor is also understood through other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). The state of being "possessing ancestors" (*pitṛmatva*) in the case of Soma consists either in Soma being the substratum for the groups of ancestors beginning with Soma, or in Soma being something to be used by them. This twofold proximity to the ancestors leads, by means of an indicative mark (*liṅga*), to the understanding that Soma has the nature of an ancestor. Thus says the Śruti: "Soma indeed has the ancestors as its deity. Furthermore, this "possession of ancestors" is not a mere secondary characteristic (*upalakṣaṇa*) of Soma, but rather a qualifying attribute (*viśeṣaṇa*). Considering that this serves a visible purpose, it is understood that the ancestors, acting as the qualifying attributes, function as co-deities (*sahabhāvena devatārthatvam*). As for the rejection of Tvaṣṭṛ’s status as a deity in the passage "Tvaṣṭṛ, drink the Soma," that is unobjectionable; for in the injunction prescribing the deity, Tvaṣṭṛ is like a vessel that holds the entire portion (*kavalapātrīvat*). Moreover, the *Hārīta-smṛti* also indicates the ancestral nature of these two (Soma and Agni).

With the stirring-ladle in hand, being permitted, when he offers to Soma accompanied by the ancestors, he thereby gratifies the ancestors who have Soma as their chief and those who drink Soma; when [he offers] to Yama, son of Aṅgiras, he thereby gratifies those seated on the sacrificial grass who have Yama as their chief; when [he offers] to Agni Kavyavāhana, the maker of good offerings, he thereby gratifies those who have Agni as their chief and those who are consumed by fire; and when he puts down the stirring-ladle, he thereby gratifies his own self. Thus it is said.

Furthermore, since Kavyavāhana Agni and Soma, accompanied by the Pitṛs, are seen to function as deities in the Pitryeṣṭi included within the Cāturmāsya sacrifices, their nature as Pitṛs is established. Moreover, in that sacrifice, the worship of these two is observed to be performed with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvīta*); therefore, it must be the same in the *piṇḍapitṛyajña* oblation and the *agnaukaraṇa*. Thus, this rite being established as having the Pitṛs as its deities, the oblation must be performed by one wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder, in accordance with the Smṛti rule: "The *prācīnāvīta* belongs to the Pitṛs. Furthermore, the use of the word *svadhā* is observed in the oblation mantra.

"Oblation and homage to Soma accompanied by the ancestors; oblation and homage to Agni, the bearer of the *kavyas*. Thus [it is said]. And the utterance of "svadhā" is the unique cause of the satisfaction of the ancestors. Accordingly, the *Śatapatha-śruti* states: "One should worship Speech as a cow. It has four udders: the utterance 'svāhā', the utterance 'vaṣaṭ', the utterance 'hanta', and the utterance 'svadhā'. Of these, two udders the gods subsist upon—the utterance 'svāhā' and the utterance 'vaṣaṭ'; humans [subsist upon] the utterance 'hanta'; and the ancestors [subsist upon] the utterance 'svadhā'."
Thus it is said. Therefore, it should be performed with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītin*). Furthermore, the *Manusmṛti* explicitly prescribes the *prācīnāvīta* mode:
"Having placed the offering to the fire in the *apasavya* manner, one should perform the entire circumambulation in reverse order."
"One should offer pure water with the hand not turned to the left (apasavya).

Thus [says the text]. Furthermore, Kātyāyana in the *Chandogapariśiṣṭa* states: "He offers two oblations into the fire for the gods. Intending that the oblation constituting the *pitṛyajña* is divine (*daivika*) by virtue of the scriptural injunction for the gods mentioned in the section on the *piṇḍapitṛyajña*, and considering that the *agnaukaraṇa* oblation—which is a modification (*vikṛti*) of that [original rite]—is likewise divine, he holds that the *agnaukaraṇa* oblation must be performed while wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*upavītin*).
He offers to the gods while facing the east.

Having first stated that the rite must be performed while wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*yajñopavītin*) based on such scriptural authority (*śruti*), he has now declared, by means of another logical argument, that the duty is to be performed with the thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*). He says: "Or it should be performed with the thread over the right shoulder and facing south;
for once the oblation has been set aside for one [deity], it is not offered to another."

The meaning of this is as follows: In the Piṇḍapitṛyajña, the offering (*nirvāpa*) is performed only once with the mantra "I offer what is pleasing to you, O Fathers," for both the purpose of the *homa* deity and the purpose of the *piṇḍa* deity. Consequently, by the force of the *nirvāpa* mantra, it is understood that Soma and Agni function as deities precisely in their capacity as Fathers (*pitṛ*). If one were to accept them as deities in their capacity as gods (*deva*), it would result in the illogical conclusion that what was offered for one [set of] deities is sacrificed to another. Therefore, since the *homa* of the Pitṛyajña is characterized by the nature of the Fathers, it is performed with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvīta*) and other such ancestral rites; Āśvalāyana, considering that this very position is superior, stated in his *Piṇḍapitṛyajñasūtra* that the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña-homa* possesses the ancestral (*paitṛka*) characteristics according to his own view, while stating that it possesses the divine (*daivika*) characteristics according to the view of others: "Wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*), taking [the food] with the stirring-spoon (*mekṣaṇa*) in the manner of a formal portion (*avadāna*), he should sacrifice with the words: 'Svadhā! Adoration to Soma accompanied by the Fathers! Svadhā! Adoration to Agni, the bearer of the *kavyas*! [Then], wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*yajñopavītī*), he sacrifices first to Agni with the utterance of *svāhā*. Thus, this *agnaukaraṇa-homa* must be performed by one who wears the sacred thread over the right shoulder.

To this it is replied: The wearing of the *yajñopavīta* (sacrificial thread) is established by the perception that the rite is a *daiva-karman* (a rite for the gods), brought about through its connection with deities whose divinity is directly indicated by Vedic scripture. This overrides the notion of the *pitryatva* (character of a rite for the ancestors) of the oblation, which would have been induced by conforming to the deity characterized as a "father" inferred from signs such as being the "carrier of offerings to the ancestors" (*kavyavāhana*). Thus, the direct scriptural statement says: "Having taken it out, he offers two oblations in the fire; indeed, he approaches the gods for the sake of the gods."

"He who has established the sacred fires and performs the New and Full Moon sacrifices has thereby performed the Pitṛyajña; thus he makes amends to the gods, and being impelled by the gods, he gives this to the ancestors. Furthermore, the ritual for the gods must be performed while wearing the sacrificial cord over the left shoulder (yajñopavītin); likewise, it is heard in the context of the Piṇḍapitṛyajña: "Then the gods, having become yajñopavītins, sat down after bending their right knees.
For otherwise, this scriptural statement would be inexplicable. Indeed, [the rule] always applies.
In rites pertaining to the gods, the left hand should be used; otherwise, it would be purposeless.
Therefore, because this *homa* is directed toward the gods (*daivika*), it must be performed by one wearing the sacrificial thread over the left shoulder (*yajñopavītī*).

But if it is indeed directed toward the gods, does this not contradict the mantra for the pouring out of the oblation (*nirvāpa*), which says: "I pour out what is pleasing to the ancestors" (*pitṛbhyo juṣṭaṃ nirvapāmi*)?

Not so. Just as in the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifice, when rice grains have been set aside for multiple deities and are to be sprinkled with water, the phrase "I sprinkle you, who are pleasing to Agni" (*agnaye vo juṣṭaṃ prokṣāmi*)—where the word "you" (*vaḥ*)—applies only to certain grains and not to all; likewise, the phrase "I set you aside, who are pleasing to the ancestors" (*pitṛbhyo vo juṣṭaṃ nirvapāmi*) applies only to those portions intended for the *piṇḍas* (funeral cakes) and does not extend to those mixed in for the purpose of the *homa* (oblation). However, under the view that the entire setting aside is performed silently (*tūṣṇīm*), there is no suspicion whatsoever of a conflict with the mantra. This view is indeed possible; thus says Āpastamba: "He sets [the rice] aside in an earthen vessel with the formula 'I set you aside, who are pleasing to the ancestors,' or silently. Under the view that the setting aside is performed separately and silently, there is even less room for suspicion of conflict, and this view is held by the author of the Carakādhvaryu-sūtra.

When the *pavitra* has been removed, he offers the *caru* three times while wearing the sacrificial cord over the left shoulder (*yajñopavītī*) with his right hand; three times while wearing it over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*) with his left hand; and finally, while wearing it over the left shoulder again, he should offer oblations with the stirring-spoon (*mekṣaṇa*), saying: "Svadhā to Soma accompanied by the ancestors! Svadhā to Yama accompanied by the Aṅgirases and the ancestors! Svadhā and obeisance to Agni Kavyavāhana! Svadhā and obeisance! Therefore, there is no contradiction with the mantras for the pouring out of the grain. Furthermore, the instruction to wear the sacrificial cord over the left shoulder is observed both in the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña*—which serves as the archetype for the *agnaukaraṇa* offering—and in the *agnaukaraṇa* itself. Regarding this, Vaijavāpa states:

Having poured out the clarified butter and removed it [from the fire], wearing the sacrificial cord over the left shoulder (yajñopavītī), he offers two oblations with a stirring-spoon (*mekṣaṇa*) on the *anvāhāryapacana* fire: the first to Agni, and the second to Soma.
Thus [it is said]. The *anvāhāryapacana* is the southern fire (*dakṣiṇāgni*).
Āpastamba also says:

The *adhvaryu*, wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*upavītī*), having bent his right knee, having spread a base of ghee in the stirring-ladle (*mekṣaṇa*), having taken a portion with it and poured ghee over it, offers it in the southern fire (*dakṣiṇāgni*) with the formula: "To Soma accompanied by the ancestors, *svadhā*! Homage! With the formula: "To Yama accompanied by the Aṅgirases and the ancestors, *svadhā*! Homage! he makes the second offering; with the formula: "To Agni, the bearer of the *kavyas*, *svadhā*! Homage! he makes the third offering. Having offered the rice grains with the stirring-ladle, he places the ladle back silently. According to one view, he does not offer to Yama; thus says Sāṃkhyāyana.

Bending his right knee, wearing the sacrificial cord over the left shoulder (yajñopavītī), and sitting facing east, he offers with the stirring-spoon (*mekṣaṇa*), saying: "Svāhā to Agni Kavyavāhana; Svāhā to Soma Pitṛmat.

Now, it may be objected that the authors of the *Sūtras* have prescribed the sacrificial cord for the offering only in reference to the Piṇḍapitṛyajña, and since that [cord] is already taken up by the primary offering and is Vedic in nature, it cannot apply to this secondary (*aprakṛta*) Smārta offering made in the fire (*agnaukaraṇahoma*). Rather, it is the *prācīnāvīta* prescribed by the Smṛtis that finds its application there.

Not so. Just as the *piṇḍapitṛyajña*, although prescribed in the Śruti, is performed in the Smārta fire by virtue of a specific injunction; and just as the *prayāja* offerings and others, though belonging to the primary *Āgneya* and other sacrifices, come to be connected with the secondary *Saurya* and other sacrifices; so too shall the *upavīta* (sacred thread), which is connected to the primary *piṇḍapitṛyajña* prescribed in the Śruti, be connected—by means of extended application (*atideśa*)—to the *agnaukaraṇahoma* of the secondary Smārta rite. And this extended application is based on a direct scriptural statement. Thus says the *Āśvalāyanagṛhya*: [1324]...

Having taken up food smeared with ghee, he asks for permission, saying, "I shall offer in the fire," or "I will offer," or "I shall offer. The response is, "Please do so," or "Do it," or "Perform it. Then he offers into the fire as previously stated. The word "previously" (purastāt) means in the preceding section on the Piṇḍapitṛyajña.
This is also stated in the Kātyāyana-gṛhya-sūtra.
Having taken up food smeared with ghee, he asks, "Shall I offer in the fire? and being permitted with the words, "Do so," he offers as in the Piṇḍapitṛyajña.

Now, although the term *piṇḍapitṛyajña* (the sacrifice to the ancestors with rice-balls) is, by its primary sense, the name for the offering of the rice-balls themselves, nevertheless—just as in the case of the word "staff-bearer" (*daṇḍin*)—it should be understood that it applies to the oblation (*homa*) as well through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), just as the name *Vaiśvadeva* applies to the first seasonal festival (*parvan*) among the Cāturmāsyas. Thus, since the extension of the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) of the oblation is established by the rule "like the Piṇḍapitṛyajña," the fact that the *agnaukaraṇa* has the character of the *yajñopavīta* (wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder) becomes logically consistent.
Yājñavalkya also says:
"Having been permitted with the words 'Perform [it],' having offered [the oblation] into the fire like the Pitṛyajña..."
Pracetas also says:
"Having been authorized with the words 'Do so,' offer oblations into the fire as in the Pitṛyajña.
Thus Pāraskara also says.

"Authorized by his paternal ancestors, he offers oblations like the Pitṛyajña. [1325] Therefore, by virtue of this extended application (*atideśa*), the *agnaukaraṇa-homa* must be performed while wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*upavītī*). Furthermore, there is a direct injunction (*upadeśa*); thus says Vaijavāpa in the Gṛhya-sūtra:

"Having addressed [the fire] with the words, 'Wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder, I shall perform the offering into the fire,' one should perform the *agnaukaraṇa* (offering into the fire)," so says Gobhila. "One should offer by scooping with the stirring-spoon (*mekṣaṇa*): the first oblation with the formula, 'Svāhā to Soma accompanied by the ancestors'; the second with, 'Svāhā to Agni, the carrier of the *kavyas*. Thereafter, [the sacrificer] should wear the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*)."

In the *Chāndogya-gṛhya-sūtra*: "I shall offer in the fire"—this is the invitation. Being told by the other, "Do so," he should take portions from the sacrificial oblation (*caru*) into a bronze vessel and offer them with a stirring-ladle (*mekṣaṇa*), dipping it in each time: first with the formula, "Svāhā to Soma accompanied by the ancestors," and the second with, "Svāhā to Agni, the bearer of the offerings to the ancestors. After this, [the rule] states, "wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder" (*prācīnāvītī*).

Because the instruction to wear the thread over the right shoulder occurs after the oblation, it follows that at the time of the oblation itself, one should be wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*yajñopavītī*); this is what is intended.

But if that is so, then what is the status of the *Manusmṛti* passage beginning, "Having thus performed the circumambulation to the left around the fire, one should perform the entire rite in reverse order"?

It is replied: If this Smṛti were intended solely to enjoin the *prācīnāvīta* mode of wearing the sacred thread, then, according to the maxim "but when there is a contradiction, it should be disregarded," it would simply be set aside by the direct Vedic text (*śruti*). In reality, however, this Smṛti does not actually enjoin the *prācīnāvīta*. Accordingly, Medhātithi has provided an entirely different explanation of this verse, both according to his own view and that of others. According to the view of others: The action characterized by the casting of oblations, such as saying "Svadhā! Adoration to Agni Kavyavāhana," must be performed with the right hand while the thread is worn over the right shoulder (*apasavya*). It is not, however, to be done with both hands released, for fear of violating prohibitions such as those regarding the release of both hands. Having thus explained it according to the view of others—namely, that it refers to either both hands joined or the left hand alone—Medhātithi provides his own explanation: "The sequence (*āvṛt*) of the oblations offered in the fire—that is, the order of those being turned around—all of that one should perform *apasavya*. The meaning is that one should offer the oblations ending toward the south, not ending toward the north. Furthermore, regarding the pouring of water, as in "one should pour pure water with the *apasavya* hand," this pouring of water known as *avanejana* (sprinkling) serves to exclude the extension (*atideśa*) of the water-vessel prescribed in the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña* of the Vājasaneyī Śākhā, which states, "Then, taking a vessel of water, he sprinkles. Therefore, this Smṛti does not enjoin the *prācīnāvīta*. Alternatively, following the *Smṛticandrikā* of Śaṅkha and others, it may indeed be injunctive; even so, it will apply only to a limited number of performers who follow the Sūtras of Kātyāyana, Āśvalāyana, and so forth. For in the *Śrāddhakalpa*, Kātyāyana says regarding the *agnaukaraṇa* oblation: "Having offered as in the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña*... And regarding the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña* oblation, he himself says: "He offers with the *mekṣaṇa* ladle, saying 'To Agni' and 'To Soma'. On the occasion of explaining this Sūtra, Upādhyāya Karka stated: "The oblation should be performed by one wearing the *yajñopavīta* and facing east, because it pertains to the gods (*daivata*), for the Śruti says: 'Having taken them out, he offers two oblations in the fire, saying "To the Gods"'. [Objection: "Or rather, it should not be performed by one wearing the *yajñopavīta*, but rather by one wearing the *prācīnāvīta* alone, because it is a subsidiary part (*aṅga*) of a rite for the ancestors (*pitrya*), and because of the principle of the primary [application] to the subsidiaries (*pradhānanyāya*); for in the *Mahāpitṛyajña*, the *yajñopavīta* is enjoined for the taking of the divine clarified butter (*ājya*): 'Having become one wearing the *yajñopavīta*, he takes the clarified butters. [Reply: This rule, being an injunction to preclude the *prācīnāvīta* that might otherwise occur due to its status as a subsidiary of a rite for the ancestors, is understood to permit the *prācīnāvīta* for purposes other than the taking of the clarified butter. [Objection: "Let it be a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the *prācīnāvīta* already established by its status as a rite for the ancestors. [Reply: No, because there is no purpose for such a restatement, and because the sentence is intended to be an exception (*apavāda*) to the *prācīnāvīta*. Although two positions are seen here, nevertheless, since the position of the *prācīnāvīta* is mentioned later and is directly practiced by the followers of Kātyāyana, it is inferred to be their settled conclusion (*siddhānta*). And they are seen to observe the *prācīnāvīta* starting from the request for permission to perform the *agnaukaraṇa*. Therefore, what is stated in the *Nāgarakhaṇḍa* regarding the *prācīnāvīta* starting from the question should be adopted only by those who follow the school of Kātyāyana.
Then, O best of kings, having taken the cooked food, he should ask the Brahmins:
"I shall perform a fire-oblation (homa) for the sake of my ancestors."
O sir, let permission be granted to me who stand with my right shoulder uncovered.

"Then" means after the worship of the Brahmins representing the ancestors (*pitrya*). From the request beginning with the words "let permission be granted," which is made while remaining in the *apasavya* (left-shoulder) position, it is understood that one should wear the *prācīnāvīta* (sacred thread over the right shoulder). The *Āśvalāyana-sūtra*, however, has already been shown [to prescribe otherwise]. Although in that text the *prācīnāvīta* is mentioned first and the *yajñopavīta* (sacred thread over the left shoulder) afterwards, nevertheless, because it is observed by those belonging to that specific Vedic school (*śākhā*), the *prācīnāvīta* alone is determined to be the established rule (*siddhānta*). On the other hand, some are seen to perform the request for permission while wearing the *yajñopavīta*, yet subsequently adopt the *prācīnāvīta* during the sequence of rites that follows it. In the *Matsya-purāṇa*, however, having prescribed the *yajñopavīta* for the items from the request for permission up to the sprinkling of water (*paryukṣaṇa*), the *prācīnāvīta* is prescribed thereafter.

Having performed the sprinkling of water and other preliminary rites while wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (yajñopavītin), everything thereafter must be done by one who knows the rules while wearing it over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītin).

This too—namely, that which is prescribed in the *Śākhās* and *Gṛhyasūtras*, or by whomsoever the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) or the ancestral thread (*prācīnāvīta*) is not mentioned at all—must be adopted by those very persons. As for the statement that fire and the other deities possess the nature of ancestors (*pitṛ*) based on such indicative marks as being the "carrier of oblations to the ancestors" (*kavyavāhana*), that is not correct. For there is no authority whatsoever to establish that [fire] must necessarily have the nature of an ancestor simply because it is the carrier of oblations to the ancestors or is associated with them; therefore, the oblation does not acquire the character of a rite for the ancestors (*pitrya*) through such a connection.
Now, if...

May the ancestors who dwell among the gods be satisfied by what is offered into the fire; may those who dwell among the ancestors be satisfied by the twice-born who have been gratified; and may those who dwell among animals be satisfied by what is given upon the earth—may the ancestors be ever satisfied.
Thus, by the words of Śātātapa and others, the nature of the *homa* as pertaining to the ancestors (*pitrya*) is stated.

That is not so. Since this statement is in the form of an *arthavāda* (explanatory praise), it lacks injunctive power; therefore, the status of the *homa* and other rites as being for the ancestors (*pitrya*) is not enjoined here. Rather, the *śrāddha* is praised exactly as it is understood through other means of knowledge. The use of the word *svadhā* is an indicative mark (*liṅga*) of its being for the ancestors. Yet, by direct scriptural statement (*vacana*), the word *svadhā* is used even for the gods (*daiva*), just as the *aindrī* verse is used for the worship of the *gārhapatya* fire. Furthermore, the use of the word *svadhā* is appropriate in the *agnaukaraṇa-homa* even when the rite is for the ancestors, such as in the *nāndīmukha* ceremony, because there is an option between wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvīta*) or over the left (*upavīta*). Indeed, this rite is of a mixed nature, possessing both divine and ancestral forms. It must be performed according to either the divine or the ancestral rule, since both are seen in the mantra "svadhā namaḥ. For *svadhā* is a mark of the ancestral, while *namaḥ* is that of the divine; and thus says the Śruti: [1328] "The *svadhā* belongs to the ancestors, and the *namaḥ* to the gods."
"The utterance of *svadhā* belongs to the ancestors, and the salutation (*namaskāra*) belongs to the gods; for both are worshipped.

Regarding this, some say that because there are more injunctions concerning the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*upavīta*), the oblation must be performed by one wearing it in that manner, according to the principle that "the majority should determine the rule. Others, however, maintain that the application of the *prācīnāvīta* (worn over the right shoulder) and the *upavīta* is determined according to the specific *śākhā* (Vedic school).
Thus says Kātyāyana:
" Svāhā, svadhā, and namaḥ, as well as the left-hand and right-hand methods; and whatever the number of oblations may be, that should be understood according to one's own sūtra. Thus it is said.
Thus concludes the determination regarding the *prācīnāvīta* and other [ritual modes].
Now follows the determination regarding the locus for the *agnaukaraṇa-homa*.

The locus (*adhikaraṇa*) is of two kinds: that which has the form of fire (*agnirūpa*) and that which does not have the form of fire (*anagnirūpa*). Regarding the determination of that which has the form of fire, some say: because of the scriptural statement in the section on the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña*, "He offers in the *Dakṣiṇāgni*," and because of the traditional rule (*smaraṇa*), "And he should offer in the fire for the ancestral sacrifice as in the *Pitṛyajña*," the oblation (*homa*) is performed in the *Dakṣiṇāgni* by virtue of extension (*atideśa*). Others, however, say: since the *Śrāddha* is prescribed in the *Gṛhya-sūtras*, the fire-oblation (*agnaukaraṇahoma*) included within it is also *Gṛhya*; and since it is understood to be connected with the *Gṛhya* fire under discussion, [the oblation is performed] in the *Aupāsana* fire. Furthermore, this rite is indeed *Smārta* (based on tradition), and therefore it must be performed in the *Gṛhya* fire alone.

As Yājñavalkya has said: "A householder should perform the *smārta* rites daily in the marriage fire, or in the fire brought at the time of partition; however, he should perform the *śrauta* rites in the *vaitānika* fires."

"Smārta karma" refers to rites such as the Vaiśvadeva, the Upāsana, and the Agnihotra; these are to be performed "in the marriage fire," that is, in the fire produced at the time of marriage; or "at the time of inheritance," meaning when brought from a Vaiśya family and consecrated, one should perform them in the *aupāsana* fire. It is further implied that "śrauta karma"—rites such as the Agnihotra—should be performed in the *vaitānika* fires, namely the Āhavanīya, Dakṣiṇāgni, and others. Manu also says:
"One should perform the domestic (*gṛhya*) rite in the *aupāsana* fire according to the prescribed rule."
"The performance of the five sacrifices, the cooking of food, and whatever other domestic duties there may be. Thus [it is said].

Regarding this, those who maintain that the *aupāsana* fire serves as the locus for the rite hold that it is logical for the extended injunction (*atideśa*) to be set aside by the direct instruction (*upadeśa*). However, those who maintain that the *dakṣiṇāgni* fire is the locus argue as follows: Since the logic of parsimony in sublation (*bādhalāghava*) establishes that even an extended injunction should be favored when its sublation would otherwise be necessary, and since the sublation of what is already established is understood to be extremely defective, they conclude that—given that both the direct instruction and the extended injunction can be accommodated without mutual sublation—it is improper to accept a sublation of the extended injunction based on a logic of "no other way" (*ananyagati*). Furthermore, considering that the general statement beginning with "the rite is *smārta*" (*karma smārtam*) finds its scope in rites such as the *aupāsana*, they believe it refers to matters other than the *agnaukaraṇa*. Now, one might object: "The extended injunction is weaker than the direct instruction. What follows from this? It is not the case that something is sublated merely because it is weak; rather, that which is weak is sublated only when it has a different scope. Moreover, this extended injunction is scriptural (*vācanika*) and does not differ from the direct instruction. Therefore, whether there is a total absence of the *āhavanīya* and *aupāsana* fires due to no installation of the fires (*sarvādhāna*), or whether they exist through a partial installation (*ardhādhāna*), the *agnaukaraṇa* oblation must be performed in the *dakṣiṇāgni* during the *Amāvāsyā* Śrāddha for those who have maintained the sacred fires. However, in a Śrāddha on another lunar day, since the ritual separation of the fires (*viharaṇa*) is absent and the *dakṣiṇāgni* is unavailable, the *agnaukaraṇa* oblation must be performed in the hand of a Brahmin by one who has performed a total installation, and in the *aupāsana* fire by one who has performed a partial installation or one who maintains the fires.

[Objection: But surely, since the domestic fire (*gṛhyāgni*)—which is obtained through a general statement—is set aside by the *dakṣiṇāgni* brought in by a scriptural extension (*vācanikātideśa*), how could it regain its status as the locus for that [fire-oblation] through a subsequent return?

[Reply: Not so. For it is only when the *dakṣiṇāgni* is actually present that it would exclude that [domestic fire], but not when it is like the son of a barren woman. Therefore, the general statement excludes the performance of the fire-oblation (*agnaukaraṇahoma*) when the agent possesses the *dakṣiṇāgni*, but not the performance of that same oblation when the agent lacks such a fire. Consequently, in the absence of the *dakṣiṇāgni*, it should be performed in the *aupāsana* fire.
Regarding this, Mārkaṇḍeya says in the Viṣṇudharmottara:
"One who has maintained the sacred fires (āhitāgni), being composed, should offer oblations in the southern fire (dakṣiṇāgni);
but one who has not maintained the sacred fires (anāhitāgni) should offer them in the aupāsada fire, or in the absence of fire, in a brahmin or in water."
The *aupasada* is the domestic fire (*gṛhyāgni*). Regarding the alternative view that [the offering] may be made "in water," Kātyāyana has shown its specific scope:
"As for the view that one should perform the *agnaukaraṇa* oblation in water—that rule is to be understood as applying to a *śrāddha* ceremony when it takes place near water."
As for that which states:
"The preparation of food and the offering into the fire (agnaukaraṇa) are performed with the aupāsana fire."

Thus, the statement of Prajāpati refers specifically to the case where one possesses only the *aupāsana* fire. Therefore, according to Śambhu, Śaṅkhadhara, and others, the oblation is offered in the *dakṣiṇāgni*; however, in its absence, it is offered in the *aupāsana* fire. Others, however, maintain that when the *aupāsana* fire is present, the oblation is offered there alone, and only in its absence is it offered in the *dakṣiṇāgni*. For they consider that the extended injunction (*atideśa*), "one should offer as in the *pitṛyajña*," being a general statement, must—by conforming to the general nature of the primary instruction—apply to the extension of ordinary ritual elements other than the *dakṣiṇāgni*.
And so says the Vāyu Purāṇa:
"Having diligently brought forth the Dakṣiṇāgni for the purpose of the oblation,
or even a common fire for the sake of the fire-ritual, one should offer the sacrifice for the successful accomplishment of the rite."

The meaning of this has been explained by Aparārka. In this sentence, the word *agni* refers to the fire under discussion; and in the injunction for the performance of the *śrāddha*, the *gṛhya-agni* (domestic fire) is the subject, because the performance of the *śrāddha* is governed by the *Gṛhya-sūtras*. Since the *Gṛhya-sūtras* proceed under the heading of the *gṛhya-agni*, it is only in its absence that the injunction for the *dakṣiṇāgni* (southern fire) or the *laukika-agni* (worldly fire) in its stead would be appropriate. But if it exists, since its function is accomplished by that very fire, what is the use of prescribing another fire? Furthermore, the injunction for the performance of the *śrāddha* found in the *Dharma-śāstras* is not different from that stated in the *Gṛhya-sūtras*, due to the recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) of identity. Therefore, even in the *Dharma-śāstras*, the *gṛhya-agni* is the subject; thus, it is correct that in the phrase "for the sake of the fire" (*agnyartha*), the word *agni* refers specifically to the *gṛhya-agni* because of its being the subject. Having thus explained the meaning of this sentence, he likewise describes the meaning of Mārkaṇḍeya’s statement, "But one who has maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) should offer oblations in the *dakṣiṇāgni*," in accordance with his own view. For instance, when this injunction for an *āhitāgni* to offer in the *dakṣiṇāgni* occurs, it applies when there is no *aupāsana-agni* due to a complete installation (*sarvādhāna*); however, in the case of a partial installation (*ardhādhāna*), where the *aupāsana-agni* exists, the offering is made in that very fire and not in the *dakṣiṇāgni*. As for the statement, "And one who has not maintained the fires (*anāhitāgni*) [should act] at the *aupasada*," this is intended to establish eligibility, having raised the doubt that—due to the injunction for the *agnaukaraṇa* rite in the *dakṣiṇāgni*—one who has not maintained the fires would lack the capacity to perform the offering due to the absence of the *dakṣiṇāgni*, and thus would have no entitlement to the *pārvaṇa-śrāddha*. Therefore, its meaning is: "One who has not maintained the fires should perform it at the *aupasada*," and not "Only one who has not maintained the fires [should act] at the *aupasada*. However, this is incorrect. In the statement "But one who has maintained the fires should offer in the *dakṣiṇāgni*," no qualification of the *āhitāgni* such as "either [one who has maintained all fires] or one devoid of the *aupāsana-agni*" is heard. Nor can it be so inferred, as no grounds for such an inference are perceived. If it is argued that the inferential ground is the thought that the injunction "Smṛti rites are performed in the marriage fire" (*karma smārtaṃ vivāhāgnau*) should not be sublated, we say no. For general rules (*utsarga-śāstra*) do not apply to the domain of specific rules (*viśeṣa-vidhi*) or to the domain of exceptions (*apavāda-śāstra*). If they did, then in the case of "Let curd be given to the Brāhmaṇas, but buttermilk to Kauṇḍinya," there would follow the consequence that the specific rule and the exception would both concern the absence of curd. Now, if it is claimed that because the phrase "having fetched the *dakṣiṇāgni*" mentions "for the sake of the fire" (*agnyartha*), and since the injunction for the *dakṣiṇāgni* is understood to apply to the function of the *gṛhya-agni*, the *gṛhya-agni* is primary and the injunction for the *dakṣiṇāgni* therefore concerns its absence—that is not so. Even in the case of an unmodified (*avikṛta*) function, a modification (*vaikṛta*) is seen to sublate the original (*prākṛta*) rule, as in the case of the *phalacamasa* sublating the *soma* even in the archetype (*prakṛti*). Therefore, even regarding the function, it is logical that the *gṛhya-agni* is sublated by the *dakṣiṇāgni* in the injunction. In fact, in the phrase "for the sake of the fire," it is more logical that the word *agni* denotes the *dakṣiṇāgni* itself, as it is presented in the same syntactical unit (*ekavākya*), rather than the *gṛhya-agni*; for the proximity of the syntactical unit (*vākya-saṃnidhi*) is stronger than the proximity of the context (*prakaraṇa-saṃnidhi*). Thus, it is proper that the worldly fire (*laukika*) is prescribed here for the function of the *dakṣiṇāgni*.
