And by "worldly" here, the *smārta* *gṛhya-agni* alone is intended, not some other unrefined fire, for there is a prohibition stating that the *paitṛka-yajñiya* offering is not to be made in a worldly fire. As for that which... [text ends].
One should always cook food either in the domestic fire or in the common fire;
in whichever fire one cooks the food, in that very fire the oblation is prescribed to be offered.

Thus, in the statement of Aṅgiras, having designated the domestic fire (*gṛhya-agni*) by the term "household fire" (*śālāgni*), and having referred to any other unrefined [fire] by the term "worldly" (*laukika*), the prescription for performing oblations therein is stated; that refers specifically to the *vaiśvadeva* sacrifice.
As they say:
"Regarding 'in the household fire,' this is the sentence uttered by Aṅgiras."
"That procedure for the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice is not applicable to this oblation. Thus [it is said].

Therefore, by the word "worldly" (*laukika*), only the domestic fire (*gṛhya-agni*) is meant. And there is no purpose for an injunction regarding that [fire] with reference to the action indicated by it; for an object being enjoined in one place does not come to exist elsewhere. Nor is an injunction possible regarding what is indicated by that [fire], because the injunction of the constituent elements (*padārtha*) occurs subsequent to the establishment of the action in the archetype (*prakṛti*). Therefore, in the phrase "for the sake of the fire," it is proper to denote the southern fire (*dakṣiṇāgni*) alone by the word "fire. As for the statement made here to remove the doubt regarding the lack of qualification for the rule "if he is one who has established the fires (*āhitāgni*) and is performing the *aupasada* rites," that too is untenable, because no such doubt arises regarding the injunction of the southern fire when the *aupāsana* fire is absent. Consequently, it is established that: if one is an *āhitāgni*, the fire-oblation (*agnaukaraṇa-homa*) is performed in the southern fire; if one is not an *āhitāgni*, it is in the *aupāsana* fire; if both those fires are not present, or if they are entirely absent, it is to be performed in the hand or similar [substitutes]. In this regard, the author of the *Smṛticandrikā* has spoken following the opinion of Aparārka: For one who is not an *āhitāgni* but possesses the *aupāsana* fire, and for an *āhitāgni* who has performed partial establishment (*ardhadhāna*) and thus possesses the *aupāsana* fire, the fire-oblation is performed in the *aupāsana* fire itself. However, if that fire is absent due to travel abroad or other reasons, it is performed in the hand of a twice-born (*dvija*) or in water. For an *āhitāgni* who lacks the *aupāsana* fire because he has performed full establishment (*sarvādhāna*) or established only the *aupāsana* fire, it is performed in the southern fire. If that is also absent, it is in a worldly fire (*laukika-agni*) or in the hand etc. One who is devoid of fire—whether because he has formally adopted the *aupāsana* fire, because his fires have been extinguished, or because he is widowed—should perform it in the hand of a twice-born or in water, but never in a worldly fire. "One who possesses a sacred fire [should perform the rite] in the fire; one without a sacred fire, however, [should do so] in the hand of a twice-born or in water.
It is settled that the daily rite should always be performed in the fire using the *laukika* (worldly/common) fire.

In this context, the prohibition of the *laukika* fire applies only to one who maintains both the non-sacred and the sacred fires—that is, to the *ardhadhānin*—and not to the *sarvādhānin*. For the latter, it is said: "For the sake of the fire, or even in the *laukika* fire, one should offer oblations for the successful completion of the rite."

Since the injunction regarding the worldly fire has been shown here [in this verse], a twice-born man who maintains a sacred fire should perform the *agnaukaraṇa* offering either in his hand or in the fire.

And because of this traditional teaching (*smaraṇa*) of Parāśara: "In this context, by the word *agni* (fire), the domestic fire (*gṛhyāgni*) is meant; for as long as that exists, there is no room for the alternative of using the hands. Therefore, by the word *agni* here, either the southern fire (*dakṣiṇāgni*) or the common worldly fire (*laukika*) is designated. And by the term *sāgnika* (one who possesses the sacred fires), only those who have performed the *sarvādhāna* (complete consecration of all fires) are meant. Regarding this, first of all, the claim that an oblation (*homa*) may be offered in the southern fire only when the domestic fire (*aupāsana*) is absent has already been refuted. Furthermore, the claim that for one who has performed the *sarvādhāna*, the oblation is offered in the common worldly fire—this too has been rejected by the statement in the rule "or the worldly [fire] for the sake of the fire," where it was stated that the word "worldly" denotes the *smārta* (traditionally taught) fire, and by the fact that the term *sarvādhāna* is not heard [as a requirement]. As for the argument that since there is no room for the hand-alternative when the *aupāsana* fire exists, the word *agni* in Parāśara’s statement refers to the southern fire or the worldly fire and not to the *aupāsana* fire—that applies equally even when the southern fire is present. If there is room for the hand-alternative in the proximity of the southern fire, then it will likewise exist when the *aupāsana* fire is present. The author of the *Smṛticandrikā* has also stated another point: "When the *aupāsana* fire is unavailable due to the *sarvādhāna*, there is simply an omission of the *agnaukaraṇa-homa* prescribed by Āpastamba. For in that case, because it is *smārta*, the rule 'the Śrauta rite is performed in the *vaitānika* fires' does not result in the acquisition of the southern fire. Since it lacks the characteristics of the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña*, the extension (*atideśa*) 'one should offer like the Pitṛyajña' does not apply either. And since fire cannot be substituted, the principle of substitution does not allow for the acquisition of the southern fire or a worldly fire. Thus, due to the absence of a locus (*adhikaraṇa*), the oblation is omitted. For this very reason, Dhūrtasvāmin stated regarding the absence of the *aupāsana* fire due to *sarvādhāna*: "The *Śrāddha* should be performed after the oblation; the Brāhmaṇas are for the purpose of the *Āhavanīya* fire, because that [feeding] is also a primary element. This means that for one who has performed the *sarvādhāna*, only that portion of the *Śrāddha* subsequent to the oblation—consisting of the feeding of Brāhmaṇas and the offering of rice balls (*piṇḍa*)—should be performed. This is understood from the consideration of statements such as "the Brāhmaṇas are for the purpose of the *Āhavanīya*," since the feeding of Brāhmaṇas is also recognized as a primary element. This [position] must indeed be reconsidered, because even if it lacks the characteristics of the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña*, the acquisition of the southern fire is possible through the extension of a specific scriptural injunction (*vacanātideśa*). Furthermore, even if a locus in the form of fire is unavailable, a locus in the form of the hands is available, as prescribed by the *Smṛtis* and *Purāṇas* which are common to all. Thus, the matter remains open to investigation.
Regarding this, the *Gṛhyapariśiṣṭa* states:
"The *Anvaṣṭakya* on the day before, the monthly [offering] every month, then the *Pārvaṇa*, the optional [offering],
that for a festival, on the eighth [lunar day], and finally the *Ekoddiṣṭa* as the eighth."
"In the first four [rites], the oblation for those who maintain the sacred fires is prescribed to be offered into the fire;
in the latter four, it should be placed into the hand of the Brahmin representing the ancestors."

In this context, there are indeed eight types of *śrāddha* offerings. The *anvaṣṭakya* is the *śrāddha* performed on the ninth lunar days following the *aṣṭakās*; the *pūrvedyuḥ* is the *śrāddha* performed on the seventh lunar days preceding the *aṣṭakās*. The *pārvaṇa* is the *śrāddha* performed every month on any day of the dark fortnight, being occasioned by the new moon (*amāvāsyā*). The *kāmya* is that performed with the desire for specific results, such as sons and so forth. The *abhyudaya* is that performed on occasions of prosperity, such as the birth of a son or a marriage; it is also that performed on the eighth lunar day known as the *aṣṭakā*. Regarding the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, because it possesses the dual nature of both the primary *ekoddiṣṭa* (which lacks the *agnaukaraṇa* rite) and the *pārvaṇa*, it is designated by the term "ekoddiṣṭa" through figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*). In the first four of these *śrāddhas*, the oblation (*homa*) is offered into the fire itself for one who maintains a sacred fire (*sāgni*). In that regard, even if a certain *āhitāgni* (one who has consecrated the fires) lacks the presence of the *dakṣiṇāgni*—which is prescribed for the purpose of Vedic rites during the *aṣṭakā* and other ceremonies—and also lacks the presence of the *aupāsana* fire due to having performed a *sarvādhāna* (complete consecration), nevertheless, because the rule mandates offering into the fire, he must perform the *viharaṇa* (the ritual separation of the fires) specifically for that purpose and then perform the *homa*. This rule is to be understood as applying only to those for whom this *Pariśiṣṭa* is intended, and not to everyone.
Thus concludes the determination of the locus for the fire-form oblation (*agnirūpahoma*).
Now follows the definition of the fire that serves as the locus for the oblation,
according to the *Brahmavaivarta* and *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇas*.
One should offer oblations into a fire that has abundant dry fuel, is well-kindled, is especially free of smoke, and possesses a pure color, for the successful accomplishment of the ritual action.
A fire that is radiant, compact, cool, resembling clarified butter or gold,
glossy, and moving clockwise shall lead to the increase of one's fame.
Whoever performs a fire-oblation (homa) with such characteristics in the sacred fire attains eternal honor from hosts of men and women; likewise,
by him the ancestors become eternally honored.
Furthermore, it is declared in the Śruti: "If one who is ignorant offers oblations into a fire accompanied by smoke, the sacrificer, along with his sons, shall become blind."
Furthermore, a fire that has little fuel, or is dry, or is covered with sparks,
or turns away from the right— such a fire leads to failure.
That which is foul-smelling, blue, and especially black,
as well as that which sinks into the ground— such a place brings about defeat.
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*: "He who, possessed of hunger, thirst, anger, or haste, offers a deficient mantra into a fire that has not been kindled or is smoky, shall become blind in another birth."
When the fire is very small, dry, emitting sparks, turning counter-clockwise, terrifying,
filled with half-burnt wood, and hissing;
If one offers an oblation into a fire that has black flames, emits a foul odor, and likewise licks the earth,
his destruction will certainly occur.
In the Devīpurāṇa: [He is] radiant with the color of molten gold, bearing the luster of the sun and vermilion;
auspicious, resembling a conch shell, a kunda flower, or the moon, and like clarified butter or milk.
One that resembles the Japā flower, the Aśoka blossom, or lac-dye, and is like the color of vermilion, bestows auspiciousness for all undertakings; indeed, the opposite brings no success.
There was an auspicious sound like that of clouds, kettledrums, conchs, flutes, and lutes;
it was honored by the cries of bulls, peacocks, and ruddy geese, as well as the song of the cuckoo.
When worshipped, it possesses the white fragrance of saffron, agallochum, and camphor;
it is auspicious, bearing the forms of a swan, an umbrella, an elephant, a cow, a water-pot, and a lotus.
A fire that resembles a lion, a peacock, or a mountain; one that emits smoke shaped like a chowrie; one that has the fragrance of smoke and nectar; one resembling a parrot or a bee;
or one whose flames are broken or which weeps—such a fire is not desired for ritual acts.
A fire with a high-towering crest is auspicious; one that rises upward even in the wind, licks [the offering], is beautiful, radiant within its hearth, and grants boons, is a giver of blessings.
In the *Bahvṛca-pariśiṣṭa*:
"The man who offers oblations into a fire that lacks flames or one whose coals are extinguished is born with weak digestion, afflicted by disease, and indeed destitute."
Therefore, one desiring health, long life, and ultimate prosperity should offer oblations only when the fire is well-kindled, and never when it is unkindled.
It has been stated that one must offer oblations into a well-kindled fire. Thereafter, he describes the manner of kindling it:
"Whether desiring to sacrifice or having already sacrificed, [one should do so] with the hands, a winnowing basket, a dipping-spoon, and other such implements."
One should not blow on the fire; rather, one should fan it with a fan or similar means.
"One should blow upon the fire with the mouth alone, for it was born from the mouth;
however, as for the saying 'not [blowing] on the fire with the mouth,' that applies to the case of ordinary (laukika) fire.
Thus ends the definition of fire.
Now follows the determination of the locus for the *homa* when fire is absent.

In that regard, it has already been stated previously that even for one who maintains a sacred fire (*sāgnika*), if at some time due to travel or other reasons the fire is not present, the *homa* may be performed in the hand of a twice-born man, which constitutes a locus where no fire is present;
"A twice-born man who maintains a sacred fire should perform the *agnaukaraṇa* either in the hand or in the fire."
Thus [it is said]. Now, the oblation for one who does not maintain a sacred fire (*anagnika*) is described as being performed in the hand and so forth.
On this point, Manu and Śātātapa state:
"In the absence of fire, however, one should offer it into the hand of a Brahmin."
For that which is fire is called the twice-born by the Brahmins who perceive the mantras.

For by the statement beginning with "He who is Agni," etc., [the Brahmin] is praised through the disclosure of his capacity for the function of the fire that serves as the locus for the oblation; "by the seers of mantras" means by those who know the Veda. Furthermore, praise is seen even in the Taittirīya Śruti:
"This very one is Vaiśvānara Agni, namely the Brāhmaṇa; he offers him into Vaiśvānara Agni indeed."

Since the statement regarding the non-difference of fire is intended to express similarity, and even the description of [the Brahmin] as having the nature of the transcendental fire is based solely on superimposition (*āropa*), there is no contradiction in the Brahmin being a secondary alternative (*anukalpa*).
For this very reason, in the verse of Yama, praise is offered precisely through the similarity to fire:
"As are the fires, so are the Brahmins; as are the Brahmins, so are the fires."
"But in the absence of fire, the oblation is prescribed to be made in the hand of a Brahmin.

Regarding this "absence of fire," some say it is caused by the non-acceptance of a wife, caused by the failure to accept the fire after such acceptance, caused by the extinction of the fire once accepted, or caused by its non-proximity.

Others, however, maintain that since one whose fire has been extinguished lacks the entitlement to perform the *pārvaṇa* śrāddha and thus lacks the fire for the *agnaukaraṇa* rite, the rule regarding the hand does not apply to an absence of fire resulting from extinction.
Others, however, say:
"In the absence of fire, one should give into the right hand of a Brahmin;
the state of being without fire is traditionally held to last as long as one has not found a wife."

Thus, because the statement of Gārgya and Jātūkarṇya shows a restrictive conclusion (*upasaṃhāra*), they maintain that even when there is an absence of fire due to an undertaking made after the formal acceptance of a wife, the rule regarding the joining of hands (*pāṇi*) does not apply.

Others, however, hold that the absence of fire is certain prior to the formal acceptance of a wife; therefore, by means of that clearly perceived [absence], the absence of fire occurring even after the acceptance of a wife is indicated by the scriptural statement, but the literal hearing of "absence" is not restricted [to that specific time].

Others, however, maintain that regarding the statement, "In the absence of fire, one should offer into the hand of the Brahmin," the exclusion of other substrates—such as the absence of ordinary (laukika) fire—is effected by the word *eva*; this is established by the statement of Gārgya, which specifies that this applies only when the absence of fire is caused by the non-acceptance of a wife, and not in cases where the absence of fire occurs after marriage. Furthermore, it does not mean that the hand ceases to be a locus for the oblation even in those instances where the fire is absent subsequent to marriage. On this point, let the teachers deliberate and adopt the most reasonable position.

Here, the view of Jayantasvāmin is presented by Harihara: regarding the verse beginning with "But in the absence of fire for a Brahmin," its subject matter is specifically one who possesses fire but whose fire is sometimes or somewhere not present. For when something has a relationship with another, such usages occur even when that thing is sometimes or somewhere absent; it is possible, for instance, to have a relationship with a horse and yet employ the expression, "In the absence of a horse, you should go having mounted a mule," provided the relationship with a horse is not absolutely impossible. This is the position favored by Jayantasvāmin; however, he himself has refuted the view that this [rule] applies to all three social classes (*traivarṇika*) without exception.
For in the *Matsya Purāṇa*, the offering into the fire (*agnaukaraṇa*) is explicitly stated for the *āmanna-śrāddha* (śrāddha with raw food):
"When the giver of the śrāddha, knowing the rule, performs an *āma-śrāddha*,
he should then perform the *agnaukaraṇa* with that [raw food] and offer the funeral cakes (*piṇḍas*) with that very same [food]."
"By that very [means]" means by means of raw food (*āmadravya*).

A *śrāddha* with raw food is explicitly prescribed for a Śūdra who has not undergone the consecration by fire (*agnisaṃskāra*); for others, however, it is obtained by logical necessity as an occasional practice in the absence of cooked food.
Likewise, a Śūdra also performs the ordinary *vṛddhi-śrāddha* in the same manner.
"A wise person should perform [the rite] with the mantra 'namaskāra', just as one would with raw grain. Thus it is said.

Therefore, for a *śūdra* who is not without fire (*anagni*), since the *agnaukaraṇa* is prescribed by explicit statement (*vacana*) in the context of the *amānna-śrāddha*—whereby the specific rule of "having no material substance" (*amadravyakatva*) is enjoined as a restatement of the *agnaukaraṇa*—the *agnaukaraṇa* is performed in the hand, which is implied by that [absence of fire]. In this regard, although it is stated generally as "of the *vipra*," nevertheless, because the subject under discussion (*prakṛta*) is at hand and there is no reason to abandon what is proximate, it is understood as referring specifically to the *vipra* who is the recipient of the *śrāddha*. Furthermore, because the repetition of every limb of the principal act is forbidden, and because the singular number in "of the *vipra*" is intended to be significant, it refers only to the single person who is seated first due to his preeminence and priority. As for those who perform this oblation according to the rules of rites for the gods—with the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*yajñopavīta*) and the utterance of *svāhā*—it should be done in the hand of the *vipra* representing the gods. However, by those who perform it according to the rules of rites for the ancestors—with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvīta*) and the word *svadhā*—it should be done in the hand of the *vipra* representing the ancestors. Or rather, it may optionally be done in either the hand of the one representing the gods or the one representing the ancestors by all. Although the word "hand" (*kara*) is common to both, the oblation must nonetheless be performed with the right hand, because of the traditional teaching (*smaraṇa*) that the right hand is the performer in all rites, and because of the scriptural statement: "One should place [the offering] in the right hand. Regarding this, Kātyāyana states that the oblation is to be made in the hand of the ancestor-seated *vipra* who was seated first.
For that paternal ancestor who ascends the row, one who does not maintain a sacred fire should offer into his hand with the mantra;
for the others, he should silently place [the food] into their vessels.

The performer of the *śrāddha* who does not maintain a sacred fire (*anagnika*) should, after offering oblations into the right hand of the Brahmin seated at the head of the row—who serves as the locus for the sacrificial food offered in honor of the father, grandfather, and others—using the mantra beginning with "To Agni Kavyavāhana," place the remaining food silently into the bowls of those seated in that same row starting from the head of the row, but not into the bowls of those seated in the row for the gods. This will be explained further regarding the disposal of the remnants.

Now, an objection may be raised: since one offers two oblations into the fire with the words "to the gods," and because the *agnaukaraṇa* oblation—offered to the god Agni Kavyavāhana and to Soma Pitṛmat—is part of the rite known as the *pitṛyajña*, it shares the same characteristics as other divine rites; therefore, by virtue of its proximity, shouldn't it be performed in the hand of a Brahmin (the *daivika-viprakara*)? Why then is it said to be performed specifically in the hand of a Brahmin representing the ancestors (*paitṛka-viprakara*)? To this, it might be replied: that *agnaukaraṇa* oblation which is offered into the fire is divine, whereas that which is offered into the hand is ancestral—or indeed, he may offer it directly into their hands, for the Brāhmaṇa states: "The gods have fire as their mouth; the ancestors have the hand as their mouth."
Thus, in the Āśvalāyana Gṛhya-sūtra, because of the citation of the Śruti.

Do not say so. Since the scriptural injunction, "One offers to the gods," establishes that this *homa* has the gods as its deities, one cannot conclude that it has the ancestors (*pitṛ*) as its deities based merely on the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*)—"The ancestors have hands as their mouths"—which serves to praise the injunction regarding the hands. This is because the explanatory passage is consistent with the attribution of a paternal character (*paitṛkatva*) due to its association with the ritual acts of offering rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) and feeding Brahmins, which are dedicated to the ancestors. Alternatively, since even the *agnaukaraṇa-homa* has the satisfaction of the ancestors as its intended result, the ancestors' mouths can be figuratively attributed to the hands by way of the hands being a cause of their satisfaction; thus, the praise is logically consistent. Therefore, the claim that this *agnaukaraṇa-homa* is sometimes for the gods and sometimes for the ancestors is incorrect.
Regarding this, they say: "To offer to the gods in the fire for the ancestors—this is inconsistent.
If it is for the gods, it should always be offered to the gods; if it is for the ancestors, it should indeed be offered to the ancestors."
Therefore, when there is an obstacle caused by fate, a fire offering (homa) must be performed.
Thus Kāśyapa said:
"When a Brahmin who lacks a ring finger performs a Pārvaṇa Śrāddha..."

"In that case, the oblation in the *daivakarman* should be performed like the *agnaukaraṇa*. Here, because a logical repetition of the oblation for each individual Brahmin of the *vaiśvadeva* group is impossible, and because a collective compound (*ekaśeṣa*) would involve unnecessary complexity, the compound *viprasya karaḥ* is formed with the singular ending alone. Thus, by virtue of the intended singular number, it refers to only one deity.
This has been stated in the *Vāyupurāṇa*:
"When many twice-born men should be present at a single Vaiśvadeva rite, then the oblation should be offered with a single hand; such is the prescribed rule."

First, when one adopts the position that "one [brāhmaṇa] at each [of the two groups], or one at both," then it is established that the oblation (*homa*) is to be performed in the hand of only one brāhmaṇa at the *vaiśvadevika* rite. Even when adopting the position of multiple brāhmaṇas in pairs—such as "two for the gods" and so forth, resulting in two, four, six, or eight brāhmaṇas at the *daivika* rite—the oblation must still be performed in the hand of only one. For by that alone the injunction for the oblation would be fulfilled; indeed, the entire enjoined oblation would be accomplished. Here, the fact that what is enjoined has been performed (*vihitakṛtatva*), i.e., that it was performed according to the injunction (*vidhikṛtatva*), or that its purpose was served by the injunction (*vidhikṛtārthatva*), is presented as a counter-reason (*pratihetu*), which renders the [opposing] argument futile. Therefore, the oblation is in the hand of only one, and by the previously stated principle, it is in the right hand of the very first seated brāhmaṇa. Thus, according to the aforementioned determination of the agent (*kartṛvyavasthā*), the oblation should be performed either in the hands of all the brāhmaṇas representing the gods, or as an equal option (*samavikalpa*) in the hands of the brāhmaṇas representing the ancestors. As for the one who...
One should perform the Vaiśvadeva rite for the twice-born in the same manner as the *agnaukaraṇa* offering;
however, one should give that [offering] directly into the hand, and never into the fire for the ancestors (*pitrya*).

Thus, although it appears as if there is a prohibition of the *pitrya* (ancestral) hand, this is for the purpose of praising the *daiva* (divine) hand and not for the purpose of excluding the *pitrya* hand. Alternatively, the meaning is that once the oblation has been offered into the hand of the foremost guest of the *daiva* row, one must not again offer it into the hand of the foremost guest of the *pitrya* row. In this context, when an *agnau homa* (oblation into the fire) is performed in a New Moon *śrāddha* dedicated to the ancestors (such as the father or grandfather), or when it is performed in a ritual procedure (*prayoga*) involving the performance of the *vaiśvadevika* rite, then—due to the identity of the factors of place, time, agent, and locus—the offering into the fire (*agnaukaraṇa*) is performed by a single ritual procedure (*tantra*), just like the *vaiśvadeva*. Therefore, intending to offer into such a *vaiśvadevika* hand, one should offer into the hand of only one person seated at the head of the *daiva* row. However, when the *vaiśvadeva* rite is performed separately, then, because of the difference in the locus, one should perform the offering separately even when offering into the hand of a *dvija* belonging to the *vaiśvadevika* rite. Accordingly, two separate offerings must be made into the hands of the two principal *dvijas* seated at the heads of the two *vaiśvadevika* rows.

But even so, a *homa* performed in the fire situated in the same place and time as that performance, or in the hand of a twice-born man intended for the *vaiśvadeva* portion of the *tantra*, would benefit both *śrāddhas*. Likewise, let there also be a distinction between the *vaiśvadeva* offerings. Otherwise, one would have to resort to the repetition of the primary acts (*pradhāna*) merely out of deference to the subordinate factor (*guṇa*) known as the locus (*adhikaraṇa*).

Not so. For the oblation is not repeated here merely because another section (*adhikaraṇa*) has already fulfilled its purpose; rather, it is determined that the hand-oblation (*pāṇihoma*), performed in the hand of a Brahmin who is not intended for any other *śrāddha*, serves as an auxiliary (*upakāraka*) to the principal rite called the *mātāmaha-śrāddha* so that it may be endowed with its full qualities. Therefore, when one intends to offer the oblation in the hand of a second Brahmin belonging to the *vaiśvadeva* portion while the *vaiśvadeva* rites are being performed separately, one must indeed repeat the *agnaukaraṇa* (the offering into fire) in the hand of that second *vaiśvadeva* Brahmin. By this very principle, the oblation in the hand of the Brahmin representing the ancestors (*pitrya*) is also explained. Thus say Aparārka, the author of the *Smṛticandrikā*, Madhumiśra, and others. However, there is this distinction: even when the *tantra* (ritual framework) belongs to the *vaiśvadeva* portion, the oblation must still be repeated due to the difference in the substratum (*adhikaraṇabheda*).
Regarding this, Kātyāyana says:
"Even when there is a difference [in lineage] for the maternal grandfather, one who maintains the sacred fires (sāgnika) should perform [the rite] according to the common procedure (tantra)."

The meaning of this is as follows: When one intends to perform the *homa* into the hand of the principal Brāhmaṇa representing the ancestors during the primary *pārvaṇa* and other rites, then, having offered into the hands of the principal twice-born seated in the row of the father, grandfather, and so forth, one should also perform a separate *homa* into the hand of that Brāhmaṇa who is related to the maternal grandfather (*mātāmaha*). This separate performance of the *homa* into the hand of the Brāhmaṇa related to the maternal grandfather should be understood to apply whether the Vaiśvadeva rite is performed separately or by way of a single ritual procedure (*tantra*). Sometimes there is also a *homa* into the hand of a twice-born even for one who maintains the sacred fires (*sāgnika*). The term "one who maintains the sacred fires" is merely illustrative (*upalakṣaṇa*), because this principle of repetition applies equally to a *pāṇihoma* performed by one who does not maintain the sacred fires when such a locus [the hand] is used. Thus concludes the determination regarding the hand as the locus for the *homa*.
Now, there are also other substrates for the oblation that do not take the form of fire.
In the *Matsyapurāṇa*:
"In the absence of fire, however, [the oblation] may be offered into the hand of a Brahmin or even into water."
Either at Ajakarna or Ashvakarna, or in a cow-pen, or near a Shiva-temple.

In the case of the expression *ajakarṇe* (goat-ear) or *aśvakarṇa* (horse-ear), since there is no reason for the gender to be disregarded, the masculine gender is indeed intended. Here, although the hand of a Brāhmaṇa is the primary option (*mukhyakalpa*) and must necessarily be present in a *śrāddha* rite that includes the *agnaukaraṇa* offering, leaving no room at all for *ajakarṇa* and the like; nevertheless, because the direct Vedic revelation (*pratyakṣaśruti*)—"This Brāhmaṇa is indeed Agni Vaiśvānara"—declares the Brāhmaṇa to be fire itself, the *ajakarṇa* and other items—seen only in Smṛti texts rooted in indirect (*parokṣa*) revelation—are inferior and thus subject to absolute sublation (*atyantabādha*). Therefore, an equal alternative (*samavikalpa*) must be accepted. When a *darbhavaṭu* (bundle of *darbha* grass) is substituted in the place of the Brāhmaṇa, room should be made for the *vāja* and other such offerings.
Śaṅkha said: Kātyāyana declared that one should place the fire in the right ear of an unborn calf, in the right hand of a Brahmin, in water, or in a bundle of *kuśa* grass.

"Fire always dwells in silver and gold. By this demonstration of the presence of fire, its application (*viniyoga*) in rites pertaining to fire is shown; for if this were merely an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), it would result in its being purposeless. Thus, in the *Saura Purāṇa*:
In the absence of fire, however, one should offer it into the hand of a Brahmin,
or in the presence of Mahādeva, or in a cow-pen, being well-composed.
In the *Kūrmapurāṇa*: "In the absence of fire, the oblation is prescribed to be performed into the hand of a Brahmin,
or before Mahādeva, or in a cow-pen, by one endowed with faith."

Thus concludes the determination regarding the locus for oblations not performed with fire. Now follow the substances for the questions and answers which constitute the ancillaries of the *agnaukaraṇa* oblation.
Regarding this, Yājñavalkya says:
Intending to offer it in the fire, he takes up the food soaked in ghee and asks for permission;
being granted leave with the words "Do so," he offers it in the fire as in the sacrifice to the ancestors (pitṛyajña).

The performer of the *śrāddha*, desiring to perform an oblation (*homa*) in the fire, should take food mixed with a large amount of clarified butter (*ājya*) in a praiseworthy vessel such as a ladle, and ask the Brāhmaṇas who are partakers of the *śrāddha* for permission in the form of the question, "I shall offer in the fire. Being authorized by those Brāhmaṇas with a statement such as "Do so," he should offer the oblation according to the *piṇḍapitṛyajña-homa* prescribed in his own *Kalpasūtra*. Regarding this, some also read the words "agnau kariṣye" and "ādāya"; in that case, the syntactical connection is: "having taken the food soaked in ghee, he should ask, 'I shall offer in the fire.'"

Kātyāyana also says: "Having set aside food smeared with ghee, he asks, 'Shall I offer in the fire? Being permitted with the words, 'Do so,' he offers as in the Piṇḍapitṛyajña; having offered, he gives the remainder of the offering, touches the vessel, and mutters [the prayer]."

Regarding the statement, "Having taken food here, he asks, 'I shall perform [the offering] in the fire,'" since it would otherwise be of no visible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*), one concludes that its intent lies in making known the food as the substance for the oblation (*homa*). Once it is determined that this very food is to be taken, the act of "taking out" (*uddhṛtya*)—which consists of the mental conception of separating it from the food currently being cooked—is already established by the sense of the situation; therefore, the word "having taken out" is understood to mean "lifting up. Pracetās says:
"Intending to offer in the fire, he takes up the food soaked in ghee and asks [permission]."
"Having been authorized with the words 'Oṃ, do so,' one should offer oblations as in the Pitṛyajña.
Thus [it is stated]. In the Saurapurāṇa: "Having said, 'I shall perform [the rite] in the fire,' [one proceeds] with the authorization 'Do so.'"
One should offer food soaked in ghee into the fire, as in the ancestral sacrifice (pitṛyajña).
In the Kūrma Purāṇa: Having composed his mind, he should indeed address [the officiants], saying "I shall perform [this]";
and being permitted by the best of the twice-born with the words "Do so" and "So be it," he should proceed.
Taking his wife and sons, he should offer them into the consumer of oblations.
The *Nigama* states in the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*: "Having taken up the food and sprinkled it with clarified butter, one asks, 'I shall perform [the offering] in the fire.'"

Having said, "I shall offer in the fire," and being told by them, "Let it be done," he should offer oblations according to the very procedure prescribed in the Gṛhya-sūtras and cause [the portions] to be placed in the vessels.

The meaning is that, having offered [the oblation], one should pour the remains of the offering into the vessels of the ancestors and the Brahmins. The restrictive particle *eva* in the phrase "only by that which is stated in the Gṛhya-sūtra" is not intended to exclude the procedures stated in the Smṛtis and Purāṇas; for, since there is recognition [of these as belonging to the same tradition] and since all ritual acts are uniform everywhere, and given that all scriptures stand in mutual dependence, it is logical to synthesize all the dharmas. Therefore, this particle *eva* should be construed thus: "only according to the rule. Baudhāyana says:

Then, having caused [the recipient] to accept water mixed with sesame seeds and having adorned it with perfume and garlands, and being permitted with the words, "I shall offer it in the fire," he kindles the fire, strews grass around it, and offers three oblations of clarified butter: "To Soma accompanied by the ancestors, *svadhā*! Adoration! *Svāhā!*"; "To Yama accompanied by the Aṅgirases and the ancestors, *svadhā*! Adoration! *Svāhā!*"; "To Agni Kavyavāhana, the maker of good offerings, *svadhā*! Adoration! *Svāhā!*. Having sprinkled the food with the remainder of that [clarified butter], he should offer these same three [oblations] for him.

‘Then’ (*atha*) means immediately after the Brāhmaṇas have been seated. ‘These’ (*etān*) refers to the Brāhmaṇas. ‘Having established the fire’ (*agnim upasamādhāya*) means having kindled the fire situated in the fire-pit; ‘having strewn around’ (*saṃparistīrya*) means having strewn it all around with *darbha* grass. The word ‘thus’ (*iti*) marks the conclusion of the clarified-butter oblation (*ājyahoma*). ‘With the remainder of that’ (*taccheśeṇa*) means with the remainder of the clarified-butter oblation. ‘Food’ (*annam*) refers to the boiled rice set aside for the purpose of the oblation; ‘having sprinkled that over’ (*tad abhighārya*) means having poured the remaining clarified butter over it. Having cut off portions of the food, one should offer three oblations with these very same mantras.
In the *Matsyapurāṇa*:
"Having been authorized by the Brahmins, the Brahmin should perform the rite in the fire according to the prescribed rule;
then, having prepared the *caru* oblation in a bronze vessel (*kāṃsya*) according to the procedure taught in his own *Gṛhya-sūtra*..."

However, even for that best of the twice-born who maintains only a single fire, having first performed the *āyana* of the fires dedicated to Agni and Soma, or when the *dakṣiṇāgni* has been brought forward;
Hārīta says:

Having approached the water-vessels, he pours water into them while reciting "They come together," sprinkles *sumanas* flowers, and, being permitted by the Brahmins, places fuel on the fire with the *sāmidhenī* verses. Having invoked the Agniṣvātta ancestors and others, he honors the Brahmins standing there with water-vessels as appropriate. Holding the stirring-spoon in his hand and being permitted, when he offers to Soma accompanied by the Pitṛs, he thereby gratifies the Soma-drinking ancestors who have Soma as their chief; when [he offers] to Yama accompanied by the Aṅgirases, he gratifies the Barhiṣad ancestors who have Yama as their chief; and when [he offers] to Agni Kavyavāhana, the Sviṣṭakṛt, he gratifies the Agniṣvātta ancestors who have Agni as their chief. By placing down the stirring-spoon, he gratifies his own self. Having given the remnants of the oblation to the Brahmins, he should set aside portions for the funeral cakes (*piṇḍas*).
Regarding the phrase "sāmidhenyeti," Hariharā has shown the reading "samitsu etīti" and explained the statement as follows: tad yathā | [He explains it as follows:]

Having poured water into the *arghya* vessels with the mantra, "Some come together, others approach," and having thrown flowers (*sumanas*) upon them, one should perform the purification (*utpavana*) without a mantra, just as in the case of the *prokṣaṇī* water. Then, being authorized by the Brahmins with the words, "O Brahmins, do you consent? (*samītsva*), one should place the fuel-wood (*idhma*)—the wood intended for kindling the fire—into the fire. From the observation of the word of authorization, it is inferred that, by implication, the performer of the *śrāddha* should previously utter a request such as, "I shall kindle the fire. Having thus offered the fuel-wood and invoked the ancestors with the invocation-mantras (*āvāhana-mantra*), one should subsequently worship Agniṣvātta and the others—by the use of the word "etcetera" (ādi), including the Havirbhuk and so forth—with the water-vessels prepared beforehand, according to the purpose; that is, with whatever honors are required for the fulfillment of the *śrāddha*'s objective for each specific caste. These [deities] are designated by Manu and others as "the Somapas, who are the [ancestors] of Brahmins," and so on. Alternatively, the conceptualization (*saṃkalpa*) of Agniṣvātta and the others occurs at the very moment of invocation, in their capacity as presiding deities over the deceased father and the rest. However, the actual worship (*arcana*) is performed using the names of the three ancestors—the father, grandfather, and great-grandfather—according to the rule, "according to the purpose. In this way, it is established that for one whose father is living, there is worship of two [ancestors]. Then, holding the stirring-spoon (*mekṣaṇa*) in hand, one asks, "I shall perform the offering in the fire," and so on. Being authorized with the words, "Do so," one offers three oblations (*āhuti*) to Soma and the others, and finally places the stirring-spoon into the fire. Having placed a small portion of the remains of the oblation into the bowls of the Brahmins representing the ancestors, one should set aside the remainder for the sake of the funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*). Thus it is said.
It has been stated that one should set aside the food; regarding that food, a specific detail is shown in the *Brahma Purāṇa*:
"Then, having taken the prepared food smeared with ghee while it is still warm, one who is self-restrained should request the twice-born, saying: 'I shall offer these into the fire.'"
Also in the *Mahābhārata*: "Then, O bull of the Bharatas, having been authorized by those twice-born ones and having uttered 'Oṃ,' a man should offer food, excluding condiments and salt."

In this context, by the word "condiments" (*vyañjana*), curd, milk, buttermilk, molasses, black pepper, and so forth are meant. As for vegetables, soups, and the like, which are seasoned with the flavor of salt, their prohibition is already established simply by the exclusion of the salty taste itself. "Alkaline substances" (*kṣārāṇi*) refers to items possessing a salty flavor.
Regarding that which is stated in the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*:
"Of flowers, fruits, and edible foods, [one should exercise] great care..."
Having extracted this [mantra] from all [the Vedas], one should offer it into the Jātavedas fire.

Thus, there is a traditional injunction (*smaraṇa*) regarding the offering (*homa*) of vegetables and other items mixed with salt and the like, which have been prepared for the sake of the ancestors (*pitṛ*). This refers to those whose *Gṛhya-sūtra* prescribes a mantra-less offering into hot ashes—using food distinct from the sacrificial oblation (*haviṣya*) and mixed with other substances—as a subsidiary part following the *agnaukaraṇa* offering; hence, there is no contradiction. Furthermore, that offering is demonstrated in the *Āpastamba-sūtra*.

There is no offering of alkaline or salty substances, nor is there an offering of food belonging to others or of that which is not fit for sacrifice; having pushed aside the hot ashes toward the north, one should offer therein, for thus it becomes both offered and unoffered in the fire.

Alternatively, this statement from the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa* refers to the case when a *śrāddha* is performed with bulbs, roots, fruits, and the like due to the absence of cooked food (*anna*). In this context, the rites of the fire-oblation (*homa*) and the rice-ball (*piṇḍa*) proceed only when the *śrāddha* is performed with cooked food, because of the rule that those two must consist of cooked food as their substance. Having set forth this view of Jayantasvāmin, Harihara refuted it by raising an objection regarding its contradiction with the previously cited passage from the *Matsya Purāṇa* beginning with "when one should perform the *śrāddha*... and so forth.
It has been stated that one asks [for permission] when about to perform [the rite] in the fire. Regarding the expectation there as to whether it be for all [of them] or for one, Manu says:
"Having brought water for them, along with *tila* seeds and *pavitra* blades, the Brāhmaṇa, being authorized by the Brāhmaṇas, should perform [the offering] in the fire."

Having honored the Brāhmaṇas with perfumes, garlands, and other offerings, having poured water into their hands, and having given them sesame seeds along with *pavitra* grass, the performer—being authorized simultaneously by all the Brāhmaṇas acting together—should perform the *homa* in the fire. From the mention of "authorization" (*anujñā*), a formal inquiry is also inferred. From the expression "together" (*saha*), it is understood that the inquiry must be directed toward all [the Brāhmaṇas]. If the inquiry were made to only one, while authorization was being granted by all, it would follow that the inquiry serves no visible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*). Furthermore, this position of inquiring of all is optional. Now, having taken up the fire, he asks all of them—the foremost of the row—whether he shall perform the rite in the fire, according to the statement of Hārīta: "He asks all. Since it is well understood here that this inquiry is made to one person facing him individually and to all persons facing them collectively, there is no need to state any uncertainty regarding the Brāhmaṇas' granting of authorization, nor any intention behind the inquiry, nor any further occasion for questioning.
It has been stated that "one should offer the oblation after being permitted. In response to the inquiry as to by whom one is permitted, Pāraskara says:
"Having offered perfumes and the like, as well as incense, one should take up the oblation mixed with clarified butter;
permitted by the paternal ancestors, he offers according to the ritual of the Pitṛyajña."

In the phrase "by the paternal [ancestors]," the word "Brāhmaṇas" is to be supplied as the ellipsis. By this, it is understood that the question also is directed toward the paternal [ancestors] alone. Here, the manner of the question and answer—"I shall perform [the offering] in the fire" and "Perform it"—is already well known. Another method is also shown in the *Āśvalāyana-gṛhya-sūtra*:

"Having taken up food smeared with ghee, he asks for permission, saying 'I shall perform [it] in the fire,' or 'I will perform [it],' or 'I am performing [it]'; the response is 'Let it be done,' 'Perform it,' or 'Do it. Then he offers into the fire as previously stated.
Āpastamba, however, states the manner of question and answer for those in the north.

The northern practice, however, is as follows: for those seated on their seats, the bringing of water-vessels to their hands is prescribed; he addresses them, saying, "Let [the oblation] be lifted up, and let it be offered in the fire," and they respond, "Let it be lifted up as you wish, and let it be offered in the fire as you wish. Once thus authorized, he should lift it up and offer it. In this regard, he distributes [the offerings] toward the east and the north, just as a swan separates milk from water.
May that Sarasvatī protect us, for the sake of the grammatical perfection of words for the learned.

Thus, according to the statement of the ancients, the meaning is that the conduct (*vṛtti*) or practice (*ācāra*) of those who belong to the northern region—those who are "northerners" (*udīcyāḥ*)—is being described. "Bringing water-vessels" refers to the offering of the *arghya* (water of respect). He "invites" (*āmantrayate*) the Brahmins, making them face him with a request for permission. "Permitted" (*atisṛṣṭaḥ*) means authorized by the Brahmins.

In this context, by the statement "as in the Pitṛyajña," the extension of the ritual procedure (*itikartavyatā*) of the Pitṛyajña to the *agnaukaraṇa* oblation is established; and that procedure has been shown by Āpastamba and others in the section on the Piṇḍapitṛyajña. Regarding this, Āpastamba says:

He brings sacrificial grass (*barhis*) that has been cut once together with its roots, or he brings grasses that have been cut once and trimmed at their bases. Having strewn the southern fire-altar (*dakṣiṇāgni*) with *darbha* blades whose tips point toward the south and east, and having bent his right knee, he makes an under-layer of ghee in the stirring-spoon (*mekṣaṇa*), takes a portion from it, sprinkles it with ghee, and offers it into the southern fire with the formula: "To Soma accompanied by the ancestors, *svadhā*! Homage! He offers a second oblation with: "To Yama accompanied by the Aṅgirases and the ancestors, *svadhā*! Homage! and a third with: "To Agni Kavyavāhana, *svadhā*! Homage! Having offered those rice grains which were in the stirring-spoon, he silently places the stirring-spoon [into the fire], and so forth.

Āśvalāyana also says: "Wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītī), having added fuel to the fire, and having taken portions with the stirring-spoon, he should offer them according to the requirements for sacrificial portions, saying: 'To Soma accompanied by the ancestors, svadhā! Homage! To Agni, the bearer of the offerings to the ancestors, svadhā! Homage! Or [he may offer] with the utterance of 'svāhā'; in this case, he should first offer to Agni while wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (yajñopavītī). In this manner, other sūtras concerning the Piṇḍapitṛyajña should also be examined regarding the determination of the prācīnāvīta and yajñopavīta positions. Furthermore, this extension of the ritual rules of the Piṇḍapitṛyajña is explained in detail in the statement of Hārīta.

"Having been authorized with the words 'Do so,' [the performer], when the fire has been previously taken out and strewn around with grass cut once and trimmed near the roots, facing east, having offered two oblations with the *mekṣaṇa* spoon according to the ritual procedure for the fuel-sticks (*samit*), should place the *mekṣaṇa* into the fire itself.
This is the meaning explained by the author of the *Smṛticandrikā*.

"In the fire previously brought forth" means in the fire that has been kindled even before the time of the *paristaraṇa* (spreading of grass). When the fire has been strewn with *darbha* grass—cut in a single effort near its base—one should take a single fuel-stick (*samit*) for the sake of both oblations according to the *tantra* (combined ritual procedure). Having offered the two oblations with a *mekṣaṇa* made of sacrificial wood, one should throw the *mekṣaṇa* back into the fire itself. By the phrase "the fuel-stick according to the *tantra*," the rule of the *pitṛyajña* is indicated; for in the *pitṛyajña* there is no placing of a fuel-stick, whereas here another rule is taught. Thus it is said.
In the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa* as well, the placing of fuel sticks is mentioned here:
"Having placed a fuel stick inside [the mouth of the fire], one should offer oblations to Kavyavāhana.
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*, however, the placing of three fuel sticks, each a span in length and smeared with clarified butter, is mentioned.
Being told by them, "Oṃ, do so," he should summon the Dakṣiṇāgni fire;
having spread darbha grass with its tips pointing southward in the four directions, he should remain silent.
One should offer three fuel-sticks (samidh) of the length of a span (prādeśa) into that fire;
having offered the fuel-sticks smeared with ghee while facing southward and accompanied by mantras,
one should also offer three oblations with a ghee-smeared stirring-ladle (mekṣaṇa).
And the trees suitable for sacrificial fuel are mentioned right there:
the *palāśa*, *phalguna*, *nyagrodha*, *plakṣa*, *aśvattha*, *vikaṅkata*, as well as the *udumbara*, *bilva*, *candana*, and those trees fit for sacrifice.
The Sarala, Devadāru, Sāla, and Khadira—
these trees are especially recommended for the purpose of sacrificial fuel.
Those trees that have thorns and those which are fit for sacrifice should be gathered for the purpose of sacrificial fuel,
having been honored according to the word of the ancestors.
Listen as I describe the fruit of that rite for one who offers oblations into the fire with fuel-sticks smeared with clarified butter:
it is indeed inexhaustible, fulfilling all desires, and possesses the merit of a horse sacrifice.

However, the following are unworthy of being used as fuel: the *śleṣmātaka*, the *naktamāla*, the *kapittha*, the *śālmalī*, the *nīpa*, and the *vibhītaka*; these are censured in the performance of the *śrāddha* rite.
The *cirabilva*, the *ṭaṅka*, the *tinduka*, the *āmrātaka*, the *tilbaka*,
and the *kovidāra*— these are censured at a *śrāddha*.
Those trees that are the dwellings of insects, those that are censured, those unfit for sacrifice,
and those surrounded on all sides by thickets and creepers [should be avoided].
The best of the twice-born should avoid the dwellings of birds and all other such places that are unfit for sacrifice.

‘Palāśa’ is *kiṃśuka*. ‘Phalgu’ is *kākodumbarikā*. ‘Nyagrodha’ is the banyan tree (*vaṭa*). ‘Plakṣa’ is the *jaṭī*. ‘Aśvattha’ is the *pippala*. ‘Vikaṅkata’ is the *sruvavṛkṣa*. ‘Udumbara’ is the *jantuphala*. ‘Bilva’ is the *śrīphala*. ‘Candana’ is *malayaja*. ‘Sacrificial trees’ (*yajñiyāḥ*) include the *kāśmarya*, *śamī*, and others. ‘Sarala’ is the *pītadruma*. ‘Sāla’ is the *sālavṛkṣa*. ‘Khadira’ is the *bālapatra*. ‘Thorny trees’ (*kaṇṭakinaḥ*) include the *iṅgudī* and others. ‘Śleśmātaka’ is the *selu*. ‘Naktamāla’ is the *karañja*. ‘Kapittha’ is the *dadhittha*. ‘Śālmali’ is the *sthirāyu*. ‘Nīpa’ is the *kadamba*. ‘Cirabilva’ is the *pūtikarañja*. ‘Ṭaṅka’ is the *ahimāraka*. ‘Tinduka’ is the *sphūrjaka*. ‘Āmrātaka’ is the *kapītana*. ‘Tilbaka’ is the *rodhra*. ‘Kovidāra’ is the *kāñcanāra*. ‘Non-sacrificial trees’ (*ayajñiyāḥ*) include the *picumarda*, *pāribhadra*, and others.
Suyajña said:

"Having swept around, sprinkled water around, and strewn grass around, having bent the right knee, wearing the sacrificial cord over the left shoulder, and sitting facing east, one offers with a stirring-spoon.
Śaṅkha and Likhita [state this].

"Having adorned [the Brahmins] with incense, perfumes, and garlands, and having offered them food with ghee, one should strew Darbha grass with its tips pointing south around the fire and offer oblations.
Thus [ends the section on] the questions, answers, and materials that constitute the ancillaries of the *agnaukaraṇa*.
Now follow the variations regarding the number of oblations and the mantras for the deities of the *agnaukaraṇa*.
Having first performed the invocation for Manu and Bṛhaspati, as well as for Agni, Soma,
and Yama, one should afterwards satisfy the ancestors according to the rule by the offering of oblations.

Having performed the satiation of the deities known as Agni, Soma, and Yama with the first oblation, he should afterwards satisfy the ancestors, who have the Brahmins as their locus, by the offering of the sacrificial food—that is, by the provision of the aforementioned food.

This is the commentary according to Medhātithi and Hariharā. The word "of Agni" (*agneḥ*) is used in the genitive case with the sense of the dative (*caturthy-arthe*). One deity is Agni alone; the second is a single deity residing in two substrata in the form of Soma and Yama. This is because, from the *dvandva* compound "Soma and Yama," unity is understood just as in the case of "Agni-Soma. Furthermore, this should be understood as applying only to those for whom such a nature of the deities is stated in their respective *Gṛhya-sūtras*.

To this we reply: although here, because Soma and Yama function as deities (*devatā*), the use of the dative case-ending would be appropriate, nevertheless, when they are construed with the word *āyana* in the sense of "causing to swell" (*poṣaṇa*), they must take the genitive case-ending. If it is argued that the genitive is not used here because they are deities, then the form *agneḥ* [in the verse] would likewise not occur. If you say that it is explained as having the sense of the dative, we say no; for it is construed with the word *āpyāyana*. As for the genitive, since it expresses a general relation, its restriction to a specific relation is already accepted; thus, there is no contradiction with its nature as a deity. Furthermore, since we observe independent injunctions and oblation-mantras (*āhutimantra*) establishing Soma and Yama as deities individually, they do not constitute a single deity when joined together. Nor do the learned (*śiṣṭa*) find them to be deities in that state in any *Gṛhya* text. Moreover, a different reading of this statement is seen in other authoritative works: "And having first performed the swelling (*āpyāyana*) of Agni, Soma, and Yama."
Yama said: Then one should offer oblations to Agni, Soma, and Yama;
thereafter, one should offer the sacrificial food with the mantra: "Svāhā to Agni Kavyavāhana!"
Having performed the nourishment of Soma, as well as of Yama Aṅgiras, who is accompanied by the Pitṛs,
and of Agni Vaivasvata;
Having offered into the fire according to this proper rite, the knower of mantras should,
after observing it, consume the remainder of the oblation with the word "svadhā."
Śaṅkha and Likhita state:
"One should offer oblations with the words: 'Svāhā to Agni Kavyavāhana; Svāhā to Soma accompanied by the Pitṛs. [1355] In the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa:
"Oblation to Agni Kavyavāhana, Svāhā!"—this is the first oblation; "Oblation to Soma Pitṛmat, Svāhā!"—thus should the other be performed.

The word *vai* is not to be employed at the time of recitation because it serves only to complete the meter. In the *Gobhila-Śrautasūtra*, however, these two same mantras are stated with the *svāhā*-utterance placed first and in the reverse order:

"One should offer the oblation by scooping with the stirring-spoon (*mekṣaṇa*), saying 'Svāhā to Soma accompanied by the ancestors' for the first [offering], and 'Svāhā to Agni, the bearer of the offerings to the ancestors' for the second; from this point onward, one should wear the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*).

In the *Brahmāṇḍa-Purāṇa*, however, three oblations are prescribed with three mantras ending in *svadhā* and *namaḥ*, and the specific application of each is described according to the distinct locations of the fire where each oblation is offered.
Having diligently brought forth the Dakṣiṇāgni for the purpose of the oblation, while reciting:
"Svadhā! Adoration to Agni Kavyavāhana!"

Saying "Svadhā! Adoration to Soma accompanied by the ancestors," and saying "Svadhā! Adoration to Yama, the lord of the Aṅgirases"—these are the oblation mantras for the three [ancestors] in their proper order.
"To the south for Agni constantly, and likewise to the north for Soma;
between these two, one should always offer oblations to Vivasvat.
The term "Lord of the Aṅgirases" is an epithet of Yama.
In the *Brahmavaivarta*, however, "to Vaivasvata" is shown as a qualification for Yama, while "to Aṅgiras" is shown as a qualification for both Agni and Soma:
"To Agni Kavyavāhana, svadhā, and to Aṅgiras, obeisance;
and to Soma accompanied by the ancestors, svadhā, and to Aṅgiras, obeisance."
"Yamāya vaivasvatāya svadhā namaḥ"— speaking thus,
these indeed are the oblation-mantras for the three [ancestors] in their proper order.
"To the south [he offers] always to Agni, and likewise to Soma to the north;
between these two he should always offer to Vivasvat.
Thus Āśvalāyana speaks with reference to the Piṇḍapitṛyajña.

Taking [the portion] with the stirring-spoon (*mekṣaṇa*), he should offer it according to the requirements of the sacrificial cutting (*avadāna*): "To Soma accompanied by the ancestors, *svadhā*! Adoration! and "To Agni, the bearer of the offerings to the ancestors (*kavyavāhana*), *svadhā*! Adoration! Or else, he may first offer to Agni with the utterance of *svāhā*.

Thus says Āpastamba in the section on the Piṇḍapitṛyajña: "He offers in the southern fire [with the formula]: 'To Soma, who has been drunk by the ancestors, *svadhā*! Adoration! A second [offering] with: 'To Yama, accompanied by the Aṅgirases and the ancestors, *svadhā*! Adoration! A third [offering] with: 'To Agni, the bearer of the offerings to the ancestors, *svadhā*! Adoration! Some say that one does not offer to Yama."
Regarding the *pitṛyajña* specifically, Sāṃkhyāyana says: "He offers with the stirring-ladle (*mekṣaṇa*), saying: 'Svāhā to Agni Kavyavāhana; svāhā to Soma Pitṛmat; svāhā to Yama Āṅgirasvat Pitṛmat.
Regarding the *pitṛyajña* specifically, Vaijavāpa says:
On the Anvāhāryapacana fire, he offers two oblations with the stirring-ladle: the first with "To Agni," and the second with "To Soma."

In this context, Agni and Soma alone, without any further qualification, constitute the deities. Although these options for the mantras used in the oblation to the deities were mentioned in the section on the Piṇḍapitṛyajña, they certainly apply to the *agnaukaraṇa* by way of extended application (*atideśa*). Furthermore, these rules regarding the deities and so forth must be understood according to the established principle that they belong specifically to those *kalpasūtras* and *gṛhyasūtras* in which they are stated. Therefore, when Āpastamba has prescribed a *agnaukaraṇa* consisting of thirteen oblations in his own *gṛhya*, the author of the *Smṛticandrikā* maintains that this rule belongs only to those who follow that specific *sūtra*. For he says as follows:

He addresses them, saying, "Let the fire be drawn out, and let the oblation be prepared. Having been granted permission, saying, "As you wish, let it be drawn out; as you wish, let it be prepared," he should draw out the fire and offer the oblation.

Thus, following the questions and answers as stated in the Dharmaśāstras and Sūtras, one should take out food and perform the rites from the kindling of the fire up to the *ājyabhāga* offerings. This is because the sequence of rites beginning with the kindling of the fire and ending with the *ājyabhāga* offerings is declared at the outset of the *Āpastambīya Gṛhya Sūtra* to constitute the entire set of preliminary subsidiary elements (*aṅgakalāpa*) preceding all principal oblations (*pradhānahoma*). After the *ājyabhāga* offerings, one should perform the principal oblation known as the *agnaukaraṇa* using the substances of both food and clarified butter (*ājya*), with the mantras beginning with "yan me mātā" and so forth.
Accordingly, the *Āpastambīya Gṛhya Sūtra* states: [text follows].
He offers oblations of food with the subsequent [verses], and oblations of clarified butter with the following ones.

Having taken small portions from the food that has been set aside, according to the rule for *avadāna* (cutting portions), one should offer six oblations to the triad beginning with the father and the triad beginning with the maternal grandfather (*mātāmaha*) using the subsequent verses. The meaning is that among the verses recited in the section on mantras, those whose application has already been stated are followed by the verses being recited hereafter; these "subsequent" (*uttara*) verses are to be used for the six final oblations of food. Although the application of these six subsequent verses is indeed understood through their respective deity-indicating marks (*devatā-liṅga*) and the order of the text as being divided into *ājya*-oblations for the deities beginning with the father, nevertheless, for the sake of clarity, to inform one of the number of oblations, and to demonstrate the practical performance, he states the application for each pair: "With the two verses, *yan me mātā pralulobha carati* and *yās tiṣṭhanti*, ending with *amuṣmai svāhā*. Here, the word "he offers" (*juhoti*) is supplied. In the phrase *amuṣmai*, one should take the name of the father in the dative case and offer two oblations. Similarly, with the two verses *yan me pitāmahī pralulobha carati* and *antardadhe parvataiḥ*, ending with *amuṣmai svāhā*—here, taking the name of the grandfather in the dative case—one should offer two oblations. With the two verses *yan me prapitāmahī pralulobha carati* and *antardadhe ṛtubhiḥ*, ending with *amuṣmai svāhā*—here, taking the name of the great-grandfather in the dative case—one should offer two oblations. In this manner, one should offer two oblations to the maternal grandfather using the verses applied to the father's oblation; two to the maternal great-grandfather using the verses applied to the grandfather's oblation; and two to the maternal great-great-grandfather using the verses applied to the great-grandfather's oblation. However, a modification (*ūha*) must be made here. In the first mantra, the modification is: *yan me mātāmahī pralulobha, tan me reto mātāmaho vṛddhām*. In the second mantra, the modification is: *antarmāṃ mātāmahād vṛdhaḥ*. In both mantras, in the place of *amuṣmai*, the name of the maternal grandfather should be taken in the dative case. In the third mantra, the modification is: *yan me mātuḥ pitāmahī pralulobha, tan me reto mātuḥ pitāmaho vṛddhām*. In the fourth mantra, the modification is: *antarmāṃ mātuḥ pitāmahād vṛdhaḥ*. In both mantras, in the place of *amuṣmai*, the name of the maternal great-grandfather should be taken in the dative case. In the fifth mantra, the modification is: *yan me mātuḥ prapitāmahī pralulobha, tan me reto mātuḥ prapitāmaho vṛddhām*. In the sixth mantra, the modification is: *antarmāṃ mātuḥ prapitāmahād vṛdhaḥ*. In both mantras, in the place of *amuṣmai*, the name of the maternal great-great-grandfather should be taken in the dative case.
Regarding this, the author of the *Gṛhyabhāṣyasaṃgraha* says:
"In place of the words 'father' and so forth, the words 'maternal grandfather' and so forth should be employed during the offering of food,
as well as during the touching [of the vessel] and the giving of water, rice-balls, and the like."
"May my grandmother... and so forth—this would serve as an example therein, and so on.

Regarding the touching of the food intended for the Brāhmaṇas’ meal, he touches it with the three mantras beginning, "O Father, this honeyed wave of Sarasvatī is for you" (*sparśe*). Then, having cut portions as before, he offers one oblation with the verse, "And those ancestors who are here" (*ye ceha pitaraḥ*). Having thus offered the food oblations, he offers six oblations of clarified butter (*ājya*). In that regard, the first and second [oblations] are made with the mantra *svāhā pitre* (preceded by the utterance of *svāhā*). Having offered the third and fourth butter-oblations with these same two mantras, he offers the fifth with the mantra *svadhā svāhā*. He offers the sixth with the mantra *agnaye kavyavāhanāya svāhā*. Then, having offered the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation, he takes a small portion from all kinds of sacrificial food, such as what is fit to be chewed or eaten; having pushed aside some hot ashes toward the north, he offers it silently into those hot ashes. Then, having performed the remaining northern subsidiary rites—such as silently anointing the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) with the drippings from the two smearings and casting it into the fire—as prescribed by extension from the *caru*-offering in the *sthālīpāka* for Agni, up until the final sprinkling (*pariṣecana*), he should place the remnants of the offerings into the bowls of the Brāhmaṇas.
The author of the *Gṛhyabhāṣyasaṃgraha* has stated all of this as follows:

"Having performed the rites to be accomplished by kindling the fire and so forth, up to the end of the *ājyabhāga* offerings, one should then take portions [of the food] and perform the oblations in the fire with the seven *annahoma* mantras, reciting each mantra individually, beginning with 'yan me' and ending with 'svāhā'. Then, having offered the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation and removed the ashes, one should perform the *anna-homa*, smear the remnants on the two ladles (*darvī*), and complete the remaining rites up to the final sprinkling (*pariṣecana*). One should then place the food remaining from the oblation into the vessels. Thus it is said.

The statement "with seven *annahoma* offerings" is made with reference to those for whom the mantras have not been modified (*anūhita*). For if the mantras were modified (*ūhita*), the number would become thirteen, and thus the expression "with seven" would be incorrect. Furthermore, this *agnaukaraṇahoma* must be performed by one wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*), because it pertains to the ancestors (*paitṛka*). Thus, Āpastamba has stated at the beginning of his *Gṛhya-sūtra*: "In the dark fortnight, the rites for the ancestors are performed with the sacred thread over the right shoulder; moving counter-clockwise, the conclusion is toward the south.

Even here, when the ancestral acts such as the pouring of the *āghāra* libation and the kindling of the fire are to be performed, they should be done by one wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder.
Regarding this, the author of the *Bhāṣyārthasaṃgraha* says:

"First, in the case of the pouring of the oblation, the sacrificial wood, the mouth of the fire, the two portions of clarified butter (*ājyabhāga*), the circumambulation, and the following behind [the fire]..."
"For the two libations and for the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, the sacrificial thread (*yajñopavīta*) should indeed be worn by the one with matted hair (*kapardin*).
Thus end the options regarding the number of oblations to the deities of the *agnaukaraṇa* and the mantras.
Now, regarding the questions and so forth concerning the oblation performed with the hand as the receptacle,
according to the *Śaunakagṛhya*: "If there is no fire, one should take clarified butter and perform the *agnaukaraṇa* in the [guests'] own fires."
"As before, so let it be. Thus.

The meaning of this is as follows: having placed *ājya*—that is, food mixed with clarified butter—in the *arghya* vessel and other such vessels, and having lifted that vessel and held it in the hand, one makes the designation of the locus and the object of the action by saying, "The *agnaukaraṇa* (offering into the fire) is in you [the Brahmins] alone. The rest is as before. The meaning is that one should employ a verbal form such as "I shall perform" (*kariṣye*), "I will perform" (*karavai*), or "I do perform" (*karavāṇi*), just as in a *homa* where the fire is the locus. This implies that the Brahmins should grant permission by saying, "So be it" (*tathāstu*). Here too, the phrase "as before" should be connected [to the preceding], like the eye of a crow or a ball; thus, the words of permission, "Let it be done," "Do it," or "Perform it," are obtained. Furthermore, the extension of other ritual properties (*dharmātideśa*) from the *agnaukaraṇa* to the *pāṇihoma* (hand-offering) should be understood. Thus, for the food intended for the *homa*, there is the division into the front and back halves; there is the sprinkling (*abhighāraṇa*) and re-sprinkling (*pratyabhighāraṇa*); and after cutting off two portions with the *mekṣaṇa* (sacrificial ladle), the *homa* is performed. Regarding this, the author of the *Smṛtyarthasāra* stated: "In the *pāṇihoma*, there is no *mekṣaṇa*, no fuel-sticks (*idhma*), and no permission from the Brahmins; the sweeping (*parisamūhana*) and the sprinkling around (*paryukṣaṇa*) do take place."
Regarding this, the author of the Smṛticandrikā says:

The statement by the author of the *Smṛtyarthasāra* regarding the absence of permission from Brahmins in this context is to be disregarded, as it is based on a failure to observe the immediately preceding statement of Śaunaka beginning with "if he is without fire" (*anagniś cet*). Furthermore, the mention of the absence of the stirring-stick (*mekṣaṇa*) is to be considered doubtful, since no other rule is seen prescribing anything else for the function of the stirring-stick. And the mention of the presence of sprinkling (*paryukṣaṇa*) and sweeping (*parisamūhana*) is improper, because the visible purpose—namely the removal of dust—is lost, and a mere unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) resulting from a restrictive rule is not sufficient to justify their performance. However, for one for whom the effect of the strewing (*paristaraṇa*) is indeed a refinement (*saṃskāra*) consisting solely of an unseen merit, that [purpose] certainly exists.
And likewise Yama says:
"In that case, the oblation in the hand of the deity should be like the *agnaukaraṇa* [offering];
having spread out the scattered *darbha* grass, for it is indeed equal to fire."

‘*Daivakaraḥ*’ refers to the hand of the Brāhmaṇa for the Vaiśvadeva rite. The mention of the *deva* (deities) is intended to include the *pitrya* (ancestral) rite by implication. ‘*Paryastadarbhāḥ*’ means the *darbha* grasses to be strewn all around; that is to say, the *darbhas* used for the ritual strewing (*paristaraṇa*). Other authors of legal digests (*nibandhakāra*), however, read: “having sprinkled water and having strewn the *darbhas*. Since there is a traditional rule stating, “the fuel-stick (*samid*) of the *idhma* is for the purpose of kindling,” its omission is universally accepted when it is absent. However, because the acts of sweeping around (*parisamūhana*) and sprinkling water (*paryukṣaṇa*) are merely ritual requirements (*dharmamātra*), they are not omitted. The teacher Karka, fearing redundancy in the *Kātyāyana-sūtra*—specifically in the phrase “having been permitted with the words ‘Do so,’ and having offered [the oblation] like the Piṇḍapitṛyajña”—with regard to the phrase “like the Piṇḍapitṛyajña,” resolved that it serves to restrict the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) to only those elements possible therein, such as the strewing and sweeping around. Consequently, we understand that the practice of performing a mere oblation (*homamātra*) devoid of the procedures of sweeping, sprinkling, the *mekṣaṇa* ladle, and so forth, was initiated only by those following his opinion. Whatever is reasonable in this matter should be adopted.
Thus are the inquiries regarding the oblation performed with the hand as the receptacle.

The fire-oblation (*agnaukaraṇahoma*) performed with the goat’s ear and so forth as the receptacle possesses the same ritual characteristics as the oblation performed with the hand as the receptacle. The only distinction here is that the inquiry is simply: "I shall perform the fire-oblation.
Thus are the inquiries regarding the oblation performed with the goat’s ear and so forth as the receptacle.
[1362] Now follows the procedure for the remnants of the oblation (*hutāvaśiṣṭapratipatti*).
Having described the fire-oblation (*homa*) therein, Yājñavalkya says:
With a concentrated mind, one should offer the remnants of the oblation into vessels,
especially those made of silver, as they may be obtained.

In this context, because of the mention of silver, which is dear to the ancestors (*pitṛpriya*), it is understood that [the offering] is to be placed in vessels belonging to Brahmins on behalf of the ancestors.
And so says Yama:
"One should present the remainder of the *agnaukaraṇa* rite into the vessels intended for the ancestors."
Having offered it to the ancestors, one should not, however, give the Vaiśvadeva offering.

In this context, because of the term *agnaukaraṇa*, the statement may refer either to an oblation into the fire or to an oblation performed in both types of receptacles—namely, those consisting of fire and those not consisting of fire—since the word *agnaukaraṇa* functions as a name (a technical designation). Accordingly, after describing the oblation into the hand of the foremost of the lineage (*paṅktimūrdhanya*) belonging to the ancestors, Kātyāyana says:
"Having offered with the mantra, one should silently pour [the remainder] into the vessels of the others."
Since the word "other" (anya) refers to those of the same class as the subject under discussion, it is understood to mean "in the vessels of the Brahmins seated in the row for the ancestors.
For this very reason, Yama says:
"One should pour the remainder from what was offered into the hand of the [Brahmin] representing the ancestors into the vessels of the ancestors."
One should not, however, offer the remnants of the *agnaukaraṇa* rite during the *vaiśvadeva* ceremony.

In this context, the mention of the "hand of the ancestors" (*pitrya-pāṇi*) is illustrative. Therefore, even when the oblation (*homa*) is performed in the hand of the twice-born invited for the Viśvedevas (*vaiśvadevika*), the remainder of the food must be placed only into the vessels of the ancestors (*pitṛ-pātra*), and not into the vessels of the gods (*deva-pātra*). For this very reason, the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa prohibits the placing of the remnant of the oblation into the Vaiśvadevika vessels as a common practice for all:
"One should not give the remnant of the *agnaukaraṇa* into the Vaiśvadevika vessel;
for the Viśvedevas are not recorded by those who know the Purāṇas as partakers of the remnant. (1363)
It has also been prohibited by Yama:
"One should present the remains of the *agnaukaraṇa* offering to the ancestors;
however, one should never give the remains of the *homa* to those of the *vaiśvadeva*."

The meaning of the phrase "never" (*na kadācit*) is as follows: when the *agnaukaraṇa* oblation is made into the hand of the foremost Brāhmaṇa of the row for the Viśvedevas, then the remainder of that oblation must not be poured into the vessel of that same person or into the vessel of another Brāhmaṇa belonging to the Viśvedeva group. Likewise, when the oblation is made into the hand of a Brāhmaṇa representing the ancestors (*pitrya*), or into the fire, or into some other receptacle, even then the remainder of the oblation must not be poured into the vessel of a Brāhmaṇa representing the Viśvedevas. Furthermore, the pouring of the oblation-remainder into the vessels of those representing the Viśvedevas is specifically forbidden by that very [text]: "A twice-born man who does not maintain a sacred fire, having performed the *agnaukaraṇa* into the hand of a Brāhmaṇa representing the gods (*daiva-vipra*)."
One should set aside [a portion] for the ancestors and the Brahmins; likewise, one should set aside [another portion] for the sake of the funeral cakes (piṇḍas).
In the *Vāyupurāṇa*:
"Having offered [the oblation] into the hand of the deity in the absence of fire, one should present the remainder to those of the ancestral rite;
for the Viśvedevas are not recorded by those who follow the Purāṇas as partakers of the remnant."

The word "in the vessel" (*pātre*) is understood as referring to the *pitrya* [vessel]. "By those who know the Purāṇas" (*purāṇagaiḥ*) means by those who are experts in the Purāṇas; this is also an elliptical expression for those who are conversant with the Śruti, Smṛti, Itihāsas, Kalpasūtras, and so forth.
However, in the Vājasaneyaka-Pariśiṣṭa-Nigama, the disposal of the remains (*śeṣapratipatti*) is stated to be in the hands of the Brāhmaṇas:
"One should offer the remaining food with the hand into their hands, like a *piṇḍa*."
