By the phrase "like the *piṇḍas*," only the utterance of the word *svadhā* is extended by analogy; however, the acts of pouring water (*avanejana*), re-pouring water (*pratyavanejana*), the firebrand (*ulmuka*), and so forth, are not. This is because Yama’s statement, "One should take the remainder of the oblation with the word *svadhā* alone," serves as a restrictive enumeration (*parisaṅkhyā*) that excludes other ritual elements. Alternatively, its meaning is as follows: "'Like the *piṇḍas*' means as in the case of the *piṇḍas*. What is intended is this: just as the remainder of the *agnaukaraṇa* offering is poured into the *piṇḍapātra* for the sake of the *piṇḍas*, so too [should it be done] into the hands of the Brāhmaṇas. Or else, the term "*piṇḍavat*" contains the possessive suffix *-mat*. The meaning is that the remainder should be placed in the hands of the Brāhmaṇas in such a way that it is "connected to the *piṇḍas*" (*piṇḍasaṃbandhi*) even by a small portion of food, but not the entirety of it. Furthermore, the rule "one should leave a remainder for the sake of the *piṇḍas*" should be understood to apply even when the oblation is offered into the fire or into the hands of the ancestors (*pitryavipra*). This is because the purpose of leaving a remainder is understood to be for the sake of the *piṇḍas*.

[Objection: But surely, since the instruction is that only the remainder from what was offered into the hand of the deity (daivapāṇi) is for the purpose of the *piṇḍas*, the status of the remainder from what was offered into the hand of the ancestors (pitryapāṇi) as being for that same purpose cannot be obtained.

[Reply: Not so. In the injunction, "One should set aside a portion of the food being offered into the hand of the deity for the sake of the *piṇḍas*," if the qualifying attributes such as "the hand of the deity" were intended to be significant (*vivakṣā*), it would result in a qualified object of reference (*viśiṣṭoddeśa*). Therefore, this is connected with the sense that one should set it aside together even with a portion offered in any locus, such as fire or the hand.
For this very reason, Vṛddhavasiṣṭha says: [He provides the verse of Vṛddhavasiṣṭha here.]
Having offered the oblation into the fire for the ancestors without delay, one should pour the remainder into the vessels;
one should set aside a portion from the *piṇḍas*, but one should not give anything at all to the *vaiśvadeva* deities.

In this context, although it is possible to prepare a sufficient quantity of *piṇḍas* from the remainder [of the food], nevertheless, since it will be stated later that one should not extract any of the food currently present for the sake of the *piṇḍas*, it is understood that the remnant of the *agnaukaraṇa* serves as an auxiliary to the *piṇḍas* merely by being mixed with the extracted food. And thus, the throwing of this [remnant] into the *piṇḍa*-vessel is established by the very force of the sense. Furthermore, although the necessity of retaining the remnant is perceived here—both because of the hearing of the injunction "one should leave a remnant" (*śeṣayet*) and because the understanding that it is for the sake of the *piṇḍas* indicates it is a primary act (*arthakarman*)—nevertheless, since it is understood to be a secondary act (*pratipatti*) as a refinement of the substance already employed, its non-necessity and its lack of causal efficiency (*aprayojakatva*) toward the remnant are determined. This is because subsidiary acts (*śeṣakarmāṇi*) lack causal efficiency. Even in the case of primary acts (*arthakarman*) that serve as substrates (*āśrayikarman*), such as the sacrifice of the *prastara* grass-bundle and so forth, their lack of causal efficiency toward the substance is intended precisely through their inclusion within the category of secondary acts (*pratipatti*).
Yama said:
[1365] "Once the fire has been properly offered with this mantra according to the rule, the knower of mantras, having reflected, should take the remainder of the oblation, saying 'Svadhā'."

Having looked at the food remaining from the *homa*, one should take it [to the guests] saying "Svadhā"; the meaning is that after placing a small portion into the vessels of the Brahmins invited for the ancestors (*pitrya*), one should set aside the remainder for the sake of the funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*). Therefore, this is an option to the rule "one should place [the food] silently into the vessels," or rather, the arrangement is according to one's own *Gṛhyasūtra*. In this matter, although the *homa* is indeed completed merely by the oblation reaching the fire and merely by its reaching the palms of the hands, and the completion of the disposal of the remainder is achieved merely by its reaching the vessels, nevertheless, because of the scriptural injunction regarding the two remnants of the offering, the Brahmins must consume them.
Regarding this, Gārgya said:
"Whatever food is given, whether placed in the hand or in a vessel,
that indeed shall be eaten by the Brāhmaṇas seated in the row of the ancestors."

And that [food] must not be eaten at the very moment it is placed [on the hand], nor should it be separated from other food being prepared for the purpose of eating. Thus, it is said in the *Bahvṛcapariśiṣṭa*:
"The foolish eat first the food given upon the palm of the hand."
By that [offering], the ancestors are satisfied; they do not obtain the remaining food.
Whatever is placed in the palm of the hand and whatever else has been prepared should be enjoyed as one; no distinction exists between them.
In the Āśvalāyana Gṛhyasūtra:

"If, after they have sipped water while their hands are still held, he designates other food, then the food remaining from the oblation in the fire is given as 'sṛṣṭa' (released), which is called 'arddhuka' (prosperous)."

Harihara, fearing that one might mistakenly think the *ācamana* (ritual rinsing of the mouth) prescribed here—occurring before the serving of food after the *homa*—would necessitate its own specific occasion and thus result in the actual consumption of the oblation at that very moment, has explained the meaning as follows: when one should offer the oblation into the hands of the twice-born (*dvija*), then, once those twice-born who have been made the locus of the *homa* have performed their *ācamana*—that is, when they have completed the ritual rinsing—one should "assign" (*anudiśet*) other food, meaning one gives it. And here, the *ācamana* is connected with the act of eating (*abhyavahāra*). However, since there is the scriptural statement, "The twice-born is said to have his hand as his mouth," the eating here consists merely of contact between the food and the palm of the hand, not actual primary consumption. For if it were primary consumption, it would contradict such statements as, "And that which is placed on the palm of the hand. Then, immediately thereafter, one should give to the Brāhmaṇas the food remaining from what was offered into the fire; the meaning is that one should place it in the vessels of the Brāhmaṇas for the ancestors (*pitṛ*). Because other food being given mixed together with that [remnant] becomes "prosperous" (*arddhuka*), meaning it specifically brings about prosperity and is beneficial to the ancestors. Here, the mention of "in the fire" (*agnau*) is intended as an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*), in accordance with other scriptural texts; it should be understood to apply to the hand and so forth as well.

Baudhāyana, however, having prescribed three oblations of clarified butter with the three mantras beginning with "To Soma accompanied by the Pitṛs, svadhā namaḥ," and having stated that the remaining clarified butter is to be poured over the food, described the time and manner for consuming the remnants of that food after he has offered three oblations with it:
"Whatever food one should sprinkle with the remainder of the *agnaukaraṇa* [offering],
when that has been consumed, one should give the food that was originally prepared."
And this subsequent disposal (*pratipatti*) is intended solely for the *agnaukaraṇa* as taught by Baudhāyana.
Thus concludes the disposal of what remains after the oblation.
Thus concludes the determination of the *agnaukaraṇa*.

Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Oblation into the Fire" (*agnaukaraṇa*), within the section on the afternoon rites of the day of the *śrāddha*, in the *Śrāddhakalpa* of the *Pariśeṣakhaṇḍa* of the *Caturvargacintāmaṇi*, composed by the illustrious Hemādri, the scholar and sovereign minister of all affairs to the illustrious Mahādevī, the supreme queen of great kings.
[1367] Chapter Fourteen:
Now, the serving of food.
And Pracetas states that this should be performed after the disposal of the remnants of the *agnaukaraṇa* offering:
"Having given the remains of the oblation to the ancestors, one should serve the food—
consisting of sacrificial grains, honey, meats, milk-rice, and cakes."
Paiṭhīnasi, however, says:
"Having adorned the Brāhmaṇas, one should set down meat, cakes, curd, honey, ghee, milk-rice, rice-and-pulse, preparations of fruit, and fish.
Having adorned the Brāhmaṇas with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, one should "set down"—that is, serve—the meat, cakes, and other items.

By the word "having adorned" (*alaṃkṛtya*), only the precedence of the act of adorning relative to the serving of food is expressed, not an immediate precedence; therefore, since the purpose of the statement is fulfilled even if the serving is performed after the *agnaukaraṇa* (the offering into the fire) following the adorning, this should be explained without the great contradiction [implied by the former view]. The particle *iti* denotes a category and serves to group together the various kinds of foods, such as soups, vegetables, and so forth. Furthermore, the mention of fish is intended to highlight that among meats, fish-meat produces the greatest satisfaction for the ancestors. Prior to the serving, one should—while still wearing the *yajñopavīta* (sacred thread over the left shoulder)—take clarified butter with a ladle and, silently, perform the under-layering (*upastaraṇa*) in the eating vessels, beginning with those of the gods. This is because the vessels serve as the substratum for the sacrificial oblation to be offered to the deities and are thus comparable to garlands and other such offerings, and also because it is the practice of the learned (*śiṣṭa*). Some, however, employ the following mantra during the under-layering.
"O Āmāsu, bring the cooked [food] up to the sun; cause it to rise in the sky.
Like Dharma, may it be well-prepared for the one who delights in songs (Girvaṇas), a vast offering made with hymns by those who have performed penance.
Then, for the sake of convenience in serving, the vessels containing the prepared food should be brought to the place of the Śrāddha.
Regarding this, Manu states the procedure: "Having personally taken the increased portion of food with both hands,
one should place it down slowly near the Brahmins while meditating upon the ancestors."

"Annasya vardhitam" refers to a vessel filled with food; having taken it from the kitchen with both hands and brought it there, he should place it near the invited Brahmins—those connected to the Śrāddha being performed—in a location free from the risk of contact with food-leavings. "Gently" means in such a way that no breaking of the vessel or noise is produced. The word "himself" is stated as the primary rule, since the assistance of a wife or others mentioned in other Smṛtis for serving the food is even more possible in the case of bringing the vessel, which is merely an auxiliary act.

The author of the *Smṛticandrikā*, however, has explained that "the increased portion of food" (*annasya vardhitam*) refers to a vessel filled with food for serving; having grasped it with both hands, one should deposit the food therein into the eating bowls. Medhātithi, along with the aforementioned explanation, also accepted this interpretation. Yet, he himself stated the fault in lifting and bringing [the food] with only one hand, or in the act of serving:
"When food is brought that has been released from both hands, the Asuras, being evil-minded, suddenly seize it."

When food that has been "released"—that is, not yet grasped—by both hands is brought forward for serving, the "Asuras," those of evil nature who are enemies of the gods, being "evil-minded," seize and scatter it "suddenly" by force. The word "ubhayoḥ" (of both) is used in the locative case of location; "muktam" means not supported or not resting [in the hands]. He [Manu] himself stated that food brought in this manner is what should be served: "Edibles and foods according to rule, roots and fruits, as well as heart-pleasing meats and fragrant drinks."
Having brought all this, being well-composed and purified, he should serve it with the Hanakas while extolling all its qualities.

‘Eatable’ (*bhakṣya*) refers to *śaṣkulī*, *modaka*, and so forth; ‘food’ (*bhojya*) refers to *ghṛtapūra* and the like. Other foods to be served here should also be understood from the section concerning the types of food to be accepted. ‘Having brought near’ (*upanīya*) means having brought it into the presence of the Brahmins; ‘he should serve’ (*pariveṣayet*) means he should place it into their eating vessels. ‘Proclaiming the qualities of the food,’ such as sweetness and so on, means making it known by saying, “This is sweet,” “This is sour,” “This is astringent,” and so forth. In this regard, it has been established in the section on the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) that even the serving for the ancestors (*pitrya*) should be performed while wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*yajñopavītī*).
In the Kālikā Purāṇa: Then, being self-restrained and with speech controlled, he should take the vessel with both hands,
bring it before the Brahmins, and serve the foods.
Yama said:
Then, having brought pure food, one who is self-restrained should feed the twice-born:
rice, ghee, vegetables, meat, curd, milk, and honey.
Having brought all of this together, one should satisfy [the recipient] according to one's pleasure.

The meaning is that, having brought all this together and offered it with the ancestors (pitṛs) in mind by means of serving, one should satisfy the Brahmins by feeding them at their pleasure. And Śaunaka states that this serving must be performed starting with the gods (daiva):
"Having brought all the cooked food and having presented each item separately, one should begin the serving according to the rule, starting with the gods."

Having made it known to the Brāhmaṇas by means of such a statement as "This is sweet," and so forth; and this [announcement] pertains to the serving prior to the commencement of the meal, which is preceded by [invoking] the gods. But after that, the serving should be performed according to one's desire in whatever order suits. Whatever may please the Brāhmaṇas, that he should give, free from envy.

Thus, because Yama has stated that in the act of serving food one should follow the wishes of the Brahmins, this service must be performed by the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), his wife, a pure attendant, or someone else. Regarding this, Dharma states that when the service is performed by the sacrificer himself, the fruit is infinite:
"The infinity of the fruit is declared for serving food oneself.

Here, "oneself" refers to the sacrificer. By this statement regarding the infinity of the fruit—which is intended to demonstrate the superior merit of the act—it is understood that the performance of the service by the wife and others is also permitted as being commendable.
And so it is stated in the *Bhaviṣyottara*:
"At the time of the Śrāddha, service [of food] by the wife is indeed recommended.
Also in the *Vāyupurāṇa*:
The serving of food in rites for the ancestors should be performed by the wife;
for she is traditionally remembered as the companion of the ancestors, the gods, and men.

Thus, from these statements which possess the character of a reason, it is understood that in the act of serving food, the wife is primarily the agent herself, while her husband is merely an assistant; she does not hold a subordinate role. Furthermore, by virtue of the praise expressed, permission for even another attendant to serve food is granted. Moreover, the service must be performed by a wife of the same caste (*varṇa*) as the husband, and not by one of a different caste. And so says Nārāyaṇa:
"Whatever substance is pure, whatever is fit for the ancestors, and whatever brings happiness—"
To twice-born men, [a gift] is given by the hand of a woman of the same caste who is not an Ārya.

In this regard, it is stated in the *Padma* and *Matsya Purāṇas* that for the sake of excellence in merit, the serving [of food] should be performed with hands joined by *darbha* grass together with sesame seeds:
"Then, having taken [the food] with both hands,
one should serve it with a tranquil mind, specifically with sesame and *darbha* in hand."

And this serving [of food] at a rite for the ancestors (pitrya) must be performed with the right hand assisted by the left; for Āśvalāyana and others prescribe such a right hand as the instrument for casting ancestral offerings, and because of established custom.

Even with such a hand, it should not be done with the bare hand alone, but rather with it covered by another vessel containing substances other than iron, or in the absence of that, even covered by leaves and the like; thus it is stated in the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa:
"Not with anything impure, not with one hand alone, nor without *kuśa* grass."
At a śrāddha ceremony, one should serve food using iron vessels with iron implements alone.

"By iron" means made of black iron; or rather, one should not serve [food] with an iron vessel at all. Regarding this serving, many statements should be consulted in the section on serving vessels that prescribe using vessels such as those of gold or silver while requiring the hand to be covered by another vessel, or that prohibit the bare hand and forbid iron vessels.
In this context, Kārṣṇājini states the rule for serving certain foods with a ladle (*darvī*) and the prohibition for others:
"Cooked food and all condiments should be given with a ladle."
He who desires to give water or cooked food with a ladle is a thief, he is most wicked; one should designate him as a slayer of a Brahmin.

"Boiled food" (*śṛtānna*) refers to milk-rice (*pāyasa*), boiled rice (*odana*), and the like; "cooked food" (*pakvānna*) refers to sweetmeats (*modaka*) and the like. Since the use of a ladle is prohibited when giving water and other such items, the gift should be made using another vessel, as the prohibition against using the bare hand has also been demonstrated.
This is also stated in the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*:
"That which is to be given with the hand [is forbidden] if given with a ladle; that which is to be given with a ladle [is forbidden] if given from the hand."
He who should eat these things in reverse would be eating pus and blood.
The prohibition regarding ladles made of iron is shown in the *Bhaviṣyottara*:
"Whatever food is offered during the Śrāddha rite with an iron ladle,
or even whatever is offered with the hand, that is appropriated by Rākṣasas."
The serving of food must be performed while the vessels remain directly on the ground, and not when they are placed upon other receptacles such as wooden stands or stone slabs.

Regarding this, Manu says: "One who is self-controlled and composed should properly place on the ground itself the condiments, soups, vegetables, and so forth, as well as milk, curd, ghee, and honey."

‘On the ground itself’ means when the vessels have been placed directly upon the ground. ‘Qualities’ refers to those things denoted by the word *guṇa*. In response to the question of which ones these are, it is said: ‘soups, vegetables, and so forth. ‘Soup’ (*sūpa*) is food such as rice and the like, prepared with mung beans and other pulses, which is designated by the term *varānna* (excellent food) and is to be eaten after being mixed with boiled rice and the like. ‘Vegetables’ (*śāka*) refers to cooked tubers, roots, fruits, leaves, and so on. By the word ‘and’ (*ca*), the various kinds of food previously shown—beginning with ‘eatables and chewables’ (*bhakṣya-bhojya*)—are included. This being the case, it is stated that the serving must be done when both types of vessels are situated on the ground: namely, the large vessels that serve as the base for milk-rice (*pāyasa*), boiled rice (*odana*), cakes (*apūpa*), and so on; and the small vessels well-known for being placed upon the large ones, which serve as the base for water, *kāmbalika*, ghee, milk, drinks, and the like—and not when they are situated in another container.
For this very reason, Hārīta says:
"One should place [the vessels] on the ground itself; one should not place vessels upon other vessels."

"Upper bowls" (*uparipātrāṇi*) refers to those bowls that are well known for being placed upon other bowls. The meaning is that one should place them on the ground itself, not upon another bowl nor upon any other support. In the *Mānavamaitrāyaṇīyasūtra*, however, mantras are prescribed for the serving of milk-rice (*pāyasa*) and other foods: "May there be milk on the earth"—with this, one should give milk-rice; "The winds are honey for the righteous"—with this, honey; "May he grant long life"—with this, one should give clarified butter (*ghṛta*). Here, the mantra beginning with "madhuvātā" has already been shown. The remaining two mantras are as follows: "May there be milk on the earth, milk in the plants, milk in heaven, and milk in the intermediate space. May the quarters of the sky be full of milk for me. "O Agni, giver of life, enjoying the oblation, having clarified butter as your face and clarified butter as your source, protect these people like a father protects his son, after you have drunk the clarified butter and the sweet, lovely product of the cow."

In the *Kaṭhasūtra*, however, another mantra is prescribed for the touching of food such as milk-rice (*pāyasa*) and for the pouring of ghee and milk: "Having touched the prepared food, [one recites] 'This cooked [food] is in these [vessels],' and having poured ghee and milk. In the *Prabhāsakhaṇḍa* of the *Skanda-purāṇa*, however, other mantras are stated:
"Milk-rice mixed with jaggery, sacrificial food filled with jaggery..."
"Obeisance to you, O Pitṛs, who are the essence"; thus he should consecrate the food being served.
With the mantra "Thou art splendor, thou art semen," he offers the clarified butter; with "O Dadhikrāvan," the curd;
the milk with the mantra for swelling; and likewise the various side dishes.
Having recited the mantra "Thou art the Year," the twice-born man should cause Indra to bestow all kinds of food, both solid and soft, and with that [water] he should offer water.
The word "should cause to be given" (*dāpayet*) is to be connected with every [clause].

Regarding this, Hārīta says that whatever foods, in whatever quantity and possessing whatever excellence of qualities, have been served in the bowl of one person, those same foods, in those same quantities and possessing those same excellences of quality, must be served in the bowl of another as well; they must not be served in reverse order.
Furthermore, for those seated in the row, the food, including the perfumes and other items, should be equal.
One should not give unequally in a row, nor should one beg, nor cause others to give.
Regarding the fault in giving unequally, Yama says:
"He who gives unequally to those seated in a single row takes away the misdeed of the row, and the giver as well as the recipient incur it."
For one who obstructs a river or a bridge, for one who creates obstacles for a maiden,
and for one who gives unequally at a funeral feast, no expiation is possible.
Yama and Vyāsa have also said:
"He who, in a single row, gives unequally—
whether out of affection, fear, or for the sake of wealth— "
The sages declare that this is the sin of killing a Brahmin, as proclaimed by the ancient seers and sung in the Vedas.
In this regard, whatever food is served in the vessel for the Brāhmaṇas must be served at that very same time in the vessel for the piṇḍas; here is an indicative mark seen in the *Brahmapurāṇa*:
"Then he gave food that was delicious and savory, beginning with milk-rice (*pāyasa*);
at one time it was freshly cooked, not stale, and of the highest quality."
He likewise gave to the brahmins into their alms-bowls food with little leafy vegetable but many fruits, possessing the six flavors and resembling nectar.
Thus ends the serving of food. Now follow the holding of the vessels, the silent recitation (japa), and the placing of the thumb [into the food].
Regarding this, Kātyāyana says:

Having given the remains of the oblation and touched the vessel, he recites: "The earth is your vessel, the sky the lid; I offer the nectar into the mouth of the Brāhmaṇa, svāhā!"—either with a verse addressed to Viṣṇu or with a Yajus formula. Having dipped his thumb into the food, and having scattered sesame seeds while reciting "Apo hatā," he should give warm, steaming food. [1375]

Having recited the mantra beginning with *pṛthivī te pātram* and ending with *svāhā*, and immediately thereafter having muttered the Vaiṣṇava ṛc, *idaṃ viṣṇur vicakrame tredhā nidadhe padaṃ samūḍham asya pāṃsure*, and then having recited the Yajus, *viṣṇo havyaṃ rakṣasva*, one should dip the thumb into the food remaining from the *agnaukaraṇa* rite placed in the ancestral vessel, insert it [into the fire], perform the rites beginning with *apahatāḥ*, and then give—that is, serve—the food. This is the meaning.

In the *Nigama*, however, after describing the dipping of the thumb and the subsequent serving of the food, it shows a different reading for the mantra regarding the grasping of the vessel and the recitation (*japa*):

"Having offered the remaining food with his hand into [the guests'] hands like a funeral ball (*piṇḍa*), and having dipped his thumb into the food, he should give warm and abundant food; then, touching the vessel, he recites: 'The earth is your vessel, the sky is your lid; I offer you, who are nectar, as nectar into the midst of the out-breath and in-breath of the Brahmins—Svāhā!'"

In the *Maitrāyaṇīya-sūtra*, however, after stating that the dipping of the thumb [into the food] occurs specifically with the remainder of the *agnaukaraṇa* offering, another mantra is prescribed for the grasping of the vessel: "The sky is the vessel, *svadhā* is the lid; I offer you, the nectar, into the mouth of the Brahmins, who are the Pitṛs—*svadhā*! The word "in the remainder" (*avaśiṣṭe*) refers to the food remaining from the *agnaukaraṇa* oblation, which has been placed into the vessel of the Pitṛs.

In the Baudhāyana-sūtra, however, a specific requirement is stated for the thumb to be devoid of a nail, and other mantras are prescribed according to the division of the positions of the ancestors and others.

Then, having announced the remainder to the Brāhmaṇas, he assigns it to the Brāhmaṇa with his thumb, excluding the nail, saying: "The earth is your level ground; Agni is your overseer; the Ṛg-verses are your greatness. For the non-neglect of what has been given: the earth is your vessel, the sky is the lid; I offer the nectar into the mouth of the Brāhmaṇa. I offer you into the out-breath and in-breath of the learned Brāhmaṇas. You are uninjured. May you be the best among my fathers in that world yonder. He assigns the second portion, saying: "The atmosphere is your level ground; Vāyu is your overseer; the Yajus-formulas are your greatness. For the non-neglect of what has been given: the earth is your vessel, the sky is the lid; I offer the nectar into the mouth of the Brāhmaṇa. I offer you into the out-breath and in-breath of the learned Brāhmaṇas. You are uninjured. May you be the best among my grandfathers in that world yonder. He assigns the third portion, saying: "The heavens are your level ground; Āditya is your overseer; the Sāman-chants are your greatness. For the non-neglect of what has been given: the earth is your vessel, the sky is the lid; I offer the nectar into the mouth of the Brāhmaṇa. I offer you into the out-breath and in-breath of the learned Brāhmaṇas. You are uninjured. May you be the best among my great-grandfathers in that world yonder."

"Other" refers to the food remaining after the *agnaukaraṇa* offering; "having presented it to the Brāhmaṇas" means having poured it into the vessels of the Brahmins invited for the ancestors (*pitrya*). Thus, by this sequence of statements, it is taught that the touching of the vessels and the recitation (*japa*) occur prior to the serving of the food, while the insertion of the thumb occurs in the remainder of the *agnaukaraṇa*. However, Pracetas has stated that the touching of the vessels, the recitation, and the insertion of the thumb occur only after the serving of the food. And [it is said]: "Having given everything as prescribed, one should touch the vessel and recite [the mantra]."

"Having given"—that is, having served—all that has been prepared for the sake of the present *śrāddha*, such as food fit to be chewed or swallowed (*bhakṣya-bhojya*), one should mutter [the mantra]. The words "pṛthivī te pātram" and so forth are to be understood as the remainder [of the instruction].
It is also stated in the *Nāgarakhaṇḍa*:
"Having seen the food thus offered, and having touched the vessel, one should mutter [the mantra]."
The word "then" (*tataḥ*) refers to the time following the disposal of the remnants of the *agnaukaraṇa* offering. "Seen" (*dṛṣṭaṃ*) means that which is required by the ancestors and the twice-born.
Regarding this, Yājñavalkya states the mantra for recitation (*japya*) by way of its opening phrase:
"Having given food, [saying] 'the earth is the vessel'"—this is the consecration of the vessel.
Having performed this with the mantra "idaṃ viṣṇuḥ," he should place the thumb of the twice-born into the food.
Paiṭhīnasi, however, states the complete mantra:

"The earth is your vessel, the sky is the lid; I offer the nectar into the mouth of the Brāhmaṇa, svadhā. With this, having placed his thumb into both the food and the water, he recites: "Viṣṇu strode across this."

Regarding this, some explain that the placing [of the thumb] in water is for the purpose of washing the thumb after it has been placed in the food; others, however, say that it is the placing [of the thumb] in water already brought forth beforehand for the sake of drinking, just as the food was already served beforehand for the sake of eating. Both of these views are observed. However, in the *Mānava-maitrāyaṇīya-sūtra*:

The grasping of the thumb is performed with this verse, "This [is] Viṣṇu"; having taken the thumbs of the Brāhmaṇas with the words, "Viṣṇu strode forth," one places them in the Vaiśvadevika rite with "O Viṣṇu, protect the *havya* (oblation to the gods)," and in the Pitrya rite with "O Viṣṇu, protect the *kavya* (oblation to the ancestors)," and then pours water into their hands.
But Yama says: "One should say 'O Viṣṇu, protect the *havya* and the *kavya*' in due order."
One should place that thumb into the waters that have been first offered.

The meaning is that one should say "O Viṣṇu, protect the *havya*" in the rite for the gods (*daiva*), and "O Viṣṇu, protect the *kavya*" in the rite for the ancestors (*pitrya*). The word "it" (*tam*) refers to what was established in the preceding mantra. Regarding the phrase "among those to whom the first portion has been given": this means among those seated before the Brāhmaṇas, or those to whom food has already been served like rice.
For this very reason, it is stated in the *Brahmapurāṇa*:
"Then, having given the entire meal in due order up to the water-offering..."
Then one should perform the formal offering to all the gods.
Having taken hold of the twice-born’s thumb, one should recite the mantra while restraining speech;
reciting "The earth is your vessel," one should contemplate the food as nectar.
One should recite: "O Viṣṇu, protect this my offering.
Then, with that same mantra, one should present it to the ancestors, respectfully taking hold of the thumb of each individual Brahmin. Thus it is said.

"Food" (*bhojana*) refers to that which is to be eaten—namely, items to be chewed, swallowed, licked, sucked, and drunk. "Having given" (*datvā*) means having served; "offering" (*pratipādana*) means relinquishment (*tyāga*). By the passage beginning with "having grasped the thumb of the twice-born," the procedure to be performed prior to the relinquishment is stated.
However, Śaṅkha and Likhita have stated that upon placing the thumb, one should touch the knees and meditate on the ancestors:
"Having taken hold of the thumb, and having sat down on the ground with the knees [bent], [one should say] 'This is Viṣṇu... regarding the ancestors.
"Meditating with the mind"—this should be understood as follows:

in rites for the ancestors (*pitrya*), one meditates on the *Viśvedevas*; in rites for the gods (*daiva*), one meditates on "all the gods. Furthermore, the sitting upon the knees should be understood according to the distinction that it is with the right knee in rites for the gods, and with the left knee in rites for the ancestors. And this is intended as an illustration for all the ritual characteristics (*dharma*) pertaining to both the gods and the ancestors.
In the *Kālikā Purāṇa*, the rotating of the thumb within the food is prescribed.
Having held the thumb of the twice-born and having stirred [the offering] soaked in ghee and honey,
one should protect the offerings to the gods and ancestors with the mantra "pṛthivī te."

By the mantra "pṛthivī te," the sequence beginning with "pṛthivī te pātram" and ending with "viṣṇo havyam" (including "idaṃ viṣṇuḥ" and so forth) is indicated. Having recited all of this, one should place the thumb of the twice-born into the food served that is saturated with ghee and honey, and having rotated it—that is, having moved it around—one should protect that food from Rākṣasas and other malevolent beings by means of that thumb.
For Viṣṇu, in the form of the thumb, is the protector of that food.
Thus says Yama:
The Blessed Viṣṇu, the size of a thumb, wanders the earth for the sake of slaying the Rākṣasas; upon whom will he strike today?

Therefore, in all *śrāddha* rites, the protection of the thumb is prescribed. Any *śrāddha* performed without the thumb, or that which is held outside the knees—all that is consumed by the *asuras*; it becomes entirely demonic.
Hārīta also says:
"A *śrāddha* performed without the thumb does not indeed gratify the ancestors;
therefore, one should recite the mantra with a concentrated mind while pressing upon the thumb."
"Viṣṇu strode through this [universe]"—
just as food placed in a vessel is covered by a lid and thus reaches a state of preservation,
so too does that which is consecrated by the thumb reach its proper place.
Another mantra for grasping the thumb and a specific rule for its rotation are stated in the *Pippalāda-sūtra*:

"Grasping the thumb in the vessel, one should rotate it clockwise for the gods (*daiva*) and counter-clockwise for the ancestors (*pitṛ*); then, having separated the knees on the ground, one should mutter: 'May the gods protect us from where Viṣṇu [is]'.
"Counter-clockwise" (*apasavya*) means not clockwise.

"Therefore may the gods protect us from where Viṣṇu strode forth with the seven stations of the earth"—this mantra is to be understood here as taught by its opening words (*pratīkena*). This too is to be employed together with the previously mentioned Vaiṣṇava *Yajuḥśiras*. Regarding the instruction "having separated the two knees on the ground," one should understand the distinction that the right knee is for the gods (*daiva*) and the left for the ancestors (*pitrya*), but not that both knees should be placed in each [direction] individually. (Kauśikasūtra)
Having grasped the thumb [of the Brahmin], one should mutter the verse "idaṃ viṣṇuḥ" while circumambulating to the right for the gods and to the left for the ancestors, having knelt upon the ground.
Regarding the specific manner of grasping the thumb, Dhaumya has stated:
"Having turned around, one should place the thumb of the twice-born into the food of the twice-born."
That indeed becomes fit for Rākṣasas; it does not reach the ancestors.

"Alteration" (*parivartana*) refers to changing the natural position [of the hand]. Therefore, it is meant that one should not place the thumb after having "turned over" (*parivṛtya*)—that is, having turned upward—the hand of the twice-born. The sacrificer also must not grasp the thumb with his own upturned hand, for it has been stated that a fault arises from doing so.
Rather, the placing of the twice-born's thumb should be done with an upturned hand:
"The twice-born who, out of delusion, performs this [otherwise], that indeed goes to the *rakṣas*."
Thus end the acts of supporting the vessel, the recitation of mantras, and the placing of the thumb.
Now follows the formal dedication (*saṃkalpa*) of the food.

Therein, intending to perform the dedication of the food for the sake of the ancestors beginning with the father, one should contemplate—so as to ensure the firmness of that contemplation—the ancestors, distinguished by their lineage, relationship, and names, as being endowed with the forms of the Vasus and other deities; the food as the oblation (*havis*); the Brahmins as representing the *āhavanīya* sacrificial fire; the site of the *śrāddha* as the sacred site of Gayā; the eaters as Gadādhara (Viṣṇu); and the food-vessel as silver. Having thus contemplated them, one should likewise proclaim them accordingly.
In the *Prabhāsakhaṇḍa*:
"Having placed the entire food in the vessels of the twice-born, one should perform the formal declaration (*saṃkalpa*);
for no connection with those [vessels] is seen when [the food] is situated in a ladle or similar implement."

For the sake of accomplishing the *śrāddha* currently under discussion, one should set aside portions from all the various collections of food that have been prepared—portions whose quantity is estimated to be sufficient to satisfy each individual twice-born guest—and having served them into the eating vessels placed before the guests, one should perform the formal dedication (*saṃkalpa*) and the act of relinquishment (*tyāga*) intended for the ancestors and others. The meaning is that the connection of those ancestors with the food does not arise merely by its presence in the ladles, pots, and so forth, but rather through the formal dedication itself; therefore, one must perform the *saṃkalpa*. Even though it is stated that "one should perform the *saṃkalpa* after placing the entire food into the vessel," if the vessel is too small, then those items which would otherwise cause a loss of flavor due to mutual mixing, or those which were forgotten at the time of serving, or those already served but later realized to be required by the guests—even while the guests are eating—must indeed be served again. This is because following the well-known methods of dining is accepted even in the case of a *śrāddha*.
On this point, some say:
"The pure should give to the pure, and that which is to be given should be pure;
because the recipient is defective, it is for this reason that [giving] in such a manner is not appropriate."

Thus, the meaning is that because the recipient is rendered impure by the act of eating leftovers, giving while they are still eating is not appropriate. Furthermore, a gift given after the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) has been made does not connect with the ancestors and would therefore be entirely useless.

To this it is said: This fault would apply to one who makes the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) once the food has already been served; however, it does not apply to one who makes the resolve even while the food is yet to be served, provided he does so at the very time [the recipient] possesses the status of a recipient (*saṃpradāna*) and is pure. For this very reason, all learned authorities (*śiṣṭa*) employ the formula for the resolve as follows: "That which has been served and that which is yet to be served. Furthermore, the determination of the agent regarding the resolve was made by Trikāṇḍamaṇḍana:
"But one should perform the act of relinquishment (*tyāga*) in every way; even in that case, one of the two [the giver or the recipient] may do so."

"If both are incapable, anyone who has been appointed may abandon [the rite]. Regarding this, "of the two" refers to the husband and wife; it means either one of them. Furthermore, this abandonment must be performed without having given the water for *apośāna* (water for sipping) into the hands of the twice-born. Atri states the fault incurred by doing otherwise:
"He who performs the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) when the Brahmin has not yet taken the *apośāna* water..."
"That food, when eaten by the Asuras, does not reach the ancestors.
In this regard, Viṣṇu has established that the formal dedication (*saṃkalpa*) of the food must be preceded by the *vaiśvadeva* rite, as well as a portion of the ritual formula (*prayogavākya*).

Saying "Salutation to all the gods," one should first offer food to two [guests] facing east; then, to the father, grandfather, and great-grandfather, by means of their names and lineages, to those facing north.

The phrase "namo viśvebhyo devebhyaḥ" (Salutation to all the gods) is merely a portion of the formula for offering (*nivedanavākya*), as it lacks the specific mention of the object to be offered. The term "of the two facing east" refers to the two twice-born (*dvija*) invited for the *vaiśvadeva* rite; for these two are taught to occupy the position of the *āhavanīya* fire by means of the *apasavya* (leftward) procedure. The use of the locative case (*prāṅmukhayoḥ*) is because they serve as the substratum upon which the sacrificial oblation is being abandoned. The word "at first" (*ādau*) is in relation to the Brahmins invited for the ancestors (*pitrya*); by this, it is understood that [the offering] is made "afterwards" to the Brahmins of the ancestors. Even there, the portion of the ritual formula is indicated by implication through the words "to the father, to the grandfather," and so forth. Furthermore, this offering of food must be performed by pouring water held in the hand together with sesame seeds. Likewise, for the Brahmins of the ancestors, it is done with a formula ending with the word *svadhā*.
And likewise in the Viṣṇudharmottara:
"With the mantra 'Oṃ namo viśvebhyaḥ' and with water containing sesame seeds,
one should consecrate that food which is offered while [the Brahmins] face the east."
Facing north, the wise and disciplined practitioner, being well-composed, should recite the names and lineages [of the ancestors] with mantras ending in "svadhā" as the offerings are presented.

One should "recite"—that is, make manifest—the formula of renunciation beginning with, "That food which has been served, that is an offering to the Viśvedevas," and so forth. However, for the rites pertaining to the ancestors (*pitrya*), one should recite the names and *gotras* followed by the word *svadhā*, which constitute parts of the formula of renunciation.

Regarding this, Atri states that the sentence for the presentation of food in the *vaiśvadevika* rite should end in *svāhā*, while in the *pitrya* rite it should end in *svadhā*; he also prescribes the use of the word indicating the item to be presented and the touching of the vessel at the time of presentation:
"One should utter the words 'This food' regarding the food and other items not yet released from the hand."
And then one should utter "svāhā," thereby effecting the withdrawal of one's own existence.
Likewise:
Having uttered the names connected with the lineage along with "this food" and "svadhā" from that [lineage],
according to the paternal succession, one should cause one's own existence to cease.

The meaning is: "one should cause one's own existence" (*svasattām*)—that is, the presence of one's ownership—to "cease" (*vinivartayet*), which means one should employ the word *namaḥ* as an expression denoting the renunciation of ownership effected by the mind. Regarding the term "unreleased" (*amuktam*), it refers to that which is being touched; in the phrase "with the hand," it should be understood as "with the left hand," because the right hand is occupied in holding the water for the purpose of renunciation. Regarding "food" (*annādyam*), this refers to the vessel intended for holding food, and not the food itself. For this very reason, the *Caturviṃśatimata* states: "A twice-born man should touch the vessel while uttering: 'This food is for you.'"

In this context, regarding the rite for the gods (*daiva*), the *Brahma Purāṇa* states that when taking hold of the vessel and when sprinkling the water of renunciation (*tyāga-jala-prakṣepa*), there is a connection with the *devatīrtha*; furthermore, in the formula of renunciation, the conjunction of the syllable *oṃ* and the word *namaḥ* at the end of the word *svadhā* is prescribed. Then, having taken warm food mixed with sesame seeds and smeared with honey and clarified butter, one should [offer it] again by means of the *devatīrtha* and with the *praṇava* alone.
Having said, "This is your food," he should cause all the gods to recite [the mantra].

Having prepared the served food together with honey, clarified butter, and sesame seeds, and having taken it with the right hand using the *devatīrtha* (the part of the hand sacred to the gods) while supporting the vessel, one should first utter the *praṇava* (*om*), invoke the Viśvedevas, designate the food by saying "This food is for you," and then recite over the Viśvedevas. The phrase "this food is for you" (*etad vo ’nnam*) is an alternative to "this here is the food" (*etad idam annam*), as they possess the same meaning. Because of the designation "for you" (*vaḥ*), the use of the vocative case is intended here to indicate the deities.
For this very reason, in this same Purāṇa, within the statement regarding the non-abandonment of food offered to the ancestors, this application of case endings is clearly set forth:
"Then one should give food to the ancestors with this invocation:
'O [Name], of such-and-such lineage, this food is for you; Svadhā! Homage!'"

Nor should one suspect that this contradicts the rule that "the dative case should not be used in the giving of food," because of the expression "having addressed [him], [saying] 'to you'. Furthermore, since the phrase "of such-and-such a lineage" has the same meaning as "to the father, to the grandfather," and so forth, it is merely an option.
In the *Sāṅkhyāyana-gṛhya*:
"Having assigned the food, saying 'This is for you,' he should feed him."

In the Kaṭha-sūtra: having made the formal resolve (saṃkalpa), "The earth is your vessel," and having consecrated [the food] according to its specific characteristics with the formulas, "Svadhā, obeisance to such-and-such; svadhā, obeisance to such-and-such," one should feed [the guests].
This is the formal resolve regarding the food.
Now follows the ritual procedure for taking up the bowl and so forth.

Therein, the performer endowed with the *daiva-dharma* (rites for the gods) should first sprinkle the food contained in the vessel of the *vaiśvadevika* Brahmin who was seated first, using the *Sāvitrī* mantra preceded by the *praṇava* and the *vyāhṛtis*. Then, touching the vessel with both hands turned upward, he should recite the mantra beginning with "The earth is thy vessel" (*pṛthivī te pātram*) and ending with *svāhā*. Following this, he should recite either the verse "May the gods protect us from here" (*ato devā avantu naḥ*) or the verse "Viṣṇu strode across this" (*idaṃ viṣṇur vicakrame*). With his right hand not turned upward, he should grasp the thumb of the Brahmin who is likewise not turned upward, and place the food into the vessel while reciting the *vaiśvadeva-yajus*: "O Viṣṇu, protect the sacrificial offering" (*viṣṇo havyaṃ rakṣasva*). Then, taking water mixed with barley and *kuśa* grass, and touching the vessel with his left hand, he should announce: "The *Viśvedevas*, known as Purūravas and Ārdrava, are the deities; this food is the sacrificial offering (*havya*); the Brahmin serves as the *āhavanīya* fire; the wielder of the conch, discus, and mace is the eater; the golden vessel is the receptacle. Having said this, he should pour that water onto the ground with the *devatīrtha* (the part of the hand sacred to the gods), reciting: "To the *Viśvedevas* known as Purūravas and Ārdrava, along with their attendants—this food, served and yet to be served, sufficient for the satisfaction of the Brahmins, is *svāhā*; obeisance, obeisance! Oṃ Tat Sat. Thereafter, he should perform the same sequence, from touching the vessel to the renunciation of the food, for each of the subsequent *vaiśvadevika* Brahmins. Immediately after that, the performer endowed with the *pitṛ-dharma* (rites for the ancestors) should substitute the word *svadhā* for *svāhā* and the word *kavya* for *havya*. Having performed the previous rites up to the placement of the thumb in the vessel of the first seated *pitṛ* Brahmin, he should take water with three *kuśa* blades folded double and sesame seeds in his right hand. Touching the vessel with his left hand, he should announce: "Our fathers of such-and-such *gotra*, named so-and-so, together with their wives, are the deities in the form of Vasus. Reciting the rest as before up to "the wielder of the mace is the eater," and saying "the silver vessel is the receptacle," he should address them as: "To the fathers of such-and-such *gotra*, named so-and-so, together with their wives, in the form of Vasus. Then, reciting: "This food, along with its accompaniments, served and yet to be served, sufficient for the satisfaction of the Brahmins, is *svadhā*; obeisance, obeisance! Oṃ Tat Sat," he should pour that water onto the ground with the *pitṛtīrtha* (the part of the hand sacred to the ancestors). In this manner, having made the renunciation for the *pitṛ* Brahmins in order, he should do the same for the *prapitāmaha* Brahmins, using their names and describing them as being in the form of Rudras; and for the *prapitāmaha* Brahmins, using their names and describing them as being in the form of Ādityas. Finally, he should perform the same for the *mātāmaha* Brahmins, using their respective names and describing them as being in the form of Vasus and the other classes of ancestors.
Thus concludes the ritual procedure for grasping the vessel and so forth.
Now follows the recitation of the Sāvitrī mantra and other rites. Regarding this, Pāraskara says:

Having made the formal resolve for the ancestors and the gods, having recited the Sāvitrī and the Madhumatī verses, having offered the Śrāddha, having given the *apośāna* water, and having issued the *juṣapraiṣa* command, then follows the meal.

Having mentally dedicated the food to the gods and the ancestors and having offered it according to the prescribed rule, one should recite the *Sāvitrī*—the *Gāyatrī* whose deity is Savitṛ—and the "Honeyed Verses" (*madhumatī*). Then, having announced the *Śrāddha* and performed the declaration of its flawlessness (*acchidravācana*) in the manner that will be shown, and having given the *apośāna* water into the hand of the twice-born, one should feed them with the command: "Enjoy [the meal]" (*juṣadhvam*). Regarding the mixing of honey into the food and the consecration with the "Honeyed Verses," there is an indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the *Brahmapurāṇa*.
Food for the ancestors, purified with sesame seeds, clarified with ghee, and sprinkled with honey,
was consecrated with the mantra "Pṛthivī" and the verse beginning with "Madhu vātā."
Varāha spoke thus. Yama has described this method of reciting the *acchidra* [formula] beginning with the pouring of honey (*madhusecana*):
"Having made the food consist of honey and having consecrated it with the mantra 'madhuvātā'..."
Whatever may be deficient in food, deficient in ritual action, or deficient in mantra,
one should say, "All is without flaw," and then diligently feed [the guests].

Immediately after saying "without flaw" (*acchidram*), one should say "may it be born" (*jāyatām*), because Baudhāyana has shown the usage "may it be born without flaw" (*acchidraṃ jāyatām*). In this context, the Brahmins should say, "May everything be without flaw" (*sarvam acchidraṃ jāyatām*), since this sentence is intended for the purpose of making a formal request. Furthermore, this must be performed precisely before the offering of the *āpośāna* water; for if it is performed later, a fault is stated by Pracetas:
"Because they have spoken of the 'flawlessness' of those who have taken the *āpośāna* water, the ancestors depart hopeless along with the gods—of this there is no doubt."
In this regard, Yājñavalkya states that the recitation of the Sāvitrī must be preceded by the Vyāhṛtis:

"Having recited the Gāyatrī together with the Vyāhṛtis, and the three verses beginning with 'madhu vātā,' they should eat while remaining silent, speaking only as much as necessary for their comfort."
The meaning is that one should say, "Enjoy [the food] as you please.

However, in the *Mānava-Maitrāyaṇīya-Sūtra*, specific details are shown, such as the requirement of beginning with the *praṇava* (Oṃ), the nature of the *vyāhṛtis*, and the threefold repetition of the *gāyatrī*. Having recited "Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ, tat savituḥ" three times, and having recited the three verses of the *madhu-vātā* hymn ("madhuvātā ṛtāyate," etc. three times, saying "Madhu! three times, he should—remaining silent—offer the most desired foods while saying, "May the fathers, grandfathers, and great-grandfathers be pleased.
Furthermore, Pracetas states that the recitation of the *sāvitrī* should take place after the offering of the *apośāna* water.
Then, having offered the *apośāna* water, he should recite the *Sāvitrī* three times,
as well as the three-verse hymn beginning with "madhu vātā" and likewise the triad beginning with "madhu."
Kātyāyana also prescribes the recitation of the Gāyatrī three times or once immediately after the offering of the *apośāna* water:
"Having offered the *apośāna*, one should then recite the Gāyatrī preceded by the *vyāhṛtis*, either three times or once."
Therefore, the recitation of the *gāyatrī* and other rites should be performed either before or after the offering of *apośāna*, in accordance with one's own *gṛhya-sūtra*.
However, in the *Brahma-purāṇa*, it is stated that the scattering of sesame seeds and other items should also be done before the offering of *apośāna*:
"Water mixed with sesame and *kuśa* grass should be placed before them."
He should scatter [food] for those ancestors while reciting the mantra "apahatāḥ" (driven away).
To them he should offer the *apośāna* water, saying, "May you partake, sirs."
And while the *apośāna* rite is being performed, the offering of the *bali* on the ground must not be made.
Thus says Bharadvāja:
"He who, having taken food for the ancestors, offers the *bali* [on the ground]..."
By that theft, the Brahmin becomes a perpetrator of every kind of theft.

"Food for the ancestors" (pitṛṇām annam) refers to the food prepared for the purpose of the gods and ancestors; therefore, even prior to the formal renunciation (tyāga), no bali offering should be given to Citragupta and others.
For this very reason, Atri states:
"Whether it has been offered or not yet offered, he who should place a bali on the ground..."
After giving a small portion of the first-fruits of the meal as an offering to the King of Dharma (Yama) and to Citragupta,
the Brahmin shall indeed obtain the fruit of his theft.
Regarding the specific instructions for the serving of food here, the *Vārāha-purāṇa* and the *Viṣṇu-purāṇa* state:
"Having offered them food that is savory, most excellent, highly desired, and well-prepared, one should say these gentle words according to one's wish: 'Please enjoy [this] as you desire.'"
In the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa, however, it is said:
"Having touched the vessel and having offered the food according to the prescribed rule, one should say without harshness: 'O sirs, please enjoy this at your pleasure.'"
And here, Lord Hari, the imperishable soul, the master of sacrifice, the consumer of all *havya* and *kavya*,
is present; by his proximity, may all *rakṣas* and all *asuras* immediately depart.

Having recited this and declared, "May the Blessed Lord Yajñapuruṣa, who is the very form of the ancestors, be pleased," one should pour water mixed with *kuśa* grass and sesame seeds onto the ground near the Brahmins with the right hand; that one should then pay homage to the twice-born is to be understood from the practice of the learned. Vyāsa says:
"Addressed with the words 'Enjoy [the food],' they, having properly steadied their vessels and observed silence, should eat immediately after the *apośāna* rite."

In this context, the taking of the *prāṇāhuti* (vitality-oblations), which is established by the rule for the unrestricted daily meal, must certainly be performed. Then the sacrificer should perform the recitation (*japa*) of the mantras shown in the section on recitation, beginning with "The father, the grandfather," and so forth.
Kātyāyana says:

"While they are eating, he should recite the *Gāyatrī* preceded by the *vyāhṛtis*, together with the *praṇava*, once or thrice; as well as the *rakṣoghnas*, the *pitṛ-mantras*, the *Puruṣasūkta*, the *Apratiratha*, and other purifying hymns."
And this has already been largely explained in the section on recitation (*japa*).
From the *Vārāha-purāṇa* and the *Viṣṇu-purāṇa*:
"One should recite mantras that destroy demons while spreading the ground with sesame seeds."
Having performed this, those very best of the twice-born should be meditated upon as one's own ancestors.
In the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*:
"A man, free from anger, should give while praising [the recipient] and enticing him;
he should mutter mantras that destroy demons and scatter sesame seeds upon the ground."

Then the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) should feed the Brahmins. He should not fail to provide foodstuffs such as those to be chewed or eaten, nor should he look on with indifference. Repeatedly offering what has been requested, and not failing to offer it, he should stimulate their appetite by praising the qualities of the various foods. Uttering slowly, "I give," and showing this or that while asking about the qualities of the sacrificial oblation (*havis*), he should occasionally have them drink cool, clear water that is delicious to taste. Looking upon those who are eating, full of faith and meditating upon the ancestors (*pitṛs*), he should feed them very slowly, avoiding desire, anger, greed, delusion, deceit, egoism, envy, harsh speech, wretchedness, shedding tears, and so forth; these and other rules for the feeder (*bhojayitṛ-niyama*) mentioned in that context should be observed. The Brahmins who are eating should observe the following rules for the eater (*bhoktṛ-niyama*) mentioned in that context: they should remain silent, not looking here and there, and not allowing the restlessness of the senses except for the act of eating. They should be free from anger, laughter, fear, and astonishment. They should not step upon anything with their feet, such as another's foot, sandals, or a seat. They should not drop their knees to the ground. They should not touch one another. If they should touch by accident, they must not abandon their eating. They should not describe the qualities of the sacrificial food even by means of hand gestures. Except for vessels for drinking water and the like, they should not lift their bowls from the ground. Their vessels should not be left empty. Their elbows should not protrude outside, nor should their knees or hands. They should take morsels without extending the thumb or forefinger. They should not make sounds such as hissing (*phūtkṛta*). They should drink what remains after sipping, and eat what remains after tasting. They should not leave in the bowl the remnants of food bitten off by the teeth or dropped from the mouth. They should not make the food hot with the breath of the mouth. They should not spit. They should not touch the head, feet, or private parts with the left hand, nor touch the eating vessel with the foot. They should not eat in excessive measure, and they should not eat everything except for curds, honey, milk, barley-meal (*saktu*), and clarified butter (*sarpiḥ*); thus should they eat. These and other rules for the eater should be understood as stated in that section.
Thus concludes the recitation of the Sāvitrī and so forth. Now follows the scattering of the *vikira* offerings and so forth;
therein, first, the sequence of the ritual rules.
The Dharma says:
For some, there is first the scattering of food (vikira), and for others, the inquiry as to whether they are satisfied;
then for yet others, the scattering of food follows after the inquiry.

The scattering [of food] is considered by some to be prior to the *amṛtāpidhāna* (the covering with nectar), while for others it is held by the learned to be after that. For some, it occurs before the recitation of the *gāyatrī* and other mantras; for others, immediately thereafter.

Relying on the position that the scattering [of food] occurs prior to the covering with nectar (amṛtāpidhāna), the inquiry regarding satisfaction and so forth, and the recitation of the Gāyatrī and other mantras, Kātyāyana says:

Having recognized that they are satiated, he scatters food, offers water once for each, and first recites the *gāyatrī*. He then recites the "Honey-verses" (*madhumatī*) and the words "Honey, honey, honey," and asks, "Are you satisfied? When permitted with the reply, "We are satisfied," he says, "Without asking for permission regarding the remaining food. Having ascertained by inference that the Brahmins are satisfied, he takes all kinds of food prepared there, places them in a single vessel, and scatters them sparsely upon the ground that has been consecrated with the rites to be described. For the purpose of releasing the silence of the vessel and granting fearlessness, he eats [the scattered food] with the mantra, "Thou art the covering of nectar" (*amṛtāpidhānam asi*). Then, having offered water once for each, he recites the *gāyatrī* three times or once, the three verses beginning with "The honeyed wind" (*madhu vātā*), and utters the word "Honey" three times. Finally, the sacrificer asks the Brahmins, "Are you satisfied? (*tṛptāḥ stha*).

In this context, since no visible purpose for perceiving satiety is observed, there is a restrictive rule (*niyama*) that in all inquiries, only the head of the row (*paṅktimūrdhanya*) should be questioned, and not everyone. Furthermore, the purpose of perceiving satiety must be stated as follows: food is not served again to those known to be already satiated. This is because, having ascertained that they are satiated, a mouthful of water (*gaṇḍūṣa*) is given for the sake of rinsing the mouth (*pātravimocana*). Moreover, even when referring to a single individual, the plural number is used for the sake of honor. To this, it is replied:

Even though the purpose [of the rite] is unseen (adṛṣṭārtha), because of the instruction using the plural number, all [the invited] must be asked; as for the option [regarding the number], let that apply to other cases. When they have said, "We are satisfied," and the request has been made for permission regarding the disposal of the remaining food by asking, "What shall be done with the rest of the food?", and when the Brahmins have replied, "Let it be eaten together with the most eminent ones, or let it be given to us," then one should offer the *piṇḍas*—this is the connection with what follows. In this matter, one should act according to whatever method of disposal the Brahmins authorize.
And so says Yama:
Then, once they have finished eating, he should present the remains of the food;
he should act according to what those twice-born ones say, having been authorized by them.
Bṛhaspati also says: "One should question the Brahmins, and then one should act according to what they say. Thus it is stated in the Nāgarakhaṇḍa.
Then, knowing the Brahmins to be satisfied, one should scatter food in front of them with the mantra beginning "Agnidagdhāś ca ye... and so forth.
Having offered water once for each, one should recite the Gāyatrī three times.
Having recited the verse beginning with "madhu vātā," he should then question the best of the twice-born.
"O Indra among kings, one who is devoted should then request permission for the sake of feeding his kinsmen with the remaining food, saying, 'Are you satisfied? Gobhila has also said:
Knowing them to be satisfied, he scatters food, recites "agnidagdhāḥ" and so forth once each time, pours water once each time, and again mutters the verse "madhu vātā.
This [verse] "madhu vātā" is indicative of the recitation of the *gāyatrī* and other mantras as prescribed by Kātyāyana and others.
It is also stated in the *Kauśikasūtra*:
"Having known them to be satisfied, one should scatter food and give water once, once. Thus it is stated in the *Vārāha Purāṇa*:
"When those Brahmins are satisfied, one should scatter food upon the surface of the earth."
One should give them water for the purpose of sipping (ācamana) once each.
In the *Kūrmapurāṇa* as well:
"Then, once they have eaten, one should offer food by scattering it on the ground in front [of them].
By the word "scattering," the laying down of the food in a solid mass (*piṇḍībhūta*) is precluded.

In this regard, Yājñavalkya speaks by adopting a sequence that is the reverse of the order stated by Kātyāyana and others—namely, the recitation of the *gāyatrī* and other mantras, followed by the inquiry regarding satisfaction (*tṛptipraśna*), and subsequently the offering of mouthfuls of water (*gaṇḍūṣadāna*)—as follows:

"Having recited purificatory verses (*pavitra*) until they are satisfied, as well as the previously mentioned *japa*, and having taken food [from the vessel], he should ask, 'Are you satisfied? and obtain permission regarding the remainder."
One should scatter that food upon the ground and offer water once, one after another.

The "preceding recitation" (pūrvaja-pa) is that which was set forth by the passage beginning with "the Gāyatrī together with the Vyāhṛtis," and so forth. Here, the recitation of the Gāyatrī, the Madhumatī verses, and the rest should be performed in such a way that the Brāhmaṇas hear them. And thus say Śaṅkha and Likhita:

Having caused the *gāyatrī* to be recited and having ascertained that they are satiated, one should request permission regarding the remaining food and perform the scattering of the ordinary food (*prakṛtānnavikira*).

The grammatical connection is: "having ascertained that they are satiated, one should cause the *gāyatrī* to be recited. Immediately after this, the recitation of the *madhumatī* verses must be performed. Thus says Śaunaka:
Knowing them to be satisfied, one should recite the *madhumatī* verses.
In the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*:
"When they have been satisfied by the [recitation of the] *pṛṣṭhas*, and say, 'Are you satisfied? and 'We are satisfied.'"
Once permitted, the man should scatter food on the ground in every direction;
having given that, he should give water once for each instance for the purpose of sipping (ācamana).
Vyāsa says: When they are asked, "Are you satisfied?", they should reply, "We are satisfied.
Thus it is stated in the Brahmapurāṇa.
When the Brahmins had finished eating, he asked them, "Are you satisfied? and they replied, "We are satisfied. Then the god [the host] gave the signal to break the silence once.
He gave water for rinsing the mouth for the purpose of releasing the vow of silence; this refers to the Sacrificial Boar (*yajñavarāha*).
In the *Mānava-maitrāyaṇīya-sūtra*:
"Are you satisfied? he asks. When they have replied, "We are satisfied," and they have sipped water once, [he pours water] on the ground.
One should offer the scattered food (vikira).
In the Saura Purāṇa: "Afterwards, one should cast the scattered food and then speak regarding the remaining food."

In the *Brahmapurāṇa*, however, it is stated following this sequence: first the offering of water for rinsing the mouth (*gaṇḍūṣodaka*), then the questions and answers, and then the scattering of food (*vikira*).
Having given the "seal of nectar" (*amṛtāpidhāna*) to the Brahmins once each, he should say to them: "O Brahmins, has this been well-prepared by me? [1394]
They said, "It is well-prepared," and he spoke to them again:
"Are you sated with food? and they replied, "We are sated."
He said to them again, "Where should the remainder of this food be given? They replied to him, "Let it be given to those who are disciplined."
Then, having ascertained that they are satisfied, one should discard the food right there on the ground.
In the Baudhāyana Sūtra: "Having had those who are satisfied sip water and having obtained their permission, they scatter the remains of the food with the verse, 'Those who were consumed by fire...'"
Thus concludes the rule for the sequence. Now follows the detailed exposition of questions and answers.
Regarding this, Pracetas said:
"Are you satisfied? "We are satisfied. "Plenty? "Plenty," they said. Here, one instance of the word *prabhūta* is the question, while the second is the answer.
Viṣṇu and Āśvalāyana state another question:
"Having scattered the prepared food of the guest.
Here, by implication, the answer is also understood to be of this same nature.

In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*, however, the application of these two questions and answers together with the previously mentioned questions and answers is shown, as well as the practice of falling upon one's knees:
"The Brahmins should be questioned with devotion while kneeling on the ground:
'Are you satisfied? Is all well with you?'"
When they have said, "We are satisfied," and then, "It is well-prepared," the faithful and composed donor should devoutly offer water for sipping (ācamana).
In the Kūrma Purāṇa: Having asked if they have been satisfied with that food, he should then give them water for sipping (ācamana).
Once they have sipped water, he should dismiss them, saying, "May you rest at ease."
In this context, the answer "we are delighted" is understood by implication. Here, in this specific section on faith (*śraddhā*), a particular question and answer is stated;
namely, in the *Maitrāyaṇīya-sūtra*.

Having offered the scattered food (vikira), he should ask those who are satisfied whether it was "well-tasted" (svadita); at a rite for prosperity (ābhyudayika), he should ask whether it was "excellent" (saṃpanna). Thus says Hārīta.

When they are satisfied, he should ask, "Was it well-tasted? and they reply, "It was well-tasted. For offerings to the gods (*daiva*), he asks, "Was it remembered? and for those to the ancestors (*pitrya*), "Was it long-lived? Having offered and [the guests] having sipped water, he should pour the scattered food (*vikira*) upon the ground. Viṣṇu says: "In the rite for the ancestors, one should say 'It was well-tasted' (*svaditam*); among the cattle-pens, [it is said] 'It was well-heard' (*suśrutaḥ*)."
In rites for prosperity and those for the gods, one should say "it is prepared" or "it is pleasing."
Thus ends the detailed exposition of questions and answers.
Now follows the method for sipping water (ācamana), giving, and receiving.
Regarding this, Viṣṇu says:

One should first offer water for rinsing the mouth (*ācamana*) to those facing north, and thereafter to those facing east. The sipping of water (*gaṇḍūṣa*) must be performed without having washed the hand that is still smeared with food. Regarding the fault incurred by doing otherwise, Marīci says:
"The foolish man who washes his hands and then drinks the rinsing water [from them]..."
That śrāddha becomes demonic; it does not reach the ancestors.
In the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa:
"That unwise man who, having washed his hands, drinks the rinsing water (gaṇḍūṣa),
destroys the offerings to the gods, the ancestors, and himself."
In the Varāha Purāṇa: "If a twice-born man always washes his hand after eating and then drinks water,
that food has been consumed by the Asuras, and the ancestors depart disappointed."
Thus ends the procedure for the offering and receiving of the ritual sipping (ācamana). Now follows the ritual performance regarding the scattering of grains (vikira).
Regarding this, the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa states:

Then one should perform the scattering (*vikiraṇa*) by means of the ritual procedure as seen in the *vidhi*— that is, in the scripture— by means of the "action" (*karman*) consisting of the specific sequence of duties (*itikartavyatā*).
In this context, there are the purification of the place for the scattering, the purification of that [place], and the purification of the nature of the food to be scattered.
In that regard, according to the *Padma* and *Matsya Purāṇas*:
"Having ascertained that [the ancestors] are satisfied, one should then perform the scattering (*vikira*) for all classes;
having taken up food along with water, one should cast it upon the ground together with sesame seeds."
Devala says:
Then the wise man, having taken various kinds of food for himself into a vessel,
should place it in the spot where their leavings were left by means of that vessel.
‘Of those’ brahmins, ‘in the place of the remnants,’ that is, near the vessel used for eating.
And so it is stated in the Manusmṛti and the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa:
“O King, when they have finished eating, then [one should give] near the vessel...”
Having gathered food of all kinds and sprinkled it with water,
one should cast it upon the ground before those who have finished eating, scattering it about.

"Consisting of all kinds of grains" (*sārvavarṇika*) refers to the various types of food—such as milk-rice, boiled rice, cakes, soups, vegetables, and so forth—prepared for the purpose of the śrāddha under discussion. By this, the nature of the food to be distributed has been stated. "Having brought together" (*saṃnīya*) means having drawn small portions from each cooking vessel and collected them in a single vessel, such as a ladle;
that is, whatever has been offered to the ancestors, from each of those respective portions, one should take a share into an auspicious cup (*camasa*).

This is because of the statement in the *Brahma Purāṇa*. The term "camasa" is an indicative mark for any excellent vessel. Having "overflowed" or sprinkled [the food] with water mixed with sesame seeds and *darbha* grass, the purification of the food to be distributed is thus shown. In the phrase "near the edge of the vessel," it should be understood as "near the edge of the vessels of the Brahmins invited for the ancestors (*pitrya*).
For this very reason, the *Viṣṇudharmottara* states:
"Now, when the Brahmins have finished eating, hear from me as I describe the ritual procedure."
Then, in front of the Brahmins facing north, [he should place] water along with [the other items].
One should scatter food with devotion; that is remembered as the portion for the ancestors.
Then, one should place it with water before the Brahmins who are facing north.

Facing north, for the Brahmins, [the offering] is accompanied by water—that is, together with the water intended for sprinkling upon the ground that serves as the locus for the scattering, according to the meaning previously explained. This is what is meant: "Having sprinkled the ground with water mixed with sesame seeds and *darbha* grass, and having likewise moistened the food with that same [mixture], one should scatter that food upon that ground. The "portion" (*bhāga*) refers to the cause of satisfaction for the deceased ancestors, such as the *sapiṇḍas* and others; those to whom this portion belongs have been shown in the section on deities (*devatā-prakaraṇa*). They are also to be understood from the indicative marks (*liṅga*) of the mantras that will be shown later. Furthermore, the sprinkling of the ground is explicitly stated in both the *Vāyu Purāṇa* and the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*.

Having sprinkled the ground and first cleared it, one devoted to the ancestors should spread a layer of darbha grass together with sesame seeds upon that ground; this is stated in the *Brahma Purāṇa*:
"Upon the area for the impure remains, one should cause darbha grass with sesame seeds to be placed with their tips pointing toward the south."
The term "ucchiṣṭa" refers to the vessel containing the remnants.
However, in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*, a specific method for consecrating the food is stated:
"Having sprinkled the food along with the blades of grass, one should recite the mantra: 'I gaze upon me (Viṣṇu) through the food.'"
"Satṛṇam" means with *darbha* grass placed upon it; having sprinkled that [water] with the mantra "Māmekṣeṣva...
The mantra is as follows: "Māmekṣeṣva bahu me pūrtam astu brāhmaṇo me juṣatām atrānnaṃ sahasradhāram amṛtodakaṃ me puratas tv etat parame vyoman."
Also in the Kaṭha-sūtra:
"Sprinkle the food along with the grass, saying, 'Look upon me.'"— thus Viṣṇu.

When the Brahmins have eaten and reached satiety, and they have looked at me [the performer], one should sprinkle water over the food along with the grass and perform the scattering of the *vikira* (food-offering) in front of the remains of the meal. Thus [ends the section on] the location for the *vikira*, its purification, the nature of the food to be scattered, and its preparation.
Now, the mantras for the *vikira*:
Regarding that, first is the *vikira* (scattered offering) for the Vaiśvadeva;
Gobhila says:
"And those gods who do not drink Soma and are deprived of their sacrificial portions..."
I shall give them food as a scattered offering during the Vaiśvadeva rite.

It is understood from the indicative mark (*liṅga*) that this *vikiro* (scattered offering) is connected to the *vaiśvadeva* rite because it is to be given with this mantra. Consequently, it is to be performed there accompanied by the specific rules pertaining to that rite, and it is to be offered near the vessel containing the remnants of the twice-born intended for that purpose. Because it belongs to the deities, it is to be performed before the *vikiro* belonging to the ancestors (*pitrya*). Furthermore, since this is not practiced by many refined people (*śiṣṭas*), it should be performed only by those who follow their own traditional custom.
Now, the mantras for the ancestral *vikiro*:
In the Kaṭha-sūtra: "And for those beings who have been consumed by fire," one should scatter food upon the ground. Thus said Pracetas.
Having perceived that [the ancestors] are satisfied, he should take food together with sesame seeds and recite as before.
Having been granted permission, he should ask, "Are you satisfied? and then scatter [the food] on the ground with the words, "Those who are in the fires... and so forth.
In the Pippalāda-sūtra: "Having ascertained that they are satiated, one should perform the scattering of food (vikira) with the mantra 'ye agnidagdhāḥ'. Bṛhaspati says:
And when the Brahmins have sipped water,
he should scatter food with water before them and recite this mantra:
