May those living beings in my family who have not been cremated by fire, and those who have been cremated by fire, find satisfaction through what is given upon the earth; being satisfied, may they go to the supreme goal.

Kātyāyana: May those who were cremated by fire and those who were not cremated by fire, the living beings born in my family, be satisfied by what is given upon the earth; being satisfied, may they go to the supreme goal.

Gobhila: May those living beings in my family who were cremated by fire, as well as those not cremated by fire, be satisfied by what is given upon the earth; being satisfied, may they go to the supreme goal.
In the *Padma* and *Matsya* [Purāṇas]:
"One should cast [the food] before those who have eaten, scattering it upon the ground:
'May those living beings in my family who have not been cremated by fire, and those who have not yet been cremated [attain satisfaction].'"
May those who have been given on this earth be satisfied; being satisfied, may they go to the supreme goal.
To those who have no mother, no father, no kinsman, and likewise no prepared food or even food itself—
this food is given upon the earth for their satisfaction.
May they indeed proceed for the happiness of the world.

In the *Brahmapurāṇa*: "Those ancestors in our family for whom the rites of the rice-ball (*piṇḍa*) and water-libation (*udaka*) have been omitted; those who have not yet had their tonsure ceremony (*cūḍā*) performed; and those who have passed away while still in the womb."
May those for whom no cremation is performed, and others who have been consumed by fire,
find satisfaction through what is offered upon the earth, and may they attain the supreme goal.
Thus end the mantras for the scattering of the ancestral offerings (pitr-vikiraṇa). What is to be done after the scattering of the offerings is stated in the Brahma Purāṇa:
"Then, having washed both hands and sipped water three times, one should meditate upon Hari."
Then, having offered the portion for the hungry ghosts, one should perform it for the sake of pacifying through expiation.
Likewise, one should recite the Gāyatrī mantra together with the Vyāhṛtis and the Praṇava;
one should also recite the meritorious Madhumatī verses, as well as "madhu, madhu."

In this context, although the ritual disposal (*pratipatti*) of the scattered food (*vikira*) involves the application of many items to be mentioned later, it is explained right here because of its connection with the *vikira*.
Regarding that, Gautama first states the time for the disposal:
"One should dispose of the *vikira* with the remnants (*ucchiṣṭa*). [1401]

In the word "ucchiṣṭaiḥ," the instrumental case is used in the sense of accompaniment (*sahārthe*). By this, the following meaning is established: when the remnants (*ucchiṣṭa*) are taken from the place of the vessels and deposited in a certain spot, one should then perform the disposal of the scattered food (*vikira*) according to the instruction.
Otherwise, Vyāsa states the fault in performing it [without the remnants]:
"One should always dispose of the scattered food with the very remnants."
But for him who acts otherwise, the deities become hopeless.
Regarding the specific manner of disposal (*pratipatti*), Bhārgava says: "Taulvali stated that the disposal of the *vikira* should be like that of the *piṇḍas*.

Regarding the phrase "like the *piṇḍas*": the sage named Taulvali declared that whatever disposal is performed for the *piṇḍas*, the same should be performed for the *vikira*. Consequently, the disposal of the *piṇḍas* prescribed in such passages as, "One should give the *piṇḍas* to cows, goats, or Brahmins, or [dispose of them] in fire or water," must also be performed for the *vikira*.
In the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*:
"Regarding that which has been stated concerning the rite of offering the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) and the scattering of food (*vikira*),
one should cast the rice-balls into water, but one should throw the scattered food into the fire."

On this point, some hold the following view: there are two optional locations for the scattering of food (*vikira*). One is in the vicinity of the leavings (*ucchiṣṭa*), and the other is in the vicinity of the funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*). In that case, when the *vikira* is offered in the vicinity of the leavings, its disposal must be performed in a manner similar to the disposal of the leavings at the very time those leavings are disposed of. However, when the *vikira* is performed in the vicinity of the funeral cakes, then at the time of their disposal, the same procedure should be followed. To support the position that the *vikira* must indeed be performed even in the vicinity of the funeral cakes, they cite a statement from the *Kālikāpurāṇa*.
As before, having performed the worship, one should cause the rice-balls (piṇḍas) and the water-offering (arghya) to be given separately;
afterwards, one should scatter food for both those cremated by fire and those not cremated by fire.

In this context, since the ritual for the *vikira* (scattered offerings) follows immediately after the *piṇḍa-pūjā* (offering of rice balls) and no specific location is mentioned, it is understood that when a location is required, it should be in the vicinity of the *piṇḍas*.
[The text continues: "One should offer the *piṇḍas*, composed in meditation, with the size of a *kapittha* fruit."
Scattering that [water] equally, one should offer the rice-balls (piṇḍas) upon those [spots] at a distance of six finger-breadths.
Thus ends the ritual for scattering the offerings (*vikira*).

Thus concludes the section on the *Śrāddha-kalpa* within the *Pariśeṣa-khaṇḍa* of the *Caturvarga-cintāmaṇi*, composed by the illustrious Hemādri, the scholar and sovereign minister of all affairs to the illustrious Mahādevī, the supreme queen of great kings.
The fourteenth chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Vikirā and Other Offerings," is completed.

It is a ground for doubt, resembling the multitude of thick waves of the Ocean of Milk.
This is that Śrī Hemādri, whose creeper of fame— having as its companions the pearls released from the vicinity of the breasts of celestial women— always sports on high;

Now, regarding the offering of the rice-balls (piṇḍadāna): as for the times [for this],
here some perform the offering of the rice-balls even before the feeding of the Brahmins, while others do so afterwards.
Regarding this, Manu says:
"Some perform the offering of the rice-balls (piṇḍa-nirvapaṇa) even beforehand.
From the use of the word "some," it is understood that there is a twofold division: some do it beforehand, while others do it afterwards.
And likewise, the *Sāṃkhyāyana-gṛhya* states: "When they have finished eating, one should offer the rice-balls (*piṇḍas*); one [ball] in front. Śaṅkha also says:
"The wise should perform the offering of the rice-balls (piṇḍa) either in the vicinity of the food-leavings or first; thereafter, one should perform the fire-rite according to the rules.
However, some perform it while the feeding of the Brahmins is actually taking place.
Likewise, Viṣṇu states, following the phrase "while the Brahmins are eating":

"In the vicinity of the leavings, upon grass-blades with their tips pointing south, one should place a single *piṇḍa* for the father, saying, 'The earth is a sacrificial ladle, imperishable,' and so forth."

Regarding this, those who perform it first do so either immediately after the worship of the Brahmins and before the *agnaukaraṇa*, or after the *agnaukaraṇa*. Concerning the performance immediately after the worship, Devala says:
"Then, having taken up a water-pot filled with water and containing *darbha* grass..."
"Having sat down in front of them, he should announce the offering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍāvāpa*)," and so forth.
In the aforementioned statement of Śaṅkha, this very time for the offering of the rice-balls is observed.
Manu, however, states that the offering of the rice-balls, which occurs prior to the meal, is to be performed immediately after the *agnaukaraṇa* (the ritual of making offerings into the fire).

Having performed everything in counter-clockwise (apasavya) fashion around the fire, he should offer pure water with his left hand. Then, being composed, he should form three pindas from the remainder of that sacrificial offering. Thus [it is said].

"Therefore, from the remnant of the oblation" means from the remnant of the oblation used for the *agnaukaraṇa* rite. The word "remnant" (*śeṣa*) has already been explained previously. As for those who perform [the offering] afterwards, some do so while the Brahmins have not yet sipped water (*anācānta*), while others do so after they have sipped water (*ācānta*). And thus says the *Āśvalāyana-gṛhya-sūtra*: "One should place the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) after they have eaten but before they have sipped water; according to some, after they have sipped water."

Kātyāyana also, having prescribed the offering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) when the Brahmins have rinsed their mouths but have not yet properly performed the final sipping (*ācamana*), states: "Some [do it] when they have sipped. For this very reason, Kātyāyana, having established the sequence beginning with "the remaining food" and ending with "having requested permission," stated as follows: [1405] Having explained according to the aforementioned order up to the point of "having requested permission," he said: "Then, having scattered the food-remnants, one should give water for rinsing the mouth once each to the Brahmins, and then perform the recitation of the *Gāyatrī*, etc. Thus, he indicates that the scattering of the remnants and the subsequent rites are to be performed even after the sipping has been completed.
