Having set aside all the food from one place, he should offer three balls of rice each upon *darbha* grass near the leavings after pouring water over them; some say this should be done once they have sipped water.

One should place all the food into a single vessel. The word "all" (*sarva*) signifies the entirety of the types of food under discussion. Therefore, taking a little bit from each of the various kinds of food—such as meat, milk-rice (*pāyasa*), boiled rice (*odana*), cakes (*apūpa*), and soup (*sūpa*)—which have been prepared for the performance of the *śrāddha* at hand, one should collect a quantity of food sufficient for the *piṇḍas* into one vessel; this is what is meant. "In the vicinity of the leavings" (*ucchiṣṭasamīpe*) means in a place separated from the area of the leavings by a distance of three *vyāmas*, three *ratnis*, two arms, or the like. Here, the ritual procedure (*upacāra*) is the same as in the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña*. Because the sūtra states "pertaining to the ancestors" (*pitrya*), the use of *darbha* grass is implied as an illustration of what is cut once with the root. Some say it is for the purpose of exclusion (*parisaṃkhyā*). "Abluting" (*avanejya*) means that for each individual *piṇḍa* about to be offered, one should address the name and lineage of each respective ancestor (father, etc. who is the intended recipient, and having uttered those, pour water mixed with sesame seeds from the vessel while saying "May you wash yourself" (*avanenikṣva*). The repetition "three each" (*trīn trīn*) is with reference to the three *piṇḍas* for the maternal grandfather and others. "One should offer the *piṇḍas*" (*piṇḍān dadyāt*): a *piṇḍa* is food that has attained a state of mass by abandoning its division due to mutual contact. According to the opinion of some, one should offer the *piṇḍas* after the *brāhmaṇas* have finished eating and before they have rinsed their mouths (*anācānteṣu*), having performed the *gāyatrī*-recitation and other rites for the sake of releasing the vessels, while the *brāhmaṇas* hold a mouthful of water once. Then he states the opinion of others: "When they have rinsed their mouths, one... (*ācānteṣv eka*). One should not think that because of the singular number ("one"), this position is merely the view of another; for Karka stated that since both are scriptural, there is an option (*vikalpa*). And let it be that because of the word "one," this is the latter's position due to its posteriority. However, some take the food for the scattering (*vikiro*) even while the guests have not yet rinsed their mouths, cause the permission for the remaining food to be given after the question regarding satisfaction, scatter the *vikira*, give water once to each of the *brāhmaṇas*, and subsequently perform the offering of the *piṇḍas*.
For this very reason, Yājñavalkya, beginning with the words "having taken food" and proceeding in that same sequence until the end of the phrase "once each," stated:
"Having taken all the food together with sesame seeds, facing south,
one should offer the rice-balls (piṇḍas) in the vicinity of the leavings, as in the Pitṛyajña."

Some, however, perform the offering of the *piṇḍas* even while the guests have finished eating but before they have performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*); having offered the scattered food (*vikira*) and caused the *svadhā* to be uttered.
To this effect, Śaṅkha and Likhita state:

Having caused the *gāyatrī* to be recited, and having ascertained that they are satisfied, he should ask, "Is it well-tasted? and, having obtained permission regarding the remaining food, he should make the *vikira* offering from the food served. Having caused the word *svadhā* to be uttered, he should place three *viṣṭara* grass seats. He should also set down three water-vessels containing sesame seeds and *pavitra* strainers, made either of clay, stone, or udumbara wood. He should present incense, perfumes, garlands, a mirror, a lamp, collyrium, and other such items. Taking all varieties of food, he should place the *piṇḍas*.

The meaning of this is as follows: Having "caused the *gāyatrī* to be heard"—that is, having uttered it so that the Brāhmaṇas may hear it—one should ascertain that they are "satisfied" (*tṛptān*), meaning well-fed. Then, having asked "Is it *svadita*?"—whereby the answer "It is well-eaten" (*svaditam*) is understood to mean "it is very well-eaten" (*susvaditam*)—one should obtain permission through question and answer, asking, "What shall be done with the remaining food? May it be eaten with those you desire. Having obtained permission, one should set aside a portion of the permitted food and scatter it upon the ground. Having caused the *svadhā* to be recited by means of the formula beginning with "I shall cause the *svadhā* to be spoken," one should place three *viṣṭaras* (seats) on the ground for the purpose of the three *piṇḍas*; each *viṣṭara* serves as the support for each individual *piṇḍa* that is about to be placed. A *viṣṭara* consists of twenty-five blades of *darbha* grass tied together with their tips pointing eastward. For the purpose of performing the *avanejana* (sprinkling) for each individual *piṇḍa*, there should be exactly three water-vessels made of either clay, stone, or copper, each accompanied by a *pavitra* (purifier). "Incense" (*dhūpaḥ*) refers to the resin of *guggulu* and the like. "Fragrances" (*gandhāḥ*) refers to the fragrant ointments prescribed for the *śrāddha*. "Garlands" (*mālyāni*) refers to strung flowers suitable for the *śrāddha*. "Mirror" (*ādarśaḥ*) is a looking-glass; it is called *ādarśa* because form (*rūpa*) is seen (*ādṛśyate*) in it. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), Hariharācārya explains that items for adornment such as vermilion (*sindūra*) are included. "Lamp" (*pradīpaḥ*) is well-known. "Collyrium" (*añjanam*) refers to *sauvīra* and the like. The word "etcetera" is intended to include other useful substances such as unguents and clothing. These one should "bring near," that is, place in the vicinity of the place where the *piṇḍas* are offered. Taking all the varieties of food, combining them into one, and making *piṇḍas* from that, one should place them down.

Some, however, perform the offering of the rice-balls (piṇḍa) while the guests have not yet sipped water, and the scattering of food (vikira) once they have sipped; for this very reason, Bṛhaspati says:
"And one should perform the offering of the rice-balls near them [the guests]."

Having described the offering of the *piṇḍas* with the words beginning "ityādinā," the offering of the *vikira* is described with the words beginning "upasṛṣṭodakānāṃ tu. Some performers, even when the Brahmins have sipped water (*ācānta*), perform the *piṇḍa-dāna* without performing the ritual items such as the request for permission to depart (*abhiramaṇānujñā*). Others do it after that [the *ācamana*], and others after the dismissal of the Brahmins (*brāhmaṇa-vimārjana*). In this regard, because of the expression "when they have sipped water," it is understood that the time immediately following the *ācamana* is intended. However, Yama states that it occurs at a time subsequent to the request for permission to depart and so forth: "One should dismiss those who have sipped water, having saluted them with palms joined in reverence."
Sirs, rejoice here, having understood the characteristics of what is permitted.
One should say "Svadhā" and likewise, "May the ancestors be pleased.
When the twice-born are satisfied, the words "The gift of food is inexhaustible" should be spoken.
Thereafter, one should perform the offering of the rice-balls (piṇḍas). Thus it is said.

"May you, sirs, enjoy yourselves"—this half-verse beginning with these words is the formula of permission (*anujñā-vacana*). Having understood its essential nature to be "conducting oneself as one pleases," which is the characteristic of one who has been permitted, [the priest says], "May you, sirs, enjoy yourselves," meaning "may you conduct yourselves as you please. However, some perform the offering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa-dāna*) after the dismissal of the Brahmins.

Thus Hārīta says: "One should ask those who are satiated, 'Was it well-tasted? and so forth; having recited the post-meal mantras ending with 'Vāja-vāja,' he says: 'One should place the remaining portions as rice-balls according to the ritual for the ancestors (*pitṛ-yajña*')."
And these times for the offering of the funeral rice-ball (piṇḍa) are to be understood as established according to the different Vedic schools (śākhā). Thus says the Smṛti:
"The offering of the rice-ball which has been prescribed by the sages at various distinct times..."
A wise person should perform that which is the doctrine of his own Vedic branch wherever it may be.

"At which time": at that time when [the rite] being performed is authorized by one's own *śākhā*, it should be done. This is an elliptical expression for authorization by one's own *gṛhya-sūtra* and so forth. Regarding the distinction between the times before and after the meal, Laugākṣi says:
"In unholy sacrifices, the washing of the *piṇḍas* comes first."
"But one should prepare the excellent food only afterwards. Thus [it is said].

"In unholy sacrifices" refers to the *preta-śrāddhas* performed prior to the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*. Regarding "pouring water" (*avanejana*), the author of the *Smṛticandrikā* states that it is the offering [of water] with the palm turned downwards. It may also be explained that by the term "pouring water"—which is a constituent element at the commencement of the offering of rice balls (*piṇḍa*)—the giving of the rice balls itself is indicated. "Before the meal" means prior to eating. "Hallowed" refers to that which is performed in *śrāddhas* such as the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* and others, which occurs only after the meal at the appropriate time. And this rule applies only to certain followers of specific Vedic branches (*śākhās*), because in the *smṛtis* of Manu and others, as well as in the *Purāṇas* such as the *Matsya*, [it is stated otherwise].

Regarding the primary *pārvaṇa* or the *piṇḍānvāhāryaka* rite, there is an injunction for the time of offering the *piṇḍas* specifically before the feeding. For this very reason, the statement of the author of the *Smṛticandrikā* that in the *pārvaṇa-śrāddha* it occurs only after the feeding should likewise be interpreted in this manner. However, for those for whom no specific time for the offering of *piṇḍas* is mentioned in the *Gṛhyasūtras* and other texts, it is proper to adopt this very position—that it occurs when they have sipped water (*ācānta*)—on account of its practical convenience. In this context, the alternative times for the offering of the *vikira* (scattered food) have also been explained incidentally.
Thus ends the section on the times for the offering of *piṇḍas*.
Now, the places for offering the rice-balls (piṇḍas).

In that regard, first, having performed the offering of the *piṇḍas* near the fire in the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña*, the procedure is to be conducted as in the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña*. Furthermore, because the ritual details (*vidhyanta*) of the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña* are extended by analogy (*atideśa*) to rites such as those for the ancestors (*pitrya*), one should offer the *piṇḍas* in the very vicinity of the fire when that fire is present. Accordingly, Devala—describing the offering of *piṇḍas* prior to the feeding of the Brahmins—states that after placing the *piṇḍas* on the ground and adorning them with collyrium and other items, he prescribes the *agnaukaraṇa-homa* immediately thereafter, specifying that this oblation is to take place in the proximity of the *piṇḍas* previously placed there.
Having thus offered oblations into the fire in the vicinity of the rice-balls (piṇḍas),
the twice-born man should immediately thereafter cause an offering of cooked food to be given to those rice-balls.

Thus, having offered oblations into the fire in the manner described while in the vicinity of the *piṇḍas*, one should immediately thereafter offer a *bali*—in the form of a food offering (*naivedya*)—consisting of cooked food, to these *piṇḍas*. By stating that the fire-oblation takes place in the vicinity of the *piṇḍas*, it is implied that the *piṇḍas* themselves must also be in the vicinity of the fire. However, in the absence of fire, Madhuśarman and others maintain that one should offer it near the remnants of the meal (*ucchiṣṭa*), based on the instruction found in the previously cited statements of Śaṅkha, Kātyāyana, and Yājñavalkya that it should be "in the vicinity of the *ucchiṣṭa*."

In that regard, although the area immediately adjacent to the leavings is unfit for the offering of the rice-balls (piṇḍa) due to its impurity, Vyāsa—having postulated its fitness based on scriptural injunction—stated the required distance from the area of the leavings for those intending to perform the offering there, in order to restrain potential donors: "One should cause the three rice-balls to be offered at a distance of one cubit (aratni), such that no drops [of water] reach them even when they are performing the ritual sipping (ācamana). Thus he said.

"In that context"—in this procedure for the *śrāddha*—one should offer the rice-balls (*piṇḍas*) in the space remaining after setting aside a region measuring one *aratni* from the place where the remnants are located. A hand with the little finger extended is called an *aratni*. This distance of separation is to be understood as applying when the Brāhmaṇas are highly skilled and well-behaved, such that they do not defile the area for offering the rice-balls with drops of water from their ritual rinsing (*ācamana*). However, if there is defilement by drops of rinsing water, one should set aside even more than that space.
Thus it is said:

Regarding the passage beginning with "yatropaspṛśatām" (where those who sip water...), the offering of the *piṇḍas* should take place in that spot which the drops of water do not reach when the Brahmins are sipping or rinsing their mouths (*upaspṛśatām*).
Accordingly, Pāraskara states that one should leave a space greater than a cubit (*aratni*):
"The offering of the *piṇḍas* is prescribed at a distance of one arm's length from the Brahmins."

The meaning is: "beyond the distance of one arm," having taken the Brahmins who partake in the *śrāddha* as the limit. Regarding the term "of the Brahmins" (*viprāṇām*), there is an alternative reading, "of the vessels" (*pātrāṇām*).

Even in that case, when there is a suspicion of water droplets reaching [the ground], Atri—explaining the meaning of the statement concerning proximity to the leavings and prescribing the restriction of direction—states that one should abandon even more than the distance of one arm:
"In front of the place where the ancestors are seated, at a distance of three *aratnis*."

The "placing of the leavings" (ucchiṣṭasaṃnidhāna) occurs there, in the vicinity of the seat for the leavings, [referring to] "of the ancestors" (pitṝṇām), meaning the Brahmins invited for the ancestral rite (paitrya). This is also an elliptical indication (upalakṣaṇa) for the Brahmins invited for the rites to the gods (daiva). For it is required that there be an intervening space between those leavings and the others.

Because the same logic applies. "From the place of sitting" means from the proximate area suitable for the limit (*avadhi*). And that [proximity] is indeed the portion immediately preceding that space, because a fixed interval is thereby obtained. Otherwise, there would follow an indefinite interval due to the distinction between crowded and uncrowded areas; and thus, at times, the offering of the rice-ball (*piṇḍa*) might result in being made upon a spot touched by food leavings. Furthermore, since a fixed interval is obtained, it is illogical to assume an indefinite one. Alternatively, the "place of sitting" for the ancestors is the extent of space with which the ancestors are joined while they are eating. Therefore, the vessels are obtained as the limit, for it is within that extent of space that the ancestors are joined. "In front" means to the east. This is the restriction of direction, meaning not behind or on the sides.
Regarding this, Jātūkarṇya states that one should avoid even the slightest suspicion of water drops falling [on the food], prescribing a further renunciation:
"Having left a space of one fathom (vyāma), one should cause the funeral cakes (piṇḍas) to be offered there,
so that no drops reach those who are performing the ritual rinsing."

The distance between the two arms extended horizontally together with the chest is called a *vyāma*. However, when there is no apprehension that the drops from the water used for sipping (*ācamana*) might reach a place measured by a cubit (*aratni*) or similar units due to the Brahmin’s virtuous character and other qualities, then—since proximity to the remnants (*ucchiṣṭa*) is prescribed by scriptural injunction—one should offer the funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*) at a distance measured precisely by a cubit or the length of an arm, in order to favor the primary degree of proximity to the remnants. With this intention, it is stated: "Or, [the distance] of those who sip water, such as a pond," and so forth. Therefore, statements regarding measurements such as the cubit serve merely as indicators (*upalakṣaṇa*) for a location near the remnants that is free from the reaching of the sipping-water drops; they do not have the purpose of being restrictive rules (*niyama*). In a cramped sacrificial space (*śrāddha-pradeśa*), however, one should perform the offering of the cakes after carefully contracting the splashing of the sipping-water drops and ensuring that the area separated by a cubit or more is not defiled; such is the settled rule (*vyavasthā*).
Regarding the balls of food (piṇḍas) to be offered prior to the feeding of the Brahmins, Devala states the specific requirements for the location and other details:
"Having anointed them with honey and ghee, one should cast them upon a heap of Kuśa grass."
And in the shadow of an elephant, in the presence of a grandson of Vastu.

The "elephant-shadow" (*hasticchāyā*) applies to the offering of the rice-ball (*piṇḍadāna*) when performed by a king or one favored by him, because others lack the capacity to provide it. Wherever the offering of the rice-ball is to be performed, the excellence of that location is to be established by ensuring the presence of the elephant-shadow. And this is for the sake of enhancing the sixfold excellence (*ṣāḍguṇya*). For from other scriptural statements, it is understood that the elephant-shadow and such are more highly praised in the context of the *śrāddha*. Therefore, even in the absence of the elephant-shadow and so forth, the offering of the rice-ball certainly takes place. This being the case, it is understood that the offering of the rice-ball, even if occurring after the feeding of the twice-born (*dvija*), is to be prescribed in this location for the attainment of the sixfold excellence. Alternatively, this specific location, when joined with the rites of sacred fords (*tīrtha*) occurring within the *śrāddha* and with the independent offering of the rice-ball, will bring about the sixfold excellence; so what is the point of insisting on the specific context? And this is clear in the section concerning the elephant-shadow.
Thus end the locations for the offering of the rice-ball (*piṇḍa*).
Now follows the ritual procedure for the offering of the rice-ball.

Regarding that, there is the taking of permission. And concerning this, Devala says that for one desiring to perform the offering of the rice-ball, it must be preceded by the taking up of a vessel of water and nectar (*amṛta*).
Then, having taken a water-pot filled with water and containing *darbha* grass,
and having sat down to their east, he should announce the offering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*). Then, permitted by them, he should go toward the southern direction.

For the purpose of offering the *piṇḍas*, having properly grasped with both hands a water-pot (*kalaśa*) filled with water (*ambhasā*) along with *darbha* grass and a *pavitra* strainer, and having sat down in front of the Brāhmaṇas, one should inform them of the *piṇḍa*-offering about to be performed by means of a question intended to solicit their permission, saying, "I shall perform the *piṇḍāvāpa*. Then, being permitted by those Brāhmaṇas with the words "Do so," he should go toward the southern direction. Although the sacrificer’s own facing of the south is established by the very fact that he asks the question while facing the Brāhmaṇas, it is nonetheless improper to go toward the southern direction in relation to the row of Brāhmaṇas standing facing north—since Atri has stated that the giving of the *piṇḍas* must be done in front of the twice-born and not behind them. Nevertheless, for the sake of making the injunction "he goes toward the southern direction" meaningful for one who is already standing facing south, it is understood that he should move two or three steps from his place of questioning. Alternatively, having sat down in front [of the Brāhmaṇas], he should sit facing east and ask the question; then, by the rule "he goes toward the southern direction," he should turn to face south and perform the offering of the *piṇḍas*. As for the grasping of the pot, it is for the purpose of taking up the water required for all the rites such as cleansing and sprinkling (*avanejana*) used in that *piṇḍāvāpa*. Or rather, since the grasping of the pot serves the function of the pot itself—as in the rule, "Being restrained, he should satisfy the ancestors with a water-jar from that [pot]" (*prayataḥ pitṝn*)—its grasping is only for those specific rites prescribed to be done with the pot. However, the sprinkling (*avanejana*) and other such acts are to be performed with water contained in a vessel common to all *śrāddha* rites.
Śālaṅkāyana clarifies the point that this collection of funeral cakes (piṇḍa) applies only to certain individuals by stating that the receiving of permission occurs even without such a collection:
"Having obtained permission for the offering of the funeral cakes, with speech, body, and mind restrained,
he should then offer all the funeral cakes with food mixed with sesame."
Thus ends the taking of permission.
Now follows the preparation of the place for offering the rice-balls (piṇḍas).
Devala says:
In a clean place that has been smeared [with cow dung], one should prepare a large site made of sand,
either circular or square, sloping toward the south.

"Smear" (*upalipte*) means smeared with cow dung and cow urine on the surface of the earth; this is because of the statement of Matsya: "with the water of cow dung and urine. Even though purity is established by the removal of prior impurity once the smearing has been performed, the word "pure" (*śucau*) is used for the purpose of removing the impurity arising from subsequent contamination. Or rather, it is said "on the pure [surface]" precisely because it has been smeared. "Sandy" (*saikataṃ*) means a place consisting of sand; "one should make" (*kurvīta*) means one should fashion a plot of ground to serve as a support for the *piṇḍas*. He describes its shape: "either circular (*maṇḍalaṃ*) or square (*caturasraṃ*). "Circular" means round in shape; "square" means four-cornered. "Sloping toward the south" (*dakṣiṇāvanataṃ*) means inclined toward the south. "Large" (*mahat*) means clearly visible from the surrounding area and possessing sufficient width to accommodate the placement of the *piṇḍas*; although the required width is already implied, this restatement is for the sake of clarity. Alternatively, the injunction is intended to ensure a width slightly greater than what is merely sufficient for placing the *piṇḍas*. And this preparation of a sandy spot is for some [traditions] only; for this very reason, in the *Matsyapurāṇa*, the surface of the earth itself is directly prescribed as the support for the *piṇḍas*: "on the surface of the earth smeared... and so forth.
Thus concludes the arrangement of the place for offering the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*). Now follows the consecration of the place for offering the rice-balls.
Among these, the smearing with cow-dung has already been described; however, the scraping and other rites are now being stated.
Regarding this, Devala says:
"With a single blade of darbha grass, one should scratch that center three times and discard it.
"That center" refers to the middle of the place where the *piṇḍas* are placed. "Scratch" means one should make it marked with lines. "Three times" means three repetitions.

Is it not the case that the scratching for the sake of the ancestors should be performed only once? And so it is stated in the *Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa*: "Now, to the south of the *Anvāhāryapacana* fire, he scratches once; that constitutes the preparation of the altar (*vedi-bhājana*). Here, "the preparation of the altar" means that which serves as the place of the altar. It is also stated in the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*:
"Breaking, grinding, and likewise the act of scratching—these should be done only once for the ancestors (pitṛs), but for the gods (devas), it is said they should be done thrice.

Here, "breaking" refers to the cutting of sacrificial grass (*barhis*) and so forth; "grinding" refers to rubbing the ground and similar acts; and "the act of scratching" refers to the making of lines. Since [these are prescribed] "only once for the ancestors" in rites for the ancestors, how can there be three scratches here?

It is said: [the requirement for three times] will be fulfilled either by an alternative rule (*vikalpa*) or by a specific injunction (*viśeṣa-śāstra*). Alternatively, there may be one marking for each individual *piṇḍa*; thus, even when performed only once, it becomes threefold. Or, there may be one marking for each ancestral group (*pitṛ-varga*); in this way, it is indeed performed three times, since the offering of *piṇḍas* sometimes involves the groups of the father, mother, maternal grandfather, and so forth. By this, it is also shown that when the offering of *piṇḍas* is for two groups, there are two markings, whereas when it is for only one group, there is only one. "By a single blade of *darbha*" means by a single tip of *darbha*. And this applies in the absence of a wooden sword (*sphya*). For, according to the statement of Āpastamba and others—"In the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña*, having marked once with the *sphya*..."—and according to the statement of Yājñavalkya and others—"One should offer the *piṇḍas* as in the *Pitṛyajña*," the *sphya* is obtained through extension (*atideśa*). Nor is this [use of the *sphya*] set aside by the instruction regarding *darbha*.
Since this very doubt regarding sublation (*bādha*) was addressed in the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*:
"O twice-born one, he should scratch that earth with either a thunderbolt (*vajra*) or even with *kuśa* grass";

and since "thunderbolt" (*vajra*) refers to the wooden sword (*sphya*), according to the Vedic scripture, "The wooden sword is indeed the thunderbolt"; and although it is established by the statement "he should scratch with the wooden sword" that it is held in the hand, Pāraskara speaks [the following] in order to remove such expectations as whether it is held in one hand or held in both hands.
"A twice-born man should scratch the earth with his two hands, using either a wooden sword (sphyam) or kusha grass.
When it is stated "with his two hands," a question arises as to what specific positioning those hands should have; in response, the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa states:
"The twice-born man should perform the scratching with his left hand placed above the right."

"Savya" means the left. Those two hands between which the "uttara" (upper) hand—that which is situated above—are placed are called "savyottarau. This is what is meant: "When pressing the *sphya* with both hands for the purpose of scratching, the left fist should be placed above the right fist. Even when scratching with *darbha* grass in the place where the *sphya* was laid down, the hands must likewise be 'savyottarau. Furthermore, the scratching should not be performed by moving the *sphya* or the *darbha* toward oneself; rather, one should move them while facing eastward (*prāṅmukha*). And that [scratching] should also be done facing forward at the front. For Āpastamba states in the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña*: 'Having dug up the altar (*vedi*) toward the south-east and away from oneself (*parācī*). The direction situated between the south and the east, known as the south-eastern corner (*āgneyī*), is the one delimited here; it is "south-eastern" (*dakṣiṇāprācī*). "Away from oneself" (*parācī*) means facing away from the sacrificer. The meaning is: having scratched with the *sphya* while moving away from the sacrificer. Āśvalāyana also, having introduced the south-eastern direction, states in his *Paribhāṣā-sūtra*: 'All rites [of the ancestors] follow that direction. The meaning is that all ancestral rites (*pitrya*) should be performed taking recourse to that direction. By this, it is established that the performer faces the south-east. Indeed, one who faces another direction cannot directly perform rites directed toward that [south-east]. Therefore, facing the south-east, the performer should draw a line facing the south-east. This same facing of the south-east applies to the spreading of *darbha* grass to be described later, as well as the washing of the feet (*avanejana*) and the offering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*). For scratching is performed as a consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the ground that is about to be used as the support for the rice-balls. Consequently, the *darbha* grass serving as the support for the rice-balls must also be spread facing that same direction. If it were spread facing south, then the *darbha* grass—which would not have the earth as its support—would result in being without a foundation. Since the seating of the ancestors follows the support, and the washing and other acts follow the seating, everything is directed toward the south-east. And this is optional; for since the Śruti says, 'The south is the direction of the ancestors,' one understands that facing south and so forth is also permitted, and we see instances of facing south and ending toward the south. Regarding the mantra for drawing the line, it is found in the *Brahmapurāṇa*."
I shall destroy everything that is impure; all the gods and dānavas have been slain by me,
as well as the rākṣasas, yakṣas, and hosts of piśācas.
And all the Yātudhānas have been slain by me.
The application (*viniyoga*) of this mantra, along with its explanatory commentary (*sārthavādaka*), is found in that very same place:
"With this mantra, one whose self is well-restrained should once scratch the altar (*vedi*) with a blade of *darbha* grass."
Desiring certain and auspicious prosperity,
a twice-born man should cast [the seed] having gone toward the northern direction.
Indeed, in whatever region this mantra is recited, the Rākṣasas avoid that very place.

The word "should cast" (*kṣipet*) implies that he should cast the *darbha* grass used for scratching. "To the northern direction" is said in relation to the *darbha* grass to be cast; by this, it is understood that he should cast it toward the southern direction from his own perspective. Furthermore, another mantra beginning with "apahatā" is seen in the context of making the scratch-line.
Thus, Kātyāyana states in the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña-sūtra*:
"He scratches with [the blade] to the south, or according to others, behind [the line]."

"To the south or to the west" means to the south or to the west of the fire. The meaning is that one should scratch [the ground] with this mantra: "The Asuras, the Rakṣases who sit upon the altar, are struck down.
Āpastamba, however, states this same mantra with a slight addition of syllables:
"The Asuras, the Rakṣases, and the Piśācas who sit upon the altar are struck down," [recited] between the Gārhapatya and Anvāhāryapacana fires, or to the south-east of the Anvāhāryapacana.

The phrase "having raised the altar" (*vedim uddhṛtya*) is to be connected with what follows. After scratching [the line], one must perform the sprinkling (*abhyukṣaṇa*). For Āśvalāyana states in the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña*: "With the wooden sword (*sphya*), he should scratch a line, saying, 'May the Asuras and Rakṣasas who sit on the altar be driven away,' and then he should sprinkle it. Immediately after the sprinkling, Āpastamba prescribes a consecration (*abhimantraṇa*) in the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña* with a mantra that indicates the invocation:
"Having looked at it, he consecrates it, saying, 'O Pitṛs, come hither with the speed of thought.'"
[1418] After the scraping, Kātyāyana states that the firebrand (ulmuka) is placed afterwards: "He places the firebrand behind with the words, 'Those forms...
In the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa as well, the placement of the firebrand after the scraping has been mentioned.

Then he places a firebrand to the rear. For if he were to give this to the ancestors without having placed the firebrand, the Asuras and Rakṣases would surely disturb them; thus, by doing so, the Asuras and Rakṣases do not disturb the ancestors. Therefore, he places the firebrand to the rear. "Those who, assuming various forms, being Asuras, move about with the *svadhā* offering, and those who bring down the *parāpuḥ* and *nipuḥ*—may Agni drive them away from these worlds," he says, for Agni is the repeller of the Rakṣases; therefore, he places it.
Then, one should perform the spreading of darbha grass characterized by such distinctions as having a single root;
and so Devala says:
"In that place, one should then [spread] many auspicious darbhas with a single root."
One should strew all those [blades] evenly, with their tips pointing south and their bases facing north.

‘In that place’ (tasmin) means where the rice-balls (piṇḍas) are to be offered. ‘Then’ (tataḥ) means immediately after the scraping and other preliminary acts. ‘Darbhas’ refers to *kuśa* grass; in its absence, one may use *kāśa* and the like previously mentioned. They should have many tips joined to a single root. Regarding the word ‘auspicious’ (*śivān*), this means they should have their tips intact and be characterized by such qualities as having uncracked tips. Fearing that the plural number might be understood as ending at the number three, the author says ‘many’ (*bahūn*). As for this plurality, since no specific number is stated, there is no fixed limit other than starting from three per rice-ball, as desired and as available; however, there is no restriction on the number sufficient to cover the ground, because the purpose of spreading them is a visible one (*dṛṣṭārtha*). If it is argued that there is a restriction because we understand that the rice-balls require another substrate to separate them from the earth, we say no; for even in the absence of a total separation from the earth, the separation from the substrate-ground is accomplished by just a few *darbha* blades. Furthermore, there is no understanding of a total separation. ‘With tips toward the south’ (*dakṣiṇāgrāḥ*) means those whose tips face south. ‘With roots toward the north’ (*udakpādāḥ*) means those whose roots point north. ‘He should spread them’ (*stṛṇuyāt*) means he should extend them. ‘Evenly’ (*samam*) means with a level surface, with equal intervals, or with equal tips and roots. From the very injunction of having a single root, their state of having common roots is also understood.
Regarding this, Jātūkarṇya says:
"Having spread the *darbha* grass near the base, in the vicinity of the food-leavings.

"Near the base" means close to the roots; the implication is that one should spread those [blades] which have been cut while leaving the roots intact. And thus, regarding the state of being with the roots, there is the *Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa*.

That which is cut at the knot belongs to the gods; that which is between the knots belongs to human beings; that which is cut with the root belongs to the ancestors. The sacrificial grass (*barhis*) has its roots intact for the sake of distinction. Regarding those cut near the roots, their being cut once is stated in the *Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa*: "Now, they are cut once and near the roots. The top is, as it were, the portion of the gods; the middle, that of human beings; and the root, that of the ancestors. Therefore, they are cut near the roots. They are cut once, because the ancestors have departed once and for all; therefore, they are cut once."
‘Ditāni’ means cut. This is the past participle form of the root *do*, meaning ‘to cut. It is also stated in the Taittirīya Śruti:
“The sacrificial grass is cut once, for the ancestors are, as it were, one.”
Āpastamba: He brings sacrificial grass (barhis) that is cut once together with its roots, or grass that is cut once and split at the base.
‘Bahiḥ’ refers to *kuśa* grass; ‘tṛṇāni’ refers to *kāśa* and other such grasses. Āśvalāyana says:
“Having strewn them down after cutting them once.”
The word "on the line" (*lekhām*) is to be understood as the ellipsis.
And so says Kātyāyana:
"Having made [the grass-blades] cut once near their bases on the line."
And when that line runs toward the south, one should spread the *darbha* grass with its tips pointing southward as well.
Thus it was said by Devala:
"With the tips pointing south and the bases facing north."
In the *Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa* as well, it is said:
"The sacrificial gifts (dakṣiṇās) are the grasses; they turn toward the south for the ancestors.
Here, "turning toward the south" (*dakṣiṇāvṛt*) means in the manner of the south.
Regarding those [blades] cut once, it is stated in the *Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa*:
"Those [blades] are to be spread out toward the south.
It is also stated in the *Matsya Purāṇa*.
Having placed the darbha grasses according to the rule with their tips pointing southward, being well-composed,
he should then offer three balls of rice each, all of them mixed with sesame seeds.
But when the line is drawn by resorting to the south-eastern direction, then even the *darbha* grasses are to be spread with their tips pointing toward the south.
This, along with other particulars, is stated in the *Vāyupurāṇa*:
"One facing south should spread the *darbha* grasses only once for the sake of the funeral cakes (*piṇḍas*)."
"Immediately thereafter, one who is self-restrained should offer the pindas with their tips pointing toward the southeast.
Here, "once" (*sakṛt*) means a single time. It is indeed possible to perform the spreading for many [pindas] at once. "Southeast" (*prāgdakṣiṇā*) refers to the direction of Agni.
In this regard, Āpastamba has shown the mantra for the spreading of darbha grass in the Piṇḍapitṛyajña.

"Once-cut grass, soft like wool, a pleasant place; for the ancestors I bring you. May my ancestors—the Soma-loving fathers, grandfathers, and great-grandfathers—sit upon this together with their followers," [with these words] he strews the sacrificial altar with once-cut grass.
Regarding this, Śaṅkha and Likhita have stated that three mats (viṣṭara) should be placed on the ground where the rice-balls are offered:
"He should place three mats."

In this context, because of the correspondence in number, it is understood that one *viṣṭara* (seat-grass bundle) should be placed for each individual, as they serve as the support for each single *piṇḍa*.
However, Yama states a specific rule here:
"One should place three *viṣṭaras* there, accompanied by [the mention of] the names and *gotras*."
"Having sprinkled [the seats] with water according to the rule and having scattered sesame seeds over them.

This means that one should do so preceded by the utterance of sentences such as, "This is the seat for our father Devadatta Śarman, belonging to the [so-and-so] gotra," including both name and lineage (*nāma-gotra*).
After spreading the *darbha* grass, Devala describes the preparation of the places for the ancestors, preceded by their invocation (*āvāhana*).
Then, rising with palms joined in reverence and remaining standing, one should invoke the ancestors:
"May my ancestors be gracious; may the grandfathers depart."
"Reciting this, he should remain silent for a moment without breathing out;
having invoked [the ancestors], he should designate their places with the tips of *darbha* grass.

Thus, holding *darbha* grass in his hand, he should point out the places in this sequence: "This is the place for the father; this is the place for the grandfather; this is the place for the great-grandfather. The rest is clear.
Immediately after the arrangement of the seats, that same author states the sprinkling and the scattering of sesame seeds therein:
"While they are seated, one should offer the water for sprinkling with a vessel;
having washed [the hands], one should scatter there sesame seeds of various colors."
By this [verse], the vessel for sprinkling is prescribed.

Āpastamba, however, has prescribed the *añjali* (cupped hands) and the mantra: "May my fathers sprinkle themselves; may my grandfathers sprinkle themselves; may my great-grandfathers sprinkle themselves. With these words, he pours three handfuls of water onto a single line.
And Atri sprinkles [the fire] counter-clockwise; the Vājasaneyins prescribe three water-vessels.
In this regard, Āśvalāyana has stated a different mantra.

Wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītī), he should sprinkle water three times upon the line with the words: "May the fathers be purified; may the grandfathers and great-grandfathers be purified.
Regarding the phrase "upon the line," this refers to the line spread out with a single layer of *sakṛdācchinna* grass; "he should sprinkle with water" means he should moisten it with water.

However, Sumantu, in the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa, has described a specific variation for the act of pouring water (*avanejana*) at the place of sprinkling (*mārjana*), following the laying down of the *darbha* grass.
Saying "May this one wash himself," he should perform the washing three times for each person with one hand.

In the phrase "asau" (so-and-so), one should pronounce the names of the ancestors in order, preceded by their lineage (*gotra*) and connected with their relationship, ending in the vocative case, and say "may you wash yourself. Then, for the purpose of washing—the cleansing of the hands of the ancestors—one should offer water. This should be done three times for each individual ancestor; accordingly, one should understand that this is repeated three times directed toward the father, and so forth.

But surely, in all mantras, one observes that in place of the word *asau* (that one), the mere name is employed; for example, "he utters the name *asau*. This is likewise heard in the *Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa*. So how is it explained here that there is the inclusion of all three: the lineage (*gotra*), the relationship, and the name?

Not so. By the word "asau" (this one), the presentation of a distinguishing term (*vyāvartaka-śabda*) is effected. Names such as *gotra* (clan) and the like are indeed distinguishing factors. Nor should it be said that because exclusion is accomplished by the name alone, the mention of *gotra* and so forth is unnecessary; for their inclusion is prescribed by such rules as: "The name and the *gotra*, as well as the relationship, are what establish eligibility for the *havya* and *kavya* offerings. Furthermore:

"At the offering of the *arghya*, at the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*), and likewise at the offering of the funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*) during the *kṣaya-śrāddha*, one should correctly declare the *gotra*, the relationship, and the names."

And this is because of the statement of Pāraskara: "Nor, in this context, is there an exclusion of the *avanejana* (the sprinkling of water) on the grounds that the word 'offering of the *piṇḍas*' denotes only the principal act, for it is observed in practice as including the ancillaries as well;
indeed, the offering of the *piṇḍas* and the water must always be performed, even in obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites, by addressing [the ancestors] by name and lineage."

Thus, because Vyāsa has stated that the mention of the *gotra* (lineage) occurs even during the act of *avanejana* (the pouring of water for washing), one should address [the ancestors] by name and *gotra*, and even in the case of "constant and occasional" offerings of rice balls (*piṇḍa*), the offering of the rice ball and the water for washing must be performed. Regarding the phrase "by name and *gotra*," the sequence between name and *gotra* is not intended to be fixed; since various sequences are observed in the scriptures for the terms "relationship," "name," and "*gotra*," the usage may be made according to one's preference, or the order may be determined by the specific Vedic branch (*śākhā*). Furthermore, this *avanejana* should be performed with only one hand, neither with both hands joined as an *añjali* nor with a vessel.
It is stated in that very same source that all libations for the *śrāddha* must be performed with one hand:
"At the time of the *śrāddha* libation, one should offer [the water] with one hand;
however, in the case of the *tarpaṇa*, one should use both hands—this is the rule as remembered."

In the case of *tarpaṇa*, however, one should employ "both," meaning both hands, as the instrument. For even when the *avanejana* (sprinkling) is performed with only one hand, it must be done with the right hand alone.
Thus Manu says:
"One should offer pure water with the hand [in the] *apasavya* [position]."

With the *apasavya* hand—that is, the right hand—one should *nirvapet*, or pour out, pure (*śuci*)—meaning uncontaminated—water upon the spread *darbha* grass for the sake of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*). One should pour that water through the space between the index finger and the thumb, because that is the *pitṛtīrtha* (the sacred path of the ancestors).
Thus it is said in the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*:
"With a concentrated mind, one should offer water to them by means of the *pitṛtīrtha*."

"To them" means to the ancestors. Kātyāyana, however, prescribes the washing with a vessel: "He performs the washing with a water-vessel, either with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (apasavya) or with the left hand, because of the capacity for lifting [the vessel]; he says, 'O so-and-so, wash yourself,' three times, beginning with the father of the sacrificer."

A vessel containing water is an *udapātra*. "With the *apasavya*" means by way of the *pitṛtīrtha* (the thumb and forefinger). "With the *savya*" means by way of the *manuṣyatīrtha* (the middle three fingers). "By virtue of the capacity for drawing out" means by virtue of the authority of the *Śatapatha-śruti*, which states, "They draw [the offering] out for men. "O horses, wash yourselves" is the mantra. The mention of the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) is because the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña* is performed by the *adhvaryu* priest. The fact that words such as *apasavya* refer to the *pitṛtīrtha* and so forth has been established by Upādhyāya Karka. This is also stated in the *Śatapatha* immediately after the drawing of the lines and the placing of the firebrand (*ulmuka*).

Then, taking a water-pot, he performs the ritual rinsing (*avanejana*), saying: "O [Name], rinse yourself! for the sacrificer’s father; "O [Name], rinse yourself! for the grandfather; "O [Name], rinse yourself! for the great-grandfather. This is just as one would sprinkle water [on the hands]; that is what it means. Regarding the phrase "as one would sprinkle":
just as there is the sprinkling of water on the hands and so forth of a person who is about to eat, such is this rinsing for the ancestors.
Gobhila also states in the *Rāṇāyanīya-sūtra* that the rinsing is performed with a vessel itself.

Taking the water-vessel with his left hand alone, he should pour it out upon the Darbha grass in the eastern furrow, bending forward; having uttered the father’s name, "O [Name], wash yourself (avanenikṣva), and those who follow you here—wash yourself for them too," and saying, "This is for him, Svadhā! he should touch water. In this very same manner, he should do for the other two.

The meaning is that, having taken a water-vessel with the left hand—as indicated by the phrase "with the left hand" (*savyena pāṇinā*)—one should pour out the water being sprinkled from the vessel held in the left hand into the right hand using the *pitṛtīrtha* (the part of the hand sacred to the ancestors). This is because the word *apasavya* is a synonym for *pradakṣiṇa* (counter-clockwise) and thus denotes the *pitṛtīrtha*. Furthermore, the three furrows (*karṣū*) here occupy the place of the lines that serve as the altar (*vedi*). Those learned in traditional conduct (*ācāra*) maintain that "touching water" (*apām upasparśanam*) means merely touching water with the hand. "Of the other two" refers to the remaining two furrows. And this touching of water must be performed individually at each instance of offering the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*), the pouring of water (*avanejana*), and the presentation of perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, and food. For Ācārya Gobhila will state exactly this in those respective places. Moreover, this water for the pouring should be understood as containing sesame seeds (*tila*).
And likewise Uśanas says:
"Having sprinkled water mixed with sesame seeds, one should offer the funeral cake (piṇḍa) upon ground strewn with darbha grass."

In this matter, it should be understood that there is either an option (*vikalpa*) between using both hands joined in *añjali*, a single hand, or a water-vessel (*udapātra*), or a fixed rule (*vyavasthā*) according to the specific Vedic school (*śākhā*). It is not the case that the right hand assists the washing (*avanejana*) by holding the vessel, while the vessel assists by holding the water; for although there is a difference in their instrumental functions (*dvārakāryabheda*), let there be no combination (*samuccaya*) of the two, because the hand is understood to be the means of performing the washing independently of the vessel. Furthermore, the hand is capable of accomplishing the washing directly as a support for water even without depending on the vessel. Regarding this, the formula for the performance of the washing according to the view of Kātyāyana and others is: "O our father of such-and-such gotra, Devadatta Śarman, be washed (*avanenikṣva*)," and so forth. By Āśvalāyana and others, however, "May the fathers be purified (*śundhatāṃ pitaraḥ*)" and so forth is stated. By Āpastamba and others, however, "May my fathers cleanse themselves (*mārjayantāṃ mama pitaraḥ*)" and so forth is stated. Here too, as before, there is either an option or a fixed rule. Likewise, Sumantu and others have stated "May the fathers be purified," etc., while Kātyāyana has stated it even prior to that. Therefore, regarding the sequence of the washing and the spreading of the sacrificial grass (*barhistaraṇa*), there is either an option or a fixed rule according to the specific Vedic school. Although the washing does not constitute a consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the place where the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) are placed, nevertheless, because its nature consists in the pouring of water and because it falls within the scope of the lines drawn and the spreading of the grass, it is mentioned among the consecrations. The invocation (*āvāhana*) is also mentioned for the same reason, namely that it falls within that same scope.
Thus concludes the sacrament of offering the rice-balls (*piṇḍadāna*). Now follows the preparation of the rice-balls.
Regarding this, Jātūkarṇa says:
"Having performed the *avanejana* (sprinkling of water), one should offer three *piṇḍas* according to the prescribed rule.

Here, the word "three" refers to each single group beginning with the father. This is because in the statements of Kātyāyana and others, the repetition "three by three" is observed, and from this it is understood that in the *amāvāsyā* śrāddha, the offering of *piṇḍas* for the group beginning with the maternal grandfather (*mātāmaha*) is also required.
Accordingly, an indicative mark (*liṅga*) is seen in the Vārāha Purāṇa, in a passage concerning the śrāddha performed by Varāha which explains the division of food for the purpose of the *piṇḍas*.
Then, taking the alms-bowl, he gave it to his wife;
she divided that food into two parts, and then made each of those threefold. Thus it is said.

‘According to rule’ (*yathāvidhi*) means without transgressing the prescribed injunctions. These injunctions will be shown to concern the substance of the *piṇḍas*, the quantity of the *piṇḍas*, and the manner of preparing the *piṇḍas*. Among these, first, the injunction regarding the manner of preparation is stated as the procedure for the large-scale offering of food. Here, in the case of the offering of *piṇḍas* performed prior to the feeding of the Brahmins and before the *agnaukaraṇa* (the pouring of oblations into the fire), the *piṇḍas* must be made from the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) intended for the *agnaukaraṇa* and other rites. Devala states this, along with its accompanying ritual details:
"Then, having taken the *caru* with his hand provided with the *pavitra* [strainer]..."
One should divide the balls of food, anointed with ghee, into four parts using a vessel;
having smeared them with honey and clarified butter, one should cast them upon a heap of *kuśa* grass.

Having taken the *caru* (cooked sacrificial rice) in a vessel, one should divide it into four parts with a hand equipped with the sacred grass (*pavitra*). Immediately thereafter, one should form four balls (*piṇḍas*) by making one ball from each portion of the *caru*. These should be "smeared with ghee" (*ghṛtākān*), meaning either smeared with ghee or mixed with ghee and honey, and one should "offer" (*vapet*) them—that is, place them—using a "vessel" (*bhājanena*), meaning a bowl. Here, the phrase "into four" (*caturdhā*) is intended as an illustration for the number of divisions corresponding to the number of balls one intends to make. However, when the offering of balls is performed at a time subsequent to the *agnaukaraṇa* (the rite of offering into the fire), the balls should be made from the remnants of the *agnaukaraṇa*.
And likewise, beginning with the words "having placed [the vessel] to the left of the fire," Manu says:
"Therefore, having formed three pindas from that remnant of the sacrificial oblation, being composed,
he should offer them facing south by the very same rite as the water-offering."

"Therefore, from the remnant of the oblation" means from the remnant of the oblation used for the *agnaukaraṇa* rite. "He should pour out water with his hand while the sacred thread is over the right shoulder (*apasavya*)"—this is the rule regarding the water offering (*audaka*). However, regarding the offering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) which occurs after the meal, Kātyāyana states: "Having set aside all the food together, he should wash [his hands] near the leavings and offer three rice-balls each upon *darbha* grass. Thus it is said.

The word "all" (*sarva*) here signifies the totality of all types of food under discussion, not a numerical or quantitative totality. Therefore, having taken small portions from each of the various kinds of food prepared for the *śrāddha*—such as boiled rice, milk-rice (*pāyasa*), cakes (*apūpa*), and lentil soup (*sūpa*)—and having collected them together in a single vessel, one should fashion *piṇḍas* (rice-balls) from that food. Then, at a spot removed by a cubit or more from the area where the leftovers were placed, and upon a line drawn with the wooden sword (*sphya*) or other implements, one should perform the sprinkling (*avanejana*) according to the method previously shown. Upon the *barhis* grass spread there, which has been cut in a single stroke, one should offer three *piṇḍas* each. The repetition "three each" (*trīṃs trīn*) is intended to indicate that there may be multiple groups of *piṇḍas*. Furthermore, all these varieties of food should be mixed with the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) remaining from the *agnaukaraṇa* rite.

And so says Āśvalāyana: "From whichever food has been consumed, from each of those he should take a portion for the sake of the *piṇḍas* and, having combined it with the *sthālīpāka*, he should place the *piṇḍas*. The phrase "food that has been consumed" implies [the food] by the Brāhmaṇas at the Śrāddha. Having taken a little from each of those, and having mixed it with the *sthālīpāka* remaining from the *agnaukaraṇa* offering, he should place the *piṇḍas*. The mixing with the *sthālīpāka* has been explained in detail in the section concerning the disposal of the remnants of the *agnaukaraṇa*. Furthermore, this food should be prepared joined with honey, clarified butter, and sesame seeds.
And likewise in the Vāyu Purāṇa:
"The wise man should offer three balls of food mixed with honey, ghee, and sesame.
This [injunction] does not intend to establish a mandatory rule regarding the combination of these three—honey and so forth—but rather aims to indicate their excellence.

For this very reason, Bṛhaspati states that they should consist of only two pieces of honey and sesame: "From all the prepared food, one should offer balls of rice mixed with honey and sesame to the fathers, maternal grandfathers, and others, according to the rules of the Gṛhya-sūtras."
Nor is there a rule that it must be accompanied by two pieces of honeyed sesame;
for this very reason, Yājñavalkya states that it should be accompanied by at least a single sesame seed:
"Having taken all the food together with sesame, [the performer], facing south..."
One should offer the rice-balls (piṇḍas) near the remains of the meal, as in the Pitṛyajña rite.
In the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa* as well, the inclusion of even a mere sesame seed is stated:
"Then, O son, one should offer three funeral cakes (*piṇḍas*) made of food mixed with sesame seeds upon *darbha* grass near the remains of the meal, dedicated to the ancestors."
Thus ends the rule concerning the subject matter of the alms-food (*piṇḍārtha*).
[1429] Now follows the rule concerning the measure of the alms-food (*piṇḍaparimāṇa*).
Regarding this, Vyāsa says: "Just as a two-year-old calf can comfortably take twenty mouthfuls, so should one determine the size of the rice balls; this is the measure spoken by Vyāsa."
"Dvihāyanaḥ" means two years of age.
Regarding the rule for other measurements, the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa states:
"Three balls [of food], in successive order, increasing by the size of a fist together with the thumb."

‘In due order’ means according to the sequence of the father, maternal grandfather, and so forth, which will be described later. ‘Sāṅguṣṭhamuṣṭivardhanāḥ’ means those whose growth (puṣṭi) is such that they [fit] a fist together with the thumb; that is to say, they are the size of a fist including the thumb. Alternatively, they are called ‘Sāṅguṣṭhamuṣṭivardhanāḥ’ because they cause the fist to grow when the thumb is included; for when they are placed within a fist along with the thumb, the fist expands slightly due to the extra bulk, resulting in a small protrusion of the thumb. Aṅgiras also mentions other measurements:
"One should offer balls of food according to the prescribed rite, the size of a wood-apple (*kapittha*) or a bilva fruit;
or the size of a hen's egg, or equal to *āmalaka* fruits;
or even equal to jujube (*badara*) fruits—one should give them endowed with faith. Thus it is said.

Since the satisfaction, pleasure, and auspicious destinies of the ancestors are achieved even through the offering of a *piṇḍa*, one should, having fixed one's faith in such a rite, offer *piṇḍas* even if they are only the size of a jujube fruit (*badara*). One should not, however, offer them while manifesting a lack of faith by thinking, "What will these jujube-sized offerings do for the ancestors? Furthermore, the determination of these measurements should be understood according to the difference in one's capacity.
Regarding this, Marīci states some other measurements established by different rules:
"In the *pārvaṇa* [śrāddha], one should make the *piṇḍas* the size of a fresh *āmalaka* fruit."
In the Ekoddiṣṭa rite, one should offer a single funeral ball (piṇḍa) the size of a bilva fruit.
In the *navaśrāddha*, one should offer a piṇḍa that is even larger than that; during the period of impurity (*āśauca*), it should be offered every day, each time being larger than the preceding.

"In the *pārvaṇa* [rite]" means in a *śrāddha* other than the *ekoddiṣṭa*. The mention of *pārvaṇa* is for the purpose of establishing a restrictive rule (*vyavasthā*). Since the connection with the *pārvaṇa* is already established by the context, the author of the *Smṛticandrikā* maintains that the mention of *pārvaṇa* is a mere restatement (*anuvāda*). However, we consider that he did not fully reflect upon the second half of the verse. Here, one should not explain it as "one should make the *piṇḍas* in the *pārvaṇa* exactly the size of an *āmalaka* fruit"; rather, it means "only in the *pārvaṇa* [should they be] the size of an *āmalaka*. Consequently, this does not contradict the observed practice of offering *piṇḍas* larger than the size of an *āmalaka* even in the *pārvaṇa* rite. By the phrase "the size of a *bilva* fruit," only a measurement smaller than a *bilva*—such as that of an *āmalaka*—is excluded, but not a larger one; thus, the conduct of the learned (*śiṣṭācāra*) is upheld. "The *navaśrāddha*" is the *śrāddha* prescribed during the period of impurity (*āśauca*) on the first, third, and so forth days, as well as on the eleventh day. Although it is of the *ekoddiṣṭa* type, one should not offer a *piṇḍa* there the size of a *bilva*, but rather something even thicker than that. Even apart from the formal *śrāddha*, during the period of impurity, one should offer every day (*aprativāsaram*) a *piṇḍa* even thicker than the *piṇḍa* of the *navaśrāddha*.
Regarding the increasing size of the three *piṇḍas* associated with each successive group beginning with the father, it is stated in the *Maitrāyaṇīya Piṇḍapitṛyajña Sūtra*:

"Having lifted them with the ladle, he places the *piṇḍas* upon those [spots] while saying: 'O Father, by name [so-and-so], this is for you and for those who follow you here; to you and to them, *svadhā*! First, [he places] the largest in the middle for the grandfather by name; the largest of all in the south for the great-grandfather by name; and wiping the smear at the base while pronouncing the names of the two descendants, [he places the smallest].
This is the rule concerning the dimensions of the *piṇḍas*.
[1431] Now follows the ritual formation of the performer, which constitutes a subsidiary part of the offering of the funeral cakes (piṇḍanirvāpa).

This [form] consists of wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvīta*), placing the left knee on the ground, facing south, and extending the right hand forward, and so forth. Although this is common to all ancestral rites (*pitrya-karma*), it is defined here with a desire to encompass the various scriptural injunctions that specifically prescribe these details in connection with the offering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa-nirvāpa*). In this regard, first, the *prācīnāvīta* must be performed, according to the Taittirīya Śruti: "To the south, one should wear the thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*). Also, from the Āśvalāyana Sūtra which prescribes the *prācīnāvīta* starting from the ritual washing (*avanejana*): "Wearing the *prācīnāvīta*, one should lead water three times over the line. Furthermore, from the Āpastamba Sūtra which prescribes the *prācīnāvīta* starting from the sprinkling (*mārjana*): "From this point upward, one performs the rites wearing the *prācīnāvīta*"; from the Gobhila Sūtra regarding the commencement of drawing the line: "The rite is to be performed by one wearing the *prācīnāvīta* and remaining silent"; and from the Kaṭha Sūtra: "Then, wearing the *prācīnāvīta*, having smeared the ground and drawn the lines... Thus, this *prācīnāvīta* is to be maintained by the performer of the rite from the smearing of the ground until the disposal of the rice-balls, setting aside those specific exceptions that will be mentioned later. Just like the *prācīnāvīta*, from the smearing of the ground onwards, one must also place the left knee upon the ground.
And so it is stated in the *Brahmāṇḍa-purāṇa* and the *Vāyu-purāṇa*:
"The wise man, devoted to the ancestors, should offer three balls of rice mixed with honey, ghee, and sesame seeds, having placed his left knee upon the ground."

By the word *jānu* (knee) used in this [verse]—which expresses a prior time—and by the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*), which overrides the order of the recited text (*pāṭhakrama*), it is established that the act of prostrating with the knee must be performed at a time prior to the offering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*). From the mention of "the left" (*savyam*), it follows by implication that the right knee is to be placed on the ground. Consequently, it is stated that the performer of the *śrāddha*, sitting upon a rug in a squatting posture (*utkaṭaka*), should place his left knee on the ground while not placing the right one, and thus remain seated.
Then, having formed a ball (piṇḍa) of one of the aforementioned measurements, he should take it with his right hand and offer it according to the water-rite (audaka-vidhi), facing south.

This is because of the previously cited statement of Manu: "He should take the ball in a vessel held by the right hand, or in a vessel such as a sword-bowl; the offering of the ball in a sword-bowl among vessels is prescribed."
Either with silver or with udumbara wood, or else with the hand itself.
Thus, from the words of Marīci.

*Khaḍga* refers to a specific beast of prey called the rhinoceros; a vessel produced from the frontal bone of that animal is a *khaḍgapātra*. *Rājata* means made of silver. *Audumbara* means made of copper. Since the rhinoceros and other such superior materials are prescribed as the primary options, in their absence, the offering of the *piṇḍa* should be performed with any vessel mentioned in the section on vessels. Thereafter, one should incline the *pitṛtīrtha* (the part of the hand sacred to the ancestors) while the left hand’s fingers are joined together, the right hand is turned upward, and the thumb does not touch the *piṇḍa*, according to one's capacity.
In that regard, the joining of the left hand has been stated by Śaṅkha and Likhita:
"One should place the ball of food with the left hand, preceded by the right hand.
Thus, having joined the left [hand] with the right, the state of having the hands turned upward is prescribed in the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa.
"One should offer [the water] with the palm turned upward while facing the south.
Regarding the touching of the thumb, Devala has stated:
"With the sacred thread over the right shoulder (aprasavya) and excluding the thumb (apāṅguṣṭham)."

And this statement will be shown in the subsequent section. Furthermore, Āpastamba has prescribed the lowering of the *pitṛtīrtha* during the *piṇḍapitṛyajña*: "Having turned the left hand [around], one whose hand has its palm facing downward... (*savyaṃ cānvācyāvācīnapāṇiḥ*). An "avācīna" hand is one that is turned upward (*uttāna*) but with the *pitṛtīrtha* portion made downward; he who is the performer [of the rite] in such a state is described as "one whose hand has its palm facing downward."

Āśvalāyana states that by the word "parācīna" (turned away), he means "āvācīna" (turned toward oneself): "Upon that [line], one should place the pindas with the hand turned away. By the word "tasyām" (upon that), he refers to the line strewn with darbha grass upon which the water-offering has been performed. Furthermore, there is the lowering of the hand at the *pitṛtīrtha* (the part of the hand sacred to the ancestors) for the purpose of offering the pindas by means of that *tīrtha*.

For this very reason, the Śatapatha Śruti prescribes the offering of the rice-balls (piṇḍa) by means of the *pitṛtīrtha* (the ancestral part of the hand). It states: "He gives with the words ‘sa vā’; for they offer oblations to the gods with the word ‘iti’, they take up [food] for men with the word ‘iti’, and thus it is for the ancestors. Therefore, he gives with the words ‘iti dadāti’. The phrase "he gives" (*dadāti*) demonstrates the imitation of the hand as it is used when giving by way of the *pitṛtīrtha*. Furthermore, in the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) beginning with "for they offer oblations to the gods with the word ‘iti’," the specific connection between the *tīrthas* of the gods, humans, and ancestors and their respective acts of offering, taking up, and giving is established precisely through the structure of these imitative formulas.
It is also stated in the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*:
"Having lowered the left knee to the ground, one should diligently offer the rice-balls (piṇḍas) by means of the *pitṛ-tīrtha*, uttering the word 'svadhā'."
Thus ends the section on the arrangement of the officiants.
Now, the principal rite called the offering of the *piṇḍas* (rice-balls) is described, together with its deities, mantras, sequence, number, and alternatives.
Regarding this, Kātyāyana says:
"He gives the rice-balls exactly as they have been washed, saying, 'O [Name], this is for you,' and 'And those who follow you'— thus for each one."

"Yathāvaniktam" (according to the washing): wherever and in whatever sequence the washing was performed for each individual, there and in that same sequence one should offer the *piṇḍa* for each of them. Regarding the washing, because of the statement "three starting with the father," the number of *piṇḍas* is obtained by this very term "yathāvaniktam" as being accompanied by the deities in the form of the intended ancestors and others. This statement occurs within the section on the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña*; and since in that context only one group consisting of the triad beginning with the father is the object of intention, there is a restriction to the number three of the *piṇḍas*. However, in the *Śrāddha* on the new moon day and so forth, because other groups are also objects of intention, the restriction to the number three does not apply. For this very reason, Kātyāyana says in the *Vājasaneyi-Śrāddhakalpa*:
"Having sprinkled water, one should offer three balls [of food] each.
In this context, at the place of the word "asau" (so-and-so), the mention of the lineage (*gotra*), the relationship, and the name is intended as that which must be performed.
For this very reason, Pāraskara says:

"At the offering of the *arghya*, at the formal declaration (*saṃkalpa*), at the offering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*), and likewise at the time of dissolution, one should duly provide the lineage, the relationship, and the names. Thus it is said.

By the word *saṃkalpa* here, the renunciation (*tyāga*) of the feeding of the twice-born is denoted. By the statement, “one should present these [items] here according to rule,” it is understood that there is no deficiency even if any one of these is missing elsewhere. Regarding the requirement of how the lineage (*gotra*), relationship (*saṃbandha*), and name (*nāman*) should be expressed—with which case-ending—one first considers this: the word *te* found in the mantra *etat te* is not the form of the pronoun *tad* in the nominative plural or nominative dual, because that would be irrelevant to the context. Therefore, it must be the form of *yuṣmad* in either the dative singular or the genitive singular. Since the deity is of the nature of a recipient (*saṃpradāna*), it is appropriate for the word denoting it to end in the dative. Consequently, the lineage, relationship, and names—which require syntactic connection with this [word *te*]—must be expressed in the dative singular alone. Furthermore, the status of the ancestors (father, etc. as deities is manifested only when such an expression is made, and not otherwise. Thus, the expression should be performed exactly as stated. Another, however, says: since the pronoun *yuṣmad* refers to a person who is present and not remote, and since the vocative is most appropriate for the purpose of addressing one among many who are standing before one, it is proper to express the lineage, relationship, and names ending in the vocative. Moreover, there is no evidence for disregarding the nominative indication in the phrase *asau* (e.g., *asau devadattaḥ*). As for the usage in common parlance, such as “How does he act like a hero? He betrays; from where will he defeat you, O Caitra?”, that is used either to denote the agency of the person in that state, or to refer to the basis of the meaning of *yuṣmad* as addressed by another means, or for the sake of stating a reason, or for the sake of praise. But in the present case, none of these possibilities apply to any of them. For since the lineage, relationship, and names belonging to a previous birth of one who has died do not exist at present, they serve only to characterize a particular conscious self (*kṣetrajña*), and thus cannot convey their own meaning in the form of an agent or other grammatical roles. Therefore, the lineage and so forth should be expressed only in the vocative. And in another Sūtra, the expression is seen exactly like this: “This for you, O Father; this for you, O Grandfather; this for you, O Great-grandfather,” and so on. The word *etat* (this) is a reference to the rice-ball (*piṇḍa*) about to be offered.
Now, how can there be a designation of a word in the masculine gender by means of a word in the neuter gender?

It is said: Since the word *piṇḍa* is seen to be used in both the feminine and neuter genders in the *Mahābhāṣya* and other works—such as in the statement, "Having entered, the *piṇḍa* falls upon the mass of the wall"—the designation in the neuter gender is not contradictory. However, the teacher Karka stated that the word *anna* (food) must be supplied [as an ellipsis]. But the author of the *Smṛticandrikā* does not accept this; for he says: "An ellipsis should be supplied only when there is no other recourse (*ananyagatitve*). But here there is no lack of recourse, because the neuter gender of the word *piṇḍa* has already been demonstrated. To this, we reply: This ellipsis is not intended merely to justify the neuter usage; rather, it is for the purpose of completing the mantra sentence. And an ellipsis for the purpose of completing a sentence is indeed accepted—as in the case of "for food (*iṣe*) thee," which is completed by "I cut (*ucchidmi*)," and so forth. Furthermore, such usage is observed in common worldly practice: "This field, this house, this wealth is given to you. Moreover, in Karka’s commentary, the word *anna* is used merely as an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*). Therefore, after the words "this is yours" (*etat te*), one must supply either "food" (*anna*) or "the *piṇḍa*" (*piṇḍam*).
And regarding the regulation of these two, Laugākṣi says:
"In the Mahālaya, at Gayā, in the Śrāddha for the deceased, and during the ten-day period, the term 'piṇḍa' (rice-ball) should be employed; elsewhere, one should mention 'anna' (food)."

"At the *mahālaya*," that is, at a specific sacred site (*tīrtha*). "At the *pretaśrāddha*" refers to the *śrāddhas* performed at the conclusion of the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*. "At the *daśāhika*" refers to the offering of rice balls (*piṇḍadāna*) to be completed within ten days, even apart from the formal *śrāddha* rites. Immediately after the word "food" (*anna*), the word "svadhā" should be employed; for Devala states: "One should say 'svadhā' preceded by the mantra.
Śāṭyāyani further states that the word "namaḥ" should also be employed immediately after "svadhā":
"Having said, 'O [Name], this is for you,' and at the end of that, 'svadhā namaḥ'."

In this regard, those who are proficient [in the ritual] recite the mantra ending with the words *svadhā* and *namaḥ*, and then, pointing to the food with the word *idam* (this), they utter the word *namaḥ* while designating the ancestors (*pitṛ*s) and others by means of those very same names, such as their lineage (*gotra*), etc., in the dative case. Now, one might ask: since the status of the ancestors as deities has already been manifested by the word *te* (them) in the dative case within the mantra itself, for what purpose is there a further employment of the lineage names, etc., in the dative case? Or, if it is thought that the deities must also be manifested by means of the lineage names, etc., and therefore they are employed again— [The response follows: This is not so; because the mantra is addressed to the ancestors (*pitṛ*s), the word *te* (them) does not denote the deities [of the offering]. For the word *devatā* (deity) is used in the sense of "one who receives a portion" (*bhāga-grāhin*). However, the ancestors do not receive a portion from the mantra; rather, they receive it through the mouth of the officiant (*ṛtvij*). Therefore, the ancestors are not the deities here. Consequently, the lineage names, etc., are employed again in order to manifest them as the deities of the offering. Furthermore, the word *namaḥ* is uttered at the end of the mantra for the sake of indicating the completion of the mantra. Otherwise, if the word *namaḥ* were not uttered, the mantra would remain incomplete, as it would lack its concluding part. Thus, the word *namaḥ* is uttered once more to indicate the conclusion of the mantra. It is not the case that the word *namaḥ* is uttered twice over; rather, the first *namaḥ* is part of the mantra, while the second is uttered separately after the mantra to signify its conclusion. Therefore, the objection is refuted. Furthermore, the word *svadhā* is uttered at the end of the mantra to indicate the conclusion of the mantra, just as the word *namaḥ* is. If the word *svadhā* were not uttered, the mantra would remain incomplete, as it would lack its concluding part. Thus, the word *svadhā* is uttered at the end of the mantra to indicate its conclusion. Therefore, the objection is refuted. And so on. Thus ends the section on the offering to the ancestors (*pitṛ-yajña*). Next, the procedure for the offering to all beings (*baliharaṇa*) is described. Regarding this, the following is stated: "Having performed the offering to the ancestors, he should perform the offering to all beings. The meaning is that he should perform the offering to all beings immediately after the offering to the ancestors. Regarding the phrase "having performed the offering to the ancestors," the word *pitṛ-yajña* refers to the offering to the ancestors, which consists of the *svadhā-kāra*. The word *kṛtvā* (having performed) indicates the sequence of actions. The word *atha* (then) indicates the immediate succession. The word *balim* (offering) refers to the *bali* offering. The word *haret* (he should offer) means he should present it. The word *sarvabhūtebhyaḥ* (to all beings) means to all living creatures. The word *iti* (thus) indicates the end of the section. That is not so; for even in the case of "O Devadatta, this garment is given to you," there would result the necessity of employing the dative case once again. To this we reply: although the act of relinquishment (*tyāga*) is already manifested by the mantra-text, it is nevertheless further expressed by a worldly sentence in accordance with established custom.
