In that regard, the formulaic sentence (*prayogavākya*) is as follows: "O our father of such-and-such lineage, named such-and-such Śarman, this food is yours; *svadhā*! Homage! This is for our father of such-and-such lineage, named such-and-such Śarman, and not mine. However, the formulaic sentences for others will be shown in their respective places. And here, some authors of Sūtras prescribe the remainder of the mantra, "ye ca tvām anu," immediately after "asāv etat te. But that remainder of the mantra is not to be employed by the Vājasaneyins. For this very reason, its use is prohibited in the *Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa* following a deprecatory explanatory passage (*arthavāda*).

He gives [the gift], saying, "N.N., this is for you," specifically for the sacrificer's father; and some say that one should modify the formula to include those who follow him, saying, "and those who follow you. However, one should rather recite it thus: "N.N., this is for you" for the sacrificer's father; "N.N., this is for you" for the grandfather; and "N.N., this is for you" for the great-grandfather. For these [ancestors] belong together with him, and those who are together with them [belong together]; therefore, one should speak thus.

Regarding the phrase *ye ca tvām*, its ultimate meaning (*pāramārthika*) is as follows: [The literal sense] is a censure, namely: "This rice-ball (*piṇḍa*) is for those who, having become your followers (*anu*), exist together with you. Alternatively, it means: "May this rice-ball also be for those who exist in a state of following (*anu*) you after you have passed away. This, however, is an inauspicious expression. For when one offers the rice-ball, by means of the mantra *ye ca tvām anu*, he says "together" (*saha*) with reference to those deceased persons; thus, he himself becomes one who exists together with them in their wake (*paścādbhūta*). Consequently, it appears as though he is offering the rice-ball to himself. And so, this is inauspicious. Therefore, the meaning of this Vedic revelation (*śruti*) is that one should not speak in such a manner. Devala, however, while prescribing this very remainder of the mantra, states a number of rice-balls exceeding three.
And one should slowly recite the names of the three [ancestors], preceded by their father's name,
with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (apasavya), the thumb outside [the fingers], preceded by the mantra, and ending with "svadhā."
"O father, this for you and those who follow you"—with these words he should offer [the first portion] to the father;
likewise for the grandfather, and likewise he should offer for the father of that [grandfather]. This is the common [portion]; thus he should offer the fourth ball to the remaining ancestors.

The meaning of this is as follows: One should recite the names of the three ancestors, beginning with the father, in their proper order—first the father, then the grandfather, and so on. The instruction that one should "pronounce the names in the vocative case" (*saṃbuddhyantāny abhidadhīta*) is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the lineage name (*gotra*) and other such details. Immediately after, having uttered the mantra, one should say *svadhā*. The mantra is shown by the formula beginning with *etat te tata* ("this, O father, is for you"). Here too, immediately after the words *etat te*, one should employ either *annaṃ* ("food") or *piṇḍam* ("the rice-ball"). Having thus offered the food with a sentence ending in *svadhā* accompanied by the mantra, one should also utter the worldly formula—"to the father, not to me"—consisting of the lineage name and other terms in the dative case, as before, and then offer the first rice-ball. By substituting the word "grandfather" (*pitāmaha*) in place of "father," and the grandfather's name in place of the father's name, one should offer the second ball to the grandfather. In the same way, making the appropriate modifications for the relationship and the name, one should offer the third ball to the great-grandfather. For the remaining three ancestors beyond the great-grandfather, one should offer the fourth ball with the general formula: "This food is *svadhā* for them, not to me. Regarding the phrase "with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*apasavyam*) and excluding the thumb (*apāṅguṣṭham*)," the meaning is that one should offer it with the right hand, using the thumb as an instrument (i.e., without the thumb touching the ball). Here, the touching of the rice-ball by the left hand is forbidden, but the grasping of the right hand is not. Alternatively, *apasavyam* may mean "by the *pitṛ-tīrtha*" (the part of the hand used for offerings to the ancestors); the fact that the word *apasavya* denotes the *pitṛ-tīrtha* is accepted as being in accordance with the views of Karka and others. The practical formula here is: "O [Name], of the [Gotra] lineage, our deceased father, this food is for you; and for those who follow you, *svadhā*. This is for [Name], of the [Gotra] lineage, our deceased father, not to me. These rice-balls should be given ending toward the south. The fourth offering is optional; it should be given without mentioning the name, lineage, and so forth of the ancestors beyond the great-grandfather. Showing another mantra for this, Āpastamba says:

When the sacrificial grass has been cut once, he offers the rice-balls (piṇḍas) ending toward the south, with each mantra respectively: "This for you, O father, [Name], and those who follow you," and so on; the fourth is offered silently. He may perform this either way—whether the names are recited or not—and the offering goes to the great-grandfather and the others.

Those whose completion or conclusion is toward the south are called "those ending to the south" (*adakṣiṇāpavargāḥ*). This means that having first placed the first *piṇḍa* on the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), one should place the second to the south of it, the third to the south of that, and the fourth to the south of that as well; thus one should give them. "With each mantra" (*pratimantram*) means that one should offer each *piṇḍa* with a single mantra. He shows the mantras with the words beginning "This for you, O father... (*etat te tāta...*) and so forth. These mantras, recited in sequence in the *Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa*, are indicated by the Sūtrakāra through the utterance of the first mantra alone. The word "so-and-so" (*asau*) is for the purpose of explaining the specific name. However, the fourth *piṇḍa* should be offered silently, without a mantra. The phrase "done or not done" (*kṛtākṛtaḥ*) indicates it is optional. The term "starting from the great-grandfather" (*prapitāmahaprabhṛtīn*) is a *bahuvrīhi* compound where the qualifier is included in the meaning (*guṇasaṃvijñāna*). The meaning is that this [fourth *piṇḍa*] is to be given intended for the three ancestors beyond the great-grandfather. He states the reason for this: "It does not go [to the deity] unless the name is grasped. Without the mention of the name, the offered oblation (*havis*) does not reach the deity. From the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of another mantra, it is understood that this fourth *piṇḍa* is offered with intent for all deceased relatives—excluding paternal uncles and others who are mentioned by their lineage, relationship, and name.
And this mantra was shown by Laugākṣi:
"Those who have died in the paternal lineage, and likewise those in the maternal lineage;
those of the preceptor, the father-in-law, and kinsmen, and whatever other relatives have died."

Those in my family for whom the funeral offerings have been interrupted, those deprived of sons and wives, those whose rites have been neglected, as well as those born blind or lame; [may they all attain satisfaction].
To those who are deformed, to those with undeveloped embryos, and to those in my family— whether known or unknown—
may this ball of rice offered by me reach them as an inexhaustible offering.

Āśvalāyana, however, states a different mantra for the offering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) to the father and others: "This is for you, O father, [named] so-and-so, and for those who follow you. Gobhila, on the other hand, states yet another mantra.

"This is your *piṇḍa*, and for those who follow you here and those whom you follow; for them, *svadhā* to you!"—this is for the *Maitrapiṇḍapitṛyajña*. "This is for you, my father, [name]," thus taking the father's name; "This is for you, my grandfather, [name]," thus for the grandfather; "This is for you, my great-grandfather, [name]," thus for the great-grandfather. He should append: "And for those who follow you here, *svadhā* to them. "This is for you, father of so-and-so; this is for you, grandfather of so-and-so; this is for you, great-grandfather of so-and-so"—thus [the formula is used] when the sacrificer is away on a journey, and the *adhvaryu* performs it.
Śaṅkha and Likhita state:
"Having taken all varieties of food, one should place the piṇḍas upon darbha grass, consecrating each one three times with the formula, 'O [Name], this is for you.

Regarding this, the authors of the *Mahārṇavaprakāśa* say: 'One should place each individual piṇḍa after consecrating it three times with each respective mantra beginning with "The earth protects this," and so forth, using the formula, "O [Name], this is for you.'"
Applying each mantra to each individual ball, Yama shows those mantras by citing their opening words:
"One should first offer the ball to the ancestors with the mantra beginning 'pṛthivī'."
One should cause [the water] to be given to the grandfather with the mantra: "To the other, the intermediate space."
Then one should offer the third portion to the great-grandfather with the mantra "dyaur darviḥ"; this is the ancient Vedic injunction.
Viṣṇu also said:

"In the vicinity of the leavings, upon Darbha grass with its tips pointing south, one should place a single rice-ball for the father with the formula, 'The earth is the sacrificial ladle, it is imperishable. A second for the grandfather with the formula, 'The intermediate space is the sacrificial ladle, it is imperishable,' and a third for the great-grandfather with the formula, 'The sky is the sacrificial ladle, it is imperishable.'"

Hariharā has explained the meaning of this: "The earth is the inexhaustible ladle, satisfaction is the *svadhā* that does not spill over. With this mantra—"O Agni, live upon the earth as you would upon an inexhaustible ladle, a satisfaction that is *svadhā* and does not spill over; and those who follow you here, let there be *svadhā* for them"—one should place one *piṇḍa* for the father. "The intermediate space (*antarikṣa*) is the inexhaustible ladle, satisfaction is the *svadhā* that does not spill over. With this mantra—"O Vāyu, live upon the intermediate space as you would upon an inexhaustible ladle, a satisfaction that is *svadhā* and does not spill over; and those who follow you here, let there be *svadhā* for them"—one should place the second *piṇḍa* for the grandfather. "The sky (*dyu*) is the inexhaustible ladle, satisfaction is the *svadhā* that does not spill over. With this mantra—"O Sūrya, live upon the sky as you would upon an inexhaustible ladle, a satisfaction that is *svadhā* and does not spill over; and those who follow you here, let there be *svadhā* for them"—one should place the third *piṇḍa* for the great-grandfather.

The meaning of the mantra has also been explained by that very same [author]: "This well-known earth is this very thing existing in the form of the first *piṇḍa* (funeral cake). By this, it is understood that one should form the notion of 'earth' regarding the first *piṇḍa*. And because she is the means for food (*anna*) and the substratum thereof, she is like a *darvī* (ladle); or, because she removes suffering (*dūri-ta-dāraṇāt*) by becoming the instrument for good deeds (*sat-karma*), she is a *darvī*. 'Inexhaustible' (*akṣitā*) means 'satisfaction' (*tṛpti*); it means inexhaustible satisfaction. Even though she is daily subsisted upon as the means of satisfaction by moving and non-moving beings, she does not perish—this is the sense. 'Svadhā' because she is the cause of supramundane gratification for the ancestors. 'Unfailing' (*anupadastā*): the root *das* means to perish; thus, it means not perishing, free from decay. "Subsist upon—that is, eat—that earth, the *darvī*, the inexhaustible satisfaction, the *svadhā*, the unfailing, in the form of the first *piṇḍa*. Here, in the word 'asau' (so-and-so), the name of the father or other ancestor who is the object of the first *piṇḍa* should be used in the vocative case, such as 'O Father! or 'O Maternal Grandfather! "'Like Agni': just as Agni, having become the lord of the earth, subsists upon the well-known earth, so too [the recipient] should form the notion of equality with Agni regarding the one intended for the first *piṇḍa*—this is understood. 'And those who follow you': those who are established here in the next world following you, being your attendants—they too shall subsist. 'This is your *svadhā*': this *svadhā* is for your sake; [the word] 'becomes' (*bhavati*) is to be supplied. "The intermediate space (*antarīkṣa*) is a *darvī* because it dispels darkness and is a means for food. And you are a means for food because you are a cause of satisfaction. For from the intermediate space, rain is produced. "'Like Vāyu': just as Vāyu, having become the lord, subsists upon the intermediate space, so do you [subsist] upon this *piṇḍa* of such a nature. By this, it is understood that one should form the notion of equality with Vāyu regarding the grandfather and others intended for the second *piṇḍa*. "But heaven (*dyau*) is a *darvī* because it dispels suffering. For heaven consists of unsurpassed bliss, and thus it is the dispeller of suffering. 'Like Sūrya': just as Sūrya, having become the lord, subsists upon heaven. By this, it is understood that one should form the notion of equality with Sūrya regarding the great-grandfather and others intended for the third *piṇḍa*. Here, in the word 'asau', the name of the great-grandfather and others intended for the third *piṇḍa* should be used in the vocative case. The rest is self-evident. In the *Śrāddhakalpa* of Śaunaka and the Atharvaṇas, after stating that the food for the *piṇḍas* is to be drawn out with these very mantras, the offering of the *piṇḍas* starting from the great-grandfather down to the father in reverse order is stated with the mantras: "This is for you, O great-grandfather," "This is for you, O grandfather," and "This is for you, O father. "Having drawn out all varieties of food with the three [verses] beginning 'Heaven is the *darvī*, inexhaustible,' and having mixed them with clarified butter, he places three separate *piṇḍas* with the mantra 'This is for you, O great-grandfather. In the *Śrāddhakalpa* of Pippalāda and the Atharvaṇas as well: "Having drawn out all varieties of food with 'Earth is the *darvī*', and having mixed them with clarified butter, and having strewn *darbha* grass with tips pointing south using 'Seated on the sacrificial grass' (*barhiṣadaḥ*), he should give three separate *piṇḍas* with 'This is for you, O father' (*etat te tataḥ*). Thus, since these mantras describe the father and others as being comparable to Agni, Vāyu, and Sūrya, it is understood that, by implication, they should be meditated upon through their similarity to Agni and the others.
In the words of Vyāsa, however, it is revealed that one should perform the meditative identification [of the rice-ball] with the forms of Varuṇa and the others:
"The first deity is Varuṇa, the second is Prajāpati, and the third is remembered as Agni; this is the rice-ball, and this is declared to be the ritual for the rice-ball."

Regarding this, the author of the *Smṛticandrikā* has stated that this statement is intended to mean that the ancestors and others, who are essentially the deities of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*), should be meditated upon in the form of Varuṇa and the other gods. Alternatively, the meditation on the deities within the rice-balls should be performed according to the method described in the *Bhaviṣyatpurāṇa*, beginning with the words, "The god Aniruddha himself... For in that text it is said: "In that rite, the performer of the *śrāddha* should meditate on his own form as Aniruddha; the first person to be addressed [the father] as Pradyumna, the second as Saṃkarṣaṇa, and the third as Vāsudeva. All of this has already been explained in detail previously. Here, the conclusion reached is this: while identifying the ancestors and others with the forms of Varuṇa and the rest, one should offer the rice-balls directed toward them.
Vyāsa states another mantra for the offering of the rice-balls (piṇḍa):
"In the śrāddhas, being composed, one should recite the Sāvitrī at each and every rice-ball;
likewise, one should say 'to Soma' and also 'to the Pitṛmat'."
Now, regarding a performer who has two fathers, Āpastamba teaches a specific rule in the Piṇḍapitṛyajña-sūtra:
"If one should have two fathers, one should designate both [fathers] upon each individual rice-ball."

For one who has two fathers, such as a son born of the wife (*kṣetraja*), when offering the rice balls (*piṇḍas*), he should indicate and designate two for each single rice ball: in the first rice ball, the two fathers; in the second, the two grandfathers; and in the third, the two great-grandfathers.
This also has been explained previously in detail. However, regarding the offering of rice balls when the names of the father and the others are unknown, that same author shows other mantras.

If one does not know the name [of the deceased], one should offer the first rice-ball with the formula: "Svadhā to the ancestors who dwell on earth"; the second with: "Svadhā to the ancestors who dwell in the intermediate space"; and the third with: "Svadhā to the ancestors who dwell in heaven. By the word *bandhu*, the name is designated. Thus says Gobhila.

If one does not know the names, one should place the first *piṇḍa* with the formula: "Svadhā to the ancestors dwelling on earth"; the second with: "Svadhā to the ancestors dwelling in the intermediate space"; and having placed the third with: "Svadhā to the ancestors dwelling in heaven," he mutters: "O ancestors, rejoice here! [1444] Regarding the ignorance of the *gotra*, Vyāghrapāt says: "In the case of the loss of the *gotra*, [use] Kāśyapa."
If the lineage is unknown, one should adopt the Kāśyapa lineage, because the Kāśyapa lineage is common to all.
Thus says the Śatapatha Śruti:
"Therefore they say that all creatures are of the Kāśyapa lineage."
Whatever has been stated regarding the ignorance of the lineage (*gotra*) and name of the father and others should be understood to apply to the maternal grandfather and others as well.
Regarding the performer who has his father living, Āpastamba states a prohibition concerning the offering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*):
"If the father is living, he should not offer; having performed the oblations (*homa*), he should desist."

And this [prohibition], although stated with reference specifically to the *piṇḍapitṛyajña*, is indeed capable of prohibiting other offerings of rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) as well, because the underlying principle is the same. Furthermore, this prohibition is optional; this has already been established at length previously. In this regard, whether it be a *śrāddha* for six deities and so forth, or an independent offering of rice-balls dedicated to the maternal grandfather and others, the ritual performance should be carried out by employing the names and lineage-connections of the maternal grandfather and others in place of the names and lineage-connections of the father and others.
Thus says the author of the *Āpastambagṛhyabhāṣyārthasaṃgraha*:

In place of words such as "father" (*pitṛ*) and so forth, one should employ [words] such as "maternal grandfather" (*mātāmaha*) and so forth, in the case of the *anna-homa*, the ritual touching, and the offering of water and rice-balls (*piṇḍa*). In that regard, the formula beginning with "Whatever [sin] my maternal grandmother [committed]" (*yan me mātāmahī*) serves as the illustration. Thus it is said.

Regarding the *anna-homa* (oblation of food) performed with the mantras beginning with "yan me mātā pralulobha caraty anuvratā" during the *agnaukaraṇa*; regarding the "touching" (*sparśa*) of the food intended for the Brāhmaṇas with the mantras beginning with "eṣa te tata madhumān ūrmiḥ sarasvān"; and regarding the "offering of water and rice-balls" (*jalapiṇḍādidānaka*) with the water-offering mantra beginning with "mārjayantāṃ mama pitaraḥ" and the rice-ball offering mantra beginning with "etat te 'sau ye ca tvām anv"—in these places, the words "grandmother" (*mātāmaha*) and so forth should be substituted in place of the words "father" (*pitṛ*) and so forth. The phrase "yan me mātāmahītyādi" serves as an illustration of this. Thus, when substituting the word "grandmother" for "father" and the rest, in the mantra "yan me mātā pralulobha caraty anuvratā tan me retaḥ pitā vṛṅktām," when the *homa* is to be performed for the grandfathers, one inserts the word "grandmother" (*mātāmahī*) in place of the word "mother" (*mātṛ*) found in the mantra; thus the modification (*ūha*) becomes "yan me mātāmahī pralulobha. This is an illustration of the desired modifications such as "tan me reto mātāmaho vṛṅktām. This modification should be adopted by those following the *Āpastamba-gṛhya-sūtra*. Others, however, taking this as an illustration, should modify the words "father" and so forth found in the mantras prescribed by their own respective *Gṛhya-sūtras*. In that regard, in a rite for six deities, having made a line for the rice balls for the group of fathers, one should make a line for the rice balls for the group of grandfathers. Having performed the sprinkling (*avanejana*) for each individual in the place of the three rice balls for the group of fathers, one should perform the sprinkling in the place of the three rice balls for the group of grandfathers. In this way, having completed each ritual act for the rice balls of the paternal group, one should complete it for those of the maternal grandfather's group; this sequence of ritual acts (*padārthakrama*) is to be observed. When a Śrāddha for nine or twelve deities is undertaken, and the offering of rice balls is to take place, if there is an intermediate rite for female deities—whether independent or part of that same rite—the application should be made using feminine forms for the lineage (*gotra*), relationship, and names. The mantra "ye ca tvām anv" should be used as "yāś ca tvām anv. In that case, for a rite for nine deities, one should make a line for the rice balls of the paternal group, then to the west of that, a line for the rice balls of the maternal group, and further to the west of that, a line for the rice balls of the maternal grandfather's group. The sprinkling, the spreading of grass (*barhis*), and other such acts should also be performed according to this same order.
This very point has been stated in the *Āpastamba-Gṛhya-Sūtra* with reference to the groups of ancestors and maternal ancestors:

"Having spread out Darbha grass with its tips pointing south in two rows, having poured water upon them with the subsequent [mantras], and having offered [the oblations] ending toward the south with the subsequent [mantras]."

Having spread *darbha* grass with its tips pointing south over the area that has been scraped, in such a way as to make it twofold—there, on the eastern part, is the spreading for the group beginning with the father, while on the western part is that for the group beginning with the mother; for it is stated by the author of the *Gṛhyabhāṣyārthasaṃgraha*: "The funeral cakes (*piṇḍas*) for the women should be here on the west," and by the statement of the author of the *Śāṅkhāyana-gṛhyasūtra*, who teaches an additional distinction: "When they have finished eating, one should give the cakes; some [place] the cakes to the east, others to the west of those [cakes] for the wives, having placed something as a partition. This means that having placed something such as grass as a partition to the west of the cakes for the paternal ancestors, one should give the cakes to the wives of the father, grandfather, and great-grandfather.
In the *Matsyapurāṇa*: "Then, during the Kṛta interval, the wise man should offer *kuśa* grass to their wives;
likewise, he should perform the offering of the *piṇḍas* and so forth, as well as the invocation (*āvāhana*) and the dismissal (*visarjana*)."
With the subsequent mantras beginning with "mārjayantām," and again with the subsequent ones beginning with "etat te tatāsau," [the offerings are made].
However, in the *Śaunakātharvaṇa-śrāddhakalpa*, the offering of the rice-balls for the group of maternal ancestors is said to be to the south of the group of paternal ancestors.
"To the south, for the wives: 'This is for you, O wives.
And Devala has stated that four pindas are offered for the group of women:
"Then, taking a handful of the remains of the sacrificial oblation, [he offers] one for each from the beginning."
One should perform the offering of rice balls (piṇḍa) for the wives of the ancestors in successive order.
Then, taking a large portion of the prepared sacrificial oblation,
he should offer it as common to the entire circle of his kinsmen.

[1447] Thus, it is established that first the offering of the rice-ball (*piṇḍa*) is for the group of paternal ancestors, then for the group of maternal ancestors, and then for the group of maternal grandfathers.
Regarding this, Satyavrata says:
"The offering is first for the paternal ancestors, and immediately after that for the maternal ancestors."
Then, the sequence for the maternal grandfathers is proclaimed in this same manner.
And this sequence applies to a *śrāddha* for nine deities performed at all times, but not exclusively to that which is accomplished at the time of the *aṣṭakā*.
As for the statement from the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*:

"One should first give to the fathers, then immediately after to the mothers, and then to the maternal grandfathers; this is remembered as the sequence for the Anvaṣṭakya. This, however, is intended as an illustration. Thus, in the rite for the nine deities, it has been stated that the group of mothers is to be placed in the middle, both spatially and temporally.
Uśanas states the fault in doing otherwise:
"If one performs a śrāddha or offers the rice-balls (piṇḍas) for the mothers by placing the maternal grandfathers in between, it does not reach the fathers."
Satyavrata said:
"He who performs a Śrāddha or offers the rice-balls (piṇḍa) to his mothers while placing his maternal grandfathers in between goes to hell."
Gārgya also said:
"That man who places the Mothers at the end in the Śrāddha rites,
being a fool, goes head-first to the Kālasūtra hell."
However, that which was stated is a contradictory statement:
"In the *tarpaṇa*, the *anvaṣṭakā-śrāddha*, and at a sacred ford (*tīrtha*), this sequence is prescribed: first the fathers and maternal grandfathers, and immediately after them, the mothers. [1448]

May this [work] lead to the welfare of those for whom the purpose has been carried out through the lineage of their ancestors. Furthermore, as for this placement of the group of mothers (*mātṛvarga*) that has been mentioned, it applies to rites dedicated to nine deities other than the *nāndīmukha*; however, in the *nāndīmukha* rite itself, their placement occurs at the very beginning.
For this very reason, the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata* states:
"In the case of the anniversary of death (*kṣayāha*), they should be performed alone; in the case of prosperity (*vṛddhi*), they are proclaimed to be at the beginning."
For in all cases, the mothers should remain neutral; they must never be made the final arbiters.
"In all cases" refers to the offering of *piṇḍas* and other rites in the *mahālaya*, the *anvaṣṭakā*, *gayā-śrāddha*, and so forth.

In this regard, those authors of *gṛhya-sūtras* who have prescribed a separate *mātṛ-śrāddha* for the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*) and other occasions must perform a *śrāddha* dedicated to twelve deities.
Wherever the paternal ancestors (*pitaraḥ*) are worshipped, there the maternal grandfathers (*mātāmahāḥ*) are certainly [to be worshipped] as well.

Because of this statement, when the *mātāmaha-śrāddha* (ancestral rite for maternal grandfathers) is also to be performed, it follows by the maxim that "the modified rite (*vikṛti*) is like the model rite (*prakṛti*)" that a separate *śrāddha* must be performed for the group of maternal grandmothers as well; furthermore, it is the consensus of the learned that the *mātāmaha-śrāddha* is a modification of the *pitṛ-śrāddha*.
For this very reason, the author of the *Āpastamba-gṛhya-bhāṣyārthasaṃgraha* has demonstrated the extension of the rules of the *pitṛ-śrāddha* to the *mātāmaha-śrāddha*:
"In the same manner, one should diligently perform the *śrāddha* for the maternal grandfathers."

In this rite, the group of maternal grandmothers is placed at the very end, following the maternal grandfathers. The sequence for performing the constituent elements (padārtha) has already been largely explained here. However, for those authors of Gṛhyasūtras who have not prescribed a separate Śrāddha for the mothers on the new moon day, they must include the mention of the wives when performing the rite dedicated to the fathers and others on the new moon and similar occasions.
Thus concludes the primary rite called Piṇḍadāna, together with its variations regarding the deities, mantras, order, and number.
[1449] Now follows the wiping of the hands.
This is stated in the *Maitrāyaṇīya Piṇḍapitṛyajña Sūtra* as being performed with mantras upon the *darbha* grass immediately after the offering of the rice balls (*piṇḍa*).
He wipes the smearings on the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) with the mantra: "O Fathers, where you are, there, according to your respective portions, rejoice; O Fathers, rejoice here!

In the *Mānava-Maitrāyaṇīya-Piṇḍapitṛyajña-Sūtra*, however, for the first mantra, it is shown that the application is solely for recitation while facing south, as it says: "Looking toward the southern direction, he mutters. The word "on the sacrificial grass" (*barhiṣi*) refers to the *darbha* blades.

Regarding the requirement that the wiping and cleansing (avalepamārjana) should be performed at the root, middle, and tip of the *darbha* grasses—specifically at one of these points—Viṣṇu, teaching another mantra, says:
"At this point, 'O ancestors, rejoice! [is said] while rubbing the hands over the roots of the *darbha* grasses.
However, the consensus of many is that the application (*viniyoga*) of this mantra is merely for its recitation (*japa*) while facing the funeral cakes (*piṇḍas*); that will be shown later.
Vyāghra also says:
"One who is composed should wipe the smearings from his hands at the roots of the *darbha* grass.

Here, in response to the expectation as to which object follows which, at the roots of which *darbhas*, and with reference to which ancestors the wiping of the smearings (*lepamārjana*) is to be performed, Manu says:
Having offered clusters of flowers to the ancestors according to the rule with a purified mind,
he should wipe that hand on those darbha grasses for the sake of those who partake of the scrapings.

Having placed it upon the *puṣpa-darbha* grass, the term "prayataḥ" (diligent) refers to one possessing a specific kind of effort. Here, the mental quality consisting of one-pointedness and so forth is to be understood as the effort useful for avoiding negligence in the form of forgetting the ritual details. This is a restatement (*anuvāda*), because such effort is already established by virtue of being required for all ritual performances. The phrase "according to the prescribed rule" (*vidhipūrvakam*) is intended to include the rules observed in other scriptures; for if it were meant merely to state that the procedure is according to the rules declared in Manu’s own scripture, its inclusion would be redundant. "Upon those *darbha* grasses" refers to those upon which the offering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) was made. "Him" (*tam*) refers to the person by whom the offering of the rice-balls was performed. "For the partakers of the scrapings" (*lepabhāginām*) means with reference to the ancestors who partake of the scrapings; these are shown in the *Matsyapurāṇa*.

"Those beginning with the fourth [descendant] are partakers of the lepa (the smearings); those beginning with the father are partakers of the piṇḍas; the giver of the piṇḍa is the seventh among them; such is the sapinda relationship extending over seven generations. Thus it is said.

"The fourth and the others" refers to the great-great-grandfather (*vṛddhaprapitāmaha*) and so forth. Thus, this performer of the *śrāddha*, addressing the three ancestors beginning with the great-great-grandfather and declaring, "May this portion be for them," should wipe his hand on the roots of the *darbha* grass that serve as the base for the first *piṇḍa*. This wiping (*nimārjana*) consists of attaching to the *darbha* blades any food or water adhering to the hand in order to remove it. Consequently, one opinion holds that if there is a smear on the hand, the wiping must be performed for the sake of the disposal known as removal, and not otherwise.
Furthermore, another opinion has been presented by Medhātithi and Harīhara, as follows:

"Even if nothing at all remains in the hand, one must nevertheless wipe the hand. For this is not merely a *pratipatti-karman* (a disposal rite) such that it would not be performed when there is no purpose for pouring out [the remainder]. Indeed, it is not heard here that 'one should wipe what is stuck to the hand'; rather, it says simply 'the hand'."

But surely it is heard [in the scripture]: "to those who partake of the smearings. In that case, if there were no smearings, [the rite] would not apply. It is said in reply: the physical form of the food itself never actually adheres [to the hand]. However, while the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) remain [on the hand], the essence of the food and its heat certainly transfer to the hand; and that very thing is called the "smearing of food" (*annalepa*). Furthermore, the genitive case here expresses the connection of the wiping with those who partake of the smearings. And yet, those who partake of the smearings are not perceptibly visible, such that one could establish a relationship of ownership and so forth for the smearing with them. Therefore, even though there is no direct smearing of food, one should indeed wipe [the hand] at the base of the *darbha* grass, saying: "Let this portion belong to those who partake of the smearings," referring to the essence of the food or its heat which has transferred to the hand under the name of "smearing."
For this very reason, Viṣṇu has stated that one should rub the hands against the roots of the *darbha* grass: "The rubbing of the hands against the roots of the *darbha* grass.
After wiping away the residue from the hands, Yama prescribes the libation with a water-pot:
Then, he should wipe that hand on the *darbha* grass for those who partake of the remnants of the smearings;
thereafter, being self-restrained, he should satisfy the ancestors with a water-pot.
And by stating that this libation (*tarpaṇa*) occurs after the giving of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), Devala has also shown its procedure:
"Then, having taken a handful from within the oblation himself,
and having likewise taken both [the handful and] a jar filled with water..."
Flowing from the tips of the hands of the ancestors and the Brahmins, he should,
facing outward, offer all those rice-balls (piṇḍas) in sequence with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (apasavya).
In this manner, three times, having circumambulated the water contained in the vessel, one should cause it to be heard softly;
and having completed the circumambulation, one should overturn that very vessel right there.
Thus ends the wiping of the hands.
Now follow the ritual acts beginning with the sipping of water (ācamana), which constitute the subsidiary elements following the offering of the rice balls (piṇḍadāna).
Regarding this, Manu says:
Having sipped water and turned toward the north, and having slowly restrained the breaths three times,
one should pay homage to the six seasons and to the ancestors with the appropriate mantras.
After wiping the hands, one should perform the sipping of water (*ācamana*). This *ācamana* should be performed three times, preceded by the washing of the hands.
Thus it is stated in the *Brahma Purāṇa*:
"Then, having duly wiped both hands upon *darbha* grass..."
Then, having washed with water and performed the ritual sipping (ācamana) three times, one should meditate upon Hari.

Having performed the ancestral rites (*pitṛkarman*) three times, this is for the purpose of setting aside the rule that "one should perform the sipping of water (*ācamana*) once. That [sipping] must be done while wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*yajñopavītin*). Immediately after the sipping, one should discard the *darbha* grass previously held and take up other *darbha* blades. Some perform this sipping of water immediately after offering the perfumes (*gandha*) and other items to the ancestors; others, however, perform it both there and here. After the sipping, "having turned toward the north" (*udak parāvṛtya*) means having turned around toward the northern direction, thus becoming facing north. "Three times" (*triḥ*) means three times. "Restraining" (*āyamya*) means suppressing. "Gently" (*śanaiḥ*) means so that no excessive pain occurs. "The vital breaths" (*asūn*): Medhātithi says that one should perform the three breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) prescribed by such rules as "the Gāyatrī together with the Śiras, conjoined with the Praṇava. However, the view of Karka and many others is that one should restrain the breaths even without a mantra. They consider that only the mere suppression of breath is intended, because the statements of Kātyāyana and others mention only the restraint of the breaths. One should pay homage to the seasons (*ṛtu*), beginning with spring, and one should pay homage to the ancestors (*pitṛ*). And these two acts of homage should be performed "with mantras," that is, conjoined with mantras.
In that regard, the mantra for the salutation is found in the Brahmapurāṇa:
"Salutations to you, O Spring; salutations again and again to Summer;
and always salutations to the rains, and to the season known as Autumn."
"Salutation to you, O Hemanta; salutation to you, O Śiśira;
and salutations again and again to the months, the years, and the days.
This is the mantra for the salutation to the ancestors (*pitṛ*).

The mantra beginning with *namo vaḥ pitara iṣe* and so forth will be shown [later]. Here, the turning away toward the north is preceded by the consecration of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa-anumantraṇa*). And that [turning] is performed either keeping the left limb forward or with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*apasavya*). Furthermore, the breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*) is to be performed while standing facing north. As for the salutation (*namaskāra*), it is to be performed immediately after the rites ending with the loosening of the waist-knot (*nīvimokṣa*), such as turning toward the rice-balls; these specific details are to be adopted from other scriptures. In that regard, the *Kātyāyana-sūtra* states:
"Having said 'O Fathers,' they turn toward the north and, until they are satisfied, mutter the verse *amīmadanta*."
Here, by citing the opening words "O Fathers," the entire mantra is indicated. Its application (viniyoga) along with its explanation is recorded in the *Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa*:
"There he mutters: 'O Fathers, rejoice here; according to your respective portions, be satisfied'—this means, 'Eat according to your respective portions.'"

Regarding the phrase "therein" (*tatra*), it means when the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) have been placed. Standing facing the rice-balls, one should mutter the mantra beginning with "O fathers" (*atra pitaro*) and ending with "rain down [upon us]" (*āvṛṣāyadhvam*). He explains the passage beginning with "according to their respective portions" (*yathābhāgam*) by saying "eat according to their respective portions" (*yathābhāgam aśnīta*), and so forth. "He sits facing north" (*udaṅgāste*) means he should remain sitting while facing the north. According to Upādhyāya Karka, this turning toward the north is performed by not turning clockwise. And it is stated in the Āśvalāyana-sūtra:

"One should address those who have returned [from the world of the ancestors] with the mantra: 'O fathers, rejoice here; rain down [upon us] according to your respective portions,' while turning away to the left and facing north."

"Covered" (*nivṛtān*) means those which have been placed upon the *darbha* grass according to the prescribed rule. "Turning to the left" (*savyāvṛt*) means turning in a counter-clockwise manner, keeping the left limb forward and moving away from the right; the meaning is that one should turn away from the right. By the phrase "having gone northward" (*udaṅgatya*), it is understood that the turning must be performed toward the north.

Viṣṇu has also stated: "Having offered the *piṇḍas*, one should address those covered [with grass] with the mantra: 'O ancestors, rejoice here; come hither each according to your share. Then, having turned back while facing north and turning to the left..."
And this counter-clockwise turning is performed by only certain performers, not by all.
Regarding this, the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata* states:
"Some declare that the turning with the left hand ends toward the north."
[1454] "All [this was taught by] Gautama, Śāṇḍilya, and indeed Śāṇḍilyāyana. Thus it is said.

"By the left" means having placed the left limb in front. "Until the north" means for as long as he remains facing north, and no longer. "Some," namely, the sages other than the sages named Gautama, Śāṇḍilya, and Śāṇḍilyāyana; however, Gautama and the others prescribe "all," that is, every manner of turning—both by the left and by the right (apasavya). Regarding the phrase "he remains facing north," he states the limit of time: "until exhaustion" (*ātamanāt*); "exhaustion" (*tamana*) means fatigue, and that is the limit. Since exhaustion cannot occur merely by standing facing north, the cause of exhaustion taught in another scripture—consisting of the suppression of breath—is indicated here as something to be practiced.
Regarding this, Āśvalāyana says: "Having sat without breathing, according to one's ability.
"According to one's ability" means without exceeding one's capacity; "without breathing" means having performed the restraint of the breath (prāṇāyāma).
Regarding this, Viṣṇu says:
"Having performed the restraint of the vital breaths according to one's capacity.

Immediately after that, "having turned back" (āvṛtya) means having returned toward the *piṇḍa* by means of the action called turning; and Karka maintains that this turning is by the same path [by which one went out].
Therefore, it is said in the *Karmapradīpa*:
"Having restrained the breath and drawn it in, meditating upon the ancestors as is appropriate,
and performing the recitation (japa) while turning [the breath] by that same [path], one should then release the breath."

The word "japet" (he should mutter) implies the mantra "amīmadanta" as its object. "By that very same path," meaning by the left path alone; "he should release the breaths," which means he should exhale. Here, the repetition of the muttering is established. However, in the tradition of Kātyāyana and others, the muttering occurs after the repetition; this is the only difference. He mutters "amīmadanta" during the repetition. By citing this opening phrase (*pratīka*), the entire mantra is indicated.
All of this—including the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), the commentary, and the complete mantra—is heard in the *Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa*.

Then he turns away; for the ancestors are, as it were, hidden from men, and so it becomes hidden. "He should remain until he is tired," they say, "for he is indeed as much as that. Having sat for just a moment and then having leaned down, he mutters: "The fathers have rejoiced; they have partaken according to their portions. By this he means to say, "They have eaten according to their portions."

"In *atha* [here], after the recitation of the mantra beginning with *pitaraḥ*, etc.; *parāṅ* means facing away from the *piṇḍas*, that is, turned toward the north (*udaṅmukha*). *Parāvartate*: while remaining seated, he moves as if turning counter-clockwise. *Parāṅ paryāvartate* is not a statement of reason; it is an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) similar to a formal declaration. "The ancestors are indeed hidden (*tiraḥ*) from humans"—*tiraḥ* means concealed. The word *iva* has the sense of *kila* (it is said) or the sense of *hi* (for/indeed); for it is said that while eating, the ancestors desire to become hidden from humans out of modesty."
And likewise, in the Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa, it is said: "He turns away, for the ancestors are modest."

*Hrīkāḥ* means "possessing shame" (*hrīmantaḥ*). *Tiraḥ* refers to turning away. Since the ancestors, who are eating the food in the form of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) from the south, are rendered invisible to the performer facing north, this act—being both appropriate and required—is considered to have been performed for the sake of the ancestors. *Ātamitoḥ* means "until exhaustion," that is, until the point of distress caused by the suppression of breath. For it is said, "The vital breath (*asu*) is indeed only this much. This implies that life lasts only as long as there is exhaustion; thus, he states that this limit is not intended to be strictly observed. "He [should remain] for just a moment (*muhūrta*)"—here, by the word *muhūrta*, some period of time prior to the exhaustion produced by the suppression of breath is indicated. *Upapallayya* means having turned back again toward the rice-balls. *Āśiṣuḥ* means "having eaten."
Āśvalāyana also says:
"Turning around, [one recites] 'The ancestors have rejoiced; they have partaken according to their portions'.
The meaning is that one should consecrate the rice-balls (*piṇḍas*) with this mantra.
Regarding this, Viṣṇu says:
"Having turned around, one should address [the ancestors] with the words 'They have rejoiced'.
However, Gobhila, the author of the Rāṇāyaṇīya-sūtra, has stated that the recitation of this mantra, "They have rejoiced," should be performed by the one who is turning around.

Having deposited the rice-balls, he mutters: "O ancestors, rejoice here; partake according to your respective portions. Without turning away, while turning back before exhaling, he should mutter: "The ancestors have rejoiced; they have partaken according to their respective portions. Here, after the deposition of the rice-balls, Āpastamba has shown the application of the two mantras mentioned by Kātyāyana and others, preceded by the presentation of alternative mantras.

"Whatever my mother has done through negligence, whatever she has done contrary to her vows—may my father take that seed; may another [seed] be produced for life. To the fathers who partake of the *svadhā*, *svadhā*! Homage! To the grandfathers who partake of the *svadhā*, *svadhā*! Homage! To the great-grandfathers who partake of the *svadhā*, *svadhā*! Homage! Having thus performed the worship, he says, "O fathers, enjoy yourselves here according to your portions," and turns away with his back toward the offerings until the steam has subsided. He waits until the steam has subsided, and then turns back, or he does not turn back at all.

The meaning is: "until the cessation of heat," that is, taking the disappearance of the heat from the rice-ball (*piṇḍa*) as the limit. Immediately after that, one should turn back toward the rice-balls with the mantra beginning with *amīmadanta*. Regarding this, some have stated that after the words *amīmadanta*, one should smell the food remaining from the rice-balls and then perform the *pratyavanejana* (the secondary sprinkling).
Thus it is said in the Āśvalāyana-sūtra:
"One should always consume the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) by inhaling it, and [perform] the pouring out."

One should eat—that is, smell—the remainder of the *caru* in such a way that it is accomplished by the *prāṇa* (breath) flowing through the nose; the meaning is that one should sniff the food remaining from the *piṇḍas*. Immediately thereafter, "constantly" (*nityam*) means as a rule, there is the "pouring out" (*ninayanam*), which means the pouring out of water for the ritual rinsing (*pratyavanejana*). Viṣṇu has also stated: "Having consecrated [the remains] with the mantra *amīmadanta*, having smelled the remainder, and having poured out water as before with the words *śundhantāṃ pitaraḥ*. Thus.

In the *Āpastamba-sūtra*, however, after stating the smelling of the remnants of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) and the optional consumption of them accompanied by a mantra, the ritual rinsing (*pratyavanejana*) is described:

"He smells what remains in the vessel [with the mantra]: 'Those ancestors who are equal and of one mind in the realm of Yama—for them is this world; Svadhā! Homage! May the sacrifice be prepared among the gods. It should be consumed by one who is ill with the words 'O ancestors, grant me a hero'; it should be consumed by one desiring food; or it may be consumed by one capable of digesting food. As before, he should pour three handfuls of water onto the single wooden sword (*ekasphyā*)."

"Āmayāvī" means one who is ill. From the context, it is understood that this refers either to the desire for the cessation of disease or, in the case of one afflicted by an incurable illness, the desire for a superior state of existence. "One desiring food and drink (annādya) may eat"; or, one who is capable of eating food but does not eat it—meaning, even though possessed of food, eats it due to the absence of a sufficiently sharp digestive fire (vaiśvānara) and thus lacks an abundance of sacrificial oblation (havis)—such a person may also eat out of a desire for relish (ruci). Both of these cases are stated in the *Maitrāyaṇīya-Pariśiṣṭa* immediately after the salutations: "One should smell the remaining food like a scent, or one who is ill, or one desiring food and drink, may eat it."
In this regard, the Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa states that the smelling of the remainder is a commendatory declaration (arthavāda):

"The exponents of Brahman say: 'Should one eat [of it] or should one not eat? If one were to eat it, he would eat the lowest kind of food and would be liable to die; if he were not to eat it, it would not be an oblation and he would be cut off from the ancestors. Therefore, it should only be smelled—it is as if eaten, yet not eaten."

The "expounders of Brahman" (*brahmavādinaḥ*) are those who expound the Vedas; they "say," meaning they determine after deliberation. "Inferior" (*jaghanya*) means inauspicious. "One prone to die" (*pramāyukaḥ*) means one subject to untimely death. Because there is an absence of the ritual disposal (*pratipatti*) consisting of eating the remnants, [the food] becomes unfit for offering (*āhaviṣṭva*). For this very reason, that food would be "cut off" (*āvṛścyeta*) from the ancestors; the meaning is that it would be severed. The smelling of the remnants has been mentioned, while the smelling of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) will be shown later.

Regarding this, Kātyāyana states that the offerings of the rice-balls consist of the rites beginning with the pouring back of water (*pratyavanejana*) after the silent recitation (*japa*) of the mantra "They have rejoiced" (*amīmadanta*), and ending with the placing of the fire-brand (*ulmukanidhāna*).

He mutters, "They have rejoiced," and having performed the ritual rinsing (*avanejana*) as before, he loosens his waist-knot (*nīvī*). With the formula, "Homage to you," he makes the *añjali* gesture; with the formula, "This for you," he offers the threads—either woolen fringes or [woolen] strips—into each ball of earth (*piṇḍa*), or else [he offers] the hair of the sacrificer on the northernmost one. With the formula, "Strength," he pours water [on them], and then the sacrificer smells [them]. The firebrands and the *sakṛdācchinna* grass-blades are cast into the fire. Here, the connection is with "having performed the ritual rinsing as before. By the phrase "as before," the procedure of the previous rinsing is extended by analogy (*atideśa*). That [procedure], consisting of the water-vessel and so forth, has already been shown previously.

The Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, however, demonstrating that same act even during the secondary washing (*pratyavanejana*) by means of instruction itself, describes the secondary washing along with its explanatory passage (*sārthavādaka*):

"Then, taking a vessel of water and pouring it out, he says, 'O so-and-so, pour water for the father of the sacrificer! [and] 'O so-and-so, pour water for the grandfather! [and] 'O so-and-so, pour water for the great-grandfather! That is just as one would sprinkle someone who has already eaten.

‘To one who has eaten’ (*jakṣuṣe*), meaning to one who has finished his meal; ‘having loosened the *nīvī*’—the *nīvī* is the concealment of the hem of the lower garment in the left armpit; ‘having loosened’ (*visraṃsya*) means having unfastened it. From the injunction to loosen it, it is understood that prior to this, it was to be worn in the ordinary manner. ‘He makes the *añjali* with the words “Homage to you”’—he makes the *añjali* for each salutation with the mantras beginning with “Homage to you, O Pitṛs, for the essence” (*namo vaḥ pitaro rasāya*). An *añjali* is the hollowing of the hands; the meaning is that, having formed the *añjali*, he should perform salutations to the Pitṛs while facing the rice-balls (*piṇḍas*). And those mantras are recited by the Vājasaneyins as follows:

"Obeisance to you, O fathers, for the essence; obeisance to you, O fathers, for the sap; obeisance to you, O fathers, for life; obeisance to you, O fathers, for the *svadhā* offering; obeisance to you, O fathers, for the terrible; obeisance to you, O fathers, for wrath; obeisance to you, O fathers, obeisance to you!"—thus [it is stated] in the Āśvalāyana-sūtra.

Then he should worship them with these [verses]: "Homage to you, O fathers, for food; homage to you, O fathers, for strength; homage to you, O fathers, for prosperity; homage to you, O fathers, for the terrible; homage to you, O fathers, for life; homage to you, O fathers, for sap; *svadhā* to you, O fathers; homage to you, O fathers; homage! These are yours, O fathers; these are ours. May we, being alive here, belong to you. And with the four verses beginning, "We call the mind hither," [he says]: "We call the mind hither with the *Nārāśaṃsa* Soma, and with the hymns of the fathers. Let the mind come back again for wisdom, for skill, for life, so that we may long behold the sun. May the divine folk, O fathers, give us back our mind; may we all increase the company of the living."
In the Āpastamba-sūtra: "When the rice-balls have lost their heat, he mutters the salutations: 'Obeisance to you, O fathers, to the essence! In the Taittirīya-brāhmaṇa:

He pays homage: for in homage to the ancestors, he says, "Homage to you, O fathers, for the sap; homage to you, O fathers, for the vigor; homage to you, O fathers, for life; homage to you, O fathers, for the *svadhā* offering; homage to you, O fathers, for the wrath; homage to you, O fathers, for the terrible; homage to you, O fathers, who abide in this world—may they follow you; and those who are in this world—may they follow us. You who abide in this world, may you be the most excellent among them; and as for us in this world, may I be the most excellent. "We invoke the mind with the *Nārāśaṃsa* Soma and with the hymns of the fathers. May the mind come back again, having made it ready for skill and for living, so that we may long behold the sun. May the divine folk, O fathers, give back our mind to us, so that we may summon the host of the living."
In the Maitrāyaṇīya-sūtra.

Having made a gesture of reverence with joined palms, he whispers: "Homage to you, O fathers, for your fury; homage to you, O fathers, for your vigor; homage to you, O fathers, for your strength; homage to you, O fathers, for your breath; homage to you, O fathers, for your essence; homage to you, O fathers, for your power; homage to you, O fathers, for that which is life; homage to you, O fathers, for that which is terrible; *svadhā* to you, O fathers, homage, homage to you, O fathers! Those among us here who are deceased fathers, may they follow you; those among us here who are living fathers, may they follow us. O deceased fathers who are here, may you be the most excellent among them; O living fathers who are here, may I be the most excellent among them. Thus.

And the *nihnava* (concealment) is performed by placing [the hand] over the two palms; for this is well-established in such passages as "Then they conceal [the hand] on the sacrificial grass" (*prastara*).
Gobhila is the author of the *Rāṇāyaṇīya-sūtra*.

Then, they conceal themselves. In the eastern furrow, having placed their hands with the palms turned upward toward the south, they recite: "Homage to you, O fathers, for life; homage to you, O fathers, for sapidity. In the middle furrow, with the left palm turned upward: "Homage to you, O fathers, for the terrible; homage to you, O fathers, for essence. In the northernmost furrow, with the right palm turned upward: "Homage to you, O fathers, for the *svadhā*-offering; homage to you, O fathers, for wrath. Then, having made the *añjali* gesture, he mutters: "Homage to you, O fathers; O fathers, homage to you."

Regarding the phrase "the right hand turned upward" (*dakṣiṇottānau*), the meaning is that one should turn the right hand upward and place the left hand, with its palm facing downward, upon its northern side. By reversing this, it should be understood that the left hand is turned upward.

However, Āpastamba, in his own Gṛhya-sūtra, has presented the mantras for the worship (*upasthāna*) according to the division of the offering of rice balls (*piṇḍa-dāna*) dedicated to male deities and female deities.

In this regard, the presentation of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa-upasthāna*) for the sake of the paternal ancestors is performed with these mantras: "Those of yours who are here, and those among us for whom you pray—let them carry [the offerings]; may you be satisfied, may you be satisfied, may you be satisfied. It should be understood from the indicative marks (*liṅga*) of the mantras that the presentation of the rice-balls for the sake of the group of women is to be performed with these mantras: "Those of yours who are here, and those among us for whom you pray—let them carry [the offerings]; may you be satisfied, may you be satisfied, may you be satisfied. Furthermore, in another Vedic branch (*śākhā*), these mantras are as follows:

"May you fathers be satisfied—those who follow you and those who hope for us from us; may they who hope for us be satisfied. May you grandfathers be satisfied—those who follow you and those who are your great-grandfathers, and those who hope for us from us; may they who hope for us be satisfied. May you mothers be satisfied—those who follow you and those who hope for us from us; be satisfied! May you grandmothers be satisfied—those who follow you and those who hope for us from us; be satisfied! May you great-grandmothers be satisfied—those who follow you and those who hope for us from us; be satisfied! Thus [he says].

And these have been explained by Harihara: "O ancestors, may you be satisfied; and those who are 'after you'—those who are your followers—may they also be satisfied. The plural number is used with reference to paternal uncles and others, according to such statements as 'of brothers born of the same womb,' and so forth. In the same way, this should be applied appropriately to the grandfathers and the rest. And those who hope for us—those such as the *adagdha* (the unconsumed) who offer expectations of the sacrificial oblation (*havir-āśaṃsā*)—may they too be satisfied by this rite. At the end, the repetition of the word 'tṛpti' (satisfaction) is for the sake of emphasizing excellence. The rest is clear in meaning. [This is from] the Kaṭha-sūtra.
In this regard, he denies it with the words: "Obeisance to you, O Pitṛs; may we live.
In the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa* it is said: "One should always recite this mantra with the left hand placed over the right."
"Obeisance to you, O ancestors, with food," thus he should recite correctly and without weariness.

The meaning is: having turned the right hand upward with the left and right hands, one should form the *añjali* gesture over it with the left hand facing downward. He states the number of prostrations as "six times. This is heard in the *Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa* along with its explanatory passage (*arthavāda*): "Then, having lifted the hem of his garment, he pays homage. The hem of the garment belongs to the ancestors; therefore, having lifted the hem, he pays homage. Homage is indeed the sacrifice; thus he makes these [ancestors] worthy of sacrifice. He pays homage six times; there are six seasons, and the ancestors are the seasons; therefore, he pays homage six times."
In this regard, the *Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa* prescribes the salutation after the rinsing and the loosening of the waist-cloth (*nīvī*).

However, in the *Manusmṛti*, the rinsing is prescribed after the salutation; furthermore, its specific location is stated to be accomplished in the same area as the water used for the preceding rinsing. And it is said: "The knower of the mantras should pay homage to the six ancestors and to the ancestors themselves."
"One should then slowly pour the remaining water near the rice balls. Thus it is said.

One should pour another portion of that very same water—the remainder of which one part was poured at the place of the first *piṇḍa*—near the other *piṇḍa*, that is, in the vicinity of the second *piṇḍa*, in the form of an *avanejana* (sprinkling). This is the final disposal (*pratipatti*) of that water; thus, the use of the word "remainder" (*śeṣa*) becomes appropriate. Therefore, Medhātithi states that if such water were somehow absent, there would be no pouring: "In the *Gṛhya-sūtra*, however, it is stated that the pouring is obligatory. And this is correct. For this very reason, it is also stated in Āśvalāyana’s *Piṇḍapitṛyajña*: "The pouring is obligatory. Here, the sequence mentioned regarding the *avanejana* and the salutation (*namaskāra*) should not be adopted by those who follow [Kātyāyana], because it is directly contradicted by Kātyāyana and the *Śatapatha-brāhmaṇa*. Furthermore, the sequence stated in the *Śatapatha-brāhmaṇa* is widely accepted. As for the specific location and the specific quantity of water mentioned therein for the *avanejana*, those should indeed be adopted, since no contradiction with the direct scriptural texts is observed.

In another Smṛti, however, the ritual rinsing with the water used for washing the alms-bowl is prescribed: "Then, one should rinse [the feet] once again with the water from the washing of that bowl. Vyāghra also says:
Having washed that vessel with water, one should perform the *avanejana* (sprinkling) for each *piṇḍa* as before,
and then turn the *piṇḍa*-vessel face down.

In this matter, even those who follow the *Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa* should adopt the practice of turning the alms-bowl upside down. However, they must certainly not offer the water used for washing the bowl as the water for rinsing (*pratyavanejana*). For the *Śatapatha*, in censuring the throwing of the wiping-cloths (*sruc-sammārjanāni*) into the fire—stating, "One should not do that; rather, one should make him drink the very water with which one has washed the vessel from which one brought food; therefore, one should indeed cast these away"—employs as an illustration the well-known worldly practice of offering the rinsings of a vessel to one who is about to be fed, one who is being fed, or one who has already been fed. By this observation of another matter, it is understood that the rinsings of a vessel are not to be given elsewhere either. With the Yajus formula, "This, O ancestors, is your garment," one should place threads upon each individual ball of rice (*piṇḍa*). From the plural number, it is understood that there are three of each. "'Ūrṇā' or 'ūrṇāḥ'" refers to the wool of a sheep. "'Daśā' or 'daśāḥ'" refers to the threads at the hem of a garment. Although these could have been included under the single term "threads" (*sūtra*), they are mentioned separately to indicate their inferiority compared to other types of thread. For this very reason, the prohibition of using hem-threads is recorded in some Smṛti texts.
"A wise person should avoid [a garment] that has reached its end, even if it is made of new cloth. Thus [it is said].

"In the later stage of life, or the hair of the sacrificer. Having divided the hundred-year lifespan into two equal parts, two stages of life are established. Regarding the "hair of the sacrificer" belonging to one who is in the later, or upper, stage of life—since these are parts of the body that are highly esteemed, only those situated on the upper part of the body should be taken; for another *sūtra* is seen stating, "In the later stage of life, the hair of the chest. By the word "or" (*vā*), the possibility of using threads and so forth even in this stage of life is shown as an alternative. Furthermore, these threads and such should be given in place of clothing if clothing is absent; however, if clothing is present, clothing itself should be given. For this very reason, after stating "one should give clothing," Āśvalāyana said:

"A fringe or a tuft of wool, for those over fifty years of age; 'O fathers, this garment of your own hair is for you; O fathers, provide us with something other than this!'"—here, "a tuft of wool" (*ūrṇāstukā*) means a fragment of wool.
And it is also stated in the *Vāyupurāṇa*:
"Or even just thread for the purpose of clothing.
One should not think that only thread should be given for the purpose of clothing and never clothing itself;
for Viṣṇu says:
Alternatively, in the absence of a garment, [he offers] a fringe of wool, with the mantra: "O ancestors, this is your clothing; O ancestors, clothe yourselves in something other than this.
This is also stated in the Brahmapurāṇa.
"One should give garments in sequence, or else a fringe from a white cloth," so it is said.
Furthermore, as Vyāghra has stated:
"O ancestors, may this garment give a fringe to each of you individually."
That too should be explained as being in the absence of cloth. Here, another mantra favored by Kātyāyana is shown in the statements of Viṣṇu and Āśvalāyana;
Āpastamba has also shown another mantra:

"O fathers, these are your garments; O fathers, do not seek anything other than this," having cut off the fringe of the garment, he should set it down, or else a tuft of wool, saying, "In the former stage of life, in the latter stage of life, [I place] your own hair."
Gobhila, the author of the *Rāṇāyaṇīya-sūtra*, however, prescribes a different mantra along with specific ritual details such as the counter-clockwise direction (*apradakṣiṇa*):

"Having taken a thread of the cord with the left hand alone, one should place the rice-ball (*piṇḍa*) in the eastern furrow, moving from right to left (*apasalavi*). Having uttered the father's name, [saying] 'O [Name], this is your garment; and those who follow you here, and whom you follow—to him, to you, be *svadhā*! Having touched water, he should do exactly the same for the other two.
In this context, the mention of the name is illustrative (*upalakṣaṇa*) of the inclusion of the lineage name (*gotra*) and so forth.
Therefore, in the *Brahma Purāṇa*: "Reciting 'This garment, O ancestors,' for each one separately, he should then recite: 'O you of such-and-such lineage, this garment is for you.'"
However, a certain distinction is shown in the *Maitrāyaṇīya-piṇḍapitṛyajña*:

"‘These are your fathers,’ with these words he applies a lock of wool or a fringe; ‘May [this] not be ours,’ with these words he looks at what remains; he should place a hair on the upper part of his age, saying, ‘The fathers are one thing, the mothers another; may they not consume us.

In the *Mānava-maitrāyaṇīya-piṇḍapitṛyajña-sūtra*, however, the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) of the fringe and other items to be offered upon the funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*) is prescribed prior to their offering.

Having sprinkled wool or a fringe of cloth with water, he places it in the location of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*). For one in the later stage of life, having cut off a lock of hair or a fringe of the garment, he should place it [with the formula]: "One for us, another for the fathers; may we not come to harm. Thus [it is said]. Viṣṇu states another mantra:
"To those who are deceased ancestors, and to those..."—thus the garment should be given.
Also in the *Śrāddhakalpa* of the Kaṭhas:
"One should place the garments with the words, 'Those who are our ancestors here who have passed away.
Here, by means of citing the opening phrase (*pratīkagrahaṇa*), the complete mantra employed is shown. [1466]

"Those ancestors here who have passed away, may they follow you; those ancestors here who are living, may they follow us. O ancestors here who have passed away, may you be the most excellent among them; O ancestors here who are living, may we be the most excellent among them. These are your garments, O ancestors; therefore, O ancestors, do not take away our life-span. Bestow upon us, O ancestors, heroic sons.

In this regard, in numerous sources other than the *Kātyāyana-sūtra*—namely, in various Vedic branches (*śākhā*), ritual manuals (*kalpasūtra*), legal codes (*smṛti*), and Purāṇas—it is stated that prior to the giving of the thread (*sūtradāna*), there are the rites of the house-consecration (*gṛhadīkṣaṇa*), the inspection of the rice-balls (*piṇḍāvekṣaṇa*), and the application of collyrium and ointment (*añjanābhyañjana*).
Regarding this, Gobhila says:
"He looks at the house, saying, 'O fathers, give us houses'; he looks at the rice-balls, saying, 'O fathers, may we always give to you.'"

With the mantra "O Fathers, give us houses," he looks at the house or at his wife, because it has been stated [in the scripture] that "the house is the wife. With the mantra beginning "May we sit together" (*sado vaḥ*), he looks at the funeral cakes (*piṇḍas*). However, the Vājasaneyins read *satova* in place of *sado vaḥ*.
In the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, however, because this mantra expresses the sense of a benediction (*āśis*), its function is understood to be that of a means for worship (*upasthāna*).

"O Fathers, give us houses," for the Fathers indeed desire houses; "this is the ritual act of blessing for this [offering]," thus it is possible to perform the *upasthāna* (reverential salutation) even while looking at the houses, since there is no contradiction. Therefore, even by those who follow the *Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa*, the *piṇḍopasthāna* must be performed while looking at the houses.

Āpastamba states the application of these two mantras for the *upasthāna*: "With the mantras, 'O Fathers, give us houses' and 'May we dwell with you, O Fathers,' he performs the *upasthāna* to the Fathers."
In this case as well, since there is no contradiction, one should understand that the attendance [upon the teacher] is to be combined with both [the provision of] a house and alms-food.
Regarding the application of collyrium and ointment, however, the *Vāyupurāṇa* states:
"One should provide collyrium and ointment, as well as the fastening of the sacred thread."
Furthermore, by means of these rebirths in Kāśī, one shall obtain the fruit of the horse sacrifice (aśvamedha). Thus it is said.

The mention of *kāśa* grasses is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*) for *kuśa* and other such materials. Therefore, from among the prescribed *darbha* grasses or purifying blades of grass, one should perform the application of collyrium (*añjana*) and the rubbing with oil (*abhyañjana*) using whichever is most excellent or whichever is available. Here, by the word *añjana*, any well-known black substance suitable for the adornment of the eyes is intended. *Abhyañjana* refers to an oily substance. The two actions accomplished by these two substances are expressed by the terms *añjana* and *abhyañjana*. Certain specific details required here are shown in the *Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa*.
Having taken three blades of *darbha* grass according to the prescribed rule,
one should offer the finest collyrium to the ancestors with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*apasavya*).
Having pronounced the names of the ancestors, one should offer thread for the sake of clothing; then,
holding a single purificatory blade (pavitra) in the hand, one should offer oil and beneficial ointment for the ancestral cakes (piṇḍas), each time reciting the mantra once for each ancestor.

In this regard, there is one specific rule: that on each individual *piṇḍa*, the ointment (*añjana*) is applied with three blades of *darbha* grass. Another rule is that [the rite] is performed with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*apasavya*). "The best" (*uttama*) means the most excellent; the meaning is that he gives the *traikakuda* (sulfur from Mount Trikakud). Regarding the phrase "having uttered the names," what is intended is the utterance of the names together with the lineage (*gotra*) and the relationship. "A single purifier" (*ekaṃ pavitram*) refers to a purifier with a single tuft; having taken that in his hand, the oil-ointment (*abhyañjana*) is offered once upon each *piṇḍa* for the ancestors using that purifier and the mantra well-known from the *Kalpasūtras* and other texts, whereby it becomes "beneficial" (*hitam*), i.e., conducive to welfare. The ointment (*añjana*) must likewise be performed with the mantra alone. The expression "once each" (*sakṛt sakṛt*) is an option to be chosen in contrast to the "three times each" (*tris tris*) that will be shown later, or it may be followed according to one's own specific *śākhā*.

In this regard, while the specific quality of being derived from the *tri-kakud* mountain is explicitly stated for the collyrium (*añjana*), the Brahma Purāṇa also shows a further specific quality regarding the oil for anointing (*abhyañjana*), namely that it is oil from black sesame seeds carefully preserved with effort:
"They say that collyrium from the *tri-kakud* is always the best;
and [the oil] should be oil from black sesame seeds, diligently well-protected."

"Trikakuda" refers to that which originates from Mount Trikakut, widely known in the world by the term *nīlāñjana*. Sages say that this is the best for application as a paste (*piṇḍopacāra*). From the statement "they say it is the best," it is understood that if it is unavailable, the use of collyrium (*kajjala*) is permitted. Regarding this, Āśvalāyana states the specific order and the mantra for the application of collyrium and ointment:
"With the words, 'O [Name], anoint yourself! O [Name], anoint yourself! one should give the ointment and collyrium upon the funeral cakes (*piṇḍas*), and then give the garment."

Viṣṇu also says: "Then he should offer ointment [with the words], 'O So-and-so, anoint yourself,' and collyrium [with the words], 'O So-and-so, apply collyrium. Here, "then" means immediately after the washing (*avanejana*). He should offer ointment upon each *piṇḍa* with the formula, "O So-and-so, anoint yourself. By the term "So-and-so," it is intended that the names of the ancestors, such as the father, together with their gotra and relationship, are to be uttered in the vocative case. He should offer collyrium upon each *piṇḍa* with the mantra, "O So-and-so, apply collyrium."

Gobhila, however, the author of the *Rāṇāyanīyasūtra*, following the very sequence stated in the *Vāyupurāṇa*, mentions another mantra: "Having taken a blade of *darbha* grass with the left hand alone, moving counter-clockwise (*apasalavi*), one should place it upon the rice-ball (*piṇḍa*) in the eastern furrow, uttering the father’s name: ‘O [Name], this collyrium is for you, and for those who follow you here, and for whom you follow; to him, *svadhā*! Having touched water, one does exactly the same for the other two [ancestors]. Likewise with oil, and likewise with fragrant substances such as perfumes and garlands.
“*Darbha*-grass blade” (*darbhapiñjūlī*) refers to one smeared with collyrium. “Fragrant” (*surabhi*) refers to scents, garlands, and so forth.
In the *Maitrāyaṇīya Piṇḍapitṛyajña* as well, another mantra accompanied by this same sequence is shown:
"He places a collyrium-impregnated stick for each ball, saying, 'Anoint yourself, O so-and-so! with the collyrium; 'Anoint yourself, O so-and-so! with the ointment.
‘Śalākāḥ’ refers to the tips of *darbha* grass.
It is also stated in the *Mānava-maitrāyaṇīya-sūtra*:
“Saying ‘Anoint this one,’ one should wipe away the smear of collyrium from each lump; saying ‘Anoint this one,’ [one does so] with the collyrium.”

Āpastamba: "He offers collyrium and ointment, and a garment, three times for each *piṇḍa*, saying: 'Anoint yourself, O [Name]! 'Anoint yourself, O grandfather [Name]! 'Anoint yourself, O great-grandfather [Name]! Thus for the collyrium; likewise for the ointment, he modifies the mantra to 'Anoint yourself. If he does not know their names, he modifies the mantra for the collyrium to: 'May my fathers anoint themselves; may my grandfathers anoint themselves; may my great-grandfathers anoint themselves,' and likewise for the ointment, 'May they anoint themselves. "He should offer three times for each *piṇḍa*."

‘*Anupiṇḍam*’ means on each individual *piṇḍa*; ‘*tris*’ means three times. One should offer the collyrium (*añjana*) and other items. Having pronounced the names of the father and others in the vocative case by saying ‘*asau*’, if the performer of the *śrāddha* does not know the names of the father and others, then he should offer the collyrium using the formula: “May my father be anointed,” and so forth. In the same way for the ointment (*abhyañjana*). By the word ‘*evam*’ (thus), it is stated that there is an adaptation (*ūha*) of the mantra used for the collyrium; this is called ‘*sannamana*’, which means modification. Regarding the instruction “he sprinkles water with ‘*ūrjam*’,” the mantra is enjoined by citing the opening words ‘*ūrjam*’. That mantra is: “Carrying strength (*ūrj*), nectar (*amṛta*), clarified butter (*ghṛta*), milk (*payas*), sweet juice (*kīlāla*), and flowing liquor (*parisrut*), you are the *svadhā* offerings; satisfy my ancestors. With this mantra, the sprinkling of water mixed with sesame seeds should be performed at the base of the *piṇḍas*. A commentary on this has been made by Hariharācārya. Here, by implication, the word ‘*āpaḥ*’ (O waters) is supplied: “O waters, you are *svadhā*, you become the sacrificial oblation for the ancestors; therefore, satisfy my ancestors. What do you do?
