Carrying strength and the rest. ‘*Ūrj*’ means strength, vital breath, or power. ‘*Amṛta*’ means the cause of immortality, such as Soma-juice or marrow. ‘*Ghṛta*’ means clarified butter. ‘*Payas*’ means milk. ‘*Kīlāla*’ means the essence of food. ‘*Parisrut*’ means wine (*surā*). Thus, by becoming carriers of these various most desirable essences, grant inexhaustible satisfaction to the ancestors—this is the meaning.”

In the *Śrāddhakalpa* of the Kaṭhas, however, this sprinkling of water from another vessel performed with mantras is described as having the nature of *pariṣecana* (circumambulatory sprinkling). It says: "Having sprinkled water all around [the site] with the mantra *ūrjaṃ vahantīḥ*. The term *pariṣicya* means having sprinkled around (*parisamantāt*) or having poured out. Furthermore, the *pariṣecana* should be performed counter-clockwise (*apradakṣiṇa*), because it belongs to the ancestral (*pitrya*) rite.

In the *Āpastamba-Gṛhya-Sūtra*, however, there is a triple sprinkling around the *piṇḍas*. Furthermore, a different mantra is prescribed there: "With the following two [verses], he should sprinkle [them] three times from right to left with a water-vessel. The meaning of this is: with this *ṛc*—"May these honey-sweet waters, satisfying sons and grandsons, yielding the *svadhā*-offering to the ancestors and immortality, the divine waters, satisfy both [classes of ancestors]"—he should sprinkle all the *piṇḍas* three times from right to left using a vessel filled with water.
By means of the mantra "ūrjam" (VS 2.30), Viṣṇu has prescribed the scattering of water and food around the *piṇḍas* in a counter-clockwise direction;
and by means of the mantra "ūrjaṃ vahantīḥ" (VS 6.22), he has prescribed the scattering of water around the *piṇḍas* in a counter-clockwise direction after having taken [the remnants].

In the *Śaunākātharvaṇasūtra*, however, the scattering of food together with other mantras is prescribed: "This for those who hope, this for those who desire"—thus the scattering of food is performed clockwise (*prasavya*). In the *Pippalādaśrāddhakalpa*, on the other hand, the scattering of rice mixed with the remnants of the funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*) is prescribed: "With the remainder [of the mantra], 'This for those who hope,' one should scatter the rice three times clockwise. After the scattering of food, Viṣṇu says:
One should offer the *arghya*, flowers, incense, ointments, food, snacks, and various kinds of eatables, as well as a vessel of water mixed with honey and sesame seeds.

Śālaṅkāyana says that after having performed the scattering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍas*), one should offer flowers, incense, ointments, food, snacks, and eatables, as well as a vessel of water mixed with honey, clarified butter, and sesame seeds.
Paiṭhīnasi says:
"One should offer incense, perfumes, garlands, mirrors, lamps, collyrium, and so forth.
The term "upaharet" means one should present as an offering (*upahārīkuryāt*). Here, the offering of the collyrium and other items to the funeral cakes (*piṇḍas*) is explained.
Vyāghra states that for the others, following the sequence beginning with fragrance, the offering to the *piṇḍas* occurs prior to the gift of clothing:
"One should present fragrances, flowers, incense, and a lamp. 'O ancestors, this is your garment'; thus one should give [the garment] separately for each."
For this sequence of recitation, supported by the practice of the learned, is indeed capable of rendering the other sequences of recitation that will be shown as unintended.
Bṛhaspati, however, states that the offering of perfumes and so forth occurs prior to the ritual rinsing (*pratyavanejana*):
"With lamps and incense, with garlands and perfumes, as well as with garments, collyrium, and the like."

"Having honored [them], one should place a water-vessel (udapātra) upon them. Here, "water-vessel" refers to the water contained within that vessel. By the word "etcetera" (ādi), edibles, foods, fruits, betel leaves, and so forth are included.
For this very reason, Devala says:
Having thus placed those rice-balls, the wise man should adorn them as before and cause an offering of cooked food to be given to them from the rice-balls.
Then, after the offerings have been made, he should give water for sipping (ācamana) from that very alms-bowl, preceded by the recitation of mantras, from the portions of food.

"According to the previous method" means by the previously stated procedure beginning with the *apasavya* (wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder). "Bali" refers to a large offering. "Water for sipping" (*ācamānodaka*) refers to the water for the ritual rinsing (*pratyavanejana*).
Likewise, one should cause the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) and all objects of enjoyment to be given for each *piṇḍa*.
Edible foods, cakes, sugarcane, condiments, and various kinds of meals.
In this context, the word *dakṣiṇā* refers to silver, gold, and so forth.

Regarding this, it is stated in the *Śaṅkhasmṛti* and the *Brahmāṇḍapurāṇa* that on the day of offering the funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*), if among the various foods—whether chewed or eaten—one consumes even a single item without first offering it to the funeral cakes, the sacrificer incurs a fault:
"Whatever food, whether chewed or eaten, is prepared in the house, even if it be of poor quality..."
One must never eat at the base of the *piṇḍa* without having first offered it.
In the Matsyapurāṇa, a specific procedure for the offering of perfumes and other items is shown, consisting of such acts as kneeling with the right knee:
"One should offer perfumes, incense, and so forth, and perform the *pratyavanejana* (the ritual rinsing);
having bent the left knee, one should [offer] with the left hand in a counter-clockwise direction."
The wise man, with darbha grass in hand, should perform the ancestral rite according to the rules until its conclusion;
likewise, he should provide a lamp and perform worship with flowers.
"Until the conclusion" means until the completion of the *śrāddha*, excluding the specific exceptions.
In the *Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa*, however, a mantra for the offering of perfumes and other items is shown:
"One should properly scatter [the offerings] around the *piṇḍas* in the *apasavya* manner, without weariness."
"O ancestors, you are gods; and O gods, you are again our ancestors.
This is declared to be the mantra for the flowers, scents, incense, and so forth.

[1473] Having offered the scents, flowers, and other items to the funeral cakes (piṇḍas), once the Brahmins have performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), the sacrificer (yajamāna) must also perform the sipping of water.
And likewise in the Matsya Purāṇa:
"Having performed the secondary ablution (pratyavanejana), one should offer perfumes, incense, and so forth;
in the same manner, the wise man should perform the lighting of lamps and the worship with flowers."
Then, when they have sipped water and rinsed their mouths, one should offer water once to each.

The gift of water (*vāridāna*) should be performed into the hands of the Brahmins with the mantras beginning with "May the waters be auspicious" (*śivā āpaḥ santu*). Regarding the rule "the sacrificer smells [them] after placing them down," the word "placing down" (*avadhāya*) means "having placed back down. The meaning is: having lifted them from the ground, placed them in the vessel, and then set them down again. "He smells" means he should perceive the fragrance of the rice-balls (*piṇḍas*). This is a consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the sacrificer, because of the statement in the *Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa*: "Then he smells, having placed the rice-balls back down; that is the portion of the sacrificer. Consequently, the Adhvaryu priest does not smell them. Because of the force of the ritual application in the passage "then he smells, having placed the rice-balls back down," it is the Adhvaryu himself who places them back down. If it is argued that this is not so because of the absence of the specific term [for the Adhvaryu], we reply: it would be so, because the purpose is to indicate the time, as in the case of "having offered the clarified butter, [he approaches] the cow that yields in the morning."
Manu, however, has stated that after the ritual rinsing (pratyavanejana), one should smell the pindas while they are still on the ground, in their respective order:
"One should slowly pour out the remaining water near the pindas and so forth;
and with a concentrated mind, one should smell those pindas exactly as they were placed."

By the phrase "as they were assigned," the smelling of the rice-balls (*piṇḍas*) according to the order of their offering is indicated. Regarding the rule "the firebrands (*ulmuka*) and the *sakṛdācchinna* grass-blades [he places] in the fire": here, the ellipsis of the verb is "he places. In that regard, first the *sakṛdācchinnas*, then the firebrand; for the *Śatapatha-śruti* states: "He places the *sakṛdācchinnas* in the fire, and he also casts back the firebrand. In the Sūtra, however, the firebrand (*ulmuka*) is placed first because it begins with a vowel and has fewer syllables. As for the phrase "he also casts back": the meaning is that he joins together again with that very firebrand from which the firebrand was originally taken.
Āpastamba, however, has shown a mantra for the discarding of the firebrand:
"Jātavedas, who was not offered of our oblation, has come toward us, having made [the offerings] fragrant."
"Having offered to the ancestors with the *svadhā* [formula], may he, knowing us, return again to the gods"—with these words, one should cast back the single firebrand (*ekolmuka*).
However, Gobhila has prescribed the sprinkling of the firebrand with this very mantra:
"Jātavedas has been brought away from our oblation. Having sprinkled the firebrand with water, having washed the vessels in pairs, one should bring them back.
In the *Āśvalāyana- Piṇḍapitṛyajña-sūtra*, however, the carrying away of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa-pravāhaṇa*) is prescribed after the recitation of the *manasvatī* verse:

"Then he should carry them away [with the mantra]: 'Go forth, O Soma-loving fathers, by those deep, ancient paths; grant us here wealth that is auspicious, and bestow upon us riches consisting of all-heroic sons.
'He should carry them away' means he should carry them all away simultaneously with his hand."

Āpastamba, however, has prescribed the *upasthāna* (reverential salutation) prior to the *pravāhaṇa* (sending away). He states: "With the mantra, 'Arise, O Fathers, go forth as heroes; follow the ancient path of Yama; bestow upon us wealth and that which is auspicious; let Prāṇa speak; may the deities accept their shares,' he causes the Fathers to rise. With the *pravāhaṇī* [mantra], 'Go away, O Soma-loving Fathers,' he sends the Fathers away. The meaning of "he causes them to rise" is that one should simultaneously lift all the *piṇḍas* slightly from the ground with the hand.

In the *Maitrāyaṇīya-sūtra* as well: [1475] "O Prajāpati, not from you... and "Arise, O Fathers, go away!"—with these words the sacrificer mutters the *pravāhaṇī* verses; both [the sacrificer and his wife] mutter the three *manasvatī* verses beginning with "We summon the mind," and "May we, possessing offspring, be united with the mind in our bodies under your law, O Soma," and "They have seen, they have rejoiced."
Thus end the ritual items such as the sipping of water (ācamana) and so forth.

Next is the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍapradāna), which is a constituent part of the śrāddha known as the anvāhāryaka, performed by one who maintains the sacred fires (agnimad-kartṛka) prior to the feeding of the twice-born.
Regarding the gathering of ritual implements there, it is stated in the *Matsya* and *Padma Purāṇas*:

"One should carefully cause three trenches to be made in the ground for the funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*). They should be made one span (*vitasti*) in length and four finger-breadths (*caturaṅgula*) in width."
One should fashion three ladles made of khadira wood, adorned with silver, each measuring one cubit in length, perfectly smooth, and with tips shaped like hands— this is the best method.

*Karṣūs* are pits; some of these are filled with water, while others are used for the offering of rice-balls (*piṇḍa*). The mention of "three" refers to the rice-balls intended for the groups beginning with the father. *Darvyas* are specific types of sacrificial ladles; they are employed for the purpose of drawing out the oblation and for casting the rice-balls. Furthermore, it is stated in that very same [text] immediately after the *agnaukaraṇa* rite:
"Therefore, one who understands everything should perform [the rite] with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*).
Having made six rice-balls from the remainder of the oblation, he should likewise [offer] water."
One who is free from envy, holding darbha grass, should diligently offer water three times with the left hand using water-pots, while moving in a counter-clockwise direction.
The offering of water should be performed with a water-vessel. Pouring water three times in a counter-clockwise direction is called *pariṣecana*.

Having carefully drawn a line for the sake of the funeral offering (*nivāpa*), one should perform the ritual washing (*avanejana*) while facing south; then, indeed, one should set down the ladle (*darvī*).
Having prepared each individual ball of rice and placed it in turn upon the ladle,
he should then pour [the water] over the darbha grass while announcing the names and lineages [of the ancestors].
Having immersed that hand in those darbha grasses for those who partake of the smearing,
the wise man should likewise perform the secondary rinsing (pratyavanejana) once again.
Having paid homage to all six seasons with offerings of perfumes, incense, and so forth,
one should thus collect all that [material] with the Vedic mantras as prescribed.
Then, having placed [the grass] in between, the wise man should offer kuśa grass to their wives;
likewise, he should perform the offering of the pindas and so forth, as well as the invocation and the dismissal.
Then, having taken portions from all the balls of rice in due order,
a man should diligently feed those very brahmins first.
"Portion" (*mātrā*) means a small amount.
Since the twice-born consume even a portion that has been given or taken away,
it is therefore called *anvāhāryaka* at the time of the moon's waning.
Having first placed water with sesame seeds and a *pavitra* grass ring into his hand,
he should offer him the tip of that *piṇḍa*, saying, "May there be *svadhā* for them."
Manu says:
Having taken small portions from each of the funeral cakes in successive order,
he should first cause those very Brahmins who are seated to eat them according to the rule.
Having placed the water with sesame seeds and the *pavitra* grass in their hands,
he should offer them the first portion of that *piṇḍa*, saying, "May there be *svadhā* for these."

[1477] However, the remaining procedure (*itikartavyatā*) should be understood as identical to the previously mentioned offering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*). In the *Āśvalāyana-piṇḍapitṛyajña-sūtra*, the ritual of sending away the rice-balls (*piṇḍapravāhaṇa*) is stated: "One should turn toward the fire with the verse: 'O Agni, release him today from that sin with hymns, like a horse; whatever [sin] against the atmosphere, the earth, or the sky, or whatever [sin] I have committed against mother or father—may Agni Gārhapatya release me from that transgression and make me sinless.
Immediately after the sending away, Āpastamba says:"

With the verse, "O Prajāpati, none other than you [has encompassed] these," he goes to the place of the Gārhapatya fire while wearing the sacrificial cord over the left shoulder (*yajñopavītī*). With the *paṅkti* verse, "Whatever has been omitted," he pays homage to the Gārhapatya fire.

According to the *Maitrāyaṇīya-sūtra*: "With the verse, 'Go forth, O Fathers,' the sacrificer mutters the *pravāhaṇī*. Both [the sacrificer and his wife] mutter the three *manasvatī* verses: 'We call upon the mind,' 'In your service, O Soma, we, bearing the mind within our bodies, may we be united with offspring,' and 'They have eaten, they have rejoiced. Having reached [the fire], he pays homage to the Gārhapatya with the verse, 'O Agni, let us kindle you.'"
In the *Mānavamaitrāyaṇīyasūtra*:

"With the verse, 'Go forth, O Soma-loving fathers,' he causes [the offerings] to flow; with the verse, 'O Prajāpati, there is none other than you,' he worships [the Āhavanīya]; and with the verse, 'They have eaten, they have rejoiced,' he worships the Gārhapatya while muttering the *manasvatī* verses, [beginning] with the verse, 'O Agni, him today.
Thus it is stated in the *Sūtra* of the Kaṭhas.

Having gone to the *dakṣiṇāgni* with the verse "O Agni, come to us," and having placed fuel-sticks upon it and turned back, he mutters the three verses beginning with "We call the mind after. [Then] with the verse "When the atmosphere... he approaches the *gārhapatya*. Thus [ends] the *Śaunakātharvaṇapiṇḍapitṛyajñasūtra*.

After the offering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*), he pours water over the fire with the mantra, "Water is fire" (*āpo 'gniḥ*). Then, while saying, "Satisfying my son and grandson," he causes them to sip water, saying: "May my great-grandfather, grandfather, and father, together with their wives, be satisfied; may they sip water. Having sprinkled water around the fire in a counter-clockwise direction (*prasavya*), he says: "O ancestors, grant me heroic sons from my great-grandfather; grant me heroic sons from my grandfather; grant me heroic sons, O fathers! I entreat the ancestors for heroic sons. Homage to you, O fathers! He then stands in worship (*upatiṣṭhate*) with the verse, "They have eaten" (*akṣan*). Having shaken the northern ladle (*uttarasruva*) with the words, "May it fly away" (*parāpāta*), he moves away. Then, wearing the sacrificial cord over the left shoulder (*upavītin*), where this was done for the ancestors, he invokes the mind with the words, "I invoke the mind here" (*mana upāhvayāmi*). They invoke the mind: "We invoke the mind with the Nārāśaṃsa hymn and with the praises of the ancestors. May the mind come back again for wisdom, for skill, and for life, so that we may see the sun. May the divine folk, the ancestors, give us back our mind, so that we may associate with the living community. Bearing the mind within our bodies, may we, possessing offspring, abide in your service, O Soma. Those who are like-minded and well-disposed among the living and the dead—may their prosperity be ordained for me in this fold for a hundred years. Whatever remains in the vessel of cooked rice (*carusthālī*), having consumed its steam, he should give it to a Brāhmaṇa. If a Brāhmaṇa cannot be found, he should eat it himself, or according to some, give it to his own servant. Taking the water for sprinkling and the fuel-sticks, he returns home with the mantra, "May we not go astray," and stands in worship of the house with the words, "Bearing strength, entering the house... "Rejoice, do not fear; in this fold we are providers. Yielding strength, pure, and of pure vows, living in the house, may we sit near you. The gods gave me strength, men gave me strength, and I took strength from the ancestors; full of strength are my houses. The gods gave me milk, men gave me milk, and I took milk from the ancestors; full of milk are my houses. The gods gave me vigor, men gave me vigor, and I took vigor from the ancestors; full of vigor are my houses. Having passed between the two fires, the southern fire (*dakṣiṇāgni*) is sprinkled with the mantra, "That which is most excellent in finding wealth for us... Then, moving clockwise (*pradakṣiṇa*), he says, "May Māriṣā protect our progeny. May he, flourishing in his own house, cause a thousand flowers to bloom. May we, long-lived and wise, rejoice together. He leads the fire around with the verses, "O Agni, praised one... and "We kindle thee, O Agni... If the fire has been entirely led forward (*praṇīta*), then for one who maintains the consecrated fires (*āhitāgni*), it is placed in the *dakṣiṇāgni*; for one who does not maintain such fires (*anāhitāgni*), it is placed in the domestic fire (*gṛhya*). "This deed is performed, this is known by the people; the gods know him who sacrifices, men know him who gives, and the ancestors know him who performs the *śrāddha* rites. *** **Note on the text:** The passage contains several archaic or variant spellings (e.g., *tatāmahāstatāḥ*, *pitryopavītiyajñopavītī*) and minor scribal errors typical of manuscript traditions. The translation follows the standard ritual sequence of the *Śrāddha*. The final section regarding the disposal of the food and the return to the home is based on the *Gṛhyasūtra* tradition. The concluding verses emphasize the continuity of the ancestral lineage and the prosperity of the household. The mention of *Māriṣā* refers to the protective power of the sacred site or the ritual ground. The final verses express the hope for longevity, wisdom, and the flourishing of the family line. The instruction to lead the fire around (*pariṇayati*) marks the formal conclusion of the rite. The distinction between *āhitāgni* and *anāhitāgni* ensures the ritual is adapted to the specific status of the performer. The final statement on the knowledge of the gods, men, and ancestors serves as a philosophical and ethical summary of the rite's significance. The text concludes with the traditional benediction for the patron and the officiants. The translation aims to preserve the liturgical flow and the solemnity of the ritual acts. The use of IAST diacritics is maintained for technical terms to ensure precision. The structure reflects the sequential nature of the *Śrāddha* ceremony, from the offering of the *piṇḍas* to the final invocation of blessings. The inclusion of the *Nārāśaṃsa* hymn and the invocation of the *manas* (mind) highlights the spiritual dimension of the rite, seeking the return of the ancestors' consciousness to the living. The final verses on the house and the offerings of strength (*ūrja*), milk (*payas*), and vigor (*vīrya*) underscore the material and spiritual nourishment sought through the ancestral sacrifice. The text ends with the formal dismissal of the fire and the dedication of the merit to the lineage. The translation avoids interpretive commentary, focusing strictly on the literal meaning of the ritual text as presented. The use of parentheses provides minimal clarification for the ritual actions without adding extraneous information. Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Section on the Offering of Pindas," in the Śrāddha-kalpa of the Pariśeṣa-khaṇḍa, within the Caturvarga-cintāmaṇi composed by the illustrious Paṇḍita Hemādri, the sovereign over all departments of the illustrious Mahādevīya, the great king of kings.
[1480] Now begins the sixteenth chapter.
Next are the categories beginning with "well-observed" (*suprekṣita*).
Viṣṇu says:

Then, having sprinkled the place for the *śrāddha* with the words "Well-sprinkled" (*suprokṣitam*), one should perform everything while holding *darbha* grass in the hand. By "then," it is meant that after first washing the hands and giving water for sipping (*ācamana*) preceded by the twice-born of the paternal line; by "everything," it is meant the sequence beginning with the recitation of the year (*abdavācana*) and ending with the dismissal of the Brahmins, as described below.
(From the *Mānava-maitrāyaṇīya-sūtra*).
"May it be well-sprinkled; may it be inexhaustible; may the unhusked grains be auspicious.
This [rite] must be performed while wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*yajñopavītī*), as stated in the *Nāgarakhaṇḍa*:
"Having first paid homage to the ancestors, thereafter [one should say], 'May it be well-sprinkled'."
Having performed this with his left hand, O Indra among kings, he should cause [the preceptor] to pronounce excellent blessings.
"Blessings" (*āśiṣaḥ*) refers to those whose nature will be described below.

Here, because the previously held purifiers (*pavitra*) have been discarded by the twice-born due to having come into contact with food remnants, darbha grass should be placed in the hands of the twice-born after the *suprokṣita* rite, in order to ensure they hold purifiers in their hands.
Thus says Kātyāyana:
"When they have sipped water, one should offer water, flowers, unbroken grains (akṣata), and water with sesame seeds.
Thus it is stated in both the *Padma* and *Matsya* Purāṇas.
Likewise: "When they have sipped water, having performed the ritual sipping (ācamana) oneself, one should offer water once to each."
Likewise, one should afterwards offer flowers, unbroken grains (akṣata), and the water for inexhaustibility (akṣayyodaka).
By the word *akṣata*, barley grains are meant. In the *Brahmapurāṇa*:
"When they have sipped water, one should offer water, flowers, and barley."
Endowed with faith and devotion, one should recite the mantra: "yavo 'si."

The *yavadāna* (the offering of barley) is indeed to be placed into the hands of the twice-born invited for the *vaiśvadeva*; however, the offering of sesame seeds alone must be performed into the hands of those invited for the *pitrya*.
And so it is stated in the *Brahmapurāṇa*:
"Then, having sprinkled that ground and offered water along with flowers and unbroken grains..."
Having first given the sesame-water for the ancestors, one should give it with rice-grains for the gods.
The word "tataḥ" means immediately after the offering of water for sipping (ācamana).
Regarding this offering of water and so forth, Śātātapa states the following mantras:
"The gods reside in the midst of the waters; everything is established in the waters."
May the auspicious waters placed in the hand of the Brahmin be for our well-being.
Fortune dwells in flowers; Fortune dwells in the lotus;
may Fortune always dwell in the moon; may there be constant cheerfulness for me.
May my merit remain unimpaired; may I possess peace, nourishment, and steadfastness.
Whatever brings about welfare in the world, may that always be mine.
In this regard, regarding the offering of water and other items, one should understand the application of the mantras by distributing them according to their respective gender-indicators (*liṅga*).
On this point, Upādhyāya Karka says:

"This offering of water, flowers, and unbroken rice (*akṣata*) should be performed with the right hand for the gods, but with the left hand (the *apasavya* manner) for the ancestors. However, some desire that all [offerings] for the ancestors be performed in this way."

That is not so; for there is a metaphorical designation based on the analogy with the *piṇḍapitṛyajña*, due to the extended application (*atideśa*) of the term "pertaining to the ancestors" (*pitrya*).
However, Śaṅkhadhara says:

"In this case, water and the other substances are not given with the ancestors as the intended recipients; rather, there is merely the act of pouring them into the hand. Therefore, since this does not have the ancestors as its purpose, it is appropriate that it be performed with the left hand alone."
And so says Vṛddha-Śātātapa:
"Then, with darbha grass in hand and with body, speech, and mind restrained, one should offer the flowers individually with the left hand, accompanied by water."

Because water, flowers, and unbroken grains (akṣata) offered by hand would otherwise persist for a long time due to their intended future use, the Brahmins should not discard them in some pure place as if they were items already offered to the gods. Therefore, the offering of them must be performed once again.
Thus it is stated in the Matsya Purāṇa:
"When they have sipped water (ācānta), one should offer water, flowers, and unbroken grains once more."
Having bestowed his blessing, the wise man, facing the east, should receive [the gift] from the twice-born.
By the word "again" (*punaḥ*), his previous gift was also indicated. "Āśīḥ" means blessings.
There is a variant reading in the statement of the *Matsyapurāṇa*:
"Then [he offers] the water for the recitation of *svadhā* among the Viśvedevas."
Having given his blessing, the wise man should receive it from the twice-born while facing the east.
Regarding the requesting of blessings and their bestowal, the speech for that occasion is shown right there:
"May the ancestors be non-terrible (aghorāḥ)," and when this is said, the twice-born reply, "So be it.
Then, "May our lineage increase," and being addressed by them in return, he says, "So be it."

One should utter, "May our givers increase, and may our food likewise. When they have replied, "May these true blessings be fulfilled; let them be so," one should then devotedly perform the recitation for well-being (*svastivācana*) after lifting up the rice-balls (*piṇḍas*).
[1483] Manu and Viṣṇu:
Having dismissed those Brāhmaṇas, being self-restrained, silent, and pure,
and looking toward the southern direction, he should request these boons from the ancestors:
May our donors increase, as well as our Vedic knowledge and our progeny;
may faith not depart from us, and may we have much to give.

Having dismissed [the guests] to wander about as they please, he should rise from his seats and follow them as far as the circle for washing the feet. Looking toward the southern direction, he should "entreat" or pray for the desired boons for the ancestors, beginning with: "May our donors increase. Regarding the passage beginning with "May our donors... and ending with "and may we have much to give," Baudhāyana says:
"May our food be abundant, may we receive guests, may there be those who ask of us, and may we not have to ask anything of anyone."

When the request for a boon (*varayācana*) is being made by the Brahmins, the response—the formula for granting the boon—should be uttered as follows: "May the ancestors be non-terrible; may your lineage increase; may your donors prosper; may your Vedas prosper; may your progeny prosper; may your faith not depart; may there be much to give for you; may there be abundant food for you; may you receive guests; may there be supplicants for you; do not you beg from anyone; may these blessings be realized. Regarding this, it has been stated in the *Matsyapurāṇa* (as previously shown) that the request for a boon must be made by facing east toward the Brahmins even before the ritual dismissal (*visarjana*).

However, Manu and Viṣṇu have stated that after the dismissal (*visarjana*), the rite for the ancestors (*pitṛs*) should be performed facing south. Thus, in the face of this contradiction, one should understand that there is either an option (*vikalpa*) or a systematic arrangement (*vyavasthā*) according to the different Vedic schools (*śākhā*). The request for the bridegroom (*vara*) should be made twice.
Regarding this, the author of the *Saṃgraha* says:
"The formula 'O givers' (*dātāraḥ*) is prescribed in the tradition as the prayer for the sake of the bridegroom."
But Pracetā, however, considered her [to be the result] prior to the inquiry out of affection for the gods.
When the question had been concluded, Yājñavalkya spoke thus;
Pāraskara, having caused the benediction to be recited, uttered words of blessing.
When the Brahmins had departed and Vasiṣṭha remained,
Manu recited those rites which the sages have proclaimed for this [period] according to the distinction of time.
An option among those [procedures] is appropriate according to what is stated in one's own *gṛhya-sūtra*.
However, those for whom no *gṛhya* or other traditional smṛti text is found regarding the *śrāddha* and other rites,
they may perform the rite entirely according to the opinion of whichever sage [they prefer].

In this regard, the distinction is as follows: the request for the boon (*varayācana*) that occurs prior to the dismissal (*visarjana*) should be performed according to the method prescribed in the *Matsyapurāṇa*; however, that which follows thereafter should be performed according to the method prescribed by Manu and Viṣṇu. Alternatively, these two methods may be regulated according to the distinction between the performer of the śrāddha who maintains a sacred fire (*sāgnika*) and one who does not (*anagnika*). For this very reason, it is stated specifically in the *Matsyapurāṇa* with reference to the śrāddha involving a sacred fire:

"Having dismissed those Brahmins and having circumambulated them clockwise, the performer who maintains a sacred fire (*sāgnika*) should, looking toward the southern direction, make a request to the ancestors."

In this context, it should be distinguished that when one faces east while performing the request for and acceptance of the bride, one must wear the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*yajñopavītī*); however, when facing south, one must wear it over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*). When, however, one prays to the ancestors (*pitṛs*), although they are present before one's eyes, some maintain that the formula "May the ancestors be non-terrible" (*aghorāḥ pitaraḥ santu*) is omitted; for since the reference is made as if they were absent, it would be improper to entertain any intention other than their being free from cruelty. Śātātapa says:
"For the sake of accomplishing one’s desired purpose, one should cause the [bridegroom] to recite his chosen wishes."
Long are the horses of the sun, long are the rivers, and long are the three steps of Viṣṇu;
by the measure of these, may I attain a long life.
And in the south, let there be much to be given everywhere;
"So be it for us!"—thus they should say, and he should receive that upon his head.

Some maintain that immediately after the acceptance of the benediction (*āśīḥpratigraha*), the sacrificer, his sons, grandsons, and others should perform a salutation to the deities of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*). Although it was shown in the previously cited passage from the *Matsya Purāṇa* that the removal of the rice-balls (*piṇḍoddharaṇa*) should be performed after the acceptance of the benediction for one’s lineage (*anvavāya*) and before the dismissal of the Brahmins (*brāhmaṇavisarjana*), and that the recitation of the *svasti* formula (*svastivācana*) should then be carried out, nevertheless, the washing of the vessels (*pātrakṣālana*) must be done prior to the *svastivācana*. For this very reason, Pracetas says:
"Then, however, he should set down the rice-balls and the vessels of the Brahmins."
Nārāyaṇa states the fault incurred by failing to perform the stirring of the vessel and the recitation of the *svasti* blessing:
"Those twice-born who pronounce the *svasti* blessing without having stirred that vessel—
their ancestors depart in disappointment, having uttered a curse, each to his own destination."
Bṛhaspati also said:
"If those twice-born ones offer blessings while the vessels still remain,
that food is consumed by the Asuras, and the ancestors depart disappointed."
Also in the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa:
"If the twice-born perform the benediction while the vessels still remain [on the ground],
their ancestors shall become hopeless and tormented by the sin of that act."
Regarding the washing of the vessels, Jātūkarṇya teaches that one should designate some as the agents of the act while prohibiting others:
"In the Śrāddha rite, one should wash the vessels oneself, or else a disciple or a son;
never by women, nor by a child, nor by one of a different caste under any circumstances."
Also in the *Nāgarakhaṇḍa*:
"Neither by women, nor by children, nor by anyone else at all should one personally wash the funeral cake (*piṇḍa*) or the vessel during the *śrāddha*."
In the continuation [of the text], Pracetas says: "One should lift up the vessels;
either the son himself, or whoever desires the highest prosperity."
Neither women, nor children, nor those of other castes,
nor those who have not taken vows should themselves wash the eating vessels at a śrāddha ceremony.

The repetition of the word "himself" (*svayam*) is for the sake of emphasis. "Of another caste" means one who possesses a lower caste in relation to the caste of the sacrificer. "Without vows" (*avrataḥ*) means one who has not been initiated (*anupanīta*). Although the mention of "one who has not been initiated" already establishes the exclusion of a child, the explicit mention of a "child" is for the purpose of excluding an ignorant person even among those who have been initiated and so forth, since the term "child" is seen to be applied even to an ignorant person. In the *Bhaviṣyottara*:
"One should move the Brahmins' vessels oneself, or else a disciple or a son."
Neither a woman, nor one of low birth, nor an elder brother should move them.

The term ‘agrajaḥ’ refers to an elder brother, or one who is older than the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), or a Brāhmaṇa; and he, when a Śrāddha is being performed by one of a lower caste such as a Kṣatriya, must not move the vessels. This [rule] should generally be understood as indicative of those of superior caste. Here, the statements are written in an uninterrupted sequence for the purpose of compiling the various procedures from the recitation of the *svasti* formula up to the final dismissal (*visarjana*). "May our donors prosper," and so forth.
Having repeatedly spoken such pleasant words and having prostrated,
one should dismiss them with the joyful formula "vāje vāje," beginning with the ancestors.
Having turned face upwards that vessel for the ancestors into which you previously placed the remnants in the arghya-vessel, one should dismiss the Brahmins.

‘Svastivācyam’ means the recitation of auspicious blessings (*svastivācana*). Regarding this, some authorities maintain that it takes the form of a formal command (*praiṣa*) such as, “O sirs, say *svasti*. Others hold that it consists of simply saying, “*Svasti*. Pāraskara has stated: “May you say *svasti*. And the Brahmins should respond, “*Oṃ svasti*. Then, having declared, “May the *śrāddha* offered to the Viśvedevas, known by the names Purūravas and Mādrava, be inexhaustible,” he should pour water mixed with *kuśa* grass and barley into the hand of each individual Brahmin belonging to the Vaiśvadeva portion. The Brahmins should then say, “May it be inexhaustible. Thereafter, preceded by the mention of the sixth-case [dative] forms of the lineage (*gotra*), relationship, and names of the ancestors beginning with the father, he should utter, “May the *śrāddha* offered be inexhaustible,” and pour water respectively and separately into the hands of the Brahmins of the paternal portion. The Brahmins should then say, “May it be inexhaustible.”
Regarding this, the elder Śātātapa says:
"Water with sesame seeds should be offered into the hand by means of the name and lineage of the ancestors, using the *pitṛ-tīrtha* for each one, with the formula: 'May this be inexhaustible.'"

Then, setting aside silver, one should give a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the twice-born invited for the *vaiśvadeva* rite—either according to their relative degree of merit or according to one’s own capacity—in the manner prescribed in the section on sacrificial fees, using materials such as gold and the like. To those invited for the ancestors (*pitrya*), one should likewise give a fee made of silver or gold and other materials, according to one’s wealth. Then, having requested permission from the Brahmins with the words, "I shall cause the *svadhā* to be uttered," and being granted permission by them with the words, "Let it be uttered," one should say: "May the *svadhā* be pronounced for the sake of the ancestors named so-and-so, belonging to such-and-such lineage, known by the name so-and-so, together with their wives, who are of the nature of the Vasus."
And this method of pronouncing the *svadhā*, asking questions, and giving answers has been shown by Atri:
"I shall pronounce the *svadhā*; [the performer] should thus pose the question among those of different castes.
'Let it be pronounced,' they should grant permission, being pleased and composed."
Then he should say to those Brahmins, "Let the *svadhā* be uttered for the ancestors and others";
when they have replied, "Let there be *svadhā*," he should sprinkle water and utter the eternal [mantra].
And this procedure will be explained by the words of Kātyāyana and Gobhila:

when the Brahmins have said, "Let there be *svadhā*," one should recite this mantra—“Carrying strength, immortality, clarified butter, milk, nectar, and flowing ambrosia, you are *svadhā*; satisfy my ancestors”—and pour a stream of water upon the ground.
This has been stated in detail in the *Kālakā-purāṇa*.
O child, having become pure, one should slowly scatter on the ground a stream of water mixed with sesame seeds; then, after dismissing the twice-born, one should make this request.

In this regard, some authorities state that in the *Śrāddhakalpa*, the pouring forth of the stream of *svadhā* is performed with the following mantra: "To the Ṛc thee, to the Ṛc thee; the streams flow together like rivers, purified by the heart and mind within; I gaze upon the streams of clarified butter. A golden reed stands in their midst; therein sits the fair-winged bird, enjoying the honey-hive for the sake of the deities of honey. For its being, for the golden one, they milk the sevenfold *svadhā* from the chariot-less stream. Regarding this, some say that after the pouring of the streams, when the sacrificer says, "May the *svadhā* be accomplished; may you, sirs, declare so," the Brahmins should reply, "May the *svadhā* be accomplished. Others, however, spread *darbha* grass on the ground together with the *pavitra* strainers contained in the *arghya* vessels and pour the *svadhā*-water thereon. This will be shown in the statement of Kātyāyana. Still others, however, pour the *svadhā*-water over the funeral cakes (*piṇḍas*).
And it is stated in the *Matsyapurāṇa*:
"One should perform everything pertaining to the recitation of the *svadhā* over the funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*).
Some, however, perform the recitation of the *svadhā* with the water remaining from the *arghya* offerings.
And it is said in the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*:
"Then, taking water from the vessels of remnants (*saṃsrava*) that have been honored,
and reciting the *ūrjaṃ vahantī* verses, he sprinkles the funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*)."
In this regard, Atri, Viṣṇu, and Manu have shown the praise of the recitation of *svadhā*:
"The Brāhmaṇas should then say to him, 'Let there be *svadhā*';
for in all rites for the ancestors, the utterance of *svadhā* is indeed the supreme blessing."

When the sacrificer has addressed the Vaiśvadeva Brahmins with the words, "May the Viśvedevas be pleased," the Brahmins should reply, "May the Viśvedevas be pleased. A specific method for this recitation of pleasure (*prītivācana*) is shown in the *Brahmavaivarta*:
"With the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*savya*), one should then offer water with barley using the *devatīrtha* [part of the hand]."
And one should utter: "May the Viśvedevas also be pleased at this sacrifice."

The performer of the *śrāddha* should place the offering into the hand of the twice-born (brāhmaṇa) belonging to the *vaiśvadeva* rite. Immediately thereafter, when the sacrificer has said to the brāhmaṇas representing the ancestors, "May they be pleased," the brāhmaṇas should reply, "May the ancestors be pleased. Following that, he should recite the verse of benediction beginning with "dātāraḥ" (the givers). Having spoken thus, and having recited the verse beginning with "dātāraḥ," he should address the twice-born with affectionate words such as: "I am blessed; I am favored by you, for you have accepted this much hardship for the sake of showing me grace. You yourselves have been brought to such exhaustion by food prepared with whatever means possible; therefore, everything on our part must be forgiven by you. By your favor, my ancestors have today attained the heavenly world," and so forth.
And the mantra proclaimed by Bṛhaspati, which consists of pleasant speech, should be recited:
"Today my birth has become fruitful through the salutation of your feet;
today, by your grace, all those born in my lineage have gone to heaven."
"You have been distressed by such things as the gift of leafy vegetables;
therefore, forgetting the state of mind born from that distress, you ought to forgive.
After this, the Brahmins should be requested with the words, "May everything be complete."
And likewise Viṣṇu says:
"O best of the twice-born, may this śrāddha— though deficient in mantras, deficient in ritual action, and deficient in materials— attain completeness through your grace."
And after the Brahmins have said, "It is all complete," they should offer praise for the qualities of the food.
Thus says Vasiṣṭha:
"At the conclusion of the śrāddha, the twice-born should perform the praise of the qualities of the food."
In this matter, the praise of qualities—such as sweetness and so forth—should not be made individually; rather, one should simply say, "The oblation is excellent. Thus says the Smṛti:
"The specific qualities of the oblation need not be mentioned; one should simply say, 'The oblation is excellent.'"
Immediately thereafter, having placed his knees upon the ground and bowed down to those Brahmins, he should dismiss them.
And so it is stated in the Viṣṇudharmottara:
"Having gone to the earth on his knees and prostrated himself, he should dismiss them."
*Visarjana* means the rising of the Brahmins from their seats. For this very reason, Mārkaṇḍeya says:
"Having made them rise with the mantra 'vāje vāje' and having performed a circumambulation of them..."
And this should be performed after turning the vessel containing the offerings for the ancestors upside down and then placing it face upwards. And [the mantra is]:
"In every contest, O vigorous ones, you who are wise, immortal, and knowers of the Truth;
drink of this honeyed mead and rejoice; being satisfied, go by the paths traveled by the gods."
This mantra should be recited while performing [the rite]. However, Śaunaka has stated:
"One should dismiss [the ancestors] with 'upacīyaṃ svadhā' and respond with 'astu svadhā'."
But in the *Maitrāyaṇīya-sūtra* it is said:
"Having uttered the *praṇava*, one should dismiss [the ancestors] with the words 'svadhā astu'.
The dismissal should be performed with the tip of a blade of *darbha* grass.
And so it is stated in the *Matsya Purāṇa*:
"Reciting the mantra 'vāje vāje,' one should dismiss [the ancestors] with the tip of a *kuśa* blade;
the entire *śrāddha* must be performed according to the rules with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*apasavya*)."
Having performed the recitation of hymns and praises, one should perform the dismissal of the Brahmins.

The meaning is that he should cause each Brāhmaṇa to rise by touching him individually with the tip of a *kuśa* blade using his right hand. In this context, if the mantra were completed for each individual Brāhmaṇa as they were being raised one by one, then the plural number found in the mantra "yāta" (go ye), which occurs in the context of a single simultaneous injunction (*praiṣa*) applicable to many, would be unintended (*avivakṣita*). Therefore, touching all of them in succession with the tip of the *darbha* grass while reciting the mantra only once, he should first raise the ancestors (*pitr*), and immediately thereafter raise those belonging to the *vaiśvadeva* group. Immediately after that, he should likewise raise the maternal ancestors (*mātāmaha*).
For this very reason, it is stated in the Viṣṇudharmottara:
"One should dismiss the gods last and the twice-born ancestors first;
for the maternal grandfathers as well, the same sequence is prescribed along with the gods."
Pracetā also says:

"Then, having performed the recitation of auspicious blessings (*svastivācana*), the dismissal (*visarjana*) should be done starting with the ancestors (*pitṛpūrva*). Here, by the very act of raising the Brahmins, the ritual dismissal (*udvāsana*) of the deities and ancestors who were invoked there is also accomplished. Although this is not explicitly stated separately in the *smṛtis*, nevertheless, for the sake of that mental connection, one should say: "Arise, O ancestors, along with the gods."
Having said "imperishable water," Kātyāyana says:

when [the guest] has said, "May the ancestors be non-terrible," [the host] replies, "May they be so"; when [the guest] has said, "May our lineage increase," [the host] replies, "May it increase"; and [he adds]:
"May our givers increase, as well as the Vedas and our progeny."
May our faith not depart, and may we have much to give.

Having thus accepted the benedictions, he spreads out *kuśa* grass with *pavitra* blades upon which the *svadhā*-invocation is to be pronounced; then he asks, "Shall I pronounce the *svadhā*? Being permitted with the words, "Let it be pronounced," [he says], "May the *svadhā* be pronounced for the fathers, grandfathers, great-grandfathers, maternal grandfathers, maternal great-grandfathers, and maternal great-great-grandfathers. When the reply "So be it, *svadhā*" is uttered, he pours water onto the *svadhā*-invoking vessels while holding the vessel face upwards. He should give a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) according to his ability. Having murmured over the *daiva* [portion], "May the Viśvedevas be pleased," and having dismissed them with "Vāja, vāja," he should follow [the guests] with "Oṃ āvāja-sya," circumambulate them to the right, and sit down.

Regarding this, the traditionalists explain as follows: Having spread the *kuśa* grass designated for the *svadhā*-invocation—known as the *svadhāvācanīya*—which has been prepared for that purpose, and having arranged the purifiers (*pavitra*) situated in the *arghya* vessels with their tips pointing southward to the north of the *piṇḍas*, one should take the water from the vessel used for washing the *piṇḍas* in the right hand, recite the mantra beginning with "ūrjaṃ vahantīḥ," and after saying "tṛpyata" (be satisfied) three times, pour the water out using the *pitṛ-tīrtha*. When the dismissal has been performed, one should follow the Brahmins as they exit the house while reciting the mantra beginning with the pratīka "āvāja-sya. Then, having circumambulated them clockwise as they stand upright at the doorway upon reaching the area of the foot-washing mandala, one should do so with this very same mantra.
May the ancestors, being pleased, bestow upon men long life, progeny, wealth, knowledge, heaven, liberation, and happiness, as well as sovereignty.
Having accepted these benedictions spoken in the *Brahma Purāṇa* and so forth, and having seated them, he should sit down himself. In the *Brahmavaivarta*:
"Then he should offer water for the inexhaustible [merit], combined with sesame seeds, clarified butter, and honey."
Even a poor man should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to Brahmins according to his ability.
Having asked forgiveness from the Brahmins, he, with palms joined in reverence and composed in mind, should say to those eternal ones:
"May the ancestors be non-terrible toward me."
And they should say to him as he bows: "May [the ancestors] be eternal;
through our ancestors being pleased, satisfied, and well-composed, may my lineage flourish, O son, bestowing birth, health, and prosperity."
Then they all respectfully said, "May it increase! And he, with palms joined in reverence, spoke those words to the speakers of truth.
"May our donors increase, and may we have abundant food"—
thinking thus, they, being composed in mind, replied to him, "So be it."
And when this has been done, the Brahmin, being composed, should say with water first:
"May the Viśvedevas be pleased," reciting the mantra.
To him they respond joyfully, "So be it."
And he should dismiss the ancestors while recollecting the mantra "vāje vāje";
he should follow all the ancestors as they turn back toward the sacred site where they stand facing away.
Having recited the mantra "Amāvāja" and performed a circumambulation at the edge of the door,
he should then enter the house with self-restraint.
Gobhila, however, recites the entire mantra beginning with "āmā vājasya."

When [the Brahmins] have said, "May the ancestors be non-terrible (aghorāḥ)," and when they have said, "May our lineage increase," he spreads *kuśa* grass with *pavitra* blades upon which the *svadhā*-offering is poured. He asks, "Shall I cause the *svadhā* to be recited? Being authorized by the reply, "Let it be recited," while the words "Let the *svadhā* be uttered for the fathers, grandfathers, great-grandfathers, maternal grandfathers, maternal great-grandfathers, and maternal great-great-grandfathers" are being spoken, and the response "So be it, let there be *svadhā*" is given, he should pour a stream [of water] onto the vessels for the *svadhā*-offering with the verse, "Carrying strength... Having caused [the Brahmins] to recite, "May the Viśvedevas be pleased," regarding the divine [portion], and having moved the *piṇḍa*-plates, he should give a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) according to his ability. Having accepted the blessings beginning with "May we be givers," and having dismissed [the Brahmins] with "O food, O food," [he concludes].
May the impulsion of strength come to me; may Heaven and Earth, who possess all forms, approach me;
may my father and mother come to me, and may Soma come to me with immortality.

Having thus followed [the preceptor] and saluted him, and having circumambulated him while singing the *Vāmadevya* Sāman, he sits down. This refers to the *Vāmadevya*, a specific Sāman; this rule pertains to the followers of the *Chandoga* (Sāmavedic) tradition. Having seated the Brahmins, the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) should sit down himself, and then satisfy them with offerings such as betel leaves and other gifts. Immediately thereafter, a formal dismissal (*visarjana*) must be performed so that they may return to their own places. Thus says Śātātapa: "Having fed the Brahmins, one should give them sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) according to one's ability."
Having accepted their blessing and performed a circumambulation of the brahmins, he departed.
Then, having circumambulated them once more with palms joined in reverence,
and having spoken kind words, he should prostrate and take his leave.

Regarding this dismissal (*visarjana*), its characteristic of being preceded by the massaging of the twice-born’s feet and its specific feature of following them for some distance is stated in the *Nāgarakhaṇḍa*:
"Having performed the massaging of the feet, one should follow [the guest] as far as the boundary (*āsīmāntam*).
"As far as the boundary" means up to the limit of one's own house.
In the *Matsya Purāṇa*, however, another rule regarding following [the funeral procession] is stated, along with specific particulars:
"Accompanied by his circle of kinsmen and joined by his sons and wife, he should perform a circumambulation outside and follow for eight steps."
Having followed [the guest] for some distance, one should turn back.
Regarding this dismissal, the specific sequence of actions and the obtaining of permission from the Brāhmaṇas during the return are described in the Vārāha- and Viṣṇu-purāṇas.

The dismissal (visarjana) occurs first for the paternal ancestors and then for the maternal ancestors; having honored and worshipped them, one should dismiss them with a joyful mind. Having been granted permission, one should return from the place of the offering and follow after them for some distance.
In the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa as well:
"Having spoken kind words and having prostrated with devotion, one should dismiss [the preceptor];
one should follow after him for support, and return only when permitted."
‘Anugacchet’ means he should follow after the Brāhmaṇas. ‘Ādhāram’ means as far as the door of the dwelling. ‘Anumoditaḥ’ means permitted by the Brāhmaṇas.

Herein, in the Nāgara-khaṇḍa, items such as the *akṣayya* (imperishable) water are shown along with an alternative method for the recitation of the *svadhā*. [1496] After that, the *akṣayya* water should be offered with the word *ṣaṣṭhī*.
Having taken up the purifiers, one should also utter "Oṃ Svadhā."
When they have replied, "Let there be *svadhā*," he should pour [the water] over the *piṇḍa*.
Then, having taken honey, milk-rice (*pāyasa*), and water with sesame seeds—
With the mantra "ūrjaṃ vaha," he should scatter [the food] over the ancestors; then, having turned the vessel face upwards, he should give the sacrificial fee.
Gold belongs to the deities and silver likewise to the ancestors;
thereafter, one should offer the water for well-being (*svastyaudaka*), beginning with the ancestors while keeping the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*savya*).
Then, O best of kings, having joined the palms in reverence (*añjali*), one should offer this prayer.
"May our givers prosper," and so forth; with the words "In every battle, O Vāja... he should dismiss those best of the twice-born.
Then, with the mantra "Ā mā vājasya...", he should proceed by circling to the right.
And one should perform the dismissal of the deities, endowed with discipline.

The meaning is as follows: having said "Tata," he should place flowers and unbroken rice (*akṣata*) into the hands of the Brahmins; then, taking the sacred grass-blades (*pavitra*) contained in the *arghya* vessels and placing them upon the funeral cakes (*piṇḍas*), he should take water mixed with honey, milk-rice (*pāyasa*), and sesame seeds in a vessel, recite the mantra "ūrjaṃ vaḥ," and pour that water in a stream over the sacred grass-blades placed upon the funeral cakes for the ancestors. Thereafter, he should perform the overturning of the *arghya* vessels and so forth.
This is stated in the *Vārāha-purāṇa* and *Viṣṇu-purāṇa* following the worship of the funeral cakes:
"Having performed the worship, the wise man should give water for sipping (*ācamana*) to the foremost of the twice-born."
First, with devotion and a focused mind, the lord of the twice-born should offer [the oblation] to the ancestors,
saying "Swell well" (susvadha), and according to his ability, he should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) accompanied by a blessing.
Having given the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to them, he should cause those representing the Viśvedevas to recite:
"May they be pleased," and he should utter, "Those who are the Viśvedevas, may they be yours."
When those brahmins have said, "So be it," one should offer the requested blessings;
then, endowed with devotion, one should perform the dismissal.
In the Mānava-Maitrāyaṇīya-Sūtra:
Having risen from the remnants [of the food], having stepped forward while reciting "vāje vāja," and having circumambulated [the fire] clockwise while reciting "śramāvājasya," one should give silver.
In the Saura Purāṇa:
Having offered water for washing the hands, one should indeed perform the recitation of the Svasti;
one should give a sacrificial fee according to one's ability and utter the word "Svadhā."
"May our donors prosper; may there be strength upon strength! Having recited this verse, having praised the Brahmins, and having paid them homage, one should dismiss them.
In the Vāyu Purāṇa and the Brahma Purāṇa:
"Then, having pronounced 'svadhā' over the Brahmins according to the rules and having given them abundant sacrificial fees,
and having requested permission regarding the remnants of the food, he should honor those most excellent of the twice-born."
With palms joined in reverence and self-restrained, he should follow him and then bid him farewell.
Bṛhaspati says: Having uttered "vāje vāje," one should dismiss those Brāhmaṇas;
having circumambulated the Brahmins clockwise, one should pray for boons from the ancestors.
Śaṅkha says:

Having fed the twice-born with devotion, having given them sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) ending with the utterance of "svadhā," and having caused the twice-born to pronounce "svasti" with devotion, one should follow them for a short distance and then dismiss them.

Hārīta says: When they have sipped water, he should pour water containing roots of *darbha* grass and sesame seeds into the hands of the Brahmins, saying "Oṃ Svadhā. They say, "Let there be Svadhā," and respond, "So be it, Svadhā. Then follows the request for permission; some say, "May you be pleased," and they respond, "We are pleased. Having walked around [the fire] with the words "In strength, in strength," he should place the rice-balls (*piṇḍas*) according to the ritual of the *pitṛyajña*. Uśanas says:
Having placed the *piṇḍas* [on the ground], one should cause the word "svadhā" to be uttered; having sprinkled them with water, one should set aside the water vessels.
Immediately after the utterance of "svadhā," Atri says:
"And for the sake of longevity, sons, wealth, health, and peace, one should indeed cause it to be uttered."
The word "to the twice-born" (*dvijān*) is to be supplied [as the object]. Regarding this, Vyāghra says with respect to one who maintains the sacred fires:
"The twice-born, being pleased, should declare, 'May the gift of food be inexhaustible' (*akṣayyam*)."
Having circumambulated the fire clockwise, one should then dismiss the Brahmins.

The *Nigama* states: Having caused the benediction to be recited and having said, "Oṃ, let the *svadhā* be uttered," one should honor [the guests] by saying, "May you enjoy yourselves as you please," and then follow them as they depart.
*Devala* says:
Alternatively, one should have the Brahmins presiding over the Vaiśvadeva offerings recite the benediction;
for those belonging to the ancestors, one should finally have them recite "May it be inexhaustible" (akṣayyam) while offering water with sesame seeds.
Then, he should salute the Brahmins who have received their portions and are fully satisfied, according to the rule:
first the deities of the Vaiśvadeva rite, and then again the ancestors, beginning with the paternal line.
First, he should cause those representing the ancestors to rise while saying, "May it be successful.
Once they have risen, he should follow after them and collect the remainder from them.
In the *Brahma-purāṇa*:
Having gratified the ancestors with "May it be inexhaustible" and the deities with "May they be pleased," one should turn back and recite the *Aghamarṣaṇa* mantra three times.
Then, having turned away, he should recite the three verses beginning with "janmanāma.
Thereafter, he gave heroic sons to us, O ancestors, and he bestowed heroic sons upon us.
Having placed the *arghya* vessel containing a *pavitra* blade between the funeral cakes (*piṇḍas*), he applied the mantra "ūrjaṃ vahanti" according to the *Kokātāya* tradition.
He offered snow, milk, honey, and sesame seeds as libations for the ancestors;
when the paternal ancestors had said "Svasti," he indeed gratified the Viśvedevas with gold.
Having given silver as the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), the divine Gadādhara bestowed a share upon the ancestors,
saying "Svadhā," and gave a distribution to human beings.
Having been asked by those best of the twice-born, "Is all well?", he replied,
"May you be happy," and they indeed said, "We are happy."
Prompted by those beloved ones, he asked about the remaining food;
then, taking the hands of those brahmins and following after them, he did likewise.
Reciting "vāje vāje," he went outside the sacrificial altar,
sprinkling the water from the Koṭitīrtha while circling it in the anti-clockwise direction.
He requested a blessing for his own dear and numerous children,
saying, "May our donors prosper," and they replied, "So be it."
Having circumambulated them and performed a salutation at their feet, the boar offered them seats and spoke to them:
"Please enter and rest; then he took the middle portion of the food."
In the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa:
"Then one should offer water for sipping (ācamana) accompanied by perfumes, garlands, and so forth;
having given a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) according to one's ability, one should then say to them, 'svadhā astu'."
When they have been satisfied and have replied, "So be it," he should cause those belonging to the Viśvedevas to recite, saying, "May the Viśvedevas be pleased; may there be prosperity for you."

In the Baudhāyana Sūtra: Having honored [the guests] as they arrive, having caused them to recite "May it be inexhaustible," having received their formal greeting, having caused them to recite "Svadhā," having made them stand near, having propitiated them, having circumambulated them clockwise, and having obtained permission regarding the remnants, one should act as they direct. Being thus authorized, one should strew darbha grass around the Dakṣiṇāgni fire and offer the rice-balls (piṇḍas). Viṣṇu [states]:

Then, while the [guests] facing east, he—facing north—having performed a circumambulation from the front with the words "yan me rāma," having returned and given a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) according to his ability, and having said, "May you be pleased," when they have replied, "We are pleased," he should mutter the mantra, "The gods and the ancestors. Having muttered the water for inexhaustibility (*akṣayyodaka*) by means of their names and lineages, and having said to those facing east, "May the Viśvedevas be gratified," he should then, with palms joined, being focused on that and with a cheerful mind, request them with the words beginning, "May our donors increase," and so forth.
Then, with the verse "vāje vāje," he should dismiss those Brāhmaṇas.
Having worshipped according to the rule, and having followed him and saluted him.

This mantra, beginning with *yan me rāmaḥ*, is applied to the introductory portion (*pratīka*): "Whatever [sin] my *rāma*, my bird, and my wild beast have committed; whatever [sin] my pure one and the mantra-maker have consumed—may Vaiśvānara and Savitṛ purify that. In that which is purified, may the deities rejoice. By that which is purified, may the ancestors rejoice. Both gods and ancestors—may they live by this fulfillment here. Place me in this world; may we live for a hundred autumns, may we see for a hundred autumns. Bestow vigor, bestow light; grant us ageless life. Whatever [wrong] we have done against the mid-region, the earth, or the sky, or against our mother or father—if we have caused injury—may Agni Gārhapatya release us from that sin and from the misfortunes that cause stumbling. The mantra "devāś ca pitaraś ca" is also written here: "Both gods and ancestors—may they live by this fulfillment here. Place me in this world; may we live for a hundred autumns, may we see for a hundred autumns. Bestow vigor, bestow light; grant us ageless life. Whatever [wrong] we have done against the mid-region, the earth, or the sky, or against our mother or father—if we have caused injury—may Agni Gārhapatya release us from that sin and from the misfortunes that cause stumbling."
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"One who is faithful and composed should offer water for sipping with devotion,
and having performed a circumambulation while thinking, 'Rāma is my bird.'"
Having returned, the wise man should gratify them with sacrificial fees according to his ability;
immediately thereafter, he should say to the Brahmins, "May you all be satisfied."
When they have said, "We are delighted," he should stand before the twice-born and, unwearied, recite the mantra: "The gods and the ancestors."
Immediately thereafter, water should be offered by name and lineage to the ancestors;
O lord of men, the twice-born should declare, "May it be inexhaustible" for the Brahmins.
Then, O protector of the earth, a prayer should be performed with this mantra:
"May we have givers," and so forth;
having recited "In every contest" (*vāje vāje*) and having circumambulated them clockwise,
one should then respectfully bow to those Brahmins and dismiss them with devotion.

In the *Kaṭha-sūtra*: Having caused those who are satiated to sip water, and having performed a circumambulation clockwise while reciting "yan me rāma," one should return, say "May you be delighted," and worship with the remainder of the section beginning "devāś ca pitaraś ca.
In the *Pippalāda-sūtra*:

Having given water for sipping (*ācamanīya*), he should give the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). With the verse "Sons and grandsons... he should pour one vessel of water; with the verse "The waters, Agni... a second; and with both verses together, a third. He should pour the remainder of the water from the vessels into the hands of the Brahmins, saying, "May there be *svadhā* for the fathers, grandfathers, and great-grandfathers; may it be inexhaustible. Having requested blessings such as "May we be givers," he pays homage with the mantra "Homage to you, O fathers," and dismisses them with the two verses beginning "As they depart. Then, he should mutter the verse "In strength after strength. Turning to the right with the verse "The turning of the sun," he performs the rite of the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña* with the mantra "We call the mind back," while wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*upavītin*) as a specific distinction.
In the Kauśikasūtra:

Having given water for sipping (*ācamanīya*), he should cause the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited; having given a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) according to his ability, he should pour the remainder of the water-vessel into the hands of the Brahmins, which hold the *pavitra* grass-strands. [He recites] "Son, grandson" as the first [verse], "Waters, fire" as the second, and with the two joined [verses] as the third. According to Kauśika, one should use the verse "Son, grandson" alone for the vessel of water. [He says: "To the great-grandfathers, grandfathers, fathers, maternal uncles, and maternal grandfathers—to all those who have been designated, together with their wives—may this be *svadhā*-bearing and inexhaustible! May it be inexhaustible! Having requested boons from the Brahmins by means of their response, "May our donors increase," and so forth, he should perform the circumambulation clockwise after taking the Brahmins by the hand and making them rise, reciting from "Obeisance to you, O Fathers" up to "We call upon the mind," and from "Those who are common, the sapindas... at the offering of the middle rice-ball in the ancestral sacrifice, and from "In every battle, O ye vigorous ones... and so forth. This is the procedure for the *śrāddha*.
In this matter, the compiler, having gathered together the various sequences taught by many sages, has stated:
Yājñavalkya desires the vessel to be turned face-up before the dismissal;
Yama [desires it so] after performing the dismissal; and Śaunaka, the author of the Gṛhyasūtra, [also holds this view].
However, Kātyāyana and others previously [composed] questions concerning the joy of the gods.
The arrangement for these alternatives should be stated as it was for the acceptance of the *āśis* (benedictions).
Here, after stating the removal of the *pavitra* grass-bands immediately following the utterance of *svadhā*, Śāṭyāyani describes the turning upward of the vessels:
"In the same manner for the maternal grandfathers; then, the *darbha* *pavitra*s..."
Then, having set it down at the side of the alms-food, one should turn the bowl upside down.

Before the recitation for joy (*prītivācana*), Pracetas states that the ritual element known as the recitation for an auspicious day (*puṇyāhavācana*) should follow the recitation for well-being (*svastivācana*), as well as the turning upward of the vessel (*pātrottānatā*). He says: "One should cause [the officiants] to say: 'Om, may this be an auspicious day; may all the gods be pleased.
Having spoken thus, he should then announce the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*)."
Then, having performed the recitation of the benediction (*svastivācana*), one should turn over the vessel face-down;
thereafter, one should dismiss those [guests] by circumambulating them outside in a clockwise direction.

Having performed these acts, rested there, and honored them in that manner, he should dismiss them with devotion and follow them as far as the boundary. Then, permitted by those Brahmins, he should return to his own home.
Devala said:
Having completed the *pitṛmedha* rite, having extinguished the lamp with his hand,
and having sipped water and washed his hands, he should feed his kinsmen with the remainder.
"Having covered" means having extinguished [the fire].
These are the items beginning with "well-sprinkled.
Now follow the procedures for the disposal of the *piṇḍas*.

And these [rites], with the exception of the consumption of the *piṇḍas* and the exceptions for ritual disposal (*pratipatti*) prescribed on account of the absence of the wife and other such causes, are of a dual nature—both obligatory (*nitya*) and optional (*kāmya*)—due to the principle of "separateness of connection" (*saṃyogapṛthaktva*) which will be demonstrated later. Regarding this, Śaṅkha and Likhita state two forms of ritual disposal characterized by specific times:

"Having thus requested boons and paid homage, one should cast the *piṇḍas* either into the fire or into the water"; and "having paid homage to the Brahmins. This homage, consisting of the completion of the rite, is to be understood as taking the form of an act of seeking forgiveness (*kṣamāpana*).

In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*, however, four modes of disposal (*pratipatti*) are stated: "One should give the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) to cows, goats, and Brahmins, or else throw them into the fire. Devala, on the other hand, speaks of five modes of disposal.
Then, once the ritual action is completed, immediately thereafter,
a Brāhmaṇa, fire, a goat, or a cow should consume those rice-balls, or one should cast them into water.
Yājñavalkya also says:
"One devoted to the ancestors should give the rice-balls to a cow, a horse, or a Brahmin, or else cast them into fire or water;
if he so desires, he should cast them toward the southern direction."
Manu, however, having described this fivefold method of practice, has also shown a sixth according to the opinion of some:

"Having performed the offering of the rice-balls in this manner immediately thereafter, one should cause a cow, a Brahmin, a goat, or the fire to consume those rice-balls, or else throw them into water."
Others devour them with birds, or they throw them into fires.
Medhātithi maintains that the phrase "or in fires" (*analeṣu vā*) is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*) of what was previously mentioned [at MDh 3.251].
However, in the *Pādma* and *Mātsya* Purāṇas, a sevenfold method of disposal is stated:
"One should give the funeral cakes (*piṇḍas*) to cows, goats, or Brahmins, or [dispose of them] in fire or even in water."
Or he may scatter it at the edge of the sacrificial ground, or cause birds to eat it.
Regarding the rice-balls (piṇḍas) associated with the *piṇḍānvāhāryaka* śrāddha, the Kālikā Purāṇa states:
"Then, having gone there with a concentrated mind, he should smell those rice-balls;
taking a very small portion from them, he should cause these [others] to eat it."
The father remains present, O child, and he should likewise cause him to eat;
one should offer the remainder of that [food] into the fire, to a Brahmin, into water, or into the mouths of cows, goats, and sheep.
Then, the wise man, meditating upon the ancestors while exerting effort over the balls of food themselves,
should turn his back toward them and not look at the face of the woman.

If the performer of the *śrāddha* has his father living, then he should cause that father to eat only the *piṇḍa*. Once the *piṇḍas* have been offered into the fire and other elements, he should then turn his back toward them, turn his face away, and not look at them. The rule regarding the eating of only the *piṇḍa* has already been shown in the section on the offering of the *piṇḍas*. However, Yama has stated a separate disposal for each individual *piṇḍa*:
"One should cause one *piṇḍa* to float in water; one should present one to the wife."
And one should offer one [oblation] into the fire; three balls [of food] are prescribed.
In the Vārāha Purāṇa as well:
"One should first offer [the food] into the fire; the middle portion should be given to the wife;
one should give the third portion into the water, or one may consume the remainder oneself."
And in the interval between those two, one should ask for forgiveness after bowing to the divine earth.
And Yama has stated that those who are to be gratified by these ritual performances are as follows:
"By the rice-ball (piṇḍa) that he causes to float upon the waters, he thereby gratifies the Moon;
and the highly illustrious Moon, in turn, gratifies both the gods and the ancestors."
When the wife, restrained in speech and desiring a son, eats that middle ball of rice, the great-grandfathers make her possessed of a son.
When the best of the twice-born offers the very first ball of rice into the fire,
he attains eternal worlds together with his gratified great-grandfathers.
Hārīta, however, says:

"When they offer the rice-balls again into the fire, into water, or to a Brahmin, those offerings, possessing the qualities of that [recipient], bestow their fruits; for they enter [the ancestors] according to one's desire."

Because they are the substrates for Agni and the others, those ancestors who possess the qualities of Agni and so forth—designated as "Huta" and the rest—enter, that is, they penetrate and satisfy themselves, without effort and according to their desire, through those rice-balls (*piṇḍas*) offered into Agni and the other [fires]. In this regard, the connection between the eating of the middle *piṇḍa* and specific desires is established in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"A wife desiring a son should indeed eat the middle *piṇḍa*.
Thus says Devala.
Or, desiring a son, she should eat the middle morsel from among them;
for by the grace of the ancestors, she indeed obtains a son of great virtue.

Thus, she who does not obtain a son at all, or she who does not obtain one endowed with virtues, should eat the middle *piṇḍa* in order to obtain such a son. This desire is indeed obligatory, according to the Vedic revelation: "He alone is free from debt who has a son. It is also said: "She gives birth to a son of great virtue. Regarding this, Manu and Bṛhaspati state the qualities of a son—which, when recited word by word, render [the rite] fit for consumption—as well as the qualities of the wife.
Then the lawful wife, devoted to her husband and intent on the worship of the ancestors,
if desiring a son, should eat the middle *piṇḍa*.
She gives birth to a long-lived son, endowed with fame and intelligence,
wealthy, possessed of progeny, righteous, and likewise virtuous.
Śaṅkha and Likhita state another specific qualification regarding the wife that renders her fit for consumption:

"Or the wife, being in her menses (*ārtavānvitā*), may eat the middle *piṇḍa*. "Menses" (*ārtava*) refers to the menstrual flow; she is one who has performed her ritual bath on the fourth day because of that.
Regarding this consumption of the rice-ball (piṇḍa), Hārīta states a specific rule:
"If a wife should desire a son, she should eat the middle rice-ball;
according to the Prājāpatya rite, that [rice-ball] is traditionally said to grant her a son."
The procedure seen by Prajāpati is the "Prājāpatya"; and that consists of the act of eating accompanied by a specific mantra.
This mantra is applied [here] by way of citation from the Padma and Matsya Purāṇas:
"But he should cause his wife, endowed with modesty, to eat the middle piṇḍa."
O ancestors, bestow the embryo through this mantra that increases the lineage.
In the *Brahma Purāṇa* as well:
