"Having rested and entered them, he then took the middle *piṇḍa*;
the lord gave that *piṇḍa* to his great consort, who was composed of shadow."
Having said, "O ancestors, bestow the embryo," that beautiful woman took the funeral cakes (piṇḍas) from the brahmins and performed the salutation of their feet.

Āśvalāyana recites this mantra in its complete form: "He should cause the wife to eat the middle of the *piṇḍas* with [the verse]: 'O ancestors, bestow a fetus, a boy adorned with a lotus-wreath, so that he may be one who does not die. For the Chāndogas, there is a different reading of that mantra: "'O ancestors, bestow a fetus, a boy adorned with a lotus-wreath, so that there may be a man here. Āpastamba, however, states a different reading for the mantra used when placing the *piṇḍa* into the hand of the wife for consumption, and for the mantra of consumption itself, [substituting] "of waters and of plants."

"I cause you to consume the essence of the waters and the plants; do thou bear a fetus created by the beings. With these words, he gives the middle *piṇḍa* to his wife, saying, "O Fathers, bestow a fetus—a boy adorned with a lotus-wreath—so that there may be a man here. The wife then consumes it. However, Bṛhaspati prescribes another method of disposal for the middle *piṇḍa* when the wife is unfit to consume it:
"If the wife has gone to another country, or is pregnant, or is ill..."
Then that [meat] deserves to be eaten by a worn-out bull or a goat.
In the *Vāyupurāṇa*:
"If the wife has gone to another country, or is lost, or has died,
what is the fate of the middle *piṇḍa* there, and what is its purpose?"
Whether it be a calf or an ox that eats [the food], one should place the middle portion there;
or else, in that very same spot, or then cast it into water.
Also in the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*:
"If a man's wife is staying in a foreign land when her menses occur,
what becomes of his *piṇḍa* when the time for the *śrāddha* arrives?"
But for that horse whose vigor has departed, and likewise for the ox of such a kind—
for these two, a morsel of food should be given, since their seed does not sprout.
Āpastamba says:
"If the wife is in a foreign land, or has been abandoned, or is dead, or is wicked or unfaithful— what is the fate of her funeral cake?"
Standing in water and facing south, one should cause the funeral ball to go toward the sky;
for the sky is the abode of the ancestors, and the south is indeed their direction.

Now, there are also other practices connected with desire (*kāma*). Regarding this, Āśvalāyana, having stated that "one should cause the wife to eat the middle *piṇḍa*," says: "The other two [the first and last *piṇḍas*] should be cast into water, or into the consecrated fire (*praṇīta*), or he who has no desire for the destination [of the ancestors] should eat them; or one afflicted by a severe illness may eat them, and he goes to one of the two destinations. Among the two destinations—consisting of liberation from disease and the attainment of a distinguished world—he attains one or the other. However, Āpastamba has prescribed a mantra for the eating of the *piṇḍas* when the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) is the agent.
"Those who are equal and of one mind, living beings among living beings, who belong to me— may their prosperity be ordained for me in this world for a hundred years.
With these words, the sacrificer eats one of the remaining portions.

In this regard, the distinction is that the first morsel should be eaten by one afflicted by disease, while the last morsel should be eaten by one desiring food. Likewise, there is an indication of another purpose in the statement of Hārīta:
"The first morsel is said to bestow longevity; the second is remembered as bestowing sons."
The third indeed bestows supernatural power; therefore, one should cause [the disciple] to consume the middle [portion].
"The wife of the sacrificer desiring a son"—this is the implied meaning.
From the *Vāyu Purāṇa* and the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*:
"A man who desires enjoyment should always offer the funeral ball (*piṇḍa*) into the fire."
One desiring offspring should indeed give the middle one to his wife, preceded by the recitation of the mantra.
Seeking the highest goal, one should always bestow [cows] upon the cows;
one should cause the funeral cake to be placed in the waters, which grant command, progeny, glory, and fame.
Desiring long life, he offers [meat] to the crows;
and seeking delicacy, he offers it to the cocks.
"One may cause [the offerings] to go into space while standing in water or facing south;
for space is the abode of the ancestors, as is the southern direction. Thus end the procedures for the disposal of the rice balls (*piṇḍa*).
[1510] Now, the removal of the remnants (*ucchiṣṭodvāsana*).

In this regard, the removal of the [food] for the purpose of cleaning the dining area, as well as the washing of the place where the remnants were left and so forth for the sake of feeding the household members, children, relatives, and others, is established by the very nature of the matter and is not explicitly taught in the scripture. However, a specific time related to that is stated. That time is primarily after sunset, while before it is secondary. In this context, the primary time is indicated in the *Kūrmapurāṇa* by way of prohibiting the secondary one.
One should not remove those leavings until the sun has set.
Vasiṣṭha states that this non-removal is purposeful for as long as that period lasts:
"In a Śrāddha, the leavings are not to be removed until the end of the day."
Streams of nectar indeed trickle down; those who have not yet performed their water-libations drink them.

As long as the remnants [of the food] are not cleared away, "streams of nectar"—streams of *amṛta*—drip and flow forth from them. Those deceased ones for whom the offering of water (*udakadāna*) is prohibited, or even those for whom it has not been performed by anyone, drink these while existing in the state of the *preta* realm and other such births.
As stated in the *Kālikā Purāṇa*:
"O best of the twice-born, as long as the cleansing of the remnants has not been performed..."
For that long, the ancestors eat food mixed with the essence of nectar.
In the Vārāha Purāṇa: "As many remnants of the Brahmin's meal as remain upon the earth,
for that long the ancestors, being nourished, remain in one's house."

"O Pitṛs"—here, the remainder [of the sentence] is "those who partake of the leavings. And they are those previously mentioned who have not yet had water offered to them, as well as those shown in the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa:
"One should not wipe away the leavings until the sun has set."
From that, inexhaustible streams of milk flow for those who share in the merit of their journey.

"Saṃcaraḥ" means a path; this is an indicative term for impure places. Therefore, the meaning is those who frequent impure places—beings born from the wombs of *bhūtas*, *pretas*, *piśācas*, and so forth, as well as the *sapiṇḍas* and *samānodakas* of the performer of the *śrāddha*.
Manu also establishes that they are partakers of the remnants of the *śrāddha*:
"The remnant fallen upon the ground belongs to one who is straightforward and free from deceit."
They declare that to be the ancestral portion for the class of slaves.
In this context, the group of servants should be understood as those who have died while related to the primary father.
Vasiṣṭha says:
"The established rule (or sacred tradition) is that for those who have died before initiation, [the rites apply] along with the servants."
Manu has declared that both the leavings on the plate and the remnants of food are one's allotted portion.

"Bhāgadheya" means a portion that is to be shared. "Ucchiṣṭa" refers to that which clings to the bowls, hands, or mouths of those eating, as well as what has fallen on the ground; furthermore, when, due to being fully satiated or for some other reason, food is intentionally left over from a heap of food, that is called "uccheṣaṇa. Manu has declared that both of these constitute the "bhāgadheya," or allotted portion, for the "sampreṣyās," that is, the servants. This is what the Śruti says.

Even the leavings (uccheṣaṇa) are not their share when remaining in the vessel; rather, they are that which is placed upon the ground. Therefore, it is understood that the Brāhmaṇas should intentionally place [the food] on the ground. And that should be relinquished by the sacrificer for the sake of those belonging to the class of servants and so forth who have entered the wombs of ghosts and other such states.
Vasiṣṭha states this very point:
"The leavings fallen on the ground, the scattered grains, the smears, and the water-offering."
One should bestow it upon those who have died childless and without a long life.

One should offer [the food] to the groups of slaves who have died while following their principal master, or to those who died in childhood and left no offspring, with the intention of following the principal ancestors. Having declared, "May this leavings (ucchiṣṭa) or remnant (uccheṣaṇa) be presented to such-and-such a deceased one," one should discard it with water containing sesame seeds, poured from the *pitṛ-tīrtha*. Manu and Viṣṇu state: "For those who die without having received the sacraments, for those who abandon [their kin], and for women of the family..."
The remnant and whatever is scattered upon the darbha grass shall be their allotted portion.

The term "unrefined" (*asaṃskṛtāḥ*) refers to those for whom the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*) has not been performed, as well as women for whom the marriage ceremony has not been performed. Those called "renouncers" (*tyāginaḥ*) are suicides who take their own lives by means of water, fire, poison, weapons, hanging, falling from a cliff, and so forth. It is the same regarding women of good family (*kulayoṣitām*) for whom the water-libation (*udaka*) has not yet been performed. Alternatively, it may be explained as referring to those who have abandoned women of good family without a valid cause. Regarding the statement that the removal of leftover food (*ucchiṣṭodvāsana*) occurs when the sun has set, this is also an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*) for washing on dry ground (*sthalaprakṣālana*). As for the verse: "When the sun has set, the vessels of the Brahmins [should be placed] in water... [and so forth].
Having become purified, one should deposit all of them with their openings facing downward.
On the second day, by washing all the vessels in that manner,
an infinite satisfaction arises for the ancestors at all times.

Thus, in the *Brahmapurāṇa*, after describing the placing of the food vessel upside down in the midst of water immediately following sunset, it is stated that the vessel is to be washed on the second day; this should be understood to apply when another vessel is available. Furthermore, as for the instruction to leave the remains (*ucchiṣṭa*) until evening, that too should be understood to apply when another house exists for the purpose of feeding sons, friends, and others.
For this very reason, Pracetas says:
"Surrounded by his circle of servants and his kinsmen, he eats the remainder of the *kavya*."
Until evening, one should not sweep away the remnants of the food left by the twice-born in the hall where the Śrāddha is performed.
In this context, the qualification "remnant" (*ucchiṣṭa*) refers to that which has been eaten in this dining hall; it is understood as such.
However, in the absence of another house or another vessel for eating, a later time is shown as a secondary option in the *Manu* and *Matsya Purāṇas*:
"The remnant (*uccheṣaṇa*) shall remain until the Brahmins have been dismissed."
Therefore, one should perform the domestic offering; thus the Dharma is established.
Yājñavalkya expresses this very same time by way of prohibiting other times:

"While Brahmins are present, one should not clear away the remnants of the twice-born. The word "present" (satsu) means while they have not yet been dismissed for the purpose of returning to their own places.

In this regard, if there is some food fit for eating that has been left over by the Brāhmaṇa who has eaten at the *śrāddha*, then it is not blameworthy to give it to his own disciple or son who is fit to eat the remnants; however, giving it to Śūdras and others is indeed blameworthy.
For this very reason, Śātātapa stated:
"He who, having eaten at a *śrāddha*, gives the leavings to a *vṛṣala*..."
That fool goes headfirst to the Kālasūtra hell.

By this prohibition against *vṛṣalas*, it is implied that giving their leavings to a member of the three higher castes (*traivarṇika*)—such as a son, a disciple, or a wife—who is fit to eat the leavings of twice-born eaters, is permitted.
However, even among those of the three higher castes, one who has not been initiated (*anupanīta*) must not be given [the leavings].
And so it is stated in the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*:
One should not cause the remnants of a *śrāddha* to be given to a *śūdra* who has not been initiated (*anupeta*).
If one should give it out of passion or delusion, that [offering] certainly does not reach the ancestors.
Therefore, in the performance of a śrāddha rite, no food or other edibles should ever be given as leftovers,
except for curd and clarified butter;
however, one may give everything at will to a disciple or a son.
By the statement "except for curd and clarified butter," the giving of the remnants of curd and clarified butter to an uninitiated person and to a Śūdra is permitted and established.
Jātūkarṇya says:
"One should collect all that remains after the twice-born have eaten into one place."
A wise person, having carefully buried it in clean ground, should cover it over.

In this regard, one should first bury what remains after being given to the sons, disciples, and others. However, if there are no sons or others to receive it, then one should bury everything. Here, if the removal of the *ucchiṣṭa* (food remnants) is performed immediately after the dismissal of the twice-born, then the performance of the five great sacrifices (*pañcamahāyajña*) with the remainder of the *śrāddha* should be done thereafter. But if the *ucchiṣṭas* are kept until sunset, then [the sacrifice] should be performed immediately after the dismissal; and that has already been stated previously. Thus ends the removal of the *ucchiṣṭas*.
Now follows the consumption of the remainder.
In that regard, the *Brahma Purāṇa* states:
"Thus, by a householder, the deities and likewise the ancestors are to be properly worshipped with *havya* and *kavya*, and guests and kinsmen with food."
Beings, servants, the infirm, animals, birds, and ants;
mendicants who beg, and whatever other supplicants are in the house.
"Deficient" refers to those who are blind, deaf, mute, and so forth.
Manu says:
"Having washed his hands and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), he should designate the food as being for his kinsmen."
Having given what is honored to his kinsmen, he should also honor his relatives.

"Kinsmen" (*jñātayaḥ*) refers to the *sapiṇḍas* on the paternal side; the meaning is that one should act so that the food remaining from the *śrāddha* reaches them, and thus feed them with that food. Having given that food to them with due honor, one should "worship" the "relatives" (*bāndhavān*), meaning those on the maternal and father-in-law's sides. In this regard, if the food is asked, "What should be done with the remainder? and the Brahmins say, "Let it be given to us," and they take it for themselves, then the kinsmen, relatives, and others must be fed with a separate cooking. However, if permission is granted by saying, "Let it be eaten together with those you love," then they may be fed with that remainder. Alternatively, when it is said, "What should be done with the remainder of the food? if they reply, "Let it be given to those you love," then—since it is traditionally taught as a mandatory rule that the remainder of the food must not be accepted by the twice-born—the remainder should not be taken at all, and the kinsmen and others should be fed with that [original] food itself.
In the Devalasmṛti and the Kūrmapurāṇa:
"Having washed his hands and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), he should feed his kinsmen with the remainder.
And when the kinsmen are satisfied, he should thereafter feed his own servants."
In the Ādityapurāṇa and the Brahmapurāṇa:
"Sisters and kinsmen are indeed always to be honored at śrāddha ceremonies;
even one afflicted by poverty, one who is wretched, or one with missing limbs or extra fingers [is to be honored]."
Those born in vain, those who are disaffected, and those afflicted by disease—
these are always and in every respect worthy to eat the food of the one who provides it.
Furthermore, bards, panegyrists, and actors skilled in the triple symphony,
if they fail to obtain gains at the funeral feasts (śrāddha), cause one’s great fame to perish; therefore,
they too should be distributed for, and provided with, their full share.

‘Those born in vain’ refers to eunuchs, the blind, the lame, and so forth. ‘The venerable ones’ (*vandya*) and others have already been explained. ‘The triple symphony’ (*tauryatrika*) consists of dance, song, and instrumental music. ‘Those who have not obtained their share’ (*alabdhalābhāḥ*) means those who have not received food; ‘they are to be divided’ (*vibhaktavyāḥ*) means that they should be made sharers in this [meal]. Having thus fed his kinsmen and others, he himself should also eat. And so says the *Nigama*: “Having been permitted, one should eat after satisfying the children and the elderly at home.”

"Permitted" means being permitted by those who have eaten at the *śrāddha* with the words, "Please eat together with those you desire. By this, it is also indicated that one should eat only the remnants of the *śrāddha* food and nothing else. Therefore, Śātātapa says:
"Immediately thereafter, one should eat the remaining food once permission has been granted."
The wise man, being well-composed, should perform [the rite] according to the rules together with those he holds dear.

By the phrase "together with those he likes," it is meant that he should sit in the same row as those who eat from his own line. By the word "according to rule" (*vidhivat*), it is established that the meal is characterized by the ritual procedures such as *āpośāna* and so forth, and is endowed with the constant rules of dining, such as holding the vessel and observing silence. "Intelligent" (*buddhimān*) means one who knows the rules for eating. "Composed" (*samāhita*) means free from the restlessness of hands and other limbs. Regarding the practice of silence therein, it is shown in the *Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa*:
"Restraining his speech, he should eat the remainder together with friends and kinsmen."

By the word "together" (*sārddham*), it is also understood that they sit in a single row. This should be explained in the same way for what follows as well. Here, after the feeding of kinsmen and servants has been mentioned, the *Kūrma Purāṇa* states:
"Afterwards, one should personally partake of the remaining food together with one's wives."
On this point, Kātyāyana has also shown another alternative:
"Or the householder may eat first.
Therefore, having fed the householder, the wives should eat either in a row or [separately].
Bṛhaspati said:
Having thus gratified both the gods and the ancestors, the best of the twice-born,
as a householder accompanied by his sons, friends, and others, is entitled to eat.
According to the *Brahma-purāṇa* and the *Mārkaṇḍeya-purāṇa*:
"Then the man should eat that food together with his servants and others.
In the *Vārāha-purāṇa*:
And having honored them, he should eat together with his servants, kinsmen, and others—
his friends, relatives, and connections— being himself pure and attentive.
Uśanas: Having been authorized by them, he should give the remainder to those he loves and eat it himself.
Yājñavalkya.
Having circumambulated [the place] clockwise, one should eat what was served to the ancestors.
In the *Padma Purāṇa*:
"Then, being tranquil, one should eat together with loved ones what was served to the ancestors."

Regarding the phrase "served by the ancestors" (*pitṛsevita*): one should eat the remnants of whatever food was eaten by the ancestral Brahmins. From this, it is understood that what was not given to the guests at the *śrāddha* through negligence must certainly not be eaten. Furthermore, even all that was consumed by the ancestors should be eaten little by little.
Thus, it is said in the *Matsyapurāṇa*:
"Then, at the conclusion of the *vaiśvadeva* rite, together with his servants, sons, and kinsmen..."
Accompanied by guests, he should eat everything that has been partaken of by the ancestors.

In this context, even though items such as beans and meat were consumed by the ancestors (*pitaras*), they must not be eaten by one who has performed the *anvādhāna* (preparatory rite) during a *śrāddha*, because of the prohibition in the Vedic scripture: "One should observe the vow without beans and without meat. However, by one who has not performed the *anvādhāna* and who is without the sacred fires, meat and other such items consumed by the ancestors may be eaten even on the fifteenth day (*pañcadaśī*), according to the statement: "One should eat everything consumed by the ancestors. As for the prohibition: "By eating meat on the fifteenth day, one destroys the family up to the seventh generation," that applies to consumption prompted by worldly desire (*rāga*) and is thus unable to invalidate the scripturally mandated (*vaidha*) consumption. Furthermore, even by one who has undertaken a personal restriction (*niyama*)—such as "I shall never eat honey, meat, and so forth, until such-and-such a time" or "always"—that [restricted food] must be eaten at a *śrāddha* and similar occasions.

And so Bṛhaspati says: "In a sacrifice or a Śrāddha, because it is an ancillary part of that rite, one who has been invited— even if he is observing a vow— may eat even meats when questioned about them, lest he violate the command of the Brahmins."

"In the *kratu*," that is, at an animal sacrifice (*paśubandha*) or a *śrāddha*, because of the non-breach—that is, for the sake of not violating—such an injunction of a Brahmin as "meat must be eaten at this meal," the sacrificer, and likewise the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) who has been chosen by him, remains truly observant of his vow (*vraty eva*) even during the "subsequent engagement" (*anuyoga*), that is, even while under the vow of non-eating. He does not have a broken vow. By the phrase "even meat," it is indicated: "how much more so anything else he might eat?
Likewise.
One who is afflicted by disease, one who has performed a sacrifice according to the rules, and likewise one invited to a śrāddha—these four may eat meat; this enumeration has been proclaimed.

"In the case of disease" means when it can be cured only by eating meat. "According to rule" means that which is offered according to the rules for the *madhuparka* or *śrāddha* rites. "Offered" refers to the sacrifice involving animal slaughter (*paśubandha*); in that case, even a sacrificer, or a priest chosen by him who is observant of vows, may eat meat. This is an "exclusive specification" (*parisaṃkhyā*) regarding these four instances, serving as an exception to the general prohibition of eating meat. Others, however, say that in the context of a vow of non-eating, one should merely smell the meat at a *śrāddha*. Thus says Jātūkarṇya: "But one who has desisted from honey and meat should perform the ritual acts at a *śrāddha*."
"By smelling the fragrance contained in the vessel, one becomes free from debt to the ancestors.

Here, "contained in the vessel" refers to that which rests upon the meat and other offerings placed in the eating vessel. By the phrase "free from debt to the ancestors," it is indicated that the ancestors attain satisfaction both from the consumption of the food they have partaken of and from its scent.
Thus it is stated in the *Brahmavaivarta*:
Whatever is offered here to all the ancestors and the twice-born,
by eating that very thing, a human being indeed gratifies the ancestors.

And this meal, when one has the capacity, should be taken until satiety; however, in the absence of that, one should take a little from each of the foods consumed by the ancestors, combine them into a single morsel even if it is only the size of one mouthful, and then eat. Regarding this, Āpastamba says:
"Having taken portions from all [the foods], he should eat at least one mouthful of the remainder with the subsequent *yajus* formula."
"Established in the vital breath, I offer the immortal; may my self [attain] immortality in Brahman.
This subsequent *yajus* verse declares the necessity of eating.
For this very reason, Vyāsa states the prohibition against fasting on the day of a *śrāddha*.
On the day of the Sun, during a solar transit, on the eleventh day of the dark fortnight, during an eclipse,
or when a Vyatīpāta yoga occurs, a householder who has sons should not fast after having performed a Śrāddha.
Devala, however, has also spoken of the fault in fasting:
"If a Brahmin, having given at a *śrāddha*, never eats thereafter,
the gods do not accept the sacrificial offerings (*havis*), nor do the ancestors accept the ancestral oblations (*kavya*)."

On the day of fasting, the performer of the *śrāddha* must indeed smell all that has been partaken by the ancestors; this position as well has been established with reasoned deliberation in the *Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa*: "O Nārada, when the day of fasting arrives and there is a *śrāddha* for the ancestors or any other [rite], listen then to how it should be performed."
The violation of a vow is a great sin; by serving that which remains after being released, one incurs this fault.
Listen now as I describe what must indeed be done in that regard.
Having gathered all the food with the right hand, one should then perform the smelling;
otherwise, there would be a violation of the vow.
"But if the smelling [of the food] is not performed, O best of sages, O Nārada, the śrāddha is rendered void by him; he becomes a slayer of his mother and a slayer of his father.
Knowing this, a means was devised by the wise twice-born. Thus it is said.
Vyāsa also said: "When a fast is obligatory and a *śrāddha* is occasional,
one should then perform the fast after having smelled that which has been partaken by the ancestors."
By the term "occasional" (*naimittika*), it is indicated that on the day of fasting for a compulsory ancestral rite (*nitya-śrāddha*), smelling [the food] should not be performed.
This was stated in the *Prabhāsakhaṇḍa* with reference to the fast of the Śivarātri vow:
"O Goddess of Gods, even the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) [is forbidden] when the day of Śiva has arrived."
It is said to be equal to eating what is forbidden; how much more so, then, any other action of mine?
Whenever there is a Śrāddha on the fourteenth day, as well as an occasional (naimittika) rite, one should then observe a fast after having smelled that which was partaken by the ancestors.

Thus, when a fast is observed on a Śivarātri-Ekādaśī, which yields great merit, or when it is abandoned, which incurs much sin, one should simply perform the smelling (of the food). However, on an occasion where neither of these two applies, one should perform the smelling, or take food unasked, or eat only one meal.
For this very reason, the specific fruits of each of these—fasting, eating unasked, and eating one meal—are stated individually in the *Prabhāsakhaṇḍa*:
"If a *śrāddha* should somehow occur on the day of fasting..."

By fasting, one obtains the merit of the sacrifice called Aśvamedha; by eating only when not invited, that of the Rājasūya; by eating only once a day, the eater obtains the merit born of the Vājapeya and the Agnihotra.

The merit arising from the *agnihotra* sacrifice is the remainder [of the sentence]. Therefore, it is established that on the day of fasting, if a *śrāddha* has been performed, one must either smell the remaining food or eat it.
Regarding the time for eating in that case, Jātūkarṇya says:
"On the very same day, however, the twice-born must eat once the *śrāddha* has been performed."
Otherwise, the ancestral rite becomes demonic when one partakes of food cooked by others.
In the *Nāgarakhaṇḍa*: "Therefore, one should offer the *bali* and then partake of food;
O lord of men, this should be done in silence for as long as the sun remains in view."
And if a man who performs a *śrāddha* eats when the sun has set, that *śrāddha* goes to waste; therefore, one should not feed [the guests] at night.
Thus concludes the consumption of the remnants.
Thus concludes the primary ritual procedure for the *pārvaṇa* śrāddha.
Now follow the secondary ritual procedures for the *pārvaṇa* śrāddha.
Regarding this, Kātyāyana states that for one who is unable to perform the primary rite, the performance may be carried out by means of a secondary substitute:
"Since the Vedic injunction must be fulfilled, it should be performed even by way of a secondary substitute."
Therefore, when the time for the śrāddha has arrived, one should give according to one's ability.
Śātātapa states that even when one performs a secondary alternative (*anukalpa*) due to the impossibility of the primary rite, the primary fruit is attained:
"In cases such as the waning of the moon, one should perform the obligatory rites by any means possible;
even in the absence of suitable recipients, materials, and so forth, he shall obtain the primary fruit."

"In whatever way possible" means with some reduction of constituent parts. "Obligatory rites" (*nityāni*) refers to those prescribed as to be performed for as long as one lives, such as the *darśapūrṇamāsa*, the *piṇḍapitṛyajña*, the *śrāddha*, and so forth. "At the waning of the moon and other times" refers to the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) and other such occasions. "Vessels" (*pātrāṇi*) refers to Brāhmaṇas possessing the previously mentioned characteristics. "Substance" (*dravya*) refers to honey, meat, milk-rice (*pāyasa*), boiled rice, soup, vegetables, and the like.
In the *Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa*: "He who performs a substitute *śrāddha* (anukalpa) in consideration of his caste, condition, and so forth..."
Even that man who possesses faith obtains the primary fruit of the śrāddha.

‘With respect to caste (*jātyapekṣayā*): for example, a Śūdra, with regard to his own Śūdra status, performs a *śrāddha* that is deficient in limbs consisting of mantras and deficient in limbs consisting of cooked food, taking the form of a secondary option (*anukalpa*); or likewise, a woman performs one deficient in mantras. Although such a *śrāddha* is indeed the primary (*mukhya*) one for women and Śūdras, nevertheless, in comparison to the primary *śrāddha* performed by the twice-born (*dvija*), it is designated here by the term ‘secondary option’ because of its deficiency in limbs, as if it were being performed by the twice-born themselves. ‘With respect to circumstance (*avasthāpekṣayā*): for example, one who is uninitiated (*anupanīta*), one who is without a wife (*apatnīka*), or a traveler (*pravāsī*) performs either an *āmānnam* (raw-food) or *hema-śrāddha* (gold-based *śrāddha*) while being devoid of mantras. By the word ‘etcetera’ (*ādi*), the requirement of the absence of suitable recipients, materials, and so forth is also included.
Vyāsa states that one who possesses the capacity for the primary performance, yet performs the secondary alternative, does not obtain the fruit of the ritual action:
"He who is capable of the primary rule but proceeds by means of the secondary alternative certainly does not obtain its fruit in the hereafter."

In this case, when there is an absence of multiple Brahmins and when food sufficient for feeding multiple Brahmins is unavailable, one should perform the *ṣaḍdaivatyam* (rite for six deities) *ṣaṭpiṇḍa-śrāddha* with only a single Brahmin.
Likewise, it is stated in the *Prabhāsakhaṇḍa*:
"In the event of a lack of resources or the unavailability of twice-born [Brahmins], I shall explain the procedure according to its true nature."
For even with a single Brahmin, one should perform the Śrāddha rite consisting of six balls of rice.
One should cause six blades of *darbha* grass to be given to him, and likewise offer a seat to the six;
one should also invoke the six there and likewise offer oblation to the six.

The phrase "non-availability of twice-born" refers to the non-availability of multiple twice-born men. And when one should perform the rite for six deities with only a single Brahmin, then one should invite a Brahmin endowed with all excellent qualities.
For it is said in the Kūrma Purāṇa:
"Or else, one may feed a single Brahmin who has mastered the Vedas."
One who is endowed with learning, virtuous conduct, and other such qualities, yet is devoid of auspicious marks.

For even when a Śrāddha for the six deities is being performed by a single Brāhmaṇa, it must indeed be performed together with the Vaiśvadevika rite. Regarding that, Vasiṣṭha states the manner of performing the Vaiśvadevika even in the absence of a second twice-born guest: "If one should feed only a single person at a Śrāddha, how should the portion for the gods (daiva) be handled there?"
Having set aside food from all that has been prepared into a vessel,
and having placed it in a temple of the deities, one should then proceed with the śrāddha.

The meaning is that one should proceed with the *śrāddha*, the rite for the ancestors, as follows: having set aside a portion from each type of food prepared for the present *śrāddha*, and having placed a vessel in a place suitable for the Vaiśvadeva deities—namely, a spot where the twice-born are seated—one should serve the food therein. Then, having invoked the Viśvedevas upon their respective seats and meditated upon them as if they were standing before one, one should mutter the mantra beginning with "The earth is your vessel" (*pṛthivī te pātram*). Having said, "To the Viśvedevas known as Purūravas and Ārdrava, this food, Svāhā! Om Tat Sat," one should commence the ancestral rite.
In the *Kūrmapurāṇa*:
"Having set aside from all the food prepared that which is in the vessel,
one should offer it to these deities in the temple and then proceed with the rest."
Śaṅkha also said:
"Alternatively, one should feed even a single Brāhmaṇa who purifies the assembly;
having first prepared the food offering for the gods, one should then present it to him."
"In the place of that brahmin representing the ancestors," Śātātapa says:
"Having paid homage to the gods, one should first cause the portion to be offered."

"Previously" means before [the offering] to the ancestors; "portion" refers to the food to be given to them. However, in the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*, the installation of the fire is prescribed in the place of the Vaiśvadeva offering:
"When there is only one Brahmin and a second is not available..."
In rites for the ancestors, the Brahmin should be appointed; but in rites for the gods, one should appoint the fire.
Regarding this ancestral rite (*pitrya*), Bṛhaspati states the manner of resolving upon the food:
"If, however, because the substance available is very small, one should feed only a single person at the *śrāddha*,
one should take out small portions from each [of the intended recipients] and present that food to him."

From a collection of various kinds of food sufficient to satisfy a single Brāhmaṇa, one should repeatedly take portions from that same kind of food to prepare six separate groups. Having served each group either upon a single dish or in a single vessel, one should offer each group to each of the deities of the Śrāddha—beginning with the ancestors—in their proper order. Alternatively, one may take small portions from the very same collection of food and, mentally conceiving them as distinct, offer them. Having consecrated the food for the gods and the ancestors respectively and performed the recitation of the Gāyatrī and other rites, a specific disposal (*pratipatti*) of the Vaiśvadeva food must be performed at the time when the Brāhmaṇas invited for the ancestors are eating.
Vasiṣṭha said to him:
"One should consume that food in the fire, or else give it to a celibate student (brahmacārin). [In the] Kūrmapurāṇa:
Then he should eat the food, or else give it to a student (brahmacārin) into the fire.
The word "then" (tataḥ) means having performed the ancestral rite (pitrya) up until the point of receiving permission to eat.
Regarding this, Śātātapa describes the manner of satisfying several ancestors through a single Brāhmaṇa.
But if there is only one Brahmin at a śrāddha and the food prepared is very little,
and since three ancestors are said to be invited, how can those three be satisfied?
The ancestors eat from the chest; the grandfathers from the left side;
the great-grandfathers from the right; and the descendants follow from behind.

The "followers" (*anuyāyinaḥ*) are the wife of the father and others. Regarding the term "followers," there is an alternative reading, *piṇḍatarkakāḥ*, which should be explained as referring to the great-grandfather and others who are entitled to a portion of the *piṇḍa*-leavings. Furthermore, according to the *Prabhāsakhaṇḍa* and the *Devalasmṛti*: "The father eats from the hand of the twice-born; the grandfather eats from [his] mouth."

The great-grandfather is said to reside in the palate, the maternal grandfather in the throat; the maternal great-grandfather is in the heart, while the elder [maternal great-great-grandfather] is situated in the navel. Thus it is said.
"Vṛddhaḥ" refers to the great-grandfather.
Regarding this, it is stated in the *Prabhāsakhaṇḍa* that even if a single Brāhmaṇa cannot be found, another alternative procedure (*anukalpa*) should be followed:
"O beloved, in the absence of a Brāhmaṇa, a young student (*baṭu*) made of kuśa grass should be employed."
In this manner, one should perform the *śrāddha* for the six deities with a concentrated mind.
However, he who should effect a division [of the rite] becomes a slayer of his ancestors (*pitṛhā*).

"Made of *kuśa*" (*kauśa*) means consisting of *kuśa* grass; a "boy" (*baṭu*) is a small human effigy. Having conceptualized that boy as a Brahmin, one should perform the entire *śrāddha*. "Division" (*vibhakti*) means the cutting or the omission of the ritual act; one must not do that.
Devala states the procedure for the *śrāddha* involving young students (*baṭu*):
"Having placed the student-representatives made of *darbha* grass upon their seats, being composed in mind,
he should carry out the ritual procedure joined with the primary and secondary injunctions."

"On seats" means on those suitable for the Brāhmaṇas to sit upon. "Welcome to you; I shall perform the Śrāddha; please grant me leave for the Śrāddha; I shall invoke the gods and the ancestors; I shall perform the *agnaukaraṇa* (offering into the fire)"—such questions are "directions" (*praiṣāḥ*). Their answers are "subsequent directions" (*anupraiṣāḥ*). One should personally perform the "procedure" (*vidhānam*) consisting of both of these, which is the section on the ritual requirements (*itikartavyatā*) of the Śrāddha. In that regard, he himself also states what must be done with the food intended for the rite:
"In the absence of [proper] vessels, a man, having performed the ritual procedure for the Pitṛyajña..."
Even after pointing out the food and setting it aside, one's destination is determined by the vessel from which it was taken.
"In the absence of a vessel, one should cast [the offering] into the fire, or give it to a cow, or likewise into water;

for there is no omission of what has been obtained, especially that which pertains to the ancestors. Thus it is said. And in the event of the unavailability of the primary substances, there are other secondary alternatives as well.
In this regard, those called *āmaśrāddhas* are described here in the *Parāśara-smṛti*, the *Viṣṇu-purāṇa*, and the *Vārāha-purāṇa*:
"One who is incapable of giving cooked food may, according to his ability, give grain."
One should indeed bestow even a very small sacrificial fee upon the twice-born.

The meaning of this is as follows: In the absence of cooked food, one should offer to the invited twice-born (dvijas) the very grains—such as barley, wheat, rice, and so forth—which serve as the raw materials for the food suitable for a *śrāddha*, dedicating them to the Viśvedevas and the ancestors (*pitṛs*) and treating them as if they were cooked food. Since grain is not directly edible, there would otherwise be an omission of the entire category of religious duties associated with the meal; this is indicated by the word *āśa* (that which is eaten), which qualifies the grain. This signifies that once those Brahmins have returned to their own homes, they should make that grain fit for eating and consume it, but must not employ it for any other purpose. Otherwise, the term *āśa* would be meaningless.
Regarding this, Vyāsa states a specific rule concerning the agent:
"Gold alone that is received for a *śrāddha* from a Kṣatriya or others may be employed at will; the Brāhmaṇa himself may consume it."

Regarding the phrase "from a Kṣatriya and so forth," this refers to Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Mūrdhāvasiktas, and others. Although it is stated here in general terms that "it may be employed as one pleases," nevertheless, it must not be employed in rites such as the Śrāddha; for it is improper to make a renunciation intended for one deity after it has already been renounced for another deity. Therefore, it should be understood that while it may be employed in worldly matters such as eating from a vessel or performing actions, it may also be employed in non-worldly matters—such as ritual fees (dakṣiṇā) prescribed by Śruti and Smṛti—for obligatory (nitya) and occasional (naimittika) rites. However, regarding what is obtained from a Brāhmaṇa, it is restricted by the rule "by himself alone. Here, one should not think the restriction means that whatever is accepted must be eaten by him alone; rather, it should be determined that he should eat it himself until satisfied, and thereafter perform the appropriate disposal of the Śrāddha remnant for another. Regarding what is accepted from a Śūdra, however, it should not be employed in any obligatory or occasional rite, but should be used only for one's own food or the food of others; thus it is stated in the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*.
Whatever raw food from a Śūdra is accepted as part of a Śrāddha offering,
all of that is fit for consumption, but not so for obligatory or occasional rites.
Regarding this, Vyāsa states the quantity of grain to be given and the procedure:

"O son of Kuntī, one should give uncooked grain, or one should give cooked food four times that amount; whatever rule applies to cooked food, that same rule applies to the *āma-śrāddha* (the śrāddha with uncooked grain)."
O Bhārata, all rites beginning with the invocation (āvāhana) should be performed, as well as the offering of the rice-balls (piṇḍa).
Whatever one gives to the twice-born, whether it be cooked or uncooked,
with that one should perform the rite of making offerings in the fire (agnaukaraṇa), and with that very same substance one should offer the rice-balls.
In the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*, another alternative regarding the offering of funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*) is also stated:
"At that time, the performer of the śrāddha who knows the rule should perform an *āma-śrāddha*;
he should perform the *agnaukaraṇa* rite in the hand of the Brahmin according to the injunction."

"Fourfold" means that one should give four times as much grain as is required to prepare enough food to satisfy each individual Brahmin; this is the meaning. Regarding the inability to give fourfold, an alternative has been stated by that same author:
"O son of Kuntī, for one giving raw grain, that gift becomes twofold, threefold, or even fourfold, but one should never bestow only a single portion."
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "invocation and so forth," the offering of *arghya* and other rites are included. Thus it is said in the *Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa*:
"The invocation should be performed, and likewise the offering of *arghya*."
This very same rule applies wherever a śrāddha ceremony is performed.
In the *Kūrmapurāṇa* and the *Yamapurāṇa*:
"A Brāhmaṇa who is beset by calamities may subsist perpetually on raw grain;
with that he should perform the *agnaukaraṇa* rite, and with that very same substance he should offer the funeral cakes (*piṇḍas*)."
In the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*, another alternative regarding the offering of rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) has also been stated:
"When one performs an *āma-śrāddha* (a śrāddha with raw grains), how should the offering of rice-balls be performed?
Having set aside a portion from the household cooking, it should be done with barley meal (*saktu*) or with milk-rice (*pāyasa*)."
Free from envy, one should offer balls of food along with sesame seeds according to what is available.
Even the scattering of food and other such acts must be performed with raw materials alone. Thus says Pracetas:
"One who offers a raw-food śrāddha [should offer] the rice-balls as well as that which is the offering into the fire."
Whatever may be offered there as part of the ancestral rite (śrāddha), one should give that very thing there with that same [intention].

The meaning is that whatever else there may be, such as scattered offerings (vikira) and so forth, that too must be performed with raw food alone. Regarding the ritual for an Āmaśrāddha, it is recorded in the Smṛti: "In the invocation, in the utterance of Svadhā, and at the dismissal, the mantras are to be recited; in other rites they are not to be modified. This is the prescribed rule.

In the invocation mantra *atta vaḥ*, the modification (*ūha*) is *svīkarta vaḥ*. In the *svadhākāra* mantra beginning with *namo vaḥ pitaraḥ*, the word *iṣaḥ* is to be modified to *āmadravyasya*. Regarding the dismissal mantra *vāje vāje*, the meaning is that the word *tṛptāḥ* must be modified to *tarpasva*. Furthermore, it has already been stated previously that even when cooked food is available, a Śūdra should perform an *āma-śrāddha* (a śrāddha with raw grains). The procedure for its performance is shown in the *Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa*: "If Śūdras who desire merit and know the dharma perform [it]..."
And the mantra for the offering into the fire is prescribed as being one of salutation (namaskāra).
Listen to how the invocation and other rites should be performed by a Śūdra:
for the gods and deities, as well as for the ancestors, one should offer the funeral cakes (piṇḍas) and so forth by name and lineage; O hero, likewise by name and lineage.

"Namaskāraḥ" means the word "namaḥ. "Homage to Agni Kavyavāhana; homage to Soma Pitṛmat. The phrase "in the *agnaukaraṇa*" is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*); this very mantra is to be used elsewhere as well. Thus, with reference to the Śūdra, it is stated in the *Matsyapurāṇa* and other texts:
"One should not omit the five sacrifices by means of the mantra consisting of a salutation (*namaskāra*)."
And this mantra is prescribed for the Śūdra by way of excluding other mantras. Thus, the exclusion of other mantras for him is stated in the *Matsyapurāṇa*:
"The entire śrāddha must likewise be performed by the Śūdra;
indeed, everything is ordained for the Śūdra except for the mantras."

"In the same way" means precisely according to the procedure for the *pārvaṇa* śrāddha. Since the *gotra* (lineage) does not exist for Śūdras in general, this mention of *gotra* here must refer to those Śūdras born of the twice-born (*dvija*). Alternatively, based on the Vedic revelation, "Therefore they say: all progeny are descended from Kaśyapa," the *gotra* for all Śūdras should indeed be Kāśyapa. For this very reason, Vyāghrapāda established the rule: "But when the *gotra* is lost, [the *gotra* is] Kaśyapa. Furthermore, if even raw rice (*āmānna*) is unavailable, a śrāddha with gold (*hemaśrāddha*) should be performed. And so says Marīci:
But even in the absence of cooked food, a wise man should perform the śrāddha with gold of great luster that is four times the value of the grain.

The meaning is as follows: in an *āma-śrāddha*, for each individual Brāhmaṇa, four times as much grain as is given should be given; and in a *hema-śrāddha*, for each individual Brāhmaṇa, that amount of gold which can be obtained for the same quantity of money as was used for the grain should be given. Here, although the various options regarding the doubling of grain and so forth in an *āma-śrāddha* have been set forth by considering the relative degrees of one's capacity, the specific measure of gold is understood by implication in accordance with those very principles, even though it has not been explicitly stated. Dharmasvāmin, however, says:
"Grain is declared to be double [the value], and gold likewise fourfold."
In the absence of food for the twice-born, and especially for the Brāhmaṇa, [one may take what is necessary].

The meaning is that for each individual Brahmin, one should give four times as much gold as the amount of grain obtained that is sufficient to satisfy him. By this, it is stated that twice the amount of gold should be given compared to the double amount of grain.
As stated in the *Bhaviṣyottara*:
"In the absence of food, in the absence of Brahmins, during travel abroad, or upon the birth of a son..."
And likewise, the Hema-śrāddha may be performed in a gathering, as well as for women and Śūdras.

Vyāsa says: In the absence of ritual materials, in the absence of twice-born brahmins, during travel abroad, upon the birth of a son, or when one's wife is menstruating, one should perform a *hema-śrāddha* (a śrāddha with gold).
An exception to the golden *śrāddha* is mentioned in the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*:
"In the absence of food, in the absence of twice-born [guests], during travel abroad, or upon the birth of a son—
one should perform the golden *śrāddha*, with the exception of the day of the new moon (*kṣayāha*)."

In this context, wherever the *āmāśrāddha* (funeral rite with raw food) is prescribed in other *Smṛtis* and other *Purāṇas*, the *hemaśrāddha* (rite with gold) being prescribed there should be interpreted as applying only when raw food materials are unavailable. For in this way, the eightfold fault of an optional alternative (*vikalpa*) between raw food and gold will not arise. Furthermore, since grain—which is an internal constituent of the *śrāddha* injunction by virtue of being the primary material for food—is to be employed first when available, its prior use over gold, which is an external element, is thereby supported. Thus, even when both cooked and raw food are present on the occasion of a *śrāddha* performed for the birth of a son, the *hemaśrāddha* alone is to be performed.
For this very reason, Saṃvarta says:
"Upon the birth of a son, a wise man should perform a Śrāddha;
he who desires auspicious things should do so neither with cooked food nor with raw food."
The method for offering the rice-balls (piṇḍas) is also shown here in the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa itself:
"Having taken [food] from the household cooking, one should always perform the offering of rice-balls with barley-meal or milk-rice once the golden Śrāddha has been performed."
A Śūdra, however, should offer those funeral cakes using food cooked in his own home;
it is traditionally taught that for him, they may consist of parched grain flour, roots, fruit, or milk-rice.
The phrase "for the purpose of offering the piṇḍas" is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence].
In the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*:
"There is no invitation (*nimantraṇa*), no pouring into the fire (*agnaukaraṇa*), and no transformation (*vikāra*) is offered at all."
No one at all should even pose a question regarding satisfaction in this matter.
Having stated that grain received at a *śrāddha* performed by a *śūdra* must not be employed for obligatory (*nitya*) or occasional (*naimittika*) rites, the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata* declares:
"However, gold received at such a *śrāddha* does not incur any fault;
one may perform the obligatory rites with it, for gold is not called 'food' (*anna*)."

However, he who is unable to perform the *śrāddha*—which involves various procedures such as the offering of rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) and is characterized by many constituent parts such as the extensive rites of invocation (*āvāhana*) and so forth—should perform a *sāṃkalpa-śrāddha*. Thus says Saṃvarta:
"But he who is unable to perform the complete *pārvaṇa* here..."
Furthermore, it is ordained for him at the proper time according to the rule of intention.
The renunciation of food intended for the alms-bowl is called the *saṃkalpa*.
Whatever ritual procedure (*vidhi*) is prompted by that [renunciation] is designated by it;
when connected with only that much, the rite is called a *māṅgalya-śrāddha*.
Regarding this, Vyāsa states which principal or subsidiary elements are not to be performed:
"When one performs the *sāṃkalpa* (the formal resolve), one should not perform the filling of the vessels;
there should be no invocation (*āvāhana*), no offering into the fire (*agnaukaraṇa*), and one should not cause the rice-balls (*piṇḍas*) to be given."

The vessel should not be filled with water and other substances for the *arghya*; the meaning is that the *arghya* offering itself should not be given. Furthermore, the invocation (*āvāhana*) accompanied by mantras is prohibited, but not the mere act of invocation; for without that, there would be no presence of the deity, and consequently, the completion of the *śrāddha* would be impossible. Some, however, stating that even the scattering of food (*vikira*) should not be performed during the *śrāddha*, cite a certain statement for corroboration: "When one does not perform the *śrāddha* through formal resolve (*sāṃkalpa*), [there should be] filling of the vessel."
"One should not scatter food offerings, nor should one cast away the rice-balls. Thus it is said.

Chāgaleya states that even one capable of performing the rites beginning with the invocation (*āvāhana*) and the offering into the fire (*agnaukaraṇa*), should at times perform the *śrāddha* by means of the rite of formal resolve (*saṃkalpa-vidhi*) alone:
"Whenever the offering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) is omitted during the *Maghā* asterism or other such occasions,
the twice-born man should then perform the *śrāddha* through a formal resolve, according to the rule and with faith."
Regarding the specific agent, Vyāsa states that the *saṃkalpa-śrāddha* is mandatory:
"For one who has renounced the sacred fires, there is neither the *pārvaṇa*, nor the *ekoddiṣṭa*, nor the *sapiṇḍana*.
But for one who has not renounced the fires, there is the mention of the *piṇḍa*; therefore, having made the *saṃkalpa*, one should feed [the Brahmins]."

Since the performance of the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* śrāddha is prescribed specifically for one who has not abandoned the sacred fires (*atyaktāgni*), the meaning is that one who has abandoned the fires (*tyaktāgni*) should perform only the *saṃkalpa* śrāddha.
As stated in the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*:
"When a Brahmin is without fire (*anagnika*), or likewise when his fires have been extinguished (*utsannāgni*)."
Then, having performed the ritual intention (saṃkalpa) for all the prosperity rites, one should perform the Śrāddha.

However, it is understood here by implication that one who maintains the sacred fires (sāgnika) should perform the *vṛddhiśrāddha* according to the procedure of formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*), joined with the offering of rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) mixed with jujube fruits (*badara*) and other items. But when one performs the *śrāddha* due to an inability to include all its constituent parts (*aṅga*), Vyāsa states a specific request to be made to the Brāhmaṇas:
"When one is unable to perform the constituent parts of the ancestral sacrifice (*pitṛyajña*), one should then cause the Brāhmaṇas to recite: 'May there be complete success.'"

As for the manner of recitation: when the sacrificer has said, "May all success attend this *śrāddha*; may you [Brāhmaṇas] say so," the Brāhmaṇas should reply, "May all success attend it. Devala states the secondary rule (*anukalpa*) in the event that both kinds of cooked food—cooked grain and raw grain—in quantities sufficient for the feeding of the Brāhmaṇas are unavailable, or when Brāhmaṇas suitable for the entire *śrāddha* cannot be found: "In the absence of both materials and Brāhmaṇas, a mere funeral cake (*piṇḍa*) should be offered."
But when the day of the śrāddha has arrived, he may even remain without food.
In the *Bhaviṣyottara*, however, the gift of a water-pot and other items is also mentioned:
"If one is unable [to give much], one should give even a little, such as a water-pot, to a twice-born;
or one may give a dwelling, or else offer a funeral cake (*piṇḍa*)."
Or, having bathed with a concentrated mind, he should satisfy the ancestors with water mixed with sesame seeds;
or, when the time for the śrāddha has arrived, he should burn dry grass with fire;
or he should fast on that day, or recite the Śrāddhasaṃhitā.
However, one should give according to one's ability when the time for the Śrāddha ceremony arrives.
‘Kakṣa’ means a mountain cave; ‘śrāddhasaṃhitā’ refers to the ritual manual for the śrāddha ceremony together with all its mantras. Vṛddhavasiṣṭha says:
“But one who is unable [to give much] should give even a little, such as a water-pot and so forth, to a twice-born.”
One should give grass to a cow, or otherwise offer funeral cakes;
or, preceded by a ritual bath, one should satisfy the ancestors with sesame seeds and *darbha* grass.

In the *Kūrma Purāṇa*: "Even a destitute twice-born man, having bathed with a composed mind, should gratify the ancestors with water mixed with sesame seeds, even if he can only do so with roots or *kuśa* grass."
Hārīta says:
Even with roots, or fruits, or likewise with water-libations, one should perform [the rite] when [other materials] are unavailable; however, one must not neglect that which has been obtained.
Devala says: Whatever libation an *āhitāgni* performs with water day by day,
by that very act he obtains the fruit of the annual and other rites dedicated to the ancestors.
Satyavrata says:
One may bring satisfaction to the ancestors through vegetables, roots, fruits, cooked food, clothing, cattle, land, gold, or even water, or by conversing with Brahmins.
"From the agreement with a Brahmin" means by the permission of any Brahmin whatsoever.
In the *Kālikā Purāṇa*:
"In the absence of food, whatever a man eats himself, even if it be fruits..."
Therefore, one desiring the satisfaction of the ancestors should perform the Śrāddha rite.

In the Vārāha Purāṇa: Even there, one who is lacking in capacity should bow down and give sesame seeds held in the tips of his hands to the foremost of the twice-born, specifically intending them for the ancestors.
Bowing with devotion and composed in mind, one should offer a handful of water mixed with seven or eight sesame seeds, dedicated to the ancestors.
Having obtained anything from anywhere— even a cow's daily fodder—
from cows, one should, endowed with faith, give it to Brahmins for the sake of the ancestors.
In the absence of everything, having gone to the forest, one should point toward the root of a *skanda* tree.
"Kakṣāmūlapradarśakaḥ" is an alternative reading.
A wise person should recite this aloud before the world-protectors, beginning with Indra:
"I have no wealth, no riches, nor anything else."
Therefore, I am here for the sake of the ancestral rites for my own forefathers;
may my ancestors be satisfied by this devotion, as I have raised these two arms upon the path of the wind.
Thus all this has been told; O twice-born one, he who, being devoted to filial piety toward his ancestors, performs this, by him indeed the śrāddha is truly accomplished.
From the Purāṇa:
A man who is dependent on others, a traveler, or even one who is destitute,
should perform the Śrāddha with water and sesame seeds through a mind endowed with devotion.
Likewise, it has been stated in another Smṛti by way of an illustration:
"Whatever one may not be able to accomplish by speech or action in any way,
all that the wise man should accomplish through the mind, as in the case of the ancestral sacrifice (pitṛyajña)."
Thus end the procedures for the *pārvaṇa* Śrāddha according to the secondary alternatives.

Thus [ends] the *Pariśeṣakhaṇḍa* in the *Caturvargacintāmaṇi*, composed by the illustrious Hemādri, the scholar (*paṇḍita*) and lord of all learned men (*karṇādhipati*), who is the servant of the illustrious Mahādevīya, the illustrious Great King of Kings (*mahārājādhirāja*).
In the Śrāddhakalpa, the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Primary and Secondary Rites for the Pārvaṇa Śrāddha."
[1537] Now begins the seventeenth chapter:
[on honoring] those advanced in learning and other virtues with various forms of service.
He who brings joy and bestows delight,
that Hemādri Sūri, the master of the Karaṇa,
now declares the procedure for the Śrāddha rite performed on the occasion of prosperity (Vṛddhi).
Now follows the procedure for the *vṛddhi-śrāddha*.

In that regard, this *śrāddha* should be performed after first installing the deities of the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) and the family deities (*kuladevatā*), performing the worship of the *mātṛkās*, and offering the stream of clarified butter (*vasordhārā*).
Thus it is stated in the *Caturviṃśatimata*:
When an occasion for prosperity has arrived, the installation of deities is prescribed;
it is the cause of increase for the worlds, as ordained by the customs of castes and the traditions of families.

When the *ābhyudayika-śrāddha* (prosperity rite) is set forth as that which is to be performed, the installation of deities—prescribed in the Vedas and other scriptures according to the classification of castes such as Brāhmaṇas and Kṣatriyas, and taught by family elders—is recorded as a duty. For that is the cause of the world's prosperity and a succession of auspicious events. Immediately following this, the worship of the Mothers (*mātṛ-pūjana*) must be performed.
Thus it is said in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*:
"First, however, the Mothers, together with Gaṇeśvara, should indeed be worshipped with devotion."
And this worship of the Mothers, as well as their names, is stated in the *Caturviṃśatimata*:
"Three are to be worshipped on the father’s side, and three are to be worshipped on the mother’s side;
these are declared to be the Mothers, with the father’s sister as the eighth."
The seven goddesses beginning with Brahmāṇī, Durgā, Kṣetrapāla, and Gaṇādhipa are traditionally remembered;
they should always be worshipped first for prosperity, followed by the Nāndīmukha ancestors.
Gaurī, Padmā, Sacī, Dakṣā, Sāvitrī, Vijayā, Jayā, Devasenā, Svadhā, Svāhā, the Mothers, and the Mothers of the World— these,
together with one’s own tutelary deity, are to be worshipped at the time of prosperity.

"In the paternal line" (*pituḥ pakṣe*), meaning among the group of ancestors, "three"—namely the mother, paternal grandmother, and paternal great-grandmother—are to be worshipped. Likewise, "in the maternal line" (*mātṛke*), meaning among the group of maternal ancestors, "three"—namely the maternal grandmother, maternal paternal grandmother, and maternal paternal great-grandmother—are to be worshipped. "The paternal aunt as the seventh and the maternal aunt as the eighth" (*pitṛmātṛṣvasāṣṭamī*): the paternal aunt is the seventh and the maternal aunt is the eighth to be worshipped. Thus, these eight are declared to be the mothers of men; they, being manifest, are to be worshipped directly with saffron, flowers, garments, ornaments, and food. However, those who are unmanifest are to be worshipped by invoking them upon heaps of unbroken rice (*akṣata*) and so forth, just like the divine mothers (*devamātṛ*) to be described later. "The seven beginning with Brahmāṇī are remembered": Brāhmī, Vaiṣṇavī, Māheśvarī, Aindrī, Vārāhī, Kaumārī, and Cāmuṇḍā—these are the seven divine mothers (*devamātṛ*). Likewise, "Durgā, Kṣetrapati, and Gaṇādhipa": having worshipped Durgā, the Lord of the Field (*kṣetrādhipa*), and the Lord of the Ganas (*gaṇādhipa*) with the sixteen services (*upacāras*) prior to the *vṛddhi-śrāddha*, one should afterwards worship the *nāndīmukha* ancestors with the *śrāddha*. "One's own deity" (*ātmadevatā*) refers to the family deity of one's own lineage; these [ancestors] are to be worshipped together with that. In another scripture, however, eight [divine mothers] are shown: Brāhmī, Māheśī, Kaumārī, Vaiṣṇavī, Vārāhī, Indrāṇī, Cāmuṇḍā, and Mahālakṣmī are declared to be the Mothers (*mātaraḥ*).
Śātātapa said:
Gaurī, Padmā, Śacī, Medhā, Sāvitrī, Vijayā, Jayā, Devasenā, Svadhā, Svāhā, the Mothers, and the Mothers of the World.
Dhṛti, Puṣṭi, and Tuṣṭi, together with Ātmadevatā—
to these one should offer arghya, fragrance, flowers, incense, and a lamp.
And this worship of the Mothers must also be performed during the *śrāddha* that is an ancillary part of a ritual; thus it is stated in the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*:
"In all rituals and other rites, the Mothers together with the lords of their hosts must be worshipped with effort; when worshipped, they in turn bestow worship."
The basis for their worship, such as the manifestation of a stream of wealth (*vasordhārā*) and so forth, is also described in that very same place:
"Whether they are fashioned from auspicious materials, painted on cloths and the like, or even upon heaps of unbroken grains, [they are worshipped] with various kinds of food offerings."

One should cause five streams of clarified butter to flow against the wall, or seven streams; they should be neither too low nor too high. Being composed, one should recite there the *āyuṣya* mantras for the sake of peace.

‘Āyuṣyāṇi’ refers to hymns (sūktas) primarily consisting of benedictions such as “ā no bhadra,” as well as Sāmans based on similar mantras. ‘Therein’ means at the place where the worship of the Mothers (mātṛpūjā) and the stream of wealth (vasordhārā) have been performed.
Regarding the fault incurred by not performing this worship of the Mothers, the *Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa* shows:
“He who serves the Śrāddha meal without having performed the sacrifice to the Mothers...”
Filled with rage, they inflict terrible violence upon him.
The form of the Mothers according to their monthly manifestations is described in the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa:
"Seated upon a celestial chariot drawn by swans, holding a rosary and a water-pot,
she who has arrived as the power (śakti) of Brahmā is designated as Brahmāṇī."
Māheśvarī, mounted upon a bull, bearing the trident and the boon-granting gesture,
arrived with her great serpent-garment, adorned with the crescent moon.
Kaumārī, with a spear in her hand and mounted upon a noble peacock,
Ambikā in the form of Guha advanced to fight the Daityas.
In the same manner, the Vaiṣṇavī Śakti, seated upon Garuḍa and holding in her hands the conch, discus, mace, Śārṅga bow, and sword, approached.
The power of Hari, who assumes the incomparable form of the Sacrificial Boar,
also arrived there, assuming the body of Vārāhī.
Likewise, Vajrahastā and Aindrī are seated upon the king of elephants;
having attained a thousand eyes, she is just like Śakra himself.
In the first [chapter] of the Brahmapurāṇa:
"And Mahālakṣmī is to be fashioned as dancing and holding a skull-cup;
she is to be depicted on the full moon day of Kārtika, bearing a lofty khaṭvāṅga, three garlands, and a lotus."
From Kūṣmāṇḍī, however, Pretasthā was born, who had protruding teeth and curly hair on her head.
In the *Siddhārthapṛcchā*:
"She whose rays shine forth by means of the moon, the half-moon, the nine, the eyes, the sun, and the seer— that one is proclaimed as Padmā."
She who holds in the tips of her hands the parrot, the cake, the lotus, the fan, and likewise the sacrificial fuel, is celebrated by the name Śacī.
She who holds a fuel-stick in her hands even during the night and the rainy season,
and who moves about with a palm-leaf fan, she is called Medhā.
She whose hands hold a rosary, a sacrificial ladle, a spear, and a water-pot is celebrated as Sāvitrī.
She who holds in her hands, in successive order, a bow, an arghya-vessel, the yoga-mudrā, and a small sword, is celebrated as Durgā.
She who holds the yogamudrā, a bow, a vessel in due order,
and a sword, is proclaimed as Cāmuṇḍā.
She who holds a skull-cup, a vessel, nectar,
and a noose in her hands— she is proclaimed as Vijayā by the devotees.
Successively resting upon the navel, the skull, the nectar, and the noose, her fingertips triumph; she is indeed Jayā.
And as it is stated in the *Sāgarasaṃhitā*:
"One should meditate upon Puṣṭi-Lakṣmī, who holds a mirror, a lotus bud, and a full-blown lotus;
she is white, gentle, and seated upon a lotus throne."
One should meditate upon her holding a vajra, a lotus, a jewel, and nectar;
she is indeed Tuṣṭi-Mahālakṣmī, seated upon the vīrāsana.
[This concludes] the description of the form of the image of Vināyaka in the Matsya Purāṇa.
One should visualize him eating in his right hand and likewise holding a blue lotus in the other;
on the left side, one should arrange a sweetmeat ball and an axe,
joined with the goddesses Buddhi and Ṛddhi, and below them, accompanied by a mouse.

Thus, while the specific nature of certain Mothers has been shown in detail, the general form of all of them is stated in the *Mahāpañcarātra*: "They are to be worshipped in a painting or in an image, with their hands granting boons and fearlessness. Having thus performed everything from the consecration of the deity up to the stream of clarified butter (*vasordhārā*), one should commence the *nāndīśrāddha*.
Accordingly, it is said in the *Caturviṃśatimata*:
"Thereafter, one should begin the offering of the *śrāddha* to the six ancestors."
The entire rule taught by Vasiṣṭha should be observed here in its entirety, free from worldly desire.

‘Thereafter’ means after the worship of the mother and other preliminary rites. ‘To the three belonging to the paternal group and to the three belonging to the maternal grandfather’s group’—thus, to these six. ‘The rite prescribed by Vasiṣṭha’ refers to the procedure proclaimed by sages such as Vasiṣṭha. ‘Free from meat’ means devoid of *āmiṣa*, which is flesh. Furthermore, these two types of *śrāddha* should be performed with the *mātṛ-śrāddha* (the rite for the mothers) coming first.
Accordingly, Śātātapa states the sequence of the three *śrāddhas*:
“The *mātṛ-śrāddha* should come first, and immediately thereafter that of the fathers.”
Then, on the anniversary of the birth of one's maternal grandfathers, three Śrāddhas are prescribed.
In the Matsya Purāṇa as well: "The mothers are to be worshipped first, then the fathers;
thereafter the maternal grandfathers are to be worshipped, and likewise the Viśvedevas."
Vasiṣṭha said:
One should first provide for the mothers, immediately after that for the fathers,
and then one should perform the śrāddha for the maternal grandfathers in due order.
In this regard, some declare that there is also a fourth *śrāddha* dedicated to three deities, beginning with the maternal grandfather (*mātāmaha*).
Accordingly, it is stated in the *Caturviṃśatimata* after explaining the worship of the mothers:
"And thereafter, one should worship the *nāndīmukha* ancestors there."

Having honored the paternal ancestors beginning with the mother, and then the maternal grandfathers as well, some say that the maternal grandmothers should then be honored; thereafter, an even number of twice-born men should be fed.
In the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa:
"O hero, O best of bird-eaters, with his left hand, according to the rule,
he should offer [the oblation] to Mātṛ, Pramātṛ, and Tanmātṛ, facing the east."
O bird, one should offer those [oblations] according to the rule to the father and mother;
likewise, O bird, at the end, one should offer them to the grandmother and the great-grandmother.
Having thus intended the mothers, one should indeed offer the funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*) of the *śrāddha*.
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*:
"The maternal grandmothers ending with the great-grandmother are the Nāndīmukhī Mothers;
likewise the maternal grandmothers, paternal grandmothers, and great-paternal grandmothers."
In this regard, Vyāghra has shown the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) for the ritual procedure of the *śrāddha* for maternal grandmothers and others:
"Just as men are satisfied upon seeing their wives well-honored,
so too do the ancestors rejoice when their wives are honored here."
Śātātapa states the number of Brahmins for the *śrāddha* for the mother:
"For the mothers—the wives of the three ancestors beginning with the father—one should feed twice as many twice-born men."
Since this is called the *mātṛśrāddha* (ancestral rite for mothers) here, it belongs specifically to women.

With reference to the mothers, one [set] of Brahmins from among the group of women—numbered as four, etc., in pairs—should be fed. Thus, there are four for the group of mothers and four for the group of maternal grandmothers (*mātāmahī*), making eight in total;
for this very reason, it is stated in the *Bhaviṣyatpurāṇa*:
O Lord of Birds, one should feed eight twice-born men at the Śrāddha for the Mothers;
one should also feed a visiting twice-born man as the ninth, who represents all the deities.
This should be understood as applying when such persons are available; however, in their absence, two from each group should be fed.
But regarding the absence of Brāhmaṇas, it has been stated by Vṛddha-Vasiṣṭha:
But if Brahmins are unavailable for the *śrāddha* for one's mother,
one may instead worship eight auspicious women who are accompanied by their husbands and sons, and who are filled with joy.
In the group of ancestors and others as well, only four or more Brahmins should be fed.
Thus it is said in the *Padma Purāṇa*:
"An even number of twice-born ones should be honored with garments, gold, and other such offerings."
‘Kārtasvara’ means gold.
In the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa:
"In this rite, pairs of twice-born men should be engaged; they are to be honored and circumambulated."
In the Viṣṇupurāṇa: "O lord of men, one should feed the Brahmins, seated facing the east, in pairs. In the Brahmapurāṇa:
One who is self-restrained and pure should feed an even number of Brāhmaṇas at a *vṛddhi* ceremony.
Regarding the *śrāddha* for the mother, the paternal grandfather, and the maternal grandfather, Vṛddha-Śātātapa says:
"In all three of these cases, one who is self-restrained and pure should feed an even number of Brāhmaṇas."
Regarding the number of pairs, Chāgaleya says that for the sake of showing respect for those specific numbers:
"One should honor two Brahmins for each group, and likewise two for the Vaiśvadeva; one should not indulge in excessive expansion."
In this manner, eight Brahmins are thus assembled here.
However, in the *Bhaviṣyapurāṇa*, even a ninth is mentioned:
"In the forenoon, one should feed eight Brahmins in this way, proceeding from left to right."
And likewise, O best of birds, place the ninth Brahmin in the square.

The meaning is that when the washing of feet is being performed within a square mandala, whoever may arrive as a guest—even if he is the ninth—should be fed there. An alternative view is also stated in that very same source:
"A wise man, intending for the Nāndīmukha ancestors, should according to the rule feed five excellent brahmins in a clockwise direction during a *vṛddhi-śrāddha*."
Regarding these three *nāndī-śrāddhas*, Vṛddha-Śātātapa states that they must be preceded by the *vaiśvadeva* rite:
"One should feed [the guests] starting with the gods, proceeding clockwise while keeping the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*savya*)."

A *śrāddha* performed with reference to all the gods (*viśve devāḥ*) is the *vaiśvadevika*. It has already been established in the section on deities that in the *vṛddhiśrāddha*, the *viśvedevas* are known by the names Satyavasu, and in the *karmāṅga* [śrāddha], they are known as Kratu and Dakṣa. Furthermore, it was shown in that same place that here the ancestors (*pitaraḥ*) to be honored are those designated as *nāndīmukha*; this will also be demonstrated here. Now, other specific rules regarding this *vṛddhiśrāddha* are set forth. Regarding this, Śātātapa says:
One who desires prosperity should perform the *abhyudayika* śrāddha with the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*savya*), using straight blades of *darbha* grass, and with a focused mind.
Assuming the form of the ancestors, the deity partakes of the food;
therefore, in a *vṛddhi-śrāddha*, one should always give with the left hand.
Just as one should worship the gods, so too should one worship the ancestors in a rite for prosperity (*vṛddhi*).
Śloka-Kātyāyana also says:
"One should always serve the ancestors here with devotion as if they were gods.
By this, it is stated that all those duties which apply to the Vaiśvadeva rite must be performed here, but not the duties pertaining to the ancestral Śrāddha.
For this very reason, regarding the ritual application for the *tilaka* mentioned in the *Padmapurāṇa*:
"The purpose of the sesame seeds should be fulfilled with barley, performed in due order using only the right hand;
and one should cause the best of the twice-born to recite all auspicious benedictions. [1546]

In the *Viṣṇudharmottara* it is also stated: "In *vṛddhi-śrāddhas*, barley should be used in place of sesame seeds. Regarding the application of a different ritual procedure (*dharmāntara-prayoga*) in place of the ancestral rites (*pitrya-dharma*), it is stated in the *Brahmāṇḍa-purāṇa*:
A wise person should employ the word "svāhā" in place of "svadhā."
In a *vṛddhi-śrāddha*, one should always wear the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*savya*),
and in place of *kuśa* grass, *dūrvā* grass should be used for the sake of auspicious increase.
In the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa: "The sacrificer, being composed, should perform the Vṛddhi-śrāddha facing north or facing east; never with his face turned in any other direction."

Regarding this, the rule for the orientation toward the north and the east is stated in the *Āśvalāyana-gṛhyapariśiṣṭa*: "In rites for prosperity (*ābhyudayika*), the Brahmins are to be even in number; the darbha grasses should be rootless. One facing north should offer [the water] to those facing east, or one facing east to those facing north; two darbha blades constitute the *pavitra*.
Thus says Pracetas.
Facing east, one should worship the ancestors during a rite for the elders using the *devatīrtha* (the part of the hand sacred to the gods);
wearing the sacrificial cord over the left shoulder (*savya-upavīta*), one should quickly wipe the ground.

The cleansing of the remnants (ucchiṣṭa) must be performed immediately; the meaning is that one should never wait until evening as is done during the Pārvaṇa rite. Thus it is stated in the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa.
Everything should be performed clockwise in the forenoon by one wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder;
for him there shall be nourishment, sovereignty, long life, and indeed progeny.
O Bird, if the marks shine brightly and one attains liberation in due course,
straight-cut *kutapa* cloths should be given according to the rule, not torn ones.
One should use barley for the purpose of sesame seeds, and likewise offer the *arghya* water;
