O Hero, one should perform all the rites including perfumes and incense, and perform circumambulation.
The wise man should indeed offer the *kuśa* grass with its tips pointing eastward using his left hand alone.
*Kutapas* are *darbha* grasses. *Savyam* refers to the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) placed on the left shoulder.
In the *Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa*: "The *vṛddhi-śrāddha* and the rite for the gods (*daivika*) should be performed by one wearing the sacred thread."
Likewise, one should perform circumambulation clockwise with barley grains around pairs [of vessels] facing the east.
In the *Kūrmapurāṇa*: "Everything should be done as for the gods; indeed, no rites with sesame seeds should be performed.
The *darbha* grasses should be straight, and one should feed an even number of twice-born brahmins."
One should indeed offer [the water] preceded by the gods; one should not do so without circumambulating.
And here there are prohibitions regarding the ancestral rites (*pitryadharma*). Regarding this, Śloka-Kātyāyana says:
"Indeed, the bending of the left knee never occurs [in these rites]."
In this case, the practice of wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (apasavya) is not required, nor is the ancestral (pitrya) part of the hand prescribed as the proper place for offering.
For one desiring the highest good, that threefold recitation of "madhu, madhu" which occurs there,
following the Gāyatrī and released by the Madhu-mantras, is prescribed here.
Whatever scattering of that food there is, containing sesame or barley,
in the vicinity of the leavings— that is the "reversal" (viparītaka) here when [the ancestors] are satiated.

The Vaiśvadeva rite is "provided with barley" (yavavān), while the ancestral rite (pitrya) is "provided with sesame" (tilavān). "Inverted" (viparītaka) means that all [the rites] are provided with barley.
Pracetās says:
"One should not recite the ancestral prayers (japya), nor should one cause meat to be offered there."

In this context, by the word *japya* (that which is to be muttered), it is specifically the muttering of mantras characterized as pertaining to the ancestors (*pitṛliṅgaka*) while the twice-born are eating that is prohibited, and not even those [mantras] that serve as instruments for the performance of ritual acts.
For this very reason, Jātūkarṇa says:
"Whatever rite has been prescribed by the sages with a mantra characterized as pertaining to the ancestors..."
Therefore, that very thing must be performed, since it is unaccomplished when devoid of mantra.
In the *Bhaviṣyatpurāṇa*: "One should avoid red flowers, sesame seeds, and the *apasavya* (left-hand) manner [of ritual].
This prohibition means that even a red flower originating from water must not be offered here.
Śātātapa said:
"One should not perform the *apasavya* (the rite with the sacred thread over the right shoulder), nor should one fail to circumambulate clockwise.
If one should offer anything during a *vṛddhi* ceremony while performing the *apasavya* due to some transgression,"
Neither the gods nor the ancestors are satisfied by him according to the prescribed rule.
And this Nāndīmukha-daivata-śrāddha, which is devoid of the ancestral rites (pitryadharma) and endowed with the divine rites (daivadharmayukta), should be performed in this manner.
Regarding this, Jātūkarṇya says:
"The invitation should take place on the day before or on that very day, preceded by the deities."
Having performed [the preliminary rites], being self-controlled and pure, he should invite the Brahmins in the forenoon.
Having prepared a small mandala, one should then wash their feet;
once they have sipped water and been honored, one should seat them upon their seats.
In the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa:
"O Hero, having prepared a square mandala, circumambulating it clockwise,
and having laid down *kuśa* grass with its tips pointing eastward, as well as a scattering of flowers..."
O hero, you should feed the twice-born, adorned with fragrant flowers.
On this point, Śloka-Kātyāyana says:
"Henceforth I shall declare whatever specific rule may apply here: one should invite an even number of Brahmins for both sides [of the rite] in the morning."
Having seated them, he should indeed give straight blades of kusha grass, laid down horizontally.

The meaning of this is as follows: On the previous day or on that very day, having invited Brahmins who have been consecrated with mantras, one should summon them early in the morning, specifically during the forenoon. Having worshipped them in a square mandala adorned with sandalwood paste, unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), and flowers, and having invoked the Viśvedevas known as Satya and Vasu, as well as the ancestors (the *pitṛs*) and others known as Nāndīmukha, one should wash their feet, seat them upon their seats, and offer them seats made of straight darbha grass. Regarding the phrase "on both sides," one should first seat four facing east and then seat four facing north on the other side.
Thus it is stated in the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa.
Having arranged four facing east and four facing north with straight blades of darbha grass, one should respectfully offer them seats.
Alternatively, all [the Brahmins] should be seated facing the east.
And so says Chāgaleya:
"One should seat all those Brahmins indeed facing the east."
In the first [chapter] of the Brahmapurāṇa: "One should seat the Brāhmaṇas, facing east, in a clockwise arrangement,
representing the portions of Indra, Agni, Yama, Bhānu, Ambhas, Anila, Candra, and Śiva."
One should offer to those [images], which are similar, praiseworthy, auspicious, and adorned with flowers and garlands, a seat of darbha grass, intended for the gods and the ancestors.
Śloka-Kātyāyana says:

Having seated them upon the kuśa grass after they have been given [the invitation] with the words "to the ancestors," one should cause the arghya to be offered to the ancestors, addressing them by their lineage names and personal names.
In the *Chāndogya* text, the number of arghya vessels is stated:
"There are exactly four arghya vessels for the *ābhyudayika* [rite].
These are to be distributed as follows: three for the three śrāddhas dedicated to the Mothers and so forth, and one for the *vaiśvadevika*.
The procedure for filling the vessels and so forth has been stated by Kātyāyana:
"One should indeed have the filling of the vessels and other such acts performed by the *daiva* [brahmins] alone;
they should sit with their pairs joined, the elder on the left, and the tips of their hands holding the *pavitra* grass."
Having accomplished the purpose, it should be bestowed; it is not given to each individual one by one.

Having prepared the hands of the eldest Brahmin—who is the first of the pair—such that they possess the straightness of *darbha* grass, the sacred thread on the left, and so forth, according to the ritual rules for the *vaiśvadeva* offering; such that the tips of the *pavitra* blades are positioned above the second hand (of the younger brother) and the tips of the *pavitra* blades are not at the fingertips; having done this, one should present the *arghya*. By joining the two hands of each pair together in the previously described manner and placing two *kuśa* blades with their tips pointing forward in each instance—for each group consisting of the mothers, fathers, and so forth, as well as for the *vaiśvadeva* group—the *arghya* is to be offered only once per group, not into the hand of each individual Brahmin; this is the meaning.
In the Padma Purāṇa:
"At a celebratory occasion, one should say 'It is accomplished' and offer the arghya water to each pair [of ancestors]."

In place of the question regarding satiety (*tṛptipraśna*), one should ask, "Is it complete? (*saṃpannam*). And the meaning is that one should offer the *arghya* water by joining together the hands of two Brahmins at a time. Here, in the *arghya* vessel, instead of sesame seeds (*tila*), when barley (*yava*) is to be scattered, this mantra "Thou art sesame" (*tilo ’si*) should be employed with the appropriate modification (*ūha*) to "Thou art barley" (*yavo ’si*), and so forth. For this very reason, the application of the modified mantra alone is shown in the *Āśvalāyanagṛhyapariśiṣṭa*: "He scatters barley into the four purifiers (*pavitra*) along with the *upayāma* vessels, which have been consecrated with the mantra 'The goddesses... (*śaṃ no devīḥ*)."
"Thou art barley, having Soma as thy deity, the 'cow-sacrifice' (gosava) fashioned by the gods;
mixed with nourishment by the ancients, do thou gratify for us the worlds of the Nāndīmukha ancestors, svāhā! Likewise:

"O Viśvedevas, this is your *arghya*; O Nāndīmukha ancestors..."—thus, according to the respective gender, the offering of the *arghya* is performed, followed by the receiving of the water with "May the ancestors be pleased," and the dismissal. In the same manner, the offering of the *arghya* for the grandfather and great-grandfather, preceded by the invocation (*āvāhana*), should be performed for the two subsequent ancestors as well.
And so it is stated in the Caturviṃśatimata:
"Having worshipped the Nāndīmukha ancestors according to the prescribed rule for ancestral rites,
one should then offer a seat and perform the invocation and other subsequent acts."

The meaning is that one should perform the entire collection of ritual items—beginning with the invocation (*āvāhana*) and the offering of water (*arghya*)—in the very same sequence as prescribed for the *pārvaṇa* rite.
Furthermore, the method of invocation is shown in the first *Brahmapurāṇa*:
"One should invoke the *nāndīmukha* ancestors with devotion, with palms joined in reverence (*sāñjali*)."
One should recite the purifying mantra: "O Viśvedevas, come hither!"
After the offering of the *arghya*, one should offer fragrant substances, flowers, and so forth.
Accordingly, it is stated in the *Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa*:
"Having used barley in place of sesame seeds, one should offer the *arghya* according to the prescribed rule."
O Hero, one should perform circumambulation to the right while offering all things, such as perfumes and incense.
And this [offering] of fragrance and so forth should be given twice each into the hand of each individual.
Thus it is stated in the Āśvalāyana-Gṛhyapariśiṣṭa: "The ritual procedure is performed clockwise; barley serves the purpose of sesame seeds; everything is done twice each."
Immediately after the offering of perfumes and other items, the *agnaukaraṇa* (offering into the fire) must be performed. This too has been stated in that very same [text]:
"The daily *agnaukaraṇa* and the oblation (*homa*) are to be performed with the utterance of *svāhā*.
Here, there is an alternative reading:

"In the hand [he offers] to Agni Kavyavāhana, Svāhā! To Soma Pitṛmat, Svāhā! Thus it is said. Likewise: "Rice mixed with speckled butter (pṛṣadājya) is the oblation everywhere; with half of that, he should offer two oblations each. Thus it is said.

"In all cases" refers to the fire-oblation (agnaukaraṇa), the feeding of the twice-born, the scattering of food (vikiraṇa), and the offering of rice-balls (piṇḍadāna). "Clarified butter mixed with curds" is *pṛṣadājya*; having divided the rice mixed with that [clarified butter] into two portions—front and back—one should perform the oblation after taking two portions from each.
This is the meaning.
[This is stated] in the first *Brahmapurāṇa*.
One should offer great medicinal herbs (*mahauṣadhīḥ*) as sacrificial fuel (*samidh*) into the fire for the purpose of destroying demons (*rakṣoghnīḥ*).
"Destructors of demons" refers to plants such as *palāśa*, *śaṅkhinī*, *viṣṇukrāntā*, and others.

Once the *agnaukaraṇa* (offering into the fire) has been performed, the serving of food must be done into the vessels of the twice-born. Regarding that, the food to be served is described in the *Bhaviṣyatpurāṇa*.
At the beginning, one should offer rice mixed with speckled butter (pṛṣadājya),
as well as milk-rice (pāyasa) and wholesome foods such as sweetmeats (modaka) and other delicacies of excellent flavor.
One should serve a meal that is sweet and should not serve anything sour.
In the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*: "O best of birds, one should offer auspicious food of various kinds, such as items to be chewed and eaten, as well as rice mixed with jaggery and accompanied by ghee."
One should offer *rasālā* and *modakas*, but not anything sour, pungent, or the like.
[1553] By the word "etc. (*ādi*), the inclusion of pungent and other such irritating tastes is intended here.
In the first instance, the *Brahma Purāṇa* states:
"One should offer food with the *daiva* (divine) *tīrtha*, while muttering the *svadhā* mantra."
Having served the food, one should perform the consecration of the vessels and other rites.
Regarding this, the *Āśvalāyanagṛhyapariśiṣṭa* states:

"With the verse 'Ataḥ devā avantu naḥ', there is the grasping of the thumb; with the verse 'Idaṃ viṣṇur vicakrame', [it is done] elsewhere; and in the *Nāndīśrāddha*, the grasping of the thumb is performed with this verse, 'Ataḥ devā avantu naḥ'."

"Anyatra" means "in another *śrāddha*" or "at another [occasion]"; "akṣann amīmadanta" is an alternative reading for the sixth verse. The recitation (*japa*) while they are eating is also prescribed in that very same place:
one should cause them to hear the *pāvamānī* verses, the *śambhūti*, the *raudra*, and the *apratiratha*.
In the first *Brahma Purāṇa*:
"One should recite the *Śakrasūkta*, as well as auspicious hymns accompanied by blessings;
however, one should not recite the *Pitṛsaṃhitā* for those whose faces are tearful."

The *Śakrasūkta* is the hymn beginning with "āśuḥ śiśānaḥ" and so forth. A "Svastiyukta" is any hymn containing the word *svasti*. One may recite other auspicious [texts] as well; one may also recite certain passages from the *Ṛgveda*, *Yajurveda*, and so on, which primarily consist of most excellent benedictions (*āśīḥ*). Having prohibited the recitation of the *Madhumatī* verses, Kātyāyana states elsewhere that auspicious recitations such as the *Soma-sāmans* and others should be performed.
In the *Caturviṃśatimata*: "One should scatter the offerings and likewise give the rice-balls (piṇḍas) without [strict] restrictive rules.
When they are satiated, one who is composed should say 'It is complete' at the *vṛddhi-śrāddha*."
Kātyāyana said: The question "Is it ready? is prescribed at the point of inquiry as to whether they are satisfied. When it is replied, "It is well-prepared," one should offer the remaining food.
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*:
"One should ask those who are delighted, 'Has this been prepared for me?
and they should reply, 'It is well-prepared. Then, once everything is declared ready, one should cast [the oblation] into the fire."
The meaning is that one should gather all kinds of prepared food into a single vessel and scatter it as a *vikira*. Vṛddha-Vasiṣṭha says:
"But at the inquiry regarding satiety, [one should say] 'It is well-prepared,' and in the case of the gods, 'It is pleasing.'"
"It is accomplished for the ancestors, but it is pleasing to the gods. Thus, in the *Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa*:
"When the Brahmins have thus eaten, one should, with a concentrated mind, offer the rice-balls (*piṇḍas*)."
O Lord of Birds, one should offer balls mixed with curd, parched rice, and jujube fruits;
as stated in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"Likewise, one should present the funeral cakes (piṇḍas) mixed with karkandhu fruits and curd."
In the *Brahmapurāṇa*: "Having mixed together four balls of rice, resembling bilva fruits, along with curd, honey, jujubes, and likewise barley..."
And one should offer [the oblation] to the Nāndīmukha ancestors according to the prescribed ritual.
In the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*:
"And one should offer rice-balls mixed with curd and mixed with barley."—
Vṛddhavasiṣṭha.
The rice-balls (piṇḍas) should be prepared in due order, mixed with curd and *karkandhu* fruits;
"karkandhu" refers to the jujube fruit (*badarīphala*). [From the Caturviṃśatimata].
Having fed the twice-born, the wise man should then offer the rice-balls (*piṇḍas*).
According to the *Padmapurāṇa*:
"With a clockwise ritual procedure, using curd, unbroken grains, fruits, and water..."
Facing either the east or the north, one should offer them together with jujube fruits.
In the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa: "O hero, descendant of Bharata, a wise man should offer balls of food made of curd, jujube fruits, unbroken rice, and so forth, within a square mandala using his left hand."
With the sacred grass in hand, having sipped water, seated and composed, facing the east, and remaining silent, he should offer the rice-balls with his left hand during the rite for prosperity.
And here, the offering of a rice-ball (*piṇḍa*) is optional.
Thus it is stated in the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*:
"Facing either the east or the north, [one should offer] with curd, unbroken grains of rice, and jujube fruits."
O King, one should indeed offer the funeral cakes with the *devatīrtha* according to one's desire.
"By desire" means by will. In the absence of desire, however, one should not give.
The rule regarding the performance or non-performance of the offering of the *piṇḍas* is stated in the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa*:
"O Lord of Men, one may perform the offering of the *piṇḍas*, or one may not perform it at all."
O mighty-armed one, in the *vṛddhiśrāddha*, one should indeed observe the family tradition.

By this, the rule is shown: it must be performed by those in whose family the offering of *piṇḍas* has been practiced through the succession of elders at the *vṛddhi-śrāddha*, but it need not be performed by those in whose family it is not so practiced. Furthermore, this rule applies only to those who maintain no sacred fire (*niranika*); however, it is stated in the *Brahmapurāṇa* that for those who maintain the fire (*sāgnika*), it must be performed at all times:
"But he who, even though the sacred fire exists, does not offer the *piṇḍas* during a *vṛddhi* ceremony—his ancestors fall [from heaven], and he himself is cooked in hell. [1556]
Regarding this, Vṛddha-Śātātapa states the specific location for the offering of the rice-balls (piṇḍa):
"At a rite for prosperity (vṛddhi), one should offer the rice-balls facing east by name, outside.
Here, "he" refers to the performer of the śrāddha; "outside" means outside the dining hall, and not near the remains of the food (ucchiṣṭa).
Pracetās said:

Facing the east, with the *devatīrtha* [part of the hand], one should offer the *piṇḍas* for the ancestors upon *kuśa* grass whose tips point eastward; the vessel for the *piṇḍas* should be turned face down.
"Prākkūlāḥ" means having their tips pointing toward the east.
In the *Āśvalāyana-gṛhyapariśiṣṭa*, the smearing of the ground for the rice-balls (*piṇḍas*) with cow dung is prescribed:
"The offering of the rice-balls is made upon receptacles smeared with cow dung, after having spread out *kuśa* grass with its tips pointing toward the east."
In the Caturviṃśatimata it is said: "On the occasion of a prosperity rite, one should offer two rice-balls for each person;
one should give them separately—one by name and the other silently."
In the first [chapter] of the Brahmapurāṇa:
"Then, facing eastward, one should give darbha grass and water for rinsing with milk;
a wise man should perform the rite of rice-balls and water-libations for the Nāndīmukhas."
And whatever is produced by means of the *prājāpatya* tīrtha.

Kātyāyana said: On *darbha* grass with its tips pointing eastward, having addressed the first [deceased] as before, one should pour water without sesame seeds at the base of the blades, saying, "Ablution! (*avanenikṣva*).

Having addressed the second and the third [ancestors] in the central and foremost regions respectively— having called them by their *gotra*, relationship, and names— and likewise the "second," the grandfather, and the "third," the great-grandfather; he should do the same for the maternal grandfather and the others, remaining restrained in speech.
Having set aside a portion of all the food and having sprinkled it with condiments, [one should offer it].
Then, having mixed barley, jujube fruits, and curd, he should, facing eastward,
offer funeral cakes (piṇḍas) the size of bilva fruits, just as in the ritual of the water-offering (avanejana).
Then, with the water used for washing that vessel, one should again perform the *avanejana* (sprinkling) for each subsequent *piṇḍa*,
offering them in successive order.
One becomes inferior by performing [the rite] with the hands facing downwards during śrāddha ceremonies;
therefore, in all śrāddhas—whether those performed for prosperity (vṛddhimat) or others—one should act otherwise.
One should offer the oblations so that they slightly touch the base, the middle, and the tip;
one should silently deposit the perfumes and other items, and thereafter cause the twice-born to sip water for purification (ācamana).
This same procedure, excluding barley and other such grains, would apply elsewhere as well.
Regarding the offering of funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*), it is stated in the *Brahmapurāṇa* at the beginning:
"The water-offering (*arghya*), flowers, incense, and excellent unguents [are required]."
A fine, unwashed, pure garment should be given that is appropriate and equal [to the recipient].
One should then offer grapes, roots of *āmalaka*, and barley;
these very items one should always give to the Brahmins as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
Then, having offered milk, barley-gruel, and so forth, in the place where the water for imperishability was placed, he should mutter:
"May this be inexhaustible for the Nāndīmukhas."
Kātyāyana, however, says:
"The offering of inexhaustible water (akṣayyodaka) is prescribed to be performed like the offering of the guest-water (arghya);
one should always perform it with the dative case-ending alone, and never with the dative-instrumental (caturthī)."
And the grandmothers known as the Prapitāmahīs, the Nāndīmukhī mothers,
as well as the maternal grandmothers, paternal grandmothers, and great-paternal grandmothers.
"Recite 'svadhā' for the maternal grandfathers, as well as for those designated as the 'nāndīvaktṛs,' and for those known as the great-grandfathers. "Let there be svadhā," they say to him, laughing.

In the Baudhāyana-sūtra: When they have finished eating, having murmured this Yajus-mantra—"O you who are full of sweetness, O you who are born of sweetness"—at the place intended for the *svadhā* offering, he pours out water with the words, "May the Nāndīmukha ancestors be pleased. This utterance is indeed equivalent to the *svadhā*. Śātātapa says:
One should cause [the guests] to recite: "May the Nāndīmukha ancestors be satisfied.
In the first *Brahmapurāṇa*, the giver said these words: "And may the Viśvedevas be pleased."
May they be pleased with you, and they speak to him in sweet syllables.
In the *Brahmapurāṇa*: "One should cause [the officiant] to recite: 'May the Nāndīmukha ancestors be pleased. In the *Caturviṃśatimata*:
One should say, "May they be pleased," and cast the rice-balls (piṇḍas) with the exclamation "Svāhā.
According to the Āśvalāyanagṛhyapariśiṣṭa:
"One should dismiss [the ancestors] with the words, 'May the Nāndīmukha ancestors be pleased. Thus it is said.
In the first [chapter] of the *Brahmapurāṇa*:
"Reciting 'camūṣu vājinam,' he should dismiss them;
then, he should perform the excellent *śrāddha* for the Nāndīmukhī Mothers."
By this procedure, the rites such as the parting of the hair (sīmantonnayana) and others should be performed.
Kātyāyana said: Then one should sprinkle the first ground, saying,
"May it be well-sprinkled," and [sprinkle] the even-numbered [seats] with barley-water, saying, "May the waters be auspicious."
After this, one should offer flowers with the thought, "May there be joy.
One should present unbroken grains (*akṣata*) with the words, "May there be safety and freedom from misfortune.
Then, one should perform the rite of the inexhaustible (*akṣayya*) according to the prescribed rule, beginning with the deities.
In this regard, having first employed the verses of supplication beginning with "dātāraḥ," another verse is stated in the *Bhaviṣyat-purāṇa*:
"May my mother, grandmother, and likewise great-grandmother—
may these be pleased with me and grant me auspiciousness."
Kātyāyana states what must be done immediately thereafter:
"When all the requests have been granted by the best of the twice-born,
one who has placed the vessels face-upward should sprinkle water over the *piṇḍas* covered by the purifiers (*pavitra*)."
Having always performed the grasping of the thumb of an even number of Brahmins for whom the benediction has been pronounced, one should bow to the leading Brahmin and then follow after him.
The term *dhurya* refers to the foremost person of the row. According to the *Caturviṃśatimata*:
"Having obtained permission regarding the remaining food, one should then perform the Vaiśvadeva rite."
On the day of the śrāddha, one should perform the vaiśvadeva rite with the remnants of the śrāddha offering.

The mention of the *vaiśvadeva* is intended as an illustration for those rites accomplished with food—pertaining to the gods, ancestors, humans, and elemental beings. Here, the entire collection of duties, excluding the specific exceptions previously mentioned, should be performed according to the *pārvaṇa* rite.
Thus it is stated in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"At a time of prosperity (*vṛddhi*), the learned man should always worship the *nāndīmukha* ancestors."
The specific details have been accomplished; the remainder should be performed as in the Pārvaṇa rite.
The "distinction" is that the ancestors are designated as *nāndīmukha*; this is also an illustration of all the specific rules previously mentioned. In the *Padma Purāṇa*:
"In this manner, even a Śūdra [should perform] the ordinary *vṛddhi-śrāddha* at all times."
A wise person should indeed perform acts such as giving with the mantra of salutation (namaskāra).

In this regard, the ritual manual (*prayogapaddhati*) stated by Kātyāyana is as follows: In rites for prosperity (*ābhyudayika*), the procedure is performed clockwise; there is recitation of mantras with the exception of those pertaining to the ancestors (*pitrya*); the *darbha* grasses are straight; barley is used in place of sesame seeds; the question regarding satisfaction is "Is it well-prepared?"; the others should reply, "It is very well-prepared"; the funeral cakes (*piṇḍas*) are mixed with curd, jujube fruits (*badara*), and unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*); he asks, "Shall I cause the Nāndīmukha ancestors to be addressed?"; [the response is] "May the Nāndīmukha fathers, grandfathers, great-grandfathers, and maternal grandfathers be pleased," and one should not employ the word *svadhā*; and one should feed an even number of guests. Thus it is said.

The meaning of this is as follows: "In the *ābhyudayika* [rite]" refers to a *śrāddha* performed on the occasion of prosperity (*abhyudaya*), such as the birth of a son or a marriage. By the mention of "circumambulation" (*pradakṣiṇa*), the wearing of the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*yajñopavītin*), facing the northeast (*prāgudaṅmukha*), and arranging things from east to north (*prāgudaksaṃstha*) are indicated. "Performance" (*upacāra*) means the ritual practice. Regarding "recitation of mantras excluding those dedicated to the ancestors" (*pitryamantravarjaṃ japaḥ*): this recitation of ancestral mantras while the guests are eating is prohibited; that is, with the exception of mantras containing the word "ancestor" (*pitṛ*), such as "May they come to us" (*āyantu naḥ*). "Straight darbha grasses," and not those that are doubled or bent. "For the purpose of sesame" (*tilārtha*) means that the function of sesame must be performed by barley alone. On this point, Karka states that the mantra beginning with "Thou art sesame" (*tilo 'si*) should be employed by substituting "Thou art barley" (*yavo 'si*).

In place of the question "Are you satisfied?", one should ask, "Is it well-prepared? (saṃpannam). And the Brahmins should give the reply, "It is well-prepared" (susaṃpannam). In place of the formula "I shall invoke the ancestors" (pitṝn āvāhayiṣye), the usage should be "I shall invoke the Nāndīmukha ancestors" (nāndīmukhān pitṝn āvāhayiṣye). It should be understood that wherever the word *pitṛ* (ancestor) is employed, the word *nāndīmukha* must be prefixed there. Furthermore, in place of the recitation of the *svadhā*, he asks, "I shall cause the Nāndīmukha ancestors to pronounce *svāhā*" (*nāndīmukhān pitṝn svāhāṃ vācayiṣye*). Having been authorized by the Brahmins with the response "Let it be pronounced," he issues the command: "Let *svāhā* be uttered for the Nāndīmukhas. Being authorized by the Brahmins with "Let there be *svāhā*," he modifies the mantra beginning with *ūrjam* by changing "be *svadhā*" (*svadhā stha*) to "be *svāhā*" (*svāhā stha*), and pours water upon the *dūrvā* grass spread on the ground. Here, one should feed an even number of Brahmins.
The ritual manual (*prayogapaddhati*) as stated by Gobhila:

In the *ābhyudayika* (prosperity) *śrāddha*, an even number of Brahmins are invited; the service is performed clockwise (*pradakṣiṇa*); the sacrificial grass (*darbha*) is straight; barley takes the place of sesame seeds; the rice-balls (*piṇḍas*) are mixed with curd, jujube fruits (*badara*), and unbroken grains (*akṣata*); and having caused [the Brahmins] to recite "May the Nāndīmukhas be pleased" for the divine portion, one should employ the word "svāhā" in place of the formula for the *svadhā*-recitation, saying: "Let 'svāhā' be uttered for the Nāndīmukha ancestors—paternal grandfathers, paternal great-grandfathers, maternal grandfathers, maternal great-grandfathers, and maternal great-great-grandfathers. This is the ritual manual as stated by Baudhāyana.

Now, therefore, regarding the *Nāndīmukha* rite: at the very beginning, having invited two Brahmins for the gods and others for the ancestors, and having honored them as they arrive with the shaving of the beard, anointing, and bathing, one should kindle the fire, strew grass around it, melt the clarified butter (*ājya*), purify it by straining, mix it with curds, cleanse the *sruva* ladle, seat the two Brahmins for the gods and honor them, and—without yet addressing the ancestors—set down water with barley and two blades of *pavitra* grass mixed with flowers, fruits, and unbroken rice grains. Having scattered barley and sand upon the seats at the places where food will be served, one seats those intended for the ancestors. Upon those vessels containing the *pavitra* grass, one pours out the barley-water twice from another vessel while reciting the mantra: "May the *Nāndīmukha* ancestors be pleased. Then, having honored them in this same manner, one performs the *agnaukaraṇa* (offering into the fire). Having honored them again, one takes portions of the speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*) with the *sruva* ladle and, having offered this much into the fire with the mantra "Svāhā to the *Nāndīmukha* ancestors," one draws up food that has been spread with a base of ghee and sprinkled with ghee into the plates, mixes it with the *pṛṣadājya*, places it on *darbha* grass to the south of the fire, covers it with *darbha* grass, and modifies the mantra to "of the *Nāndīmukhas*. Having spread a base of ghee twice for the Brahmins and taken two portions of the desired food twice, and having sprinkled ghee over them twice, one should feed them according to rule. Having caused the Brahmins—who represent the general class of ancestors—to hear the *svadhā*-invocations, and when they have eaten and rinsed their mouths, one scatters curd-rice, sprinkles water twice with the rinsings, gives the barley-water as before, presents sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), and causes them to say, "May the *Nāndīmukha* ancestors be pleased. Having saluted them, placing the right knee on the ground in place of the *svadhā* call and lifting the left, one mutters "Bhūḥ" from the *Dūdhāt* section; at the end of the recitation, pouring out water with the words "May the *Nāndīmukha* ancestors be pleased," he dismisses them, rises, shows them favor, circumambulates them, asks permission for the remainder, and dismisses the deities. Then, circumambulating the fire and on *darbha* grass with tips pointing east, he should offer to the *Nāndīmukha* ancestors with the mantra "Svāhā to the *Nāndīmukhas*," and sprinkles water clockwise with the rinsings while reciting "ūrjaṃ vahantīḥ. Here too, for the sake of his wife and others, he performs the *kālahomas* with *pṛṣadājya* as before; thus, this single offering is completed.

Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Vṛddhi-Śrāddha," in the Śrāddha-kalpa of the Pariśeṣa-khaṇḍa of the *Caturvarga-cintāmaṇi*, composed by the illustrious Hemādri, the great king of kings, the illustrious Mahādevīya, and the preeminent master of all branches of learning.
Now begins the eighteenth chapter. Next is the procedure for the daily *śrāddha*. Regarding this, Yājñavalkya says:
One who desires his own welfare should perform daily the rite for the ancestors with food or even with water, for the sake of their satisfaction.

And this *śrāddha* consists of the *pitṛyajña*, which is included among the five great sacrifices (*pañcayajña*). For this very reason, Nārāyaṇa, having introduced the five sacrifices, stated: "After [the offerings] to the ancestors, one should perform a gift especially to worthy recipients;
wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*apasavya*), one should perform it while meditating upon the father and grandfather."
"Tanvīta" means "he should perform. Kātyāyana says:
"He should feed even a single Brāhmaṇa for the sake of accomplishing the purpose of the Pitṛyajña."
In the Viṣṇu Purāṇa: O King, one should also feed another Brāhmaṇa for the sake of the ancestors,
provided he is known to be born in that region and established in the proper conduct required for the five great sacrifices.
By the word "one," it is indicated that if possible, one should feed several [guests] of an odd number. As stated in the *Kūrmapurāṇa*:
"O best of men, one may feed even a single Brahmin for the sake of the ancestors."
The daily śrāddha performed with that intent is a sacrifice to the ancestors (pitṛyajña) that bestows a favorable rebirth.
Manu said:
One should offer the *śrāddha* daily with food and drink,
or even with milk, roots, and fruits, thereby bringing satisfaction to the ancestors.
One should perform the Śrāddha ceremony day after day with food and drink,
or one should feed Brahmins on behalf of the ancestors, or even just a single Brahmin.
Regarding the case where not even a single Brāhmaṇa is available, or where there is an impossibility of obtaining food sufficient for a meal, Kātyāyana has stated:
"If no other recipient for the gods exists, whether it be one who eats or the food itself,
one should nevertheless set aside some food according to one's ability and in accordance with the rule."
Having said, "This for the ancestors," he should utter the word *svadhā*.
And one should take this food to the place where a Brāhmaṇa resides and give it to him, according to the saying: "Where the worthy recipient is, there is one's destination. Also in the Kūrma Purāṇa:
"Or, having collected some food according to one's ability, being composed..."
One should present it only to a twice-born man who knows the true meaning of the Vedas.

In every case, however, if no twice-born (brahmins) are available, one should perform the specific modes of disposal (*pratipatti*) taught in the section on the secondary procedure (*anukalpa*) for the *pārvaṇa* rite. And this *śrāddha* must be performed as one dedicated to the six deities.
Thus it is stated in the *Bhaviṣyottara*:
"In the daily *śrāddha*, having honored the twice-born with water-offerings (*arghya*), perfumes (*gandha*), and so forth, according to one's ability..."
One should properly feed all the groups of ancestors together, designating them collectively.

In this context, because the word "all" includes as many ancestors as are intended in the *pārvaṇa* rite, it follows that these six—namely, the father and others together with their wives, and the maternal grandfather and others—are to be understood.

Here, the offering of the *arghya* water to them which is mentioned should be understood as being merely for the purpose of honoring the Brahmins, and not as a ritual service to the deities of the *śrāddha*, in accordance with the prohibitive statements that will be shown later.
Regarding the daily *śrāddha*, Vyāsa says:
A householder should feed even a single Brahmin daily in place of the six [ancestors],
beginning with the father;
as for that which says:
"One should feed even a single Brahmin, intending [the rite] for the three ancestors"—

this statement from the *Matsyapurāṇa* likewise uses the mention of "three" as an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the six [ancestors], based on the statement of Dhaumya: "Where the ancestors are worshipped," and so forth.
And this should be performed exactly like the *pārvaṇa* rite; for this very reason, after describing the *pārvaṇa*, Devala says:
"By this procedure, one should perform the *śrāddha* once a year, twice, four times, or as the *śrāddha* tradition dictates—month by month or day by day."

By this *pārvaṇa* procedure, the *śrāddha* should be performed day after day; however, if one is unable to perform it every day, it should be done month after month; and if even that is impossible, it should be performed within a year—either in three months, six months, or once a year. This is the meaning.
Regarding this, an exception to certain *pārvaṇa* duties is stated.
On this point, Manu says:
In the performance of the five great sacrifices for the sake of the ancestors, one should feed even a single Brahmin;
however, in the Vaiśvadeva rite, one must not fail to feed at least one twice-born man.
In the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa:
"That which is called the daily *śrāddha* (nitya-śrāddha) is said to be devoid of the deities;
it should be known as lasting for six years, and it is to be performed without the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) and the funeral cake (*piṇḍa*). [1566]
In the Matsya Purāṇa: "I shall now describe the daily [śrāddha], which is devoid of the offering of water (arghya) and the invocation (āvāhana).
One should know that to be 'adaiva' (without the gods); it is remembered as the pārvaṇa [śrāddha] to be performed on the parvan days."

Hārīta said: "The daily śrāddha (nityaśrāddha) should be without offerings to the gods (adaiva), and it should be devoid of the water-offering (arghya), the funeral cake (piṇḍa), and so forth. Pracetas [said]:

The best of the twice-born should not perform the invocation, nor the fire-oblation, nor the invitation, nor the dismissal, nor the offering of rice-balls, nor [the worship of] the gods in the daily rite.
In the *Bhaviṣyottara*:
"The invocation, the utterance of *svadhā*, the offering of rice balls (*piṇḍa*), the ritual of placing [the food] in the fire (*agnaukaraṇa*), and so forth;
the observances such as celibacy (*brahmacarya*); and likewise the *Viśvedevas*."
In the daily śrāddha, one should avoid these [unfit persons] and provide food fit for consumption.
The food to be eaten is that which the sacrificer himself consumes;
for this very reason, it is said in the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*:
"Whatever food a person has, his deities have that same food."
Then, in the daily śrāddha, one should give that which one eats oneself.
By this, permission is also granted for oil and the like; however, when superior food is available, one should not give inferior food.
As Devala says:
"If one feeds a Brahmin without clarified butter in one's own house while ghee is available..."
In the next world, the householder falls into a terrible hell.
Having himself eaten choice food,
if a Brahmin subsequently feeds another Brahmin light and poor-quality food, he shall dwell in hell for a long time.
Pracetas says: There is no invocation (āvāhana), no offering into the fire (agnaukaraṇa), no funeral cakes (piṇḍas), and no dismissal (visarjana).
The Brahman’s fee (brahmadakṣiṇā) and the fees for the priests follow; and the treatment of a guest is extended to three [ancestors].

Regarding the phrase "no dismissal" (*na visarjanam*), this is a prohibition specifically of the dismissal characterized by the words "vāje vāje" and so forth, and not of dismissal in general, in accordance with the statements that will be shown later. The words "anubrahma" mean for each Brāhmaṇa, and "and the sacrificial fees" (*dakṣiṇāś ca*)—the word "should give" (*dadyāt*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. The meaning is that for the three twice-born invited to the *śrāddha*, the status of a guest (*atithitvam*) must be assigned to any additional twice-born person who has arrived at that time. This should be understood as intended to state that the *pārvaṇa* duties, other than those which are prohibited, are to be performed.
For this very reason, he himself stated other ritual duties:
"Having seated [the guest] and provided a seat, having honored him with flowers and so forth,
having instructed him and fed him, one should dismiss him after giving some small gift."
A specific rule regarding the dismissal [of the deity] is shown in the *Bhaviṣyottara*:
"One should give a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) according to one's ability and dismiss [the deity] with prostrations.
Here, by the force of the statement from the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa* previously cited which prohibits the giving of a sacrificial fee, it is understood that the sacrificial fee is optional (*kṛtākṛtā*).

Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Nitya-Śrāddha according to the Primary and Secondary Rituals," in the *Śrāddhakalpa* of the *Pariśeṣakhaṇḍa* of the *Caturvargacintāmaṇi*, composed by the illustrious Hemādri, the Paṇḍita and sovereign over all departments of the illustrious Mahādevīya, the Great King of Kings.
[1568] Now begins the nineteenth chapter.
Next is the ritual procedure for the *śrāddha* at sacred fords (*tīrtha*).
In this regard, the permission of Brahmins is first stated in the *Prabhāsakhaṇḍa*:
"At a sacred ford (*tīrtha*), the word of a Brahmin is to be accepted for bathing, *śrāddha*, worship, and so forth.
[Also] in the *Matsyapurāṇa*:
Having bathed in all the rivers, one should satiate the ancestors and the gods;
in each such place, one should likewise perform the śrāddha and other rites according to one's means.

Whether at an improper time or at the proper time, men should always perform the *tīrtha-śrāddha* as soon as it is attained; likewise, the libation to the ancestors (*pitṛ-tarpaṇa*) must be performed.

The phrase "in rivers" is an elliptical indication (upalakṣaṇa) for sacred bathing places (tīrtha) in general. "Śrāddha and so forth" refers to specific rites such as the performance of śrāddha, giving gifts, and recitation of mantras (japa). By the expression "according to one's wealth," it is established that when resources are available, the rite should be performed with an abundance of food and other offerings, whereas in their absence, it may be done with whatever is at hand. "At the proper time" refers to specific times such as the new moon (amāvāsyā), the aṣṭakā days, and the sun's passage into a new zodiac sign (saṅkrānti). "At an improper time" refers to non-specific times other than those prohibited—such as the first day of the bright fortnight (śukla-pratipad)—but not during forbidden times such as at night. As stated in the *Prabhāsakhaṇḍa*:
One should perform the Śrāddha rite together with the Sapiṇḍana ceremony according to the procedure prescribed in one's own tradition,
having invited there Brāhmaṇas who are learned in the scriptures and free from defects.

Here, by the term "without the *piṇḍas*," it is stated that no regard should be paid to specific *piṇḍas* based on particular restrictions regarding time or causes for prohibition. "Independent" (*svatantrāṇi*) means one's own domestic manuals (*gṛhya*) and so forth. "Having invited" (*āmantrya*) should be understood as follows: if there is leisure, one should invite them on the previous day; if not, then one should call them at that very moment. The phrase "knowers of the scriptures" (*śāstrajñān*) is an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) of all the aforementioned qualities. Faults such as having deformed nails or leprosy have already been explained in detail previously. As stated in the *Prabhāsakhaṇḍa*: "Those twice-born who, even if inactive, are invited on the previous day..."
They are free from greed and devoid of disease, unlike those who perform sacrifices for village communities.

This should be understood as applying specifically when such Brahmins residing at that very sacred site (tīrtha) are available. However, if they are not available, even others who are likewise qualified should first be accepted if they reside at that sacred site; only after them may others be taken.
And so it is said in the *Prabhāsakhaṇḍa*:
"O Goddess, those men who have come there for the pilgrimage [should employ] the residents of that field."
Brahmins are to be honored first in rites dedicated to the gods and those dedicated to the ancestors.
In whichever holy places there are brahmins, whichever gods, and whichever mother-goddesses,
one should not despise them if one desires a long life.
In the Padma Purāṇa: "At sacred fords (tīrthas), one should never examine a Brāhmaṇa in any way;
according to the teaching of Manu, one should feed him when he arrives seeking food."
In the *Prabhāsakhaṇḍa*:
"The forest-dweller, the celibate student, the traveler, the pilgrim,
and the guest— these should be honored during the performance of the *śrāddha* rite after [the offering to] the *vaiśvadeva*."
Regarding sacred fords (tīrtha), the *Padma Purāṇa* states:
"A śrāddha should indeed be performed there, but it must be devoid of the water-offering (arghya) and the invocation (āvāhana).
Dogs, crows, vultures, ravens, and the like do not destroy that rite by looking upon it. [1570]

The "rites" consist of the offering of funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*) and so forth; "dogs and others" refers to all such [creatures] that are inauspicious; they "do not harm," meaning they do not defile [the rite].

One should avoid the water-offering (*arghya*), the invocation (*āvāhana*), the placing of the thumb of the twice-born, the scattering of food (*vikira*), and the inquiry as to whether they are satiated (*tṛptipraśna*) even in a *śrāddha* performed at a sacred ford (*tīrtha*).
And regarding this śrāddha being performed, the obligation to offer the funeral cakes (piṇḍas) in the presence of the Brāhmaṇas is stated in the *Prabhāsakhaṇḍa*:
"The offering of the piṇḍas must be performed according to the rules in their presence.
And likewise in the *Brahmavaivarta*:
Those high-souled ones who, having bathed at a sacred ford, perform the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa) for their ancestors,
rescue all their ancestors from hell.
In the *Camatkārakhaṇḍa*:
"Likewise, the offering of the funeral cake (*piṇḍa*) is praised, for it is exceedingly dear to the ancestors;
indeed, the ancestors look out for their own kinsman who has arrived."
Endowed with supreme resolve, one should fulfill that hope for them;
one must neither delay nor act too hastily.
In the Padma Purāṇa, the materials for the composition of the *piṇḍas* are stated:
"The offering of *piṇḍas* should be performed with roasted barley flour (*saktu*), or with barley-gruel (*pāyasa*) mixed with barley,
or as ordained by the sages, with oil-cake (*piṇyāka*) or with *iṅguda* fruit."
Or always with sesame oil-cakes by men who are full of devotion.
‘With *aiṅguda*’ means with the oil-cake produced from *iṅguda* fruits.
Regarding the specific sacred site (*tīrtha*) called Gopracāra, it is stated in the *Prabhāsakhaṇḍa*:
"A man himself should offer the funeral cake (*piṇḍa*) for his own ancestors and for himself."
Even with oil-cake or even with iṅguda fruit, she is not to be grieved for, O fair-faced one.
Having done this, one should then recite this mantra there:
"Kavyavāḍ, Anala, Soma, Yama, and likewise Aryaman."
May the Agniṣvātta Pitṛ-devatās, the Barhiṣad Pitṛ-devatās, and the Somapā Pitṛ-devatās—those highly fortunate ones—come here; may they protect us in this place.
O protectors of the earth, and those who are my fathers born in my lineage, my uterine kin— O grandfathers, I have come as the giver of the funeral cakes (piṇḍa) for them.
Having spoken thus, O Great Goddess, one should then recite the mantra:
"The father, the grandfather, and likewise the great-grandfather."
The mother, the maternal grandmother, and likewise the maternal great-grandmother;
the maternal grandfather, the maternal great-grandfather, and likewise the maternal great-great-grandfather.
May this ball of rice offered by me reach them as an inexhaustible offering:
Oṃ, homage to the Sun, the Sustainer, who possesses the forms of the Moon and Mars!
Having thus bowed down to and worshipped the one whose nature consists of Jīva, Bhārgava, Saumya, Āra, Rāhu, and Ketu, one should then recite this hymn of praise.
There, having invoked the ancestors near a cow's footprint, one should offer rice-oblations (caru) that have been cooked with ghee, and present funeral cakes (piṇḍas) to them with the sacred mantras.
"Those who have died in my family and those for whom no destination is known—
I shall summon them all onto the surface of the *darbha* grass with water mixed with sesame seeds."
For the sake of the deliverance of those who have died in my paternal lineage as well as in my maternal lineage, I offer this funeral ball (piṇḍa).
And for those in my maternal grandfather’s family whose destination is unknown,
I offer this pinda for the sake of their deliverance.
And whatever members of one's kin there may be, devoid of name and lineage— whether in one's own family or another's family— for them this funeral cake (piṇḍa) is prepared.
And those who have died by hanging, and those who were killed by poison or weapons—
for the sake of their deliverance, I offer this rice-ball.
To those who were cremated by fire, as well as others who were not cremated,
and to those killed by lightning or thieves— to them I offer this funeral cake.
For the sake of uplifting those who have gone to the Raurava, Andhatāmisra, and Kālasūtra hells, I offer this funeral ball (piṇḍa).
For the sake of the deliverance of those who have gone to the terrible Asipatravana and the Kumbhīpāka hells, I offer this funeral ball (piṇḍa).
To those who have entered the womb of animals— whether birds, insects, or reptiles—
or those dwelling in the womb of trees, to them I offer this rice-ball.
To those who have been led by the rulers of Yama to dwell in incalculable hells,
I offer this funeral ball (piṇḍa) for the sake of their deliverance.
Wandering through thousands of other births by their own karma,
for those among whom the human state is difficult to attain, I offer this funeral ball (piṇḍa).
May all those who were kinsmen or non-kinsmen, and those who were kinsmen in another birth—
may they all forever attain satisfaction through this funeral cake (piṇḍa).
Whatever ancestors of mine exist in the form of hungry ghosts,
may they all always find satisfaction through this funeral cake (piṇḍa).

The ancestors dwelling in the celestial, atmospheric, and terrestrial realms, as well as kinsmen and others who have died without having received the funeral rites— for them, the *piṇḍa* offering leads to liberation.

Those who have died in the paternal lineage, as well as those in the maternal lineage, and those others who are kinsmen—teachers, fathers-in-law, and relatives—who have passed away; [for all these may one perform rites].
Those in my family for whom the funeral offerings have been interrupted, those deprived of sons and wives, those whose rites have fallen into neglect, as well as those born blind and the lame;
To those of my family who were deformed, those who died in the womb, and those known or unknown—
may this ball of rice offered by me reach them as an inexhaustible offering.
May my ancestors be liberated from the state of being a preta forever;
may whatever there is mixed with honey, cow’s milk, ghee, and milk-rice [be offered].
They say that what is given at that *goṣpada* holy site becomes inexhaustible;
likewise at the supreme *goṣpada* holy site in the midst of the Nyaṅkumatī.
Having offered the morsels of food according to the rule, one should again recite this mantra:
"May the gods, beginning with Brahmā, and the foremost of the ṛṣis, be my witnesses."
"O best of gods, having reached this sacred ford, I have performed the rite of expiation for my ancestors; I have come to this ford for the sake of the ancestral rites."
"O witnesses, all of you, I am now liberated from the three debts.
Having thus performed a circumambulation of Goṣpada, the most excellent sacred ford.
Having given sacrificial fees to the Brahmins, one should offer funeral cakes (piṇḍas) in the river;
likewise, the gift of a cow and a dear black antelope skin should be given there.
The phrase "to those who eat with faith" is the ellipsis to be supplied.
[1574] In the *Padma Purāṇa*, regarding the *śrāddha* performed by Rāma at the sacred site of Puṣkara:
"And when the Brahmins had eaten, having offered the rice-balls (*piṇḍas*) in due order..."
And having given them sacrificial fees according to their ability, they were dispatched.
It is stated in the *Viṣṇudharmottara* as being common to all sacred fords (*tīrtha*):
"At a *śrāddha* performed at a sacred ford, a wise man should always cast the funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*) into the water while facing south,
which is proclaimed to be the direction of the ancestors."

In the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*: "One should offer the *bali* facing north, or alternatively at the edge of the water. One should perform the *bali* well-known [to tradition] and cast it from a higher place to an even higher one."
First, one should cast the offering above the tips of the horns of the cows.
Praise of the Śrāddha at Sacred Fords (Tīrtha-śrāddha-praśaṃsā) in the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa:
"In this world, one who offers the śrāddha-piṇḍa shall indeed lead his ancestors to Viṣṇu;
he who feeds even a single Brāhmaṇa there who is firm in his vows."
"At the great sacred ford of Gopracāra, ten million [ancestors] are fed;
thus has the procedure for the śrāddha ceremony there been briefly described to you."
The praise of the ancillary elements of the *śrāddha* is also found in that same source:
"By the gift of fragrance one becomes rich in scent; by the gift of flowers, one gains good fortune;
by the gift of incense, one attains sovereignty; and by the gift of a lamp, one shines."
Through the gift of a banner, there is the destruction of sin; one who undertakes a pilgrimage partakes in the world of Brahmā.
Darbha grass, sesame seeds, and sacrificial food (haviṣya), when offered with faith during a ritual application, [yield great merit].
Agastya, Bhṛṅgarāja, and the auspicious hundred-petaled flower;
camphor, agallochum, sandalwood, saffron, and a leaf of Tulasī.
When offerings of balls of food the size of bilva fruits are made upon ground illuminated by lamps,
along with betel, fruits, sacrificial food (naivedya), sesame seeds, darbha grass, and water—
at a sacred ford (tīrtha)— that which is intended for prosperity becomes infinite.
Now follows the procedure for the *gayāśrāddha*. Regarding this, the *Mahābhārata* states:
"The shaving of hair, beard, nails, and so forth is not recommended."
Therefore, one who desires to perform the Śrāddha at Gayā should never undergo the shaving of the head.
Those in this land of Bhārata who are devoted to the rites for their ancestors, having maintained their hair and being permeated by supreme devotion,
have come to Pitṛtīrtha for the sake of discharging their debt.
Their debt will certainly come to an end.
Upon reaching Gayā, a man should never practice stinginess regarding his wealth;
for by practicing such stinginess, he shall not partake in the fruit of the sacred site.
Now, regarding the Brāhmaṇas for the Śrāddha at Gayā,
the Vārāha Purāṇa states:
"If a son should go to Gayā at some point due to the passage of time..."
One should feed those very Brahmins who have been designated by the officiating priest.
Those Brahmins whose station is equal to that of Brahmā and who likewise partake of the drinking of Soma,
being established in the state of Brahman, are remembered as being equal to Brahmā.
The Gayā Brahmins are superhuman, having been ordained by Brahmā;
when they are satisfied, the deities together with the ancestors are fully satisfied.
Having worshipped the Brahmins at Gayā who represent the ancestors with a concentrated mind,
one whose self is purified of all sins is glorified in the heavenly world.
And what is given into their hands, especially at Gayā, becomes inexhaustible for his ancestors; of this there is no doubt.
One need not examine their lineage, conduct, learning, or even asceticism;
for when these are honored, the gods, along with the ancestors and the Guhyakas, are satisfied.
In the *Brahmavaivarta*: "One should dwell constantly at Gayāśīrṣa and perform one's ablutions at the Phalgu river;
the offering of the funeral cake (piṇḍa) at Gayāśīrṣa is difficult to obtain even in heaven."
Having bathed at Phalgutīrtha, beheld the god Gadādhara,
and circumambulated Gayāśiras, a person is liberated from the sin of killing a Brahmin.
In the Mahābhārata:
"Then one should conclude the śrāddha according to one's capacity and according to one's strength;
one obtains divine desires, for that is remembered as the gateway to heaven."
O King, funeral cakes (piṇḍas) should be offered according to the prescribed rite on the land of Gayā to those who are of the same caste, kinsmen, friends, relatives, and well-wishers.
To his sons, to his grandsons, and even to his younger relatives— in every way—
he should offer funeral cakes (piṇḍas) even to those who have died in other births.
"They all go to heaven through this ball of rice," so says the sacred tradition;
this is proclaimed as the mantra for those whose names and lineages are unknown.
Those born in the paternal lineage and likewise in the maternal lineage,
as well as the gurus, fathers-in-law, kinsmen, and whatever other twice-born relatives there may be.
Those in my family for whom the funeral rice-offerings have been interrupted, those deprived of sons and wives,
the deformed, those who died as miscarriages, and all others known or unknown within my lineage— [may they be satisfied].
To those who have perished while performing ritual acts and to others who remain within the womb—
to them this funeral cake (piṇḍa) offered by me shall indeed reach as an inexhaustible offering.
Thus is the mantra for the offering of the rice-ball (*piṇḍa*).
Furthermore, one should cast the rice-ball there as a treasure-store for oneself;
O Greatly Wise One, let [the ancestors] go to Gayā for the sake of oneself even without sesame seeds.
The offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa) for the deceased should be performed with sesame seeds;
likewise, other members of the same lineage (gotraja) should also perform the offering of funeral cakes.
O King, those of the same caste, kinsmen, friends, relatives, and well-wishers— these too may offer the funeral cake (piṇḍa) according to the prescribed rite at Gayā-rūpa.
A wise man, being fully composed and diligent, should offer the funeral cake (piṇḍa) with every effort to his sons, to his daughters, and even to his younger siblings.
"They all go to heaven because the funeral ball (piṇḍa) has been offered"—such is the sacred tradition (śruti).
Therefore, one should, with a concentrated mind, regularly offer the funeral ball even to them.
The killer of a Brahmin, the ungrateful person, and the slayer of a cow— these five types of sinners—
all attain purification by offering funeral cakes at Gayā.
The slayer of a Brahmin, the drinker of liquor, and one who harms children, the elderly, or gurus—
even such a sinner goes to destruction if he visits Gayā.
Whether it be one's own son or even another person, whenever one causes a funeral cake (piṇḍa) to be cast into the Gayā-kūpa in the name of someone, that person shall be led to eternal Brahman.
When an eclipse of the moon or the sun occurs during the month of Makara,
the offering of funeral cakes at Gayā is difficult to obtain even throughout the three worlds.

In this regard, regarding the offerings of funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*) and ancestral rites (*śrāddha*) and so forth, one should perform the offering of funeral cakes and other such acts at those places described as praiseworthy, beginning with Gayāśiras and Viṣṇupāda.
As stated in the *Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa*: "Having gone to Uttaramānasa by this very procedure..."
Having sipped water and holding kuśa grass in his hand, he should sprinkle water upon his head.
One should go to the place called Kanaka, situated within the unstable region;
having sipped water and sprinkled one's head there, one should speak while looking at the sun.
Having bowed the head at Gayā and bathed at the station of the Grandfather (Pitāmaha),
one should behold it, enter for the ritual bath, and then perform the Śrāddha according to the prescribed rules.
One should perform this at Gayāśiras, offering the śrāddha and the piṇḍas on the fourth day;
on the fifth day, one should go to the banyan tree known as Akṣaya.
One should also bathe at Gayāvaṭa after performing the libations (tarpaṇa),
and then one should perform the śrāddha rite beneath the banyan tree according to the prescribed rules.
There stands the one known as Akṣayavaṭa, renowned throughout the three worlds;
whatever is given there to the ancestors shall certainly become inexhaustible.
By taking refuge at the foot of a banyan tree, even if only a single Brahmin is fed with vegetables or water, it is as if ten million have been fed.
The abandonment of the body and the taking up of residence at Gayā are both prescribed;
among the śrāddha, the piṇḍa offering, and the water libation, each preceding one is more highly praised than the next.
To the north of Muṇḍapṛṣṭha is the river named Kanaka;
having bathed there, one should perform a Śrāddha ceremony accompanied by the offering of rice-balls (piṇḍa).
At that moment he becomes one who has accomplished all his duties and is liberated from the three debts;
a Śrāddha performed at the Puṣkariṇī in the Suṣumṇā is said to be inexhaustible.
Having bathed in Lake Mānasa and performed the Śrāddha rite, one should then proceed;
there on the shore is a temple where one should recite the names of one’s father, mother, and other ancestors.
Then one should perform the Śrāddha at Uttaramānasa according to the prescribed rule;
he obtains divine desires and finds the means to liberation.
Whatever fruit is obtained when the sun is eclipsed by Rāhu at the Saṃnihati tīrtha,
that entire fruit is said to be attained day after day at Gayā.
If one offers a rice-ball at Gayā under the name of those who have no kin, as well as those who are kin, and even young girls, Brahman shall lead that person to his own abode.
The Śrāddha at Gayā for those who have passed away is highly commended when a full year has elapsed;
however, one should indeed offer the rice-balls (piṇḍas) even for those who are still living, as well as for oneself.
One should offer those rice-balls at the śrāddha ceremony without sesame seeds while reciting their names and lineages;
however, for those who are living or those who are deceased, sesame seeds are not forbidden in the śrāddha.
He for whose sake one releases a dark-blue bull at Gayā attains liberation;
likewise, even when released, it brings satisfaction.
That bull which is red in color, white in the face and tail,
and black in the hooves and horns, is called a *nīla*.
One should properly release a bull that is vigorous, endowed with beauty, firm, beautiful in all its limbs, pleasing to behold, and either tawny or blue.
Whether it be of such a kind or that kind, one should release a bull at Gayā;
one obtains the imperishable world and attains unsurpassed happiness.
One should burn the left side with a trident and burn it with a discus;
thereafter, one should bathe the marked image and, once bathed, release it according to the prescribed rite.
Thus it has been said: he who performs the Śrāddha at Gayā according to his capacity, having transcended all difficulties, attains the Supreme Brahman.
Concerning Dvāravatī, it is said in the Skanda Purāṇa:
"Having bathed there, a person should then satiate the gods and the ancestors;
endowed with supreme faith, he should perform the śrāddha according to the prescribed rule."
Then, the five jewels and the seven grains should be given to the twice-born.
Likewise, one should satisfy the ancestors, the gods, and human beings according to the rules;
thereafter, endowed with faith, one should perform the śrāddha for the ancestors.
And one should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) there, avoiding stinginess regarding wealth;
especially should delicious fruits be offered.
He gave Śyāmāka and Nīvāra grains, coral, antelope skins,
the seven types of grain, rice, and parched flour mixed with jaggery.
Perfumes, garlands, betel, garments, and likewise milk—
the life of that mortal is fruitful, and his existence is truly well-lived.
Regarding Viraja, it is stated in the Vārāha Purāṇa:
"There, bathing and giving gifts shall all become ten-millionfold in merit;
and there, on the new moon day (Amāvāsya), by offering rice-balls (piṇḍa) to the ancestors,"
They certainly rescue ten million members of their lineage from hell; of this there is no doubt.
In the Āditya Purāṇa:
"Having returned home, he should again worship the gods, the ancestors, and the Brāhmaṇas."
Acting in this way, one shall obtain whatever fruit is declared for those sacred fords and the like; there is no doubt in this matter.

Thus concludes the procedure for the *tīrthaśrāddha*. Now follows the procedure for the various types of *śrāddha* performed for the sake of prosperity (*pauṣṭika*), for desired objects (*kāmya*), for the purpose of a festive assembly (*goṣṭhī*), for divine rites (*adaivika*), for pilgrimage (*yātrā*), and for the purification of actions through sacrifice and charity (*iṣṭāpūrta*).
In that regard, the *Bhaviṣyottara* states: "For rites such as *iṣṭāpūrta*, one should perform the *śrāddha* in the same manner as the *vṛddhi-śrāddha*.
Pāraskara says:
At the time of conception, during the Soma sacrifice, as well as at the parting of the hair (sīmantonnayana) and the rite for ensuring a male child (puṃsavana),
the Śrāddha should be understood as a subsidiary part of the ritual, performed like a rite of prosperity (vṛddhi).
Pracetās said:
"That feeding of Brāhmaṇas is performed for the sake of purification;
it is declared to be for the purpose of purification when the Śrāddha is performed according to the Pārvaṇa rite."
In the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa:
"The śrāddha that is performed in a cow-pen is called the *goṣṭhya-śrāddha*.
O Lord of Birds, that too has been declared according to the *pārvaṇa* procedure."
In the *Bhaviṣyottara*:
"On occasions such as portents and the like, one should always perform the *nitya-śrāddha*;
indeed, for the feeding of the twice-born, one should offer it specifically for the sake of the Viśvedevas and other deities."
That should be performed like the daily *śrāddha*; it is called a *deva-śrāddha*.
In the Kūrma Purāṇa: "O child, I shall describe to you the sequence of the rules for pilgrimage,
according to the procedure of the sages, as it has been seen and as it has been heard."
Having made his resolve on the preceding day, having worshipped the ancestors and the gods,
eating only the remains of the oblations, composed in mind, observing celibacy, and sleeping upon the ground;
On the following day, having bathed, being pure, having performed his prayers and auspicious rites,
and having paid homage to his gurus and elders, he should circumambulate the village,
set out with a joyful mind while recollecting his chosen deities.
In the *Skanda Purāṇa*, in the *Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa*:
"Having circumambulated the sacred site, restrained in speech and well-composed, self-controlled and restricted in diet, one should then proceed on the path."

In the Mahābhārata: A wise man, having properly formed a formal resolve (saṃkalpa) and directed his intention toward the sacred site of the ancestors (pitṛtīrtha), should perform the Śrāddha rite at home in the presence of the ancestors.

O best of the twice-born, O most excellent one, one should avoid accepting gifts, the food of others, and strife; likewise, one should avoid other despicable things and even those who are unrighteous.
Dharma said: A man performing a journey-śrāddha according to the pārvaṇa rite should,
having abandoned what is improper and irregular, perform everything with a concentrated mind.
Regarding Gayā, it is stated in the *Brahmavaivarta*:
"One who is about to go to Gayā, having performed the *śrāddha* according to the rules,
should don the garb of a common laborer (*karpaṭī*) and perform the circumambulation of the village."
Then, having gone to another village and partaken of food remaining from a śrāddha ceremony,
he should travel every day, avoiding the acceptance of gifts.

In this context, it should be understood that the practice of going to another village on the very day of the *śrāddha* to eat the remnants of the *śrāddha*—a matter mentioned under the section concerning Gayā and established by the previously cited statement from the *Kūrma Purāṇa*—applies to occasions other than the pilgrimage to Gayā. The distinction is that the scriptural injunction, "having eaten improper or irregular food," being a general statement, is restricted specifically to the subject of the Gayā pilgrimage. Pāraskara says:
"A *śrāddha* [should be performed] upon the recovery of health and likewise upon the increase of wealth."
That Śrāddha performed according to the Pārvaṇa rite is declared to be for the sake of nourishment.

"In the accumulation of the body" means prior to the administration of medicine for the purpose of bodily nourishment; "in the accumulation of wealth" means prior to the undertaking of activities that serve as the means for accumulating wealth.
Vṛddha-Śātātapa says:
"That which is performed out of desire is called *kāmya* (optional), for the sake of accomplishing a desired object."
That too has been stated in due order according to the ritual procedure for the Pārvaṇa rite.
In this regard, the specific detail concerning those known as the Viśvedevas should be understood as shown in the section on deities.

Thus concludes the procedure for the *iṣṭāpūrta* śrāddha, which is performed for the purpose of purifying the limbs of ritual acts, for the sake of a cow-pen, for divine purposes, for a journey, and for prosperity.
By that Hemādri, who has crushed the flood of the wretched and the miserable,
all the rites that bring satisfaction to the departed spirits are now being described.

Now follows the procedure for the offerings of sesame-water (*tilodaka*), rice-balls (*piṇḍa*), the ancestral oblation (*śrāddha*), and so forth, which bring satisfaction to the departed spirits (*preta*).
Regarding that, first as for the sesame-water, Yājñavalkya says:
"From the seventh or even the tenth day, the kinsmen approach the waters."
May our sin be burned away by this [rite], while facing the direction of the ancestors.

"Relatives" (*jñātayaḥ*) refers to those who share the *sapinda* relationship and those related by water (*samānodaka*), for seven or ten days, facing the direction of the ancestors—that is, facing south—should approach the water to bathe and to offer water to the deceased. Having gone there and bathed with the *gāyatrī* verse addressed to Agni seen by Kutsa, "May the water cleanse away our sin" (*āpo naḥ śośucad agham*), they should present the water. Yājñavalkya states the extension of this rule to non-relatives:
"In the same way, the water-rite is performed for the deceased maternal grandfathers and teachers."
Water for the sake of desire (kāmodaka) should be offered for a female friend, a daughter-in-law, a sister’s son, a father-in-law, and an officiating priest.

The water-rite (udakakriyā) for deceased maternal grandfathers and others should be performed by their daughters’ sons and others in the manner previously described. For friends and the like, one should offer "water out of affection" (kāmodaka); the meaning is that if one desires to give water, then one should give it. "Prattā" refers to an unmarried daughter and so forth. Pāraskara states: "Water out of affection [is offered] for the officiating priest, the father-in-law, a friend, a maternal uncle, and a sister’s son."
Yājñavalkya states the ritual procedure for the offering of water:
"Restraining their speech, they sprinkle water once with the [deceased's] name and lineage.
On the number of days specified, kinsmen and others, restraining their speech, should sprinkle water once each day with the name and lineage.
Kātyāyana says: Then, having gone to water that is free from living beings, everyone who has touched the corpse should bathe with their clothes on,
perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), and offer the water libation for him on dry land.
At the end of the name of the lineage, one should say, "I satisfy [you].
Having arranged the *kuśa* grass with their tips pointing south, one should offer [the water] separately, along with sesame seeds.
In the Viṣṇupurāṇa:
Until the Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa rite, the ancestral rites are performed with straight darbha grass;
after the Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa, they should be performed according to rule with double the amount of grass.

Having carried out the deceased and performed the cremation rites, the relatives should approach the funeral pyre in a counter-clockwise direction and, still wearing their clothes, immerse themselves in water. Having offered the water libation for the deceased, they should offer a single rice-ball (*piṇḍa*) upon *kuśa* grass. Vasiṣṭha states:
"They should perform the water-rite with the left hand placed over the right; facing south, they should offer an odd number [of libations]."

Vaijavāpāyana says: Having gone to the edge of the water and having immersed themselves once, they scratch [themselves] in the water with the little finger of the left hand, saying, "The little finger has washed away. Into that [water], they should offer one handful of water to the deceased, saying, "To such-and-such a person, svadhā! Hārīta says:
Having gone out, having purified themselves, and having gone to water and bathed, they pour out a handful of water, saying, "May he be satisfied. Paiṭhīnasi says:
Meditating mentally and facing south, one should pour out three handfuls of water. One should cease [this practice] from the time of death until the eleventh day.
Pracetas says:
Day by day, one should offer full handfuls for the sake of the deceased;
the increase in the quantity should continue until the funeral cake (piṇḍa) is completed.
Gautama: [The performance of] water-libation rites [should be done] on the first, third, fifth, seventh, and ninth days. Pracetās: [The same].

The kinsmen of the deceased, descending into the water in order of seniority, should not splash it about, but should pour it out at the edge of the water with their sacred threads and garments over the right shoulder (apavīta), facing south for a Brāhmaṇa, facing north for a Kṣatriya, and facing east for a Vaiśya. Viṣṇu states:
"They should offer water and funeral cakes (piṇḍa) to the deceased for as long as the period of impurity lasts."

Śaṅkha: The relatives of the deceased, having entered the water in order of seniority, should not rub their bodies; they should sprinkle [water] once, facing toward the northeast. Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas do exactly the same, having placed their lower garments and sacred threads over the right shoulder (in the *apavīta* fashion). Then, saying "This is for the deceased," they emerge from the water, discard the clothes worn during contact with the deceased, and put on other clothes. It should be understood that the prescription of a number of *añjali*s greater than the standard rule is for the purpose of providing a superior benefit to the deceased.
This is the statement regarding the offering of water found in the Rāmāyaṇa.
Rāma said:
"O tiger among men, may this pure, divine,
and inexhaustible water, given by me, attend upon you in the worlds of the ancestors."
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*:
"A bath with one's clothes on (*sacela*) must be performed, for it removes all impurities.
Thereafter, water mixed with sesame seeds (*tilodaka*) should be offered by everyone upon the surface of a stone."

For a deceased person, those who have performed the *sapiṇḍana* rite should face south at a body of water, wearing their sacred threads over the right shoulder (*apavīta*). Having bathed only once, they should offer water with sesame seeds (*tilodaka*) from the *pitṛ-tīrtha* (the part of the hand sacred to the ancestors) using an *añjali* (cupped hands), directed toward the deceased, upon a stone.
Ten *añjali*s of water should be offered to each Brāhmaṇa;
twelve should be given for a Kṣatriya, and fifteen for a Vaiśya.
But for a Śūdra who has gone to the land of the departed, the gods grant [the merit] for thirty years.
Having placed the sacred thread over the right shoulder with their garments,
the Brahmins, facing south, should offer three handfuls of water into his joined palms.
Then, by means of the flow from the left thumb, either upon the ground or in some other place, one should recite this:
"May this deceased person of such-and-such lineage be satisfied."

This, however, is the method for offering water with sesame seeds for one who has not committed a mortal sin (*mahāpātaka*); for one who has fallen from his caste (*patita*), another [method] is indeed prescribed:
"But he who, out of compassion, desires to perform the satiation for a fallen person, shall summon a female slave of the same caste who has been paid her wages."
Even if she speaks according to the facts, saying, "But she has an impure jar in her hand," [the judge says]:
"O maidservant, go and bring sesame seeds quickly for a price!"
Then, seated with your left foot [resting on the ground], facing southward, throw this water-filled jar containing sesame seeds.
One should recite the *Mṛtasaṃjñāna* [mantra] and repeatedly say, "Drink!
Upon hearing his words, she—who has attained her value—performs that act.
When this is done, there shall be satisfaction for those who have fallen; it cannot be otherwise.
Thus ends the ritual for the offering of water with sesame seeds (tilodaka) for one who has fallen [from caste].
Furthermore, the praise of the tilodaka is found in the Ādityapurāṇa.
Just as a king followed by a thousand warriors proceeds,
even so water mixed with sesame seeds goes to the departed spirits.

Now follows the ritual procedure for the *piṇḍa* offering for the deceased (*preta*). Regarding this, Śaṅkha says that when the kinsmen have returned home after having offered water with sesame seeds, they should touch *dūrvā* grass, a sprout, fire, and a bull; then, having offered a *piṇḍa* to the deceased at the door of the house, they should enter afterwards.
Śunaḥśepha states by way of introducing the *piṇḍa* for the *preta*s:
"It should be offered at the doorway or in temples.
But Vṛddhapracetas says:
It should be given at the gateway, never in a temple of the gods.
And it is stated in the Āditya Purāṇa:
