"It should be given at the gateways, never in a temple of the gods."
And thus, because the place for the deities (devatāyatana) is both prescribed and prohibited, there is an option; this follows from the statement in this very *Purāṇa*:
"In a pure place, or by a river, one should cause [the piṇḍa] to flow away when the water has become old.
In the *Padmapurāṇa*:
One should perform the offering of rice-balls for the deceased for twelve days;
that is declared to be his provision for the journey, since it brings him great satisfaction.

In the Vārāha Purāṇa: "O beautiful one, having performed the formal resolve (saṃkalpa) for the funeral cakes (piṇḍa) by means of name and lineage, one should indeed offer the portion for the deceased on the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) during the forenoon itself."
Afterwards, the clansmen eat; those of the same lineage share a single meal. One should not give to one of a different lineage, since they eat together as one.
O Mādhavī, among all four castes,
men who have gone to the world of the departed are pleased by offerings given in this manner during funeral rites.
In the *Kūrmapurāṇa*:
"For ten days, all the relatives, having bathed and being well-restrained,
should offer the funeral rice-ball (*piṇḍa*) every day according to the rules, both evening and morning."
In the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*: "For one who has become a *preta*, one should constantly offer rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) and water, along with sesame seeds and *kuśa* grass, outside near a body of water."
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*: "Those who have retired to the forest must perform the offering of rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) for the deceased for ten days outside the village, near a body of water."
If the offering of alms in the forest is not performed out of delusion,
then upon death, on the very first day, one goes to the Raurava hell.
Others say that in the third [fever] there is the Mahārāva, known by a name of auspicious meaning;
but in the fourth, one passes even into the most terrible state called Tāmisra.
In the fifth [hell] is Andhatāmisra, and in the sixth is the terrible Suprabha;
on the seventh day, there is the sin-filled [hell] filled with impurities and pus.
On the eighth day, the person goes entirely to the terrible Asipatravana hell;
on the ninth day, he goes to the one known as Mahāraurava.

On the tenth day, one should perform the libation for the deceased with rice, barley flour, vegetables, or fruits, according to one's faith and in accordance with the place and time, in that terrifying realm known as Avīci.
Viṣṇu says: "For as long as the period of impurity lasts, they should offer water and one funeral cake (piṇḍa) for the deceased. [In] the Brahma-purāṇa:
On the day of the deceased, a funeral ball (piṇḍa) should indeed be offered in a single sequence.
Śātātapa says:
"Even when the period of impurity is reduced to three days, one should nevertheless offer all ten funeral balls."
Then, at the śrāddha ceremony, one should offer a single ball of rice according to the prescribed rule.
Regarding that, Pāraskara states the method for offering the ten funeral cakes (piṇḍas) during a three-day period of impurity:
"On the first day, three cakes should be offered by those who are composed;
on the second day, one should offer four, as well as the collection of the bones."
On the third day, however, one should give three [garments] as well as clothing for washing and so forth.
In the *Brahmapurāṇa*, however, regarding the matter of immediate purification (*sadyaḥśauca*), there is the offering of ten rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) simultaneously:
"When the period of impurity lasts for three days, one rice-ball is indeed to be offered on the first day,
four on the second day, and five on the third."

Indeed, in certain cases, having prioritized local customs, people cast funeral rice-balls (*pretapiṇḍa*) for the social classes (*varṇa*) in numbers equal to the periods of impurity prescribed by birth.
The tenth *piṇḍa* for kings should indeed be offered on the twelfth day;
for Vaiśyas, the tenth is likewise to be offered on the fifteenth day;
and for a Śūdra, the tenth *piṇḍa* is given on the full completion of the month.
Pāraskara states: "For a Brāhmaṇa, ten piṇḍas are prescribed; for a Kṣatriya, twelve are recorded;
for a Vaiśya, fifteen are declared; and for a Śūdra, thirty are proclaimed."
Regarding those for whom the aforementioned number is not applicable, he [the same author] states another number:
"One should offer ten balls of rice to the deceased belonging to all castes;
however, when the Śrāddha rite has arrived, only one ball of rice is prescribed."
Pracetās said: "One should offer the rice-ball for those who have not undergone consecration on the ground, and for those who have undergone consecration, on *kuśa* grass. Thus says Śunaḥpuccha.
With fruits, roots, milk, vegetables, and molasses,
one should offer a rice-ball mixed with sesame seeds upon *darbha* grass to the south.
One should silently offer water for rinsing the mouth, flowers, incense, and likewise a lamp;
one may also present these with rice, fine grains, or even vegetables.
Whatever substance is used on the first day, that same substance shall be used throughout the ten-day period.

In the *Bhaviṣyottara*: "Whatever one might give on the first day— be it boiled rice, meat, parched grain, vegetables, roots, fruits, and so forth— one should give that same thing on the following day."
In the *Gṛhyapariśiṣṭa*:
"Whether of a different lineage or the same lineage, whether a woman or a man—
whoever offers [the water] on the first day, he shall complete it for ten days."
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*:
"He who, with a concentrated mind, offers food to the deceased on the first day,
he indeed offers it even on the other nine days."
In the *Bhaviṣyottara*: "At the door of the house, in the cremation ground, at a sacred ford (*tīrtha*), or likewise in a temple—
wherever the first funeral cake (*piṇḍa*) is offered, there one should complete everything."
Pracetās said:
Having taken new vessels, as well as a water-pot and a cooking-pot,
one should then go for the sake of water, taking a man with him in front.
Holding a staff, he wards off all evils from the path.
Then, having brought rice for the deceased, he should enter the house; taking a handful of that rice, the rite of offering the funeral cake (piṇḍa) must be performed.
Having washed them thoroughly three times, one should then prepare the *caru* offering;
having prepared it and taken it up, one should place it upon *darbha* grass.
With the tips of the *darbha* grass pointing southward and facing the southern direction,
he should take up the *piṇḍa*, form it, and offer it by means of [the deceased's] name and lineage.
In the Ādityapurāṇa: "The performer, facing south upon *darbha* grass mixed with sesame seeds,
should offer the *piṇḍa* according to the name and lineage, but without mantras."
Marīci said:
Having bathed and being pure in mind, one should prepare the *caru* in the northeast and offer the *piṇḍa* for the *preta* outside, devoid of *darbha* grass and mantras.
In the Ādityapurāṇa: "One should never employ the word 'pitṛ' (father/ancestor) nor the exclamation 'svadhā';
likewise, one should here carefully avoid the word 'anu'."
One should recite: "May this ball of rice attend upon the deceased (preta)."
Whether impure, one may offer incense, sprinkled water, a lamp, and likewise flowers to those of the three castes; of this there is no doubt.
Śātātapa says: Restrained in speech and purified, he should remain standing near the funeral cake (piṇḍa).
Then, once its steam has ceased, he should cast it into a river.
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*:
"Having bathed and being well-restrained, one should take a new earthen vessel,
grasp a staff that destroys all evil-doers, and fetch water."
Then, one should kindle the fire in the northeastern direction;
there, having washed three handfuls of rice three times, one should cook it oneself.
Then, having placed at the edge of the door pure white clay mixed with sesame seeds accompanied by purificatory blades (pavitra), free from insects and hair;
Upon that [seat], he should spread darbha grass grown in the region with its tips pointing toward the south;
then, while recollecting the lineage and the name [of the deceased], he should offer the water for washing the feet.
Having sprinkled the heated ground with sesame, ghee, honey, and milk,
one standing facing south should offer the funeral cake (piṇḍa) to the deceased.
In some places, it is mixed with fruits, roots, jaggery, milk, and sesame seeds;
likewise, with water-offerings, flowers, incense, lamps, and cool waters.
One should worship the *piṇḍa* with pure garments made of woolen threads.
As long as a column of vapor rises from the *piṇḍa* up to the sky, one should remain standing facing it; then, one should cast the *piṇḍa* into the water.
In the first [round], one handful of water and one vessel are given;
in the second, two; in the third, three; and likewise in the fourth, four.
In the fifth [there are] five, in the sixth likewise five, and in the seventh seven;
in the eighth eight, in the ninth nine, and in the tenth ten.
By which there may be fifty-five handfuls of water in succession;
that many vessels of water, prepared with sesame seeds and other ingredients, [should be provided].
There are eleven impairments of the sense organs, together with the impairments of the intellect,
for all living beings as they transition to the next world.
But for those who partake of the portion of the hungry ghosts (preta) dwelling in the Raurava and other hells,
their eleven sense-faculties are purified by these five [offerings] with each of the five vessels, as well as by the añjali-gestures, according to the teaching of the scriptures.
Vṛddha-Śātātapa also says:
"Day after day, one should offer full handfuls for the sake of the deceased;
the increase [of offerings] should continue until the funeral cake (piṇḍa) is completed."
The fruit of the offering of the rice-ball (*piṇḍa*) and the water-libation is stated in the *Ādityapurāṇa*:
"Whether they belong to one's own lineage or another lineage, women as well as men—
those who have become *preta*s— are liberated from that state by that ritual act."
But having become like the wind, they always remain for as long as time permits.
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*:
"Those men who go to offer the funeral rice-ball (*piṇḍa*) to a deceased ancestor should depart from the house placing the eldest brother at their head."
Having placed short men in front, they enter the house;
having stepped over the weapon and the stone, they enter the house in succession.
For one day, having placed a water vessel at the doorway,
I resolved out of compassion that there should also be a vessel of milk for the sake of the preta.
"O preta, bathe in this cool water; then drink milk.
Reciting this for three nights, one should likewise throw a handful of cooked rice [into the water].
Śātātapa says:
"Water and milk should be placed for one day in the open air in earthen vessels.

The meaning is that, with reference to the deceased (preta), one should first place water and milk separately in earthen vessels in the "open air"—that is, elsewhere than on the ground, such as on a hanging shelf or similar object—for one full day and night.
Regarding this, an increase in the number of days is stated in the *Padmapurāṇa*:
"Because the deceased is led to the city of the dead within twelve days,
he beholds his home, sons, and wife for those twelve days."
Therefore, for ten nights,
one should certainly consume milk in the open air for the sake of pacifying all afflictions and destroying the fatigue of travel.
The word "should place" (*sthāpayet*) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence.

Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Section on the Procedure for Śrāddhas at Sacred Fords (*tīrtha-śrāddha*) and Other Rites," in the *Śrāddhakalpa* within the *Pariśeṣakhaṇḍa* of the *Caturvargacintāmaṇi*, composed by the illustrious Hemādri, the scholar (*paṇḍita*) and chief minister of all affairs to the illustrious Mahādevī, the supreme sovereign of great kings (*mahārājādhirāja*).
[1596] Chapter Twenty:
Now begins the section on the practical application of the *śrāddha* and other rites for the satisfaction of the departed (*preta*).
In that regard, the ten bodily parts to be accomplished by means of the ten *piṇḍas* are described in the *Brahmapurāṇa*: "The head of the deceased is always fashioned by the first *piṇḍa*;
by the second, the body, ears, eyes, and nose are formed in brief."
With the third [offering], one should [offer] the throat, face, arms, and chest in due order;
with the fourth lump, however, the navel, genitals, and anus.
One should always [purify] the thighs, shanks, and feet with the fifth [vow];
all the skin with the sixth; and the channels with the seventh.
The growth of the gums occurs on the eighth day; fullness and the reversal of hunger arise on the ninth, and likewise on the tenth in due order.
In the Āditya Purāṇa: "The head is produced from the funeral cake (piṇḍa) offered on the first day;
the eyes, ears, and nose are produced on the second day."
On the third day, the two arms, the chest, and the neck are formed;
the heart, the sides, the abdomen, and the seat of the vital breaths constitute the fourfold [set].
On the fifth day, the region of the hips and the anus become supple;
on the sixth day, the thighs are to be known [as formed]; likewise, on the seventh day, the fingers [and toes] appear.
The two feet are to be known in the ninth [house], and the eyes of valor in the tenth;
likewise, at the beginning, the physical form arises, as well as the auspicious and inauspicious.
Within ten days, knowledge regarding the deceased arises through the offering of the *pretapiṇḍa*,
because during those ten days the ritual of pronouncing the name and other details is performed.
That which arises merely by name is designated as the "living being" (jīva) in name only;
the wise know that its establishment as a mere name persists even when [the body] has not perished.
Now follows the procedure for the *śrāddhas* for the deceased (*preta*).
Regarding that, the number, the eligibility, and the time for these [rites] designated as "the nine" have already been explained previously. As for the purpose, Vyāghrapāt says:
"The nine *śrāddhas* should be diligently offered for the sake of purifying the house."
Then, for the sake of purifying the deceased, [one should perform the rite] on the anniversary of death for one year.

The word "then" (*tataḥ*) means after the *navaśrāddha* (the funeral rites for the newly deceased). The meaning is that, month by month on the anniversary of death, *śrāddhas* should be offered for as long as a year for the sake of liberation from the state of being a *preta*.
However, Vṛddhavasiṣṭha says:
"But without performing the *navaśrāddha*, one is not released from the state of being a *preta*."
But by receiving [the gift] before the completion of twelve days, one overcomes evil deeds.

By this, it is stated that even for those who have recently died (*navaśrāddha*), liberation from the state of being a *preta* is the purpose. "Evil deed" (*duṣkṛta*) refers to that which causes the state of being a *preta*; having received the *śrāddhas* performed from the day of death up until the end of the eleventh day—prior to the twelfth day—one crosses over [that state]. By this, it is also understood that the *śrāddhas* performed before the twelfth day bear the designation of "recent *śrāddhas*" (*navaśrāddha*).
Yama says that if these *preta-śrāddhas* are not offered, there is no liberation from the state of being a *preta*:
"For whomsoever these sixteen *ekoddiṣṭas* have not been given..."
His state as a piśāca remains firm, even by means of hundreds of funeral offerings (śrāddha) performed for him.
"Piśācatva" (the state of being a piśāca) refers to the condition of a living being denoted by the term "preta.
However, in the Bhaviṣyapurāṇa, the purpose of this is stated as the cessation of downward rebirth:
"The *navaśrāddha*, the three fortnights, the six months, and the monthly rites..."
But for that son who does not perform [the rites], his ancestors have gone to the lower realms.
Likewise, it is stated in that very same source that the qualification for the subsequent *śrāddhas* is also their purpose:
"But for one by whom the *śrāddhas*, such as the *nava-śrāddha* and others, have indeed not been performed,
he would not be qualified for those [performed] at the end of a month, six months, or a year."
In the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa: "One should diligently perform the nine śrāddhas intended for the deceased according to the procedure for the ekoddiṣṭa; never otherwise."
Chāgaleya said:
But if birth-impurity (sūtaka) should occur during the period of impurity following a death, or likewise during the impurity of a night,
the nine *śrāddhas* must be offered at the proper times and in the proper sequence.

In this context, the sequence and the time have already been shown previously in the section on time (*kālaprakaraṇa*). Regarding the *navaśrāddha* (funeral rites for the newly deceased), the non-performance of certain ritual items is stated in the *Gṛhyapariśiṣṭa*: "The *navaśrāddha* is without water, without incense, devoid of perfumes and garlands, without mantras, and devoid of rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) and water libations."
"Without water" means without the precious rice-ball (piṇḍa) and water consisting of the acts of washing and sprinkling.
Likewise:
"In all Ekoddiṣṭa rites, there is neither the utterance of *svadhā* nor the request 'May you be satisfied' (*abhiramyatām*)."
The mantra for the offering into the fire and the single offering of water with sesame seeds are given everywhere without specifically designating the deceased.

In the case of all those who are childless, there is neither the *svadhā* nor the expression of satisfaction (*abhiramyatām*). One should dismiss them with "May it be well" (*svasti astu*), saying this only once and omitting the *praṇava*.
In the *piṇḍa* of the *ekoddiṣṭa*, however, the word "anu" (after) is not used;
one should not employ the word "pitṛ" (father), for otherwise one becomes a slayer of one's ancestors.

Many commentators have explained that this refers to the *ekoddiṣṭa* rites performed prior to the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*. By the phrase "to the deceased" (*pretāya*), it is stated that the word *preta* should be employed here, and not the word *pitṛ*.
Thus says Āpastamba.

For the occasional *śrāddha*, they prepare the rite outside the village, being pure themselves in a pure place. There, one should give to those who have eaten new articles—both those by which the food is prepared and those upon which it is eaten—and one should feed them all together. One should not give the leftovers to anyone of inferior quality; thus for a year, one should perform the rite with the finest metal and a goat, and have a measuring vessel made. In the northern half of a covered area, one should feed the Brahmins; for they teach that when one sees both the Brahmins eating and the ancestors as if they were oneself, the purpose is achieved. From this point forward, the ancestors are said to be satisfied by the *śrāddha* regardless of whether it has been performed fully or partially.
By the term *naimittika*, the *śrāddhas* for the deceased (*preta*) are meant;
therefore, Gālava said:
"Starting from the cremation, the wise should offer the *naimittika-śrāddha*."
"By rule, for as long as a year"—thus was it spoken by Gālava.
The food remaining from a *navaśrāddha* (a funeral rite for the newly deceased) must not be eaten by the performer of the rite or by anyone else.
Thus says Aṅgiras:
"That which remains in the house from *navaśrāddhas*, and that which has become stale..."
And one should never eat what remains after the husband and wife have eaten.
In response to the inquiry as to how the remainder of the food at a *nava-śrāddha* (recent funeral rite) should be disposed of, Devala says:
"In the case of *ekoddiṣṭa* rites, one should discard the remainder to the Brahmins;
thereafter, one may eat it oneself at an auspicious meal."

In the *ekoddiṣṭa* rites known as the *navaśrāddha*, one should offer the remnants to the Brahmins who have eaten at the *śrāddha*; or, with their permission, one may cast them into water or similar elements. However, one must not eat them oneself, nor should one feed anyone else [with them]. ‘Then,’ that is, subsequently, when the ‘auspicious meal’ (*maṅgalabhojana*)—such as the annual anniversary rite (*sāṃvatsarika*) and others—is being performed, one should feed kinsmen and others with the remnants of the *śrāddha*. The sacrificer himself should also eat. But with food other than the *śrāddha* remnants, kinsmen, the poor, the helpless, and so forth, should be fed. Thus it is stated in the *Brahmapurāṇa* after describing the *navaśrāddha* rites:
Men should perform the śrāddha rite according to the requirements of place and time.
Those who share the same ancestry (sapiṇḍas), as well as others of the same caste, and even others who are hungry— the poor, the helpless, and the wretched— all partake of the food.
If this food has been eaten by someone who is not a relative, the expiation for that case is also stated right here:
"For those who possess discernment, purification shall come through two *taptakṛcchra* penances;
on the third and fifth [days] one should perform a bath, and likewise on the ninth."
Thus concludes the procedure for the nine types of *śrāddha* rites.
Now follows the procedure for the eleven additional *śrāddha* rites;
regarding this, the *Kūrmapurāṇa* states:
On the eleventh day, one should perform [the rite] with devotion for the sake of the deceased;
or it should be performed on the twelfth day, or indeed on any other blameless day.
One purifying blade of grass, one *arghya* offering, and likewise one *piṇḍa* and bowl;
thus should it be performed on the anniversary of death for a year, month by month.
In the Padma Purāṇa: "Then, on the eleventh day, one should feed exactly eleven brahmins— odd numbers of brahmins— at the end of the period of impurity (sūtaka), beginning with their lineage names."
On the second day, one should again perform the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite in the same manner,
according to the prescribed rule, omitting the invocation (*āvāhana*), the offering into the fire (*agnaukaraṇa*), and the rites for the gods (*daiva*).
One purifying blade of grass, one *arghya* offering, and one rice-ball (*piṇḍa*) are prescribed;
after saying "May they approach you," water with sesame seeds should be offered.
One should say "Svaditam" when two hands are joined, and "Abhiramyatām" at the conclusion;
those learned in the Vedas know that the remainder here also should be performed as previously described.
One should perform everything according to this rule every month.

In the *Brahmapurāṇa*: "On the third day, the twice-born should perform the *śrāddha* on the funeral pyre where the deceased was cremated; at the end of the period of impurity (*sūtaka*), they declare that the *ekoddiṣṭa* should be performed at home."
On the twelfth day, after a month, and after three fortnights,
and thereafter every month until the end of the year, O twice-born one, [the rite] must be performed.
In the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa:
"Listen now to that which is to be performed on the anniversary of death—the Ekoddiṣṭa rite;
it is devoid of [invocations to] the gods, possesses only a single water-offering (arghya), and likewise has only a single purifying blade of grass (pavitraka)."
One should not perform the invocation (āvāhana), as it is devoid of the fire-offering (agnaukaraṇa);
one should offer a single rice-ball (piṇḍa) for the deceased near the remains of the food.
And one should offer water with sesame seeds while keeping the sacred thread over the right shoulder (apasavya), accompanied by the recollection of the deceased's name, saying:
"May this be inexhaustible for [Name], and may it attend upon him."
Thus the performer should diligently say during the dismissal of the Brahmins;
he should say, "May you be satisfied," and they should reply, "We are satisfied.
This should be performed by men every month until the end of the year.
In the Baudhāyana-sūtra.

Now, in the case of the *ekoddiṣṭa* (rites for a single deceased person), there is no offering into the fire (*agnaukaraṇa*), no placing on the fire (*atiśrayaṇa*), no preliminary rite (*pūrva*), no rite for the gods (*daiva*), no incense (*dhūpa*), no lamp (*dīpa*), and neither the *svadhā* nor the salutation (*namaskāra*). There is no sacrificial cake (*apūpa*) here; rather, having brought all that is prepared, he should seat an uneven number of Brahmins whose hands and feet have been well washed, having given them water to sip (*ācamana*), upon seats prepared with *darbha* grass. Having taken portions from everything once each, and having sprinkled them with clarified butter, he should draw out embers mixed with ashes toward the south and offer oblations upon them, saying: "To the deceased [Name], to Yama, Svāhā! That which is offered becomes as if unoffered; he says, "May there be satisfaction for [Name]," and performs the receiving and dismissal of the water. He pays homage to [Name] without specifying others. The offering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) is directed only to those [deceased ancestors] for whom it was intended; he says, "Be satisfied," and dismisses them with "May there be satisfaction. For the others, the response is, "Salutations! May there be satisfaction. For the deceased, there is an increase by one Brahmin starting from the second day until the tenth day; at this point, the new [lineage] is severed. On the eleventh day, the *śrāddha* is performed. In the third fortnight, the second [monthly *śrāddha*] is performed. They carry it continuously, one by one, for eleven months; that reaches the twelfth month.
Baudhāyana says: The *ekoddiṣṭa* rite should take place on the very next day, or again on the twelfth day;
or else, one may perform it after that on an odd-numbered day according to one's own ability.
Whether it be half a month, a month, a season, or even a year,
the invitation for the rite to the gods should take place on the preceding day, as should the offering into the fire.
There is no *svadhā*, no announcement (*āśrāvaṇā*), nor cakes, incense, lamps, or prostration;
having kindled the fire, sprinkled it around, and strewn grass around it, one should set down the offerings.
A ladle made of udumbara wood, a vessel for clarified butter,
a large spoon, a sacrificial bowl, water for sprinkling, and likewise a vessel of sesame-water.
Having sprinkled this food along with the special offerings, having poured out the clarified butter,
and having placed it on the fire and performed the circumambulation with fire (paryagni), he should then [proceed] with both of those.
Having cleansed the *sruva* and *darvī* ladles, having removed the food and poured clarified butter over it,
one should prepare the *tilodaka* (sesame-water) for men and women with the prescribed mantras.
One should insert the word "pitṛ" (father/ancestors) everywhere except for the *svadhā* formula;
having invoked the deceased (*preta*), seated the Brahmins, and invited them [to the rite].
"May there be satisfaction for such-and-such a person"—thus one should offer the water with sesame seeds here;
and another, having offered it as well, should say "May there be satisfaction," once [the recipient] has been adorned.
Having been granted permission with "I shall do so" and urged with "Do it," he should then spread a base [of ghee] in the ladle, taking portions from all the foods once each.
Then, having sprinkled [the oblation] and set aside the embers mixed with ashes separately to the south, one should offer [the sacrifice] with the mantra beginning "To the preta," and so forth.
Then, having touched the food, offered it, and placed it down, he should dedicate it with the words,
"May they partake through this," while looking at them with the sacred mantras.
After they have eaten and sipped water, and after [the host] has expressed that it was well-prepared and offered water with sesame seeds;
having scattered [rice], poured out [water], and given the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) at the site of the funeral rite when the sun has risen.
Having saluted them, he should say, "May there be satisfaction," and they too should say, "May there be satisfaction"; then he should perform the concluding rite of permission.
Having been permitted with the words "with what remains of the food," and having offered the *piṇḍa* and sprinkled water,
he should take that *piṇḍa* along with the leavings, saying, "May you be satisfied."
Having cast that [offering] at the edge of the waters and bathed, he should go toward his home,
accompanied by the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*), lamps, full water-jars, and other such auspicious items.
At the door of his house, having seen [guests], he may eat the remaining food according to his desire;
but a Kṣatriya, immediately after bathing, may touch the mounted vehicle.

A Vaiśya should carry a goad or a whip, and a Śūdra who has performed his duties should carry a staff; by performing this rite up to the end of the Ekoddiṣṭa, the performer is indeed released from sin.

When the third fortnight has arrived, one should certainly perform the second [offering]. And month by month, according to one's desire, one may perform it; however, when the [first] year has somehow expired, some perform it on the anniversary of his death every year.
Bṛhatpracetā states: "The ancestral recitation (japa) should not be performed, nor should one utter the word 'svadita'. This is found in the Bahvṛca-gṛhya-pariśiṣṭa.
In the *ekoddiṣṭa* rice-ball offering, the word "anu" (after) is not used; one should not utter the word "pitṛ" (father).

Bhṛgu states that in the *ekoddiṣṭa*, the *kuśa* grasses should have their roots; this is a prohibition against using grass that has been once-cut. One should perform both the *avanejana* (sprinkling) and the *pratyavanejana* (re-sprinkling). Furthermore, one should not offer incense, sandalwood paste, garlands, and so forth.

The first funeral rite (navaśrāddha) is performed without water, honey, and sesame; it is devoid of perfumes and garlands, is without mantras, and is bereft of both rice-balls (piṇḍa) and water libations.

Because of this statement; and because of the statement "the remaining food," one should not say "the remaining food. Even the remainder should be given to him or cast into the water; it must not be eaten by anyone else. On the eleventh day, even by one who maintains the sacred fires (*sāgnika*), the *vaiśvadeva* sacrifice must be performed afterwards. And so says the *Pariśiṣṭa*:
"When the *pārvaṇa* śrāddha has arrived, and likewise in the *ekoddiṣṭa*..."
The Vaiśvadeva sacrifice should take place first, on the eleventh day after [the death].
And likewise, there is a specific rule regarding the gift of a bed and other items, as Satyavrata has stated:
"Even when immediate purification (*sadyaḥśauca*) applies, the gift for the deceased must be given on the eleventh day;
that very day serves as the [proper time] for his *śrāddha*, bed, seat, and so forth."
This *śrāddha* is not only for a Brāhmaṇa on the eleventh day, but this very time is also prescribed for the first *śrāddha* of a Kṣatriya and others.
Thus says Paiṭhīnasi:
"The *śrāddha* which is performed on the eleventh day is declared to be common [to all]."
"The period of impurity (sūtaka) for all four castes is indeed distinct for each. Thus [it is said].

Nor should it be suspected that a Kṣatriya or others lack the entitlement to perform the *śrāddha* there due to impurity; for even one who is impure possesses this entitlement by virtue of scriptural injunction (*vācanika*). Thus says Śaṅkha:
"One should perform the first *śrāddha* on the eleventh day, even if he is impure."
"The agent's purity is only momentary; he becomes impure once again. Thus [it is said].
The word "first" (ādyam) means that which is the archetype for all *ekoddiṣṭa* rites, namely the one known as the eleventh-day rite (*ekādaśāha*).
After this *śrāddha*, one should bathe and eat.
Likewise, there are other specific details.
Blessings are doubled; there is the benediction for victory and the recitation of auspicious verses (*svastivācana*);
likewise, there is the mention of the word "father" in relation to kinship and the word "śarma."
The invitation, the taking up of the vessel, the drawing of the firebrand and so forth,
the inquiry regarding satiety, the modification, and likewise the inquiry regarding the remnants.
One should avoid these eighteen matters at a śrāddha for the deceased: circumambulation, the formal dismissal of guests, and likewise proceeding to the boundary.
Manu:
For one who has passed away, the twice-born should perform the *asapiṇḍa* rite;
they should offer a *śrāddha* without an invitation to the gods and should cause only a single *piṇḍa* to be made.

Yājñavalkya says: The *ekoddiṣṭa* rite is devoid of offerings to the gods; it consists of a single *arghya* offering and a single *pavitraka*; it is indeed performed without the invocation (*āvāhana*) and the *agnaukaraṇa* oblation, and with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*apasavya*).
At the dismissal of the Brahmins, while standing in the place of imperishability,
he should say, "May you be pleased," and they should reply, "We are pleased."

Kātyāyana says: Now, regarding the *ekoddiṣṭa* (offering for a single deceased person), there is one *arghya*, one *pavitra*, and one *piṇḍa*; there is no invocation (*āvāhana*), no offering into the fire (*agnaukaraṇa*), and no Viśvedevas here. The question regarding satisfaction is "Is it well-tasted? (*svaditam*). In place of the word "imperishable" (*akṣayya*), [the word] "may he approach" (*upatiṣṭatām*) is used. The dismissal is "May you be pleased" (*abhiramyatām*), and the others reply, "We are pleased" (*abhiratāḥ smaḥ*). Sāṅkhyāyana says:

Now, therefore, follows the *ekoddiṣṭa* (rite for a single deceased person): there is one purifier (*pavitra*), one offering of water (*arghya*), and one rice-ball (*piṇḍa*). There is no invocation (*āvāhana*), no offering into the fire (*agnaukaraṇa*), and no Viśvedevas in this rite. The question regarding satisfaction is "Is it *svadita*? In place of the word "imperishable" (*akṣayya*), the formula is "May [the deceased] be present" (*upatiṣṭhatām*). The dismissal is "May you be pleased" (*abhiramyatām*). This is done thus for one year after death.
Regarding "one purifier," it means a purifier with a single tip. However, in the *Nāgarakhaṇḍa*, it is also stated that it may have two tips.

O best of kings, the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite should be performed devoid of the deities, with only a single offering of water (*arghya*) and a single purifying blade of grass (*pavitraka*), and excluding the invocation (*āvāhana*).
Likewise, the inquiry regarding satisfaction should be made once with the words "Was it well-tasted?
Then, the dismissal of the Brāhmaṇa should be performed with the mantra "May you be pleased."
One should prepare two blades of *darbha* grass with uncut tips and unbroken points;
one should know that as the *pavitra*, and it is prescribed for the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite.
In the *Bhaviṣyottara*: "The śrāddha which is performed on the eleventh day is declared to be general;
one should give [offerings] to eleven Brahmins on the eleventh day."

And there, having honored with devotion a single high-souled Brāhmaṇa, one should give him food, along with clothing, ornaments, and a bed; as well as whatever vehicles his father possessed, and cows, houses, seats, and female slaves.
In the Vārāha Purāṇa:
"On the eleventh day, one must diligently perform the Śrāddha for the deceased.
Having determined, 'I shall perform it tomorrow,' one should carry out the rite of inviting the Brāhmaṇas."
Having bathed and become pure, one should assign the deceased among the Brahmins, saying:
"You have gone to the divine world by the path ordained by Kṛtānta."
"O Brahmin, with my mind transformed into the wind, I shall employ you;
I will honor you with enjoyments. In this manner, one should invite the Brahmin.
When the sun had set, he went to the brahmin’s residence,
offered water for washing the feet according to the rules, and paid homage to those best of the twice-born.
Having anointed the feet of the deceased with oil out of a desire for his welfare,
when the night has turned to dawn and the sun has risen;
One should perform the shaving of the beard as well as the clipping of the nails;
one should provide the Brahmin with bathing and anointing according to the prescribed ritual.
Having taken possession of a portion of ground, one should immediately prepare a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila);
having selected a site for the water-channel, a great sacrificial mound must be constructed.
Or, if dwelling on a riverbank, one should designate that as the ground for the deceased (pretabhūmi).

O auspicious lady, those who perform the funeral offering without first setting aside a portion for the earth make the entire world dependent upon that [offering], and thus it becomes rendered as their leavings.
Neither the gods nor the ancestors ever accept offerings from him in this world;
by that leavings, O beautiful one, they fall into a terrible hell.
Having bathed with his clothes on and gone to a great river,
the wise man, having meditated upon sacred fords (tīrthas) in his mind, should sprinkle himself with their waters.
Having thus performed purification, one should quickly summon a Brāhmaṇa;
and upon seeing the twice-born guest arrived, the rites of welcome should be performed.
Then, O Mādhavī, having offered water for honor and water for the feet with a joyful and contented heart,
one should prepare a seat according to the prescribed rule and with the appropriate mantra.
Likewise:
Having seated him on an auspicious seat, one should provide an umbrella there;
that umbrella is given to the Brāhmaṇa for the purpose of protection.
Afterwards, one should give a pair of auspicious sandals that protect the feet from the scorching sands of the earth as well as from snakes and thorns.
By giving a pair of sandals to a Brahmin who has restrained his self, after performing the ritual service with sesame seeds, one causes the deceased to cross over difficult passages.
Having first uttered the name and lineage of the preta,
one who holds darbha grass in hand should then quickly summon him to the ground upon the earth.
The mantra:
"Having abandoned this world, you have gone to the supreme destination.
Having thus invoked him, one should worship with perfumes, flowers, and incense.
Then, O beautiful one, one should provide all the garments and ornaments to the Brahmin,
and thereafter one should prepare cooked food as well.
O Mādhavī, all such substances intended for the portion of the *preta*s,
beginning with the washing of the feet, [should be offered] to the four castes.
Bṛhaspati says: When an offering is made for a single person according to the procedure for an *ekoddiṣṭa* rite,
it is devoid of the invocation (*āvāhana*), the ritual of placing food in the fire (*agnaukaraṇa*), and the portion for the gods (*daiva*).
Having honored with perfumes and garlands whatever garments, ornaments, beds, vehicles, and weapons belonged to his father, he should present them to the recipient of the śrāddha feast.
One should cause various kinds of food and side dishes to be prepared;
and according to one's ability, one should likewise bestow gifts such as cows, land, gold, and so forth.
Nine, seven, or thirteen śrotriyas are to be fed,
as well as kinsmen, relatives, or other guests.
One should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to all of them according to their merit;
a Śrāddha performed by one who is not learned in the Vedas is as good as lost, and a sacrifice without a sacrificial fee is lost.
Therefore, one should give as a sacrificial fee in the ritual even a paṇa, a kārṣāpaṇa, or even a fruit or a flower; by that, the merit becomes a hundredfold.

Satyavrata says: Having risen in the morning and invited eleven Brāhmaṇas representing the deceased, one should, in the afternoon, perform the offering of funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*) according to the rules, dedicating each one to an individual, accompanied by various kinds of food, drinks, and savory dishes. Then follows the giving of gifts—clothing, gold, a female slave, shoes, an umbrella, and a water-pot—as well as the gift of a bed to a virtuous recipient. Thereafter, the rites beginning with the recitation of auspicious prayers (*svastyayana*) proceed. When the tenth day has passed, one should feed them individually; a bed should be given to one among them who is particularly virtuous. Viṣṇu says:

Then, at the end of the period of impurity, having bathed, thoroughly washed his hands and feet, and performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*), he should feed Brāhmaṇas of such a kind as before, facing north, according to his ability, after honoring them with perfumes, garlands, garments, ornaments, and so forth. In the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite, he should modify the mantras to the singular. In the vicinity of the food remnants, he should offer a single *piṇḍa* (funeral cake) using the deceased's name and lineage (*gotra*). When the Brāhmaṇas have eaten and have been honored with sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), and the water for inexhaustibility (*akṣayyodaka*) has been offered with the deceased’s name and lineage, he should prepare three trenches—four finger-breadths wide, separated by that same distance, dug to that same depth, and one span long. Near these trenches, he should establish three fires, spread sacred grass around them, and offer three oblations into one of them: "Svadhā! Adoration to Soma accompanied by the ancestors; Svadhā! Adoration to Agni, the bearer of the *kavya*; Svadhā! Adoration to Yama, the descendant of Aṅgiras. In the three locations, he should perform the offering of *piṇḍas* as previously described. Then, having filled the three trenches with curd, honey, clarified butter, and meat, he should mutter: "This is for you. He should perform this every month on the anniversary of the death.
Laghuhārīta states:
One should always personally perform the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite with cooked food alone;
in the absence of cooked food, one should fast on that day.
Thus concludes the procedure for the *śrāddha* rites performed on the eleventh day and subsequent days.
Now follows the ritual for the gift of the "bed of the deceased."
And since that [gift] is to be completed by the extension (*atideśa*) of the procedure for the gift of a bed for the living (*jīvacchayyā*), it is described as being preceded by that.
In this regard, the *Bhaviṣyottara* states:
"O scion of the Yadu lineage, I shall proclaim to you the gift of a bed."
Having given this, one shall partake of auspiciousness both in this world and in the next.
All the gods and the best of the twice-born praise the gift of a bed,
for since life is impermanent, who else will provide it after one has passed away?
Therefore, O Bharata, as long as one's kinsman or father lives,
once he is known to be dead— dead indeed— affection ceases in an instant.
Therefore, one should personally provide bedding, food, water, and so forth,
having reflected in one's mind that "the self alone is indeed the friend of the self."
If one does not honor oneself with gifts and enjoyments,
who else indeed other than that self will honor one later on?
Therefore, having obtained a bed made of strong, seasoned wood— firm, beautiful,
adorned with ivory carvings, and decorated with bands of gold;
Covered with swan-feather down, provided with beautiful pillows for the cheeks,
furnished with a bedsheet, and perfumed with incense and fragrances.
Upon it, one should place a golden image of Hari accompanied by Lakṣmī;
at the head of the bed, one should arrange a water-pot filled with ghee.
O best of the Pāṇḍavas, the wise should recognize the "sleeping pitcher" as consisting of betel nut, saffron powder, camphor, agallochum, and sandalwood. [1612]
One should devoutly place a lamp, shoes, an umbrella, chowries, a seat, and a vessel, as well as the seven types of grain, at the sides.
Whatever else is beneficial for one lying on the bed,
such as golden jars and water-pitchers, as well as a five-colored Vināyaka [image], should be provided.
Having prepared such a bed, one should cause it to be given to a Brāhmaṇa together with his wife,
after honoring him on an auspicious day according to the prescribed ritual.
Just as the bed of Kṛṣṇa is never empty of the daughter of the ocean,
so may my own bed also be never empty, birth after birth.
Since the bed of Keśava and Śiva is never empty,
may my own bed likewise remain unfilled in birth after birth.
Having thus given everything to him and prostrating, one should bid him farewell;
this is the prescribed procedure for the gift of a bed that has been proclaimed.
This same rule is proclaimed for the eleventh day as well,
if a kinsman gives for the sake of dharma when a kinsman has died.
And listen, O Indra among kings, as I describe the distinction here:
whatever was enjoyed by him, and whatever remained previously in his house.
Whatever is clinging to his body, as well as his clothing, vehicle, and vessels—
whatever may be dear to him— one should provide all of that.
Then, one should place that very golden figure upon it;
having worshipped it, the death-bed should be given away as prescribed.
In the Padma Purāṇa: On the second day after the end of the impurity caused by death, one should give a distinctive bed,
as well as a golden man, provided with fruits and garments.
Having honored the brahmin couple, adorned them with various ornaments,
and seated them upon the bed, he should then offer the *madhuparka* and speak as follows.
Having taken the frontal bone with silver, one should grind it together with curd and milk,
making it fine and incorporating diamond.
A wise person, being self-restrained, should feed a Brahmin couple adorned with various ornaments with milk-rice; this is the eternal rule.
This very same rule has been observed by the most excellent Brahmins of the Pārvatīya region.
The procedure for the Brahmin’s seating upon the bed and the duties to be performed by the Brahmin are stated in the *Vārāha Purāṇa*:
"Having grasped the hand of the twice-born with his own hand, he should cause him to rise with the mantra;
he should likewise offer a bed and a seat, as well as collyrium and a comb."
Taking his collyrium-stick and comb, that twice-born man stepped onto the bed;
having rested there for a moment, he went to the place where the water-offering was made,
and leaning against the tail of a cow, he took hold of the Brahma-hand.
Regarding the fruit of the gift of a bed, it is stated in the *Bhaviṣyottara*:
"By the power of giving a bed, that person dwells happily in heaven, in the abode of Purandara, and likewise in the residence of the Son of the Sun."
In the abode of the Son of the Sun and likewise in the city of Vaivasvata,
the terrifying-faced messengers of Yama do not torment him.
That man is never oppressed by heat or cold;
even if he is joined with sin, he goes to the heavenly world.
Mounted upon a supreme celestial palace and attended by hosts of apsarases,
he remains free from all affliction until the dissolution of the world.
O son of Pāṇḍu, the stainless gift of a bed has been proclaimed by you as a treasury of all happiness;
indeed, he who gives it according to the prescribed rite shall dwell in the world of Viṣṇu.
Free from conceptual construction, that mortal shines for an eon.
In this context, the prohibition against accepting the bed of the deceased is stated in the *Padma Purāṇa*:
"The bed of the departed is extremely defiled and must not be accepted by the best of the twice-born;
if it has been accepted, one must undergo the purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) once again."
In both the Vedas and the Purāṇas, sleeping [on a cot] is everywhere condemned;
those who accept such gifts are all destined for hell.
Thus concludes the procedure for the gift of a bed. Beginning from the eleventh day until the end of the year, a water-pot (udakumbha) must be offered daily to the deceased.
And so it is stated in the Padma Purāṇa:
O best of men, a water-pot accompanied by various kinds of food and snacks should be given for a year, preceded by offerings of sesame seeds and water.
Hārīta said: When the father has died, the son should indeed offer a pure rice-ball (*piṇḍa*) and a jar of food to a Brahmin, according to the rule for designating the deceased.
In the *Smṛtisamuccaya*: "From the eleventh day onwards, sons should offer a water-pot filled with water and food every single day until the end of the year."
Pāraskara:
Day by day, one should give food and a water-pot to this Brāhmaṇa; some, moreover, offer him a funeral cake (piṇḍa).
Yājñavalkya says:
For one whose *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* has been performed before the completion of a year,
one should also give food along with a water-pot to a twice-born man for the duration of a year.
Āpastamba says:
For one whose *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* has been performed before the completion of a year,
one should offer a water-pot filled with food every day for the duration of that year.
Laukāxi says:
For one whose sapiṇḍīkaraṇa takes place before the completion of a year,
the monthly offerings and the water-pot (udakumbha) must also be given for that entire year.
Thus concludes the section on the water-pot. Now follows the ritual of releasing a bull (*vṛṣotsarga*).

Regarding this, first are its rules, time, and location; and here, it is stated in the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata* that on the eleventh day, the release of a bull should be performed for the sake of a deceased person.
If for a deceased person the bull is not released on the eleventh day,
his state as a Piśāca remains fixed, even by hundreds of Śrāddhas offered.
In the *Bhaviṣyottara*, however, the release of the bull (*vṛṣotsarga*) is prescribed for the twelfth day:
"O Yudhiṣṭhira, it may be performed on the full moon of Kārttika, or on the new moon, or at the solstice,
or on the third day of Caitra, or on the full moon of Vaiśākha, or on the twelfth day."
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*, however, the release of a bull (*vṛṣotsarga*) is prescribed even on any anniversary of death (*mṛtāha*):
"O Lord of Men, one should perform the release of a bull on the fifteenth day of the bright fortnight of Āśvayuja,
or likewise in the month of Kārttika."
On the two principal eclipses,
as well as during the two solstices, the two equinoxes, on the anniversary of a kinsman’s death,
and at the arrival of the Kaumudī festival, one should indeed release a blue-necked [goat].

‘Nīlakaṇṭha’ refers to a dark-colored bull. ‘Kaumudī’ is the full-moon day of the months of Āśvina and Kārtika. In the *Matsyapurāṇa*, there is a censure of one who does not perform the rite of releasing a bull (*vṛṣotsarga*) for the sake of his ancestors and others: “That son who does not release a bull at a sacred bathing place, nor offers a handful of water, is merely the excrement of his father.”
‘Uccāraḥ’ means the voiding of excrement. Here, the bull named Nīla is the most excellent of all.
Regarding the locations for the release of the bull, the Devīpurāṇa states:
"That release should take place in a forest, at a sacred ford (tīrtha), or even in a cow-pen."
In the *Brahmapurāṇa*:
"The release of the bull (*vṛṣotsarga*) should be performed in a pleasant, secluded forest on ground sloping toward the east or the north"— this is the remainder [of the statement].
In the *Kālikā Purāṇa*:
"A wise man, desiring abundant fruit, should release the bull in the forest, at a crossroads, or in a cow-pen; he should not release it within his house."
Thus ends the rules regarding the time and place for the rite of releasing a bull.
Now follows the characteristics of the bull to be released.
In the Matsya Purāṇa,
Manu said:
"O Blessed One, I wish to hear the characteristics of the bull."
As well as the ritual procedure for the release of a bull, and likewise its great meritorious fruit.
Matsya said: First, one should examine a cow that is well-behaved and endowed with auspicious marks— free from physical defects, not emaciated, having a living calf, and free from disease.
With glossy color, glossy hooves, and likewise glossy horns;
captivating, exceedingly gentle, well-proportioned, and not arrogant.
She who is endowed with rightward-turning curls on the right side and leftward-turning curls on the left,
and whose hips and breasts are broad;
She whose lips are soft, firm, and copper-colored, and whose tongue is red and highly honored;
likewise, she whose tongue is not blackish, not long, not cracked, and is red.
And her eyes were coppery and clouded by sparse, hard scales,
resembling beryl and the color of honey, like bubbles upon the water.
With eyes that are red and glossy, with pupils likewise red, possessing seven or fourteen teeth, and having a dark-colored palate— such a woman would be [unlucky].
She whose six parts are elevated, whose sides and thighs are well-formed, who is broad and possesses five equal proportions,
whose head and neck are eightfold in length, and who is endowed with auspicious marks.
In which [parts] are there six elevations, and in which five are there elongations? Likewise, for which cows are the eight elongations auspicious?
Matsya said:
"O lord of the earth, the wise revere six elevated parts of cows: the chest, the back, the head, the two flanks, and the hips."
O delighter of the Ratnas, the two ears, the two eyes, and the forehead—these five are praised when they are long; likewise, the tail and the two thighs should be measured with a cord.
And four breasts, O King; thus these eight, together with the head and neck, are exceedingly long in the case of kings, according to the wise.
One should examine her son as a bull endowed with auspicious marks:
with elevated shoulders and hump, a straight tail, and a dewlap.
He has great hips, a broad chest, and eyes like lapis lazuli gems;
the tips of his horns are the color of coral, and his tail-hair is very long and soft.
One with nine, eight, or ten auspicious teeth that have sharp tips should be released; even if kept in the home, such a Mallikākṣa bestows wealth and grain.
By color, a copper-brown horse is praised for a Brāhmaṇa;
likewise white, red, black, fair-complexioned, and pale-red are recommended.
One who has a back with the luster of sapphire, is brindled, has five black spots,
broad ears, large shoulders, and smooth hair;
One that has reddish eyes, is tawny, and has red horns,
as well as one with a white belly and a black back, is recommended for a Brāhmaṇa.
A glossy color with a reddish hue is praised for a Kṣatriya;
that with a golden luster for a Vaiśya; and even a black one for one of low birth.
He whose horn always extends forward, facing his own mouth,
is the accomplisher of all goals for all social classes alike.
A tawny cat with white paws is auspicious, as is one that is tawny-brown;
a white cat with white paws is also auspicious, possessing eyes resembling jewels.
Karaṭa and Piṅgala, as well as Śvetapāda,
Svacchapādaśiras, Dvipāda, and Śveta.
Blessed is he who resembles a francolin partridge, or likewise one resembling a partridge,
whose face shines white as far as the root of the ears.
He should be known as Nāndīmukha, especially red in color;
O Lord of Cows, his belly and back should be white.
That bull named Samudra is a constant increaser of his lineage;
variegated with jasmine-like flowers, this preeminent bull is auspicious.
O Lord of the Earth, he becomes variegated with lotuses and circles;
likewise, one who has the color of an *atasī* flower is considered most auspicious.
These are the auspicious ones; O King, I shall now proclaim to you those who are inauspicious.
Those with black palates, lips, and teeth; those with rough horns and hooves;
those with indistinct coloration, who are short, and resemble tiger ashes;
those with the color of crows and vultures, as well as those resembling mice.
Those afflicted with leprosy, the one-eyed, the lame, and likewise those with squinting eyes;

Those bulls whose white feet are uneven and whose eyes are wandering should not be released, nor should they be kept in the house. I shall further describe the characteristics of those that are to be released and those that are to be kept.
Their horns were shaped like svastikas, their roars resembled the rumbling of a mass of clouds,
they possessed great vital strength, and they moved with the gait of elephants in rut.
[1620] Broad-chested, with deep breaths, and possessing great strength and prowess;
likewise, their heads, ears, foreheads, tails, and feet.
The eyes and the areas around them are praised when they are black with the luster of the moon;
these same features are also praised when white, especially in the case of a black horse.
A bull is praised when it drags its tail along the ground, possesses a thick tail-hair, and has a dark-blue hump raised high in front.
Those bulls whose row shines with the luster of spears, banners, and flags are indeed blessed;
they bring about the attainment of wealth and victory.
Blessed are those who increase the herd, their heads and necks held high, who turn back of their own accord as they proceed in a clockwise direction.
If it should be white in color with red tips on its horns and eyes,
and its hooves resemble coral, there is no one more fortunate than that person.
These bulls should be maintained with great effort, or else they should be released;
for when thus maintained or released, they cause an increase in wealth and grain.
In the *Brahmapurāṇa*:
"The bull should be of the black-spotted antelope variety, three years of age,
pleasing to the mind, handsome to behold, and endowed with all auspicious marks."
Viṣṇu said:

In that sacrifice, one should examine a bull that is the son of a cow with living calves, endowed with all auspicious marks, either dark-blue or reddish-brown, white in its tail and feet, and capable of overshadowing the herd.
Now follows the description of the bull known as the "All-Supreme Blue" (*sarvottama-nīla*).
In the Revākhaṇḍa:
"He who indeed has white spots on his chest, forehead, and likewise on his foot,
and he whose tail is white— he is indeed one who beholds heaven."
In the Kālikā Purāṇa:
"Resembling the petal of a blue lotus, with white feet and a moon-like head,
white-complexioned, youthful, and red-eyed— the bull is called 'Nīla' (the Blue One)."
In the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*: "That bull which is red in color, white at the face and tail,
and white in its hooves and horns, is called a *nīla* bull."
In the Matsya Purāṇa: "O Lord of Rays, one should designate that [bull] as 'Nīla' whose feet, face, and tail are white, while the rest of his body has the color of lac juice."
That bull alone should be released; he should not be kept in the house.
For this reason, this ancient verse circulates in the world:
One should desire many sons, so that even one among them might go to Gayā,
or marry a wife who is a Gaurī, or release a dark-colored bull.
Now follows the procedure for the ritual release (*utsarga*).
In the *Bhaviṣyottara*, there are these words of Kṛṣṇa:
"A bull that is tawny, blue, with feet like a conch-shell, marked with *pauṇḍra* spots, and having a white tail..."
One should release it accompanied by four cows; hear that procedure.
Then, O sinless Pāṇḍava, Garga spoke long ago in Gokula:
"I shall perform for you that rite prescribed by the domestic ritual manuals."
Having established the Mothers, one should worship them with flowers and unbroken grains;
thereafter, one should perform the Śrāddha for the Mothers, which always brings about prosperity.
At the root of an *arka* tree, one should place a water-pot adorned with *aśvattha* leaves;
having recited the *rudra-mantras* there, one should install it as having Rudra as its presiding deity.
Then, one should thoroughly kindle the fire preceded by the mantra;
one should offer oblations with clarified butter, each consecrated separately with the six [mantras].
Then, having subsequently offered oblations into the fire according to the prescribed rite with mantras dedicated to Pūṣan,
[he should offer] a horse that is either of one color or two colors, whether red or white.
The son of the milch-cow Jīvavatsā, beautiful in all his limbs,
was adorned along with four yearling heifers.
The Brahmin should whisper into their ears: "I give you a strong and auspicious husband;
with him, play together with joyful hearts."
Then, one should draw a trident on the left and a wheel on the right;
it should be marked with the trident and the wheel and anointed with flowers and other offerings.
One should release a powerful bull whose neck is encircled by a garland of flowers, covered with white cloths, and accompanied by three calves.
"In a temple, in a cow-pen, or likewise at the confluence of rivers—
thus has the procedure for the release of the bull been declared by the sage Garga."

In this context, it is stated that one should perform the *śrāddha* which brings about prosperity (*abhyudayika*), preceded by the worship of the Mothers; from this it is understood that the *abhyudayika-śrāddha* must be performed. Regarding that, it is stated in the *Vārāha Purāṇa* that after performing the *śrāddha*, one should satisfy even those twice-born (*dvija*) individuals other than the *śrāddha*-recipients with food and so forth, and then perform the offering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) preceded by the offering of water with sesame seeds (*tilodaka*).
"O lady of beautiful hips, having performed the *śrāddha*, the twice-born should be gratified;
having offered water with sesame seeds, one should offer the rice-balls to the ancestors and grandfathers. [1623]
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*, it is also stated that after the recitation of the *Rudra* over the water-pot (*kalaśa*), one should likewise recite the *Puruṣasūkta* and so forth:
"Having recited the *Rudra*, one should then establish the deity Rudra [therein];
in the same manner, one should recite the *Puruṣasūkta* and likewise the *Kūṣmāṇḍa* hymns."

The chapter beginning with "Rudra" and "Obeisance to you, O Rudra, whose wrath... is well known in the Yajurveda. The *Puruṣasūkta*, consisting of sixteen verses beginning with "Thousand-headed," is also included. The verses beginning with "Whatever offense against the gods, O gods... are known as the *Kuṣmāṇḍas*.
Regarding this, there is a specific detail mentioned in the *Saura Purāṇa*:
having invoked Rudra into the water-pot (*kalaśa*), [one should worship him] with perfumes, garlands, unbroken grains (*akṣata*), and so forth.
Having worshipped and touched the water-pot, he should then recite the Rudrādhyāya;
likewise, he should chant the Puruṣasūkta and the Raudrī Saṃhitā.

The *Rudrasaṃhitā* consists of eleven *sāmans*: one named *āvorāja*, four named *tad vaḥ*, three *ājyadohas*, and three *devavratas*. This is stated in the Brāhmaṇa known as the *Sāmavidhāna*: "The *āvorāja*, the *tad vaḥ* section, the *ājyadohas*, and the *devavratas*—this is the name of this *saṃhitā*; by employing it, one pleases Rudra. Following the silent recitation (*japa*), there is an oblation (*homa*). As stated in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"Having well-kindled the sacrificial fire and spread it out extensively in the midst of cows..."
The wise man, being composed, should cook a caru offering for Pūṣan with milk.

Herein, this fire-offering (*homa*) is described in sequence. In the midst of the cows, to the rear of the *rudrakalaśa*, one should perform the five purificatory rites of the ground (*pañcabhūsaṃskāra*), beginning with sweeping. Having established the fire and seated the *brahmā* priest to the south, and having set out everything required for the subsequent ritual, one should place the clarified butter (*ājya*) on the fire. [1624] Having added rice grains together with milk and cooked the *pāyasa* (milk-rice), and having added water and rice to a pot and cooked the *pauṣṇacaru* (the sacrificial oblation for Pūṣan), one should remove the clarified butter and other items from the fire. After consecrating the clarified butter and throwing the fuel sticks (*samidh*) into the fire, one should sprinkle water around the fire clockwise. Bending the right knee and while being touched by the *brahmā*, six oblations of clarified butter should first be offered with the mantra "iha ratiḥ" (*May there be delight here*). They are as follows: "iha ratiḥ svāhā"—this to Agni; "oṃ iha ramadhvaṃ svāhā"—this to Agni; "oṃ iha dhṛtiḥ svāhā"—this to Agni; "oṃ iha svadhṛtiḥ svāhā"—this to Agni; "oṃ upamoṣam asmāsu dīdharat svāhā"—this to Agni. Then, while being touched by the *brahmā*, one should offer an oblation in the northern part of the fire while meditating mentally on Prajāpati with the formula "prajāpataye svāhā," and make the renunciation (*tyāga*) "idaṃ prajāpataye. This is the eastern *āghāra* (pouring). Then, offering in the southern part of the fire with "indrāya svāhā," the renunciation is "idam indrāya. This is the northern *āghāra*. Offering in the north-eastern quarter with "agnaye svāhā," the renunciation is "idam agnaye. This is the *ājyabhāga* for Agni. Offering in the south-eastern quarter with "somāya svāhā," the renunciation is "idaṃ somāya. This is the *ājyabhāga* for Soma. Immediately after that, while being touched, one should perform the offering with the *pāyasa* for the deities mentioned in the *godhajña* [text]. It is as follows: "oṃ agnaye svāhā"—this to Agni; "oṃ rudrāya svāhā"—this to Rudra; "oṃ sarvāya svāhā"—this to Sarva; "oṃ paśupataye svāhā"—this to Paśupati; "oṃ ugrāya svāhā"—this to Ugra; "oṃ aśanaye svāhā"—this to Aśani; "oṃ bhavāya svāhā"—this to Bhava; "oṃ mahādevāya svāhā"—this to Mahādeva; "oṃ īśānāya svāhā"—this to Īśāna. Then, one oblation from the *pauṣṇacaru*: "pūṣā gā anvetu naḥ... [etc.]—this to Pūṣan. Then, while being touched by the *brahmā*, one should offer the *sviṣṭakṛt*, the *mahāvyāhṛtis*, the universal expiation (*sarvaprāyaścitta*), and the *prājāpatya* oblation. Then: "agnaye sviṣṭakṛte svāhā"—this to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt. [1625] Thus is the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering with the *pauṣṇa* and *pāyasa*. The offerings of the *mahāvyāhṛtis* and so forth are performed with clarified butter: "oṃ bhūḥ svāhā"—this to Agni; "oṃ bhuvaḥ svāhā"—this to Vāyu; "oṃ svaḥ svāhā"—this to Sūrya. These are the three *mahāvyāhṛtis*. Then, the universal expiation is performed with the five mantras beginning with "tvaṃ no agne," ending with *svāhā*: "oṃ satvan no agne pramumugdhyasmat svāhā"—this to Agni-Varuṇa; "oṃ sa tvaṃ no agne suhavo na edhi svāhā"—this to Agni-Varuṇa; "oṃ ayāś cāgne syanabhi bheṣajaṃ svāhā"—this to Agni; "oṃ ye te śataṃ svarkāḥ svāhā"—this to Varuṇa, Savitṛ, Viṣṇu, the Viśvedevas, the Maruts, and the Svarkas; "oṃ uduttamaṃ aditaye syāma svāhā"—this to Varuṇa. Then the *prājāpatya*: "oṃ prajāpataye svāhā"—this to Prajāpati. Then follows the tasting of the remnants (*saṃśravaprāśana*), the sprinkling (*mārjana*), the disposal of the *pavitra* grass, and the giving of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). Having thus completed the fire-offering, one should perform the branding of the bull and other rites.
Regarding this, Viṣṇu says:

"In the midst of cows, having strewn grass around a well-kindled fire and having cooked a *caru* offering for Pūṣan, and having offered oblations with the verses 'pūṣābhigandhe numaḥ' and 'iha ratiḥ', one should bring forward a bull and summon a blacksmith (*ayaskara*).
'Blacksmith' (*ayaskara*) means a metal-worker."
In the Saura Purāṇa: "Then, having brought a bull and stationed it to the north of the fire,
one should draw a discus on its left hip and a trident on its right foreleg."
Having first marked the left hip— the left side of the waist—
with saffron, the Brāhmaṇa, being well-composed,
[should do so]; afterwards, the blacksmith should mark the bull with molten metal.
In the Devīpurāṇa: "One should draw a wheel on the left side and a trident on the flank with molten metal; one may engrave it with gold, silver, or iron."
‘Hema’ means gold; ‘tāra’ means silver; ‘āyasa’ means iron. Viṣṇu [should be worshipped].
One should bathe [the image] which is marked on one side with a discus and on the other with a trident, using the four verses beginning with “hiraṇyavarṇā” and the verse “śanno devīḥ.”
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*: "O Lord of Men,
one should bathe the [image] marked [with the signs], and during that bathing,
one should likewise recite the four verses beginning with 'hiraṇyavarṇā'."
And also the three verses beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā," as well as "śaṃ no devī."
The four *ṛc* verses beginning with "hiraṇyavarṇāḥ śucayaḥ pāvakāḥ," which are well-known in the *Atharvaveda*, are used for the consecration (*abhiṣecanīya*). Pāraskara [states]:
"Eight water-pots with roots removed, adorned with garlands and ribbons..."
Adorned with garments and jewels, and beautified by mango sprouts.
Having stationed four [priests] in front, the bull should be bathed;
the calves should be made to lie down by four [others]. Then one should adorn them all and recite the verses beginning with "samudrajyeṣṭhāḥ" during the consecration.

The *ṛgvedic* verses beginning with "samudrajyeṣṭhāḥ salilasya madhyāt" are well known to the followers of the *Bahvṛca*. This bathing of the bull and the calves and so forth is for the purpose of performing his marriage with them. Furthermore, this procedure, including the specific number of calves and other details, has been clarified in the *Devīpurāṇa*:
"There should be four auspicious calves, or two, or even one if more are not possible."
The male child shall have all his limbs fully developed, and the girl shall be submissive.
O Sage, having adorned her as beautifully as possible, one should perform the ritual of renunciation;
for the marriage with Nīla always takes place after one year.
A ‘kanyakā’ is one who has experienced sexual intercourse. An ‘ekavatsarī’ is one who is one year of age. Likewise:
[the gift] joined with eight cows, or four, or [two], in sequence.
He was adorned with three-year-old cows that were both auspicious and beautiful in form.
"Three-year-old" means three years of age. Endowed with every excellence, that great bull, the best of all,
should be released according to the prescribed rule, as also shown by the Smṛtis.
In the Āditya Purāṇa: "Then, after the dismissal [of the guests], cows and bulls should be given to pregnant women—
either eight, or four, or as many as can be obtained."
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"O lord of men, one should then adorn those four heifers and that bull with perfumes and garlands according to one's ability."
And with delightful tinkling bells, as well as beautiful Chinese silks.
"Kiṅkiṇyaḥ" refers to small bells. In the Āditya Purāṇa:
"One should give a bell made of iron, and on its horn, an auspicious cloth-cover."
A *paṭala* is a casket fashioned from gold or other precious materials. In the *Devīpurāṇa*:
"First, having marked [the cows] and decorated them in every way, they are released."
In the *Śivadharmottara*:
"Having adorned them as beautifully as possible with red and yellow flowers, with pigments such as saffron and the like, one should worship the bulls according to one's means."
It was equipped with the sound of tinkling bells, provided with small bells and bells of various sizes,
adorned with svastikas and half-moons, and embellished with various jewels.
The *svastika* is a variety of the *vicchanda* meter. One should place upon one's chest a garland made of gold lotuses eight finger-breadths wide, or one made of silver, or even of leather.
And such a garland of back-rib bones, curved at the ends and the hump,
adorned with various ornaments and hanging halfway down the belly, made of gold,
silver, or bone, and embellished with various jewels.
It should be made of copper and adorned with various silk cloths according to what is beautiful;
its two horns should be fashioned and provided with fine cloth and chowries.
A golden lotus on the head, adorned with a crescent moon.
One should bind it with a peacock feather (*candraka*), bees, and *aśvattha* leaves, combined with jewels,
along with a divine necklace adorned with various precious objects.
A *graiveyaka* is a neck ornament.
One should fasten a pure, resonant bell made of bell-metal around the neck;
[the horse] should be adorned with hooves of gold and silver, and decorated with armlets and bracelets.
And it was adorned with various silk cloths, decorated as beautifully as possible.
Pāraskara says:
"Then, having adorned them all, one who is composed should cause them to hear the Rudrādhyāya, the Puruṣasūkta, and likewise the Pratiratha hymns."
The twelve verses beginning with "āśuḥ śiśāno vṛṣabho na bhīmaḥ" are known as the Pratiratha hymns. Viṣṇu [is the deity].

Having brought the bull, which has been bathed and adorned, together with four young cows that have likewise been bathed, one should mutter the Rudra-hymns, the Puruṣasūkta, and the Kūṣmāṇḍī mantras. One should also mutter the mantra "pitā vatse" into the right ear of the bull.
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"One should mutter the well-known mantra, 'O child, [I am] your father,' into the ear of the bull while wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*apasavya*).
"Over the right shoulder" means on the right side. The mantra "O child, [I am] your father" is famous in the *Atharvaveda*.

"He is the father of the calves, the protector of those who travel on chariots; he is the father of the great Gargas, the calf, the afterbirth, the fresh milk, and the cream. Clarified butter is his life-sustaining essence; that is his seed. Thus [it is said]. In the *Āditya Purāṇa*:
"And there one should mutter the Sāvitrī, as well as the Aghamarṣaṇa."
And one should certainly whisper [the mantra] into the ear of the bull; of this there is no doubt.
The *aghamarṣaṇa* is well known from such [passages] as "Ṛtaṃ ca satyaṃ cābhīddhāt tapasaḥ" and so forth.
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"Then, having marked [the body], one should recite this mantra with a restrained mind."
You are the Bull, the Blessed One; the Dharma is proclaimed as four-footed.
Out of devotion, I choose it; may it protect me in every way.
Pāraskara, however, having recited this very mantra, says:
"Having thus prayed to that lordly bull, and having taken handfuls of flowers,
one should circumambulate him three times and pay obeisance according to the rule."
For cows facing westward, this much procedure is prescribed;
then, one should cause the cows and the bull to face the northeast.
Having placed the cows on both sides of the bull in the middle,
one should join the neck-cloths of them all together,
saying: "This most excellent husband has indeed been given by me to you all."
And all these beautiful wives have been given by me to you.
Having yoked the bull with them, he should present it to the ancestors;
having grasped the tail of the bull with his left hand.
Then, having taken water with his right hand along with sesame seeds and kuśa grass,
he should pronounce the lineage name and say, "to such-and-such [person]."
"A bull indeed has been given by me; may it always deliver him.
Having uttered this, one should cast [the bull] upon the ground together with gold and sesame seeds.

This statement regarding the release of a bull (*vṛṣotsarga*) for the sake of a single deceased person has been spoken by Pāraskara. However, for the sake of multiple deceased persons, the mantra for the release of a dark-blue bull (*nīlotsarga*) is stated in the *Vārāha Purāṇa*: "Those men who remain here, fallen kinsmen of the ancestors—may this dark-blue bull, released according to the rule, be their savior."
Having taken an udumbara vessel and prepared water with black sesame seeds,
and having grasped the tail with his hand, he should release the bull for the ancestors.
"Udumbara" means copper.
In the *Brahmapurāṇa*:
"Svadhā [be] for the fathers, for the mothers, and also for the kinsmen, for their satisfaction."
And whoever belong to the mother’s side, and those others born of the father’s side.
Those who were born in the families of one's gurus, fathers-in-law, and kinsmen,
those who have fallen into the state of a preta, and others who have been deprived of the śrāddha rite— [for them all].
"By means of this rite of releasing a bull, may they all obtain supreme satisfaction.
With this mantra, one should offer water mixed with sesame seeds and unbroken rice grains,
as well as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the ancestors and to the Brahmins in brief.
With this mantra, one should release a bull dedicated to many ancestors. Viṣṇu says:

"I give this youth to you as a husband; sport with him, your beloved, and move about. May we not be deprived of our offspring nor of our bodies; O King Soma, let us not fall into the power of the hater."
One should drive a bull yoked with a heifer toward the northeastern direction;
"drive" means one should impel it. The remainder [of the instruction] is that this is done with this mantra.
[This is stated] in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*.
I give you this youth, a bull, the lord of cattle, the leader of the herd, full of pride;
roam with him as you desire.
At will, he should then drive that bull and all those young cows toward the eastern direction, just as he did previously.

Kātyāyana says: From a cow that has a living calf and is prolific, one should select the one that is most beautiful in form among her offspring and the herd. Having adorned that [cow], and having adorned four principal heifers of the herd, they should release them with this [formula]: "I give this young man as a husband to you; sporting with him, your beloved, move about. Being in agreement through the seven births, may we rejoice in the increase of wealth and in food. With this very [formula] they should release them, and he consecrates their backs with the remainder of the *anuvāka* beginning with "The source of bliss" (*mayobhūḥ*).
In the *Brahmapurāṇa*:
Then, once the rite of bull-liberation (vṛṣotsarga) had been performed, the donor addressed the Brahmins with some enigmatic words: "Whatever has been released by anyone in a secluded place,
let no one else take it away, nor shall it be divided or distributed out of order."
In this regard, the donor’s instruction to the Brahmins is as follows: "Whatever has been discarded here in this secluded place by anyone must not be taken away by another, nor shall it be divided.
Then Pāraskara states the place where it should be disposed of:
"That bull should be cast into a forest abounding in water and grass."
One should drive all those heifers along with him;
or else, they should be placed in a cow-pen that is auspiciously filled with many cattle.
In the *Śivadharmottara*: "And such a bull as this— the lord of cattle, capable of sustaining a herd of cows,
primarily producing female calves, and bringing forth abundant milk for the cows."
Adorned with various ornaments and endowed with its former splendor,
one should worship the Cow-Mothers and then release them into a herd of auspicious cows.
Having thus dismissed [the deities], one should perform the recitation of blessings (*svastivācana*) and other rites. Pāraskara says:
"When the lord of the cows has departed, one should have the Brahmins recite blessings there."
And one should give them a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), and thereafter feed the Brāhmaṇas.
He should give to the Hotṛ priest the Rudra-pitcher together with gold, as well as the bathing jars;
he should give all of that, and also a milch cow.
