In the Vārāha Purāṇa: "Having performed the word of the Brahmins and having given a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) according to one's ability. "The word of the Brahmins" refers to the recitation of auspiciousness (svastivācana) by the Brahmins.
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*: "Then a pair of garments should be given to the *hotṛ* priest,
along with gold and a bronze vessel containing clarified butter."
Likewise, O King, the price for the chief artisan should be paid so that he may attain satisfaction;
and the Brahmins should likewise be given food joined with curds and clarified butter.
Those with whom one may eat together [should be served] mixed with milk.
And that feeding of Brahmins should be performed in the presence of Rudra; thus it has been said:
"One should feed the Brahmins in the presence of Rudra according to the prescribed rule.
Regarding the prohibition of keeping the bull after it has been released according to this rite, Pāraskara says:
No one should restrain her; no one should make her carry loads; one should not milk that cow, nor should anyone bind her.
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*: "Neither that [person] nor his milk should ever be consumed by anyone anywhere. In the *Śivadharmottara*:
Those bulls which have been consecrated by the virtuous, marked with the trident, and beloved of Śiva— those fools, of sinful conduct and lowest among men, who drive them.
Until the time of the great dissolution (mahāpralaya), they are cooked in all the hells and other realms without exception,
accompanied by their wives, sons, and others, through various terrible tortures.
In whose kingdom there are base men who,
being wicked, compel a bull to carry loads, that sin belongs equally to him as well;
therefore, the king should prevent those bulls from being made to carry loads by them.
In the Devīpurāṇa:
"By acting thus, one indeed obtains the fruit declared for the horse-sacrifice (vājimedha);
for whichever [deity] one releases the calf with intent, that [deity] shall obtain it without doubt."
Thus, the man who performs the rite of releasing a bull with devotion for his ancestors,
having rescued them from being submerged in the mire of misfortune—
He himself attains the world of Śambhu.
In the *Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa*:
"Blessed are those who release a bull— an animal that roams at will, proud, bellowing,
a bringer of happiness to cows, humped, and the leader of the herd."
A bull that has been set at liberty purifies ten generations past and ten future generations.
Whatever water one touches after emerging from the water onto the earth,
that is declared to be inexhaustible for the ancestors when offered by means of a bull set at liberty.
And whatever water one touches with the tail or other parts, even down to the very end, all of that shall become inexhaustible for him; there is no doubt in this matter.
Whatever furrows the bull incessantly scratches into the earth with his horns or hooves,
those become inexhaustible streams of honey for his father.
The satisfaction that the ancestors obtain from a pond measuring a thousand *nalvas*, according to the sacred tradition, is surpassed by the gift of a bull.
Whoever offers sesame seeds mixed with other sesame seeds,
or honey, or blue sugar-candy at the time of the Śrāddha rite— all that indeed becomes inexhaustible.
The "blue section" refers to a blue bull.
That which scratches the earth with its horns and hooves is the proud one;
that which bellows upon seeing rival bulls is the defiant one.
That entire time brings satisfaction to the one who performs the marriage, and it leads even to the assembly of Śakra.
Thus ends the rite of the release of a bull (*vṛṣotsarga*).

Thus [ends] the section on the *pariśeṣa* (supplements) in the *Caturvargacintāmaṇi*, composed by the illustrious Hemādri, the scholar and chief minister of all affairs to the illustrious Mahādevīya, the illustrious Mahārājādhirāja.
In the Śrāddhakalpa, the twentieth chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Śrāddha with Sesame and Water and Other Rites that Satisfy the Departed Spirits."
[1636] Now begins the twenty-first chapter.
By whom, at the outset, was the earth made to possess the *avadānas* and other narratives that are devoid of the tales of beggars?
Having perfectly bestowed prosperity through his glorious sprout-like right hand,
and having likewise rendered even the heavens free from distress by means of successive series of sacrificial offerings,
that virtuous scholar Hemādri now speaks of the ritual for the Sapindikarana.
Now follows the procedure for the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite.
Regarding this, after describing the rites performed for the sake of the deceased (*preta*) up until the end of one year, it is stated in the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*:
"Then, when the year is complete, the rite is duly performed by men."
The Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa Śrāddha is also mentioned; its procedure is now stated.

In this context, "when a year is complete" is the general rule (*utsarga*). However, those exceptional times (*apavāda*) prescribed by other causes, which apply even when the year is not complete, have all already been explained previously in the section on time (*kāla-prakaraṇa*). The definition of *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, however, was explained in the section on the varieties of *śrāddha*. Its essential form, in brief, is as follows: while the feeding of Brahmins is being performed in a single ritual application (*ekaprayoga*), simultaneously according to the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite for the deceased person who has recently died and attained the status of an ancestor (*pitṛtva*), and according to the *pārvaṇa* rite for that person's predecessor; the water of the *arghya* offering for the deceased is poured into the *arghya* vessels of the ancestors, and the funeral cake (*piṇḍa*) of the deceased is divided and placed among the ancestral cakes—this is declared to be the procedure for *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, as stated in this very Purāṇa following the aforementioned proposition.
There, the Śrāddha should be performed with concentrated minds for the sake of the departed spirits;
and that too should be devoid of the deities, having only a single Arghya offering and a single Pavitra.
In that rite, there is no offering into the fire, and it is devoid of the invocation;
there too, one should feed an odd number of twice-born men with the sacred thread over the right shoulder.
One should also feed others for the sake of the three ancestors;
furthermore, there is another specific distinction therein regarding the rites performed every month.
Listen with one-pointed concentration as I describe it:
there, four vessels should be prepared, joined with sesame seeds, perfumes, and water.
O son, one should perform three offerings for the ancestors and one for the deceased;
then, one should pour the water-offering (arghya) from the vessel of the deceased into the three vessels.
Reciting "ye samānā," one should perform the remainder as previously described; this same procedure for the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite is declared to apply to women as well.
The sapindikarana rite for them is not performed in the absence of a son;
rather, the ekoddista rite must always be performed for them by their kinsmen.
In the Bhaviṣyatpurāṇa:
Having prepared four vessels and filled them with sesame seeds and water,
one should pour the contents of one vessel into the three vessels for the ancestors, pronouncing their names and lineages.
Yājñavalkya: One should prepare four vessels containing fragrant water and sesame seeds;
for the purpose of the *arghya* offering, one should pour the vessel of the deceased (*preta*) into the vessels of the ancestors (*pitṛ*).
With the two verses beginning "ye samānā," one should perform the remainder as previously described;
this Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa rite for women is also performed as an Ekoddiṣṭa.

One should prepare four vessels for the *arghya* offering for the *preta*s and others, containing water mixed with sandalwood and other fragrances, as well as sesame seeds. Having offered the *arghya* to the *preta*, one should pour the remaining water from that vessel into the vessels for the grandfather (*pitāmaha*) and the others, using the two mantras beginning with "Those who are common" (*ye samānāḥ*), which have the ancestors as their deities, in due order. As for the remainder of the ritual, such as the invitation of the Brahmins and so forth, one should perform it according to the *pārvaṇa* rite. This aforementioned procedure—wherein the *pārvaṇa* has the grandfather as its deity and the *ekoddiṣṭa* śrāddha has the *preta* as its deity—is to be understood by the name *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*. Furthermore, this must be performed for a woman as well, and not for a man alone.
In the Caturviṃśatimata:
"The sapindikarana [rite] takes place when the year is complete, or at a time of prosperity (abhyudaya);
however, according to the opinion of some, it occurs on the twelfth day, and likewise on the eleventh."
Having first placed the new deceased as the ninth,
together with the four paternal ancestors beginning with the great-grandfather, the Pārvaṇa rite is prescribed.
Being pure, one should worship four arghya vessels as before;
the wise man should pour the vessel for the preta into the vessels for the ancestors.
Having recited the three verses beginning with *madhu vātā* and the three verses beginning with *saṃgacchadhvam*,
some wise teachers desire that one should also recite the two verses beginning with *ye samānā*.
In this manner, the rite should be performed for the rice-balls (*piṇḍas*), but one should finally dismiss them.
In the Āśvalāyana-Gṛhyapariśiṣṭa:

Now, regarding the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite: there are four water-vessels—one for the deceased and three for the others. One should join the first vessel with the other three vessels while reciting, "United indeed are our intentions... In this same manner, one should join it with the funeral cakes (*piṇḍas*). With the two verses beginning with "Sweetened" and "Come together," the fourth [deceased] is thus made to be admitted. And at this point, one should not feed the gods; rather, having already offered the *arghya* and food to the gods, and having honored the vessel with perfumes and garlands, one should place the remnants of the oblation into the hands of the ancestors.
—Kātyāyana.

Then, when the year is complete, having filled four vessels with water scented with sesame and perfumes—three for the ancestors and one for the deceased—he pours the vessel of the deceased into the vessels of the ancestors while reciting the two verses beginning with "ye samānāḥ. By this, the ritual of the *piṇḍas* is explained. In the *Kūrma Purāṇa*:
"The *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* is declared to take place again when the year is complete."
O best of the twice-born, one should prepare four vessels for the pretas and the others.
Then, one should pour the water-offering for the pretas into the vessels of the ancestors with the two verses beginning "ye samānāḥ. In the same manner, one should likewise offer the rice-balls.
The Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa Śrāddha is prescribed as being preceded by the rites for the gods;
one should invoke the ancestors there, and furthermore, designate the deceased (preta).
Vaijavāpa.

Now, regarding the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite: for one year, one does not designate a separate rice-ball (*piṇḍa*) [for the deceased]. When the year is completed, he prepares four water-vessels; therein, one is for the deceased (*preta*) and three for the ancestors (*pitṛ*). He pours that vessel of the deceased into the vessels of the ancestors with the two verses beginning, "Those who are common... (*ye samānāḥ*). Likewise, he [merges] the rice-ball. Then he touches it, saying: "O ancestors, this deceased has followed you; I place him among you. May there be auspiciousness! May the remainder of you be born with long life! "May our intentions be common, may your hearts be common; may your mind be common, so that there may be great prosperity for you."

"Come together, speak together; may your minds be in accord, O wise ones, as the gods of old, being in agreement, partook of their portion"—this [rite] one should not extend to those who have been accused, the outcaste, the killer of an embryo, or a woman who has committed adultery. "Extension" (*atideśa*) means reuniting with the ancestors.
Thus says Hārīta.
When the year has concluded, one should perform the animal-śrāddha according to the rules;
one should offer four funeral cakes (piṇḍas) and first join them together.

Having offered the omentum, the animal's omentum itself, and whatever portions (avadāna) there may be according to the prescribed rule, one should pour the remainder together with the funeral cakes (piṇḍa).
From that time forward, the deceased indeed attains the commonality of the ancestors;
he finds the world of the fathers, and from that point the śrāddha ceremony proceeds.
And for as many hairs as there are on the animal, for that many thousands of years one who has been appointed by the ritual rule is glorified in the heavenly world.

Viṣṇu says: At the end of the year, one should feed Brāhmaṇas—beginning with those for the gods—to the deceased, his father, his grandfather, and his great-grandfather. In this rite, one should perform the offering into the fire (agnaukaraṇa), the invocation (āvāhana), and the washing of the feet (pādya). One should join the vessel of the deceased with the three vessels using the mantra, "May the earth unite thee," and "Like mothers. One should prepare four rice-balls (piṇḍa) near the remains of the food; the rice-ball of the deceased should be placed among the three rice-balls, just as the water from the foot-washing of the vessels was done, even when performed in proximity to the three furrows (karṣū). Thus it is stated in the Kāṭhaka Gṛhya Sūtra.

"Having set aside the fourth ball of rice and divided it into three parts, one should place them upon the [other] balls with the verses: 'May the Earth, Vāyu, Agni, and Prajāpati unite you; may you be united with the ancestors of old; be of one mind'—thus also with the water.
Thus [it is said] in the *Brahmapurāṇa*: "From among the four arghya-vessels, [one should take] one with the left hand..."
Having taken the water with sesame seeds in his right hand alone.
Reciting, "May the earth unite you," and "Those who are equal," one should pour a fourth portion of water into the hand of the deceased Brahmin.
Then, one should offer that water separately to the Grandfather (Brahmā) and the others with their respective mantras, using the two verses beginning with "ye samānāḥ."
Having offered the *arghya* to them according to that same procedure from the vessel for the deceased as before,
and having presented the *arghya* to them, he should afterwards perform the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*) himself.
Then, by that same procedure, having offered the water for washing at the root of the *darbha* grass to the father, he should devoutly offer the funeral cake (*piṇḍa*) as before.
Having offered the rice-ball (piṇḍa) and meditated upon the Lord residing within the tantra according to the eightfold method,
one should then divide that piṇḍa into three parts with blades of darbha grass made of gold and silver.
Having offered [the portion] to the ancestors beginning with the Grandfather, one should present the deceased [with the formula]:
"May the Earth, Vāyu, Agni, and Prajāpati unite with you."
One should recite this mantra with devotion, as well as "samānīva" and the two verses beginning with "ye samānāḥ"; with these, one should offer the deceased to the ancestors.
Then, having made those three balls well-rounded, one should worship them with water-offerings (*arghya*),
flowers, incense, lamps, garlands, and ointments;
having placed the principal father first, and the sages in their proper order.
Regarding this, a certain commentator on Manu says:

Although it is recorded in the Smṛti that one should feed Brāhmaṇas for the deceased (preta), as well as for his father, grandfather, and great-grandfather, nevertheless—due to the absence of separate designations and because of the favor accorded to their being together—the deceased is also included within the very same three Brāhmaṇas intended for the grandfather and the others. Just as in the Śrāddhas of the new moon and other occasions, the three ancestors beginning with the father are sometimes fed by means of a single Brāhmaṇa, so too here, the deceased is included within the three Brāhmaṇas intended for the grandfather and the rest.
Furthermore, the word "again" (punaḥ) occurs in the Smṛti:
"One should announce the Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa Śrāddha preceded by the gods;
one should invoke the ancestors there, and again designate the deceased (preta)."

The word "again" (punaḥ) is appropriate only when the deceased (preta) is included within those same three Brahmins and not separately. This being the case, his inclusion is accomplished in every respect; for this rite is performed for the purpose of integration (saṃsarga). Since the deceased is also brought into those very [Brahmins], that food becomes for the sake of the deceased as well. Furthermore, it is recorded in Smṛti: "One should feed an odd number at the rite for the ancestors (pitrya)"; that too is thus upheld. If one were to assign a separate Brahmin for the deceased, then in the case of four or more Brahmins, that [Smṛti rule] would be contradicted.

Furthermore, the statement that "one pours the *arghya* from the vessel of the deceased (*preta*) into the vessels of the ancestors" would also be inconsistent. For if the pouring were performed prior to the offering of the *arghya* to the deceased, then because that vessel would have become empty, from which vessel could the *arghya* for the deceased be offered? Nor can it be said that it is poured from the ancestor's vessel into which [the water] has not been poured; for it is not proper to offer *arghya* to one person using a vessel prepared for the sake of another, since that vessel was prepared for the sake of the grandfather and others, not for the father.

Now, if the pouring of water (*āsecanam*) is performed immediately after the offering of the *arghya* to the deceased (*preta*), then, since the *arghya* has already been offered, that pouring would not be for the purpose of that *arghya*-offering; however, there is no contradiction with the method previously stated.

This [position] is incorrect. For, according to the Smṛti, in such passages as "one should feed Brāhmaṇas for the deceased," it is stated that one should feed each Brāhmaṇa with reference to each individual ancestor. In that case, because of the specification for each person, it is not appropriate to perform the action without regard for the distinctness of the words [denoting the ancestors].
Now, if you have an extreme need for the word "separately" (*pṛthak*), then listen to the words of the authors of the *Smṛtis* and *Purāṇas*. Regarding this, Uśanas and Sumantu both state:
"In the *Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, one should feed the Brahmins as in the *Pārvaṇa* rite;
however, for the sake of the deceased, the *Ekoddiṣṭa* should be performed separately according to the prescribed rule."
"O Hero, O King, at the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite, one should perform two *śrāddhas*:
the *ekoddiṣṭa* and the *pārvaṇa*; so said the Blessed Lord Śiva."
[Objection: But if this were so, the word "again" (*punaḥ*) would not be appropriate.

[Response: It is not so; from the word "again," this meaning is understood: having performed the invocation of the ancestors (*pitṛs*), one should subsequently perform it for the deceased (*preta*). Furthermore, there is no such statement anywhere in those very *Brāhmaṇas* that "the deceased also must be invoked.
[Objection: But if this were so, the favor of performing them together (*sahatva-anugraha*) would not be achieved.

Well then, if one were to favor the principle of simultaneity (*sahatva*), it would follow that only a single person should always be fed for the sake of all [ancestors]; yet this is not tenable, because of the statement of Śaunaka: "But it is never explained that one person alone may be fed with the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) for all. Furthermore, as for the statement of Manu, "One may feed even a single learned man at both the rite for the gods (*daiva*) and the rite for the ancestors (*pitrya*"), it is impossible to claim that this refers to the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* ceremony; for where the offering is given to only one person, that is designated as the *ekoddiṣṭa*, and where it is given to three, that is the *pārvaṇa*. If, however, the *pārvaṇa* and the *ekoddiṣṭa* were to occur simultaneously at the same time, that would constitute the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*; but in the case of feeding only a single Brahmin, this would necessarily fail, since there is no separate *ekoddiṣṭa* rite. Therefore, just as there is a requirement for the simultaneity of the *pārvaṇa* when there is a plurality of Brahmins, so too must it be stated here.

As for the argument that the rule "an odd number" (*ayugmān*) would be accommodated even when the deceased is invited among the Brahmins representing the grandfather and others during the *paitṛka* rite—that is incorrect. Since these two rites, the *pārvaṇa* and the *ekoddiṣṭa*, are distinct, and since both together require four Brahmins, an odd number remains unaltered in each individual case; thus, the accommodation of the rule exists even under this alternative view. Furthermore, regarding the statement of an option—"if the pouring [of water] occurs before the offering of the *arghya* to the deceased," and so forth—that too is of no consequence. For the water is poured out specifically for the purpose of the *arghya* offering, and not by emptying the vessel entirely. Consequently, both the offering of the *arghya* and the pouring of water must indeed take place; there is no such traditional injunction (*smṛti*) that the pouring must be performed with the entire quantity of *arghya* water. Therefore, the claim that the invitation of the deceased should be made only among the Brahmins representing the grandfather and others is untenable. Moreover, this position has not been accepted by the learned (*śiṣṭas*). Thus, it is established that one should perform the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* by designating separate Brahmins for the sake of the deceased and separate ones for the sake of the grandfather and the others.

In this regard, certain commentators on Yājñavalkya explain the word *preta* in the injunction "one should pour the *preta*-vessel into the *pitṛ*-vessels" as follows: "One who has gone away from here in an eminent manner (*pra-karṣeṇa*), having fallen away from the offering of funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*) and so forth," that is, the long-deceased Great-Grandfather (*vṛddhaprapitāmaha*), is designated by the word *preta*. Therefore, his *arghya*-vessel should be poured into the *arghya*-vessels of the ancestors, and his *piṇḍa* should be merged (*saṃsṛj*) with the [other] *piṇḍas*. If, however, the word *preta* were to denote one who has died recently, then when the water from the *preta*'s *arghya*-vessel is poured into the *pitṛ*-vessels, that vessel would become empty; consequently, the offering of *arghya* to the *preta* would not take place. On the other hand, if the word *preta* denotes one who has died long ago, then there is no fault, because there is no offering of *arghya* for that deceased person (since he is already included among the ancestors). Furthermore, in such expressions as "he gives to the *pretas*," the word *preta* is employed to refer to anyone who has simply passed away. Therefore, since the word *preta* signifies merely one who is dead, that very meaning which is appropriate in those contexts is what should be accepted here.

And the author of the *Kāṭhaka-gṛhya-sūtra* has explicitly stated that the *saṃsarjana* (merging) of the offerings should take place among the balls for the great-grandfather and the others. As it is said:
"Having set aside the fourth ball and divided it into three parts, one should place them upon the [other] balls.
For this very reason, Vṛddha-Śātātapa says:
Having examined four balls of rice according to each name,
the giver of the balls should divide the first one into three parts while reciting the two verses beginning with "ye samānāḥ."

And here too, the word "first" (*ādya*) refers to the individual body of the person. If one asks how so, it is because of conformity with the statement in the *Kāṭhaka-gṛhya-sūtra*. Nor is the term "first" untenable on the grounds that the deceased body is the "last" in this context; for if the long-deceased were referred to by the word "preta," then [the verse would read]:
"He who should offer a separate piṇḍa to a *preta* whose *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* has been performed incurs sin and becomes a slayer of his ancestors."

This [objection] is not tenable, because after the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, an annual *ekoddiṣṭa* rite is prescribed for him. However, in the case of a long-deceased great-great-grandfather (*vṛddhaprapitāmaha*) who is designated by the term "preta," since there is no separate offering for him after the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, this prohibition is applicable. Therefore, the mixing of the great-great-grandfather’s *arghya* with the *arghyas* and his *piṇḍa* with the *piṇḍas* must be performed; but this is indeed improper, for if that were so, because the *arghya* and *piṇḍa* of the great-great-grandfather would come into contact with many other *arghyas* and *piṇḍas*, it would be his *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* alone, and not that of the recently deceased *preta*. Consequently, it is only logical that the mixing of the *arghya* and *piṇḍa* of the newly deceased person himself should be performed among the others. As for what was said—that if this were done, the offering of the *arghya* for the newly deceased would not take place—[that objection is refuted].

That is not so, because the offering of that *arghya* is accomplished by means of the water remaining after it has been poured into the father’s vessel; for there is no scriptural statement that the pouring must be done until nothing remains. As for the claim that the term *preta* refers to the great-grandfather (*vṛddhaprapitāmaha*) based on the etymology "one who has departed (*ita*) from here (*pra*) with excellence," that too is made without due consideration, since Yājñavalkya states:
"Food should be given to the *preta* for three days according to the procedure of the *piṇḍayajña*."

Having thus established this in the section on impurity (*āśauca*), it is now stated again: "one should pour out the vessel for the deceased (*preta*). Therefore, since the one who has recently died is the subject under discussion and remains present in the mind, it is appropriate to denote him by the word *preta*, and not an elder who is not the subject at hand. If, however, the great-grandfather were denoted here by the word *preta*, then—once the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite has been performed—he would be released from the state of being a *preta*.
Thereafter, mortals attain the status of ancestors (*pitṛ*) every year.
On the anniversary of his death, the Śrāddha ceremony should be properly performed by those who are fully composed.

If one were to argue that liberation from the state of a *preta* is being described by such passages, that would not be consistent. For at that time, the state of being a *preta* does not depart for the great-great-grandfather; nor does his death (*pramītatva*) cease in its entirety. Nor, by the cessation of that specific state denoted by the word *preta*, would he acquire the designation "father" (*pitṛ*), since that specific state arises for him [only] later, as his status as a father was already established previously. Furthermore, the *śrāddha* rite prescribed to be performed every year would also not be applicable to him. It is said: "The fourth *piṇḍa* does not go [to him]."
Water should be offered for three [ancestors], and the rice-ball offering proceeds for three;
the fourth is the one who bestows these, and a fifth is not possible.
This is because [the status of the deceased] is denied by such statements as these. Furthermore, Gārgya has expressed this even more clearly regarding one who has been recently cognized as deceased:
"At the end of the year, the son should unite the deceased with the ancestors;
from that time forward, the *pārvaṇa* śrāddha is performed on the anniversary of death, and not otherwise."

However, when it is stated that "the *pārvaṇa* śrāddha begins with him," then only one who has recently died is fit to be understood here by the word *preta*, not the great-grandfather (*vṛddhaprapitāmaha*). For it is not proper to perform the *pārvaṇa* śrāddha beginning with him, due to the prohibition, "not for those beyond [him]," and because it contradicts established custom. Furthermore, if the great-grandfather were intended by the word *preta*, then—according to the statement of Viṣṇu, "One should feed the Brahmins for the *preta*, for his father, for his grandfather, and for his great-grandfather"—the feeding of Brahmins would have to be directed toward the great-grandfather, the grandfather, and so on; and it has already been stated that this is not tenable. As for the argument that the word *preta* is seen applied to anyone who has simply died—as in "he gives to the *pretas*"—and thus the great-grandfather can also be designated by the word *preta*, that too is incorrect. Even in that case, the word denotes only one who is eligible for the offering, and not the great-grandfather who is ineligible for it. Furthermore, as for the statement that "having set aside the fourth *piṇḍa* and divided it into three parts, one should place them among the *piṇḍas*," that also holds true only in our view, not in yours. For the "fourth" is called such because it completes the number four; and such a [fourth] *piṇḍa* does not belong to one who has merely passed away. Because: [The verse continues: "Having offered the *piṇḍa* to the deceased, he should offer another to the father, and another to the grandfather; then, having offered the fourth *piṇḍa* to the great-grandfather, he should divide it into three parts and place them upon the [other] *piṇḍas*. (Gobhila Gṛhya Sūtra 4.3.20) This clearly shows that the fourth *piṇḍa* belongs to the great-grandfather, who is still living. If he were dead, he would have already received his share at the time of the *sapindana*. Therefore, the division of the fourth *piṇḍa* applies only when the great-grandfather is alive. Thus, the rule regarding the *piṇḍas* is consistent only with our position. Consequently, the word *preta* here refers exclusively to the person who has recently died. It is not possible to apply the term *preta* to the great-grandfather based on the mere fact of his having died in the past. Therefore, the *pārvaṇa* śrāddha must be performed starting from the recently deceased. This is the correct conclusion. Thus ends the section on the *Pārvaṇa-śrāddha*. Now follows the section on the *Ekoddiṣṭa-śrāddha*. Regarding this, the following is stated: "The *ekoddiṣṭa* is for one year, until the *sapindana* is performed. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.255). This means that for one year, the śrāddha for the deceased is performed as an *ekoddiṣṭa*. After the *sapindana* has been completed, however, the śrāddha becomes *pārvaṇa*. As stated: "After the *sapindana*, the śrāddha is *pārvaṇa*. (Viṣṇu Smṛti 78.1). The *sapindana* is the rite of unifying the *piṇḍas*. As stated: "The *sapindana* is the unification of the *piṇḍas*. (Viṣṇu Smṛti 78.2). This unification occurs at the end of the first year, or at the anniversary of death, or at the completion of the twelve months. As stated: "The *sapindana* is performed at the end of the year, or at the anniversary of death, or after the twelve months have elapsed. (Viṣṇu Smṛti 78.3). Therefore, until the *sapindana* is performed, the śrāddha is *ekoddiṣṭa*; thereafter, it is *pārvaṇa*. This is the settled rule. Thus ends the section on the *Ekoddiṣṭa-śrāddha*. Now follows the section on the *Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa-śrāddha*. Regarding this, the following is stated: "The *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* is the rite of uniting the *piṇḍas*. (Viṣṇu Smṛti 78.2). This rite is performed at the end of the first year, or at the anniversary of death, or after the twelve months. As stated: "The *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* is performed at the end of the year, or at the anniversary of death, or after the twelve months have elapsed. (Viṣṇu Smṛti 78.3). This rite is essential, for without it, the deceased cannot attain the status of a *pitṛ*. As stated: "Without the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, the deceased does not attain the state of a *pitṛ*. (Viṣṇu Smṛti 78.4). Therefore, this rite must be performed diligently. This is the settled rule. Thus ends the section on the *Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa-śrāddha*. Now follows the section on the *Navaśrāddha*. Regarding this, the following is stated: "The *navaśrāddha* consists of eight rites. (Viṣṇu Smṛti 78.5). These are: the first-day śrāddha, the third-day śrāddha, the sixth-day śrāddha, the tenth-day śrāddha, the monthly śrāddhas for nine months, and the śrāddha at the end of the year. As stated: "The first-day, third-day, sixth-day, tenth-day, and monthly śrāddhas for nine months, and the annual śrāddha—these are the eight *navaśrāddhas*. (Viṣṇu Smṛti 78.6). These are to be performed diligently for the sake of the deceased's welfare. This is the settled rule. Thus ends the section on the *Navaśrāddha*. Now follows the section on the *Śuddhiśrāddha*. Regarding this, the following is stated: "The *śuddhiśrāddha* is for the purification of the impurity. (Viṣṇu Smṛti 78.7). This is performed at the end of the period of impurity. As stated: "At the end of the impurity, the *śuddhiśrāddha* should be performed. (Viṣṇu Smṛti 78.8). This rite is necessary for the purification of the performer. This is the settled rule. Thus ends the section on the *Śuddhiśrāddha*. Now follows the section on the *Pratyābdika-śrāddha*. Regarding this, the following is stated: "The *pratyābdika* is the annual śrāddha. (Viṣṇu Smṛti 78.9). This is performed every year on the anniversary of death. As stated: "The *pratyābdika* is the śrāddha performed annually on the anniversary of death. (Viṣṇu Smṛti 78.10). This rite is essential for the satisfaction of the deceased. This is the settled rule. Thus ends the section on the *Pratyābdika-śrāddha*. Now follows the section on the *Vṛddhiśrāddha*. Regarding this, the following is stated: "The *vṛddhiśrāddha* is for occasions of prosperity. (Vi
Having commenced the two types of *śrāddha*, one should perform the offering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) together;
for those two, first comes the rite for three ancestors (*tripuruṣa*), and after that, the *ekoddiṣṭa*.

Thus, since the *Purāṇa* prescribes the performance of the *ekoddiṣṭa* for one who has recently died after the time of the *pārvaṇa*, and because its *piṇḍa* is prescribed as that which completes the number four;
so too it is stated in the *Kaṭha-pariśiṣṭa*:
"Having offered the *piṇḍas* to the ancestors, he should then offer according to the law one to the deceased."

"But having divided that ball into three parts, one should continuously place them in succession into the three balls; this is the rule for the mixing [of the offerings]. Furthermore, if it is asserted that in the phrase "one should divide the first into three," the word "first" (ādya) refers to the primordial ancestor (ādipuruṣa), then—since the word "first" would denote the very first [ancestor] in such passages as "the first is the father, his father, and whoever is his father too"—there would be the fault of lack of systematic consistency (avyavasthā-doṣa).

Furthermore: From the statement, "Having set aside the fourth *piṇḍa*, having divided it into three parts, one should place them among the *piṇḍas*," it is understood that the division and the joining (*saṃsarjana*) among the *piṇḍas* occur immediately after the setting aside of the fourth. This, however, is not consistent if the subject refers to the *piṇḍa* of the great-grandfather (*vṛddhaprapitāmaha*). For, if the offering of the *piṇḍa* for the great-grandfather—which is an element of the *pārvaṇa* rite dedicated to the grandfather and others performed previously—were separated by the offering of the *piṇḍa* for the newly deceased person, which is an element of the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite performed immediately thereafter, then the division and the joining would likewise be separated. But if the subject refers to the *piṇḍa* of the newly deceased, then since there is no intervening offering of another *piṇḍa*, the division and joining performed immediately thereafter are more appropriate. Nor is it untenable for the phrase "one should divide the first into three" to refer to the newly deceased; for the word "first" (*ādya*) denotes primacy, and here the *piṇḍa* of the newly deceased is primary, because the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* has the purpose of consecrating the newly deceased. There is indeed a Purāṇic text stating, "having made the primary [deceased] the father," and a Smṛti text stating, "at the end of the year, [offerings are made] to the deceased, his father, and his grandfather. The injunction regarding the priority of the *piṇḍas* of the grandfather and others over the *piṇḍa* of the newly deceased is intended for that very purpose, and thus the word "first" is used accordingly, leaving no room for the aforementioned objection. As for the claim that the prohibition—"one who has performed the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* for the deceased"—is inappropriate because an annual *ekoddiṣṭa* is prescribed for the newly deceased after the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, that too is incorrect. That prohibition is justified either as being for the purpose of an optional *pārvaṇa* rite, or as being restricted to the annual rites performed by sons such as the legitimate son (*aurasa*), or as referring to *śrāddhas* for those killed by weapons on occasions other than the fourteenth day. In fact, this prohibition is even less applicable if it were directed at the great-grandfather, for according to texts such as "water should be offered to the three," the offering of *piṇḍas* is entirely prohibited for him on the anniversary of death and similar occasions; since the separate offering of a *piṇḍa* never arises in that case, what would be the point of prohibiting a separate *piṇḍa*? Furthermore, there exists a specific class of living beings called *preta*, like a planet, spirit, or demon; and there is scriptural authority from the Smṛtis and Purāṇas that the state of being a *preta* for the newly deceased is something to be terminated by the post-mortem rites ending with the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*.
And likewise in the Brahma Purāṇa: "Prior to the Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa rite, the deceased is indeed a preta; once the Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa has been performed, he attains the status of a Pitṛ. Thus it is said.

Therefore, the word *preta* applies by convention (*ruḍhi*) to the specific state of one who has recently died; however, it applies to the great-great-grandfather (*vṛddhaprapitāmaha*) through etymological derivation (*yoga*). And since conventional meaning is stronger than etymological derivation, [the term does not apply there]. Furthermore, the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite belongs to that very person for whom the sixteen *śrāddhas* are prescribed.
For this very reason, Śātātapa says:
"The *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, however, is to be understood as taking place here at the end of the year."
"The rites for the deceased (*preta-kriyā*) are to be known by the wise as ending with the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*.

By this [statement], it is understood that the one designated by the term "deceased" (*preta*) in the monthly rites (*māsika*) and so forth is the very same person in the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite; therefore, it is established that the vessel of water-offering (*arghya-pātra*) belonging to a father or other ancestor who has recently died must be joined with the vessels of water-offering belonging to the grandfather and others, and his *piṇḍa* must be joined with their *piṇḍas*. If the grandfather is still living but the father has died, the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* should be performed by excluding the grandfather and joining [the father] with the three ancestors starting from the great-grandfather.
And so it is stated in the *Brahmapurāṇa*:
"If the father has died but the grandfather still lives,
then three rice-balls (*piṇḍas*) must be offered by him, beginning with the great-grandfather."
And for them, the ancestral rice-ball (piṇḍa) should be offered as before;
however, no rice-ball should be given to one who is still living, since he would be dead [only] when that [other] person dies.
But for one who is still living, taking a morsel of food from his hand would be equivalent to cutting off his head.

And it should be understood that this method of performing the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* for one whose grandfather is still living is intended as an illustration of the various methods for the *pitṛyajña*, including the offering of the rice-ball (*piṇḍa*) by those who have a living father and other such eligible persons.

In this regard, some maintain that even when the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* has already been performed together with the grandfather (*pitāmaha*) and others, if the grandfather subsequently passes away, the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* of the father must again be performed together with that grandfather during the funeral rites (*aurdhvadehika*) concluding with the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*. Otherwise, they argue, the *śrāddha* to be performed at times such as the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) would not be properly accomplished. When the grandmother (*pitāmahī*) is still living, the same principle as stated for the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* of the father should be applied to the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* of the mother. Accordingly, it is stated in this very *Purāṇa*: "But when the mother has died while the grandmother is still living..."
"Everything should be performed starting from the great-grandmother; in that case as well, this is the rule.
[1650] Now, another specific detail regarding the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* for women is stated:
In that regard, first, Śatānīka raises a doubt by way of a question in the Bhaviṣyapurāṇa:
"How should the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite for a mother be performed by her sons?
Should she be joined with her maternal grandfather, or should she be led into the family of her husband?"
The meaning of this [question] is: should she be joined for the *sapiṇḍana* rite with her maternal grandfather and others, or rather with the family of her husband?
Intending to describe the decision on this matter, Sumantu said:
"Alas! What a great hardship you have described; it is indeed difficult to discern."
For there is indeed a twofold nature here for all people; nevertheless, O King, let it be heard.
Firm is the sky, firm is the earth, firm is this entire world;
firm are all these mountains, and firm are women within their husband's family.

Having established this prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that she is to be united with the maternal grandfather and others through the *sapiṇḍana* rite, it is understood that the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that she is to be joined with her husband's family.
Furthermore, even for a deceased woman, the connection with her husband’s gotra is observed in the offering of rice-balls (*piṇḍa*), water, and so forth, and not separation from it.
Thus says Hārīta:
A woman falls from her own lineage at the seventh step of the marriage;
her rites of funeral cakes and water-libations must be performed by the lineage of her husband.
Uśanas said:
"She has attained oneness with her husband regarding the funeral cake (piṇḍa), the lineage (gotra), and the period of impurity (sūtaka).
Therefore, one should offer both the water and the cake under the husband's lineage."
Bṛhaspati says:
"By means of the mantras of the fourth oblation, together with her flesh, marrow, and bones, she attains oneness with her husband; therefore, she shares his lineage."
The mantras recited at the taking of the hand remove the woman from her father’s lineage;
therefore, the offering of rice-balls and water for women should be performed with the lineage of the husband.
Likewise: "One should perform the *sapiṇḍana* for the mother by means of her husband's lineage and name;
silently, one should separate the ancestors from the two *piṇḍas* of the couple with *kuśa* grass. Thus it is said.
"Antarayan" means concealing.
Vyāsa said: "Because the act of covering the head was performed in front of the father-in-law..."
That [funeral rite] should be performed with Darbha grass by sons who desire their mother's exaltation.

Thus, it is established that the *sapiṇḍana* of the wife must be performed together with her paternal family. Regarding this, Śātātapa states the following, beginning with a doubt as to with whom it should be done:
"How should the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* of the mother be performed by her sons?
Her rite of *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* should be performed together with her paternal grandmother."
The meaning is "together with the paternal grandmother, the great-grandmother, and the great-great-grandmother.
Regarding this, Gārgya states another view:
"The *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* for a woman must be performed by her husband alone."
For even though she was dead, she attained unity with him through mantras, fire-oblations, and vows.

"Mantras" refers to such [formulas] as "That which is your heart, let that be my heart," and so forth; "oblations" refers to those included within the marriage *homa* and other rites; "vows" refers to celibacy (*brahmacarya*), the avoidance of pungent or salty food, and so on—the meaning is "by these.
This is also stated in another *Smṛti*:
"The *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* for the mother is ordained to be performed together with the husband."
For it is held that for women devoted to their husbands, he alone is their ultimate refuge.
And it is said in the *Bhaviṣyat-purāṇa*:
"In the Vedas, the wife is sung of as half the body of the man;
for she who is born is indeed half of one's own self, O King."
Therefore, her *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* is ordained to be performed together with her husband;
for once the marriage has been completed, on the fourth night,
she is joined [to him] by means of mantras through the bones, flesh, skin, and other [constituent parts].

The mantras, however, are: "I join your vital breaths with my vital breaths, your bones with my bones, your flesh with my flesh, and your skin with my skin. Thus, while it has been stated in some scriptural passages that the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite for a mother should be performed together with her paternal grandmother and others, and in others that it should be performed together with her husband, the specific determination of the applicable cases is found in the *Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa*: "One whose father is living should perform the *sapiṇḍana* of his mother together with his paternal grandmother;
one whose father is deceased [should do so] with his father; and the son of an appointed daughter (*putrikā*) [should do so] with his father's father."
"By her father" means by the mother's father;
as stated in the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*:
"The *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* for the mother must be performed by the sons within one year."
If her husband, however, is still living along with her paternal grandmother.
Lokākṣi said:
"A woman should perform the sapinda-rite for her mother along with her paternal grandmother and other female ancestors;
however, while her father is still living, she should do so only when he has passed away."
Śātātapa said:
"A woman who has followed her husband in death is entitled to share a funeral rice-ball (piṇḍa) with him and to dwell in heaven until the dissolution of all beings."

This being the case, while the father is alive, the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* must be performed with the paternal grandmother and others alone. However, when the father has died, if the mother has ascended the funeral pyre (*anvārūḍhā*), the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* is performed with the father alone; whereas if she has not ascended the pyre (*ananvārūḍhā*), it is performed with the paternal grandmother and others. Thus, the settled rule (*vyavasthā*) is established. If, however, the *sapiṇḍana* were to be performed with the father alone even when the mother has not ascended the pyre, then the statement concerning the woman who has ascended the pyre would be rendered meaningless. If that statement is considered meaningful as a restrictive rule—namely, "she who has ascended the pyre is to be *sapiṇḍita* with the husband alone"—then the statement "one whose father is deceased [should perform it] with the father" cannot be taken as a restrictive injunction; thus, the lack of a fixed rule (*aniyama*) is established.

Furthermore, as for what was stated in the *Aparārka*—that when the paternal grandmother is living, the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* of the mother is performed together with the father—that is not correct; for in such a case, the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* with the paternal great-grandmother and others has been shown to be prescribed by the *Brahmapurāṇa*.

Alternatively, let there be the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* with the paternal great-grandmother and others as stated in the *Brahmapurāṇa* when both the father and the paternal grandfather are living; whereas when the paternal grandmother is living and the father is deceased, the *sapiṇḍana* is performed together with the father—such is the settled rule.
As for what Śātātapa says:
"When the father has died, however, the mother's *sapiṇḍatā* should not be performed [separately];

through the father’s very *sapiṇḍatā*, that [status] shall belong to her as well. This [rule] refers to the case of a son who is utterly incapable [of performing rites], or it should be understood as the opinion of certain authorities.
But when the husband performs the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* for his wife, Paiṭhīnasi states that it should be performed together with his own mother and the others:
"When a woman dies without a son, the husband shall perform the *sapiṇḍana*;
her *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* shall take place together with her mother-in-law and the others."

This being the case, and since the husband’s entitlement to perform the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* for his wife has been established, the statement that "the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* for women does not exist in the absence of a male [relative]" should be understood as a prohibition applicable when there is an absence of a son accompanied by an absence of a husband. Vyāsa states:
"But when a woman has died without a son, the husband shall perform the *sapiṇḍana*."
Together with his three mothers-in-law, he thus conformed to the Dharma.

Thus, by this extensive discussion, it has been stated that the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* of the mother must be performed within the husband’s family alone, together with the paternal grandmother and others, or with the father. However, there is also this alternative view that the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* should be performed in the maternal grandfather’s family as well.
Āpastamba says:
"Just as the sons of a cuckoo live depending on another's connection [to their parents], so too is the case for the mother."
When nourished, they return to their own family; such is the woman who has died as a virtuous wife (satī).
In the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa: Just as water situated in the sky, having fallen upon the surface of the earth,
returns to its own source, so too does a woman who dies as a chaste wife (satī).
One should not abandon the *gotra* of the father and adopt that of the husband;
for women, the paternal family remains [the primary one] both at birth and in times of misfortune.
Just as a calf finds its mother among hundreds of thousands of cows,
so too, O King, does a woman go to her father’s family, leaving behind the husband’s clan.
Just as water flows toward the low ground once it has left its source, O lord of men,
so does a woman, having abandoned her husband’s family after death, return to her own kin.
The father and grandfather [become free] from their mothers when a full year has passed with their sons;
likewise for the mother and maternal grandfather—so said the Blessed Lord Śiva.
"Yojyaḥ" means one who is to be united [with the ancestors].
And so it is stated in the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa:
"Just as by the sons, upon the completion of a full year for the father's grandfather..."
Likewise, according to the statement of Uśanas, the sapinda relationship extends to the mother’s maternal grandfather.

Thus, while some maintain that she is to be united with the paternal lineage (*pitṛkula*) through *sapiṇḍana*, others hold that it is with the maternal grandfather’s lineage (*mātāmahakula*); regarding this contradiction, the following rule for determining the scope is stated: For a woman married by any one of the forms of marriage known as Brāhma, Daiva, Ārṣa, or Prājāpatya, union with the husband’s family must be performed, as well as the offering of rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) and so forth according to his lineage. For she was made the property of the husband by her father through a gift free from conditions; therefore, even when deceased, she is not fit to be deprived of that family and lineage. However, for a woman married by any one of the Gāndharva, Āsura, Rākṣasa, or Paiśāca forms, union with the maternal grandfather’s family must be performed, as well as the offering of rice-balls and so forth according to his lineage. For she was given by her father to the groom of her own accord and without opposition; thus, she is not fit to be displaced from her maternal grandfather’s family or his lineage.
Therefore, Bṛhat-Śātātapa says:
"In the case of marriages such as the Brāhma and others, whatever girl has been wedded,
the offerings of rice-balls (piṇḍa) and water for her must be performed by means of her husband's gotra."
And among others, such as the Āsuras, one who knows the Dharma [should perform the rite] according to the paternal lineage (pitṛgotra).
[1656] Herein is another arrangement.
On this point Vyāsa says: "One should perform the offering of rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) and water for the mother according to the lineage (*gotra*) of the maternal grandfather."
The son of an appointed daughter (putrikā-putra) should perform [the rites]; this is the eternal law (sanātana-dharma).
Unity with the husband lasts only so long as a son is not born;
once a daughter has given birth to a son, her unity with the husband ceases.
And as for the other statement, "The son of the appointed daughter (putrikā) belongs to her father," that has already been demonstrated.
Here too, the settled rule is stated:
"By the same path his fathers have gone, by which his grandfathers have gone..."
The paths of the virtuous have been traversed by him; therefore, one who follows them does not incur fault.

Because of this statement, those who perform the *sapiṇḍana* with the paternal lineage according to family tradition should do so accordingly, while others should do otherwise. Regarding this very subject, having cited mutually contradictory statements, Sumantu declared in the *Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa*: "O Bhārata, such is the diversity of scriptural practice in all rites, just as there is a difference in the performance of the *homa* whether it is offered after sunrise or before sunrise."
"Therefore, a wise man should practice the customs handed down through his family lineage.
Thus ends the specific rule regarding the *sapiṇḍana* for women.

Thus concludes the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Procedure for the *Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*," in the *Śrāddhakalpa* section of the *Pariśeṣakhaṇḍa* of the *Caturvargacintāmaṇi*, composed by the illustrious Hemādri, Paṇḍita and Chief Administrator of all departments under the illustrious Mahārājādhirāja, the illustrious Mahādevīya.
[1657] Now begins the twenty-second chapter.
Next, the procedure for the annual *śrāddha* (ancestral rite).
Now, for some, these rites for the deceased ending with the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* should not be performed before the completion of one year, even after having performed the *nārāyaṇabali*.
Regarding this, Gautama says:
"They should not associate with those who have committed sinful acts, nor with women who practice sorcery."
Vṛddhayājñavalkya states:
"For those killed by serpents, poison, or by horned animals, fanged beasts, and reptiles,
as well as for those slain by the rod of a Brahmin's curse, a Śrāddha ceremony must not be performed."
Saṃvarta says: For those who have committed great sins (mahāpātakin) and likewise for those who commit suicide,
the offering of water, the giving of funeral cakes (piṇḍa), and whatever śrāddha has been performed [are ineffective].
None of that reaches him; it is all plundered by the rākṣasas.
From another Smṛti:
"Those killed by lightning, a cow, a king, a Brahmin, water, a horned animal, a fanged beast, or fire;
those born in vain, great eunuchs, those who have taken vows, and those who are not vessels for the [Vedic] word."
‘Udabhājanāḥ’ means vessels for the water of respectful offering (*arghyodaka*).
And so it is said:
“In the case of one killed by a Brāhmaṇa or others, one who is ill, one who has fallen [from his status], or one who is devoid of attachments...”
And if he dies out of the order of succession, the inheritance should be given to those very persons to whom he himself would have given it.
A monk who is "free from attachment" [is one who]—
according to the *Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa*— may die by his own will through the agency of a Brahmin, or by means of horned animals, fanged creatures, or reptiles.
By being bitten by the most venomous snakes, by poison, by hanging, and by being beaten by oneself.
Or else, for those whose limbs are fully intact,
poison may be extracted by means of falling into water or fire, entering a womb, or likewise through fasting and other such methods.
Those who think in this way are indeed said to be doers of evil;
they have taken refuge in heresy and are likewise great sinners.

Women who are unchaste, as well as those who have fallen from their status after being elevated, are not entitled to the rites of bathing or consecration; for them there is no *śrāddha* and no *sapiṇḍana*.
Indeed, the sixteen *śrāddhas* that have been prescribed do not apply to them at all.
One should cast the Vaitāna fire into water and the domestic fire at a crossroads;
one should burn the ritual vessels in the fire in the case of a sinner who maintains a sacred fire.
In the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*:
"If one should cause his own death by means of fire, water, or other such methods,
for him no period of impurity is prescribed, nor should any water-libation rite be performed."
One should not perform a *śrāddha* for those killed by snakes, horned animals, fanged beasts, or reptiles, nor for those who have committed suicide.
Death from a Caṇḍāla, water, a serpent, a Brāhmaṇa, lightning,
or from fanged beasts and wild animals, befalls those who have committed evil deeds.
The water libations, the offering of funeral cakes, and whatever śrāddha ceremony has been performed—all that does not reach them; it remains suspended in the intermediate space.
Out of fear of public reproach, men should perform the Nārāyaṇabali;
therefore, food together with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) must be given even to them.
The Nārāyaṇabali, however, will be described later. Therefore, "after" the Nārāyaṇabali;
likewise:
"Having first performed the Cāndrāyaṇa penance, the rites should be performed according to the rules."
Out of fear of public reproach, men should perform the Nārāyaṇabali rite.

One should give desired and beloved food, along with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), to a Brahmin. Thereafter, one should perform the rites of the rice-balls (piṇḍa) and the water libations, as well as the release of a bull (vṛṣotsarga) and other ceremonies;
likewise, one should perform the Ekoddiṣṭa and Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa rites.

This Nārāyaṇa-bali, which has been prescribed for those who have died by fire, water, and so forth, is intended only for those who commit suicide through the influence of anger, intoxication, grief, and the like, but not for those who die through negligence or by accident.
Thus it is said in the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa:
"Now, if someone should die through negligence by means of fire, water, and so forth..."
One should perform all the preparatory rites for him according to the prescribed rule, beginning with the saṃskāras.
In some places, he states an exception to this:
"One should not go [to the funeral] out of negligence or even by desire, nor if one has died from a snakebite.
"One should not go" means that one should not proceed toward the rites such as the cremation; the meaning is that without the serpent-worship to be described, one is not fit for those rites.
In the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*:
"Now, if someone dies through negligence by means of fire, water, or the like,
impurity must be observed for him and the water-libation rite must be performed."
Baudhāyana says:
For those who intentionally kill a limb, the omission of the ritual act is prescribed;
and for them alone is the scriptural statement regarding the defilement of the consecrator cited.
Having had the corpse of those who died an unnatural death burned by Śūdras alone,
as well as that of others who met with an evil death due to their sinful deeds.
As before, there is the burning of the body and then the reconstruction of the corpse;
one should perform the consecration with Palāśa stalks according to the ritual of the Pitṛmedha.

For those who have maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) but die a sinful death, the avoidance of a substitute body is the primary rule; they burn the fire-maintainer with his very own body, along with the sacrificial vessels, and thus these [substitutes] do not perform the consecration for them.
Brahmagarga said:
"He who, afflicted by a great disease, is unable to perform [the rites]..."
Thus, one who performs fire rituals, water offerings, and great processions does not incur fault in the next world.
Vivasvān said:
For one who is detached from all the senses, aged, who has performed his duties,
and is afflicted by disease, death at a sacred ford is remembered as superior even to asceticism.
Likewise, Gārgya also spoke specifically concerning the householder:
"One should not desire to live in vain, [but rather choose] the journey on the Great Departure, entering fire or water, or even leaping from a precipice."
‘Bhṛgu’ refers to a mountain ridge. ‘Vainly’ means devoid of the performance of dharma. With reference to the forest-dweller (vānaprastha), Manu says:
"Having taken his stand in the unconquered [direction], he should proceed straight toward that quarter."
By abstaining from taking life, one is glorified in the world of Brahmā.
The Aparājitā is the north-eastern direction; facing it, one should proceed with a concentrated mind until the fall of the body, inhaling neither crooked water nor wind.
Having stood firm in the conduct of the great seers and having cast off the body composed of evil, the Brahmin, freed from sorrow, becomes fit for absorption into Brahman.
Regarding those killed by cows or Brahmins, there is a specific rule in the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*:
"In the case of those killed by cows or Brahmins, as well as those who have become outcasts (patita),
one should perform all the funeral rites (*aurdhvadehika*) after the lapse of one year."
Now follows the procedure for the Nārāyaṇabali.
Regarding that, first is the rule for the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) and so forth in the Baudhāyana-sūtra.

Now, therefore, we shall explain the Nārāyaṇabali. For those who have been accused of crimes, those who have fallen from their caste, those who have drunk liquor, those who have abandoned themselves, and those killed by Brahmins—for these, one should perform the rite for twelve or three years at the very place where death occurred. Having summoned [representatives] in a village, one fashions a human figure out of Palāśa wood of uniform leaf-pattern upon a black antelope skin; or one should perform the consecration according to the ritual of the Hotṛ priest or that of the Pitṛmedha. Having extracted the mantras used for the application of the limbs, there is a separate application of the mantras of the Puruṣasūkta verse by verse in their place; or else everything may be performed silently. There is no nourishment with the Yāmyasūkta; the worship is done with the Puruṣasūkta; the rest is the same. Having bathed at a sacred ford (tīrtha) and performed the water-libation for the deceased, one should mentally contemplate the name and lineage and utter: "O Nārāyaṇa, this water is for you. In this very manner, he performs it morning and evening for ten nights, or for three nights. In the offering of the rice-balls (piṇḍa), the distinction is: "O [Name], this rice-ball is for you. On the eleventh day, they perform the Ekoddiṣṭa rite.
Regarding the procedure for the funeral rites (*saṃskāra*), it is stated in that very same work:

"For those who have died from snakebite, one should offer three oblations with the mantra 'Homage to the snakes' (*namo ’stu sarpebhyaḥ*). For those who have died in water, one should offer oblations with the mantra 'To the ocean, go away with the wind' (*samudrāya vāyunāpeta*). Regarding him, we do not know his angry truth. They say that the rite of bodily purification (*dehasaṃskāra*) applies to those embodied beings who have died through knowledge; others say it applies to all. Furthermore, the ritual application for the *Nārāyaṇabali* is shown in the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*.
Their sons, grandsons, or other heirs,
being overwhelmed by [the power of] Viṣṇu’s name, perform the ancestral rites (śrāddha) as they have been heard.
Having paid homage to the Self-Existent One, I shall likewise fully declare to you [the merit of] having observed the eleventh lunar day (ekādaśī) of the bright fortnight.
The *nārāyaṇabali* is to be performed; this is the remainder [of the statement]. A specific detail regarding this is shown in the *Bhaviṣyottara*:
"When a full year has passed for them, then it should be performed by the compassionate ones, having reached the eleventh lunar day (*ekādaśī*) of the bright fortnight."
Having likewise worshipped Viṣṇu and Yama with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings,
one should place ten rice-balls, anointed with ghee and mixed with honey, upon blades of darbha grass.
Wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder, meditating upon Viṣṇu and Yama,
he should silently offer each of those [portions] while facing south.
Having lifted the prepared rice-balls, he should cast them into the water of a sacred ford or similar place.
And it is stated in the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata* that this should be performed preceded by meditation on Viṣṇu:
"Having brought Viṣṇu to mind, one should then cast [the offering] into the river water."
In the *Bhaviṣyottara*:
"One should quickly utter the name of Viṣṇu for the sake of that deceased person;
then one should again worship Viṣṇu and Yama with flowers and sandalwood."
With incense, lamps, and food offerings consisting of various kinds of eatables and edibles,
one should fast on that day and likewise invite Brahmins.
Endowed with noble lineage, learning, and austerity, and possessed of beauty and virtuous conduct—
nine, seven, or five [disciples] according to one's own capacity.

In the Baudhāyana-sūtra: "Now, therefore, we shall explain the Nārāyaṇa-bali. It should be performed on the twelfth day of the dark fortnight, either during the sun's southern course (dakṣiṇāyana) or its northern course (uttarāyaṇa). On the preceding day, one should invite six or twelve Brāhmaṇas who are endowed with excellence of birth, lineage, Vedic learning, and conduct. [Also] in the Bhaviṣyottara-purāṇa:
When another day had arrived, at midday, being well-composed,
he worshipped Viṣṇu and Yama and attended upon those brahmins.
Facing north, recollecting the form of the ancestors according to their seniority,
he should perform the rites beginning with the invocation and the offering of *arghya*, accompanied by Viṣṇu and Sūrya.
Remembering the deceased in the realm of the departed, one should indeed recite the name of Viṣṇu;
wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder, one should perform the rite while proclaiming the name of the deceased.
Remembering the deceased, Yama, and Viṣṇu, one should bring the śrāddha ceremony to completion.
In the Baudhāyana-sūtra.

Likewise, on the following day, having kindled the fire in a temple or on a riverbank and having strewn grass around it, he prepares the *praṇītā* water. Rising, he invokes the deity in front of the fire with the *Puruṣasūkta*. Having recited two verses, he invokes the deity with the *vyāhṛtis*. Then he bathes the deity with the *Puruṣasūkta*; then, having worshipped him with perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, and the eight-syllable mantra, he satiates him with water, saying, "I satiate Keśava," using the twelve names. Having performed the rites from the laying of the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) up to the "mouth of the fire" (*agnimukha*), he offers oblations of cooked food with the verse "In the succession of Viṣṇu" as the invitatory verse (*puronuvākyā*), and offers with the offering verse (*yājyā*) "Beyond the measure. Having invoked, he offers additional oblations with these very names, saying, "To Keśava, svāhā! He presents food mixed with molasses, milk-rice, and ghee, saying, "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, I present this to Viṣṇu. He mutters the seven *vyāhṛtis* with the word *svāhā*. With the *vyāhṛtis*, he offers water for sipping. Then, having invited the Brahmins and seated them in places prepared with *darbha* grass, and having honored them with garments, perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, and garlands, and having obtained their permission, he offers the oblation mixed with ghee with his hand, saying: "To the ancestors, svadhā! Adoration to Nārāyaṇa, svāhā! To the grandfathers, svadhā! Adoration to Nārāyaṇa, svāhā! To Agni Kavyavāhana Sviṣṭakṛt, svadhā! Adoration to Nārāyaṇa, svāhā! Thus, having satisfied the Brahmins with food...
The ellipsis is to be supplied as "one should perform what is about to be described.
In the *Bhaviṣyottara*:
"Then, having ascertained that the Brahmins are satiated, one should ask them about their satisfaction according to the prescribed rule."
Then, for the purpose of offering the rice-balls (piṇḍas), one should set aside portions from all the cooked foods.
One should offer five funeral cakes (piṇḍas) in sequence upon separate blades of darbha grass;
first, one should offer them to Viṣṇu, to Brahmā, and to Śiva.
Then, for Yama together with his attendants, and likewise for the preta, one should remember the fifth [offering];
one should recall his name and lineage and proclaim the word "Viṣṇu."
One should offer the fifth pinda preceded by a salutation;
thereafter, one should give water for sipping (ācamana), as well as betel-leaf and a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
One should honor an especially excellent Brahmin with gold,

while remembering that deceased person, according to one's ability, with cows, land, clothing, food, and other gifts. Then, one should offer sesame seeds into the hands of the Brahmins, which are joined with *darbha* grass.
Recalling the name and lineage, one should give [the gift] while saying, "May Viṣṇu be pleased."
Having followed behind the twice-born, he should then, facing south,
announce their names and lineages and cast [the remains] upon the ground, saying, "May there be satisfaction.
Restrained in speech, he should eat the remainder together with his friends and kinsmen.
In the Baudhāyana-sūtra.

Having caused them to sip water, he gives them a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) according to his ability. Having circumambulated [the fire] from left to right and having asked for permission regarding what remains, he strews *darbha* grass with its tips pointing eastward to the south of the fire and offers the oblation (*bali*) upon them, saying: "Homage to the Viśvedevas! Homage to the Sādhyas! Homage to all the gods! Homage to all the deities! Homage to Viṣṇu Nārāyaṇa! Homage to the Soul of Sacrifice! Homage to the Person of Sacrifice! Homage to the Lord of All! Thus, from the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering onwards until the granting of the boon of the cow, he attains all the ancestors and is glorified in the world of Brahmā; he is glorified in the world of Brahmā—so said the venerable Baudhāyana.
Regarding the Nārāyaṇabali in the *Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa*:
"When this is performed, even those who have committed sinful deeds will go to the heavenly world;
however, once the Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa and other rites have been performed, they no longer attain it."
Likewise:
"In this manner, he who, abiding by the doctrine of Viṣṇu, should give [the gift] to one who has committed suicide, swiftly rescues that person; no doubt should be entertained in this matter."
Thus concludes the ritual procedure for the Nārāyaṇa-bali.
Now follows the ritual procedure for the worship of the Nāgas.
In the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa: "Whether one has died through negligence, by one's own will, or from a snake or serpent,
one should worship the Nāgas on both fortnights, specifically on the fifth lunar days."
One should fashion an image of a serpent out of flour on the ground;
one should worship it with white flowers, along with perfumes and sandalwood paste.
One should offer incense and lamps, scatter white rice grains,
and likewise present food made of raw flour as well as milk.
Having approached him, one should say, "Release, release [the name] so-and-so," and on that day one should give sweets; in this manner one should practice for a year.
Then, according to his means, that best of the twice-born should give a golden serpent,
and thereafter he should give a cow with its calf, saying, "May the King of Serpents be pleased."
One should perform the rites, even those pertaining to the past, according to their respective divisions;
yet this further instruction has been declared for the sake of liberation from the serpent:
"Having liberated the twice-born, may the serpents be well-pleased."
Thus ends the ritual procedure for the worship of the Nāgas. Now follows the procedure for cremating one who has died while away from home and so forth.
Regarding this, the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata* states:
How should the elaborate rites, such as cremation and others, be performed for those who have gone to another country, who were not seen, but are heard to have died?
Regarding this, Vṛddha-Manu states the specific time:
"When twelve years have passed for one who has been away,
upon reaching the thirteenth year, one should cause the funeral rites to be performed."
In the *Bhaviṣyottara*: "If a father has gone abroad and there is neither news of him nor any report of his arrival,
after fifteen years have passed, one should fashion an image of him."
Then one should perform his consecration according to the ritual for consecration;
thereafter, one should cause all the remaining rites to be performed, beginning with those very same ones.

In this context, the making of a substitute should be understood as occurring only when bones are not obtained; however, if they do exist, there is a specific rule mentioned in another treatise, as follows:

Here, the specific procedure for one who has died while away from home is described. Before the cremation, the *agnihotra* must be offered by one wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*). One should not perform the strewing of grass around the fire, nor the circumambulation, nor the sprinkling of water. To the south, one should remove hot ashes and place the vessel upon them; there is no lighting of the wick or pouring of liquids. One should take it down to the south and set it down once. Without a formal call (*praiṣa*), one should draw the offering once, carry the fuel-sticks, and drop the knee on the left side. The placing of the fuel-sticks consists of a single casting of all of them at once. Then, on a black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*), one should fashion the shape of a man with the bones, anoint them with ghee, cover them with wool, and join the vessels as before; the cremation is performed with fires produced by friction. On the fourth day, the collection of the bones (*saṃcayana*) and subsequent rites are as previously described.
In the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*:
"If his bones are lost, however, the cremation is performed with *brahmadarbha* grass;
this was stated by the wise Kātyāyana in the absence of the deceased."
One should fashion a figure of the deceased out of darbha grass using three hundred and sixty blades, or else with palāśa fuel-sticks; this is the number that has been proclaimed.
Then one should fashion the form of a preta, marked with hands, feet, and other signs;
having recited the mantra "Apeta," one should indeed cremate it according to the prescribed rite.
Regarding this, Yajñapārśva states the division of the number of *kuśa* blades according to the different parts of the corpse, such as the head and neck:
"One should place forty in the place of the head,
ten in the neck, one hundred in the region of the chest, and sixty in the belly."
One should assign one hundred bones to the place of the two arms, twenty to the knees and shanks;
one should assign four to the penis, six to the two testicles,
and ten to the toes of the feet— thus one should arrange the collection of bones.
Having covered it with woolen threads and anointed it with clarified butter, one should join the vessel as before and burn it with fires produced by friction. Thus it is said in the *Bhaviṣyottara*:
"One should give fifty [coins] on the head, and ten indeed on the neck."
One should likewise give one hundred on the two arms and twenty on the chest.
One should give twenty [offerings] to the abdomen, thirty to the two regions of the hips,
one hundred to the thighs, and thirty to the knees and shanks; ten to the toes of the feet— this is the ritual arrangement for the deceased.

In this regard, Madhuśarman Miśra states that one should fashion a human figure out of *kuśa* grass upon a black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*), place *palāśa* stalks therein, and that the division of the number [of stalks] occurs right there.
In the *Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa*: "If a householder who has gone abroad should happen to die somewhere at home..."
When the period of impurity has passed, one should commence the śrāddha rite there.
If, upon returning, he learns of what previously occurred in the house,
then there shall be impurity for the householder regarding that property and so forth.

The Śrāddha rite that has been commenced by one who is childless or otherwise disqualified must be completed by him in its entirety; even during that performance, the householder should remain at a great distance.
Vṛddha-Manu states what must be done immediately thereafter:
"Having heard that one for whom the funeral rites (aurdhvadehika) have been performed is actually alive,
he should perform the Smārta expiation and then establish the sacred fires."
In this case, the expiation should be understood as the re-performance of the sacraments (*saṃskāra*), beginning with the birth-rite (*jātakarman*) and ending with marriage.
For this very reason, it has been stated by that same author:
"If he should return while still living, one should immerse him in a vat of clarified butter."
Having lifted him up and bathed him, one should perform for him the birth-rite and other ceremonies.
Likewise:
he should observe the vow for twelve days, or for three nights;
then, having bathed, he may marry a wife, or another woman in the absence of the former.
Having established the sacred fires according to the rules, he should either perform the Vrātyastoma sacrifice,
or likewise, having gone to a mountain, he should perform the Aindrāgna animal sacrifice there.
Then one should perform the *āyuṣmatī* sacrifice and the desired rites;
