by "the *āyuṣmatī* sacrifice" is meant the sacrifice for the desire of long life. Thus concludes the ritual procedure for the cremation and other rites for one who has died while away from home.
Now, the scholar Hemādri— whose mind has been rendered stainless by the destruction of all waves of defects— expounds upon the annual Śrāddha.
Now follows the procedure for the annual *śrāddha*.
Regarding this, the time, the qualified performer, and the deities have already been explained [at 1670]. Logākṣi says:
One whose father has died must personally perform the śrāddha rite every month on the new moon day,
as well as at the time of the lunar increase and annually.

The inclusion of the word "himself" (*svayam*) is for the sake of emphasis, and not for the purpose of excluding the group of sons, disciples, and so forth; for another *smṛti* states: "With the mantra 'This is for you,' the officiating priest and others should offer the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) to the father of the sacrificer. This [rule] should be understood to apply when the sacrificer is incapable due to being preoccupied with more important duties, or in cases where the proper time has elapsed. Jābāli says:
"Thousands of eclipses and tens of thousands of new moons..."
But the śrāddha offered on the anniversary of the day of death shall indeed become inexhaustible.
Kārṣṇājini stated the fault in failing to perform [the rite]:
"Just as a seed sown in saline soil does not sprout,
so it is with that which is not given to them on the anniversary of their death."
The intention is that [the gift] must necessarily be given on the anniversary of death.
In the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*: "Some say the gift should be given to one person after a year; others have declared it should be given to three."
Therefore, you ought to hear the decision in accordance with the Smṛtis.

By the phrase "giving to one," the procedure for the annual Śrāddha is stated to be like that of the Ekoddiṣṭa; by the phrase "to three," it is stated to be like that of the Pārvaṇa. First, the statements prescribing the Ekoddiṣṭa are written down. Regarding this, Yama says:
"After the Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa, every year the son [should perform the rite]."
One should perform the ekoddiṣṭa rite for one's parents; otherwise, for others, one should perform the pārvaṇa rite.
Vyāsa: After the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite, wherever an offering is made,
there the triad [of ancestors] must be included, except on the anniversary of the day of death.
Wherever an annual Śrāddha is offered for one's mother and father,
one should feed those who are not deities (i.e., Brahmins) and offer a single pinda.
Gārgya says: Even when the offering of the funeral rice-ball has been performed and the commonality of group membership has been attained,
the annual Śrāddha is prescribed for that very person alone.
Laukāxi also said:
"Before the Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa rite, the son should perform the Ekoddiṣṭa for his father;
after that, he should perform the Pārvaṇa rite annually, while others [should do so] by the other method."
"By the other" means by the procedure for the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite.
Śātātapa says:
"At the time of a solar transit (*saṃkrānti*), during an eclipse, at a festival (*parva*), on a great festival day (*utsava*), and during the *mahālaya* [period]."
On the anniversary of death, the son should offer three funeral cakes, or even just one.
Āpastamba says: "The first *śrāddha* for a single person is performed before the end of the year; the monthly rites continue until then.
The annual rite is to be performed every year, and they know the remaining rites to extend to three generations."
Yama, however, has stated that after performing the annual *ekoddiṣṭa* rite, there is a fault in its omission:
"If one performs the *pārvaṇa* rite while abandoning the *ekoddiṣṭa*, one should know that it is as if unperformed; such a person is a slayer of his mother and father."
Now, the scriptural injunctions prescribing the *pārvaṇa* rite are set forth. Regarding this, Śātātapa says:
"In whatever [rites] there is the offering of these [ancestors] after the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*..."
In that regard, one who desires prosperity should understand that the śrāddha is to be performed according to the rules of the pārvaṇa rite.
Those deceased ancestors for whom the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* has been performed—for them there is no separate rite;
nor is the offering of a separate *piṇḍa* prescribed for them thereafter. For they have crossed over from the state of being a *preta* and have attained the ranks of the *pitṛ*s.
And because it is so, he says again:

"He who should offer the deceased who has already been united with the ancestors (sapiṇḍīkṛta) separately in a funeral ball (piṇḍa) becomes a destroyer of the ritual injunction and is born as a slayer of his father."
Pulastya says:
The *ekoddiṣṭa* rite must be performed until the *sapiṇḍana* of the parents is completed;
thereafter, after the *sapiṇḍana*, the *ekoddiṣṭa* ceases.
Prajāpati also said: "One should perform the Ekoddiṣṭa rite for deceased ancestors who have not yet undergone the Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa.
After the Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa, it is declared that they share equality with the three [ancestors]."
And because it is thus, for that very reason it is *dharma*: the *pārvaṇa* [śrāddha] at the time of a festival (*parvan*), as well as [the rites] for the attainment of desire and wealth;
and at a time of prosperity (*vṛddhi*), by means of the procedure for prosperity, through the joining of one [rite] with another.
Having thus established that after the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite, the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite is no longer applicable, the same author states:
"For those who have been united [with the ancestors], there should always be only one [offering], and never otherwise;
because the cause for their consecration is common, a separate performance is not appropriate."

Thus, having set aside the *ekoddiṣṭa* for one whose *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* has been performed, that same author states the *pārvaṇa* rite for the anniversary of death every year by way of restating the *māsika* and other *ekoddiṣṭa* rites:
"The first *śrāddha* for a single ancestor is the *māsika* before the end of the year;
after the *saṃnayana*, even on the anniversary of the death of the parents, it is *pārvaṇa*."
Likewise: "That *pārvaṇa* rite belongs to that son by whom his aged parents have been brought together through the perfection of ritual; it is otherwise for anyone other than him."

Therefore, setting aside the *vṛddhi-śrāddha*, in all other cases—always and everywhere, including on the anniversary of death (*mṛtāha*) and so forth—one must perform only the *pārvaṇa* for a father for whom the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* has been performed. Likewise:
"The father, indeed, having been led to the state of divinity by the perfection of the mantras..."
He does not return to the state of a preta, even when being led away by his sons.
All the deities are independent, and the state of being a sapinda is independent;
furthermore, the abode of the departed is devoid of that separate agency.
Just as the ancestors, gods, and sages, having established themselves in the highest state,
do not desire a miserable rebirth, so too do even those who have been made solitary ghosts (pretas) [not desire it].
Pāraskara says:
Having included the deceased among the ancestors during the offering of the rice-balls (piṇḍa) and the water-offerings (arghya),
one should rescue the deceased from hell and not cause him to fall there again.
Śambhu said:
"But in the case of the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite performed according to the rule at any time,
because of the superior force of its association with that [ancestral lineage], it pertains to three generations in every instance."
For this very reason, Jātūkarṇya says:
"From that point onward, the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite should never be performed;
it has been declared by the Mudgalas that it ends with the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*."
Likewise: "Then, when a full year has passed and the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite has been performed,
the ancestors depart disappointed once the invitation for only one [the deceased] has been made."
And here, the invocation is intended to be without a mantra. As stated in the *Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa*:
"O King, when a full year has passed and the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* has been performed..."
The ancestors depart disappointed when the invocation is performed for only one.
The *ekoddiṣṭa* rite must be performed until the *sapiṇḍana* of the parents;
O King, after the *sapiṇḍana*, the *ekoddiṣṭa* ceases.

Therefore, from that point forward, the offering of individual funeral cakes (piṇḍa) for all the deceased (pretas) here is not prescribed; rather, [the rite] is performed using the mantra that has been assigned.
Having crossed over the state of being a preta, he indeed attains the company of the ancestors;
however, he falls from the world of the ancestors due to the separate offering of the funeral rice-ball (piṇḍa).
Just as a married woman does not go back to her father’s family,
so too, O Great King, the deceased, once united with his ancestors, never departs from them.
As long as a year has passed, that [rite] shall be the Ekoddiṣṭa;
but when a year has elapsed, it is said to be common with the three [other rites].
Having accomplished their purpose here once the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite was performed,
those hosts went to the world of the ancestors, just as the Blessed Lord Śiva has said.
"Having performed the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, the wise man should always perform [the rite] like the *pārvaṇa* ceremony every year; thus spoke Viṣṇu."
The Śruti also says:

"Having slain the Asuras by means of the gods, he obtained the state of being a Pitṛ; saying, 'All have been seized together,' those who are our equals take back their own respective shares from you; thus it came to pass."

Regarding the verse "ye naḥ samānā," the meaning is as follows: those ancestors who are "samānāḥ" (equal) to us—meaning similar, equivalent, and those with whom the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* has been performed—they are the gods; they are the ancestors who, from behind, receive their own respective portions. It was exactly thus that it came to pass. From this, it is understood that after the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, when an offering is to be given to the ancestors, one should first give to the gods and afterwards to the ancestors. Consequently, it is determined that the *pārvaṇa* śrāddha must be performed every year on the anniversary of death (*mṛtāhani*), especially since the specific *pārvaṇa* procedure is observed therein.
Jātūkarṇya said:
A son should perform [the rites] for his father who has entered the assembly of the ancestors according to the *pārvaṇa* method;
this eternal rule is to be understood as applying both annually and monthly.

"Abiding in the group of ancestors" means one for whom the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* has been performed. "Sanātanaḥ" means obligatory. Śātātapa says: "Having performed the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, one should always perform [the rite] according to the *pārvaṇa* method."
The wise one should perform this rite every year, according to the procedure taught by Chāgaleya.
Jamadagni says: Since a Śrāddha performed without a deity is declared to be fruitless,
therefore, in all Śrāddhas— even on the anniversary of death— the Pārvaṇa rite must be observed.
In the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa:
"O King, some praise the *ekoddiṣṭa* on the anniversary of death;
others, O King, praise the *pārvaṇa* on the anniversary of death."
Having performed the *pārvaṇa* śrāddha, one should not perform the *ekoddiṣṭa*;
by performing it, one goes to hell, especially on the anniversary of the day of death.
O hero, the preta has been dispatched, commissioned along with the ancestors.
He does not exist for even a moment, just as a son cannot exist without his mother.
Just as one who separates a young calf from its mother would go to hell,
so too does a man who quickly joins a deceased person with the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite [go to hell].
One should perform the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite on the anniversary of death for one year;
after that, however, when [the bones] have been gathered, the *pārvaṇa* rite should be performed on the anniversary of death.
Henceforth, one should never perform the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite;
rather, after the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, it should be performed every year on the anniversary of the day of death.
O King, the pārvaṇa rite must be performed, and never the ekoddiṣṭa;
likewise, a water-pot should always be given on the anniversary of the day of death.
Gārgya said:
At the end of the year, the son should unite the deceased with the ancestors;
from that time forward, the Pārvaṇa Śrāddha should be performed on the anniversary of death, and not otherwise.
The Śruti also says:
"Month by month, season by season—specifically at the beginning of each winter, summer, and rainy season—and every year, the gods and the ancestors remain together.
The meaning is that the Viśvedevas and the paternal ancestors, grandfathers, and so forth, stay together to partake of the śrāddha.
Sumantu said: "O King, the pārvaṇa rite must be performed; the ekoddiṣṭa is never to be done. Many statements on this matter sung by the sages shall now be declared."
"O King of kings, the *ekoddiṣṭa* is prescribed for fewer [days];
therefore, by the force of the statement, the *pārvaṇa* should be performed on the anniversary of death.
By "by the force of the statement," the meaning is "by the force of many statements."

This very same point was also stated by Jaimini: "In a conflict of contradictory properties, that which possesses the majority of properties shall prevail. Thus, when there is such a duality of scriptural statements, a determination regarding the scope of application must be made.
Jābāla says:
Where there is a conflict between two Vedic texts, both are remembered as Dharma;
but where there is a conflict between two Smṛtis, their respective scopes must be distinguished.
In this regard, first of all, those statements prescribing the *pārvaṇa* [śrāddha] should be understood as referring to the legitimate (*aurasa*) son.
For this very reason, Jamadagni says:
"Having established the identity of the funeral rice-balls (*sa-piṇḍatva*), the legitimate son performs the rite according to the rules."
One should perform the śrāddha for one's mother and father on the anniversary of their death just as one does for the new moon.
Among sons, the son of one's own body (aurasa) and others who are merely sons [of other women] should always perform the Pārvaṇa rite for their father and for his paternal lineage.
The mention of the *aurasa* (legitimate son) is also an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) of the *kṣetraja* (son born of the wife).
For this very reason, Jābāli says:
"The *aurasa* and *kṣetraja* sons [should perform the rite] by means of the *pārvaṇa* procedure."
Every year, the other ten sons should perform the ekoddiṣṭa rite.
Sumantu says: Every year, the *kṣetraja* and *aurasa* sons perform the rite according to the *pārvaṇa* procedure alone; the other ten types of sons should perform the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite.

The two sons— the *kṣetraja* and the *aurasa*— who are conversant with the ritual injunctions, should perform for their father who has entered the company of the ancestors the rites as prescribed for the *darśa*, both annually and every month.

"Annually" means on the anniversary of death; "monthly" means on the new moon day (*darśa*) and so forth. Because of the mention of the *darśa*, it is understood that even for the son of an appointed daughter (*putrikāputra*), the *pārvaṇa* rite alone is prescribed on the anniversary of his mother's death, since he is equal to a legitimate son (*aurasa*), and because the rule regarding the *ekoddiṣṭa* applies specifically to the *darśa* rites.
Dharma says:
"On the anniversary of death, for those who have been brought together from two lineages (*dvigotrin*), [the rite] is performed with reference to one [ancestor]."
Therefore, that [rite] is pārvaṇa; elsewhere, it is performed according to the specific qualification in each case.

Before the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite, on the anniversary of death every month, a *śrāddha* intended for one [ancestor] must be performed by the son of an appointed daughter (*putrikāputra*). However, for those whose *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* has been completed, on the anniversary of their passing—and not only then, but also on other occasions such as the sun’s passage into a new sign (*saṃkrānti*) or the *vyatīpāta* yoga—a *pārvaṇa* rite alone must be performed; this is the meaning. Śāṭyāyana says:
"But that son who is authorized to perform the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* for his father..."
He himself should perform the Śrāddha on the anniversary of the death, just as he would for the Darśa sacrifice.

And this should be understood to apply only when there are many sons, such as the *aurasa* (legitimate) and others; for even when there are many sons, the right to perform the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* belongs primarily to the *aurasa* and the rest.
Thus it is said in the *Garuḍa Purāṇa*:
"The primary son alone should perform the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* for his father."
The legitimate son born of one's own body (aurasa) is the primary heir; in his absence, the son born of the wife (kṣetraja) is likewise.

[1679] Even by those who maintain the *aurasa* (legitimate) fire and others, the *pārvaṇa* śrāddha must be performed every year on the anniversary of death, provided they possess the sacred fires (*sāgnibhiḥ*).
For Manu says:
"The oblation belonging to the ancestral sacrifice is not ordained for the common (*laukika*) fire."
For a twice-born man who has maintained the sacred fires, there is no śrāddha without the Darśa sacrifice.

The meaning is that a Śrāddha devoid of the rite characterized by the *darśa* (new moon) must not be performed by one who maintains the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*); rather, it must be performed precisely according to the *darśa-śrāddha* procedure. However, it should not be interpreted to mean that no other Śrāddha whatsoever—such as the *kṣayāha-śrāddha* and so forth—should be performed apart from the *darśa-śrāddha*, for that would entail the undesirable consequence of the non-performance of those rites as well.
Yama also says:
"Manu has declared that among those whose Śrāddha rituals are unified, [certain offerings] are praised."
For a twice-born who has maintained the sacred fires, there is no ancestral rite (śrāddha) without the performance of the Darśa sacrifice.
Manu says:

For those Brahmins who maintain many sacred fires as well as those who maintain only a single fire, after the *sapiṇḍana* rite has been performed, the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite is prescribed, not the *pārvaṇa*.
In this context, the connection is that the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite is not [performed]. For this very reason, Kārṣṇājini states:
"In the householder's stage of life, the performance of all [rites] has the fire as its primary element."
By virtue of that connection, those who have acquired the requisite capacity are entitled everywhere to perform the pārvaṇa rite.
In the *Bhaviṣyatpurāṇa*:
"Every year, the twice-born who maintains a sacred fire should indeed perform the *pārvaṇa* rite;
however, O hero, one who does not maintain a sacred fire should perform the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite on the anniversary of death."

Therefore, those who maintain the sacred fires—namely, the legitimate son (*aurasa*), the son born of the wife (*kṣetraja*), and the son of an appointed daughter (*putrikāputra*)—must perform only the *pārvaṇa* rite every year on the anniversary of the death, and not the *ekoddiṣṭa*.
As for the statement of Gārgya:
"One whose father has died should perform the *śrāddha* at the time of a festival according to the prescribed rule..."
On the anniversary of death, a rite may be performed according to one's preference; on occasions of prosperity, it is performed with joy.

The view that one may perform either the *pārvaṇa* or the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite according to one's preference as an option between them applies to the case of a son born of the womb (*aurasa*), a son born of the field (*kṣetraja*), or the son of an appointed daughter (*putrikāputra*) who maintains no sacred fires (*niragni*).
For Dharma says:
"A triad of rites is prescribed for one who possesses the sacred fires; it does not exist for one devoid of fires."
And it is said that for him, the ritual is not performed according to the procedure for an Ekoddiṣṭa.

"O [Name], this is for you"—this is for the father of the sacrificer; "O [Name], this is for you"—this is for the grandfather; "O [Name], this is for you"—this is for the great-grandfather: such is this triad of injunctions. And this applies only to one who maintains the sacred fires (*sāgni*); however, for one without fires (*niragni*), there is an option between the *ekoddiṣṭa* and the *pārvaṇa*. Nevertheless, those for whom the *pārvaṇa* has been performed through tradition should perform that very rite, and those for whom the *ekoddiṣṭa* has been performed should perform the *ekoddiṣṭa* alone—according to the path by which one's fathers have gone, and by which one's grandfathers have gone.
Therefore, one should follow the path of the virtuous; by not following it, one does not incur fault.

Thus, according to the statement of Manu, the *pārvaṇa* rite should be performed optionally on the anniversary of death (*mṛtāhani*) by those who maintain no sacred fires (*niragni*), as well as by the legitimate son (*aurasa*), the son born of the wife (*kṣetraja*), and the son of an appointed daughter (*putrikāputra*). However, for those who maintain sacred fires (*sāgnika*), the *pārvaṇa* alone must be performed; and for the other ten types of sons, such as the adopted son (*dattaka*) and so forth, it is established that the *ekoddiṣṭa* alone is to be performed.
And it has been stated in the *Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa*:
For a son born of the legitimate womb who is without the sacred fire, the Ekoddiṣṭa rite is prescribed on the anniversary of death;
for one who maintains the sacred fire, the Pārvaṇa rite is prescribed every year. However, for others, the Pārvaṇa rite is not performed.
[1681] Regarding the ten types of sons, such as the *dattaka* (given son) and others,
Pulastya states:
"The ten sons should perform this annual *śrāddha* for each one."
One who is without the sacred fire and is a legitimate son should perform [the śrāddha]; however, one who possesses the sacred fire should perform the pārvaṇa rite.
But surely—
“If the time of a festival (parvakāla) and the anniversary of death (mṛtāha) should coincide on one and the same day,
the pārvaṇa rite must be performed there, and never the ekoddiṣṭa.”

If one’s father has passed away on the new moon day (amāvāsyā) or during the fortnight of the ancestors (pretapakṣa), the pārvaṇa rite must be performed there; the ekoddiṣṭa rite is never to be performed.

According to this statement: "One should perform the *pārvaṇa* rite for a father who has died during the fortnight of the ancestors (*pretapakṣa*). For men who have paternal uncles or brothers, the rite is *ekoddiṣṭa*, not *pārvaṇa*."

Because of this statement, it might be argued that the *pārvaṇa* rite should apply only to those with consecrated fires (*sāgni*) who have legitimate sons (*aurasa*), specifically on the new moon day of the fortnight of the deceased (*pretapakṣa*) when the sun is in the sign of Cancer (*kṣayāha*), and not universally. To this it is replied: by these sentences, the *pārvaṇa* rite is restricted for the three types of sons, beginning with the legitimate son (*aurasa*), who are without consecrated fires (*niragni*), on the new moon day of the fortnight of the deceased. For instance, after prohibiting the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite through the supplementary clause "never the *ekoddiṣṭa*," the restriction to the *pārvaṇa* rite is established by these very sentences. Furthermore, the application of the *ekoddiṣṭa* applies only to those without consecrated fires, not to those with them; because for those who have maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*), the *pārvaṇa* is mandatory according to the rule: "For a twice-born who has established the sacred fires, there is no *śrāddha* apart from the new moon. Therefore, the *pārvaṇa*, which is already applicable to those without fires during the fortnight [of the deceased], is restricted to the new moon day of the fortnight of the deceased when the sun is in Cancer, such that "this alone must be performed here, and not the *ekoddiṣṭa*."

Furthermore, if it were restricted that for those who maintain the sacred fires (*sāgni*)—such as the *aurasa* sons and others—the *pārvaṇa* rite is to be performed only on the new moon day, the fortnight of the deceased (*pretapakṣa*), or the anniversary of death (*kṣayāha*), and not elsewhere, then it would follow as a consequence that they could have no *śrāddha* on the anniversary of death other than those specific occasions. If it is argued that, because of the restriction to the *pārvaṇa* rite on those occasions, the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite would apply elsewhere;

No; for by the statement, "The ten sons perform the *ekoddiṣṭa*," that [rite] is restricted exclusively to the ten types of sons, such as the *dattaka* (adopted son) and others. Furthermore, although this annual *śrāddha* follows the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) of the *pārvaṇa* rite, it must be performed on the anniversary of the father's death for the three ancestors—the father, grandfather, and great-grandfather—alone, and not for the maternal grandfathers as well. As the author of the *Saṃgraha* says: "The time [for *śrāddha*] was declared by Yājñavalkya as the new moon day and so forth."
This applies without distinction to both the father and the maternal grandfather.
And he should be understood simultaneously from the statement that is about to be made;
for the *tantra* exists indeed through the non-differentiation of time and the non-differentiation of place.
Therefore, from the injunction of the *tantra* [common ritual procedure], simultaneity is understood;
thus, at times such as the new moon (*amāvāsyā*), the rite is performed together with the maternal grandfather.
However, on the anniversary of death (*mṛtāha*), because that [simultaneous procedure] does not apply, a separate performance would not be appropriate.

The meaning of this is as follows: By the statement of Yājñavalkya, "The new moon day, the Aṣṭakās, the Vṛddhi [rites]," and so forth, a general time for both the *pitṛśrāddha* and the *mātāmahaśrāddha* has been specified, such as the new moon day. Furthermore, that [time] is to be understood as being subsidiary (*aṅga*) to the *pitṛśrāddha* and *mātāmahaśrāddha* when they are performed simultaneously;
for the maternal grandfathers (*mātāmaha*) as well, the *vaiśvadevika* rite is likewise a single performance (*tantra*).

For this reason, within that very context, the description of the *vaiśvadeva* ritual as a common procedure (*tantra*) is only appropriate when the rites are performed simultaneously. Therefore, since the *śrāddha* for the paternal ancestors (*paitṛka*) and the maternal ancestors (*mātāmaha*) are understood to be performed at one and the same time, their shared procedure is logical. However, on the anniversary of death (*mṛtāha*), because the lifespan of each individual differs, the days of the passing of the father and the maternal grandfather are distinct; thus, the day of the father’s passing is not the time for the maternal grandfather’s *śrāddha*. Consequently, a shared procedure based on other [texts] is not tenable.

But surely, by this very logic, because of the difference between the anniversary of the father’s death and that of the grandfather’s death, one should not perform the *śrāddha* for the grandfather and others on the anniversary of the father’s death.

Not so. Because of the extended injunction (*atideśa*), “One should perform the *śrāddha* as in the case of the new moon (*darśa*”), the grandfather and great-grandfather also possess the status of deities on the anniversary of the father’s death. Nor should it be argued that the status of the maternal grandfather and others as deities follows from the extended injunction “as in the case of the new moon” and from the statement, “Wherever the fathers are worshipped, there the maternal grandfathers are certainly [to be worshipped] as well.
Vyāsa says:
When the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* has been performed, the offering should be like that of the *darśa* sacrifice; there is a three-generation designation.
Pāraskara says: "For a legitimate son, once the father has attained the state of a deity, [the offering] extends to three generations."
In all cases, for those of various lineages, [the rite is performed] on the single anniversary of the death of one [forefather].

"For one who has attained divinity"—that is, for one who has acquired the status of a *pitṛ* through the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite—"of the father," on the anniversary of his death (*kṣayāha*), "of the legitimate" (*aurasa*) son, "a three-generational" (*tripauruṣa*) *śrāddha*, meaning one dedicated to three deities, must be performed. Regarding "those of various lineages" (*anekagotrāṇām*), meaning those of different *gotras* such as daughters' sons (*dauhitra*) and others, the meaning is that the *śrāddha* for childless maternal grandfathers (*mātāmaha*) and so forth is exclusively of the *ekoddiṣṭa* type. Consequently, although the extension (*atideśa*) from the rule regarding the new moon (*darśa*) would have applied [the *tripuruṣa* form], by restating "three-generational" in the context of the six deities, there is an exclusion (*parisaṃkhyā*) of the maternal grandfathers and others on the anniversary of the father's death.

Now, as for the statement "that which pertains to three generations belongs to the legitimate son," since the legitimate son is restricted with reference to the three generations, and because the qualifying attribute of the referent (the three generations) is not intended to be significant, there is an exclusion (*parisaṃkhyā*) of the maternal grandfather and others.

It is not so, because on the anniversary of death (*kṣayāha*), there is no application of the *śrāddha* for three deities. If it is argued that—on account of the statement, "On the [anniversary] day, as at the new moon (*darśa*), there should be an offering to three [ancestors]"—there is a general application of the three-deity rite even on the anniversary of death after the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* has been performed; [we reply: in that case, by this very [rule], the exclusion (*parisaṃkhyā*) of the maternal grandfathers and others will be established. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "for the legitimate son (*aurasa*), [the rite] extends to three generations," if the mention of "three" were not intended to be significant (*avivakṣita*), then the sentence would indeed be purposeless. For there is no such thing as a *pauruṣa* (pertaining to one person) or *apauruṣa* (not pertaining to one person) *śrāddha* on the anniversary of death, such that this sentence could serve to establish a distinction that "the *pauruṣa* belongs to the legitimate son and the *apauruṣa* to others. And by this same logic, the offering should not be made to those accompanied by their wives (*sapatnīka*). Nor should it be said that the offering is made to those accompanied by their wives according to the *pārvaṇa* rule, based on such statements as, "The mother eats the *śrāddha* together with her own husband."
As Vyāsa has said:

"On the Anvaṣṭakā days, on the occasion of a family prosperity rite (vṛddhi), and likewise at the annual anniversary—on these occasions the Śrāddha for the mother is performed separately; on other occasions, it is together with her husband."

Even when, by chance, the time for the annual *śrāddha* for the father and the time for the annual *śrāddha* for the mother coincide, one should not designate the father and others together with their wives in the father’s annual *śrāddha*. Rather, following the sequence of their deaths, one should perform the cooking for both annual *śrāddhas* simultaneously (*tantra*), but the rites from the invitation of the twice-born until their dismissal should be performed separately. However, when the sequence of death is unknown, the two *śrāddhas* should be performed such that the father’s annual *śrāddha* comes first and the mother’s afterwards, because of the father’s primacy. In the same way, even when the days for the annual *śrāddhas* of brothers and others coincide, multiple *śrāddhas* must be performed according to the order of seniority and so forth. All of this has been explained in detail in the section on the coincidence of times (*kālasaṃnipāta*).
Regarding the practice of *anvārohaṇa* (the widow following her husband onto the funeral pyre), Laugākṣi describes the procedure for the *śrāddha* of the couple:
"On the anniversary of death, the offering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) is performed collectively;
however, the *navaśrāddha* (funeral rite for the newly deceased) for both husband and wife is performed only when she follows him in death."
"In brief" means concisely; it refers to the offering of the funeral rice-ball (piṇḍanirvapaṇa).

Just as in a *śrāddha* for two fathers, a single *piṇḍa* is offered by designating both fathers, saying, "to [Name] and to [Name]," so too here, having made the designation for both parents on a single *piṇḍa*, saying, "to [Name] and to [Name]," only one *piṇḍa* should be given. And because this *śrāddha* possesses the characteristic of being directed toward multiple recipients (*anekoddeśya*), it follows the ritual rules (*dharma*) of the *pārvaṇa* rite. Therefore, the *vaiśvadevika* offering should be performed here by way of a single procedure (*tantra*). As for the statement, "The *navaśrāddha* for the husband and wife is separate," the *navaśrāddha*—the *śrāddha* performed during the days of the *navaśrāddha* prior to the tenth day—must be performed separately for the father and for the mother.
As for that which was stated by Gārgya: "If a husband and wife have both ascended the same funeral pyre and met their death,
one should perform the Śrāddha for them separately, and offer the cooked rice (odana) separately for each."

"Odana" means a lump of boiled rice; however, that refers to the context of the *nava-śrāddha* (the first-year funeral rites) and not to the context of the annual (*sāṃvatsarika*) rites, so there is no contradiction with the previous statement.
As for what was stated by Bhṛgu: "The devoted wife who performs the ascension to her husband's funeral pyre..."
When the anniversary of her death arrives, one should offer her a separate funeral ball (piṇḍa);
likewise, every year, one should perform the new-anniversary śrāddha (navaśrāddha) and conclude it all at once.

Thus, for these *dattaka* (adopted) sons and others, the annual *śrāddha* for the mother and father is ordained according to the procedure of the *ekoddiṣṭa*. Regarding that, the meaning of the rule "one should complete the *navaśrāddha* simultaneously" is as follows: when the death days of the mother and father coincide, and the mother has performed the *anvārohaṇa* (self-immolation) on the same funeral pyre (*ekacityā*), one should perform the *navaśrāddha* for the father and the *navaśrāddha* for the mother at the same time with a single offering of cooked food (*ekapāka*). Having first performed the preliminary set of rites (*pūrvāṅgakalāpa*) because of the father’s primacy, one should then perform the *śrāddha* for the father first and for the mother afterwards, and perform the subsequent set of rites (*pāścātyāṅgakalāpa*) by way of a single performance (*tantra*). If several mothers have performed the *anvārohaṇa* on the same funeral pyre, one should perform the *navaśrāddha* immediately after the father's, then for the biological mother (*sākṣānmātuḥ*), and then for the stepmother (*upamātuḥ*), following the order of seniority starting with the eldest. This refers to the annual *śrāddha* for the mother.
The procedure for the annual śrāddha is described in the Viṣṇudharmottara:
"Every year, men and women should perform the ekoddiṣṭa rite on the anniversary of death according to the prescribed rule, just as it has been declared here for men."
Just as the *śrāddha* for men is performed with mantras, so too the *śrāddha* for twice-born women who have been married is likewise performed with mantras. Marīci says:
"The *śrāddha* for women is without mantras, as is that for Śūdra women and for him [the Śūdra]."
And before the initiation into the twice-born status and the instruction in the vows, they should perform those very same rites in that same manner.

“Without mantras” means devoid of the recitation of Vedic mantras. By the phrase “without mantras,” the meaning is that only the recitation of the [bride’s] name and lineage (*nāma-gotra*) should be performed. Even in that regard, based on such statements as “a woman falls from her own lineage,” it is understood that she should be given away using the husband’s lineage.
One should not perform the rite by abandoning the father’s lineage; rather, one should do so through the husband’s lineage.

By the phrase “by the father’s *gotra* alone,” etc., the following rule is established: in the event of a disagreement, for a woman married through an *āsura* or similar form of marriage who has been designated as an appointed daughter (*putrikā*), or for one who has been given away in marriage, the *śrāddha* is performed by the father’s *gotra* alone; however, for a woman married through a *brāhma* or other approved form of marriage, it is performed by the husband’s *gotra*. And this refers specifically to the *śrāddha* for women who have already been married. This is because unmarried women, being devoid of sacramental rites (*saṃskāra*), lack the eligibility to recite Vedic mantras. Regarding the statement, “And they should perform it in that very same way,” the word “they” refers to those such as the *pāraśava* sons and others. Furthermore, since the twice-born are unrefined prior to their initiation (*vrata*), even for fathers, paternal uncles, and so forth who have already been initiated, the *śrāddha* is to be performed without mantras.
Regarding this, Kātyāyana states the rule for the *ekoddiṣṭa* and *pārvaṇa* rites:
"O twice-born one, whatever rite a son always performs for his father every year—
whether it be the *pārvaṇa* or another— he should perform that same rite for his mother."

The term "anyat" (other) refers to the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite. As for what was stated by that same author— "The *ekoddiṣṭa* is always prescribed for paternal uncles, brothers, and mothers"— that should be understood as referring to the co-wife of one's mother (*mātṛ-sapatnī*), because of the association with paternal uncles and others mentioned therein.
Āpastamba states regarding the annual śrāddha for those who have no sons:
"For whatever persons— whether women or men— who are remembered as being sonless, an ekoddiṣṭa must be offered for them, and not a pārvaṇa."
One should indeed offer the monthly *śrāddha* to friends, kinsmen, and sapindas, as well as to women and maidens; the annual *śrāddha* is otherwise than this.
Pracetas says:
After the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite,
the *ekoddiṣṭa* is prescribed for all those who are without sons, as well as for those who have no wives.
‘Apatnīnām’ means those who have not performed the marriage ceremony.
Atri says: To a brother, a sister, a son, a master, and a maternal uncle...
For the paternal uncle and the preceptor, the śrāddha is of the ekoddiṣṭa type, not the pārvaṇa.
Jātūkarṇya says:
"For paternal uncles, brothers, and mothers who are childless,
as well as for a childless maternal grandfather, the Śrāddha and other rites should be performed just as for one's father."
[1688] To illuminate the necessity of this duty, Pracetas states that on the anniversary of death (kṣayāha), the *pārvaṇa* rite alone must be performed by all sons for renunciants (*saṃnyāsins*):
"For an ascetic (*yati*), there is no *ekoddiṣṭa* here because of his adoption of the triple staff (*tridaṇḍa*);
due to the absence of the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, the *pārvaṇa* belongs to him always."
Śātātapa says:

One should not perform the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite, the offering of water, the funeral cake (*piṇḍa*), the period of impurity, or the funeral ceremonies for one who has become a Brahman, other than the *pārvaṇa* rite, for such a mendicant.

Therefore, on the anniversary of death (kṣayāha), ascetics must always have the *pārvaṇa* rite performed by all their sons, and not the *ekoddiṣṭa*. Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Annual Śrāddha," in the *Śrāddhakalpa* of the *Pariśeṣakhaṇḍa* of the *Caturvargacintāmaṇi*, composed by the illustrious Hemādri, Paṇḍita and Chief Administrator of all departments under the illustrious Mahādevīya, the Great King of Kings.
[1689] Now begins the twenty-third chapter.
He who observes the vow for the universal benefit shall perform this rite on the fortnight of the ancestors (the dark fortnight) out of faith.
Hemādri, the lord who brings prosperity to all and the foremost among the virtuous, speaks with a wealth of eloquence that flows like the pure essence of ripened nectar— words that,
like a shower of ambrosial drops, bring divine joy to the vicinity of the ears without interruption.
Now follows the ritual procedure for the śrāddha of the dark fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada.

In this regard, if the capacity for cooking and so forth exists within the bodies of all the Brāhmaṇas invited, then everyone—including those with fires, those without fires, widows, students, and others—should perform the rite for all [the ancestors] every day from the first day (pratipad) until the new moon (amāvāsyā), excluding the fourteenth day (caturdaśī). However, on the fourteenth day, it should be performed only for one who was killed by a weapon. But when there is no possibility of cooking or other such preparations, then they must certainly perform it for all [the ancestors] even on a single day, according to the scriptural injunction: "One should not let the dark fortnight pass by even with mere vegetables. It has been established in the section concerning the time of the dark fortnight of Bhādrapada that, if the primary time known as the dark fortnight of Bhādrapada is unavailable, the rite should be performed on the fifteenth day of the festival of lamps (dīpotsava). Furthermore, this Śrāddha should be performed for nine deities (navadaivatyam).
Dharma said:
"In the Mahālaya, at the Gayā-śrāddha, at a rite for prosperity (vṛddhi), and at the Anvaṣṭakās, the offering here shall be to nine deities; they know the remainder to be for six ancestors."
"Remaining" refers to a *śrāddha* other than the sixteen *śrāddhas* and so forth.
Kātyāyana says:
"Excluding that which is accompanied by the *karṣū* (the sacrificial pit), as well as the first of the sixteen *śrāddhas*..."
And for the remaining [deceased], there should be six rice-balls at the annual anniversary; this is the established rule.

By the word *karṣū*, the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite is meant. And here, the state of having nine deities (*navadevatyatā*) is as follows: one group is that of the fathers (*pitṛvarga*), the second is the group of mothers (*mātṛvarga*), and the third is the group of maternal grandfathers (*mātāmahavarga*). Furthermore, within the group of maternal grandfathers, women are designated together with their husbands and not separately.
Thus says the *Karmapradīpa*:
"One should not give [offerings] separately for women, except on the day of the funeral anniversary (*avasānadina*)."
Their satisfaction is proclaimed to come from the mere funeral cakes (piṇḍa) offered by their own husbands. Chāgaleya says:
"On the anniversary of death (kṣayāha), they should be worshipped alone; at a rite of prosperity (vṛddhi), they are proclaimed to be worshipped first."
For in all cases, the mothers should remain neutral; they should never be made the final arbiters.
In all cases—whether at the Mahālaya, the Anvaṣṭakā, or the Gayā-śrāddha—the placement [of the offerings] is strictly in the middle. Satyavrata says:
"The offering to the fathers comes first, and immediately after that, the offering to the mothers."
Then [he should offer] to his maternal grandfathers, and to his paternal uncle and to him [the deceased].
Uśanas says:
He who performs a Śrāddha or offers the rice-balls (piṇḍas) for his mothers while omitting their maternal grandfathers goes to hell.
Jābāla says:
That man who places the Mothers at the end in the Śrāddha rites goes,
being a fool, head-first to the Kālasūtra hell.
In the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa:
"One should first give to the paternal ancestors, then to the maternal ancestors, and thereafter to the maternal grandfathers; this is the sequence prescribed for the Anvaṣṭakya rite."
In the *Caturviṃśatimata*: "Except for the anniversary of death (*kṣayāha*), there is no separate rule for women;
yet some excellent brahmins desire a separate śrāddha for women."

A twice-born man should always offer separate funeral cakes (piṇḍas) to these: to his teachers, gurus, and disciples; to his friends and kinsmen; to all his paternal ancestors, and likewise to their wives, specifically during the month of Bhādrapada.
Regarding this, Jātūkarṇya states the rule for the *pārvaṇa* and *ekoddiṣṭa* rites:
"After the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, the *pārvaṇa* rite is indeed for the parents alone;
for paternal uncles, brothers, and mothers, the *ekoddiṣṭa* is always prescribed."
Regarding this, Marīci states the rule for the sequence between the Pārvaṇa and the Ekoddiṣṭa rites:
"If the Ekoddiṣṭa and the Pārvaṇa should occur on the same day,
one should complete the Pārvaṇa first and then conclude the Ekoddiṣṭa."
In this case, the cooking must be performed by a single person acting as the agent for all.
Thus says Atri:
"Whether there be many or even two [performers], if the Śrāddha occurs on an even day..."
Having performed the cooking by means of a single thread, one should perform the separate Śrāddha rites.
Pulastya says: At the Mahālaya, at the Gayā-śrāddha, and on the anniversary of death (kṣayāha),
one should perform the cooking by a single method (tantra) and then perform the śrāddhas separately for each.

And it is established that, beginning from the first day of the dark fortnight of Bhādrapada—excluding the fourteenth day and continuing through the days up to the new moon—one should perform the *aparapakṣa-śrāddha* for paternal uncles and others who have no sons, as well as for others, daily according to the *pārvaṇa* procedure; or, if one is unable to do so every day, by preparing food once according to the *tantra* method during that same period, one should perform the rites for the nine deities according to the *pārvaṇa* rite and for the others according to the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite, separately for each.

Now, the specific procedure for the *śrāddha* on certain lunar days of the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*) is described. Among those, first, the *pañcamī-śrāddha* is prescribed in the *Baudhāyana-sūtra*.

Having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*): "I shall perform the *pañcamī-śrāddha* for the sake of obtaining a son; for that purpose, I shall cause the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha-vācana*) to be recited," he should cause the *puṇyāha* to be recited. Having said, "May the deity of the *puṇyāha*, Agni, be pleased," he should again cause the *puṇyāha* to be recited. This should be performed starting from the month of Mārgaśīrṣa. Having performed the re-establishment of the fire (*agnisaṃdhāna*) if it has been discontinued, and having completed the rites from the opening of the fire (*agnimukha*) up to the end of the *praṇītā* water, he should place the vessel for the *svadhā* offering to the south of the fire. He should sprinkle it with water while reciting: "O raw grains, O Fathers, come from the path of the gods! You are sesame, whose deity is Soma; you are the cow-sacrifice (*gosava*), created by the gods. Offered by the ancients, come as *svadhā*! Delight these Fathers and these worlds for us; *svadhā*! Homage! Then, with the three verses beginning "The winds are sweet for the righteous one" (*madhuvātā ṛtāyate*), and with the formulas "You are the splendor of Soma" (*somasya tviṣir asi*), "Cast out, do not release my head" (*nirastaṃ na mucyeḥ śiraḥ*), and "The divine waters for our aid" (*śanno devīr abhiṣṭaye*), he mixes the *svadhā* offering. Having honored it with perfumes, flowers, and unbroken rice (*akṣata*) saying, "Homage to the Fathers, homage to the Grandfathers, homage to the Great-grandfathers," he should cover it with *darbha* grass. At the place of eating, he sprinkles with water while reciting: "The Asuras, Rakṣases, Piśācas, and those who sit among the Fathers and dwell upon the earth—let them go elsewhere, wherever their minds are directed. He invokes the Fathers with the verse: "May they rise, the lower, the higher, and the middle ones, the Soma-loving Fathers; those who have gone to the life-force, the harmless ones who know the Truth—may they protect us, O Fathers, at our invocations. He says: "Come, O Soma-loving Fathers, by your ancient, deep paths; grant us progeny, wealth, and long life for a hundred autumns. Having made two offerings to the All-Gods (*Viśvedevas*) with the formula "A moment must be made for the Viśvedevas," and having given clothing, ornaments, and food, as well as perfumes, flowers, incense, and lamps, he washes the feet of three Brahmins intended for the Fathers. He offers the *svadhā* with the formulas: "Svadhā, homage to the Fathers; svadhā, homage to the Grandfathers; svadhā, homage to the Great-grandfathers. Having honored them with clothing, food, perfumes, flowers, incense, and so forth, and having obtained permission from the Fathers, he makes the resolve: "I shall perform the fire-oblation (*agnau kariṣyāmi*). He performs the consecration of the clarified butter (*ājya*), carries out the cleansing of the *sruk* ladle, places the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*), anoints the fuel-sticks, lays down the fuel, and performs the sprinkling around the fire. He offers the two *āghāra* libations, and having offered the oblations with the verses "Yoked, you carry the offerings" (*yukto vahasi*), "To us, the auspicious ones" (*ā no bhadraḥ*), "Virūpākṣa" (*virūpākṣam*), "I [offer] to the transverse one" (*ahaṃ yā tiraścī*), "To the prospering one" (*saṃrādhanyai*), "To the accomplishing one" (*prasādhanyai*), and the *vyāhṛtis*, he wears the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*). He offers five oblations with the verses beginning "The ancestors have come" (*udīratām avaraḥ*) and "The flesh-eater" (*yan me kravyād*). Having divided the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) into three parts: in the first part, he offers with the formula: "We offer this oblation to the powerful Soma accompanied by the Fathers; enjoy this, O swift one, *svāhā*! The offering to the gods and Fathers, *svadhā*! Homage! *Svāhā*! In the second part, having taken a portion, he offers: "They call him the peaceful one, accompanied by the Aṅgirases, for protection; he belongs to Vaivasvata, the great one, *svāhā*! The offering to the gods and Fathers, *svadhā*! Homage! *Svāhā*! In the third part, having taken a portion, he offers: "O Agni Kavyavāhana, sacrifice to the Fathers who increase the Truth; carry the offering to the gods and the Fathers, *svāhā*! The offering to the gods and Fathers, *svadhā*! Homage! *Svāhā*! Having offered these three, he should likewise make three offerings of cake (*apūpa*) with these same three mantras. Having mixed sesame seeds into the cooked food intended for the Fathers' meal, he performs twenty oblations with the *tarpaṇa* mantras. Having made the oblation in the southeast part of the fire with the formula: "To Agni Kavyavāhana Sviṣṭakṛt, *svadhā*! Homage! *Svāhā*!", he should feed the Brahmins designated as Fathers with the remainder of the food and the remainder of the *caru*. At the start of the meal, touching the food, he should mutter: "The earth is your vessel, the fire is your supervisor; the *ṛc* verses are your greatness for the non-neglect of what is protected. The earth is your vessel for the Grandfathers; the atmosphere is your vessel... the sky is your vessel... Having touched the food with his thumb while reciting "Om Bhūr Bhuvaḥ Svaḥ," he should give it with the formulas: "Svadhā, homage to the Fathers; svadhā, homage to the Grandfathers; svadhā, homage to the Great-grandfathers. The sacrificer mutters the five oblations: "You are the under-layer of immortality; *svāhā* to Prāṇa, *svāhā* to Apāna, *svāhā* to Vyāna, *svāhā* to Udāna, *svāhā* to Samāna. Saying, "For the sake of immortality in the Brahman, satisfy [them] with all desires," and "You are the covering of immortality," he should take some water and food at the end of the meal and scatter it on the ground, reciting: "Those in my family who were burnt by fire, those who are living, and those who were not burnt—may they be satisfied by what is given on the ground; being satisfied, may they go to the highest goal. Taking water with sesame seeds, he says "Be satisfied" (*tṛpyadhvam*) and gives the *svadhā* to those who are satisfied. After circumambulating the Brahmins clockwise, he should dismiss them. To the south of the fire, he should offer twenty-four funeral balls (*piṇḍa*) to the Fathers, beginning with "Svadhā, homage to the Fathers" and ending with "Svadhā, homage to all. He should make three oblations with the remainder of the *caru* while reciting the mantras "What my mother [did]," "What my grandmother [did]," and "What my great-grandmother [did]. Starting with the recitation and ending with the sprinkling around, the venerable Baudhāyana says: "Within a year, one obtains a son; this is the truth."
Now follows the Aṣṭakā-homa, according to the Baudhāyana-sūtra.

Now, the *Aṣṭakā* oblations should be performed on the eighth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Taiṣa, and likewise in Māgha and Phālguna. Whether the moon is waning or full, they may be performed subsequently on the full moon day, or on the seventh, eighth, or ninth day of the dark fortnight; or they may be performed specifically on the eighth day. On the preceding day, he should invite Brahmins who are endowed with noble birth, lineage, learning, and good conduct—though some say they should be unrelated, while others teach that one may invite even relatives provided they are endowed with learning and good conduct, for it is said that "the *svadhā* offering is established through learning, good conduct, and noble birth. Having honored them according to his means with shaving, anointing, bathing, and other comforts, and having bathed himself, he prepares the sacrificial ground in a clean, level place, performing the rites from the drawing of lines for the *devayajana* up to the placing of the *praṇītā* water. Taking the animal outside, he dedicates it, saying: "I dedicate this, which is pleasing, to the fathers, svāhā! To the grandfathers, svāhā! To the great-grandfathers, svāhā! Some say he should do so silently. Then he sprinkles it with water, saying: "I sprinkle this, which is pleasing, for the fathers, svāhā! For the grandfathers, for the great-grandfathers," or some say he should do so silently. They immolate the animal here, facing westward, with its head toward the north and its feet to the south. From the immolated animal, he satisfies the vital breaths with water. Silently extracting the omentum (*vapā*), he extracts the heart and the various portions (*avadāna*). Having placed these on the spit and roasted them over this very fire, he first roasts the rice, the boiled grain, the cakes, and other special dishes. Having brought all that is prepared together, he seats an even number of Brahmins whose feet have been well-washed, having made them sip water, on seats prepared with *darbha* grass, facing either east or north. If they face east, they sit with their ends toward the south; if they face north, their ends are toward the east. He says, "May your honor partake," and the others reply, "We have partaken. Then he causes them to receive water mixed with barley, saying: "To such-and-such, *svadhā* and homage! To such-and-such, *svadhā* and homage! Some prescribe three offerings of water with sesame seeds. He should give the food before the meal, the water with sesame twice, and a third time when they have finished eating. Then, having honored them as much as possible with garments, perfumes, incense, lamps, and garlands, he asks: "Shall the food be taken out? And shall it be offered in the fire? They reply: "Let it be taken out as you wish; let it be offered in the fire as you wish. Or, if he says, "I shall offer it in the fire," they reply, "Do so. Then, being authorized, he performs the rites from the laying of the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) up to the "mouth of the fire" (*agnimukha*). When the omentum is cooked, he offers five spoonfuls of oblations; this has been explained previously. Having divided the omentum into three parts, he offers it with a ladle (*darvī*) made of *udumbara* wood; this too has been explained previously. Then he offers the *Aṣṭakā* oblations: "This is she who first covered herself..."—these eight verses; "For nourishment, they saw her who was before..."—this one verse; "The image of the year..."—this one verse; thus ending with seventeen verses. Having divided the cake into eight parts and offered three portions according to the ritual of the omentum, he gives the remaining portions to the Brahmins. Having cut those portions into the *iḍā*-plates—rice, meat, and cake—and having mixed them with clarified butter, he offers the covering oblation with the *udumbara* ladle, saying: "To the fathers, *svadhā* and homage, svāhā! To the grandfathers, *svadhā* and homage, svāhā! To the great-grandfathers, *svadhā* and homage, svāhā! To the mothers, *svadhā* and homage, svāhā! To the grandmothers, *svadhā* and homage, svāhā! To the great-grandmothers, *svadhā* and homage, svāhā! To the maternal grandfathers, *svadhā* and homage, svāhā! To the maternal grandfathers' fathers, *svadhā* and homage, svāhā! To the maternal great-grandfathers, *svadhā* and homage, svāhā! To the maternal grandmothers, *svadhā* and homage, svāhā! To the maternal grandmothers' mothers, *svadhā* and homage, svāhā! To the maternal great-grandmothers, *svadhā* and homage, svāhā! To the teachers, *svadhā* and homage, svāhā! To the wives of the teachers, *svadhā* and homage, svāhā! To the preceptors, *svadhā* and homage, svāhā! To the wives of the preceptors, *svadhā* and homage, svāhā! To friends, *svadhā* and homage, svāhā! To the wives of friends, *svadhā* and homage, svāhā! To kinsmen, *svadhā* and homage, svāhā! To the wives of kinsmen, *svadhā* and homage, svāhā! To the attendants, *svadhā* and homage, svāhā! To the wives of the attendants, *svadhā* and homage, svāhā! To all, *svadhā* and homage, svāhā! To all, *svadhā* and homage, svāhā! To Agni Kavyavāhana, the maker of good offerings, *svadhā* and homage, svāhā! In the eastern half of the southern quarter, having taken the meat and rice into vessels, having added the special dishes, and having mixed them with the remains of the oblations, he places them on *darbha* grass, covers them with *darbha*, and touches them, saying: "The earth is your vessel, the sky is the lid; I offer you into the mouth of the Brahmin. I offer you into the out-breath and in-breath of the Brahmins as they eat. You are imperishable, beloved by the fathers, grandfathers, and great-grandfathers, in that world, in that place. Then, having set these down for the Brahmins, he indicates them with the thumb of a Brahmin (without the nail), saying: "To such-and-such, *svadhā* and homage! To such-and-such, *svadhā* and homage! Looking at them as they eat, he recites: "Seated in the breath, I offer nectar. Having caused the five Brahmin women to recite, he recites for his own immortality. He does not look upward, for it is known: "The fathers are modest. Satisfying them with all desired things, he should cause them to hear the *brāhmaṇa* texts associated with the *svadhā* offering, as well as those that destroy demons and those belonging to Nirṛti. When they are satisfied, he makes them sip water and scatters the remnants of the food into the pits, saying: "Those born in my family who were cremated by fire, and those who were not cremated—may they be satisfied by what is given on the earth; being satisfied, may they go to the highest goal. Having scattered the wash-water, he will announce the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), consisting of gold, bullion, gems, cloth, iron, land, vessels, cows, horses, goats, sheep, elephants, and whatever else is available, or saying "may it be inexhaustible. Having grasped their feet, having caused them to pronounce the *svadhā*, having clothed them, having gratified them, having circumambulated them, and having asked permission regarding the remainder, he goes back by the same path and presents the leftover food. He should act as they direct. Being permitted by them, he spreads *darbha* grass with points toward the south to the south of the fire and offers balls (*piṇḍa*) with the leftovers, saying: "To the fathers, *svadhā* and homage! To the grandfathers, *svadhā* and homage! To all, *svadhā* and homage! Then he sprinkles them three times with the wash-water, saying: "Carrying strength, nectar
Now, regarding the *anvaṣṭakā* śrāddha, it is stated in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"On the *anvaṣṭakā* days, the śrāddha for women must likewise be performed.
Having offered oblations according to the procedure for the *aṣṭakās*, one should perform these five [rites] in due order."

O King, preceded by the Viśvedevas, the offering of the rice-balls (piṇḍa) should be made to one's mother and grandmother; O ruler of men, that [offering] for her is performed just as for the paternal ancestors.
Now learn from me the ritual procedure there once the Brahmins have finished eating.
O King of kings, it should be one span in width and four finger-breadths in length;
its height should be exactly that much, and one should have six furrows made therein.
For the Chandogas, three furrows (karṣū) must be made.
Gobhila says:
"One should bring three furrows, each a span (prādeśa) in length and four finger-breadths (caturaṅgula) deep. However, for others, the arrangement follows their respective Gṛhyasūtras.
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"Having strewn sacrificial grass around the fire at the base of each pit,
and having performed the sacrifice to Agni, Soma, and Yama as previously described..."
At the base of the three furrows,
one should perform the offering of the rice-balls (piṇḍa-nirvapaṇa) for the male ancestors, as before, one by one according to the rule.
And one should fill those three vessels with milk from those [cows] by means of ladles.
The offering for women should take place at the base of the three furrows;
the filling of the furrows should be done with curd, meat, and milk.
O best of men, this should be performed with food mixed with water;
let it be proclaimed that for you all, this shall be inexhaustible.
[1699] Viṣṇu.

Having performed the *śrāddha* on the *aṣṭakās* and the *anvaṣṭakās* preceded by the gods, using vegetables, meat, and cakes, and having offered oblations into the fire preceded by the gods, he should likewise feed the Brahmins for his mother and paternal grandmother as before, honor them with sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), follow them as they depart, and then dismiss them. Thereafter, he should prepare six furrows. Having established fires at their base in an easterly direction and offered oblations, he should perform the offering of three *piṇḍas* according to the primary rite; he should do this at the base of one of the furrows. At the bases of the three furrows—that is, at the three roots of the furrows—he should fill the three furrows of the men with water mixed with food. He should fill the three furrows of the women with water mixed with food, milk, curd, and meat—filling each set of three furrows individually—and then recite: "May this be inexhaustible for you ladies."
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"Having offered oblations in the first pentad during *āmaśrāddhas* performed for specific desires,
one who is self-controlled should offer oblations in the middle pentad during *śukraśrāddhas*."
Having offered the supreme fivefold oblation on all new-moon days,
and having likewise offered these fivefold oblations in sequence during the three Aṣṭakās,
as well as during the Anvaṣṭakās, one should, being self-restrained, feed the twice-born.

Regarding the *śrāddha* on the thirteenth day (*trayodaśī*), it should be performed for six ancestors—namely, the triad beginning with the father and the triad beginning with the maternal grandfather—according to the *pārvaṇa* procedure; all of this has been set forth in the section on the timing of *śrāddhas* during the dark fortnight (*aparapakṣa*).
Now follows the ritual application (*prayoga*) for the *śrāddha* on the fourteenth day (*caturdaśī*). [Thus says] Pracetas:
Even for a father who has attained equality [with the gods] but was slain by a weapon,
the sons must perform the Ekoddiṣṭa rite on the fourteenth day during the Mahālaya.

The underlying intention is as follows: for one who has attained equality—that is, for one who has been *sapiṇḍīkṛta*—it is restricted that on the fourteenth day (*caturdaśī*) of the dark fortnight of Bhādrapada, known as the *Mahālaya*, the rite is to be performed only for one killed by a weapon and not for anyone else. It does not mean, however, that for one killed by a weapon it must be performed only on the fourteenth day; therefore, on the anniversary of death (*kṣayāha*) and other occasions, the *śrāddha* for even one killed by a weapon must be performed exactly as prescribed. Furthermore, when the father or mother was killed by a weapon on the fourteenth day, then setting aside the *pārvaṇa* rite occasioned by the anniversary of death, the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite for one killed by a weapon occasioned by the dark fortnight must indeed be performed.
In this regard, an alternative procedure for the *śrāddha* of the dark fortnight is stated in the *Brahmapurāṇa*:

"A man who is entirely dependent on others, one who is traveling abroad, or even one who is destitute, [should perform it] at all times during the dark fortnight with milk, roots, fruits, and vegetables."
With a mind purified by devotion, one should offer the faithful gift of water with sesame seeds.

Thus concludes the procedure for the *śrāddha* of the dark fortnight of Bhādrapada. Now follows the procedure for the *śrāddha* on the first day (*pratipad*) for the sake of a daughter’s son (*dauhitra*).
That [rite] must be performed specifically on the first day following the new moon of the dark fortnight.
Now,
one whose father is living should not perform the Darśa-śrāddha, the Gayā-śrāddha, the Aparapakṣika-śrāddha, nor even libations with sesame seeds.

If it is asked, "How can this be, since there is a prohibition against the *śrāddha* of the dark fortnight (*aparapakṣa*) for one whose father is still living?"—if you reply, "Because of the practice of the learned (*śiṣṭa-samācāra*)," we say: if the *śrāddha* of a daughter's son (*dauhitra*) occasioned by the dark fortnight is prohibited, then that same rite performed even on the first day of the lunar month (*pratipad*) would also be prohibited. To this it is said: "When the sun has entered Virgo, the ancestors indeed go toward their sons."
The entire city of the hungry ghosts is empty, as far as the sight of the scorpions extends.

Thus, since even the arrival of the daughter (the *kanyā-saṅkrānti*) is a cause for the *śrāddha*, the sons of the daughter (*dauhitras*) must perform the *śrāddha* specifically on that occasion, and not one occasioned by the dark fortnight (*aparapakṣa*). And this should be performed according to the *pārvaṇa* procedure in accordance with the practice of the learned (*śiṣṭācāra*), so say the Madhuśarman Miśras.
This concludes the ritual procedure for the *pratipad-śrāddha* of the daughter’s son.
Thus [ends the work of] the Paṇḍita, the sovereign lord of all departments of the illustrious Mahārājādhirāja, the illustrious Mahādevīya...
The Procedure for the Śrāddha of the Latter Fortnight, in the Śrāddhakalpa of the Pariśeṣakhaṇḍa, within the Caturvargacintāmaṇi composed by Śrī Hemādri.
Now begins the twenty-fourth chapter.
Next is the procedure for the Śrāddha that is an ancillary part of renunciation (saṃnyāsa).
Regarding that, with reference to renunciation, it is stated in the Baudhāyana Sūtra:

One who maintains a sacred fire should perform eight śrāddhas at the beginning according to the pārvaṇa rite. One who does not maintain a sacred fire should, at the end, perform eight śrāddhas for himself according to the ekoddiṣṭa rite—namely, those dedicated to the gods (daiva), the ancestors of the sages (ārṣaka), the celestial beings (divya), the paternal ancestors (pitrya), the ṛṣis (mārkka), humans (mānuṣa), and elemental spirits (bhautika).
Likewise:

Now we shall explain the procedure for renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*). Prior to the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) for renunciation, one should perform the *śrāddha* rites beginning from the eighth day [of the lunar fortnight]. On either the full moon or the new moon day, there are the following: the *deva-śrāddha*, the *ṛṣi-śrāddha*, the *divya-śrāddha*, the *mānuṣa-śrāddha*, the *bhūta-śrāddha*, the *pitṛ-śrāddha*, the *mātṛ-śrāddha*, and the *ātman-śrāddha*. In the *deva-śrāddha*, the three deities are Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara. In the *ṛṣi-śrāddha*, the three deities are the celestial sages (*devarṣi*), the Brahmin sages (*brahmarṣi*), and the royal sages (*kṣatrarṣi*). In the *divya-śrāddha*, the three deities are the Vasus, the Rudras, and the Ādityas. In the *mānuṣa-śrāddha*, the three deities are Sanaka, Sanandana, and Sanātana. In the *bhūta-śrāddha*, the three deities are the elements beginning with earth, the organs beginning with sight, and the fourfold collection of living beings (*bhūtagrāma*). In the *pitṛ-śrāddha*, the three deities are the father, grandfather, and great-grandfather, as well as the maternal grandfather, maternal great-grandfather, and maternal great-great-grandfather. In the *mātṛ-śrāddha*, the three deities are the mother, paternal grandmother, and paternal great-grandmother. In the *ātman-śrāddha*, the three deities are oneself, one’s father, and one’s grandfather.

Now, therefore, we shall explain the procedure for renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) as proclaimed by Śaunaka. On the preceding day, one should perform the *nāndīmukha* śrāddha. One should offer rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) and water to the gods, sages, divine beings, humans, spirits, ancestors, the mother, and oneself, using an even number of Brahmins and offering separate rice-balls for each. In the *deva-śrāddha*, one should offer three rice-balls to the three deities: Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa. In the *ṛṣi-śrāddha*, one should offer three rice-balls to the three deities: the celestial sages (*devarṣi*), the royal sages (*kṣatrarṣi*), and the human sages (*manuṣyarṣi*). In the *divya-śrāddha*, one should offer three rice-balls to the three deities: the Vasus, Rudras, and Ādityas. In the *manuṣya-śrāddha*, one should offer three rice-balls to the three deities: Sanaka, Sanandana, and Sanātana. In the *bhūta-śrāddha*, one should offer three rice-balls to the elements, beginning with the earth. In the *mātṛ-śrāddha*, one should offer three rice-balls to the three deities: the mother, paternal grandmother, and paternal great-grandmother. In the *ātma-śrāddha*, one should offer three rice-balls to the three deities: oneself, one’s father, and one’s grandfather. One should offer the rice-balls and water according to their names, lineages (*gotra*), and relationships. Immediately thereafter, one should have the auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) proclaimed.

Thus ends the section on the ritual procedure for the *śrāddha* as an auxiliary to renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) in the *Śrāddhakalpa* of the *Pariśeṣakhaṇḍa* of the *Caturvargacintāmaṇi*, composed by the illustrious Hemādri, the scholar (*paṇḍita*) and sovereign lord of all administrative departments of the illustrious Mahādevīya, the great king of kings.
[1704] The twenty-fifth chapter.
Now follows the procedure for the *ijyā-vat-śrāddha* (the śrāddha performed like a sacrifice). In the *Āditya Purāṇa*:
"When there is an abundance of place, time, wealth, faith, and resolve..."
Or a man may himself perform a śrāddha for one who is living or for the sake of one who is living.
Because of the word "or" (vā), it follows that in the absence of another performer of the *śrāddha*, one should perform the *śrāddha* for oneself by oneself. Likewise:
"Having observed the fast, well-bathed, and composed in mind on the thirteenth day..."
Then one should worship Viṣṇu, the creator, the enjoyer, and the Lord of all.
It is omnipresent in water, on land, in the sky, in form, in the ritual jar, in the lotus, and in the sun; it resides in the moon, the sun, Jupiter, cows, Brahmins, and one's mother and father.
Accompanied by sacrificial fees and sesame seeds, one should, with a concentrated mind, offer nine fresh lotuses to the ancestors in front of them, O Ocean.
Having thus performed the worship, one should give three water-cows (jaladhenu) dedicated to the father.
Regarding this, he states the mantras:
"To Soma accompanied by the fathers, svadhā! Homage!"—thus recollecting.
Recalling [the mantra]: "Svadhā and obeisance to Agni Kavyavāhana."
And one should place the third [offering] facing south on the right side, while recollecting: "To Yama, to Aṅgiras, Svadhā! Obeisance!"
Having placed them between those two, one should seat five Brahmins;
the meaning is that one should place the first to the north, the second to the south, and the third in the middle.
And having first worshipped the Viśvedevas with the invocation (āvāhana) and other rites.
"O Brahmin, I feed you for the sake of the Vasus; O Brahmin, I feed you for the sake of the Rudras;
O Brahmin, I feed you for the sake of the Sūryas"—thus he should say to them.
One should perform all the rites beginning with the invocation (āvāhana) according to the procedure for ancestral offerings (pitṛkarma).
Then, a gentle cow should be given as a gift to a Brāhmaṇa who is devoted to Indra (Vāsava).
One should offer a vessel of oil to Agni, then to Rudra, then to Yama, and then to Sūrya and the twice-born;
and then one should present a vessel of oil to the Viśvedevas.
"To Vāsava" means for those seated with the Vasus as their presiding deity;
the same applies in the subsequent cases as well.
And having given those twice-born men "svasti-udaka," that is, imperishable water.
One should dismiss [the deity] while recollecting the all-pervading Lord Viṣṇu through the eight-syllabled mantra;
thereafter, at night, one should meditate upon Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of the family of Kāma.
Having performed all this on the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight, he states what must be done on the second day:
"Then, on the fourteenth day, one should go to whichever excellent river is available;
the Brahmin by the east, the Kṣatriya by the north, and the Vaiśya by the west."
Likewise, the Śūdra, scattering barley grains, should follow by the path on the right.
"With a gentle [mood]," that is, with the northern [path], "scattering barley," meaning he should go while scattering it;
he should remember that the clothes and iron fragments are living beings.
Having gone there, he states what must be done:
Facing south, he himself should kindle the fire there and burn an effigy of Brahmā made from fifty *kuṇa* seeds.
The word "himself" (*svayam*) is for the purpose of excluding others. "Image" (*pratikṛtiḥ*) refers to a figure possessing limbs such as hands and feet.
Having performed the *śmaśānika* oblation with a full-offering (*pūrṇāhuti*), he [should burn] that very [image].

This is the meaning: if the fire has been extinguished, having established the fire according to the alternative rite beginning with *pṛṣṭhodivi*, and having performed the full-offering according to the procedure prescribed in his own *Gṛhya-sūtra*, he should offer clarified butter with the mantra for the offering of fire and then burn the image.
If he has not yet formally taken up the sacred fires, it is said that he should act as follows:
"Or, being without the sacred fires, while recollecting Yama and Rudra,
having offered oblations in the primary place, he should thereafter have her cremated."
Kātyāyana states regarding the fire from the sky (pṛṣṭodivya):
"One should bring the village fire with the mantra *anv agniḥ*, and one should place it [on the altar] with the mantra *pṛṣṭo divi*; then one should kindle it with the Sāvitrī."
The other [mantra] is known as "tat savitur vareṇyam" and "viśvāni.
The "village fire" is the common worldly fire; it should be brought from the house of one learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*). One should "establish" it, meaning one should bring it forward.
Then, one should cook a *caru* oblation mixed with *mūga* beans on another fire.
The second, however, is mixed with sesame seeds and rice, and provided with a pavitra.

The mention of "another" means that where the burning of the effigy has been performed, one should act in another place than that. Therefore, one should produce fire by the previously mentioned method for the purpose of cooking the *caru*. Regarding the phrase "with the *pavitra*," this refers to the pouring of rice grains and the sprinkling of the boiled milk while the *pavitra* is present.
He states what must be done immediately after the cooking:
One should fill three furrows with honey, milk, ghee, and water.
Near that, however, one should fill three small casket-like vessels.
One should offer the first with "Oṃ, salutation to you, Pṛthivī," and immediately thereafter the second with "Oṃ, salutation to Yama."
Oṃ, salutation to Rudra, the lord of the cremation ground;
then, [one should prepare] a blazing, kindled fire upon the ground that naturally consumes [the offerings].
Recalling the mantra, "Homage to the flesh-eating Agni and to the heated earth," one should scatter a water-pot soaked in milk for the sake of pacifying that [impurity].
Then, having entered the water up to the navel and facing the direction of Yama (the south),
one should offer seven handfuls of water to the seven known as Yama.
To Yama, the King of Dharma, to Death, and to Antaka;
to Vaivasvata, to Kāla, and to the Taker of All Life.
Together with the utterances *svadhā*, *namas*, and *praṇava*, [he performs] sevenfold [the offering], while recollecting: "Oṃ, obeisance to Rudra, the Lord of the cremation ground."
One should scatter parched grain and water upon the ground from a jar filled with both,
and offer the *avanejana* (water for washing) upon *darbha* grass pointing toward the south.
Recalling "Rudra, obeisance to you, who are of the nature of *svadhā*," one should say:
"O [Name], of the [Name] lineage, may this water with sesame seeds be for you."
This subtle body of yours is this physical form, endowed with the fragrance of water-offerings, flowers, and incense;
this oblation of incense, lamp, and food is for you, leading to heaven and imperishable.
Then, having offered ten rice-balls (piṇḍas), one should meditate upon Viṣṇu facing the north;
and that water, being devoid of heat, one should enter up to the navel.
One should cast a full water-pot into the midst of the water at each respective spot;
then, one should offer fifty-five water-libations from the pots.
One should place milk and water at the edge of the door or within the house, while recollecting:
"O living being, come here, bathe, and drink this milk."
