He should sleep on darbha grass with its tips pointing southward, facing northward;
thereafter, on the new moon day, he should perform the *jīvacchrāddha*.
One should fill three karṣukas with ghee, rice, meat, and curd;
and then, month by month, one should perform the monthly rite and subsequently the sapiṇḍīkaraṇa.
Then, at the end of the period of impurity, having recognized the instability of one's own or another's devotion, health, wealth, and lifespan, one should perform all these rites with devotion.
Now follows the procedure for the *jīvacchrāddha* as taught by Baudhāyana.

We shall now explain the procedure for the *jīvacchrāddha* (the funeral rite for one still living). He who desires his own spiritual welfare should, having reached the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight (*aparapakṣa*), prepare the necessary materials on that very day. For the rites pertaining to the deceased, he should procure six garments with golden thread, a goad, nine *pālāśa* leaves, a shoulder-hair tuft, a bundle of *palāśa* twigs, a black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*), a sacrificial fuel-stick (*idhmā*) made of *udumbara* wood, a ritual seat (*āsandi*), a water-pot (*kalaśa*), and so forth. On the following day, having bathed and stood in the water at midday, he should emerge from the water and cause others to recite "Auspicious Day! and "May there be well-being. He should then give gifts of clothing and finger-rings as sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*). With those same materials, he should eat milk-rice (*pāyasa*) while facing south. Then, having established the sacred fire according to the rules prescribed in his own *Gṛhya-sūtra*, and having strewn grass around it, he performs the *āghāra* libations and the two *ājyabhāga* offerings. Having offered three oblations of clarified butter (*ājya*) into the mouth of the fire with the *sruk* ladle, he offers cooked food. Reciting the *puro’nuvākyā* verse beginning with "Four are the horns," he offers the oblation with the *yājyā* verse "That desirable glory of Savitṛ. Reciting the *puro’nuvākyā* "Ye Vasus," he offers the oblation with the *yājyā* verse "She who lies across. Next, he offers additional *ājya* oblations with the eighteen-verse *Puruṣasūkta*. Having offered clarified butter, he should offer eight thousand or twenty-eight oblations with the *Gāyatrī* mantra. From the *Sviṣṭakṛt* offering onwards, the rite proceeds until the gift of a cow and a boon. He sits upon a single-headed seat, not at a crossroads. Having given the goad, the needle-studded shoulder-rope, and the black-bodied [image], he causes others to say, "May the servants of Yama be pleased," while reciting "Bhūḥ Svāhā. He should then place a water-pot among the rice grains, wrap it with a thread, and fashion a human figure filled with water. He places three [units] on the head, three on the face, twenty-one on the body, four on the arms, two on each of the thighs, one on the organ, and five on each of the feet. He then says, "May the blessed servant of Yama be pleased. Having prepared the ritual seat (*āsandi*) and washed it with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), he fashions a human figure on a black antelope skin using *palāśa* stalks. Having infused the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) into the pot-man and the physical form into the stalk-body, he should sleep in the middle. At sunrise, he himself should sprinkle the body with the pots. At evening, he should eat food with sesame seeds and clarified butter while reciting the *Puruṣasūkta*. He should also feed Brahmins for the satisfaction of the servants of Yama. On the fourth day, during the burning of the mechanical image (*yantra*), he should offer a water-ball (*udakapiṇḍa*) and a *sapinda* ball, saying: "O Maruts, this *sapinda* is for such-and-such a person of such-and-such a lineage; may it be *svadhā* unto him in that world," ending with a salutation. Thus he concludes the rite. Therein, the period of impurity (*āśauca*) lasts ten days, but for one's own mantra-oblations, it does not apply. On the eleventh day, the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite should be performed. Regarding this, they also cite an exception: in times of distress, a woman or a Śūdra may burn their own body by means of mechanical devices. One should stand in the water at midday and not perform all the ritual acts; such indeed is the Vedic revelation (*śruti*). For women, the rite may be either silent or with mantras, performed month after month. After a year, it is performed annually until the twelfth year, after which it ceases. When one is unable to do it oneself, then sons and others should perform it, using the formula "For such-and-such a person of such-and-such a lineage," and complete the remainder of the rite.
Moreover, they cite this:
"Even while one is still alive, one should perform the *śrāddha* for oneself, even when others are present,
by proceeding according to the rules immediately, except for the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*."
Thus, for the reason stated, one should delay [the funeral rites]; because life is impermanent, one should complete the remainder [of the ritual], so said the Blessed Baudhāyana. In the Liṅga Purāṇa:
"I shall describe the procedure for the *jīvacchrāddha* (funeral rite for the living) in brief, as it is approved by the Vedas."
It was told to the sage by Brahmā, the god of gods, in ancient times.
Now, for the distinguished Vasiṣṭha and Bhārgava,
let them listen with their whole being to this supreme means that brings about all accomplishments.

I shall explain directly the sequence of the path of ancestral rites (śrāddha), as well as the sequence for those who are worthy of such rites, and also the specific rules that are prescribed for śrāddhas performed while the ancestors are still living.
Whether on a mountain, by a riverbank, in a forest, or even in a temple,
one should diligently perform the *jīvacchrāddha* at the time of death.
When the *jīvacchrāddha* has been performed, a living person is liberated while still alive—
whether performing actions or not, whether ignorant or even possessed of knowledge.
Whether he be a learned brahmin or not learned, or even a kṣatriya or a vaiśya— provided he is devoted to the path of yoga, there is no doubt in this matter.
Having examined the ground according to the prescribed rules by means of its smell, color, taste, and so forth,
one should carefully remove a small amount of earth and prepare a sand mound on the ground.
In the center, one should fashion an auspicious sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) measuring one cubit,
or alternatively, a leveled altar (sthaṇḍila) measuring one arrow-length (iṣu), repeatedly;
having smeared it according to the rule and having drawn the lines, one should then place the fire.
[1711] Having strewn fuel according to one's own Śākhā and having swept around it on all sides.
Having strewn [the sacrificial grass] according to the procedure taught in one's own Vedic branch as handed down through the lineage,
and having completed everything beginning with the invocation of the fire (agnimukha) in due order with these mantras;
Having worshipped the fire upon the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), one should perform the oblation (homa) with fuel-sticks and other materials;
first performing the homa with fuel-sticks, and then separately with the sacrificial porridge (caru).
Having extracted that [offering] from each [portion], one should offer it individually with ghee beautified in separate vessels, and likewise to all beings everywhere.

*Oṃ bhūḥ, salutation to Brahmā. Oṃ bhūḥ, svāhā to Brahmā. Oṃ bhuvaḥ, salutation to Viṣṇu. Oṃ bhuvaḥ, svāhā to Viṣṇu. Oṃ svaḥ, salutation to Rudra. Oṃ svaḥ, svāhā to Rudra. Oṃ mahaḥ, salutation to Īśvara. Oṃ mahaḥ, svāhā to Īśvara. Oṃ janaḥ, salutation to Prakṛti. Oṃ janaḥ, svāhā to Prakṛti. Oṃ tapaḥ, salutation to Pudgala. Oṃ tapaḥ, svāhā to Pudgala. Oṃ ṛtam, salutation to Puruṣa. Oṃ ṛtam, svāhā to Puruṣa. Oṃ satyam, salutation to Śiva. Oṃ satyam, svāhā to Śiva.* *Oṃ, protect my *sarvadharā*; in the nose, [protect] smell; salutation to Bhūḥ for the All-God. Oṃ, protect my *sarvadharā*; in the nose, [protect] smell; svāhā to Bhūḥ for the All-God. Oṃ, protect my *sarvadharā*; in the nose, [protect] smell; salutation to Bhūḥ for the Consort of the All-God. Oṃ, protect my *sarvadharā*; in the nose, [protect] smell; svāhā to Bhūḥ for the Consort of the All-God.* *Oṃ, protect my *bhavajala*; on the tongue, [protect] taste; salutation to Bhuvaḥ for the God Bhava. Oṃ, protect my *bhavajala*; on the tongue, [protect] taste; svāhā to Bhuvaḥ for the God Bhava. Protect my *bhavajala*; on the tongue, [protect] taste; salutation to Bhuvaḥ for the Consort of the God Bhava. Protect my *bhavajala*; on the tongue, [protect] taste; svāhā to Bhuvaḥ for the Consort of the God Bhava.* *Oṃ, protect my *rudrāgni*; in the eyes, [protect] form; salutation to Svaḥ for the God Rudra. Oṃ, protect my *rudrāgni*; in the eyes, [protect] form; svāhā to Svaḥ for the God Rudra. Protect my *rudrāgni*; in the eyes, [protect] form; salutation to Svaḥ for the Consort of the God Rudra. In this manner, O observers of good vows, the oblation should be offered starting from Śiva and ending with Viriñca, as before; for it was previously declared that [the sequence] ending with Viriñca follows the path of emanation.
Furthermore, having worshipped the consort of Paśupati and likewise Paśupati in due order with mantras as before,
one who is composed should offer oblations in sequence, beginning first with clarified butter at the end of all [the rites] and ending with fuel-sticks (*samidh*).
Oṃ, sever all my bonds; sever my life-force and my scent; destroy my evil! Bhūḥ svāhā! Bhūr bhuvaḥ svāhā!
Having thus offered oblations separately with pure ghee alone—either a thousand, half of that, or one hundred and eight—
Having thus performed one hundred and eight oblations separately with clarified butter alone,
he should then offer oblations to Prāṇa and the others using clarified butter exclusively.

Oṃ, I offer the nectar established in the vital breath; may the auspicious one enter me for the sake of non-burning. Svāhā to the vital breath! Svāhā to Rudra, the lord of the vital breath, the speckled butter! Bhūḥ svāhā! Bhuvaḥ svāhā! Svaḥ svāhā! Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ svāhā!
In this manner, one should offer oblations in sequence, exactly as prescribed and in due order.
On the seventh day, O best of Brahmins, one should feed those Brahmins worthy of the *śrāddha*.
And for all the brahmins, he provided vehicles, beds, vessels of white copper, seats, and other utensils, all accompanied by garments and ornaments.
Gold or silver, a cow, sesame seeds, land, and a house,
as well as groups of male and female slaves, should indeed be given as sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā).
The funeral ball (piṇḍa) should be offered as before, according to the previously stated method;
furthermore, one thousand Brahmins should be fed along with ritual fees (dakṣiṇā).
Or [one may feed] even a single person who is devoted to yoga, established in Brahman, and has conquered the senses;
and for three days, one should offer the great sacrificial porridge to Rudra.

This specific instruction regarding the funeral rites (śrāddha) has been told in its entirety. Since one who is liberated while living (jīvanmukta) is himself [liberated], he may perform them after death or not perform them;
likewise, he may perform the obligatory and occasional rites (nitya-naimittika) or abandon them.
Even when a kinsman has died, no impurity whatsoever exists for him;
there is no doubt that he is purified by mere bathing alone, and there is no *sūtaka*.
And if, after a son has been born in one's own field,
[the father] performs all the rites for him, that son shall also become a knower of Brahman.
If a daughter was later born to that great-souled one—
whether of the same caste or of another, yet of equal status and observant of virtuous vows—
This indeed comes to pass, there is no doubt; even those born of his own lineage are liberated, and there is no doubt here that his ancestors are released even from hell.
Thus, both mothers and fathers are freed from all their karmic debts.
When the twice-born has passed away, one may either bury him in the ground or cremate him;
provided that the remaining duties toward a son have been performed, no fault is found.
And by his very subsequent deed,
the destiny of this great-souled one was told in its entirety by Brahmā to the sages of purified minds.
Formerly, this was heard by me in its entirety from Sanatkumāra himself through his command;
all of this has been told to you out of compassion by that wise one.
It was told to Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana himself by the son of Brahmā,
through the grace of that wise god, Vedavyāsa.
I have understood it and performed it solely by his command.
Thus I have told you all this secret, which bestows all accomplishments;
it must never be given to the wicked nor to one who lacks devotion, O observer of noble vows.

Sūta says to the listeners: "The commentary on this *Liṅgapurāṇa* shall now be told. Regarding the "path of the *śrāddha*"—that is, in the context of the *jīvacchrāddha* (the rite for one still living)—he explains the "sequence," meaning the specific method involving place, time, and other factors. "At the time of death" means when the moment of passing has arrived; "even while living" means that by means of the purification of the *sattva*, through the attainment of the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), one is indeed liberated. "In front"—that is, to the east of the sacrificial ground (*sthaṇḍila*) and other such sites intended for worship—a fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*) or another sacrificial mound should be prepared for the purpose of the *homa*. Having worshipped Brahmā and the other deities upon the sacrificial ground with these mantras to be mentioned hereafter, one should offer the fuel-sticks (*samidh*) and other materials into the fire using those same mantras. "Having extracted from oneself" means having mentally extracted and separated, one by one, the principles (*tattva*) and elements residing within oneself as revealed by their respective mantras, and then one should offer them into the fire, intending them for the deity; thereafter, one should contemplate that principle as purified. In this context, the mantra ends in *namaḥ* during worship, whereas it ends in *svāhā* during the *homa*. Therein, for the triad of the first octad beginning with Brahmā, there are the worship and *homa* for each of those respective deities; likewise for all the others from Paśupati down to the end, together with their consorts and associated with the principles starting from Earth (*dharā*). Thus, having stated twenty-two mantras according to the order of emanation (*sṛṣṭikrama*), he cites the final mantra of the first octad as the primary example to demonstrate the reverse order in the process of reabsorption (*saṃhāra*): "Oṃ, to Śiva, truth," and so forth. "In this manner" refers to the previously mentioned mantras of the eight deities from Viriñci (Brahmā) to Śiva according to the order of emanation; now, again according to the order of reabsorption, one should worship from Fire up to Śiva with "To Śiva, truth, svāhā," ending with "To Brahmā, svāhā. Likewise, having worshipped in the stated sequence from Paśupati’s consort down to the end of the list, one should offer oblations individually, following the sequence of clarified butter (*ghṛta*), sacrificial porridge (*caru*), and fuel-sticks. The mantra "Oṃ, to Sarva... and so forth is for the *homa* of clarified butter alone. Therein, at the end of the three sentences beginning with "Sarva, the Earth," the third is "Bhuvaḥ svāhā," and the fourth mantra is "Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ svāhā. "In this way, separately and separately": likewise, these four mantras beginning with "Śivasya patnī" are to be applied by modification (*ūhya*). Thus, the *homa* is performed with the four modified mantras: "O Bhava, cut my water; O Bhava, destroy the taste in my tongue; O Bhava, destroy my sin; Bhuḥ svāhā," and so forth. Likewise, there is the *homa* performed with the *viraja* mantras and with the six mantras beginning with "Niviṣṭaḥ prāṇe," as prescribed in the *śrāddha* rites and the *Gṛhyasūtras*, intended for the father, grandfather, great-grandfather, and others. Having thus offered oblations every day for seven days, on the seventh day, after honoring the Brahmins and designating the various deities starting from Earth, eight funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*) should be offered to the group beginning with Sarva. When the *jīvacchrāddha* is performed in this manner for one's own kinsman who has died, there is no period of ritual impurity (*āśauca*) nor birth-impurity (*sūtaka*). Consequently, a son born from him is also to be consecrated with the *jātakarma* and other rites, and he shall become a possessor of knowledge (*jñānin*). The same applies to a daughter. And thus, in that lineage, they are born as yogis.

Thus ends the section on the procedure for the *jīvacchrāddha* (the Śrāddha performed while one is still alive) in the *Śrāddhakalpa* of the *Pariśeṣakhaṇḍa* of the *Caturvargacintāmaṇi*, composed by the illustrious Hemādri, the great king of kings, the illustrious Mahādevīya, the sovereign of all departments, and a Paṇḍita. [1717]
Praise of the Śrāddha Ritual. In the Matsya Purāṇa:
"O protector of the earth, this much has been told to you."
The ritual procedure for the *śrāddha*, as ordained by the sages,
removes sin, increases merit,
and likewise bestows preeminence in the world.

By that illustrious Lord of the Secretariat, Hemādri, was composed this great [work], in which there was never any dense growth among the trees sprouted by his abundant merit, and which no one at all touches even slightly with barrenness.
May this work, the subject of the title *Śrāddhanibandha*, dispel the delusion of the virtuous.
Thus ends the Śrāddhakalpa.
